Under a uniform prior on unrooted topologies, what is the prior probability of any one topology for 5 and for 24 languages? Use the result to explain why a posterior probability of 0.3 for a single 24-language topology represents an enormous update, and why reporting clade probabilities is nonetheless more informative. Research You are asked to compare a Bayesian tree of 120 Bantu languages with the Guthrie zones and with Glottolog’s classification. Which tree distance would you use, how would you handle the polytomies in the classifications, and how would you incorporate the uncertainty in the Bayesian posterior rather than comparing a single summary tree? Justify each choice. A colleague proposes to test whether language families of hunter-gatherers have less balanced trees than those of farmers, using Glottolog classifications. Identify the main threats to validity (classification practice, the language/dialect problem, incomplete sampling, polytomies) and design an analysis, including null models and robustness checks, that would address them. 2.12 Further reading Felsenstein (2004), Inferring Phylogenies. The standard reference on phylogenetic inference; its early chapters on counting trees, consensus and tree comparison are a lucid introduction to the topics of this chapter. Baum and Smith (2013), Tree Thinking. An introductory textbook on reading and inferring trees, unusually careful about common misreadings (tip order, node counting, “primitive” lineages, similarity versus relatedness); its early chapters are the natural companion to Section 2.1. Warnow (2017), Computational Phylogenetics, is a more algorithmic textbook on how tree-estimation methods are designed and on their statistical properties. Semple and Steel (2003), Phylogenetics. A rigorous mathematical treatment of trees, splits, compatibility and the splits-equivalence theorem, for readers who want proofs. Paradis (2012), Analysis of Phylogenetics and Evolution with R. The book-length guide to ape and the phylo data structure, with worked examples of reading, manipulating and plotting trees. Bryant (2003): A clear classification of consensus methods, showing what each assumes and which properties it satisfies. Heled and Bouckaert (2013): Explains, with simulations, how summary trees and their node heights are constructed from Bayesian posterior samples and why the choice matters; essential for anyone reporting MCC trees. Huson et al. (2010), Phylogenetic Networks. A comprehensive introduction to split networks and explicit networks, written by the authors of SplitsTree and Dendroscope. Mooers and Heard (1997): A classic review of what tree shape can and cannot reveal about evolutionary processes. Pompei et al. (2011): A linguistic application of quartet distances to evaluate inferred language trees against expert classifications. Hillis et al. Chapter 3 Linguistic Data for Phylogenetics Phylogenetic methods do not operate on languages; they operate on data matrices. Every analysis in this book begins with a table whose rows are languages and whose columns are characters, and every result depends on how that table was built: which varieties were chosen as rows, which features as columns, how each cell was judged, and how uncertain those judgements were. Two analyses with identical models but differently built matrices can disagree more than two analyses with different models and the same matrix. This chapter is about the decisions that go into the matrix and about the evidential weight that different kinds of characters can bear. A small hand-typed Indo-European word list, turned into a cognate matrix and an automatic cognate clustering in R, lets us watch each decision in action. After reading this chapter you should be able to: Explain why cognacy, not similarity, is the linguistic counterpart of homology, and how the depth of cognate judgements affects the characters. Decide which varieties to sample as taxa, including how to treat attested ancient languages, reconstructed proto-languages and dialect continua. Code a word list as binary and multistate cognate characters in R, with loans kept, coded as missing or dropped, and describe the consequences of each choice. Identify the main sources of uncertainty in cognate judgements and of dependence between characters, and say which models or analyses account for them. Compare the evidential status of lexical, phonological, morphological and syntactic characters, including the Parametric Comparison Method. Describe CLDF, Glottolog, Concepticon and Lexibank, and evaluate automated cognate detection with B-cubed scores. 3.1 From words to characters 3.1.1 Taxa, characters and states In biology a character is a heritable feature that varies among taxa, and its values are character states. A nucleotide position in an aligned gene is a character with four states (A, C, G, T); the presence or absence of wings is a character with two. The data for a phylogenetic analysis form a matrix \(D\) whose entry \(D_{ij}\) is the state of character \(j\) in taxon \(i\). Almost every model in this book assumes that characters evolve independently along the same tree, so that the probability of the whole matrix is a product over characters (Chapter 5). The two fundamental requirements on a character are therefore that its states in different taxa be homologous, that is, comparable because they descend from a common ancestral state, and that characters be (approximately) independent of one another. In linguistics the taxa are languages, but even that is not straightforward. A “language” in a dataset is really a particular variety as documented in a particular source, at a particular time, by a particular fieldworker or lexicographer. The term doculect has been proposed for this unit (Cysouw and Good 2013). Two datasets that both contain “Hindi” may contain different doculects, and a dataset may contain several varieties that others would treat as dialects of one language. These decisions affect tree shape, the apparent density of sampling, and the estimates of rates and dates (Chapters 2 and 15). The characters can be of many kinds. The vast majority of published linguistic phylogenies use lexical characters derived from cognate judgements in basic vocabulary, because these are plentiful, comparatively easy to collect for many languages, and relatively resistant to borrowing. Smaller numbers of studies use structural (typological) characters, phonological characters such as sound changes, or morphological characters such as paradigm irregularities. Each kind of data comes with its own notion of homology and its own pitfalls. 3.1.2 Cognacy as homology The linguistic counterpart of homology is cognacy. Two words in different languages are cognate if they descend, by ordinary inheritance, from the same word in a common ancestral language. English two, German zwei, Latin duo, Russian dva and Sanskrit dvā́ are cognate because they all continue the Proto-Indo-European word for ‘two’, usually reconstructed as *dwóh₁. Their resemblance in form is a consequence of common descent, not the criterion for it. The criterion is the existence of regular sound correspondences: systematic, recurring relationships between the sounds of words with related meanings across the languages, of the kind formulated as sound laws (Campbell 2013; Hock and Joseph 1996). English t corresponds to German z [ts] not only in two/zwei but in ten/zehn, tongue/Zunge, tooth/Zahn and to/zu, a correspondence explained by the High German consonant shift. Once such correspondences have been established, they allow cognates to be recognized even when they look nothing alike (English wheel and Sanskrit cakrá- ‘wheel’ are cognate), and non-cognates to be rejected even when they look identical. The rejection of look-alikes is as important as the recognition of cognates. English have and Latin habere ‘to have’ are similar in sound and meaning but are not cognate; the regular correspondences show that have goes back to the same root as Latin capere ‘to take’, while habere continues a different root. English day and Latin dies ‘day’ are likewise unrelated, as are English much and Spanish mucho, or English bad and Persian bad ‘bad’. Chance resemblances of this kind are surprisingly frequent: with thousands of words in each language and a limited inventory of sounds, some pairs will match by accident (Ringe 1992; Kessler 2001). This is why phylogenetic analyses of lexical data are almost always built on expert cognate judgements grounded in the comparative method, or on automated methods that attempt to emulate it (Section 3.12), rather than on raw similarity of form. Cognacy is also a matter of depth. English hound and German Hund are cognate within Germanic; Latin canis, Greek kúōn and Lithuanian šuõ go back to the same Proto-Indo-European root for ‘dog’. Whether a dataset places all of these in one cognate set depends on the time depth at which cognacy is judged. Most datasets aimed at a single family code cognacy at the level of the family’s proto-language (so that Hund and canis are cognate), but there are exceptions, and analyses of subgroups sometimes use shallower judgements. The choice matters because deeper judgements create fewer, larger cognate sets and therefore fewer characters with different distributions across the tree. 3.2 Choosing and coding the taxa The rows of the matrix deserve as much thought as the columns. Phylogenetic models assume that each tip is a lineage that evolved independently of the others after it split from its sister, and that the tips are sampled in a way the tree prior can describe (Chapter 6). Linguistic taxa fit this picture to varying degrees, and three situations need particular care. 3.2.1 Dialects, languages and sampling density Whether two varieties count as one language or two is partly a political decision, and dialect continua have no natural cut points (Chapter 1). The choice still has consequences. Sampling many closely related varieties from one branch and one variety from another changes the shape of the tree, shortens some terminal branches and lengthens others, and can bias rates and dates, because the tree prior and the clock model both see the sample as if it were representative. A single variety standing for a whole branch also has a long terminal branch, which makes it vulnerable to long-branch attraction (Section 4.14). A useful rule is to decide the sampling scheme from the question: for the deep structure of a family, sample each major branch with several well-documented and well-separated varieties, preferably including its most divergent ones; for the internal history of one subgroup, sample its dialects densely but think about whether a tree is the right model at all (Chapter 8). 3.2.2 Attested ancient languages: ancestors, sisters or members of a dialect network? Written records give linguistics something that most of biology lacks: dated observations of earlier stages of the same lineages. But an attested ancient language can stand in three different relationships to the modern languages in a dataset, and they call for different treatments. An ancestor, or nearly so. The attested variety lies on the path from the root to some modern tips, with no or very little independent change of its own. The Old Norse of medieval Icelandic manuscripts, in relation to Modern Icelandic, is close to this case. In a tree it is a sampled ancestor: a tip with a zero-length branch, or a node on a branch. A sister. The attested variety belongs to a lineage that split off before the common ancestor of the modern languages and then died out. Gothic, the only well-attested East Germanic language, is the sister of the ancestor of North and West Germanic, not the ancestor of either; Hittite and the other Anatolian languages left no descendants at all. Such varieties are tips on side branches that end at their date of attestation. A member of a dialect network. The attested variety is one standardized or literary variety among many spoken ones, and the modern languages descend from its unrecorded neighbours. Classical Latin is the literary language of a speech community whose spoken varieties gave rise to the Romance languages; the West Saxon of most Old English texts is not the direct ancestor of Modern Standard English, which descends mainly from Midland dialects; and Classical Arabic stands in a similar relation to the modern Arabic dialects. Here neither “ancestor” nor “sister” is literally true: the attested variety and the real ancestor were near-contemporaries in one network, sharing most of their vocabulary but not all of it. These possibilities affect sampling, coding and interpretation. A tree prior without sampled ancestors forces a nearly ancestral variety onto a side branch with a length of its own. In dated analyses this can push the root deeper, which is the core of the debate over the “ancestry constraints” of Chang et al. (2015) and the sampled-ancestor analyses of Heggarty et al. (2023) (Sections 10.6 and 10.6.4). Coding raises its own problems. The vocabulary of an ancient language is known from a corpus, not from elicitation. A meaning that is unattested in the surviving texts must be coded as missing (?), never as absent, and the word that a corpus happens to use for a meaning may be a literary or genre-specific choice rather than the everyday basic word. The phonology behind an ancient orthography is itself a reconstruction, so cognate judgements involving ancient forms carry extra uncertainty. And the “date” of an ancient tip is the date range of a corpus that may span centuries, which is better represented by a prior on the tip age than by a fixed number (Section 10.5.1). Ancient languages typically have much more missing data than modern ones, and the way missing data enter the likelihood can influence where they are placed (Section 10.5.3). Whether the data can distinguish the three situations is an empirical question that deserves to be asked explicitly. Under a fossilized birth-death prior the probability that a tip is a sampled ancestor is, in the vocabulary of Section 6.10, identifiable under the model, but with a few hundred lexical characters and much missing data it may not be practically estimable: the posterior probability of ancestry can then be driven more by the prior on the sampling process than by the words. Two practical consequences follow. Report the prior as well as the posterior probability that each ancient tip is an ancestor, and check how dates change when ancient varieties are treated as ancestors, as sisters, or are removed and used only as calibrations. And interpret a “sampled ancestor” for a variety such as Classical Latin as a statement that it is very close to the ancestral network, not as a claim that the Romance languages descend from Cicero’s prose. 3.2.3 Reconstructed proto-languages are not data Some databases include reconstructed proto-languages alongside attested ones; the Polynesian dataset used in Chapter 17, for example, contains a Proto-Polynesian “variety”. A reconstruction is an inference from the daughter languages, made with the comparative method and usually with a particular subgrouping in mind. Including it as a tip counts the daughters’ evidence twice and builds the expected answer into the data. Reconstructions are valuable for checking ancestral state estimates (Chapter 12) and for designing cognate sets, but they should be removed before inferring a tree. 3.3 Basic vocabulary lists 3.3.1 The Swadesh lists Lexical phylogenetics inherited its data from lexicostatistics, and in particular from the word lists devised by Morris Swadesh (Chapter 1). The idea was to compare languages on a fixed list of basic meanings: concepts expected to be lexicalized in every language, independent of culture and environment, and resistant to replacement by borrowing. The original 200-item list (Swadesh 1952) contains pronouns, body parts, numerals, natural phenomena, basic actions and properties. Swadesh later reduced it to 100 items (Swadesh 1955), dropping meanings that proved hard to elicit unambiguously, culturally specific, or prone to borrowing. The Swadesh 100 and 200 lists, and variants of them, remain the most widely used meaning lists in the field. Swadesh lists have well-known problems. Many items are ambiguous as glosses: ‘lie’ (recline, or tell a falsehood?), ‘bark’ (of a tree, or of a dog?), ‘dull’ (of a knife, or of a person?). Others, such as ‘snow’ or ‘ice’, are not lexicalized separately in every language, while some, like ‘we’, may correspond to two words (inclusive and exclusive) in languages that make that distinction. Lists also exist in many slightly different versions, and two datasets labelled “Swadesh 200” may not contain exactly the same meanings. These issues are not trivial, because the choice of which word fills a meaning slot determines its cognate class. Kassian et al. (2010) provided a detailed semantic specification of the 100-item list to reduce this ambiguity, and IE-CoR has invested heavily in precise meaning definitions for the same reason (Heggarty et al. 2023). Fieldwork on poorly documented languages makes the problem concrete. Discussing Muno, a language of Papua New Guinea that he documented, Rönchen (2025) notes that its numerals above six are loans from Tok Pisin, that the word for ‘dog’ is unlikely to be older than the arrival of dogs in New Guinea, that ‘we’ has inclusive and exclusive (and possibly dual) forms, and that the very short stems of complex verbs make cognates hard to identify. He concludes that word lists should be tailored to the region and family rather than treated as universal, and that the “raw data” of lexical phylogenetics are already products of analysis. The idea is older than modern phylogenetics. McMahon and McMahon (2005) review regionally adapted Swadesh lists, among them lists for Southeast Asia and for Australia that add meanings such as ‘armpit’ or ‘goanna’, and suggest keeping a common core while substituting items within the same semantic field; in the Andes, for instance, ‘llama’ can replace ‘cow’, whose words are uniformly Spanish loans and so say nothing about relations among the indigenous languages. The price of such flexibility is comparability across families, which matters more for global analyses than for the phylogeny of a single family. 3.3.2 Lists designed from data Later lists were constructed from empirical evidence about stability or borrowability. The Leipzig-Jakarta list of 100 meanings was derived from the World Loanword Database (WOLD), which recorded loanwords for more than 1,400 meanings in 41 languages from around the world (Haspelmath and Tadmor 2009a). The meanings were ranked by a combination of how rarely they were borrowed, how often they were expressed by simple (unanalysable) words, and how old the words tended to be, and the top 100 formed the list (Tadmor et al. 2010). Its overlap with the Swadesh 100 is substantial but not complete; it includes, for instance, ‘ant’ and ‘wing’, which are not on the Swadesh 100. The ASJP list of 40 meanings was selected by the Automated Similarity Judgment Program team as the subset of the Swadesh 100 whose words were most stable, judged by how consistently they were shared within known language groups, and which gave the best classification results (Holman et al. 2008). The brevity of the list is what made it possible for ASJP to collect word lists for the great majority of the world’s languages (Wichmann et al. 2022). Other short lists include Dolgopolsky’s list of about 15 especially stable meanings, compiled for long-range comparison (Dolgopolsky 1986), and the 35-item list of S. Yakhontov used in the Moscow school of comparative linguistics. At the other extreme, project-specific lists may be longer: the Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database uses a list of 210 meanings (Greenhill et al. 2008), and IE-CoR uses 170 meanings (Heggarty et al. 2023). Both hopes are only partly met. Stability varies enormously across meanings. Some meanings, such as low numerals, pronouns and words for ‘name’, ‘eye’ or ‘water’, tend to retain the same word over thousands of years, while others, such as ‘dirty’, ‘bad’ or ‘to throw’, are replaced frequently. Pagel et al. (2007) showed that across Indo-European the rate of lexical replacement in a meaning is strongly and negatively related to how frequently the meaning is used in everyday speech (Chapter 9). Such variation among characters is not a problem in itself, since modern models allow rates to vary among characters (Chapter 7), but it is a strong reason not to assume a uniform rate, as glottochronology did. Borrowing in basic vocabulary is also not negligible. In the WOLD sample, loanwords made up on average roughly a quarter of the vocabulary, with much lower proportions in basic meanings but substantial variation across languages (Tadmor 2009). English, for instance, borrowed the basic pronoun they and words such as sky and skin from Old Norse. 3.3.4 Concepts, glosses and Concepticon Because so many lists exist, comparing or merging datasets requires knowing which meaning in one list corresponds to which meaning in another. A gloss such as “bark” or “to lie” is not enough. The Concepticon project addresses this by linking the meanings (“concepts”) of hundreds of published lists to a common set of concept sets, each with a unique identifier and a definition (List et al. 2016). A dataset whose meanings are linked to Concepticon can be aligned with any other linked dataset automatically, which is one of the foundations of the large-scale data aggregation described in Section 3.11. 3.4 Coding cognates as characters 3.4.1 A toy dataset To make the coding schemes concrete, we use a small hand-typed word list: eight meanings in twelve Indo-European languages, with orthographic forms, a rough phonetic transcription in a simplified ASCII alphabet loosely modelled on the ASJP transcription system, and expert-style cognate judgements. A meaning with \(k\) cognate classes produces \(k\) characters. The resulting matrix is analogous to restriction-site data in molecular biology, and models for its evolution (the binary CTMC, covarion and stochastic Dollo models) are the subject of Chapter 7. Binary coding handles synonyms naturally: Irish madra and gadhar are both coded 1 in their respective characters. make_binary <- function(wl, loans = c("keep", "missing", "drop")) { loans <- match.arg(loans) langs <- unique(wl$Language) if (loans == "drop") wl <- wl[!wl$Loan, ] sets <- unique(wl$CogID) M <- matrix("0", length(langs), length(sets), dimnames = list(langs, sets)) M[cbind(wl$Language, wl$CogID)] <- "1" for (cc in unique(wl$Concept)) { cols <- unique(wl$CogID[wl$Concept == cc]) ok <- wl$Concept == cc & (loans != "missing" | !wl$Loan) # a language with no (inherited) word for a meaning gets "?" for all # of that meaning's cognate sets M[setdiff(langs, wl$Language[ok]), cols] <- "?" } M } B <- make_binary(wl, loans = "missing") dim(B) #> [1] 12 39 B[, grep("^(hand|dog)", colnames(B))] #> hand-A hand-B hand-C hand-D hand-E hand-F dog-A dog-B dog-C #> English "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" "0" "0" #> German "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" "0" #> Swedish "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" "0" #> Italian "0" "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" "0" #> Spanish "0" "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" #> French "0" "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" "0" #> Russian "0" "0" "1" "0" "0" "0" "?" "?" #> Polish "0" "1" "0" "0" "0" "0" #> Lithuanian "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" #> Irish "0" "0" "1" "1" "0" "0" #> Greek "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" "0" #> Hindi "0" "0" "0" "0" "0" "1" Two features of binary coding deserve attention. The first is that characters from the same meaning are not independent. If a language has a word from class A for ‘hand’, it almost certainly does not have a word from class B, so the binary characters for a meaning are negatively correlated, and a single replacement event (say, the Balto-Slavic replacement of the inherited word for ‘hand’) changes two characters at once: one goes from 1 to 0, another from 0 to 1. Models that treat the characters as independent therefore overcount the evidence from each replacement, a point made forcefully by critics of binary coding and taken up in Section 3.5.2 and Chapter 7. The second feature is ascertainment. A binary cognate matrix never contains a column of all zeros, because cognate sets are only recorded if at least one language has them. Depending on the coding conventions, it may also exclude or include singletons (classes found in only one language) and constant columns of all ones (such as ‘two’ in our data). The likelihood of the data must be corrected for the patterns that could not have been observed, a correction known as ascertainment bias correction, which is crucial for estimating branch lengths and dates correctly (Chapter 7). informative <- function(x) { # at least two languages in each state x <- x[x != "?"] sum(x == "1") >= 2 && sum(x == "0") >= 2 } c(characters = ncol(B), constant = sum(apply(B, 2, function(x) length(unique(x[x != "?"])) == 1)), singletons = sum(apply(B, 2, function(x) sum(x == "1") == 1)), parsimony_informative = sum(apply(B, 2, informative))) #> characters constant singletons #> 39 2 22 #> parsimony_informative #> 15 Of the 39 characters, 22 are singletons and only 15 are parsimony-informative, that is, divide the languages into two groups of at least two each. One of the two constant columns is ‘two’, which every language shares; the other is the cognate set of the Russian loan sobaka, which, once the loan is coded as missing, contains only zeros. A column of zeros is exactly the kind of pattern that a cognate matrix should never contain, and it illustrates how coding decisions interact with ascertainment: such columns must be removed, and the likelihood corrected accordingly. 3.4.3 Treating loanwords Our function offers three treatments of the two flagged loanwords, which are also the three used in practice. Loans can be kept, in which case English mountain is coded as sharing a cognate class with the Romance words; this treats a borrowing as if it were inherited and will, if loans are common, pull the borrowing language towards the donor in the tree. Loans can be coded as missing, so that the language contributes no information about that meaning; this is the most common choice in Bayesian analyses. Or the loan can be dropped from its cognate set while the language is still coded 0 for all other sets of the meaning, which treats the loan as if it were a unique innovation.
