First, models with among-character rate variation, and often with covarion structure, are generally favored over a simple single-rate binary model whenever they are compared, as one would expect from the strong rate heterogeneity of basic vocabulary. Second, the topologies inferred under reversible and stochastic Dollo models are usually similar, while dates can differ more. This fits the limit relationship of Section 7.7.4: the models agree where gains are rare and disagree where multiple origins (borrowing, advergence, coding artefacts) are common. Third, in the Indo-European dating debate the largest differences between studies come not from the substitution model but from data coding, the treatment of ancient languages and the choice of constraints and calibrations (Chang et al. 2015; Heggarty et al. 2023). A substitution model can only be as good as the definition of the characters it is applied to. Fourth, agreement between inferred trees and established subgroups, as reported by Greenhill, Drummond, et al. (2010), is consistent with the models capturing the main genealogical signal, but it is not independent validation of them, for the reasons given in Section 7.3.2. Fifth, Bayes factors compare models only with each other. A model that wins a Bayes-factor comparison may still be badly inadequate, which is why absolute tests of fit matter. Sixth, and most uncomfortably for current practice, recent work suggests that relative fit can point in the wrong direction. Rönchen (2025) argues, on the basis of a formal analysis and simulation studies reported in manuscripts that form part of his dissertation (Rönchen, Häuser, et al. 2025), that the ascertainment correction used for cognate data fundamentally changes the behaviour of finite-state Markov chains such as the covarion model: under conditions that he reports to hold for many empirical and realistically simulated datasets, they come to approximate a Dollo-type model, but they overfit, so that a model with higher apparent fit can infer a less accurate tree. If this result holds up in peer-reviewed form and on other data, the Bayes-factor preference for covarion models reported in many of the studies above would say little about which model recovers the history better. Notice, finally, what the table does not contain: we know of no published comparison that sets binary models against a meaning-slot model with synonymy (row 10 of Table 7.2) on the same data. 7.10 Model adequacy Model selection asks which of a set of models is best supported. Model adequacy asks whether the chosen model could plausibly have generated the data at all. The standard tool for the second question is the posterior predictive check (Gelman et al. 1996), introduced to phylogenetics by Bollback (2002) and reviewed by Brown (2014b) (Section 6.9). Draw parameter values (and trees) from the posterior distribution; simulate a replicate dataset of the same size from the model with those values; compute a test statistic on each replicate and on the real data; and see where the observed statistic falls in the predictive distribution. In a maximum-likelihood setting, the same idea with the fitted values in place of posterior draws is a parametric bootstrap. Where the analysis produces a posterior sample of trees, replicates should be simulated on trees drawn from that sample rather than on a single summary tree, so that the check reflects phylogenetic uncertainty. The choice of test statistic is what makes a check informative, and the diagnostic column of Table 7.3 suggests statistics for each model. For cognate data, useful statistics include the number of cognate classes per language (which tests whether the model captures variation in vocabulary turnover among lineages), the site frequency spectrum, the distribution of Fitch parsimony scores (homoplasy), the number of cognate classes per meaning, and treelikeness statistics such as the delta score (Chapter 8). The code below uses the data simulated with strong rate heterogeneity in Section 7.5 and asks whether the single-rate model and the gamma model reproduce the observed proportion of characters that fit the tree with a single parsimony step. Because the “observed” data are themselves simulated, with a known misspecification of the single-rate model, the example shows that the check has the power to detect that misspecification; it says nothing about the adequacy of either model for any real dataset. one_step_prop <- function(tree, X) { pd <- phyDat(X, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1")) mean(parsimony(tree, pd, site = "site")[attr(pd, "index")] == 1) } predictive <- function(fit, nrep = 100, shape = NULL) { n <- ncol(Xv) replicate(nrep, { Y <- sim_ctmc_binary(fit$tree, 3 * n, pi1 = 0.5, rate = 1, shape = shape) Y <- Y[, colSums(Y) > 0 & colSums(Y) < nrow(Y)][, 1:n] # same filtering one_step_prop(fit$tree, Y) }) } set.seed(21) obs_eq <- one_step_prop(fit_eq$tree, Xv) obs_g <- one_step_prop(fit_g$tree, Xv) pp_eq <- predictive(fit_eq) pp_g <- predictive(fit_g, shape = fit_g$shape) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) hist(pp_eq, xlim = extendrange(c(pp_eq, obs_eq), f = 0.06), main = "single-rate model", xlab = "proportion of one-step characters", col = "grey85", border = "white") abline(v = obs_eq, col = "#d1495b", lwd = 3) hist(pp_g, xlim = extendrange(c(pp_g, obs_g), f = 0.06), main = "gamma model", xlab = "proportion of one-step characters", col = "grey85", border = "white") abline(v = obs_g, col = "#d1495b", lwd = 3) Figure 7.5: Parametric bootstrap check of two models fitted to data simulated with strong rate heterogeneity. Histograms show the proportion of variable characters requiring a single parsimony step on the fitted tree in 100 datasets simulated from each fitted model; the vertical line shows the observed value. The single-rate model cannot reproduce the excess of slowly evolving, perfectly tree-compatible characters; the gamma model reproduces it. rbind(single_rate = c(observed = obs_eq, quantile(pp_eq, c(0.025, 0.975))), gamma = c(observed = obs_g, quantile(pp_g, c(0.025, 0.975)))) #> observed 2.5% 97.5% #> single_rate 0.1155 0.008507 0.02053 #> gamma 0.1149 0.104167 0.12849 The single-rate model fails decisively: the observed data contain several times more perfectly tree-compatible characters than it can generate, because it has no slowly evolving characters. The gamma model, whose estimated shape is close to the true value (Table 7.4), reproduces the observed proportion, which lies inside the central 95% of its predictive distribution. That is expected here, since the data were simulated under a gamma model; with real data even the better of two models may fail some checks. This is how adequacy checks are most useful in practice: not as a pass-or-fail verdict, but as a pointer to the aspect of the data that a model handles least well. Posterior predictive checks of this kind are cheap and illuminating, yet they remain rare in published linguistic phylogenies. Most studies report only Bayes-factor comparisons, if they compare models at all. The most systematic exception is King (2026b), who checked the analysis set-up that has become standard in BEAST 2 in two steps. Simulation-based calibration, an implementation check, showed that the covarion parameters are recovered correctly, but that the default reweighting of partition rates by the number of observed cognates interacts with the ascertainment correction and produces poorly calibrated posteriors; an alternative that treats each meaning as drawing on a cognate set of equal size behaved correctly and fitted empirical data better. Posterior predictive simulation on a sample of Germanic, Italic and Celtic languages from IE-CoR, an empirical adequacy check, then showed that data simulated under the fitted covarion model differ from the real data in several statistics of language divergence and cognate distribution, a failure that King attributes most plausibly to semantic shift and to the non-independence of cognate replacements within meanings. The two results answer different questions: the first says that the software computes what the model specifies, the second that the model does not describe lexical evolution well. Chapter 15 argues that adequacy checks should become routine, and Chapter 16 lists the relevant tools. 7.11 What biology offers The models in common linguistic use are, with the exception of the stochastic Dollo family, simplified versions of models developed for DNA and morphology twenty or more years ago. Molecular phylogenetics has since moved on to much richer descriptions of heterogeneity among sites and lineages. Several of these could be adapted to cognate data with little effort. Mixture and profile-mixture models. In a mixture model, each character is assumed to evolve under one of several distinct processes, and the likelihood sums over the possibilities with estimated weights; unlike a partitioned model, the assignment of characters to processes need not be known in advance. Pagel and Meade (2004) introduced a general mixture model for gene sequences and discrete characters, implemented in BayesTraits. In protein phylogenetics, the CAT model of Lartillot and Philippe (2004) goes further, letting each site have its own equilibrium profile drawn from a Dirichlet process, so that the number of profile classes is itself inferred. Empirical profile mixtures for proteins (Le et al. 2008) are now standard in deep phylogenetics. For cognate data, the analogue of an equilibrium profile is the frequency of presence \(\pi_1\) together with the rate. A mixture over a few (\(\pi_1\), rate) classes would let the data separate, say, cognates that are long-lived and widespread from cognates that are short-lived and local, without the analyst having to specify which is which. Morphological phylogenetics offers a ready-made version: Wright et al. (2016) let the stationary frequencies of binary characters vary across characters according to a discretized Beta distribution, a mixture of F81 models. There the Beta is usually symmetric, because the labels 0 and 1 of a morphological character are arbitrary; for cognate presence and absence they are not, and the mean frequency of presence should be estimated. Section H.3.17 implements both versions in RevBayes and compares them by marginal likelihood with the binary Jukes–Cantor, F81 and F81+\(\Gamma\) models on simulated data. Dirichlet process rates. Huelsenbeck and Suchard (2007) replaced the parametric gamma distribution of rates with a Dirichlet process prior, which clusters characters into an unknown number of rate classes. Applied at the level of meanings, this would deliver a data-driven classification of meanings into stable and volatile groups, a direct test of the claim that the Swadesh list contains distinct strata of stability. Heterotachy mixtures. Kolaczkowski and Thornton (2004) showed that when rates shift across lineages in a site-specific way, standard models can be misled; mixtures of branch-length sets and covarion-type models address this. Hidden-rate models. The hidden Markov models of Beaulieu et al. (2013), developed for morphological characters, allow a character to switch between unobserved rate categories, as in the covarion model, but with asymmetric rates of gain and loss in each category. Structured characters. The structured Markov models of Tarasov (2019) combine dependent morphological characters into a single character with a constrained state space; applied to the cognate classes of a meaning, the same construction gives a principled meaning-slot model. Model averaging. Rather than choosing a single substitution model, bModelTest (Bouckaert and Drummond 2017) averages over a family of nucleotide models within BEAST 2 by reversible-jump MCMC; an analogous scheme for binary and multistate lexical models would remove the need for separate Bayes-factor comparisons. Data-driven partitioning. PartitionFinder (Lanfear et al. 2012) chooses partitioning schemes for molecular data by information criteria, and the same logic could group meanings into rate classes objectively. To our knowledge, none of these approaches, apart from occasional use of BayesTraits mixtures and covarion models, has been applied systematically to linguistic cognate data. Beyond these, two less obvious directions deserve mention. First, population genetics has a mature theory of the site frequency spectrum under infinite-sites and infinite-alleles models, and of how demography (expansion, bottlenecks) distorts it. The cognate site frequency spectrum computed in Section 7.7 is the linguistic analogue, and spectrum-based tests could help detect expansions or the effects of borrowing. Second, the morphological-phylogenetics literature has grappled with many of the same issues as cognate analysis, including the choice of ascertainment correction, variable numbers of states and correlated characters, and the guide by Wright (2019) is a useful source of ideas for linguists. 7.12 Practical recommendations Pulling the threads together, the following practices are sound defaults for model choice in lexical phylogenetics. Start from the historical question. Topology, dates, rates of replacement and borrowing are sensitive to different features of the models in Table 7.2; choose and check the model with the target quantity in mind. Match the ascertainment correction to the way the data were filtered. For standard cognate matrices that retain singletons and universally shared cognates, use the no-absence correction; if singletons were removed, use a correction that excludes them too. Always include among-character rate variation, ideally at the level of meanings rather than independent cognate classes, and check how sensitive dates are to the rate model. Compare at least one reversible model (with gamma and possibly covarion rates) with a Dollo-type model. Agreement between them is reassuring; disagreement points to multiple origins of cognates, which calls for a closer look at borrowing and coding. Do not treat a better marginal likelihood for a finite-state model as evidence that it recovers the tree better (Rönchen 2025). Be explicit about binary versus multistate coding and about how synonyms and missing entries were handled, and remember that binary analyses do not model the dependence among the classes of a meaning, so that their posterior intervals are likely to be too narrow. Add posterior predictive checks with statistics that matter for your question, such as the site frequency spectrum, homoplasy and cognates per language, simulated over the posterior sample of trees. If meanings are partitioned by number of cognate classes, check how partition rates are weighted, since the default weighting can miscalibrate the posterior (King 2026b). Report the full model specification (substitution model, rate variation, ascertainment correction, clock and tree prior) so that the analysis can be reproduced. Models of lexical evolution differ in their unit of observation, the process that creates and removes cognate classes, whether they allow synonyms and recurrent innovation, whether they represent the dependence among classes of one meaning, and how they treat borrowing (Table 7.2). The binary CTMC (restriction-site, Mk2) model treats each cognate class as a presence/absence character evolving independently and reversibly; its transition probabilities have a simple closed form and saturate with time. Cognate classes absent from all sampled languages are never observed. The ascertainment correction divides each character’s likelihood by the probability of observability; the appropriate correction depends on exactly how the data were filtered. Rates of lexical replacement vary by two orders of magnitude among meanings, partly predictably from word frequency. Ignoring this variation shortens trees and biases dates toward the recent past; covarion switching has similar consequences for deep dates. The stochastic Dollo model gives each cognate class a single birth followed by independent deaths; its likelihood has built-in ascertainment and is the limit of the corrected reversible model as the frequency of presence goes to zero. Pseudo-Dollo models approximate it within a standard CTMC. Multiple origins of a cognate class (borrowing, parallel semantic shift, loose coding) violate the Dollo assumption and can bias dates. Only meaning-slot models account for the dependence among the cognate classes of a meaning; binary analyses are composite likelihoods that overweight fast meanings and overstate the information in the data. Explicit models of replacement with synonymy are the clearest gap in current practice. Every model identifies only rate-time products from the data, and rate parameters are interpretable as historical quantities only relative to a given coding. Relative model fit is not adequacy, and agreement with established subgroups is not independent validation; posterior predictive checks should be routine. 7.13 Exercises Conceptual A language has two words for ‘stone’, from cognate classes B and D. Explain the difference between a parameter that is identifiable under the model and one that is interpretable as a historical quantity, using the binary loss rate and the meaning-slot replacement rate as examples. The original papers on the restriction-site model and the Mk/Mkv models, including the derivation of the ascertainment corrections; still the clearest statements of the logic. Yang (1994): The discrete-gamma approximation to among-site rate variation, used in nearly every analysis since. Tuffley and Steel (1998): The mathematical formulation of the covarion model, with a discussion of identifiability. Nicholls and Gray (2008): The stochastic Dollo model with catastrophes and its application to Indo-European; demanding but rewarding statistically. Chapter 8 Borrowing, Contact and Reticulation Languages do not evolve in isolation. Speakers of neighboring languages trade, intermarry, conquer one another and shift from one language to another, and words, sounds and grammatical patterns pass between languages in the process. Contact is the feature of language history that most clearly distinguishes it from the textbook picture of biological descent, and it was the basis of the oldest objection to the family tree, Johannes Schmidt’s wave theory of 1872. This chapter asks what contact does to phylogenetic inference, how much of it a tree can absorb, and what to use when a tree is the wrong representation. Its central distinction is between descriptive networks, which summarize conflicting signal in the data, and generative models, which propose a history of descent and contact that could have produced the data; and its central argument is that the choice among trees, networks and wave-like representations should follow from the historical question being asked. After reading this chapter you should be able to: distinguish a tree read as an approximation to a genealogy from a tree read as a statistical summary of variation, and explain why under extensive reticulation there may be no bifurcating history to approximate; match a historical question (reconstructing divergence, describing similarity, identifying innovations, estimating a dominant pattern of transmission) to an appropriate representation and method (Table 8.1); predict how local and distant borrowing affect topologies, branch lengths and dates under reversible and Dollo-type models; compute and interpret delta scores and Q-residuals, and explain why they measure conflict rather than borrowing; read a NeighborNet or consensus network correctly as a description of conflicting signal, not a history of contact; explain what explicit, generative models of contact (lateral-transfer stochastic Dollo, explicit networks) add, and what they cost; state when a wave or linkage model, rather than a tree, is the appropriate description, and what Historical Glottometry measures. 8.1 Borrowing and the tree model 8.1.1 What is borrowed, and how often Contact linguistics distinguishes several outcomes of language contact (Thomason and Kaufman 1988; Thomason 2001). In borrowing, speakers of a language adopt material from another language while keeping their own; vocabulary is borrowed first and most easily, and structural features follow only under intense and prolonged contact. In shift, a community abandons its language for another and often leaves traces of the old language, a substrate, in the new one. In extreme cases contact produces mixed languages, whose grammar and lexicon come from different sources, and creoles, which emerge from pidgins in situations of radical social disruption. Each of these processes creates a different kind of departure from treelike descent. For phylogenetics based on basic vocabulary, the central question is how much of that vocabulary is borrowed. The World Loanword Database project compiled loanword data for a standardized list of meanings in 41 languages (Haspelmath and Tadmor 2009a). Across the whole list, roughly a quarter of the words were loans on average, with enormous variation among languages (Tadmor 2009). Borrowability also varied strongly by meaning, and Tadmor et al. (2010) used these differences to build the Leipzig-Jakarta list of the 100 meanings least likely to be borrowed. Basic vocabulary is therefore resistant to borrowing but not immune. English took they, sky, skin and egg from Old Norse; the numerals of Thai and of many other languages of mainland Southeast Asia are of Chinese origin; and Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese each have a full set of Chinese-derived numerals alongside native ones. Borrowing rates in basic vocabulary vary among regions and social settings, but the rates measured in large samples are generally modest. Bowern et al. (2011) found, for example, that borrowing rates in the basic vocabulary of hunter-gatherer languages from several regions of the world were generally low, contrary to the expectation that hunter-gatherer languages borrow unusually freely. 8.1.2 Known and hidden loans Linguists handle borrowing first by identifying loans. Most large cognate databases flag known loanwords (Chapter 3), and analysts either exclude them or code them as separate characters that do not unite donor and recipient. Gray and Atkinson (2003), for instance, removed known borrowings from the Indo-European data before analysis. The difficulty is with undetected loans. Loans between closely related languages are the hardest to detect, because regular sound correspondences, the main diagnostic, may not distinguish a borrowed word from an inherited one when the languages have undergone few sound changes since their split. Loans from unrelated or distantly related languages are easier to identify. This creates an asymmetry: the borrowings most likely to slip through are those between neighbors and close relatives, and, as we shall see, these are also the ones that phylogenetic methods are least able to detect. 8.1.3 The biological parallel and the ethnogenesis critique Biologists face the same problem in other guises. In prokaryotes, horizontal (lateral) gene transfer is so pervasive that some have argued the tree of life is better described as a web (Doolittle 1999). In plants and animals, hybridization creates lineages with two parents, and introgression, the movement of genes from one species into another by repeated backcrossing, is the closest biological analogue of lexical borrowing. Within species, recombination means that different parts of the genome have different genealogies. Biologists have responded with explicit models of all three processes, which we survey in Section 8.11. In anthropology, the parallel argument was made forcefully by Moore (1994), who contrasted phylogenesis, the branching of cultures from common ancestors, with ethnogenesis, their formation by blending, and argued that human history was dominated by the latter. The empirical response has been to measure rather than assume. Collard et al. (2006) compared the fit of cultural and biological datasets to trees using the retention index, and found that cultural data were, on average, no less treelike than biological data. That comparison does not settle any particular case, but it reframes the question: how treelike is a given dataset, and how robust are the conclusions we want to draw from it? 8.2 Trees, networks and historical questions 8.2.1 Two readings of a tree A tree inferred from linguistic data can be read in two quite different ways, and much confusion about contact comes from sliding between them. On the genealogical reading, the tree is an approximation to a real history in which speech communities separated and then diverged. Internal nodes stand for proto-languages spoken by identifiable (if unknown) communities, branch lengths correspond to elapsed time or amounts of change, and borrowing is a perturbation: a set of lateral events superimposed on a history that is fundamentally branching. Every dating analysis, every reconstruction of a proto-lexicon at an internal node and every homeland inference presupposes this reading. Whether it holds is a matter of empirical adequacy and historical interpretation, in the vocabulary of Section 6.10, not something the inference itself can establish: a posterior probability for a clade is a probability given that the history was a tree. On the summary reading, the tree is a statistical summary of variation: the hierarchical arrangement that best fits the similarities in the data, in the way that a cluster dendrogram summarizes a distance matrix. Its internal nodes need not correspond to communities, and its branch lengths need not measure time. Support values measure how consistently the data favor a grouping, not whether the grouping ever existed as a speech community. The summary reading is always available, which is part of its appeal, but it licenses far fewer historical conclusions. The two readings coincide when the history really was close to a tree, and diverge sharply when it was not. Under extensive reticulation, as in Ross’s linkages (Section 8.7) or a dialect continuum in which innovations spread across overlapping sets of varieties, there may be no single bifurcating history underlying the data at all. A tree inferred from such data is then not a slightly blurred picture of the true history, with a few borrowings hidden; it is a projection of a different kind of history onto a model that cannot represent it. Its internal nodes do not correspond to proto-languages, its “divergence times” do not date separations, and high support for a clade may reflect nothing more than the fact that some grouping had to be chosen. It is sometimes reasonable to call a tree inferred from overlapping innovations a summary that hides their distribution; it is not reasonable to then treat its nodes as ancestors. Between the two extremes lies the common case of a dominant vertical signal with contact superimposed, for which a tree with lateral edges, or a network with estimated inheritance proportions, is the natural representation. 8.2.2 Descriptive networks and generative models Two kinds of network are discussed in this chapter, and they answer different questions. Descriptive networks, such as split networks, NeighborNets and consensus networks (Section 8.5), are functions of the data: they display the signal in a distance matrix or a set of trees, conflicting signal included. They have no likelihood, make no claim about what happened, and their edges have neither direction nor date. They are to a dataset what a scatterplot is to a regression: indispensable for seeing the data, silent about mechanism. Generative models of contact (Section 8.6) specify a history of descent and contact, with parameters such as borrowing rates, donor and recipient lineages, times and inheritance proportions, together with a probability model under which that history could have produced the data. Because they define a probability of the data, they can be fitted, compared, checked against data simulated from them and used to estimate how much borrowing occurred and when. Their cost is the cost of any model: they can be misspecified, they may be computationally demanding, and their parameters may be only weakly identifiable. Some methods fall between the two: perfect phylogenetic networks and minimal lateral networks posit explicit contact edges, but select them by combinatorial or heuristic criteria rather than by a probability model. 8.2.3 Choosing by the historical question Which representation to use should follow from the historical question being asked, not from a general preference for trees or for waves. Table 8.1 sets out four common questions. Table 8.1: Four historical questions and the representations and methods that suit them. Historical question What is estimated Appropriate representation Typical tools What it cannot deliver Reconstructing divergence: in what order, and when, did speech communities separate? a genealogy of communities, with dates rooted tree; explicit network if lineages merged Bayesian trees with clocks (Chapters 9, 10); lateral-transfer models; explicit networks meaningful answers where no separation into communities took place (linkages, continua) Describing similarity: how similar are the languages, and where does the signal conflict? a summary of the data distance matrix, split network, consensus network, dialectometric map NeighborNet, delta scores and Q-residuals, multidimensional scaling the direction, timing or cause of contact Identifying innovations: which changes are shared, and by which groups? the distribution of innovations established by the comparative method compatibility analysis, perfect phylogenetic network, glottometric diagram comparative method; perfect phylogenetic networks; Historical Glottometry rates, dates, or the probability of parallel change, unless modelled Estimating a dominant pattern of transmission: how much is vertical, how much horizontal, and along which tree? a tree plus the amount and location of transfer tree with lateral transfer; network with inheritance proportions lateral-transfer stochastic Dollo; minimal lateral networks; four-taxon tests; network coalescent a complete history of individual borrowing events The questions are not exclusive. A typical project begins by describing similarity, to see how treelike the data are; uses the result to decide whether reconstructing divergence is a sensible goal at all; and, if it is, estimates the dominant tree while checking whether the amount of transfer is large enough to change the conclusions. What the table rules out is the use of a method built for one question to answer another: dating the nodes of a NeighborNet, for instance, or reading a box in a split network as a borrowing event. 8.3 How borrowing distorts trees 8.3.1 Two kinds of borrowing It helps to distinguish two situations. When languages borrow from their close relatives and immediate neighbors (local borrowing), the borrowed words reinforce relationships that the tree already shows. They do not create much conflict in the data, but they make related languages look more similar than inheritance alone would, compressing the tree: internal branches become shorter and the whole tree shallower. When languages borrow from distant relatives or unrelated languages (distant or global borrowing), the borrowed words create characters that unite languages from different clades. Such characters conflict with the tree and, if there are enough of them, can pull the recipient toward the donor, distorting the topology. The effect on dates depends on the substitution model. Under reversible models and distance methods, both kinds of borrowing reduce the inferred amount of change, so dates tend to be underestimated. Under the stochastic Dollo model (Chapter 7), a cognate class present in two distant languages must have been born above their common ancestor, so distant borrowing can push inferred births, and possibly the root, deeper into the past, while forcing many parallel losses. Borrowing therefore has no single direction of bias; its effect depends on who borrows from whom and on the model used (Table 7.2). Does horizontal transmission invalidate cultural phylogenies? Greenhill et al. (2009) addressed this question by simulation. They generated binary trait data on known trees and allowed traits to be copied between lineages at a range of borrowing rates, contrasting borrowing restricted to nearby lineages with borrowing between any lineages. They then reconstructed trees from the simulated data with Bayesian phylogenetic methods and compared the results with the true trees. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, this is a study of robustness under misspecification: the inference model ignores the borrowing that the generating process contains. Their key finding was that the reconstructed topologies were fairly robust to the levels of borrowing thought to be realistic for basic vocabulary, with accuracy declining at higher rates; they also found that borrowing tended to make the estimated trees shallower, which matters for dating. A companion study (Currie, Greenhill, and Mace 2010) asked the analogous question for comparative analyses of continuous cultural traits and also found a reasonable degree of robustness to moderate horizontal transmission. These studies do not show that borrowing is harmless, only that its effects can be quantified, and that they are often smaller than critics had assumed. Their conclusions hold for the simulated scenarios, which assume an underlying tree; they say nothing about histories, such as linkages, in which there is no tree to recover. 8.3.2 A simulation in R We now run a small experiment of the same kind. Our model is a meaning-slot model: each language has one word for each of 200 meanings; along each lineage, a word is replaced by a newly coined word (a new cognate class) at rate \(r_{\text{innov}}\); and it is replaced by the word for the same meaning in another, contemporaneous language at rate \(r_{\text{borrow}}\). For global borrowing the donor is chosen uniformly among contemporaneous lineages; for local borrowing it is chosen with probability proportional to \(e^{-d/s}\), where \(d\) is the patristic distance between donor and recipient at the time of borrowing and \(s\) a scale parameter, so that close relatives are preferred. A third option, pair, restricts borrowing to one donor lineage and one recipient lineage within a time window, mimicking a specific episode of contact. The simulation steps through time in small increments, which is crude but transparent. The simulator sim_borrowing() and two helpers, meaning_dist() (the proportion of meanings for which two languages have non-cognate words) and to_binary() (binary presence/absence coding), are loaded silently below. The code of sim_borrowing() and its helpers, with an explanation of the time-stepping scheme and of the glottochronological formula used below, is in Section C.2.1. library(phangorn) family <- read.tree(text = paste0( "((((A1:0.2,A2:0.2):0.2,(A3:0.25,A4:0.25):0.15):0.35,", "((B1:0.2,B2:0.2):0.25,(B3:0.3,B4:0.3):0.15):0.3):0.25,", "(((C1:0.15,C2:0.15):0.3,C3:0.45):0.25,(C4:0.4,C5:0.4):0.3):0.3);")) plot(family, edge.width = 2, label.offset = 0.01, cex = 0.9) axisPhylo(backward = FALSE) Figure 8.1: The toy language family used in the simulations of this chapter: thirteen languages in three subgroups (A, B, C), with root age 1. We simulate datasets at six levels of borrowing, expressed as the proportion \(b\) of all replacement events that are borrowings, holding the total replacement rate fixed at 0.6 per meaning per unit time. For each dataset we infer a neighbor-joining tree from the proportion of non-cognate meanings, compute its normalized Robinson-Foulds distance to the true tree (Chapter 2), compute the mean delta score with the function quartet_stats() introduced in the next section, and estimate the root age in the manner of glottochronology: we transform distances with the formula \(\hat{t} = -\log(1 - d)/(2r)\) appropriate to the model without borrowing, and take the root height of a UPGMA tree built from them (Chapter 4). In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, this is a test of robustness under misspecification: both the tree-building method and the dating formula assume that there is no borrowing. set.seed(42) r_total <- 0.6 grid <- expand.grid(b = seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.1), mode = c("local", "global"), rep = 1:6, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) res <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) { g <- grid[i, ] M <- sim_borrowing(family, innov = (1 - g$b) * r_total, borrow = g$b * r_total, mode = g$mode) d <- meaning_dist(M) qs <- quartet_stats(d) t_hat <- -log(pmax(1 - d, 1e-3)) / r_total # = 2 x estimated divergence time c(RF = RF.dist(NJ(d), family, normalize = TRUE), delta = qs$delta, Qres = qs$qres, root_age = max(node.depth.edgelength(upgma(t_hat)))) })) sim <- cbind(grid, res) summ <- aggregate(cbind(RF, delta, Qres, root_age) ~ b + mode, data = sim, FUN = mean) knitr::kable(summ, digits = c(1, 0, 3, 3, 4, 3), caption = "Mean results over six replicate simulations per setting: normalized Robinson-Foulds distance of the neighbor-joining tree to the true tree, mean delta score, mean Q-residual, and glottochronological estimate of the root age (true value 1), as a function of the proportion b of replacements due to borrowing.") Left: mean delta score. Right: estimated root age (true value 1, dotted line). Global borrowing increases conflict in the data (higher delta scores), whereas local borrowing hardly changes the delta score; both kinds compress the tree and lead to substantial underestimation of the root age. The topology (not shown) was recovered almost perfectly throughout. The results in Table 8.2 and Figure 8.2 illustrate three general points. First, the topology of this well-structured tree survives even heavy borrowing: the neighbor-joining tree is essentially always correct. That is in line with the robustness of topology reported by Greenhill et al. (2009), although our tree, with long internal branches, is an easy case. Second, global borrowing leaves a detectable signature in the data, a rising delta score, while local borrowing leaves almost none. Local borrowing is the most dangerous kind precisely because it is invisible to treelikeness statistics. Third, both kinds of borrowing make the languages look much more similar than their true divergence times imply, and the root age estimated by the glottochronological formula falls steadily as borrowing increases. In a Bayesian analysis with calibrations, part of this bias would be absorbed by the estimated rate, because the calibrating languages would be affected too, but the compression of the tree is real and unevenly distributed. Note what the experiment does and does not show: the borrowing simulated here is superimposed on a true tree, so the experiment speaks to the genealogical reading of Section 8.2 when it holds; it cannot tell us whether a real family had a tree-like history in the first place. 8.4 Measuring treelikeness 8.4.1 Quartets and the four-point condition How can we tell from the data whether a tree is an adequate summary? The most widely used statistics work with quartets, sets of four languages. Recall from Chapter 4 that a distance matrix fits a tree exactly if and only if it satisfies the four-point condition: for every quartet \(\{w, x, y, z\}\), of the three sums \[\begin{equation} s_1 = d_{wx} + d_{yz}, \qquad s_2 = d_{wy} + d_{xz}, \qquad s_3 = d_{wz} + d_{xy}, \tag{8.1} \end{equation}\] the two largest are equal. If the true tree groups \(w\) with \(x\) and \(y\) with \(z\), then \(s_1\) is the smallest sum and \(s_2 = s_3\), both equal to \(s_1\) plus twice the length of the internal edge. Real distances never satisfy the condition exactly. The question is how far they depart from it, and whether the departures look like noise or like a systematic conflict. 8.4.2 The delta score Holland et al. (2002) proposed measuring the departure for each quartet by the delta score. Order the sums so that \(s_{(1)} \le s_{(2)} \le s_{(3)}\), and define \[\begin{equation} \delta_q = \frac{s_{(3)} - s_{(2)}}{s_{(3)} - s_{(1)}}. \tag{8.2} \end{equation}\] The delta score is zero when the quartet fits a tree exactly (\(s_{(2)} = s_{(3)}\)) and one when the quartet is maximally unresolved, with the two largest sums as far apart as the largest and smallest, which corresponds to a perfect “box” in a split network. Averaging \(\delta_q\) over all quartets gives a score for the whole dataset; averaging over the quartets that contain a given language gives a taxon-specific delta score, which can pick out languages involved in conflicting signal. Because \(\delta_q\) is a ratio, it does not depend on the overall scale of the distances. 8.4.3 The Q-residual Gray et al. (2010) introduced the Q-residual alongside the delta score in their discussion of treelikeness in language data. It measures the same departure in absolute rather than relative terms, as the squared difference between the two largest sums, \[\begin{equation} Q_q = \bigl(s_{(3)} - s_{(2)}\bigr)^2, \tag{8.3} \end{equation}\] computed after the distances have been rescaled so that their mean is one, which makes Q-residuals comparable across datasets. The two statistics behave differently when the internal edge of a quartet is short. A nearly unresolved quartet with a short internal edge can have a large delta score, because the denominator \(s_{(3)} - s_{(1)}\) is small, even though its absolute departure from treelikeness is tiny. The Q-residual is insensitive to this. For this reason, Gray et al. (2010) recommended reporting both. Implementations differ in details, for example in how distances are normalized and whether a constant factor is included, so values should be compared only when computed in the same way. Both statistics are computed by SplitsTree (Huson and Bryant 2006); phangorn’s delta.score() computes delta scores from Hamming distances. The function quartet_stats(), which computes both statistics for every quartet, and a check of its delta scores against phangorn::delta.score(), are in Section C.2.2. Delta scores and Q-residuals measure conflict in the data, not borrowing. Conflict can arise from borrowing, but also from parallel innovation, homoplasy due to rapid change, rate heterogeneity among lineages, coding errors, missing data and simple sampling noise in small datasets. Conversely, as the simulation above showed, borrowing among close relatives produces very little conflict. A low delta score does not prove that a family’s history was treelike, and a high score does not prove that it was not. The next chunk simulates a specific contact episode: during the last 40 percent of the family’s history, language B4 borrows heavily from the lineage leading to C5. We compute taxon-specific delta scores with and without the contact. Because the true history is known, this is a check of what a descriptive statistic responds to; in the vocabulary of Section 6.10 it is neither parameter recovery (no model is fitted) nor a test of empirical adequacy. set.seed(5) M_contact <- sim_borrowing(family, innov = 0.5, borrow = 1, mode = "pair", pair = c("B4", "C5"), window = c(0.6, 1)) set.seed(5) M_tree <- sim_borrowing(family, innov = 0.5, borrow = 0) d_contact <- meaning_dist(M_contact); d_tree <- meaning_dist(M_tree) qs_contact <- quartet_stats(d_contact); qs_tree <- quartet_stats(d_tree) B_contact <- to_binary(M_contact) # binary coding, used below pd_contact <- phyDat(B_contact, type = "USER", levels = c(0, 1)) tab <- rbind(no_contact = round(qs_tree$taxon_delta, 3), contact = round(qs_contact$taxon_delta, 3)) knitr::kable(t(tab), caption = "Taxon-specific delta scores for data simulated on the toy family without contact and with heavy borrowing into B4 from the lineage of C5. The recipient of the loans stands out.") Table 8.3: Taxon-specific delta scores for data simulated on the toy family without contact and with heavy borrowing into B4 from the lineage of C5. The recipient of the loans stands out. no_contact contact A1 0.070 0.118 A2 0.080 0.122 A3 0.101 0.119 A4 0.079 0.117 B1 0.070 0.137 B2 0.073 0.142 B3 0.096 0.154 B4 0.086 0.326 C1 0.076 0.118 C2 0.068 0.117 C3 0.066 0.124 C4 0.076 0.129 C5 0.070 0.149 With contact, the recipient B4 has by far the highest taxon-specific delta score, roughly twice that of any other language. Every other language’s score also rises somewhat, because every language belongs to some quartets that contain B4; the next highest values belong to the donor C5 and to B4’s former close relatives in subgroup B, whose quartets with B4 are the most disturbed. Taxon-specific scores of this kind have been used to flag languages with mixed histories before an analysis, and to decide whether to exclude them. Wichmann et al. (2011) computed delta scores across a large number of language families from ASJP word lists and explored what predicts how reticulate a family appears. 8.4.4 Other measures Several other statistics carry information about treelikeness. The consistency index and retention index from parsimony (Chapter 4) measure how much homoplasy the data require on the best tree; they were the basis of the comparison by Collard et al. (2006). Bootstrap support and posterior probabilities of clades indicate how consistently the data favor particular splits, although they confound conflict with lack of signal. Counts of characters that are incompatible with the tree, as in the compatibility methods of Ringe, Warnow and Taylor (Section 8.6), are directly interpretable for carefully chosen characters. And posterior predictive checks (Section 7.10) can use any of these quantities as test statistics, comparing their observed values with the values expected under a tree model without borrowing. That last use turns a descriptive statistic into a test of the genealogical reading of Section 8.2: if the observed delta score lies far outside what a fitted tree model generates, the tree is at best a summary. 8.5 Split networks: describing conflict 8.5.1 From trees to split systems A tree can be described by its splits: each edge, if cut, divides the languages into two groups (Chapter 2). Two splits are compatible if they can appear together on one tree, which is the case when one side of the first split is contained in one side of the second. A tree corresponds to a set of pairwise compatible splits. When data support incompatible splits, for example \(\{B4, C5\}\) versus the rest alongside \(\{B1, B2, B3, B4\}\) versus the rest, no tree can display them all. A split network (or splits graph) displays an arbitrary collection of splits by representing each split not by a single edge but by a band of parallel edges; cutting all the edges of the band separates the two sides of the split. Incompatible splits produce boxes, or more generally parallelograms, and the length of each band represents the weight of the split. A split network is therefore a picture of the signal in the data, conflicting signal included, and not a picture of a history. A box between two languages does not say that they were in contact; it says that some characters group them together and others do not. In the terms of Section 8.2, split networks are descriptive: they answer the question “how similar are these languages, and where does the signal conflict?”, and no other. Not every collection of splits can be drawn in the plane without crossing bands. Circular split systems, in which the languages can be arranged around a circle so that every split cuts the circle into two arcs, can always be drawn as planar networks. Restricting attention to circular systems keeps the networks readable and the computations fast. 8.5.2 Split decomposition and NeighborNet Two methods build split networks from distances. Split decomposition (Bandelt and Dress 1992) identifies the splits that are supported by every quartet that spans them, which yields a weakly compatible split system. It is conservative, and with large or noisy datasets it tends to give poorly resolved networks. NeighborNet (Bryant and Moulton 2004) is the method of choice for linguistic data. It is an agglomerative method, like neighbor joining (Chapter 4), but instead of joining two nodes into a cluster at each step it builds up a circular ordering of the languages, allowing a node to be paired with two neighbors rather than one. The ordering defines a circular split system, and the weights of the splits are then estimated by non-negative least squares, so that the patristic distances in the network approximate the observed distances as closely as possible. Splits with zero weight are dropped. If the distances fit a tree, NeighborNet returns that tree; the more conflict there is, the more box-like structure appears. For binary character data there are also median networks (Bandelt et al. 1995), which contain all most parsimonious trees for a set of compatible-in-pairs characters and become very complex when there is much homoplasy, and median-joining networks (Bandelt et al. 1999), which reduce that complexity heuristically. Both were developed for mitochondrial DNA within species. Finally, consensus networks (Holland and Moulton 2003; Holland et al. 2004) summarize a collection of trees, such as bootstrap replicates or a posterior sample, by displaying every split that appears in more than a chosen proportion of the trees. Where a consensus tree must discard conflicting splits, a consensus network shows them, which makes it a natural way to display phylogenetic uncertainty as well as conflict. All of these methods are implemented in SplitsTree (Huson and Bryant 2006), the standard program for split networks, and the main ones are available in phangorn. Huson et al. (2010) give a comprehensive treatment. 8.5.3 NeighborNets of simulated data The code below draws NeighborNets for the two datasets of the previous section, without contact and with heavy borrowing into B4 from the C5 lineage (Figure 8.3). par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5)) nn_tree <- neighborNet(d_tree) nn_contact <- neighborNet(d_contact) plot(nn_tree, cex = 0.8, edge.width = 1) title("no contact", font.main = 1) plot(nn_contact, cex = 0.8, edge.width = 1) title("borrowing into B4 from C5", font.main = 1) Figure 8.3: NeighborNets of data simulated on the toy family without contact (left) and with heavy borrowing into B4 from the lineage leading to C5 (right). Without contact the network is nearly a tree. With contact, a prominent band of parallel edges represents the split grouping B4 with C5, in conflict with the split grouping B4 with its own subgroup. The left network is almost a tree: the boxes that appear are small and reflect sampling noise. In the right network, B4 is drawn between subgroup B and C5, and the box that connects them is the visual signature of the conflicting splits. We can quantify the conflict by listing the heaviest splits that are incompatible with the true tree, using a helper function conflicting_splits() (listed in Section C.2.3). knitr::kable(conflicting_splits(nn_contact, family), row.names = FALSE, digits = 4, caption = "The heaviest NeighborNet splits that are absent from the true tree, for the data with contact. Each split is labeled by its smaller side.") Table 8.4: The heaviest NeighborNet splits that are absent from the true tree, for the data with contact. Each split is labeled by its smaller side. split weight B4,C1,C2,C3,C4,C5 0.0422 B4,C5 0.0258 B4,C4,C5 0.0231 All of the heaviest splits absent from the true tree group B4 with members of subgroup C: with the whole of subgroup C, with C5 alone, and with C4 and C5. This is what the simulated contact predicts. Many of the words B4 acquired from C5 are old words that C5 shares with the rest of its subgroup, so the contact appears not only as a B4-C5 split but also as a split uniting B4 with all of subgroup C. The example also shows the limits of a descriptive network. The network displays the conflict, but nothing in it identifies B4 rather than C5 as the recipient, dates the contact to the last part of the history, or distinguishes contact from, say, parallel innovation. We know these things only because we simulated them. In real applications the true tree is not known, and the analyst must judge which splits are surprising in light of other evidence. 8.5.4 Consensus networks of bootstrap trees A consensus network over bootstrap trees, or over a posterior sample of trees, shows how the uncertainty about relationships is structured. If the trees disagree only randomly, the network shows many weak, unrelated splits; if they disagree systematically, a few strong conflicting splits appear (Figure 8.4). set.seed(9) bs <- bootstrap.phyDat(pd_contact, FUN = function(x) NJ(dist.hamming(x)), bs = 200) cnet <- consensusNet(bs, prob = 0.1) op <- par(xpd = NA) # let tip labels at top and bottom extend into margins plot(cnet, cex = 0.8, edge.width = 1) Figure 8.4: Consensus network of 200 bootstrap neighbor-joining trees for the data with contact, showing every split present in at least 10 percent of the bootstrap trees. Edge lengths are proportional to the frequency of the split. The position of B4 is the main source of conflict. par(op) 8.5.5 NeighborNets in linguistics NeighborNet entered linguistics in the early 2000s and quickly became the standard exploratory tool. Bryant et al. (2005) applied it to Indo-European lexical data and found that, although the major subgroups emerge clearly, the relationships among them are surrounded by conflicting signal. McMahon and McMahon (2005) used NeighborNets throughout their book on quantitative language classification. One of their diagnostics deserves wider use. They divided the 200-item list into a sublist of meanings that are widely reconstructable and rarely replaced and a sublist of meanings that are neither, reasoning that related languages should be more distant on the unstable meanings than on the stable ones. For Quechua and Aymara they found the reverse, and concluded that contact rather than common descent accounts for most of the lexical similarity between the two families (McMahon and McMahon 2005; McMahon et al. 2005). Comparing trees or networks built from fast and slow subsets of meanings is a cheap way of locating suspected loans before borrowing is modelled explicitly, although it assumes that stability rankings transfer across families. Lehtinen et al. (2014) made a related comparison for Uralic, between networks built from basic vocabulary and from more easily borrowed vocabulary: the networks broadly supported a treelike diversification, but showed conflicting signal behind some ambiguous splits and the effect of borrowing between branches, mostly within and between the Finnic and Saami subgroups. Ben Hamed (2005) analyzed Chinese dialects and showed that their relationships are poorly represented by a tree, consistent with a long history of dialect contact and the influence of standard languages; the theme was developed further by Ben Hamed and Wang (2006). Heggarty et al. (2010) discussed how divergence measures and network analyses can help distinguish tree-like splitting from wave-like diffusion in language histories. Bowern (2010) discussed the relevance of trees and networks for Australian languages, where the extent of borrowing has long been debated. Bakker et al. (2011) used NeighborNets of typological features to argue that creoles form a typologically distinct group (Section 8.9). And Gray et al. (2010) used NeighborNets together with delta scores and Q-residuals to discuss the “shape” of language history across several families. The shape and fabric of human history. Gray et al. (2010) addressed a long-standing question: is the history of languages and cultures fundamentally treelike or fundamentally reticulate? They argued that the question is empirical and that the answer may differ among datasets and families. They proposed using delta scores and Q-residuals, together with NeighborNet visualizations, to quantify how treelike a dataset is, and introduced the Q-residual for this purpose. Applying these measures to language data, they showed that families vary in their degree of treelikeness, and argued that even fairly reticulate data can contain enough tree signal to support phylogenetic inference, provided the degree of conflict is measured and its consequences assessed. The paper’s lasting contribution is methodological: it shifted the debate from assertions about whether “language evolution is a tree” to measurements of how much conflict particular datasets contain. Those measurements describe the data; deciding whether a tree inferred from moderately reticulate data should be read genealogically or only as a summary (Section 8.2) still requires historical argument. Split networks are routinely over-interpreted. A box in a NeighborNet does not identify a borrowing event, a donor or a recipient, and it carries no information about timing. Boxes can come from sampling error, rate heterogeneity, coding inconsistencies or incomplete data as well as from contact. NeighborNet also always produces a circular split system, so it cannot represent some patterns of conflict at all, and planar drawing places languages on the circle in ways that can suggest spurious relationships between neighbors in the drawing. Use split networks to explore and display conflict, and use generative models or careful linguistic analysis to explain it. 8.6 Explicit models of borrowing Split networks describe conflict; explicit models try to explain it by positing a tree of descent plus lateral events. The approaches below differ in how far they are generative in the sense of Section 8.2. Perfect phylogenetic networks and minimal lateral networks posit explicit contact edges, but choose them by combinatorial or heuristic criteria; the lateral-transfer stochastic Dollo model and the contact-aware models for structural data define a probability for the data, and can therefore estimate borrowing rates, compare hypotheses and be checked against data simulated from the fitted model. 8.6.1 Perfect phylogenetic networks Ringe, Warnow and Taylor approached Indo-European subgrouping through compatibility: a character, such as a shared sound change, a morphological innovation or a cognate class, is compatible with a tree if it can evolve on that tree without homoplasy, that is, with each state forming a connected region. With carefully chosen characters, almost all should be compatible with the true tree (Ringe et al. 2002). The characters that remain incompatible are candidates for borrowing or parallel development. Nakhleh, Ringe, et al. (2005) formalized this idea as a perfect phylogenetic network: a tree plus a small number of contact edges, such that every character is compatible with at least one of the trees displayed by the network. In the Indo-European dataset, a network with only a few contact edges accounted for nearly all characters, and edges involving Germanic were prominent among them. The position of Germanic has long been the most problematic in Indo-European subgrouping. The approach gives explicit, interpretable hypotheses of contact, and because its characters are innovations rather than cognate sets it addresses the question of identifying innovations directly; but it requires characters coded with great care and it does not provide a probability model for weighing alternatives. Warnow et al. (2006) later proposed a stochastic model of language evolution with both homoplasy and borrowing, which could underlie statistical versions of this approach. 8.6.2 Minimal lateral networks Nelson-Sathi et al. (2011) imported a method from the study of prokaryotic genome evolution (Dagan et al. 2008) to detect hidden borrowing in Indo-European. The approach works as follows. Take a reference tree as given. For each cognate set, consider gain-loss scenarios that allow at most one gain, at most two gains, and so on; under a model allowing more gains, patchily distributed cognates are explained by multiple origins rather than by early origin and many losses. Each model implies a distribution of ancestral vocabulary sizes, the number of cognates reconstructed for each ancestral language. The criterion for choosing among models is that ancestral vocabulary sizes should resemble those of the modern languages: a model that allows too few gains produces implausibly large ancestral vocabularies. Under the selected model, cognate sets that require more than one gain are interpreted as candidates for borrowing, and the inferred multiple origins are connected by lateral links, yielding a minimal lateral network. The study argued that a non-trivial amount of borrowing had gone undetected in standard Indo-European data. List, Nelson-Sathi, Martin, et al. (2014) applied the method to Chinese dialect data, and List, Nelson-Sathi, Geisler, et al. (2014) discussed the parallels between lexical borrowing and lateral gene transfer more generally. The main limitations are the dependence on a fixed reference tree, and the fact that the method does not distinguish borrowing from parallel semantic shift or from coding error, all of which create multiple apparent origins. Networks uncover hidden lexical borrowing. Nelson-Sathi et al. (2011) analyzed the Indo-European Swadesh-list data of Dyen and colleagues, using a reference tree of the major subgroups. Their gain-loss analysis found that models allowing only a single origin per cognate set implied ancestral vocabularies far larger than any modern Indo-European language possesses, so that some cognate sets had to have multiple origins. Interpreting these as borrowings, they built a minimal lateral network linking the branches involved and argued that a non-trivial fraction of the basic vocabulary had been affected by borrowing that had not been flagged by the original coders. The study is a good example of how a method from microbial genomics can be transferred to language with minimal modification. It also illustrates the inferential trade-off: the conclusions rest on the vocabulary-size criterion and on the reference tree, and other researchers have questioned whether all inferred multiple origins are really borrowings. 8.6.3 Lateral transfer in the stochastic Dollo model The most complete probabilistic treatment of lexical borrowing so far is the extension of the stochastic Dollo model (Chapter 7) by Kelly and Nicholls (2017), row 7 of Table 7.2. In addition to births at rate \(\lambda\) and deaths at rate \(\mu\), each trait present in a lineage can be copied into other lineages that exist at the same time, at a rate governed by a borrowing parameter \(\beta\). A borrowed trait does not displace anything; it simply becomes present in the recipient, where it can subsequently die. The difficulty is computational. Without borrowing, the fate of a trait in different lineages is independent once they have split, which is what makes the pruning recursion of Chapter 7 possible. With borrowing, the presence of a trait in one lineage affects its chance of appearing in others, so the likelihood requires tracking the joint distribution of each trait across all lineages alive at a given time, and the cost grows quickly with the number of contemporaneous lineages. Kelly and Nicholls (2017) showed how to compute the likelihood exactly, given the tree, for moderate numbers of languages, and implemented the model in TraitLab. This allows the borrowing rate to be estimated jointly with the tree and the dates, and the question of whether ignoring borrowing biases date estimates to be addressed within a single model rather than by simulation. Like any rate parameter, the borrowing rate is identifiable under the model only jointly with the death rate and the tree, and borrowing among close relatives, which barely alters the patterns of presence (Section 8.3), will be hard to estimate in practice. Why borrowing breaks the pruning recursion, and the size of the state space the lateral-transfer likelihood must track, are explained in Section C.2.4. 8.6.4 Contact events on a tree: contacTrees Neureiter et al. (2022) approached the same goal in BEAST 2 with a model they call contacTrees. It infers the phylogenetic tree of a language family together with contact events between its clades, represented as contact edges between lineages that coexist in time, so that the history of an individual cognate class can follow a contact edge instead of the tree. In a simulation study the model recovered the simulated history, including the contact events, and showed that ignoring contact can bias the estimated tree height, rate of change and topology; this is parameter recovery under the model’s own assumptions (Section 6.10). Applied to a subset of well-documented Indo-European languages, it recovered known contact events and identified known loanwords. As with the lateral-transfer Dollo model, borrowing parameters are identifiable only jointly with the tree and the rates, and contact between close relatives will be hard to detect, for the reasons given in Section 8.3. 8.6.5 Contact-aware models for structural data Borrowing affects grammar as well as vocabulary, and several models address structural features. Daumé III (2009) proposed a non-parametric Bayesian model that combines a phylogenetic component with latent geographic “areas” in which features diffuse. Cathcart et al. (2018) modelled the evolution of Indo-European grammatical features with terms representing pressure from geographically neighboring languages. And the sBayes model of Ranacher et al. (2021) identifies contact zones as sets of languages that share features beyond what their family membership and global preferences predict, using a mixture of inheritance, contact and universal components. These are generative models in the sense of Section 8.2, and they move toward the joint modelling of descent and diffusion that the biology of introgression has developed (Section 8.11). Hartmann and Jäger (2024) proposed a related device for trees inferred from lexical data: a distance-based Gaussian process with latent phylogenetic distances that identifies potential contact zones and estimates how strongly geographic proximity affects clade support and pairwise distances. 8.7 Waves, linkages and Historical Glottometry 8.7.1 The wave model The oldest alternative to the family tree is the wave model (Wellentheorie) of Schmidt (1872). Schmidt observed that the Indo-European subgroups share innovations in overlapping patterns: Balto-Slavic shares some features with Indo-Iranian, others with Germanic, and so on, in a way that no single tree can accommodate. He proposed that innovations spread like waves across a dialect continuum, each covering a different, possibly overlapping, area. The wave model was never fully abandoned, and dialectologists have always worked with it, but because it offered no procedure for reconstruction comparable to the tree-based comparative method, it remained largely qualitative. The Oceanic linguist Malcolm Ross gave the wave picture a sharper typology. He distinguished families, which arise when a speech community splits into separate groups that then innovate independently, from linkages, which arise when a dialect network diversifies in place, so that innovations spread across overlapping subsets of dialects (Ross 1988; Ross 1997). In Ross’s terms, a family is innovation-defined, because each of its subgroups is defined by innovations shared by all and only its members, whereas a linkage is innovation-linked, characterized by intersecting innovations. Many Oceanic groups, in Ross’s analysis, are linkages rather than families. The distinction is fundamental for phylogenetics: a tree model is appropriate for families, and for linkages it is not merely approximate but misspecified, because there is no sequence of splits for it to approximate (Section 8.2). 8.7.2 Historical Glottometry François (2015) and Kalyan and François (2018) developed Historical Glottometry, a method that takes the wave model seriously as a quantitative framework. Its input is a set of innovations established by the comparative method, such as sound changes, morphological changes and lexical replacements, each with the set of languages that share it. No tree is assumed. Instead, for every subgroup \(G\) (any set of languages that share at least one innovation), the method computes several quantities. Let \(S_i\) be the set of languages sharing innovation \(i\). Then: the number of exclusively shared innovations is \(\varepsilon_G = |\{i : S_i = G\}|\); innovations support \(G\) if they are shared by all members of \(G\), \(G \subseteq S_i\); innovations conflict with \(G\) if they are shared by some members of \(G\) together with languages outside it, that is, \(S_i \cap G \neq \emptyset\), \(S_i \setminus G \neq \emptyset\) and \(G \setminus S_i \neq \emptyset\); the cohesiveness of \(G\) is the proportion of relevant innovations that support it, \[\begin{equation} \kappa_G = \frac{|\{i : G \subseteq S_i\}|}{|\{i : G \subseteq S_i\}| + |\{i : S_i \text{ conflicts with } G\}|}; \tag{8.4} \end{equation}\] and the subgroup strength is \(\varsigma_G = \varepsilon_G \, \kappa_G\), which weights the number of exclusive innovations by how consistently the group behaves as a unit. Innovations shared by a proper subset of \(G\) and by no outsiders are neither supporting nor conflicting: they are compatible with \(G\) as a subgroup containing smaller subgroups. A tree is the special case in which no innovation ever conflicts with any subgroup, so that every cohesiveness equals one. The results are displayed in a glottometric diagram, a map-like picture in which each subgroup is drawn as an isogloss whose thickness is proportional to its strength. The formulas above follow Kalyan and François (2018) in slightly simplified form, and readers who want to apply the method should consult the original for the treatment of details such as innovations that are uncertain or attested in only part of a subgroup. Glottometry is descriptive in the sense of Section 8.2, but it describes something different from a split network: the distribution of innovations identified by the comparative method, not overall similarity. The code below applies these definitions to a toy chain of seven languages, V1 to V7, in which innovations spread over overlapping stretches of the chain, as in a dialect continuum. innov <- c(rep(list(c("V1", "V2")), 6), rep(list(c("V2", "V3")), 3), rep(list(c("V1", "V2", "V3")), 5), rep(list(c("V3", "V4")), 2), rep(list(c("V4", "V5")), 4), rep(list(c("V4", "V5", "V6")), 3), rep(list(c("V5", "V6")), 2), rep(list(c("V6", "V7")), 5), rep(list(c("V5", "V6", "V7")), 2), rep(list(c("V3", "V4", "V5")), 2), list(c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4")), rep(list(c("V4", "V5", "V6", "V7")), 2)) glottometry <- function(innov) { key <- sapply(innov, function(s) paste(sort(s), collapse = "+")) groups <- unique(innov[!duplicated(key)]) res <- t(sapply(groups, function(G) { eps <- sum(sapply(innov, function(S) setequal(S, G))) sup <- sum(sapply(innov, function(S) all(G %in% S))) con <- sum(sapply(innov, function(S) any(S %in% G) && any(!S %in% G) && any(!G %in% S))) c(exclusive = eps, supporting = sup, conflicting = con, cohesiveness = sup / (sup + con), strength = eps * sup / (sup + con)) })) out <- data.frame(subgroup = sapply(groups, paste, collapse = "+"), res) out[order(-out$strength), ] } gm <- glottometry(innov) knitr::kable(gm, row.names = FALSE, digits = 2, caption = "Historical Glottometry for a toy dialect chain: exclusively shared, supporting and conflicting innovations, cohesiveness and subgroup strength for each subgroup attested by at least one innovation.")
