Groups such as V1+V2+V3 are also strong, despite being crossed by innovations linking V3 to V4. Groups like V3+V4, with few exclusive innovations and much conflicting evidence, are weak. The table and network (Figure 8.5) together describe a structure that a tree would force into an arbitrary hierarchy: a tree must either join V3 with V1 and V2 or with V4, discarding the evidence for the other grouping. Whichever it chose, its internal node would be a summary of the data, not a proto-language. The Torres and Banks languages of Vanuatu. The Torres and Banks Islands of northern Vanuatu are home to seventeen closely related Oceanic languages spoken in a chain of small islands. François (2015) and Kalyan and François (2018) assembled several hundred innovations in phonology, morphology and lexicon from comparative work on these languages, and found that their distributions intersect so extensively that no tree can accommodate more than a fraction of them. Their glottometric analysis showed strong subgroups among geographically adjacent languages and a pattern of overlapping groupings that follows the geography of the islands. They interpreted the result as the signature of a dialect network that diversified in place, with innovations spreading between neighboring communities after the initial settlement: in Ross’s terms, a linkage rather than a family. The case is a reminder that the comparative method itself produces evidence that may not be treelike, and that forcing such evidence into a tree can manufacture subgroups that never existed as speech communities. 8.7.3 Critiques and the place of trees Historical Glottometry has been criticized from the standpoint of tree-based historical linguistics. Jacques and List (2019) argued that many apparent conflicts among innovations can be explained by parallel innovation (especially of common, natural sound changes) or by later diffusion between languages that had already separated, and that distinguishing these possibilities requires more than counting shared innovations. They argued that tree models remain indispensable for reconstruction, and that the choice between tree and wave models should depend on the data rather than on a general preference. Their paper appeared in a special issue of the Journal of Historical Linguistics on alternatives to the tree model (Kalyan et al. 2019), together with a reply by Kalyan and François (2019), and with a study by Verkerk (2019) that took a model-based route: the multiple-topologies method of BayesPhylogenies, which lets different characters follow different trees, found evidence for more than one topology in lexical data from Sinitic, Indo-European and Japonic, but not in Austronesian, and Verkerk discusses dialect-chain break-up, borrowing, incomplete lineage sorting and properties of lexical datasets as possible sources of this reticulation. They also pointed out that glottometry, as formulated, treats all innovations as equally informative and does not model the probability of parallel change, which a probabilistic phylogenetic model does. Defenders of glottometry reply that the method is intended for exactly the situations in which the tree model fails, notably dialect continua that diversified in place, and that it makes explicit what tree diagrams hide. In the terms of Table 8.1, the two sides are partly answering different questions: glottometry describes the distribution of innovations, while tree-based reconstruction asks about the sequence of separations, and the dispute is over which question a particular body of evidence can answer. A synthesis would combine the two: a generative model with both descent and diffusion, in which the relative contributions of each are estimated from the data. The biological models of Section 8.11 show what such models can look like. One step toward such a synthesis within the tree framework is the Dialect Chain Tree of Elgh and Hammarström (2024), an extension of the tree model that represents both tree-like descent and the systematic disintegration of dialect chains, and so formalizes the notion of a linkage in a way that quantitative methods can use. Bayesian case studies point the same way. In the Timor-Alor-Pantar family, Kaiping and Klamer (2022) concluded that dialect-cluster effects played a major role in the formation of the present languages; King et al. (2024) found their Philippine results consistent with a linkage shaped by diffusion after a rapid initial spread; and Auderset et al. (2023) showed that Bayesian methods can suggest new subgroups within the Mixtecan dialect continuum while raising questions about how primary data are gathered and organized. 8.8 Dialect continua and dialectometry Dialect continua are the clearest case in which treelike descent is the wrong model. Neighboring dialects are mutually intelligible, innovations spread across dialect boundaries, and the boundaries themselves are often gradients rather than lines. Dialectology developed its own quantitative tradition, dialectometry, which measures aggregate distances between dialects from large numbers of linguistic features and analyses them with clustering, multidimensional scaling and network methods. Nerbonne (2009) and Wieling and Nerbonne (2015) review the field, including the use of edit-distance measures of pronunciation difference, statistical tests of the relation between linguistic and geographic distance, and the problem of identifying stable dialect groups when different clustering methods disagree (Prokić and Nerbonne 2008). Dialect data can also be analyzed with the categories of historical linguistics rather than with aggregate distances: Babel et al. (2013) studied the dialectology of Western Numic (Uto-Aztecan) and argued that both descent and diffusion shaped its diversification. Phylogenetic network methods entered dialectology through NeighborNet analyses such as those of Chinese dialects (Ben Hamed 2005; List, Nelson-Sathi, Martin, et al. 2014). A recurrent finding is that linguistic distance increases with geographic distance roughly as one would expect from local diffusion, so that a spatially explicit model of diffusion is often a better null model than a tree. The phylogenetic relevance of dialectometry is twofold. First, it shows that the “language” level at which most phylogenetic analyses operate is itself an abstraction over a continuum, and that the choice of which varieties to sample affects the shape of the result (Chapter 15). Second, its methods for relating linguistic to geographic distance, and for detecting where gradients become boundaries, have counterparts in landscape genetics and phylogeography (Chapter 11) that have scarcely been brought together. 8.9 Creoles and mixed languages Creoles and mixed languages strain the tree model in the most extreme way, because they do not have a single parent. Thomason and Kaufman (1988) argued that such languages are “not genetically related” to any of their source languages in the traditional sense, since the comparative method’s assumption of continuous transmission of the whole linguistic system breaks down. Mixed languages make the point vividly. Michif, spoken by Métis communities in Canada and the northern United States, combines French noun phrases with Plains Cree verbs (Bakker 1997); other mixed languages combine the grammar of one language with the lexicon of another in different ways (Matras and Bakker 2003). A tree built from lexical data alone would place Michif with French or with Cree depending on which part of the vocabulary dominated the list, and neither placement would be a meaningful statement about its history. Creoles raise a related but different question: whether they form a typologically distinct class of languages. Bakker et al. (2011) compared creoles and non-creoles on a set of structural features and used NeighborNet to show that creoles cluster together, apart from both their lexifier languages and other languages, which they took as evidence for a distinct creole typological profile. The interpretation has been contested, partly because the result depends on the choice of features and the sampling of comparison languages. The Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures (Michaelis et al. 2013) now provides a much larger standardized dataset for questions of this kind. For phylogenetic purposes, the essential point is that such languages require models with multiple parents, such as hybridization networks or admixture graphs, or should be excluded from tree-based analyses with an explicit justification. 8.10 Contact and typological convergence Contact affects grammar as well as vocabulary, and grammatical convergence among unrelated languages creates linguistic areas (Sprachbünde). The Balkan languages, belonging to several different branches of Indo-European, share features such as a postposed definite article and the loss of the infinitive; the languages of mainland Southeast Asia, from several families, converge on tone, isolating morphology and classifier systems. For phylogenetic inference from structural data, convergence is a confound of the same kind as lexical borrowing. For comparative studies of typology, it is one half of Galton’s problem: languages may share features because they share ancestors or because they are neighbors (Chapter 13). Statistical approaches that separate inheritance from contact in typological data come in several forms. Population-genetic clustering methods such as STRUCTURE have been applied to structural features: Reesink et al. (2009) analyzed the languages of Sahul (New Guinea, Island Melanesia and Australia) and identified components that combine deep inherited signal with areal spread. Dunn et al. (2008) explored the use of structural features to reconstruct deep relationships among Papuan languages of Island Melanesia, where lexical evidence is exhausted, and discussed the danger that contact-induced similarity may mimic deep relationship. The latent-area model of Daumé III (2009), the model of Murawaki and Yamauchi (2018), which estimates for each feature both its vertical stability and its horizontal diffusibility, the areal-pressure model of Cathcart et al. (2018) and the contact-zone mixture model of Ranacher et al. (2021) (Section 8.6) are explicit models for typological data. Chapter 13 discusses spatio-phylogenetic regression models that include both a phylogenetic and a spatial covariance term, which are the most widely used tool for this problem in comparative typology. Genetics now offers an independent proxy for contact. Graff, Blasi, et al. (2025) used genetic admixture between speaker populations, and location in a shared geohistorical area, as proxies for contact, and found that language pairs with such contact share noticeably more linguistic features, with a similar increase across world regions and demographic situations. The effect varied strongly among features and was only partly explained by their learnability or social function, and for some features admixture decreased sharing, which the authors interpret as a possible signal of divergence under contact (schismogenesis). Results of this kind suggest realistic orders of magnitude for borrowing in simulation studies of structural data. 8.11 Phylogenetic networks from biology The most striking contrast between linguistics and biology in this area is the sophistication of the explicit network models that biologists now use routinely. Split networks, which dominate linguistic network analysis, are implicit networks: they display conflict but do not posit reticulation events. Explicit phylogenetic networks are rooted, directed graphs in which some nodes (reticulation nodes) have two parents, each representing a hybridization or introgression event with an estimated time and an estimated proportion of inheritance from each parent (Huson et al. 2010). The implicit/explicit distinction of the network literature is the descriptive/generative distinction of Section 8.2, applied to graphs; explicit networks fitted under a probability model are the generative models that linguistics mostly lacks. Explicit networks under the multispecies network coalescent. In biology, gene trees differ from the species tree for two main reasons: incomplete lineage sorting (ancestral polymorphism sorted differently in different descendant lineages) and hybridization/introgression. The multispecies network coalescent combines both: each locus has its own gene tree, generated by a coalescent process within the branches of a species network that includes reticulation nodes. PhyloNet (Than et al. 2008; Wen et al. 2018) infers such networks by maximum likelihood, maximum pseudo-likelihood or Bayesian MCMC; SNaQ, in the PhyloNetworks package (Solı́s-Lemus and Ané 2016; Solís-Lemus et al. 2017), uses pseudo-likelihood based on quartet concordance factors and scales to large datasets; and SpeciesNetwork (Chi Zhang et al. 2018) performs full Bayesian inference of species networks in BEAST 2. The linguistic analogy is close but not exact (Chapter 16 discusses what an explicit model of lexical transmission would need for it to hold). Each meaning’s history of cognate replacement is like a gene tree, ancestral synonymy (two words for one meaning in a proto-language, sorted differently in its descendants) is like incomplete lineage sorting, and borrowing of a word into a lineage is like introgression of a locus. A language network with a reticulation node of inheritance proportion \(\gamma\) would say that a fraction \(\gamma\) of the basic vocabulary of a lineage comes from one parent and \(1 - \gamma\) from the other, which is exactly the kind of statement linguists make about heavily mixed lexicons. To our knowledge, these methods have rarely if ever been applied to lexical data. Admixture tests and graphs. The D-statistic (ABBA-BABA test) detects introgression from an excess of discordant patterns of one type over the other in a four-taxon comparison (Green et al. 2010; Durand et al. 2011); Patterson et al. (2012) developed a family of related \(f\)-statistics and admixture graphs, and TreeMix (Pickrell and Pritchard 2012) infers population trees with migration edges from allele frequencies. The four-taxon logic transfers directly to cognate data: for languages (((P1, P2), P3), O), an excess of cognates shared by P2 and P3 over those shared by P1 and P3 indicates contact between P2 and P3, and can be tested formally. Ancestral recombination graphs. Within species, the ancestral recombination graph describes how recombination gives different parts of the genome different genealogies (Griffiths and Marjoram 1997), and modern methods such as ARGweaver infer it from genome sequences (Rasmussen et al. 2014). The ARG is the natural model for dialect continua, in which different features have different genealogies, but no such model has, to our knowledge, been developed for linguistic data. Reconciliation. Gene-tree/species-tree reconciliation with duplication, transfer and loss (DTL) models infers transfers by comparing each gene tree with the species tree; Chapter 16 discusses how it could be applied to the histories of individual meanings. The obstacles to applying these methods to language are partly practical and partly conceptual. Practically, multispecies-coalescent methods need many independent loci, each with enough information to estimate a gene tree or at least concordance factors. A single meaning has only a handful of cognate classes and carries very little information about its own tree, so the methods would have to work from site patterns or quartet frequencies pooled across meanings rather than from estimated gene trees. Conceptually, borrowing in language often happens between languages that have been separated for a long time, and continuously, rather than in a few discrete pulses, which strains models built around a small number of reticulation events. And an explicit network still presupposes a mostly genealogical history with occasional merging; for linkages and continua, the ancestral recombination graph or a spatial diffusion model is the better analogy. Neither obstacle seems insurmountable, and the payoff would be large: explicit, testable statements about which languages exchanged how much vocabulary, and when. 8.12 Practical guidance For an analyst working with lexical data from a family in which contact is known or suspected, the following sequence is a reasonable default. State the historical question. Decide whether the goal is to reconstruct divergence, describe similarity, identify innovations or estimate a dominant pattern of transmission (Table 8.1), and say whether the tree is to be read genealogically or as a summary. Flag and examine known loans. Code them so that they do not unite donor and recipient, and record the decision. Analyze the data both with and without problematic items. Describe the conflict. Compute delta scores and Q-residuals for the whole dataset and for each language, and draw a NeighborNet. Look for languages with exceptionally high taxon-specific scores and for strong conflicting splits. Interpret conflict linguistically. Ask whether conflicting splits correspond to known contact situations, dialect continua, coding inconsistencies or simply poorly sampled languages. If the data look like a linkage, reconsider whether a dated tree answers any meaningful question. Assess sensitivity. Rerun the phylogenetic analysis without the most reticulate languages and without the meanings most prone to borrowing (for example, using the Leipzig-Jakarta list), and compare topologies and dates. Remember the invisible kind. Borrowing among close relatives leaves little trace in treelikeness statistics but can compress trees and bias dates. When it is suspected, consider simulation studies tailored to the family, or explicit lateral-transfer models. Use descriptive networks to explore, generative models to explain. Split networks are exploratory displays. Statements about who borrowed from whom, how much and when require generative models or careful comparative analysis. A tree can be read as an approximation to a genealogy or as a statistical summary of variation. Dating, ancestral reconstruction and homeland inference require the genealogical reading; under extensive reticulation there may be no bifurcating history for a tree to approximate. The choice of representation should follow from the historical question: reconstructing divergence, describing similarity, identifying innovations, or estimating a dominant pattern of transmission (Table 8.1). Basic vocabulary is resistant to borrowing but not immune; undetected loans between close relatives are the hardest to find and the hardest for methods to detect. Simulation studies suggest that tree topologies are fairly robust to realistic levels of borrowing superimposed on a tree, while branch lengths and dates are more sensitive; borrowing among close relatives compresses trees without creating much conflict. Delta scores and Q-residuals measure the departure of quartets from the four-point condition, in relative and absolute terms respectively; they measure conflict, not borrowing as such. Split networks (NeighborNet, split decomposition, consensus networks) are descriptive: they display conflicting signal, and their boxes have many possible causes, no direction and no date. Generative models of contact (the lateral-transfer stochastic Dollo model, contact-aware models for structural data, explicit networks) define a probability for the data and can estimate how much borrowing occurred, at the price of new assumptions and weakly identified parameters. Perfect phylogenetic networks and minimal lateral networks posit explicit contact edges without a full probability model. The wave model, Ross’s linkages and Historical Glottometry describe diversification in a dialect network; dialect continua, creoles and mixed languages require models with multiple parents or spatial diffusion. Biology offers explicit network models under the multispecies network coalescent, admixture tests and ancestral recombination graphs, almost none of which have been applied to language. 8.13 Exercises Conceptual Explain the difference between reading a tree as an approximation to a genealogy and reading it as a statistical summary of variation. Chapter 9 Clock Models and Rates of Language Change A phylogeny inferred from cognate data tells us how much change separates languages, not how much time. Turning change into time requires two things: a model of how the rate of change behaves along the branches of the tree, called a clock model, and external information that fixes the scale. This chapter follows the idea from glottochronology, which assumed that every language replaces its basic vocabulary at one universal rate, to the relaxed clocks of modern Bayesian phylogenetics, and then asks what linguistic phylogenetics has learned about the rates themselves. Its central lesson is that lexical data never identify rate and time separately. Every date is a joint product of the data, the clock model, the tree prior and the calibrations, and the first question to ask of any clock model is which of its parameters the data actually inform. Chapter 10 takes up calibration and the dates that have been obtained for particular families. After reading this chapter you should be able to: explain why rate and time are confounded in every substitution model, and state which quantities (branch lengths, relative ages, absolute ages, branch rates) are identifiable under which assumptions; derive the glottochronological formula from its assumptions, and explain which assumptions failed and why rate variation among meanings biases its dates downward; distinguish strict, uncorrelated, autocorrelated, local and random local clocks, and penalized-likelihood rate smoothing, by what each assumes about rate variation among lineages; distinguish rate variation among characters from rate variation among lineages, and interpret a published clock rate in light of how the data were coded; date a simulated phylogram under several rate models with ape::chronos(), and say which of the chapter’s simulations are parameter-recovery checks and which are misspecification experiments; evaluate empirical claims about rates of language change (word frequency, punctuational bursts, grammar versus vocabulary, population size) in terms of their design and main confounds. 9.1 Why time is hard Imagine two languages that have each replaced forty of the meanings on a two-hundred-item basic vocabulary list since they last shared a common ancestor. Did they separate a thousand years ago and change quickly, or three thousand years ago and change slowly? The cognate data alone cannot tell us. Every substitution model introduced in Chapters 5 and 7 depends on time \(t\) and rate \(r\) only through their product. The transition probability matrix for a branch is \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{P}(b) = e^{\mathbf{Q} b}, \qquad b = r \, t, \tag{9.1} \end{equation}\] where \(b\) is the branch length, measured in expected numbers of changes per character. Doubling the rate and halving the time leaves \(b\), and therefore the likelihood, unchanged. Rate and time are said to be confounded, or non-identifiable, from the data alone. This is the central problem of all phylogenetic dating, in biology and linguistics alike. It has two parts. First, we need some external information that fixes the absolute scale of time: a calibration, such as the date at which a daughter language was first written down, or the archaeologically dated settlement of an island. Calibrations are the subject of Chapter 10. Second, we need a model that tells us how rates are allowed to vary from one branch of the tree to another. Without such a model, every branch could have its own rate, and the branch lengths of a tree estimated without a clock (a phylogram) would carry no information at all about the relative ages of its nodes. A clock model is a set of assumptions, ideally probabilistic, about how \(r\) varies across the branches of a tree. The strongest assumption is that \(r\) is the same everywhere. That is the strict clock, and it is where linguistic dating began. A concrete example shows the stakes. Icelandic and Norwegian both descend from the Old West Norse spoken around the time Iceland was settled in the late ninth century CE. Over the following millennium, Norwegian replaced far more of its basic vocabulary than Icelandic did, partly through contact with Danish and Low German. A model that assumed a single rate for both lineages would place their split at different dates depending on which language it treated as typical. English and Frisian, or the Romance languages descended from a well-documented Latin, provide similar cases where the true time depth is known from written history, and where lineages have demonstrably changed at different speeds. Any credible clock model must accommodate such differences, and any credible dating analysis must say how much they matter. 9.1.1 What the data can and cannot identify It helps to be precise about what is identified, and by what. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10: Branch lengths \(b_j = r_j t_j\) are identifiable under the model from the characters alone, and with a few hundred cognate sets they are practically estimable, up to the limits set by saturation on long branches (Section 7.3.1). Relative node ages are identifiable only under a clock model that ties the rates of different branches together. Under a strict clock, ratios of node ages are identified by the data. Under a relaxed clock, they are identified only in part: how each branch length is divided into rate and time depends on the prior on rates, so relative ages are informed jointly by the data and by that prior. Absolute ages and the absolute rate are not identifiable from the characters at all. Only calibrations identify them, and their precision has a floor, set by the uncertainty of the calibrations, that no amount of additional lexical data can lower (the infinite-sites argument of Section 10.1). Branch-specific rates in a relaxed clock are identifiable as a population, through the variance of the rate distribution, but individual rates are practically estimable only for branches that carry many changes or lie close to a calibration. The rates of single terminal branches are among the most poorly estimated quantities in any dated tree. Identifiability is not the same as historical interpretability. A clock rate in a binary cognate analysis can be estimated precisely and still not correspond to any historically observable event, because it counts gains and losses of cognate classes rather than replacements of words (Section 9.6). A large coefficient of variation among branch rates is estimable, but whether it measures genuine differences in the tempo of change, or unmodelled borrowing, coding inconsistency and missing data, all of which also alter branch lengths, is a question of historical interpretation that the clock model cannot answer by itself. Nor is a parameter that is identifiable under the model necessarily robust to misspecification: the simulations in this chapter show how strongly dates depend on the match between the assumed and the real pattern of rate variation. 9.2 Glottochronology: the first strict clock 9.2.1 The model In the early 1950s Morris Swadesh proposed that a small core of basic vocabulary, the meanings that every human language has a word for and that are rarely borrowed, is replaced at a roughly constant rate in all languages (Swadesh 1952, 1955). If that were true, the proportion of shared cognates between two related languages would be a clock. Robert Lees made the proposal quantitative (Lees 1953). He compiled thirteen pairs of language stages separated by known spans of time, for example Old English and Modern English, or Latin and its Romance descendants, and measured how much of a 200-item test list each had retained. He found that, on average, a language retains about 81 percent of its basic vocabulary per thousand years. Swadesh later shortened the list to 100 items, which he argued were more stable, with a retention rate of about 86 percent per millennium (Swadesh 1955). The enterprise of dating language splits in this way became known as glottochronology. The broader activity of classifying languages by shared-cognate percentages is lexicostatistics. Chapter 1 tells the history; here we take the model apart. The model makes three assumptions. First, each meaning on the list is replaced independently of all others. Second, replacement is a memoryless process: in any short interval \(dt\), the word currently expressing a meaning is replaced with probability \(k\,dt\), where the replacement rate \(k\) is the same for every meaning, every language and every period. Third, the two daughter lineages descending from a common ancestor change independently, and a meaning that has been replaced in either lineage no longer yields a shared cognate. The first two assumptions describe a Poisson process. The probability that the original word for a meaning survives for \(t\) millennia is \(e^{-kt}\). Writing \(\rho = e^{-k}\) for the retention rate per millennium (Lees’ 0.805, or Swadesh’s 0.86), the expected proportion of the list retained in one lineage after \(t\) millennia is \[\begin{equation} R(t) = e^{-k t} = \rho^{t}. \tag{9.2} \end{equation}\] Two sister languages share a cognate for a meaning only if both have retained the ancestral word. By the independence assumption, the expected proportion of shared cognates after a split \(t\) millennia ago is \[\begin{equation} C(t) = R(t)^2 = \rho^{2t}. \tag{9.3} \end{equation}\] Solving for \(t\) gives the glottochronological formula: \[\begin{equation} t = \frac{\ln C}{2 \ln \rho}. \tag{9.4} \end{equation}\] This is the formula that appeared in introductory textbooks for half a century. If two languages share 50 percent cognates on the 200-item list, then \(t = \ln 0.5 / (2 \ln 0.805) \approx 1.6\) millennia. On the 100-item list with \(\rho = 0.86\), the same 50 percent would imply about 2.3 millennia. In the language of Chapter 5, glottochronology is a strict molecular clock combined with a very simple substitution model. Each meaning is a character, a split resets nothing, every branch has the same rate \(k\), and distances between languages are converted to time by a fixed transformation. The formula is the linguistic counterpart of using a known substitution rate to convert a corrected genetic distance into a divergence time. Glottochronology also used a distance-based route from data to tree, in the spirit of Chapter 4, rather than a model of the whole tree at once. In the terms of Section 9.1.1, it made absolute time identifiable by fiat: the universal retention rate served as a calibration imported from other languages. 9.2.2 The retention curve in R The following code draws the retention curves implied by Equations (9.2) and (9.3), and tabulates the dates that Equation (9.4) assigns to a range of shared-cognate percentages. glotto_C <- function(t, rho) rho^(2 * t) # shared cognates glotto_t <- function(C, rho) log(C) / (2 * log(rho)) # Equation (glotto) t_grid <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.05) # millennia plot(t_grid, 0.805^t_grid, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Time since split (millennia)", ylab = "Proportion", las = 1) lines(t_grid, glotto_C(t_grid, 0.805), lwd = 2, lty = 2) lines(t_grid, 0.86^t_grid, lwd = 2, col = "grey55") lines(t_grid, glotto_C(t_grid, 0.86), lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "grey55") abline(h = 0.5, col = "grey85") legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2, 1, 2), col = c("black", "black", "grey55", "grey55"), legend = c("Retained, 200-list", "Shared, 200-list", "Retained, 100-list", "Shared, 100-list")) Figure 9.1: Glottochronological retention curves. Solid lines: expected proportion of the list retained by a single language; dashed lines: expected proportion of cognates shared by two sister languages. Black: Lees’ 200-item list with a retention rate of 0.805 per millennium; grey: Swadesh’s 100-item list with 0.86. C_vals <- c(0.90, 0.75, 0.60, 0.50, 0.40, 0.25, 0.10, 0.05) glotto_tab <- data.frame( shared = paste0(100 * C_vals, "%"), t200 = round(1000 * glotto_t(C_vals, 0.805)), t100 = round(1000 * glotto_t(C_vals, 0.86)) ) knitr::kable(glotto_tab, col.names = c("Shared cognates", "Years (200-list, 0.805)", "Years (100-list, 0.86)"), caption = "Glottochronological dates implied by different proportions of shared cognates.") Table 9.1: Glottochronological dates implied by different proportions of shared cognates. Shared cognates Years (200-list, 0.805) Years (100-list, 0.86) 90% 243 349 75% 663 954 60% 1177 1693 50% 1598 2298 40% 2112 3038 25% 3196 4596 10% 5308 7633 5% 6905 9931 Table 9.1 makes one of glottochronology’s weaknesses immediately visible. The curve flattens as time increases, so at great time depths a small difference in the percentage of shared cognates translates into a very large difference in date. Going from 10 to 5 percent shared cognates adds well over a millennium on either list. Yet at those depths, a handful of chance resemblances or misjudged cognates can easily make up five percent of a 100-item list. 9.2.3 Sampling error Even if every assumption of the model held, a 100- or 200-item list is a small sample. If each meaning is retained with probability \(C(t)\) independently, the number of shared cognates on a list of \(N\) items is binomially distributed with mean \(N C(t)\) and variance \(N C(t)(1 - C(t))\). The resulting uncertainty in the date can be large. The next chunk computes exact binomial confidence intervals for the shared proportion and transforms them into intervals on the date, for a range of observed counts on the 100-item list. N <- 100 obs <- c(80, 60, 40, 20, 10) ci <- t(sapply(obs, function(x) binom.test(x, N)$conf.int)) ci_tab <- data.frame( shared = obs, date = round(1000 * glotto_t(obs / N, 0.86)), lower = round(1000 * glotto_t(ci[, 2], 0.86)), upper = round(1000 * glotto_t(ci[, 1], 0.86)) ) knitr::kable(ci_tab, col.names = c("Shared (of 100)", "Point date (years)", "Lower 95% (years)", "Upper 95% (years)"), caption = "Binomial sampling uncertainty alone in glottochronological dates on a 100-item list, assuming the retention rate is known exactly.") Table 9.2: Binomial sampling uncertainty alone in glottochronological dates on a 100-item list, assuming the retention rate is known exactly. Shared (of 100) Point date (years) Lower 95% (years) Upper 95% (years) 80 740 449 1144 60 1693 1198 2316 40 3038 2279 3955 20 5336 4083 6850 10 7633 5755 9998 The intervals in Table 9.2 widen dramatically with time depth, and they ignore every other source of error: uncertainty in \(\rho\) itself, variation of \(\rho\) across lineages, borrowing, and coding mistakes. Even in the earliest discussions of the method, its proponents knew that individual dates carried uncertainties of several centuries. What they did not anticipate was how badly the core assumption of a universal constant rate would fare. 9.2.4 What went wrong The critique of glottochronology came quickly and from several directions. Here we organize it by the assumption under attack. Excellent longer treatments are Embleton (1986) and McMahon and McMahon (2005). Rates differ between languages. The most damaging empirical test was by Bergsland and Vogt (1962), who measured retention in cases where the time depth is independently known. Their most famous example was Icelandic. Compared with the Old Norse of its medieval texts, Icelandic had retained far more of the test list than the model predicted, so the formula would have placed the separation of Icelandic from its own ancestor at a small fraction of the documented time depth. They also examined other languages with long written records, including Georgian and Armenian, and found that the amount of retention over comparable spans differed from case to case. Other test cases in the literature showed the opposite problem, languages that had replaced their vocabulary faster than expected. Blust (2000) later made the same point at the scale of a whole family. Across Austronesian, languages separated by similar time depths, as judged from subgrouping and archaeology, vary enormously in how much basic vocabulary they share, and some lineages are dramatically more conservative than others. Blust concluded that the “universal constant” assumption is simply false for Austronesian. Rates differ between meanings. Words for some meanings, such as low numerals, pronouns and certain body parts, are replaced far more slowly than words for others, such as ‘dirty’, ‘to throw’ or ‘to play’. This was clear to Swadesh himself and was one motivation for his shortened list. As we show in Section 9.2.5, rate variation among meanings does not merely add noise. It biases glottochronological dates downward, more and more severely as time depth increases. The mathematics was shaky. Chrétien (1962) argued that the mathematical models presented in support of glottochronology contained serious errors and that the claimed constancy had not been established. Later work proposed corrected formulations, including models with meaning-specific rates (see the review in Embleton 1986). Some Russian scholars, notably Sergei Starostin, developed a revised glottochronology that excluded loanwords and modified the decay function. These revisions improved some results but did not resolve the deeper problem of variable rates across lineages. Borrowing and chance inflate shared percentages. If one language borrows a basic word from its sister, or if both borrow from the same source, the pair will appear to share a cognate that they did not inherit. Chance resemblances, which become proportionally more important as genuine cognates decay, have the same effect. Both biases make languages look closer than they are and dates younger; Section 8.3 quantifies the effect of borrowing by simulation. The list and its coding matter. Different scholars coded the same languages differently, chose different words when a language has several synonyms for a meaning, and used different versions of the list. Because the formula is very sensitive to the shared percentage at great depths, small coding differences translated into large date differences. Distances are not trees. Glottochronology computed a date for each pair of languages independently. Dates for different pairs need not be mutually consistent, and nothing in the method ensured that the dated pairs fitted together into a single tree. The information in other languages about the history of a pair was ignored. Bergsland and Vogt (1962) tested glottochronology on cases where the answer was known. They compared modern languages with their own documented ancestors, so that the time depth was given by the written record. Icelandic, compared with Old Norse, had retained so much of the basic vocabulary list that the formula implied a time depth far shorter than the one documented in writing. Other cases deviated by different amounts, so no single constant could fit them all. Because the test cases were the very kind of data on which the retention constant had been calibrated, the results showed that the constant was not constant. The paper, published with a range of commentaries in Current Anthropology, is often cited as the moment glottochronology lost its credibility among historical linguists. It is worth reading with a modern eye: what Bergsland and Vogt documented is exactly the among-lineage rate variation that relaxed clocks were designed to model. It is also an early example of what Section 10.8 calls independent validation: dates checked against historical evidence that played no part in estimating them. 9.2.5 Rate variation among meanings biases dates Of all these problems, rate heterogeneity among meanings has the most instructive consequences, because it produces a systematic bias rather than random error. Suppose each meaning has its own replacement rate, drawn independently from a gamma distribution with mean \(\bar{k}\) and shape parameter \(\alpha\), the model of among-character rate variation introduced in Section 7.5. Fast meanings are lost early, so what remains shared at great depths is dominated by the stable meanings, and shared cognates decay more slowly than the exponential curve of Equation (9.3). A glottochronologist who knows the mean rate \(\bar k\) exactly and applies Equation (9.4) therefore underestimates every date. The expected estimate is approximately \[\hat{t} \approx \frac{\alpha}{2 \bar{k}} \ln\left(1 + \frac{2 \bar{k} t}{\alpha}\right),\] which is always less than the true time \(t\) and grows only logarithmically with it: the deeper the split, the worse the underestimate. The derivation of the gamma-averaged shared-cognate curve (Equation (C.7)) and of the bias of the glottochronological estimate (Equation (C.8)), a numerical check of both, and the code for Figure 9.2 are in Section C.3.1. Figure 9.2 makes the point concrete. We take a 200-meaning list with mean retention 0.86 per millennium, draw meaning-specific rates from a gamma distribution with shape \(\alpha = 1\), simulate the independent survival of each word along two lineages, and apply the classical formula to the resulting shared percentages. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, this is a test of robustness under misspecification: the data are generated with rate variation among meanings that the glottochronological formula ignores. Figure 9.2: Rate heterogeneity among meanings biases glottochronological dates. Each point is one simulated pair of languages (200 meanings, gamma-distributed replacement rates with shape 1, mean retention 0.86 per millennium), dated with the classical formula. Curves show the expected estimate implied by the gamma model for several values of the gamma shape parameter; the diagonal is the true time. With \(\alpha = 1\), a moderate level of heterogeneity, a true split of ten millennia is estimated at well under half that. Studies of Indo-European and Austronesian vocabulary suggest that rate variation across meanings is at least this strong (Sections 7.5 and 9.7). This single effect is enough to explain why glottochronology systematically produced shallow dates for old families. It also explains why the remedy is not to abandon dating. Modern phylogenetic models of lexical change include among-character rate variation, typically with the same gamma distribution, and estimate \(\alpha\) from the data (Pagel 2000; Gray and Atkinson 2003). The bias in Figure 9.2 is then removed in expectation, provided that the gamma model describes the real rate variation adequately; Section 7.10 shows how to check whether it does. It is common to read that phylogenetic dating “is just glottochronology with more computing power.” The criticism has a grain of truth: both convert amounts of lexical change into time and both depend on calibration. But the differences are substantive. Modern methods (i) model rate variation across meanings explicitly rather than assuming a single constant; (ii) allow rates to vary across lineages through relaxed clock models; (iii) estimate rates from multiple internal calibrations within the family under study rather than importing a universal constant; (iv) infer a single tree for all languages jointly, using all the data at once; and (v) report uncertainty that integrates over topology, branch lengths, rates and calibrations. Atkinson et al. (2005) and Gray et al. (2011) set out this case in detail. Whether these improvements are enough is an empirical question, and Chapter 10 and Chapter 15 discuss the evidence on both sides. 9.2.6 Lexicostatistical dating after glottochronology Distance-based dating did not disappear. The Automated Similarity Judgment Program (ASJP), which compares phonetically transcribed 40-item word lists for thousands of languages, developed an automated dating method calibrated on dozens of historically or archaeologically dated splits (Holman et al. 2011). Instead of cognate percentages, it uses a normalized Levenshtein distance between word forms (Chapter 4), which is converted to a date through an empirically fitted relationship. ASJP chronology makes no claim that the rate is universal for any single pair. It treats the calibration relationship as a statistical average with substantial scatter, and reports correspondingly wide intervals. The method is valuable for a first approximation of time depths across the world’s families, many of which have never been dated phylogenetically. But it inherits several of glottochronology’s problems: a pairwise rather than tree-based treatment, and no explicit model of lineage-specific rates. The 40-item ASJP list was itself chosen by ranking meanings according to their stability across language families (Holman et al. 2008), an empirical counterpart of Swadesh’s intuition that some meanings change more slowly than others. The generalized Bayesian dating of Rama and Wichmann (2020), discussed in Section 10.9.16, replaces family-specific calibrations by a single regression of known time depths on tree lengths. In the same comparison, an automated version of glottochronology performed worse than both it and ASJP chronology. A generalized calibration of this kind reintroduces, at the level of whole trees, the assumption of a common rate that the relaxed clocks below were designed to avoid, which is why its dates, like those of ASJP, are best read as first approximations. A cautionary contemporary of the first Bayesian datings is Forster and Toth (2003), who adapted the network methods and dating approach of genetics to a small, hand-coded set of Celtic and Indo-European word forms, including Gaulish inscriptions, and obtained a tentative date of 8100 BCE (\(\pm\) 1,900 years) for Proto-Indo-European. McMahon and McMahon (2005) criticized the very small dataset, the unexplained assignment of words to character states and the neglect of borrowing within Celtic, contrasted it with the expert cognate data and broad sampling of Gray and Atkinson (2003), and still declined, in 2005, to recommend any linguistic dating method, arguing that where contact dominates there may be no branching points left to date. 9.3 From glottochronology to molecular clocks At almost the same time that glottochronology was being discredited in linguistics, biologists proposed the molecular clock. Zuckerkandl and Pauling (1965) observed that the number of amino-acid differences between the hemoglobins or cytochromes c of different species increased roughly linearly with the time since the species diverged, as estimated from fossils. The neutral theory of molecular evolution then offered an explanation (Kimura 1968). If most substitutions are selectively neutral, the rate at which they become fixed in a population equals the mutation rate. Kimura’s argument is short and worth knowing, because it has a linguistic analog that we revisit in Section 9.10. In a diploid population of \(N\) individuals, \(2N\mu\) new neutral mutations arise per generation, and each has a probability \(1/(2N)\) of eventually becoming fixed. The substitution rate is the product, \(2N\mu \times 1/(2N) = \mu\), independent of population size. The molecular clock was never exact. Rates differ between genes, between sites within genes, and between lineages. Rodents, with short generation times, accumulate substitutions faster than primates in many genes. The nearly neutral theory (Ohta 1973) showed that if many mutations are slightly deleterious, they behave as neutral in small populations but are purged by selection in large ones, which makes the rate depend on population size after all. Over the following decades the “clock” became a family of statistical models in which the rate is a quantity to be modeled and estimated, rather than a constant to be assumed. Bromham and Penny (2003) and Kumar (2005) review this history. Ho and Duchêne (2014) and Bromham, Duchêne, et al. (2018) review modern methods, and the textbooks by Felsenstein (2004) and Yang (2014) give the mathematics. The parallel with linguistics is close but imperfect. Swadesh’s constant rate of vocabulary retention resembles the original molecular clock. The linguistic data that undermined glottochronology resemble the data showing rate variation among genes and lineages. And the response in both fields was, eventually, the same: to stop treating the rate as a known universal constant and to model its variation statistically, estimating it from calibrations internal to the group under study. Linguistics made the transition about four decades later than biology, through the work of Gray and Atkinson (2003) and others, by borrowing the biological methods wholesale (Atkinson and Gray 2005). 9.4 The strict clock Under a strict clock, every branch of the tree has the same rate \(r\). The tree is ultrametric: all tips that are sampled at the same time are equidistant from the root (Chapter 2). Branch lengths in time units, \(t_j\) for branch \(j\), are determined by the ages of the nodes at either end. The branch lengths in expected changes per character are \(b_j = r\,t_j\). Rather than \(2n - 3\) free branch lengths for an unrooted tree of \(n\) languages, a strict-clock tree has \(n - 1\) node ages and one rate. Fixing one age by calibration, or setting \(r = 1\) to obtain relative ages, leaves \(n - 2\) free parameters to estimate in addition to the rate. Even a strict clock does not tick like a metronome. Under the CTMC, changes arrive after random waiting times, so two sister lineages evolving at exactly the same rate will usually accumulate different numbers of changes; the strict clock is a statement about expected amounts of change, and a test of it must ask whether the differences between lineages exceed this stochastic scatter. The strict clock can be tested with a likelihood ratio test (Chapter 5). Fit the tree with and without the clock constraint. Twice the difference in maximized log-likelihood is approximately \(\chi^2\)-distributed with \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom, the difference in the number of free branch-length parameters (Felsenstein 2004). With linguistic data the test almost always rejects the strict clock for families of any size, which is unsurprising given the evidence in Section 9.2.4. A simpler diagnostic is the regression of root-to-tip distance on sampling time, discussed in Section 10.5.2. For contemporaneous tips, the coefficient of variation of root-to-tip distances in a rooted phylogram is a rough index of departure from clocklike behavior. A strict clock nonetheless has its uses. It is the most parsimonious model and has the fewest parameters, so it can be preferable when data are few and the family is shallow. It is also a sensible null model for Bayesian model comparison by marginal likelihoods (Chapter 6). Its single rate still needs a prior, and when not even the order of magnitude of the rate is known a prior that is uniform on the logarithm of the rate (a log-uniform prior, as in the RevBayes scripts of Appendix H) spreads the prior mass evenly over orders of magnitude instead of piling it onto the largest values allowed, as a uniform prior on the rate itself would. Several linguistic studies have compared strict and relaxed clocks with Bayes factors, and the relaxed clock is usually, though not always, preferred. 9.5 Relaxed clocks A relaxed clock allows each branch \(j\) to have its own rate \(r_j\). Because the rates are not identifiable from the data branch by branch (Equation (9.1)), they must be tied together by a model. In a Bayesian analysis, the model is a prior distribution on the branch rates. That prior encodes an assumption about how rates vary, and the posterior combines it with calibrations and the tree prior to apportion each branch length \(b_j\) between rate and time. Two broad families of models exist. In uncorrelated models, rates on different branches are drawn independently. In autocorrelated models, rates evolve along the tree, so that closely related lineages tend to have similar rates. Table 9.3 summarizes the models discussed in this section. The penalized-likelihood objective function (Equation (C.11)) and the cross-validation of its smoothing parameter are in Section C.3.4. 9.5.1 Uncorrelated relaxed clocks The uncorrelated relaxed clocks of Drummond et al. (2006) are the default in BEAST and its descendants, and they are the most widely used clock models in linguistic phylogenetics. In the uncorrelated lognormal (UCLN) model, the rate of each branch is the mean clock rate \(\bar r\) multiplied by an independent random factor drawn from a lognormal distribution with mean one. The standard deviation \(\sigma\) of the logarithm of these factors measures how “relaxed” the clock is. A more interpretable quantity is the coefficient of variation of the branch rates, \(\sqrt{e^{\sigma^2} - 1}\), which is close to \(\sigma\) when \(\sigma\) is small. Values near zero indicate a nearly strict clock. Values around 0.3 to 0.5 are common in molecular data sets, and values above 1 indicate extreme rate heterogeneity. In the uncorrelated exponential (UCED) model, rates are drawn from an exponential distribution with mean \(\bar{r}\), which implies a coefficient of variation fixed at one. Because the exponential has its mode at zero, the UCED model gives many branches very low rates. It is less often appropriate than the UCLN but is a useful alternative in model comparison. In practice, BEAST originally implemented these models by discretizing the rate distribution into as many equiprobable categories as there are branches and assigning each branch to a category. Later implementations sample continuous rates or rate quantiles. A summary statistic routinely reported is the covariance of rates between parent and child branches. If its posterior distribution spans zero, there is little evidence for autocorrelation, which supports the choice of an uncorrelated model. The uncorrelated models are attractive because they make weak assumptions and are computationally convenient. They have a less attractive property. Because a rate is drawn independently for every branch, a long terminal branch can be explained either by a long time or by a high rate on that one branch. The model has no way to borrow strength from neighboring branches. Rates and times on terminal branches are therefore identifiable under the model only through the prior, which makes them poorly estimable in practice, and the posterior can be strongly influenced by calibrations and the tree prior. This matters for ancient languages used as dated tips (Section 10.5): an ancient language on a long terminal branch tells the model little about the rate if that branch is free to have its own rate. 9.5.2 Autocorrelated relaxed clocks The intuition behind autocorrelated clocks is that the rate of evolution depends on heritable properties of lineages. For organisms, these are traits such as generation time, metabolic rate or population size. For languages, they might be the size and social structure of the speech community, literacy, or the intensity of contact. Such properties change gradually, so a daughter lineage should have a rate similar to its parent’s. Thorne et al. (1998) proposed a model of this kind, and Kishino et al. (2001) refined it into the most widely used form, the geometric Brownian motion model, in which the logarithm of the rate performs a Brownian motion along the tree with variance \(\nu\) per unit time. Rates are similar on short branches and can drift far apart on long ones. The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process, a mean-reverting alternative, has also been used. Lepage et al. (2007) compared a range of autocorrelated and uncorrelated models on molecular data and found that autocorrelated models were often preferred by Bayes factors, a finding that remains debated. To our knowledge, autocorrelated clocks have rarely been compared with uncorrelated ones on linguistic data, though they are available in RevBayes, MCMCTree and PhyloBayes. The drift variance \(\nu\) is a good example of a parameter that is identifiable in principle but hard to estimate in practice: it is informed only by the pattern of branch lengths across many branches, and with a few dozen languages its posterior usually remains close to its prior. 9.5.3 Local clocks and random local clocks Some rate variation is better described as a few discrete shifts than as continuous scatter. A local clock model allows different, internally constant rates in specified parts of the tree (Yoder and Yang 2000). One might give the Polynesian clade within Austronesian its own rate, for example, to test whether rates changed when speakers settled the remote Pacific. Local clocks require the shifts to be specified in advance. The random local clock (RLC) of Drummond and Suchard (2010) removes this requirement. Each branch has an indicator for whether the rate changes at its start, a rate multiplier applies to that branch and its descendants until the next change, and the number of changes is given a prior (for example, a Poisson distribution with a small mean). MCMC then averages over the number and placement of rate shifts. When the posterior favors zero shifts, the RLC reduces to a strict clock. When it favors many, it approaches an uncorrelated relaxed clock. The compound Poisson process of Huelsenbeck et al. (2000) is a related idea in which rate changes occur as random events along branches. Random local clocks are well suited to a linguistic question discussed below: whether particular lineages, such as those that underwent rapid geographic expansion or intense contact, show discrete rate shifts. 9.5.4 The optimized relaxed clock The uncorrelated relaxed clock is notoriously slow to mix in MCMC. Branch rates and node ages are strongly correlated in the posterior, because changing a node age while keeping its branch lengths fixed requires compensating changes in the rates of all adjacent branches; this posterior correlation is the computational face of the rate-time confounding of Section 9.1. Douglas et al. (2021) introduced the optimized relaxed clock (ORC) package for BEAST 2. It combines several improvements: a parameterization of branch rates by real values rather than by discrete categories, proposals that change node ages and rates jointly so as to keep the genetic distances approximately constant, and adaptive weighting of operators. The model is still the uncorrelated lognormal clock. What changes is how efficiently MCMC explores it, which in practice determines whether an analysis of hundreds of languages converges at all (Chapter 6). Recent linguistic analyses in BEAST 2 increasingly use the ORC. 9.5.5 Penalized likelihood and rate smoothing Before Bayesian relaxed clocks were widely available, the main tools for dating trees with variable rates were semi-parametric. Sanderson (1997) proposed nonparametric rate smoothing (NPRS), which chooses node ages that minimize the squared differences between the rates of adjacent branches. Sanderson (2002) then proposed penalized likelihood (PL), which balances the fit of a set of node ages and branch rates to the branch lengths of an estimated phylogram against a penalty on differences between the rates of adjacent branches. A smoothing parameter \(\lambda\) sets the balance. With \(\lambda\) very large, the rates are forced to be equal and the method approaches a strict clock. With \(\lambda\) near zero, the rates are free and the ages are poorly determined. Sanderson proposed choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation: drop each terminal branch in turn, predict its length from the rest of the tree, and choose the \(\lambda\) that minimizes prediction error. Gray and Atkinson’s influential dating of Indo-European (Gray and Atkinson 2003) used penalized likelihood, applied to a sample of trees from a Bayesian posterior distribution, with fourteen historically known calibrations. PL remains useful for quick analyses and for very large trees where full Bayesian dating is impractical. In R, the function chronos() in ape implements a penalized-likelihood framework with several rate models (Paradis 2013). Its "correlated" model penalizes differences between the rates of adjacent branches. Its "relaxed" model penalizes departures of the rate distribution from a gamma distribution, without regard to which branches are adjacent. Its "discrete" model assigns branches to a small number of rate categories, and its "clock" model forces a single rate. Paradis also proposed an information criterion, \(\Phi\)IC, for comparing these models. Penalized likelihood gives point estimates; uncertainty must be obtained by repeating the analysis over a sample of trees, as Gray and Atkinson did, and that captures topological and branch-length uncertainty but not calibration uncertainty. 9.5.6 Simulating and estimating clocks in R To see how the clock models behave, we simulate a time tree, impose three different patterns of rate variation on it, convert the result into a phylogram with stochastic numbers of lexical changes on each branch, and then try to recover the node ages with chronos(). We imagine a family of sixteen languages whose root is 6,000 years old, and a dataset in which about 80 lexical changes (cognate gains and losses across the whole list) are expected per millennium per lineage at the mean rate. The three scenarios are a strict clock, an uncorrelated lognormal clock with \(\sigma = 0.6\), and an autocorrelated clock with drift variance \(\nu = 0.15\) per millennium. The simulation code (time tree, branch rates under the three clock models and Poisson numbers of changes) is listed in Section C.3.3. The coefficients of variation of the simulated branch rates are 0, 0.65 and 0.4 for the strict, uncorrelated and autocorrelated scenarios. (A constant of 0.5 is added to each branch’s count simply to avoid zero-length branches, which chronos() cannot handle.) Figure 9.3 shows the true time tree and the three phylograms. Under the strict clock the phylogram is nearly ultrametric, apart from Poisson noise. Under the uncorrelated clock, individual branches are stretched or shrunk at random. Under the autocorrelated clock, whole clades are stretched or shrunk together, which makes rate variation easier to mistake for differences in time. When the data really are clocklike, the strict clock model recovers the node ages almost perfectly. When rates vary, every model makes errors of several hundred years even though the root age is known exactly, because rate and time on internal branches can trade off. In this small example, the correlated-rates model, whose penalty is designed for autocorrelated rates, does no better than the strict clock model even when the rates really are autocorrelated: with sixteen languages and a single calibration, the extra flexibility buys little, and the discrete-rates model can do noticeably worse. And the gamma-penalized "relaxed" model of chronos(), which does not tie the rates of adjacent branches together, is poorly constrained by a single calibration and can perform badly.
