The qualitative message is robust: estimated dates are only as good as the match between the clock model and the real pattern of rate variation, and calibrations do much of the work. 9.5.7 Choosing and checking a clock model Clock models can be compared like any other part of a phylogenetic model. In Bayesian analyses, the standard approach is to estimate marginal likelihoods by path sampling, stepping-stone sampling or nested sampling and compute Bayes factors (Chapter 6). Bayes factors rank models relative to one another; they do not show that the preferred model is adequate. Two other tools from biology deserve wider use in linguistics. Clock partitioning asks whether different subsets of the data share a pattern of rate variation across lineages. ClockstaR (Duchêne et al. 2014) addresses this by comparing branch-length patterns across data partitions and clustering partitions with similar patterns; linguists might ask whether, for example, verbs and nouns, or vocabulary and grammar, share a clock. Clock model adequacy asks not which model is best but whether the chosen model could plausibly have generated the data. D. A. Duchêne et al. (2015) proposed a posterior predictive approach: simulate data sets from the posterior, re-estimate branch lengths, and compare them with branch lengths estimated from the observed data. To our knowledge, neither approach has yet been applied to linguistic data, although both could be run with standard software on existing cognate data sets. Because rate and time are confounded, a clock model that fits the branch lengths well can still date the tree badly if the calibrations are wrong, and a poorly fitting clock can be partly rescued by good calibrations. Clock adequacy is therefore necessary but not sufficient for trustworthy dates. Section 10.8 discusses how dates can be validated against evidence that played no part in estimating them. Molecular rates often appear to depend on the timescale over which they are measured. Ho et al. (2005) showed that rates estimated from pedigrees or recently diverged populations are often considerably faster than rates estimated from deep calibrations, because many recent changes are transient polymorphisms or slightly deleterious variants that will be lost before they become fixed. Rates estimated over short spans therefore overestimate long-term rates, and applying them to deep divergences can produce dates that are too young. Language change plausibly has the same structure. Many lexical innovations, slang terms and semantic shifts are visible in a short time window but never become established across the speech community. Rates estimated from very recent historical splits, such as those between colonial and metropolitan varieties, might not transfer to splits several millennia old. Linguistic phylogenetics has paid little attention to the timescale dependence of rates. Two approaches from biology could address it directly: fitting explicit models in which the rate declines with the age of the calibration, and comparing rates estimated from calibrations of different ages in the same family. Both are feasible for well-calibrated families such as Indo-European and Austronesian. 9.6 Clock models in linguistic practice Most dated language phylogenies published since 2009 were estimated in BEAST or BEAST 2 (Bouckaert et al. 2019), often with model specifications generated by BEASTling (Maurits et al. 2017), or in MrBayes, RevBayes or TraitLab. The typical analysis combines a binary or multistate model of cognate evolution (Chapter 7), gamma-distributed rate variation among cognate sets or meanings, a relaxed clock (most often the uncorrelated lognormal), a birth-death or Yule tree prior, and a set of calibrations. Four aspects of the clock component deserve comment. First, the clock rate in a cognate analysis has a particular meaning. In a binary analysis, each character is a cognate set and the rate is the expected number of gains and losses per cognate set per unit of time. Because most cognate sets are present in only a few languages, this rate is not directly comparable with a rate of lexical replacement per meaning. Rates per meaning can be derived from multistate models, in which each character is a meaning and its states are cognate classes, or by summing over the cognate sets belonging to a meaning (Section 7.8). When reading a published rate, it is always worth checking which unit it refers to. A binary clock rate is estimable but only indirectly interpretable as a historical quantity. Second, the separation between rate variation across characters and rate variation across lineages is essential. Gamma rate heterogeneity (Sections 7.5 and 9.2.5) lets some cognate sets or meanings change faster than others at all times and in all lineages. A relaxed clock lets some lineages change faster than others across all characters. Neither substitutes for the other. A model with both makes the assumption that the two kinds of variation combine multiplicatively, so that a fast meaning is fast by the same factor in every lineage. That assumption is untested in most linguistic data and is likely to be violated, for example if contact affects some semantic domains more than others. Covarion models (Section 7.6) relax it partially. Third, published analyses frequently report the coefficient of variation of branch rates. In linguistic data sets these values are often substantial, consistent with the lineage-level rate variation that undermined glottochronology. The value depends on the data and model, and, as Section 9.1.1 noted, it absorbs every unmodelled process that stretches or shrinks branches, including undetected borrowing (Section 8.3) and missing data in poorly attested languages. Rather than quoting typical figures we encourage readers to check them in the papers reviewed in Chapter 10. Fourth, the clock interacts strongly with the tree prior and the calibrations. With a relaxed clock and few calibrations, node ages far from any calibration are determined largely by the tree prior and by the assumed distribution of rates. Section 10.3.2 shows how to detect this by running analyses without data (sampling from the prior) and comparing the prior and posterior distributions of node ages. Specification by default carries its own risks. King (2026b) found, by simulation-based calibration, that the default weighting of meaning-partition rates in BEAST 2 analyses of cognate data interacts with the ascertainment correction and miscalibrates the posterior, whereas an alternative weighting behaved correctly (Section 7.10). Because partition rates scale the expected amount of change on every branch, details of this kind can in principle affect dates as well as substitution parameters. 9.7 Rate variation across meanings 9.7.1 Frequency of use That some meanings change faster than others has been known since Swadesh. Phylogenetic methods made it possible to measure the rates. Section 7.5 introduced the central result: Pagel et al. (2007) estimated a rate of lexical replacement for each of the 200 Swadesh meanings across 87 Indo-European languages, on a posterior sample of trees so that phylogenetic uncertainty was carried into the rate estimates, and found that frequency of use in modern corpora accounted for roughly half of the variation, with frequent words replaced slowly. Expressed as half-lives (the time over which a word has a 50 percent chance of being replaced), the most stable meanings had half-lives of many millennia, the least stable well under a millennium. Here we add what matters for dating. The frequency effect is not an isolated finding. The same issue of Nature carried a paper by Lieberman et al. (2007) showing an analogous law for the regularization of English irregular verbs: the half-life of an irregular past-tense form scales with the square root of its frequency, so that rare irregular verbs regularize much faster than common ones. Calude and Pagel (2011) showed that the frequencies of the Swadesh meanings are strongly correlated across a sample of 17 languages from several families, which supports treating frequency as a near-universal property of meanings rather than an accident of Indo-European. Monaghan (2014) reported that the age at which children acquire a word also predicts its rate of replacement in Indo-European, with early-acquired words changing more slowly, though age of acquisition and frequency are themselves correlated. Vejdemo and Hörberg (2016) examined semantic properties of meanings and reported that they help predict rates of replacement over and above frequency. Pagel and Meade (2018) focused on numerals, arguing that number words for the lowest numbers are among the most stable elements of vocabulary, with expected lifetimes of many thousands of years. Work on borrowing, such as the Leipzig-Jakarta list of Tadmor et al. (2010), has shown that the meanings least prone to borrowing overlap strongly with the meanings that are most stable within lineages. For dating, the practical consequence is that the composition of the meaning list strongly influences the estimated rate. A clock rate is a property of a particular list, coded in a particular way, not of a language family. Different lists, or different subsets of the same list, will give different absolute rates and must be calibrated separately, and a rate estimated in one family cannot be transferred to another unless the lists and coding conventions match. This is one reason why borrowing a “universal” rate, glottochronology’s original sin, remains a temptation to resist. How should frequency be included in a phylogenetic model? So far, most analyses have estimated per-character or per-meaning rates and examined their correlates afterward. Section 7.5 sketched a regression model for meaning rates built into the likelihood. For dating, its attraction is that external data would inform the rate category of each meaning, so that fewer of the data’s degrees of freedom are spent estimating among-meaning rate variation and more are available for branch lengths. Such a model is formally similar to the phylogenetic generalized linear models used in phylogeography (Chapter 11). To our knowledge, this has rarely if ever been done in a published dating analysis. 9.7.2 Ultraconserved words and deep time If some meanings are replaced very slowly, perhaps their words could preserve signals of relationship older than any established language family. Pagel et al. (2013) tested this idea. They used reconstructed proto-words for seven Eurasian language families (Indo-European, Uralic, Altaic, Kartvelian, Dravidian, Chukchi-Kamchatkan and Inuit-Yupik), taken from an etymological database, and asked which meanings had proto-words that were judged cognate across several families. They found that the meanings with such putative cognates were precisely those predicted by frequency to be the most stable, including pronouns (‘I’, ‘thou’, ‘we’, ‘ye’), demonstratives and interrogatives, and words such as ‘not’, ‘mother’ and ‘to give’. They identified 23 “ultraconserved” meanings and inferred a tree of the seven families with a root of around 15,000 years ago, which they interpreted as evidence for a deep Eurasiatic macrofamily. The paper was strongly criticized. Heggarty (2013) argued that the underlying proto-forms, taken from an etymological database associated with the Moscow school of long-range comparison, are subjective interpretations that cannot be independently validated and that most specialists in reconstruction reject, and that the result was circular: because those reconstructions are built on family-level proto-forms that are themselves weighted toward stable meanings, finding the putative cognates concentrated in stable meanings was, in his words, “correlation in, correlation out”. A further concern raised by other critics in the same debate is that frequent meanings tend to have short, phonetically simple words, and short words are also the most likely to show chance resemblances, so the match between predicted stability and observed cross-family similarity does not by itself distinguish inheritance from chance. More generally, the probability of chance resemblance among short words can be substantial, as Ringe (1992) showed in a classic analysis of the statistics of language comparison. Most historical linguists regard the existence of Eurasiatic as unproven. The episode illustrates a general point about rates. Knowing that some meanings change slowly does not by itself make it possible to detect relationships beyond the time depth at which genuine cognates become indistinguishable from chance similarities. That limit is set by the rate of change of the slowest characters, by the size of the data set, and above all by the reliability of the cognate judgments. Long-range comparisons combine two hard problems: very low expected numbers of surviving cognates, and a high rate of false positives from chance resemblance, sound symbolism, nursery words (‘mama’, ‘papa’) and borrowing. Phylogenetic models assume that the cognate judgments are correct and say nothing about whether they are. A phylogenetic analysis of doubtful cognate sets yields a tree with the appearance of precision, and its dates inherit every error in the input. Before interpreting a deep date, ask how the cognate sets were identified and how many would be expected by chance. 9.8 Punctuational bursts at language splits 9.8.1 The idea In the clock models discussed so far, change accumulates in proportion to time. An alternative hypothesis holds that some change happens in bursts associated with lineage splitting. In biology, Webster et al. (2003) and Pagel et al. (2006) reported that, across many phylogenies, lineages that have undergone more speciation events have also accumulated more molecular change, after accounting for time. Venditti and Pagel (2010) reviewed the evidence and the possible mechanisms, such as founder effects and rapid adaptation in new populations. The linguistic analog is intuitive. When a group of speakers separates from its parent community, by migration or by social fission, the new community may innovate rapidly, deliberately or not, as a marker of a new identity. Small founding populations may also lose and replace vocabulary by drift. The test is simple. Under a gradual process, the expected root-to-tip path length \(P_i\) of language \(i\) in a phylogram depends only on the time elapsed since the root, which is the same for all contemporaneous languages. If each split adds a burst of change \(\beta\) to the descendant lineages, then \[\begin{equation} \mathbb{E}[P_i] = r T + \beta \, n_i, \tag{9.5} \end{equation}\] where \(T\) is the root age and \(n_i\) is the number of nodes on the path from the root to tip \(i\). A positive slope \(\beta\) in the regression of path length on node count, estimated with the phylogenetic non-independence of the tips taken into account, indicates punctuational change. The proportion of total path length attributable to bursts, \(\beta n_i / P_i\), measures its importance. 9.8.2 Evidence from language families Atkinson et al. (2008) applied this test to Bayesian posterior samples of trees for Bantu, Indo-European and Austronesian, all estimated from basic vocabulary. They found a significant positive relationship between path length and number of nodes in all three families. By their estimates, bursts at splits accounted for roughly 10 to 33 percent of the total lexical divergence, depending on the family. Atkinson et al. (2008) tackled the main technical objection to the path-length test, the node-density artefact (Venditti et al. 2006). In phylogenies estimated from data, branch lengths tend to be underestimated in sparsely sampled regions of the tree, because multiple changes on long branches are not detected. Densely sampled regions have more nodes and also more fully recovered branch lengths, so a positive relationship between path length and node count can arise even without any real bursts. The test of Venditti et al. (2006) looks for a characteristic curvilinear shape in the relationship, and Atkinson and colleagues reported that their data did not show the artefact. Their result has been widely cited as evidence that language change is partly punctuational. It has implications for dating: if change is concentrated at splits, branch lengths depend partly on the number of unsampled or extinct splits along each lineage, which a clock model cannot see. It would be valuable to repeat the analysis on the larger and more carefully coded data sets that have since become available, such as IE-CoR for Indo-European, and with models that build the bursts into the likelihood rather than testing for them after the fact. Figure 9.5 simulates the test. We generate a pure-birth (Yule) tree of 60 languages, then add lexical change along each branch in proportion to time, plus, in one scenario, a burst of extra change at the start of each branch, so that every split contributes. We then regress root-to-tip path length on the number of nodes. For simplicity the figure uses ordinary least squares, which ignores the shared ancestry of tips. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, this is a parameter-recovery exercise for the test statistic: the data are generated under the very process the test is designed to detect, with true branch lengths and no node-density artefact, so it shows what the test estimates in the most favorable case and nothing about its behavior on real, estimated trees. Figure 9.5: Simulated test for punctuational change. Root-to-tip path length (number of lexical changes) against the number of nodes on the path from the root, for a 60-language Yule tree under purely gradual change (left) and with a burst of change at every split (right). Lines are least-squares fits. A single simulated dataset gives a noisy slope, because tips share ancestral branches and their path lengths are therefore correlated, so the effective sample size is much smaller than the number of languages. Averaging over many replicate datasets on the same tree, with the function path_lengths() that simulates one dataset, shows what the test estimates: reps <- sapply(c(gradual = 0, bursts = 8), function(b) replicate(200, coef(lm(path_lengths(b) ~ nodes_on_path))[2])) round(rbind(mean_slope = colMeans(reps), sd_slope = apply(reps, 2, sd)), 2) #> gradual bursts #> mean_slope -0.15 8.15 #> sd_slope 1.57 1.98 The simulation code for Figure 9.5, and a version of the test that uses phylogenetic generalized least squares to account for the shared ancestry of the tips, are in Section C.3.5. In the gradual scenario the average slope is close to zero; with bursts it is close to the burst size per split. The spread of slopes across replicates is a reminder that a single family provides one noisy realization of the process, and that significance tests must account for the shared ancestry of languages. Real analyses face the additional difficulties that tree topology and branch lengths are estimated with error, that extinct and unsampled languages leave splits invisible, and that the node-density artefact can mimic the signal. A convincing case for punctuational change in a language family would therefore need a robustness-under-misspecification experiment as well: data simulated without bursts, but with saturation and uneven sampling, analyzed in the same way as the real data (Exercise 4 below). 9.9 Vocabulary, grammar and sound systems Basic vocabulary is only one part of a language. Are grammatical and phonological systems more or less stable? Claims on both sides have a long history. Some typologists have argued that grammatical features such as word order or morphological type are slow to change and preserve deep historical signals. Others have pointed out that grammatical features are few, mostly binary or low-dimensional, prone to convergence through contact, and liable to change back and forth, so that their signal decays quickly. Greenhill et al. (2017) compared rates of change in grammatical structures and basic vocabulary in a sample of Austronesian languages. They estimated rates for each lexical meaning and each grammatical feature on the same set of trees. On average, grammatical features changed faster than basic vocabulary, although the two distributions overlapped broadly and some grammatical features were among the most stable characters of all. The authors also suggested that grammatical features are more susceptible than basic vocabulary to influence from neighboring languages. And when the authors mapped the lineages with unusually fast or slow change, the two systems showed different regional patterns: the Indonesian and Malay languages, for example, showed elevated rates of lexical change, while languages of the Bismarck Archipelago, in long contact with non-Austronesian languages, showed more structural change. A lineage that was conservative in vocabulary was not necessarily conservative in grammar. The study suggests that grammar and vocabulary evolve as partly independent systems with distinct dynamics. The design of Greenhill et al. (2017) is a model for comparative rate studies. Lexical cognate data from the Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database and grammatical features coded for the same languages were analyzed on a common phylogenetic framework, so that differences in rates could not be attributed to different trees. Rates were estimated with explicit models of character evolution and compared as distributions, not just as averages. The authors then looked separately at where on the tree each system showed significantly elevated or reduced rates, and found that the two systems did not share the same lineage-specific patterns, although they did not report a formal test of correlation. This has a practical implication for dating. A clock calibrated on vocabulary cannot simply be transferred to grammatical data, and combined analyses of lexical and structural data probably need separate clock models for the two partitions. Measures of the stability of typological features have also been developed outside a full phylogenetic framework. Wichmann and Holman (2009b) estimated the stability of features in the World Atlas of Language Structures by comparing how often related and unrelated languages agree, and Dediu and Cysouw (2013) compared seven different methods for measuring feature stability, finding moderate but not perfect agreement among them. Phylogenetic estimates of rates of change for structural features on Grambank-scale data (Chapter 3) are an active area of research. Sound change poses different problems. Regular sound changes affect whole classes of words at once, so their effect on cognate-based characters is not independent across words. Hruschka et al. (2015) proposed a phylogenetic model in which sound correspondences evolve by “concerted evolution”, in the sense used for gene families in molecular biology, and applied it to Turkic. They showed that regular sound changes could be detected as correlated changes of many characters at the same point in the tree, and estimated when particular changes occurred. To our knowledge, systematic comparisons of the rates of phonological change with lexical and grammatical rates on the same trees remain rare. Phonological inventory data (Chapter 3) and sound-change databases offer obvious opportunities. A first example of such a comparison is the study of Mixtec tone by Auderset (2024). Using a database of tonal and segmental sound changes in 42 Mixtec languages, she measured phylogenetic signal with the \(D\) statistic and estimated rates with a hidden Markov model over a posterior sample of trees, and found that most tone changes carry phylogenetic signal and that tones do not, in general, change faster than segments, contrary to the common assumption that tone is inherently unstable. At the level of word forms, Cathcart (2024) used phylogenetic models of homologous words to ask why sequences of identical consonants are rare, and found that such words arise less often than others but, once present, do not die out more often, although they are replaced in basic meaning functions more frequently. 9.10 Population size and rates of change 9.10.1 Theory Does the size of a speech community affect how fast its language changes? Two opposing intuitions exist. One holds that small, tightly knit communities can tolerate and transmit idiosyncratic innovations, while large communities, with many weak ties and many adult learners, favor simplification and slow down idiosyncratic change (Trudgill 2011). Another, derived from population genetics, holds that random drift is stronger in small populations, so that small communities should both lose and fix variants faster (Nettle 1999). In the neutral model of Section 9.3, these effects cancel: the number of innovations grows with population size while the chance that any one of them spreads through the community falls. The cancellation is exact only if innovations are neutral, if every speaker is equally likely to innovate, and if the community mixes randomly. None of these conditions is likely to hold for languages. Models of language change with social structure, prestige-biased transmission or conformist learning predict a range of relationships between population size and rate. Population size might also affect the kind of change: Reali et al. (2018) used models and experiments to argue that larger populations favor simpler grammars and larger vocabularies. 9.10.2 Evidence Nettle (1999) argued from simulation and comparative data that the rate of linguistic change is not constant and is faster in smaller groups. Wichmann and Holman (2009a) tested for a relationship between population size and rates of lexical change in a large global sample of lexical data, and reported little evidence of a strong effect. Their study used distances between related languages rather than phylogenetic branch lengths. Bromham et al. (2015) brought phylogenetic methods to the question. Using a Bayesian tree of Polynesian languages, they compared the amount of lexical change along phylogenetically independent pairs of related languages that differ in population size. They distinguished the gain of new words from the loss of existing cognates. Languages with larger populations gained new words at a faster rate, and languages with smaller populations lost words at a faster rate. Both patterns fit population-genetic expectations: more speakers produce more innovations, and in small populations existing words are more easily lost by drift. Greenhill et al. (2018) extended the test to Indo-European, Austronesian and Bantu. They found less consistent support for the relationships in these larger and more heterogeneous families. The question of whether population size systematically affects rates of lexical change therefore remains open. Current population sizes are a noisy proxy for population sizes over the history of a lineage, and families differ in how much their histories have been shaped by expansion, contact and language shift. The paired-comparison design used by Bromham et al. (2015) is a standard tool in comparative biology for testing rate correlates. Each pair consists of two lineages that share a common ancestor and differ in the trait of interest, here population size. The lineages of a pair are compared on the amount of change accumulated since their split, measured as root-to-tip or ancestor-to-tip distance on the tree. Because each pair shares the same span of time and the pairs do not overlap on the tree, the comparisons are phylogenetically independent. The approach does not require a clock model, since both members of a pair have experienced the same amount of time; it sidesteps the rate-time confounding of Section 9.1 by comparing rates relative to each other rather than absolutely. It does require care in measuring the trait: in Bromham et al.’s study, population sizes were current speaker numbers, and the authors discussed the assumption that relative sizes have been reasonably stable over the history of the pairs. The Polynesian setting is especially favorable, because island populations are relatively isolated and their settlement history is well constrained by archaeology. 9.11 Rate heterogeneity among lineages The variation in rates among lineages that defeated glottochronology is now routinely estimated by relaxed clocks, and it is of interest in its own right. Which lineages are fast and which are slow, and why? Several kinds of explanation have been proposed, though few have been tested systematically. Contact and language shift. Lineages that have absorbed many speakers of other languages, or that have been in intense contact, often show high rates of lexical replacement. Norwegian and English, both heavily influenced by contact, are classic examples within Germanic. Since borrowed vocabulary should ideally be flagged and removed in cognate coding (Chapter 3), contact may affect rates through undetected loans or through contact-induced restructuring that is not itself borrowing. Founder effects and expansion. Gray et al. (2009) found in Austronesian that the expansion across the Pacific proceeded in a series of pulses and pauses (Chapter 10). Rates of lexical change may themselves vary with phases of expansion, as the punctuational analysis of Section 9.8 suggests. Literacy and standardization. Written standard languages with long literary traditions are sometimes held to change more slowly, as the conservatism of Icelandic suggests. But Icelandic is also an isolated island community with an explicit purist language policy, so literacy alone cannot explain its conservatism. Literacy may also have a different effect on vocabulary than on grammar or phonology. Population size and social structure, discussed above. Disentangling these factors requires analyses that estimate branch rates on a tree and then relate them to lineage properties, or better, that build the properties into the clock model. Two cautions apply to the first approach. Estimated branch rates are among the least well-identified quantities in a dated tree (Section 9.1.1), so a regression of branch rates on lineage properties should be repeated over the posterior sample of trees and rates rather than run once on a summary tree. And branch rates absorb every process that changes branch lengths, so a “fast” lineage may simply be one with undetected loans or many missing entries. Several families of methods developed for molecular rates could address the causes of rate variation among language lineages directly. Rate-trait correlation models. Coevol (Lartillot and Poujol 2011) jointly models the evolution of substitution rates and continuous traits (such as body mass or generation time) as a multivariate Brownian motion along the tree, and estimates the correlation between them while integrating over divergence times. Linguistic analogs of the traits might be log population size, degree of multilingualism or a measure of contact intensity, reconstructed along the tree. To our knowledge, no linguistic analysis has used a joint rate-trait model of this kind. Clocks with covariates. Instead of drawing branch rates independently, one can model the log rate of each branch as a linear function of branch-level predictors plus a random effect. This approach parallels the generalized linear models used for phylogeographic transition rates (Chapter 11). Predictors could include whether a branch led to an island colonization, a change of subsistence, or a period of documented contact. Comparative rate studies. Lanfear et al. (2010) review the extensive biological literature on why rates differ between species, covering generation time, metabolic rate, population size and life history, and the statistical designs (sister-pair comparisons, phylogenetic regression of branch rates) used to test them. Many of these designs could be transferred directly to language families with existing dated phylogenies. Episodic and random local clocks for shifts. Random local clocks (Drummond and Suchard 2010) identify the branches on which rates shift without prior specification. Applied to language trees, they could test whether rate shifts coincide with known historical events, such as island settlement or language shift, more often than expected by chance. 9.12 What biology offers, and what remains to be done Gathering the threads of this chapter, the following methods from evolutionary biology seem especially promising for the study of linguistic rates, ranked roughly by how easily they could be applied to existing data: Clock model comparison and adequacy. Routine comparison of strict, uncorrelated, autocorrelated and random local clocks by marginal likelihoods, together with posterior predictive tests of clock adequacy (D. A. Duchêne et al. 2015). These require no new data or software. Clock partitioning. Testing whether vocabulary partitions (by part of speech, frequency band or semantic domain) and structural partitions share a clock (Duchêne et al. 2014). The results of Greenhill et al. (2017) suggest they may not. Clock models for discrete morphological characters, which raise many of the same problems as linguistic characters (few characters, strong rate variation among them, ascertainment), are reviewed by Lee (2020). Time-dependent rates. Testing whether rates estimated from shallow calibrations are higher than those from deep calibrations (Ho et al. 2005), and modeling the dependence explicitly. Rate-trait correlation and covariate clocks. Joint inference of rates and lineage traits (Lartillot and Poujol 2011), or log-linear models for branch rates. Models with bursts in the likelihood. Instead of testing for punctuational change after the fact, models that include a per-node burst parameter, or in which the clock rate depends on the speciation process, can estimate the size of bursts while accounting for unobserved splits. Meaning-level predictors of rates. Building frequency, age of acquisition and other covariates into among-character rate models, so that external data inform the rates of individual meanings. All of these are within reach with current software and data, and several would bear directly on the reliability of the dates discussed in the next chapter. Cognate data determine branch lengths as products of rate and time. Branch lengths are identifiable from the data; relative ages only under a clock model; absolute ages and rates only with calibrations; individual branch rates are poorly estimable in practice. Glottochronology is a strict clock with a universal rate. It fails because rates vary among lineages and among meanings. Rate variation among meanings biases glottochronological dates downward, increasingly so at greater depths. Modern clock models let rates vary: uncorrelated relaxed clocks (UCLN, UCED), autocorrelated clocks (geometric Brownian motion), local and random local clocks, and penalized-likelihood smoothing. The optimized relaxed clock improves MCMC efficiency rather than changing the model. Rate variation across characters (gamma) and across lineages (relaxed clock) are different things and are usually both needed. A binary clock rate counts gains and losses of cognate classes and is not a rate of word replacement. In simulation, dates are recovered well only when the clock model matches the generating process; parameter recovery under the model’s own assumptions is not evidence of adequacy for real data. Frequency of use is the best-established predictor of the rate at which a meaning’s word is replaced, so a clock rate is a property of a particular list and coding. Claims that ultraconserved words reveal relationships of 15,000 years or more remain highly controversial. Path-length tests suggest that part of lexical change in several families occurs in bursts at language splits, though the node-density artefact must be ruled out. In Austronesian, grammatical features appear on average to change faster than basic vocabulary, and the two systems show different lineage-specific patterns of fast and slow change. Evidence on population size and rates is mixed. A Polynesian study found faster gain of words in larger populations and faster loss in smaller ones, but the pattern is less consistent in other families. Rate-trait models, covariate clocks, clock partitioning, time-dependent rates and clock adequacy tests are available in biology and largely unused in linguistics. 9.13 Exercises Conceptual Explain why doubling every branch rate and halving every node age leaves the likelihood of a cognate matrix unchanged. List the components of a Bayesian dating analysis that break this symmetry, and say for each whether it carries historical evidence or modelling assumptions. Two languages share 60 percent of their cognates on a 100-item list. Explain why a glottochronological date and a Bayesian relaxed-clock date for the same pair could differ even if both use the same mean rate of replacement. Which assumptions differ, and which difference would you expect to matter most at this time depth? A study reports a posterior mean coefficient of variation of 0.8 for the branch rates of a binary cognate analysis. List three processes other than genuine differences in the tempo of lexical replacement that could produce such a value, and describe a check that would help distinguish each from real rate variation. Contrast an uncorrelated lognormal clock, an autocorrelated clock and a random local clock as hypotheses about why the Polynesian languages might have changed faster than the Formosan languages. What would each predict about the distribution of rates over the Austronesian tree? Why is the clock rate estimated from binary cognate characters not directly comparable with the per-meaning replacement rate estimated by Pagel et al. (2007)? Describe how you would convert one into the other, and what extra information you would need. Why is a positive regression slope of root-to-tip path length on node count not by itself evidence for punctuational change? Name the main artefact and one way of addressing it. Which list gives the more precise date, and why? How sensitive is the ranking of the four rate models to \(\lambda\)? Use attr(fit, "PHIIC")$PHIIC to see which \(\lambda\) the information criterion would choose. Simulate the node-density artefact. Starting from path_lengths() (Section C.3.5) with burst = 0, transform each branch’s count \(x\) to a saturated value \(K(1 - e^{-x/K})\) with \(K = 30\) before computing path lengths, so that long branches are underestimated, and repeat the regression of Section 9.8.2 over 200 replicates. Does a spurious positive slope appear? Which kind of validation is this? Research You plan to date a family of 60 languages for which two medieval attestations and one archaeologically dated island settlement are available. Choose a clock model and justify the choice; specify which prior-only runs, parameter-recovery simulations and misspecification simulations you would perform before interpreting the root age; and say which results would make you abandon the clock model you chose. Design a study testing whether intense contact raises rates of lexical replacement. Define the predictor at the level of branches, choose between a two-step analysis (estimate branch rates, then regress) and a covariate clock, and explain how you would prevent undetected loans, which also lengthen branches, from producing a spurious association. Propose a test of time-dependent rates of lexical change in Indo-European or Austronesian, using calibrations of different ages. What pattern of results would support time dependence, what alternative explanations would produce the same pattern, and how would you distinguish them? 9.14 Further reading McMahon and McMahon (2005): A balanced and readable account of lexicostatistics and glottochronology, their critiques, and the transition to quantitative phylogenetic methods, written by linguists for linguists. Embleton (1986): The most thorough technical treatment of the statistics of glottochronology and its revisions. Essential for anyone who wants to understand exactly which assumptions failed. Bergsland and Vogt (1962): The classic empirical test of glottochronology on languages with known histories, with published commentaries. Worth reading as a primary source. Atkinson et al. (2005): A direct response to the charge that phylogenetic dating is merely glottochronology revisited, explaining how modern models address its failures. Ho and Duchêne (2014): A clear review of molecular-clock methods for biologists that is accessible to linguists, covering strict, relaxed and local clocks and calibration. Drummond et al. (2006): The paper that introduced uncorrelated relaxed clocks, which underlie most linguistic dating analyses. The introduction gives the intuition clearly. Pagel et al. (2007): The study linking word frequency to rates of lexical replacement in Indo-European, with Lieberman et al. (2007) on irregular verbs. Atkinson et al. (2008): A short paper on punctuational bursts of change at language splits, with supplementary material explaining the method and the node-density test. Greenhill et al. (2017): A comparison of rates in vocabulary and grammar on the same trees, with careful attention to methodological issues. Bromham et al. (2015): A test of population size effects on lexical rates, illustrating the paired-comparison design of comparative biology. References
