Chapter 10 Calibration and Divergence Times: Family by Family Chapter 9 showed that a clock model can turn a tree measured in amounts of change into a tree measured in relative time, but that the data alone never fix the absolute scale. This chapter is about the last step, anchoring relative time to the calendar, and about what that step has produced. Calibration is where historical linguistics, philology and archaeology enter a dating analysis most directly, and it is also where most disputes about published dates turn out to lie: which events can be dated, how securely, which node of the tree they belong to, and whether an attested ancient language is an ancestor, a sister or merely a witness. The first half of the chapter develops the theory of calibration and of validating dates; the second reviews the published dated phylogenies of the world’s language families. Chapter 15 takes up the broader controversies, and Chapter 11 the closely related question of where families originated. After reading this chapter you should be able to: explain, using the infinite-sites argument, why calibrations determine the precision of every date in a tree and not only its time scale; choose and justify a calibration density for a piece of historical evidence, and explain why minimum ages are usually more secure than maximum ages; distinguish specified from effective priors on node ages, and diagnose the difference by sampling from the prior; describe the ways an attested ancient language can enter a dating analysis (node calibration, dated tip, sampled ancestor, constrained ancestor), and explain how the choice affects taxon selection, coding and dates; assess whether a published date has been independently validated, distinguishing evidence used as calibration from evidence held out, and recognizing circular agreement; summarize the published dated phylogenies of the major families and identify for each the main source of disagreement. 10.1 The anatomy of a dating analysis A Bayesian dating analysis has five components, and every published date is the product of all of them: Data \(D\): usually a matrix of cognate sets coded as binary characters, sometimes multistate meaning-classes or structural features (Chapter 3). A substitution model describing how characters change: for example a binary CTMC with gamma rate variation or a stochastic Dollo model (Chapter 7). A clock model describing how rates vary across branches: strict, relaxed or local (Chapter 9). A tree prior describing the distribution of topologies and node ages before the data are seen: Yule, birth-death, coalescent or fossilized birth-death (Chapter 6). Calibrations linking some node ages, or tip ages, to absolute time. Components 2 to 4 form what Warnock and Wright (2020) call the tripartite model of Bayesian divergence-time estimation, the substitution, clock and tree models, each of which can be specified and checked separately; their short introduction, written for palaeobiologists, is a useful companion to this chapter. The joint posterior is \[\begin{equation} p(\tau, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}, \theta \mid D) \propto P(D \mid \tau, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}, \theta)\; p(\mathbf{r} \mid \theta)\; p(\tau, \mathbf{t} \mid \theta, \mathcal{C})\; p(\theta), \tag{10.1} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{t}\) are node ages, \(\mathbf{r}\) branch rates, \(\theta\) the remaining parameters, and \(\mathcal{C}\) the calibrations. The data enter only through the likelihood, which, as Chapter 9 emphasized, depends on rates and times only through their products. Everything that separates rate from time comes from the clock prior \(p(\mathbf{r} \mid \theta)\) and the time prior \(p(\tau, \mathbf{t} \mid \theta, \mathcal{C})\). A simple thought experiment shows how much this matters. Suppose we had an unlimited number of cognate sets, so that every branch length \(b_j = r_j t_j\) was known exactly. Under a strict clock, the node ages would then be known up to a single scale factor, the rate. All the remaining uncertainty would come from the calibrations: if the calibration on the root allowed ages between 5,000 and 7,000 years, then every node age would have a correspondingly proportional range. Adding more data would not narrow the interval at all. This infinite-sites argument, developed by Yang and Rannala (2006) and Rannala and Yang (2007), shows that in dating, unlike in topology estimation, uncertainty does not vanish as data accumulate. With a relaxed clock, the limit is wider still, because each branch has its own rate. Plotting the width of posterior intervals against their mean for all nodes in a tree (an infinite-sites plot) reveals how close an analysis is to this limit. If the points fall on a straight line, more data will not help, and only better calibrations can (Reis et al. 2016). The derivation of the infinite-sites limit for a strict clock, with a short R illustration of the infinite-sites plot, is in Section C.4.1. Linguistic datasets are very far from infinite. A typical basic vocabulary list has 100 to 200 meanings, yielding a few hundred to a few thousand cognate sets, many of which are present in only a few languages. In practice, therefore, both data and calibrations limit precision. Yet the infinite-sites argument contains a lesson that is easily forgotten. Calibrations do not just fix the time scale; they determine the precision of every date in the tree, and errors in them propagate to every node. 10.1.1 What is identified, and by what Section 9.1.1 classified the quantities in a dated tree by whether the lexical data identify them. Table 10.1 extends that classification to the quantities that dating analyses report, using the four questions of Section 6.10: is the quantity identifiable under the model, practically estimable with realistic linguistic data, robust to misspecification, and interpretable as a historical quantity? Table 10.1: What a dating analysis can and cannot identify. Calibrations are assumed to fix the absolute time scale; “practically estimable” refers to typical basic-vocabulary datasets of a few dozen to a few hundred languages. Quantity Identified by Practically estimable? Most sensitive to Historical interpretation Topology and branch lengths The characters Usually, for well-sampled families Borrowing, coding, saturation Shared cognates are not shared innovations (Chapter 3); topology is a summary of lexical similarity under the model Relative node ages Characters plus clock prior Yes under a strict clock; partly under relaxed clocks Clock model, among-character rate variation Order and spacing of lineage splits Absolute node ages Calibrations (with clock and tree priors) Only as precisely as the calibrations allow Calibration placement and densities; effective priors The time of the “split” depends on what a split of a dialect continuum means Mean clock rate Calibrations plus characters Yes, given good calibrations List composition, coding (binary versus multistate) A rate of cognate-class gain and loss on a given list, not a universal rate of change Individual branch rates Clock prior plus characters Poorly, especially on terminal branches Missing data, undetected loans Ambiguous: tempo of change or unmodelled processes Tree-prior parameters (speciation, extinction, sampling) Node-age distribution Weakly; often prior-dominated Taxon sampling scheme Rarely interpretable as rates of language diversification Ancestor or sister status of an ancient language Absence of unique changes in the ancient language Poorly when the language is fragmentarily attested Missing data, literary registers Whether the attested variety, or a close relative, gave rise to the descendants Two lessons follow from the table. First, the quantities that attract the most attention, absolute root ages, are precisely those that the lexical data do not identify: they are borrowed from the calibrations through the clock model. A root age is therefore only as good as the weakest of three things: the calibrations, the match between clock model and real rate variation, and the extrapolation from calibrated nodes to the root. Second, the quantities that the data identify best, topology and branch lengths, are summaries of lexical similarity under the substitution model. Agreement between an inferred topology and the subgroups of the comparative method is welcome, but it is not independent validation of either, since the cognate judgments are themselves products of the comparative method, and it says nothing at all about whether the dates are right. 10.2 Kinds of calibration information Biologists calibrate trees primarily with fossils, whose ages are determined by radiometric dating of the rocks in which they are found. Linguists have no direct equivalent of radiometric dating for languages. Instead, they use several indirect sources of absolute time, each with characteristic strengths and weaknesses. Table 10.2 summarizes them. Table 10.2: Kinds of calibration information available for language families. Source Example What it constrains Main risks Documented historical events Settlement of Iceland in the late ninth century CE; Dutch colonization of the Cape from the mid-seventeenth century Upper (and sometimes lower) bound on the split of a colonial variety from its source Dialect differentiation may predate or postdate the migration; continued contact Written attestation of an ancient language Hittite texts from the second millennium BCE; the fourth-century Gothic Bible A minimum age for the clade containing that language; or a dated tip Attestation is not origin; literary languages may not be ancestral to spoken descendants Disappearance of a common language Latin as the last common stage before the Romance split Age of a clade’s last common ancestor When exactly a dialect continuum became separate languages is a matter of definition Archaeological correlates Lapita-associated settlement of western Polynesia; first settlement of New Zealand Ages of clades assumed to correspond to an archaeological expansion Circularity if the dated tree is then used to test the archaeological hypothesis; language and material culture need not move together Datable loanword strata Latin loans in Germanic; Chinese loans in neighboring languages Relative order of events and contact dates Indirect; often constrain contact rather than splits Three general points apply. First, a calibration is a statement about a node in the tree: the last common ancestor of a specified set of languages. Its validity depends on the clade being correctly identified. If a calibration is attached to the most recent common ancestor of the Romance languages, but the tree places a non-Romance language within that clade, the calibration constrains the wrong event. In BEAST and similar programs, calibrated clades are often constrained to be monophyletic for exactly this reason. Second, most historical evidence provides minimum ages more securely than maximum ages. A written text proves that a language existed and was already distinct by the time it was written. It says nothing about how long before that the language had been separating from its relatives. Maximum ages are typically inferred from negative evidence, such as the absence of a population from a region before a certain date, which is weaker. The asymmetry is the same as with fossils, and it shapes the choice of calibration distribution (Section 10.3). Third, the split between two languages is not an instantaneous event. Dialects diverge gradually, and the date at which two varieties became “separate languages” depends on contact, mutual intelligibility and social identity. A tree model treats a split as a point in time. The calibration therefore represents a modeling idealization, and its uncertainty should be wide enough to reflect that. 10.3 Node calibrations and their densities 10.3.1 Calibration distributions In a Bayesian analysis, a calibration is a probability density on the age of a node. Several standard forms are used (Ho and Phillips 2009): A uniform density between a minimum \(a\) and a maximum \(b\), with zero probability outside. This is a hard-bounded calibration. It says that all ages in the interval are equally plausible and all ages outside it are impossible. A soft-bounded uniform, in which most of the probability lies between \(a\) and \(b\) but small tails, often 2.5 percent on each side, extend beyond them (Yang and Rannala 2006). Soft bounds allow the data to override a calibration that conflicts with the rest of the evidence, which hard bounds do not. An offset lognormal or offset exponential, in which the minimum age \(a\) is treated as a hard lower bound and the time by which the true age exceeds it has a lognormal or exponential distribution. These forms express the idea that the true age is probably not much older than the minimum but could be considerably older. Their parameters are best chosen by deciding where the bulk of the probability should lie, for example by placing the 97.5 percent quantile at the oldest plausible age, rather than by guessing the parameters directly. A normal density centered on a best estimate, appropriate when an event is believed to be dated to within a symmetric range, as with some historical events. Normal calibrations were common in early linguistic BEAST analyses. Figure 10.1 compares these shapes for a hypothetical node whose minimum age, from the earliest written attestation of one of its descendants, is 2,500 years. The offset-lognormal density (Equation (C.12)), the construction of soft bounds, functions that choose the parameters of offset lognormal and exponential calibrations from a minimum and an upper quantile, and the code for Figure 10.1 are in Section C.4.2. Figure 10.1: Four calibration densities for a node with a minimum age of 2.5 millennia (dotted line): a hard-bounded uniform (2.5 to 4 millennia), a soft-bounded uniform with exponential tails, an offset exponential and an offset lognormal. All have similar central ranges but very different assumptions about how old the node could be. Which shape is right? There is no general answer. Biologists have argued for years about how to translate paleontological knowledge into calibration densities, and have developed best-practice guidelines for justifying them (Parham et al. 2012). The same discipline would benefit linguistics. For each calibration, a study should state the clade it applies to, the evidence for its minimum and maximum, the reason for the chosen distribution and its parameters, and a reference to the historical or archaeological source. Most published linguistic analyses provide the first two; fewer justify the shape of the density. The choice matters most for the tail on the old side, because that is where the evidence is weakest and where an offset exponential and an offset lognormal with the same median can differ by centuries. 10.3.2 How calibrations interact A calibration density is what the analyst specifies. It is not necessarily what the analysis uses. The prior on node ages actually applied in an analysis, the effective prior or marginal prior, can differ substantially from the specified calibration densities, for three reasons. Truncation by ordering. A node cannot be older than its parent. If two calibrated nodes are nested and their calibration densities overlap, the joint prior is truncated to the region where the ancestor is older than the descendant. Both marginal distributions shift: the ancestor toward older ages, the descendant toward younger ones. Interaction with the tree prior. In BEAST, the joint prior on node ages is typically constructed by multiplying the tree prior density by the calibration densities. This product is not, in general, a distribution whose marginals equal the calibration densities. The tree prior pulls node ages in its own direction, and uncalibrated nodes are also affected. Heled and Drummond (2012) derived calibrated tree priors whose marginals do match the specified calibrations for the Yule process, and explained the difference between the multiplicative and conditional constructions. Yang and Rannala (2006) use a conditional construction in MCMCTree, in which the calibrations define the marginal densities of calibrated nodes and the birth-death process defines the distribution of the others conditional on them. Interaction with the clock prior. The prior on rates also contributes. Even the prior on the mean clock rate, combined with the root calibration and the tree prior, implies a prior on the total amount of change expected in the tree. Inoue et al. (2010) and Warnock et al. (2012) demonstrated with molecular examples that effective priors can differ greatly from specified ones and that the differences can drive posterior dates. The diagnostic is simple. Run the analysis without data, sampling from the prior alone, and compare the resulting marginal prior distributions of calibrated and uncalibrated node ages with what was intended. BEAST 2 and RevBayes both make this easy. A prior-only run is also the first step of implementation validation in the sense of Section 6.10: if the software’s prior does not match the analyst’s understanding of it, nothing downstream can be trusted. The following simulation illustrates truncation. A root has a normal calibration with mean 6 and standard deviation 0.5 millennia, and a descendant node has a uniform calibration between 4 and 7 millennia. Sampling from the product of the two densities and imposing the order constraint, by rejection, gives the effective joint prior. set.seed(3) m <- 2e5 root <- rnorm(m, 6, 0.5) desc <- runif(m, 4, 7) ok <- desc < root # ordering constraint op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) hist(root[ok], breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white", main = "Root", xlab = "Age (millennia)", xlim = c(3.5, 8), las = 1) curve(dnorm(x, 6, 0.5), add = TRUE, lwd = 2) hist(desc[ok], breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white", main = "Descendant node", xlab = "Age (millennia)", xlim = c(3.5, 8), las = 1) segments(4, 1/3, 7, 1/3, lwd = 2); segments(c(4, 7), 0, c(4, 7), 1/3, lwd = 2) Figure 10.2: Effective versus specified priors. Histograms show the effective marginal priors on the root (left) and a calibrated descendant node (right) after the two calibrations are combined and the ordering constraint (descendant younger than root) is imposed. Lines show the densities the analyst specified. par(op) round(c(mean_root_specified = 6, mean_root_effective = mean(root[ok]), mean_desc_specified = 5.5, mean_desc_effective = mean(desc[ok])), 2) #> mean_root_specified mean_root_effective mean_desc_specified #> 6.00 6.12 5.50 #> mean_desc_effective #> 5.06 The root’s effective prior is shifted older than specified, and the descendant’s is no longer uniform: ages near 7 millennia have become improbable, because they would usually exceed the root. With more calibrations and a tree prior, such interactions multiply. None of this is a flaw in the software. It is a consequence of the logic of probability, and the analyst’s task is to check that the effective prior expresses what she believes. The exact effective densities for this example, obtained by integration and used to check the rejection sampler, and the general form of the multiplicative and conditional constructions, are in Section C.4.3. Always sample from the prior. A posterior date that sits close to the effective prior tells you that the data are uninformative about that node and the answer was determined by the assumptions. A posterior that sits close to a specified calibration may still be strongly shaped by the tree prior or by other calibrations. Report effective priors alongside posteriors for the key nodes, especially the root. Reviewers of linguistic dating studies should ask for this, as reviewers in molecular dating now routinely do (Brown and Smith 2018). 10.4 The tree prior The tree prior specifies the distribution of node ages before the data are seen. Three classes are common (Chapter 6). A Yule or pure-birth process assumes that lineages split at a constant rate \(\lambda\) and never go extinct. A birth-death process adds an extinction rate \(\mu\) and a sampling proportion \(\rho\), the fraction of extant languages included. A coalescent prior, derived from population genetics, is designed for samples from a single population and is rarely appropriate for language families, although it has occasionally been used. The tree prior matters most for the nodes that are far from any calibration and for the root, if the root is not itself calibrated. A Yule prior tends to place nodes relatively evenly in time, whereas a birth-death prior with high extinction concentrates them near the present. A coalescent prior concentrates them near the present even more. Under weak data and few calibrations, the choice can shift root ages noticeably. Rama (2018) compared three tree priors (uniform, fossilized birth-death and coalescent) on five Indo-European datasets and found that the choice shifted the inferred root date by up to about three millennia, and changed the placement of Anatolian and Tocharian near the root, while well-established subgroups were recovered under all three priors. Ritchie and Ho (2019), testing four lexical datasets, found origin-time estimates to be fairly robust to the choice of tree prior, though less so than in comparable analyses of genetic data. They also found that speciation priors fitted better than a constant-size coalescent prior at all the taxonomic scales they examined, but that datasets with narrower taxonomic and geographic sampling fitted the expectations of a birth-death model less well. The sampling proportion \(\rho\) also matters. If a family is represented by a small fraction of its languages, a birth-death prior that assumes complete sampling will place internal nodes in the wrong places. Diversified sampling, in which one language per subgroup is chosen, violates the assumption of random sampling made by most birth-death priors, and biology has developed priors for this case. The parameters of the tree prior are themselves seldom well estimated from a single family (Table 10.1), so it is the choice of prior, not the estimated speciation and extinction rates, that usually matters for dates. 10.5 Tip-dating with ancient languages 10.5.1 Dated tips Indo-European, Semitic, Sinitic and a few other families include languages known from texts that are centuries or millennia old: Hittite, Tocharian, Latin, Ancient Greek, Vedic Sanskrit, Gothic, Old Irish, Akkadian, Classical Chinese. Such languages can be used in two ways. In node dating, they provide minimum ages for the clades containing them, and they may be excluded from the data matrix entirely. In tip dating, they are included in the data matrix as tips whose ages are fixed, or given a prior distribution, at the dates of their attestation. Because the date of a text is itself often uncertain by decades or centuries, the second option is the safer one: in palaeontology, fixing uncertain fossil ages at point values has been shown to bias estimates of divergence times and topology (Barido-Sottani et al. 2019, 2020). Their lexical data then directly inform the rate of change: a language that stopped changing 3,000 years ago should have accumulated fewer changes since the root than a living language. The idea comes from the study of measurably evolving populations in virology (Drummond et al. 2003), where viruses sampled at different times provide a direct measure of the rate. Tip dating is attractive because the ages of attested languages are among the most secure pieces of chronological information available. They do not require assumptions about when a split happened, only about when a text was written. Its limitations are also clear. Ancient languages are often attested in limited corpora, so many meanings of a basic vocabulary list are missing. They may be literary or archaic registers rather than the spoken vernacular of their time. And they raise the question of whether they are ancestors of later languages, discussed in Section 10.6. 10.5.2 Root-to-tip regression A quick check of temporal signal in heterochronous data is the root-to-tip regression, popularized in virology by TempEst (Rambaut et al. 2016). If the tree is rooted correctly and the clock is roughly strict, the root-to-tip distance \(d_i\) of tip \(i\) in a phylogram is approximately \[\begin{equation} d_i \approx r\,(T - a_i), \tag{10.2} \end{equation}\] where \(T\) is the root age and \(a_i\) is the age of tip \(i\) (zero for living languages). The slope of the regression of \(d_i\) on \(a_i\) estimates \(-r\), and the point where the line crosses zero distance estimates \(T\). The scatter around the line indicates departure from a strict clock. In virology, this plot is used to detect outliers and to check whether there is enough temporal signal to estimate rates from the tip dates alone. Because the tips share ancestral branches, the usual regression p-values are invalid. A complementary test randomizes the tip ages among tips and checks whether the observed slope is stronger than in the randomized datasets, the date-randomization test (S. Duchêne et al. 2015). We simulate a family of 24 languages with a root at 6,000 years, of which eight are known only from ancient texts, with lexical change under a mildly relaxed clock (het_phylo, with tip ages tip_age). In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, this is a parameter-recovery exercise: the data follow the nearly clocklike process that the regression assumes, so success here shows only that the method works when its assumptions hold. The code that simulates the heterochronous family is listed in Section C.4.4, together with the derivation of Equation (10.2). d <- node.depth.edgelength(het_phylo)[1:n] # root-to-tip distances fit <- lm(d ~ tip_age) root_hat <- unname(coef(fit)[1] / -coef(fit)[2]) # where d reaches zero plot(tip_age, d, pch = ifelse(tip_age > 0, 16, 1), xlim = c(0, 7), ylim = c(0, max(d) * 1.05), las = 1, xlab = "Tip age (millennia before present)", ylab = "Root-to-tip distance (changes)") abline(fit, lwd = 2); abline(v = 6, lty = 3) Figure 10.3: Root-to-tip regression for a simulated family of 24 languages, eight of them ancient (filled circles, plotted at their attestation ages). The regression line crosses zero distance near the root age; the dotted line marks the true root age of 6 millennia. # date-randomization test: permute tip ages among tips perm_slopes <- replicate(500, coef(lm(d ~ sample(tip_age)))[2]) c(rate_per_kyr = unname(-coef(fit)[2]), root_age = root_hat, randomization_p = mean(perm_slopes <= coef(fit)[2])) #> rate_per_kyr root_age randomization_p #> 76.290 6.536 0.000 The estimated rate is close to the simulated mean of 80 changes per millennium, the estimated root age is within about half a millennium of the truth (somewhat too old here, partly because of rate variation and the small constant the simulation adds to every branch), and the date-randomization test shows that the temporal signal is far stronger than would be expected by chance. In real linguistic data, root-to-tip plots are rarely shown, but they should be. They reveal ancient languages that are too divergent or not divergent enough for their age, which can indicate coding problems, missing data, misplacement in the tree, or an ancient language that is an ancestor rather than a sister of its relatives. 10.5.3 Missing data in ancient languages Ancient languages are often poorly attested, and missing data interacts with the model of lexical evolution in subtle ways. If an unattested meaning is treated as absent rather than unknown, the language appears to have lost cognates it may in fact have had, which makes it look more divergent and pushes it away from its relatives. Ryder and Nicholls (2011) developed a stochastic Dollo model that handles missing data explicitly, and applied it to dating Proto-Indo-European, building on Nicholls and Gray (2008). Their analyses showed that careful treatment of missing data matters for root ages. More generally, the way ancient languages are coded, and the way their placement in the tree is treated, became central issues in the debate over Indo-European dates (Section 10.9.1). 10.6 Ancient languages: tips, ancestors or sisters? 10.6.1 What an attested language is Ancient languages are not simply fossils in the biological sense, and the analogy, useful as it is, hides a problem that historical linguists have long recognized. An attested stage of a language can stand in at least four different relations to the later languages in a dataset: it can be (very close to) the direct ancestor of some of them, as Old Norse is of Icelandic; it can be a sister lineage with no surviving descendants, as Hittite, Tocharian and Gothic are; it can be a close relative of the real ancestor, a different variety of the same speech community. Most Old English texts are in West Saxon, whereas Modern Standard English continues mainly Anglian dialects; the Romance languages continue spoken Latin rather than the Classical Latin of the texts; the Middle Indo-Aryan languages are not the descendants of Classical Sanskrit in any simple sense; it can be a witness to a dialect network rather than to a single lineage, if its descendants or sisters arose by the diversification of a continuum in which innovations spread across overlapping areas [Garrett (2006); Section 8.7]. Which of these holds is itself an inference, made with the comparative method and philology, and it is often uncertain. It matters for three stages of an analysis. For taxon selection, it determines which ancient varieties to include (a vernacular-like variety is more informative than a literary standard, and two stages of one lineage may be better than one), and whether an ancient language should enter the data matrix at all or only provide a node calibration. For character coding, it determines how to treat register-specific vocabulary, archaisms and gaps in the corpus: a basic word unattested in a small corpus must be coded as unknown, not absent (Section 10.5.3), and a literary word that the spoken language did not use creates a spurious unique change. For interpretation, it determines what a date means: if an ancient language sits on a side branch, the split between it and its relatives must be older than its attestation, and a model that cannot place it on the line of descent will push that split, and with it the root, back in time. 10.6.2 The fossilized birth-death process Paleobiology faced the same problem as linguistics: how to combine dated extinct taxa and living taxa in a single, coherent prior. The answer was the fossilized birth-death (FBD) process (Stadler 2010; Heath et al. 2014). In the FBD model, lineages split at rate \(\lambda\), go extinct at rate \(\mu\), and are sampled as fossils at rate \(\psi\) while alive. Living lineages at the present are sampled with probability \(\rho\). The process defines a prior on trees that includes both the living tips and the dated fossil samples. Because fossils are sampled from lineages that may have continued to evolve, a fossil can be a sampled ancestor: a sample lying directly on a lineage that has living descendants, rather than on a side branch that went extinct. Sampled ancestors appear in the tree as tips with zero-length branches, and specialized MCMC moves are needed to add and remove them (Gavryushkina et al. 2014). For languages, the analogy is direct but, as the previous section showed, imperfect. An attested ancient language is a “fossil” sampled from a lineage at a known time. Latin is the standard example of a plausible ancestor; Hittite and Tocharian have no living descendants. A standard birth-death prior forces every ancient language to sit at the tip of its own branch, which must be at least slightly longer than zero. If the ancient language is really an ancestor, the model must explain the absence of its unique changes by accumulating a long branch elsewhere, and this can distort the rates and dates. The FBD prior with sampled ancestors allows the ancient language to sit directly on the lineage leading to its descendants, if the data support it. The FBD process brings two further benefits. It provides a coherent prior on the times of all nodes given the sampled ancient languages, instead of combining ad hoc calibration densities with a tree prior and suffering the interactions described in Section 10.3.2. And it allows total-evidence dating, in which the ancient languages contribute both their dates and their data, as fossils contribute both stratigraphic ages and morphology in paleobiology (Pyron 2011; Ronquist, Klopfstein, et al. 2012; Zhang et al. 2016). Table 10.3 compares the four ways of using an attested language. Table 10.3: Four ways of using an attested ancient language in a dating analysis. Treatment What is assumed What the ancient language’s data contribute Typical consequence for dates Main risk Node calibration only The language belongs to a specified clade, attested by a given date Nothing; only its date enters, as a minimum age Depends on the density chosen for the clade age Treating attestation as origin; wrong clade Dated tip, standard tree prior The language is a sister lineage that ended at attestation Its cognates, which inform both topology and rate If it is really ancestral, splits are pushed older than they should be Forced side branches; missing data read as change Dated tip, sampled-ancestor (FBD) prior It may be an ancestor or a sister; the data decide As above, plus evidence on ancestry Intermediate; depends on how well ancestry is identified Ancestry weakly identified with fragmentary data Ancestry constraint The language is (nearly) the ancestor of specified descendants As above, with its position fixed Younger splits if it is in fact a sister Encodes a philological judgment as a certainty 10.6.3 Ancestor or sister: what the data can tell How well can the lexical data distinguish an ancestor from a sister on a short side branch? The evidence for ancestry is negative: an ancestral language should show no lexical changes of its own, no cognate classes gained or lost that its descendants lack. Suppose an ancient language is attested for \(n\) meanings of the list, each replaced at rate \(k\) per millennium, and sits on a side branch of length \(x\) millennia. It is then expected to show about \(n k x\) unique replacements. If none is observed, the data are consistent with any side branch shorter than about \(3/(nk)\) millennia, the familiar “rule of three” for a Poisson count of zero. With a retention of 0.86 per millennium (\(k \approx 0.15\)), a language attested for all 200 meanings excludes side branches longer than about a century, but one attested for 50 meanings excludes only those longer than about four centuries, and one attested for only 20 meanings cannot exclude a side branch of almost a millennium. Conversely, a few apparent unique changes can arise from a literary register, a scribal tradition or a regional variety rather than from a separate line of descent, and the model has no way to tell these apart. In the terms of Section 6.10, ancestry is identifiable under the model but often not practically estimable from fragmentarily attested languages, and the posterior probability that an ancient language is an ancestor is correspondingly sensitive to coding and to the prior on sampled ancestors. The calculation behind these figures, as a short R function with a table for several list sizes, is in Section C.4.6. 10.6.4 Ancestry constraints and sampled ancestors in linguistics Chang et al. (2015) argued that much of the disagreement between phylogenetic and traditional estimates of the age of Indo-European arose from the way ancient languages were treated. Several ancient languages in their dataset are widely accepted as ancestral, or very close to ancestral, to particular modern languages, such as Latin to the Romance languages and Vedic Sanskrit to many modern Indo-Aryan languages. When these were constrained to be ancestors, the estimated root age fell considerably. Heggarty et al. (2023) later used the sampled-ancestor framework in BEAST 2, which estimates rather than imposes ancestry, on a newly compiled Indo-European dataset. Their results and the debate they generated are discussed in Section 10.9.1. Seen through Table 10.3, the two studies made different choices about how much of the philological judgment to impose and how much to leave to the data, and the previous section shows why the data alone may not settle the question. A dating study with ancient languages should therefore report its root age under more than one of the four treatments, and say which ancient languages it regards as ancestors and on what philological grounds. Goldstein (2024) examined these issues in a single, well-documented case, the diversification of Latin into the Romance languages. The study addresses three problems that recur in Bayesian dating: sensitivity to the model, the dependence of root-age estimates on uncertain interior-node ages, and the relationship between ancient languages and their modern counterparts. Its results support a gradualist account of the formation of Romance that most likely began after 300 CE, and they are consistent with treating Classical Latin as a sampled ancestor of the Romance languages, that is, as lying on the branch that leads to them. Because the history of Romance is unusually well known, analyses of this kind are among the few places where a dating method’s behavior can be compared with independent historical evidence. Several developments of the FBD framework in paleobiology have not, to our knowledge, been used with language data. Skyline versions of the birth-death and FBD processes let the rates of splitting, extinction and sampling change through time in piecewise-constant intervals (Stadler et al. 2013). For languages, a time-varying sampling rate is especially relevant: the probability that a language is attested in writing was essentially zero before the invention of writing and has increased since. A model with constant sampling through time misrepresents this. Stratigraphic range models treat a taxon known over an interval of time, rather than at a single date, as a single lineage observed repeatedly. Languages attested over several centuries in a sequence of texts, such as Latin, Greek or Chinese, are natural candidates. Total-evidence dating with morphological clocks (Zhang et al. 2016; Gavryushkina et al. 2017) combines data partitions with different clock models, which is directly relevant for analyses that combine lexical and structural data for ancient and modern languages (Chapter 9). Finally, calibration cross-validation, in which each calibration in turn is left out and its node age predicted from the others, can detect inconsistent calibrations (Near et al. 2005); Section 10.8 shows how simple it is to apply. 10.7 Calibration pitfalls Many disputes over linguistic dates turn out, on close inspection, to be disputes over calibrations. The following problems recur. Circularity. If a calibration is derived from an archaeological hypothesis, the dated tree cannot then be used to test that hypothesis. Using the date of Lapita pottery to calibrate the age of Oceanic, and then claiming that the dated tree supports a Lapita-associated spread of Oceanic languages, would be circular. Careful studies avoid this by using historical calibrations unrelated to the hypothesis under test, or by checking that the result is robust when the relevant calibrations are removed. Attestation is not origin. The date of the earliest text in a language is a minimum age for the clade that contains it, not an estimate of the clade’s age. Treating it as the age of the split, for example with a narrow normal distribution centered on it, biases dates downward. Wrong clade. A calibration must be attached to the correct node. If historical evidence dates the separation of two dialect groups but the calibration is applied to the most recent common ancestor of a larger clade, or the clade is not monophyletic in the tree, the calibration constrains the wrong event. The miscalibration scenario in the R example below shows the consequences. Overconfident calibrations. Narrow calibration densities express certainty that the evidence rarely supports. Because calibrations determine the precision of all dates (Section 10.1), overconfident calibrations yield overconfident dates throughout the tree. Unintended interactions. As shown in Section 10.3.2, several calibrations together, combined with a tree prior, can produce an effective prior that nobody intended. Extrapolation. If all calibrations are shallow, for example within the last two millennia, the root age is estimated by extrapolating the clock model far beyond the range of the calibrations. Any misspecification of the clock, for instance the time-dependence of rates discussed in Section 9.5.7, then affects the root most strongly. Undetected borrowing and parallel change. Borrowing between sister languages makes them appear more similar and the nodes that join them younger (Section 8.3). Chang et al. (2015) used the term advergence for the process by which languages in contact become more similar after their split, which can bias dates downward. Undetected borrowing from outside the family can have the opposite effect, making a language appear more divergent. Model misspecification beyond the clock. The substitution model, the treatment of ascertainment bias and the model of rate variation among characters all affect branch lengths and therefore dates. Chapter 7 discusses these; Chapter 15 gathers the evidence on how much they matter in practice. The following example explores some of these pitfalls with ape’s chronos() on a simulated family of 20 languages (cal_phylo, a phylogram with lognormally varying rates) with a true root age of 6,000 years. We date the same phylogram under six calibration schemes, including one in which a calibration has been attached to the wrong, younger node with a minimum age that belongs to an older event. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, the misattributed scheme is a test of robustness under misspecification of the calibrations, the other schemes a comparison of how much each kind of calibration constrains the dates when the calibrations are correct. calib <- function(node, lo, hi) data.frame(node = node, age.min = lo, age.max = hi, soft.bounds = FALSE) schemes <- list( "Root fixed at 6" = calib(n + 1, 6, 6), "Root between 5 and 7" = calib(n + 1, 5, 7), "Three internal (+/-15%)" = calib(cal_nodes, 0.85 * tc, 1.15 * tc), "Root window + three internal" = calib(c(n + 1, cal_nodes), c(5, 0.85 * tc), c(7, 1.15 * tc)), "One shallow internal only" = calib(cal_nodes[3], 0.85 * tc[3], 1.15 * tc[3]), "Three internal, one misattributed" = calib(cal_nodes, c(0.85 * tc[1:2], 1.6 * tc[3]), c(1.15 * tc[1:2], 2 * tc[3])) ) res <- t(sapply(schemes, function(cal) { ch <- suppressWarnings(chronos(cal_phylo, lambda = 1, model = "correlated", calibration = cal, quiet = TRUE)) est <- branching.times(ch) c(root = unname(est[as.character(n + 1)]), rmse = sqrt(mean((est - true_ages[names(est)])^2))) })) knitr::kable(round(res, 2), col.names = c("Estimated root age (millennia)", "RMSE of all node ages (millennia)"), caption = "Root age and node-age error under six calibration schemes for the same simulated phylogram (true root age 6 millennia).") Table 10.4: Root age and node-age error under six calibration schemes for the same simulated phylogram (true root age 6 millennia). Estimated root age (millennia) RMSE of all node ages (millennia) Root fixed at 6 6.00 0.19 Root between 5 and 7 6.73 0.34 Three internal (+/-15%) 6.27 0.25 Root window + three internal 6.27 0.25 One shallow internal only 6.35 0.26 Three internal, one misattributed 7.39 0.72 The simulation of cal_phylo and the choice of calibrated nodes are listed in Section C.4.5. Several lessons emerge from Table 10.4. A fixed root age gives good estimates of the other nodes, but only because we told the method the right answer. A root window lets the root age drift within the window, here toward its older end. Internal calibrations that bracket the true ages constrain the root reasonably well even without a root calibration. In this run, a single shallow calibration also happens to give a reasonable root age, but this is luck; with other seeds or stronger rate variation, extrapolating from a single shallow node can go badly wrong. And a single misattributed calibration pushes the whole tree older, with the error spreading to nodes far from the one that was miscalibrated. A penalized-likelihood analysis like this one gives point estimates only. A Bayesian analysis would show the same effects in the posterior distributions, along with the uncertainty. 10.8 Validating dates How do we know whether a published date is right? The answer depends on which of five different questions is being asked, and the vocabulary of Section 6.10 keeps them apart. Implementation validation. Does the software compute what the model says? Prior-only runs that reproduce the intended effective priors (Section 10.3.2), and agreement between independent implementations of the same model, answer this question. They say nothing about whether the model is appropriate. Parameter recovery. Are the dates practically estimable from data of this size? Simulating cognate data on trees with the family’s size, calibrations and rate variation, under the analysis model, and checking that the root age is recovered with intervals of the stated coverage, answers this question. Success shows that the data could determine the dates if the model were right. Robustness under misspecification. How much do dates change when the data are generated by processes the model ignores? Simulations with borrowing (Section 8.3), rate shifts and bursts (Section 9.8), ancestral languages placed on side branches (Section 10.6.3) and realistic missing data in ancient languages answer this question. Empirical adequacy. Could the fitted model have generated data like the real data? Posterior predictive checks (Section 7.10), tests of clock adequacy (Section 9.5.7) and root-to-tip outliers (Section 10.5.2) address this question. Independent historical validation. Do the dates agree with evidence that played no part in estimating them? This is the question most readers have in mind, and it has two forms. Calibration cross-validation leaves each calibration out in turn, re-estimates the tree, and asks whether the omitted node’s age is predicted correctly from the others (Near et al. 2005). External comparison sets the estimated dates against archaeological, genetic or documentary evidence that was not used as a calibration. External comparison is only as independent as the evidence. An archaeological date used to calibrate a tree cannot then validate it, and a root age that is “consistent with” an archaeological horizon is weak support if the credible interval is wide enough to be consistent with its competitors too. Agreement between an inferred topology and the subgroups of the comparative method is not independent validation of the topology, still less of the dates, because the cognate judgments that went into the analysis are themselves products of the comparative method, and because shared cognates include shared retentions, whereas subgroups are defined by shared innovations. The appropriate hierarchy of certainty is that a dated phylogeny estimates a root age under its assumptions; agreement with independent evidence suggests or is consistent with a historical scenario; only convergent agreement among several kinds of independent evidence, robust to the main misspecifications, comes close to demonstrating one. Published examples of the first and third kinds of evidence are recent. King (2026a) applied posterior simulation-based calibration, which simulates datasets from parameter values drawn from the posterior for a given empirical dataset, to a tip-dated analysis of Indo-European vocabulary in BEAST 2. The posteriors were well calibrated, which suggests that the dating machinery is not biased by implementation problems; but datasets simulated from the posterior did not make node ages any more precise than the original analysis, in line with theoretical limits on the identifiability of node ages (Section 10.1.1). This is implementation validation, not evidence that the model is right. Rönchen, Billing, et al. (2025), in a manuscript forming part of a doctoral dissertation (Rönchen 2025), tested robustness under misspecification instead. They simulated Indo-European vocabulary evolution with a richer model than the inference models (loans, a topology close to the consensus of historical linguists and varying rates of change) and reported that the methods of Bouckaert et al. (2012) and Chang et al. (2015) did not reliably recover the simulated root age: their inferences varied with model assumptions and with the randomness of the evolutionary process, and their credible intervals substantially understated the errors. The two studies are complementary rather than contradictory. A sampler can be well calibrated for its own model while the model is misspecified for the data, and only the second kind of study can show how much that matters for dates. Calibration cross-validation is easy to apply and catches the misattribution pitfall of the previous section. The function below leaves each calibration out in turn, re-dates the tree with chronos(), and records the predicted age of the omitted node. We apply it to the “root window plus three internal” scheme, once with all calibrations correct and once with the third internal calibration misattributed as in Table 10.4. loo_calib <- function(phylo, cal, model = "correlated", lambda = 1) { # leave each calibration out, re-date, predict the omitted node's age out <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(cal)), function(i) { ch <- suppressWarnings(chronos(phylo, lambda = lambda, model = model, calibration = cal[-i, ], quiet = TRUE)) c(predicted = unname(branching.times(ch)[as.character(cal$node[i])])) })) data.frame(node = cal$node, min = cal$age.min, max = cal$age.max, predicted = as.vector(out), outside = as.vector(out) < cal$age.min | as.vector(out) > cal$age.max) } good <- calib(c(n + 1, cal_nodes), c(5, 0.85 * tc), c(7, 1.15 * tc)) bad <- calib(c(n + 1, cal_nodes), c(5, 0.85 * tc[1:2], 1.6 * tc[3]), c(7, 1.15 * tc[1:2], 2 * tc[3])) loo <- rbind(cbind(scheme = "all correct", loo_calib(cal_phylo, good)), cbind(scheme = "third misattributed", loo_calib(cal_phylo, bad))) knitr::kable(loo, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Leave-one-calibration-out cross-validation: the age of each calibrated node predicted from the remaining calibrations, compared with its calibration window.")
