With the misattributed calibration, most of the calibrations fail: the misattributed node is predicted far younger than the window it was given, and other calibrated nodes are predicted older than theirs, because the misattributed calibration, still in place when they are left out, stretches the whole tree. Cross-validation therefore shows that the calibrations are mutually inconsistent under the clock model, but it does not by itself say which one is wrong. The largest discrepancy, here at the misattributed node, is the natural place to start, and the historical evidence behind each calibration must decide. Most language families have only a handful of calibrations, so cross-validation costs a few extra runs. 10.9 Family-by-family review The rest of this chapter reviews published dated phylogenies, family by family. For each family we describe the main studies, the data and calibrations they used, their root-age estimates, and the debates they provoked. Dates are given as years before present (BP), as reported by the authors and rounded; readers should consult the original papers for exact values and intervals, which depend on the model and data subset. We have included only studies we are confident exist, and where we are unsure of a precise figure we say so rather than guess. Chapter 11 covers the homeland inferences that many of these studies also made. Two cautions apply throughout. First, each root age is an estimate conditional on the data, coding, clock model, tree prior and calibrations of the study, and the main sources of disagreement between studies of the same family are usually to be found among these (Table 10.1). Second, several studies report that their trees recover subgroups established by the comparative method. That agreement is reassuring about data quality, but it is not independent validation of the trees, since the cognate judgments come from the same comparative tradition, and it is no validation at all of the dates (Section 10.8). When a study links its dates to an archaeological horizon, the useful question is whether that horizon was also used as a calibration. 10.9.1 Indo-European No family has been dated more often, or with more controversy, than Indo-European. Two hypotheses about its origin have dominated the debate. The steppe or Kurgan hypothesis places Proto-Indo-European in the Pontic-Caspian steppe around 6,000 to 6,500 years ago, and associates its spread with mobile pastoralists who used horses and wheeled vehicles (Anthony 2007). A key argument is linguistic paleontology. Proto-Indo-European can be reconstructed with a vocabulary for wheels, axles and wagons, and wheeled vehicles are not attested archaeologically before the late fifth or fourth millennium BCE. The Anatolian hypothesis associates Indo-European with the spread of farming from Anatolia into Europe, beginning around 8,000 to 9,500 years ago (Renfrew 1987). The two hypotheses predict root ages that differ by two to three millennia, which makes dating potentially decisive. Gray and Atkinson (2003) analyzed 87 Indo-European languages using the cognate judgments of Dyen et al. (1992) for the Swadesh 200-meaning list, supplemented with Hittite and the two Tocharian languages, for a total of 2,449 cognate sets coded as binary characters. They estimated trees with MrBayes under a binary restriction-site model with gamma rate variation, then dated a sample of trees by penalized-likelihood rate smoothing (Sanderson 2002), using 14 calibrations from historically documented events and attestations. The estimated root age fell between about 7,800 and 9,800 years BP, consistent with the Anatolian hypothesis and older than the steppe hypothesis predicts. They tested the robustness of this result to several of their assumptions, including the choice of calibrations and the treatment of the data. The paper, in Nature, launched the modern debate about phylogenetic dating in linguistics. Subsequent work examined the robustness of the result. Atkinson et al. (2005) analyzed the Indo-European dataset of Ringe, Warnow and Taylor (Chapter 4) under both a reversible model and a stochastic Dollo model, tested both methods on simulated data with borrowing, and answered several criticisms of the earlier analysis of the Dyen data. Nicholls and Gray (2008) introduced a stochastic Dollo model for cognate data, in which each cognate set arises once and can then be lost many times (Chapter 7), and found root ages broadly compatible with Gray and Atkinson’s. Ryder and Nicholls (2011) extended the model to handle missing data and also estimated a root age broadly in line with the earlier results. Bouckaert et al. (2012) combined dating with phylogeography in a single Bayesian model. They used cognate data for 103 ancient and modern Indo-European languages, treated the ancient languages as dated tips, and modeled the geographic spread of the family as a random walk on the map (Chapter 11). The analysis favored an Anatolian homeland over a steppe homeland, and the root age, which overlapped the range estimated by Gray and Atkinson, fitted an agricultural expansion from Anatolia beginning roughly 8,000 to 9,500 years ago. The paper was criticized on several grounds, including its geographic model, its treatment of language contact and its data (Pereltsvaig and Lewis 2015). Its methodological contribution, the integration of time, geography and lexical evolution in one framework, has been widely adopted. Chang et al. (2015) re-examined the question with a revised dataset, building on IELex, and argued that the earlier analyses had a systematic bias. In their unconstrained analyses, ancient languages such as Latin, Vedic Sanskrit and Old Irish were placed as side branches rather than as ancestors of their modern relatives. They argued that this, combined with advergence (convergent similarity through contact) among some modern languages, inflated the root age. When they imposed ancestry constraints, requiring the ancient languages to be ancestral or nearly ancestral to their modern descendants, the estimated root age fell to roughly 6,000 years BP (medians of about 5,900 to 6,500 years across their main analyses), consistent with the steppe hypothesis. The paper made the treatment of ancient languages, and the question of whether they are ancestors or sisters, central to the debate. These analyses appeared during the same years in which ancient DNA transformed the archaeology of Indo-European. Haak et al. (2015) reported genomic evidence for a massive migration of people related to steppe pastoralists of the Yamnaya culture into central Europe around 5,000 years ago, and argued that this migration was a source for at least some Indo-European languages in Europe. Ancient DNA does not date languages, but it identifies population movements to which language spreads can plausibly be linked, and it shifted many scholars toward the steppe hypothesis, at least for the European branches. Pereltsvaig and Lewis (2015) provide a critique of the phylogenetic approach from a linguistic perspective, defending the steppe hypothesis. Garrett (2006) argued that several Indo-European subgroups arose through convergence among already-differentiated dialects rather than through clean tree-like splits, which complicates any attempt to date them as nodes of a tree. Heggarty et al. (2023) assembled a new Indo-European dataset, IE-CoR, with cognate judgments for around 160 languages and 170 meanings, compiled by specialists in each branch under explicit and consistent protocols. They analyzed it in BEAST 2 with a sampled-ancestor model, so that ancient languages could be ancestors if the data supported it, rather than having that relationship imposed or forbidden. The estimated root age was around 8,100 years BP. The authors proposed a “hybrid” model in which Indo-European originated south of the Caucasus, with one branch later reaching the steppe and spreading from there into Europe, a scenario intended to reconcile the phylogenetic dates with the ancient DNA evidence for steppe migrations. The study is the most thorough phylogenetic analysis of Indo-European to date, but it did not end the debate. The interpretation of the root date, the coding of particular cognates and the handling of ancestry continue to be discussed. The IE-CoR data have since been published as a stand-alone, openly documented dataset of 160 languages and 170 meanings, with 4,981 cognate sets, explicit coding of known horizontal transfer and calibration data for each language (Anderson et al. 2025), so the analysis can now be re-examined independently. The first critiques have addressed the data and the topology as much as the dates. Kassian and Starostin (2025) acknowledged that the lexical data are much better curated than in earlier studies, but argued that cognate coding in places still fails to separate true cognacy from areal diffusion and from independent derivations from the same root, that both the consensus topology and the dates conflict with historical evidence in several respects, and that a list of 170 meanings may be too short to resolve the topology of so many languages robustly. Two simulation studies bearing on the reliability of Indo-European dating are discussed in Section 10.8. Indo-European dating has also been used to test methodological choices. Rama (2018) compared tree priors on several Indo-European datasets, and found that the choice affected the inferred root age. The general lesson of the Indo-European literature is that the main sources of disagreement have been calibrations, the treatment of ancient languages, the data, and the interpretation of the results in light of archaeology and genetics, more than the inference software. Chapter 15 returns to this controversy. 10.9.2 Austronesian Austronesian is one of the largest language families in the world, with well over a thousand languages spread from Madagascar to Easter Island and from Taiwan to New Zealand. Its expansion is one of the clearest cases of a language family spread by seafaring migration. The standard hypothesis places its homeland in Taiwan, with a subsequent spread through the Philippines and Island Southeast Asia into the Pacific, associated with the “out of Taiwan” or “express train” model of Austronesian settlement (Bellwood 2005; Diamond and Bellwood 2003). Gray and Jordan (2000) applied maximum parsimony to 77 Austronesian languages and found a tree consistent with the express-train model, with Formosan languages at the base and a sequence of splits following the proposed route of settlement. The Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database (Greenhill et al. 2008) then made much larger analyses possible. Gray et al. (2009) analyzed basic vocabulary for 400 Austronesian languages in a Bayesian framework with a relaxed clock and calibrations from archaeology and history. The tree placed the root in Taiwan around 5,200 years BP, consistent with the archaeological evidence. More strikingly, the dated tree revealed a pattern of pulses and pauses. After the initial split, there was a long pause of roughly a millennium before Malayo-Polynesian expanded from Taiwan into the Philippines, followed by a rapid pulse of expansion through Island Southeast Asia and into the Pacific. A second pause occurred in western Polynesia before the rapid settlement of eastern Polynesia. The authors linked the pauses to the challenges of crossing new sea gaps, such as the Bashi Channel between Taiwan and the Philippines, and the pulses to technological or social innovations such as improved outrigger canoes. The study is an example of how a dated tree can reveal the tempo of a prehistoric expansion, not just its starting date. Greenhill, Drummond, et al. (2010) examined the robustness of the Austronesian topology to borrowing, coding choices and missing data, and found that the main subgroups were robust. Greenhill and Gray (2009) addressed common misconceptions about Bayesian phylogenetic methods among Austronesianists. Some of the archaeological dates used in Austronesian work have themselves been revised. For example, high-precision radiocarbon dating has placed the initial settlement of East Polynesia, including New Zealand, later than many earlier estimates (Wilmshurst et al. 2011), which matters for calibrations of the youngest Polynesian clades. King et al. (2024) turned from the age of the family to the internal history of Malayo-Polynesian in the Philippines. They analyzed 202 doculects from the ABVD (147 Philippine languages and an outgroup of 55 Formosan ones), with 7,565 cognate sets in 185 meanings whose coding had been revised by specialists, under a covarion model with a relaxed clock in BEAST 2. They did not estimate the age of the family: the root had a narrow prior centered on 5,200 years BP, taken from Gray et al. (2009), so all their dates are conditional on that value. Under this prior, the Philippine languages began to diverge about 3,400 years BP (HPD interval roughly 2,600 to 4,200). The main results concern topology and process. The languages of northern Sulawesi (Sangiric and Minahasan) were strongly supported as sister to all other Philippine languages, and the Batanic languages nested within northern Luzon, a pattern the authors read as incompatible with a simple north-to-south dispersal out of Taiwan and as consistent with a rapid initial expansion followed by south-to-north spread. The trees carried a pervasive geographical signal, which they interpreted as evidence that diffusion across chains of neighboring languages dominated after the initial spread; the unstable position of the Gorontalo-Mongondow languages was plausibly due to later contact in Sulawesi. Language shifts to Austronesian in “Negrito” populations were dated to various points within the last two millennia, with no sign of elevated rates of lexical change on the branches where they occurred. Methodologically, the study examined which cognate sets supported each competing position of an unstable group, rather than reporting clade probabilities alone. As with other analyses of subgrouping, its agreement or disagreement with traditional subgroups is evidence about the cognate data under the model, not an independent test of either. At a smaller scale, Smith and Rama (2022) dated a phylogeny of 87 Austronesian languages of Borneo with four historical calibrations. The inferred root was shallower than archaeological estimates for the settlement of the island, which they related to a possible linguistic leveling event, and a phylogeographic analysis placed the homelands of several subgroups along Borneo’s major rivers. 10.9.3 Bantu The Bantu languages, a branch of Niger-Congo with several hundred languages spoken across central, eastern and southern Africa, spread within the last few millennia from a homeland near the border of present-day Nigeria and Cameroon. Their expansion has long been associated with the spread of farming, and, later, iron working. The main debates concern the route: whether the eastern Bantu languages descend from populations that moved around the central African rainforest to the north and east, or through it. Holden (2002) applied maximum parsimony to basic vocabulary for 75 Bantu languages and found that the tree was consistent with the spread of farming. Currie et al. (2013) used Bayesian phylogeographic methods on Bantu language trees to reconstruct the locations of ancestral populations. Grollemund et al. (2015) analyzed basic vocabulary for over 400 Bantu languages in a Bayesian framework, combined with a phylogeographic model. They inferred that the expansion began in the mid-Holocene, on the order of five millennia ago, and that the major movements of Bantu-speaking populations tracked savannah habitats, crossing the rainforest zone mainly along savannah corridors that opened within it, such as the Sangha River Interval, rather than moving through closed forest. They also argued that the rate of expansion was slower where populations had to adapt to new habitats, such as the rainforest itself. The study linked both the route and the pace of a language expansion to habitat. Koile et al. (2022) revisited the question with a different phylogeographic model and a dataset of Bantu languages, and found support for an early route through the rainforest, contrary to the conclusion of Grollemund et al. (2015). Their time frame for the expansion was broadly similar. The disagreement shows how sensitive phylogeographic conclusions can be to the spatial model and the choice of languages, even when the dates broadly agree (Chapter 11). Grollemund et al. (2015) place the start of the expansion at roughly 5,000 years ago, while Koile et al. (2022) estimate the root at about 5,100 years BP and the migration through the forest at about 4,400 years BP, well before the savannah corridor opened. Lower-level studies have since refined the picture regionally. Gunnink et al. (2022) inferred a lexicon-based phylogeny of 34 Southern Bantu languages in which all derive from a single direct ancestor; because archaeology indicates several earlier migrations of Bantu speakers into southern Africa, they argued that the languages of the first migrants were lost and that the ancestor of the present Southern Bantu languages emerged in southern Africa during the second millennium CE. Gunnink et al. (2025) placed the previously unclassified Yeyi in Wider Eastern Bantu as a lineage of its own, closest to Narrow Eastern Bantu rather than to any of its present neighbors, and suggested an early migration into southern Africa. Pacchiarotti et al. (2024) showed for part of West-Coastal Bantu how a lexical phylogeny and a diagnostic sound change can disagree about subgrouping, because the sound change itself may have spread through lexical diffusion and contact. 10.9.4 Sino-Tibetan Sino-Tibetan includes Chinese (Sinitic) and several hundred Tibeto-Burman languages spoken from the Himalayas to Southeast Asia. Its homeland and age have long been debated. Hypotheses range from northern China, associated with millet farming in the Yellow River basin, to the eastern Himalayas or Sichuan. In 2019 two independent dated phylogenies of Sino-Tibetan were published within weeks of each other. Sagart et al. (2019) analyzed lexical data for 50 Sino-Tibetan languages, with root-meaning cognate coding and a relaxed clock, and estimated a root age of roughly 7,200 years BP. They linked the origin of the family to millet farmers of northern China, in the late Cishan and early Yangshao cultures. Zhang et al. (2019) analyzed 109 Sino-Tibetan languages and estimated a root age of roughly 5,900 years BP, also placing the homeland in northern China and associating the origin with the Yangshao culture, with later westward and southward movements linked to subsequent Neolithic cultures such as Majiayao. The two studies agree on a northern Chinese origin linked to millet agriculture but differ in their root dates by more than a millennium, and in some details of the internal structure. The difference is a useful reminder of how much dates depend on data, coding and calibrations, even when the general scenario agrees. A third continental analysis, by Zhang et al. (2020), used a larger and linguistically more diverse sample. It again found a primary split between Sinitic and Tibeto-Burman but placed the initial divergence earlier, at approximately 8,000 years before present, which the authors linked to the onset of millet agriculture in the Yellow River region. Three analyses with different data and teams thus agree on the general scenario while their root ages span roughly two millennia. Later work has concentrated on parts of the family that the continental studies sampled thinly. Wu et al. (2022) extended a subset of an existing Sino-Tibetan dataset with new vocabularies for the Kho-Bwa and Hrusish clusters and neighboring languages of the Tibet-Arunachal area and inferred dated phylogenies for their internal and external relations, and Dhakal et al. (2024) collected, transcribed and cognate-coded new data for eight South-Western Tibetic languages, including partial cognates, for a Bayesian analysis. Small studies built on primary data of this kind are what any future continental analysis will rest on. 10.9.5 Dravidian The Dravidian family has about 80 languages, spoken mainly in southern India, with outliers such as Brahui in Pakistan. Kolipakam et al. (2018) collected new basic vocabulary data for 20 Dravidian languages and estimated a root age of approximately 4,500 years BP. The estimate is consistent with some linguistic and archaeological proposals. They also examined the internal structure of the family, including the relationships among its main subgroups, and discussed the possible relationship of the Dravidian languages to the archaeological cultures of South Asia, including the Indus civilization, a question the phylogenetic results alone cannot resolve. 10.9.6 Uralic Uralic includes Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian, the Saami languages and the Samoyedic languages of Siberia, among others. Syrjänen et al. (2013) analyzed the internal classification of Uralic using basic vocabulary and phylogenetic methods, and the UraLex dataset grew out of this work. Honkola et al. (2013) produced a dated Uralic phylogeny, with a root in the mid-Holocene, and argued that the timing of major splits in the family coincided with climatic and cultural changes in northern Eurasia. We do not quote a precise root date from this study; readers should consult the original. Uralic is a family with relatively few calibrations and a long history of debate about its homeland and internal structure, so dated phylogenies are particularly sensitive to calibration choices. 10.9.7 Turkic The Turkic languages extend from Turkey to Siberia and China. Savelyev and Robbeets (2020) analyzed basic vocabulary for Turkic languages in a Bayesian framework and estimated the root age at roughly 2,100 years BP, with the earliest split separating the Bulgharic branch (represented today by Chuvash) from Common Turkic. The young age reflects the well-known shallowness of the family, whose languages are closely related. Hruschka et al. (2015) used Turkic as a test case for their model of regular sound change as concerted evolution (Chapter 9). Egorov et al. (2022) reanalyzed the internal structure of the family with strictly controlled word lists, explicit treatment of derivational drift and several algorithms (distance, Bayesian and parsimony). They confirmed Chuvash as the first outlier, found the rest of the family to diversify in a multifurcation into eight branches, and argued that Siberian Turkic is an areal rather than a genealogical unit; the subtitle of their paper names the limitation that intensive contact imposes on tree-based analyses of the family. 10.9.8 Transeurasian The Transeurasian or Altaic hypothesis groups Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic, with or without Koreanic and Japonic, into a single family. Most historical linguists regard this grouping as unproven or as reflecting long-term contact rather than common descent. Robbeets and Bouckaert (2018) applied Bayesian phylogenetic methods to a dataset of putative cognates across the five groups. Robbeets et al. (2021) then combined linguistic phylogenetics with archaeology and ancient DNA. They estimated a root age of roughly 9,000 years BP and associated the family’s origin with millet farmers of the West Liao River region in northeastern China, with subsequent spreads linked to agriculture. The study was widely publicized and heavily criticized. Critics argued, in a widely discussed preprint, that the cognate sets were not established by the comparative method and included many doubtful comparisons, that the archaeological and genetic data did not support the proposed scenario, and that the triangulation framework could not compensate for weaknesses in the linguistic data (Tian et al. 2022). The debate is a reminder that a phylogenetic analysis cannot establish the genealogical unity of a family whose cognates are themselves in dispute. The individual branches are on firmer ground. For Tungusic, whose unity is not in doubt, Oskolskaya et al. (2022) analyzed 254 basic-vocabulary items for 21 doculects; their trees are consistent with two classifications proposed earlier, and they estimate the age of Proto-Tungusic at between the 8th century BCE and the 12th century CE (95% HPD), an interval whose width reflects the scarcity of calibrations. 10.9.9 Semitic Kitchen et al. (2009) analyzed basic vocabulary for 25 Semitic languages, including ancient languages such as Akkadian, in a Bayesian framework. They estimated that Semitic originated around 5,750 years BP in the Levant, and that Ethiosemitic languages resulted from a single introduction of Semitic from southern Arabia into the Horn of Africa around 2,800 years BP. Semitic is unusual in having ancient languages attested from the third millennium BCE, which makes it a promising family for tip-dating and sampled-ancestor analyses. To our knowledge, a dated phylogeny of Afroasiatic as a whole, the much older family to which Semitic belongs, has not been attempted with comparable methods, which is unsurprising given the difficulty of establishing cognates at that time depth. 10.9.10 Pama-Nyungan Pama-Nyungan is the largest family of Australian languages, covering most of the continent. Bowern and Atkinson (2012) used Bayesian phylogenetics to investigate the internal structure of the family, which had long been debated, and found support for many established subgroups. Bouckaert et al. (2018) then produced a dated phylogeography of over 300 Pama-Nyungan languages. They estimated a root age of roughly six millennia and placed the origin near the Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia, with the family spreading across the continent from there. The result is significant because Pama-Nyungan speakers were hunter-gatherers. Its spread cannot be explained by agriculture, and it challenges the view that large language families spread mainly with farming (Diamond and Bellwood 2003). The Chirila database of Australian languages supports much of this work. 10.9.11 Japonic and Ainu Lee and Hasegawa (2011) analyzed 59 Japonic languages and dialects and estimated a root age of roughly 2,200 years BP. They interpreted this as support for the hypothesis that Japonic arrived in the Japanese archipelago with rice farmers from the Korean peninsula during the Yayoi period, rather than descending from the languages of the earlier Jomon hunter-gatherers. Lee and Hasegawa (2013) applied similar methods to Ainu dialects and discussed the results in relation to the archaeology of Hokkaido and neighboring regions. Huisman et al. (2025) revisited Japonic with a new dataset of 48 Japanese (including Old Japanese) and 33 Ryukyuan lects for 256 concepts, analyzing cognate characters together with binary phonotactic characters (the presence of particular two-segment sequences) in separate partitions on a shared tree. They estimated the Japanese-Ryukyuan split at around 400 to 500 BCE, consistent with the Yayoi-period scenario, and dated the ancestor of the Ryukyuan languages to around the ninth century CE, when the first traces of cereal farming appear in the northern Ryukyus. Old Japanese was a dated tip and the age of Southern Ryukyuan was calibrated, so the agreement of the deeper dates with the archaeological record is conditional on these choices. 10.9.12 South American families South America has a large number of language families, many of them poorly documented, and phylogenetic dating is still in its early stages there. Walker and Ribeiro (2011) applied Bayesian phylogeography to Arawakan, one of the most widespread families of lowland South America, to investigate its homeland and dispersal. Walker et al. (2012) studied the Tupi family with a simpler, distance-based tree built from 40-item ASJP word lists, mapped onto geography. Within Tupi, the Tupi-Guarani branch, which includes Guarani and the extinct Tupinamba, has been studied in more detail. Michael et al. (2015) produced a Bayesian phylogenetic classification of Tupi-Guarani, and Ferraz Gerardi et al. (2023) revisited its chronology, comparing phylogenetic dates with the archaeological record of the region. A recurrent difficulty for these families is the scarcity of reliable calibrations: there are few written records before European contact, and the correlation of archaeological cultures with language groups is often uncertain. We do not quote root dates for these studies. Birchall et al. (2016) combined the comparative method with computational phylogenetic analysis for the small Chapacuran family of the Bolivian–Brazilian border region, an example of how the two can be used together where documentation is thin. Michael and Chousou-Polydouri (2019) review the computational classifications of South American families and argue that character-based methods should be preferred to distance-based ones, and that adequate comparative datasets are the main bottleneck. Two recent studies prepare the ground for dated analyses. Michael et al. (2023) identified twelve calibration points for Arawakan from archaeological sites in zones into which Arawakan peoples expanded, together with more recent calibrations from the first historical mentions of ethnonyms and early lexical sources. Ferraz Gerardi et al. (2025) produced a Bayesian classification of the Je family (14 languages, 303 concepts) with well-supported Northern, Central and Southern subgroups. 10.9.13 Uto-Aztecan Uto-Aztecan extends from the western United States to Central America and includes Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. A long-standing debate concerns whether the family originated in the south, in Mexico, with maize farmers, as proposed by Jane Hill and others, or in the north, among hunter-gatherers, with maize farming adopted later by some branches. Wheeler and Whiteley (2015) analyzed the family with a parsimony-based sequence optimization method and examined its biogeography. Greenhill et al. (2023) produced a dated Bayesian phylogeny of Uto-Aztecan and argued for a relatively recent northern origin, roughly four millennia ago, which they interpreted as evidence against a southern, farming-driven origin. As with other families, the conclusion depends on the calibrations and on the relationship between language spread and subsistence, which remain debated. 10.9.14 Kra-Dai Tao et al. (2023) compiled a lexical dataset of 100 Kra-Dai (Tai-Kadai) languages, with 646 cognate sets based on the Swadesh 100-meaning list, and analyzed it in BEAST 2 under a covarion model with a relaxed lognormal clock, a birth-death skyline tree prior and node calibrations from historical records. The estimated root age was about 4,000 years BP (mean 4,041; 95% HPD 2,741 to 5,550). A discrete phylogeographic analysis over a sample of posterior trees favored an origin in the Guangxi-Guangdong area of southern China, with later dispersal toward Mainland Southeast Asia. The authors linked the diversification to demic diffusion and the spread of agriculture under late Holocene climate change, drawing also on genetic and archaeological data; as elsewhere, the association is an interpretation of the dates, not a test of them. Buckley et al. (2025) compared phylogenies of Kra-Dai languages and of the looms used by their speakers (Chapter 14). 10.9.15 Families with few or no dated phylogenies Many large and historically important families have not, to our knowledge, been the subject of a dated Bayesian phylogeny that is comparable in scope to the studies above, or have been analyzed only in preliminary or unpublished work. These include Austroasiatic (including Vietnamese, Khmer and the Munda languages of India), Hmong-Mien, Mayan, Oto-Manguean, Trans-New Guinea, most branches of Niger-Congo beyond Bantu, Nilo-Saharan (whose unity is itself contested), Afroasiatic as a whole, Nakh-Daghestanian, and most North American families other than Uto-Aztecan. Some of these, such as Mayan, have rich traditions of lexicostatistical and comparative work, including glottochronological estimates, and ancient written records (Classic Maya inscriptions) that could provide tip dates. Others, such as Trans-New Guinea, pose difficult problems of data and classification. These families represent clear opportunities for future work, with the caveat that many depend on primary documentation and cognate judgments that do not yet exist. Some gaps have begun to close. Kra-Dai now has a dated phylogeny (Section 10.9.14); the Mixtecan branch of Oto-Manguean has been subgrouped with Bayesian methods (Auderset et al. 2023); and the Timor-Alor-Pantar family of Papuan languages has been analyzed with a systematic comparison of models (Kaiping and Klamer 2022). For Kartvelian (South Caucasian), Gavashelishvili et al. (2023) inferred a dated phylogeny whose topology agrees with the accepted one but whose mean split dates are earlier than in previous studies, and combined it with the ranges of animals and plants whose names reconstruct to Proto-Kartvelian, archaeological cultures and ancient genomes to place the homeland in the Colchis region of the South Caucasus. Both of the last two studies stress how dialect-chain histories complicate tree inference (Chapter 8). 10.9.16 Global-scale dating At the global scale, Holman et al. (2011) applied ASJP chronology (Chapter 9) to estimate the ages of many of the world’s language families. The approach uses a single empirically calibrated relationship between lexical similarity and time, so it inherits the limitations of distance-based dating, but it provides rough estimates for families that have never been dated phylogenetically, and a common yardstick for comparing them. Rama and Wichmann (2020) proposed a generalized Bayesian dating method in the same spirit: trees are inferred from automatically detected cognates in 40-item ASJP lists, and node ages are predicted from tree lengths by a gamma regression fitted to a set of known historical time depths, so that no family-specific priors or calibrations are needed. Applied to 116 families, it gave dates broadly similar to those of published family-specific studies, but in tests against known dates its errors were somewhat larger than those of ASJP chronology, although the difference between the methods was not statistically significant. 10.10 Summary of dated studies Table 10.6 summarizes the studies reviewed above. Most dated families are younger than about ten millennia. This partly reflects the method’s limits. Cognate-based methods require cognates that can be identified, and beyond roughly ten millennia, very few basic vocabulary cognates survive in a recognizable form (Chapter 9). It also reflects selection: the families that have been dated are those with well-established cognate data, which tends to mean families of moderate depth. Many root ages fall in the Holocene and coincide roughly with the spread of agriculture. Indo-European (under the Anatolian interpretation), Austronesian, Bantu, Sino-Tibetan, Japonic and, if it exists, Transeurasian have all been linked to farming expansions, in line with the farming/language dispersal hypothesis (Bellwood 2005; Diamond and Bellwood 2003). But the counterexamples are important. Pama-Nyungan spread among hunter-gatherers, and the steppe interpretation of Indo-European links it to pastoralism rather than to the first farmers. Uto-Aztecan, on the analysis of Greenhill et al. (2023), also does not fit a farming-driven origin. The coincidence of dates with farming expansions is, moreover, partly a matter of study design: where archaeological dates of farming dispersals have served as calibrations, agreement with the farming hypothesis is built in rather than discovered (Section 10.8). Expansions proceed in pulses and pauses. The Austronesian pattern of long pauses followed by rapid pulses has been influential, and similar questions can be asked of Bantu and Pama-Nyungan. The tempo of expansion is a question that dated phylogenies are especially well placed to answer, and one that cannot be addressed with root ages alone. The main disagreements concern calibrations and data, not software. The Indo-European debate has turned on the treatment of ancient languages, the reliability of cognate judgments, and the interpretation of dates in relation to archaeology and genetics. The two Sino-Tibetan studies differ in data and coding. The Transeurasian debate concerns whether the cognates are real. These are problems of linguistic evidence, and they show that dating methods cannot be separated from the comparative method on which the data rest. Few published dates have been independently validated in the strict sense. Calibration cross-validation, prior-only runs reported alongside posteriors, and comparisons with evidence held out of the analysis remain the exception in linguistic dating. Until they become routine, the dates in Table 10.6 are best read as estimates under stated assumptions, whose robustness is still being established. Molecular dating offers a model for how linguistic dating could become more systematic. Large-scale molecular dating projects now publish their calibrations in standardized form, with explicit justification of minimum and maximum ages, the specimens and stratigraphic evidence on which they rest, and the phylogenetic placement of each calibrating fossil (Parham et al. 2012). They routinely sample from the prior to report effective priors (Warnock et al. 2012), use infinite-sites plots to judge whether calibrations or data limit precision (Reis et al. 2016), perform cross-validation of calibrations (Near et al. 2005), and compare node dating, tip dating and FBD analyses of the same data. Linguistics could adopt each of these practices immediately. A shared, versioned database of linguistic calibrations, linked to Glottolog and documenting the historical evidence for each, would make dating analyses more transparent and more comparable across studies. Calibrations fix the absolute time scale and also determine the precision of all dates. Even unlimited data cannot reduce date uncertainty below the floor set by calibration uncertainty. Absolute ages and rates are not identified by lexical data; they are borrowed from calibrations through the clock model. Topology and branch lengths are identified by the data, but they summarize lexical similarity and are not validated by agreement with traditional subgroupings. Linguistic calibrations come from documented history, attestation of ancient languages, archaeological correlates and datable loans. Each provides minimum ages more securely than maximum ages, and each has characteristic risks, including circularity. Calibration densities (uniform, soft-bounded, offset lognormal or exponential, normal) express different assumptions. Their interactions with each other and with the tree prior produce effective priors that may differ from those specified. Always sample from the prior. Ancient languages can serve as dated tips. Root-to-tip regression and date-randomization tests check temporal signal. Missing data in ancient languages must be handled explicitly. An attested language may be an ancestor, a sister, a relative of the real ancestor, or a witness to a dialect network. Node calibration, dated tips, sampled-ancestor priors and ancestry constraints encode different assumptions, and ancestry is poorly identified for fragmentarily attested languages, so dates should be reported under more than one treatment. Validation of dates has five distinct senses; only calibration cross-validation and comparison with evidence held out of the analysis count as independent historical validation. Dated phylogenies exist for Indo-European, Austronesian, Bantu, Sino-Tibetan, Dravidian, Uralic, Turkic, Semitic, Pama-Nyungan, Japonic, Kra-Dai, Uto-Aztecan and several South American families. Root ages range from about two millennia (Turkic, Japonic) to roughly eight or nine millennia (Indo-European under several analyses, and the contested Transeurasian). Indo-European dates remain disputed. The disagreements concern calibrations, ancient languages, data and interpretation more than methods. Many large families remain undated with modern methods, including Austroasiatic, Mayan, Trans-New Guinea, Afroasiatic and most of Niger-Congo. 10.12 Exercises Conceptual Using the infinite-sites argument, explain why doubling the number of cognate sets in a dating analysis may leave the width of the root-age interval almost unchanged.
