The shortcut of fitting a geographic model to a single maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree does not, and it can mislead in four ways, even when the MCC topology looks plausible. It treats uncertain structure as known. The MCC tree is the sampled tree whose clades have the highest product of posterior frequencies (Section 2.5). Clades with modest support appear in it as if they were certain, and the order of the first splits, which matters most for the homeland, is often among the least certain parts of a language tree. Its branch lengths are summaries. Node heights on an MCC tree are taken from one sampled tree or averaged across trees with different topologies, and may correspond to no history in the posterior (Heled and Bouckaert 2013). Quantities that depend on branch lengths, such as diffusion rates, are then computed on a tree that no analysis actually inferred. Averaging and summarizing do not commute. Most phylogeographic outputs are nonlinear functions of the tree. The average of a reconstruction over trees is not the reconstruction on an average tree. Intervals are too narrow. An analysis on one tree ignores the between-tree component of uncertainty altogether. In phylogeography these effects are uneven. Because the Brownian homeland is a weighted average of tip locations, it is fairly robust to moderate topological uncertainty. Rates and velocities are not, because they scale directly with the dates, and discrete reconstructions of ancestral regions can vary considerably from tree to tree. The R section (Section 11.13.6) shows all three patterns on a mock posterior sample. In a two-step analysis the remedy is simple: fit the geographic model to each of 100 or more trees drawn from the posterior and pool the results, either by concatenating posterior samples (Bayesian) or by combining estimates and their variances across trees (Section 13.12.1). 11.11 Sampling bias, displacement and replacement Three features of linguistic data make phylogeography harder for languages than for viruses or most organisms. Sampling bias. The languages included in a dataset are not a random sample of the family. They over-represent well-documented regions, national and standard languages, and the decisions of compilers about what counts as a separate language rather than a dialect (Section 15.8). In continuous phylogeography, densely sampled regions attract the root because the model treats each tip as an independent observation of the end point of a diffusion process. Kalkauskas et al. (2021) showed in simulations that biased spatial sampling distorts estimates of both diffusion rates and ancestral locations under the standard models, and Guindon and De Maio (2021) proposed ways of modeling the spatial sampling process explicitly, so that the absence of samples from a region is treated as informative only to the extent that the region was searched. Both papers concern pathogens and organisms, but their conclusions transfer directly to languages, for which the sampling process is, if anything, more uneven. A related development in viral phylogeography is the use of individual travel histories to correct for unsampled locations (Lemey et al. 2020); the linguistic analogue would be to use historical records of where a speech community lived before its documented location. Displacement. The location assigned to a language is usually its location at the time of documentation, often the nineteenth or twentieth century. Many speech communities have moved within the historical period, through voluntary migration, forced relocation or the reorganization of colonial boundaries. Coding such languages at their current location distorts the reconstruction near the tips and, through the weighting of Equation (11.6), the root. Datasets such as Glottolog give a single point per language, which is a convenience, not a historical claim. For ancient languages, the attested location is that of the surviving texts, which may be far from the core area of the speech community (as with administrative languages of empires). Replacement and language shift. As Section 11.9 stressed, phylogeography models the movement of languages: a language can spread by shift without substantial migration, while people can move without their language surviving. Replacement removes branches from the tree entirely: if the earliest offshoots of a family were spoken in what is now the homeland of another family and have since died out, the surviving branches carry no information about them. The spread of Turkic across Anatolia, the spread of Hungarian in the Carpathian basin and the spread of English are cases where historical records tell us that the present distribution says little about earlier ones. In such cases the diffusion model is misspecified in a way that no amount of data from the surviving languages can detect. A practical checklist for linguistic phylogeography: (1) report the number of languages per region and test robustness to subsampling; (2) use polygons or uncertainty radii rather than single points when the location of a speech community is uncertain or historically mobile; (3) include ancient languages at their attested locations and dates whenever possible, because they provide the only direct information about directional trends; (4) compare undirected, heavy-tailed and landscape-aware models with marginal likelihoods (Chapter 6), and report the sensitivity of the root to the model; (5) run posterior predictive checks, and say which plausible misspecifications they could not have detected; (6) analyze a sample of trees rather than one summary tree, and report rates together with the dates they depend on; (7) treat reconstructed movement as movement of linguistic lineages, not of populations, unless independent evidence links them. 11.12 From the biologist’s toolbox Historical biogeography and phylodynamics have developed a large repertoire of geographic models beyond the CTMC and the random walk. Most have, to our knowledge, rarely if ever been applied to languages. DEC and BioGeoBEARS. The dispersal-extinction-cladogenesis (DEC) model of Ree et al. (2005) and Ree and Smith (2008) treats the geographic range of a lineage as a set of areas, not a single area. Along branches, ranges expand by dispersal into a new area (rate \(d\)) and contract by local extinction from one area (rate \(e\)), giving a CTMC on the \(2^K - 1\) non-empty subsets of \(K\) areas. At each speciation event, a widespread ancestral range is divided between the daughters according to explicit cladogenetic scenarios: one daughter inherits a single area while the other inherits the rest (peripheral isolation), the range is split into two disjoint parts (vicariance), or one daughter inherits a subset nested inside the ancestor’s range (sympatric subset). The R package BioGeoBEARS (Matzke 2014) implements DEC alongside likelihood versions of other biogeographic models and adds a “+J” parameter for founder-event speciation, in which a daughter lineage jumps to a new area at the moment of splitting; the +J extension is powerful for island systems but has been criticized as a model whose likelihood comparisons with DEC are not straightforward (Ree and Sanmartı́n 2018). For languages, ranges spanning several areas are the norm (a language spoken across a dialect continuum), and the cladogenetic scenarios map naturally onto linguistic processes: vicariance onto the splitting of a dialect continuum by an intrusive population, peripheral isolation onto the separation of an outlying dialect, and founder events onto island colonization in Austronesian. The Bayesian implementation of Landis et al. (2013) handles many areas efficiently, which matters for families spread over dozens of regions. To our knowledge DEC-type models have rarely if ever been used on language data. GeoSSE. The geographic state-dependent speciation and extinction model (Goldberg et al. 2011) couples range evolution to diversification: speciation and extinction rates may differ between areas, and range evolution and diversification are estimated jointly from the tree. For languages it would address a long-standing question, whether some environments promote language diversification (mountains, tropical forests, islands), without the bias that arises when ancestral areas are reconstructed under a model that ignores area-dependent diversification. The usual caveats about state-dependent diversification models apply (Chapter 16). Structured coalescent and MASCOT. Discrete-trait phylogeography treats location as a character mapped onto a tree generated independently of it. For densely sampled populations, the structured coalescent models the tree itself as arising from subpopulations connected by migration, so that where lineages coalesce depends on population sizes and migration rates. Approximations such as BASTA (De Maio et al. 2015) and the marginal approximation implemented in the BEAST 2 package MASCOT (Müller et al. 2018) make the structured coalescent practical and are less sensitive to sampling bias than discrete-trait models. For languages, the coalescent framework is most natural at the shallow end, among dialects or closely related varieties sampled from a few regions, where the “population” of speakers and the number of distinct varieties are both meaningful. Phylodynamic GLMs and landscape phylogeography. The GLM of Equation (11.4) (Lemey et al. 2014) and the landscape tests of SERAPHIM (Dellicour et al. 2016) together offer a direct way to ask what drove a language family’s spread: distance, terrain, rivers, ecological similarity, agricultural suitability. A Bantu analysis with rainforest cover, rainfall and river networks as predictors of dispersal rates, or an Austronesian analysis with distance across open sea as a predictor, would move linguistic phylogeography from describing expansions to explaining them. Beyond these, several other biological methods deserve mention. Isolation-by-distance and spatial population genetics models describe gradual differentiation in a continuum, a closer analogue to dialect geography than a branching tree, and connect to the wave-model approaches of Chapter 8. Spatially explicit simulations of expansion on a landscape, combined with approximate Bayesian computation, would allow linguists to fit models of directional, wave-of-advance expansion that the standard diffusion models cannot represent. And phylogenetic models with jumps (Lévy processes), used for trait evolution, offer an alternative to the Cauchy RRW for representing rare long-distance moves such as island colonization. 11.13 Phylogeography in R Full Bayesian phylogeography of real language families is done in BEAST 2 (with the GEO_SPHERE and BEAST_CLASSIC packages) or BEAST X (Appendix F). The basic models, however, can be explored in R with ape and phytools (Paradis and Schliep 2019; Revell 2024), and doing so makes their behavior, including their failures, easy to see. All data below are simulated. 11.13.1 Simulating a language family in space We simulate a dated tree of 30 languages with a root age of 6 (read: 6,000 years, so branch lengths are in millennia) under a pure-birth (Yule) process, and then let the location of each lineage diffuse along the branches under bivariate Brownian motion starting from a known homeland at the origin \((0, 0)\). Coordinates are in units of 100 km east and north of the homeland, and the diffusion matrix has variance \(0.36\) per millennium in each direction with a modest positive correlation. Figure 11.1 draws the resulting tree in geographic space. library(phytools) set.seed(11) tree <- pbtree(n = 30, scale = 6) # root age 6 millennia tree$tip.label <- paste0("L", 1:30) Sigma <- matrix(c(0.36, 0.10, 0.10, 0.36), 2) # diffusion matrix per kyr XY <- sim.corrs(tree, vcv = Sigma, anc = c(0, 0), internal = TRUE) tips <- XY[tree$tip.label, ] colnames(tips) <- colnames(XY) <- c("east", "north") plot(NA, xlim = range(XY[, 1]), ylim = range(XY[, 2]), asp = 1, xlab = "East (100 km)", ylab = "North (100 km)") for (i in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) { a <- tree$edge[i, 1]; d <- tree$edge[i, 2] segments(XY[a, 1], XY[a, 2], XY[d, 1], XY[d, 2], col = "gray50") } points(tips, pch = 21, bg = "gray80", cex = 1.2) points(0, 0, pch = 23, bg = "red", cex = 1.8) Figure 11.1: A simulated language family diffusing in space under bivariate Brownian motion. Lines are the branches of the tree drawn in geographic space (from simulated internal node locations), gray points are the 30 present-day languages, and the red diamond is the true homeland at the origin. Units are hundreds of kilometers. 11.13.2 Estimating the homeland Under BM the maximum-likelihood ancestral locations can be computed coordinate by coordinate with fastAnc() (equivalently ace(..., method = "REML") in ape), which also returns 95% confidence intervals. The ML estimate of the full diffusion matrix comes from evol.vcv(). We compare the phylogenetic estimate of the homeland with two naive alternatives: the unweighted centroid of the present-day languages, and a simple diversity-based estimate that places the homeland at the language whose five geographically nearest neighbors are, on average, most distantly related to it (in the spirit of the diversity principle, though much cruder than Wichmann, Müller, et al. (2010)). root <- as.character(Ntip(tree) + 1) anc_e <- fastAnc(tree, tips[, "east"], CI = TRUE) anc_n <- fastAnc(tree, tips[, "north"], CI = TRUE) est <- rbind( truth = c(0, 0), phylo_ML = c(anc_e$ace[root], anc_n$ace[root]), centroid = colMeans(tips)) # crude diversity-based estimate geo <- as.matrix(dist(tips)) pat <- cophenetic(tree)[rownames(tips), rownames(tips)] divers <- sapply(rownames(tips), function(l) { nb <- names(sort(geo[l, ]))[2:6] # five nearest neighbours mean(pat[l, nb]) }) est <- rbind(est, diversity = tips[which.max(divers), ]) colnames(est) <- c("east", "north") round(est, 2) #> east north #> truth 0.00 0.00 #> phylo_ML 0.09 -0.15 #> centroid 0.06 -0.36 #> diversity 0.67 -0.73 rbind(east = anc_e$CI95[root, ], north = anc_n$CI95[root, ]) #> [,1] [,2] #> east -1.521 1.708 #> north -1.697 1.390 round(evol.vcv(tree, tips)$R.single, 3) # ML diffusion matrix #> east north #> east 0.456 0.084 #> north 0.084 0.417 The phylogenetic estimate is close to the truth, its confidence intervals cover the origin, and the estimated diffusion matrix is close to the simulated one. This is a check of parameter recovery: the data were simulated under the model used to analyze them. Note that the confidence interval is wide, extending roughly 150 km either side of the estimate in each direction: even with a perfectly known tree and a correctly specified model, thirty languages pin down the homeland only roughly. Note also that the centroid is not much worse than the phylogenetic estimate here; under BM both are averages of the tip locations, differing only in their weights (Section D.1.3 computes the weights explicitly). 11.13.3 When the model is wrong: relaxed walks and directional expansion How reliable is the BM root under realistic violations of its assumptions? The function below simulates one family under one of three scenarios and records whether the 95% confidence interval of the Brownian root estimate (east coordinate only) contains the true homeland, as well as the error of the phylogenetic and centroid estimates. The scenarios are: (1) BM, the model used for inference (parameter recovery); (2) a relaxed random walk, with branch-specific lognormal rate multipliers; (3) BM with a directional trend, simulating an expansion that moves on average 40 km east per millennium (mu = 0.4) for six millennia. Scenarios 2 and 3 test robustness under misspecification. For each replicate the function also runs a simple adequacy check. Under BM on the true tree, the standardized independent contrasts of the tip coordinates (pic(); Section 13.5) are independent normal variables, so their kurtosis should look like the kurtosis of 29 draws from a normal distribution; the check flags a dataset whose contrasts are more heavy-tailed than 95% of such draws. kurt <- function(u) mean(u^4) / mean(u^2)^2 # about 3 for normal data set.seed(99) kurt_null <- replicate(4000, kurt(rnorm(29))) # 29 contrasts for 30 tips one_rep <- function(scenario, n = 30, T = 6, sig2 = 0.36, mu = 0.4) { tr <- pbtree(n = n, scale = T) sim_tr <- tr if (scenario == "RRW") { phi <- rlnorm(nrow(tr$edge), 0, 1) sim_tr$edge.length <- tr$edge.length * phi / mean(phi) } x <- fastBM(sim_tr, a = 0, sig2 = sig2, mu = if (scenario == "trend") mu else 0) f <- fastAnc(tr, x, CI = TRUE) k <- kurt(pic(x, tr)) # adequacy statistic c(coverage = as.numeric(f$CI95[1, 1] < 0 & f$CI95[1, 2] > 0), error_phylo = abs(unname(f$ace[1])), error_centroid = abs(mean(x)), ci_width = unname(diff(f$CI95[1, ])), flagged = as.numeric(mean(kurt_null >= k) < 0.05)) } set.seed(1) cov_tab <- sapply(c("BM", "RRW", "trend"), function(s) rowMeans(replicate(150, one_rep(s)))) knitr::kable(round(t(cov_tab), 2), caption = "Performance of the Brownian homeland estimate (east coordinate) over 150 simulated families per scenario. Coverage is the proportion of replicates whose 95% confidence interval contains the true homeland; errors and widths are in units of 100 km; flagged is the proportion of replicates in which the contrast-kurtosis adequacy check rejects Brownian motion at the 5% level.") Table 11.3: Performance of the Brownian homeland estimate (east coordinate) over 150 simulated families per scenario. Coverage is the proportion of replicates whose 95% confidence interval contains the true homeland; errors and widths are in units of 100 km; flagged is the proportion of replicates in which the contrast-kurtosis adequacy check rejects Brownian motion at the 5% level. coverage error_phylo error_centroid ci_width flagged BM 0.96 0.47 0.53 2.61 0.03 RRW 0.95 0.54 0.58 2.68 0.26 trend 0.09 2.41 2.46 2.64 0.03 Table 11.3 makes the point of Section 11.5.5 quantitatively. Under BM the intervals have close to their nominal 95% coverage, and the adequacy check rejects about as often as it should (its false alarm rate). Moderate rate heterogeneity among branches (the RRW scenario), with the tree held fixed, does surprisingly little damage to the root estimate; the adequacy check detects it in only about 26% of replicates, because 29 contrasts carry little information about the shape of their distribution. But under a directional trend the coverage collapses: the estimate is displaced toward the center of the present distribution by roughly \(\mu T\), here about 240 km, and the confidence interval, whose width does not depend on the tip locations, is no wider than before. The phylogenetic and centroid estimates fail together, because both are averages of the tips. This is the bias found in realistic simulations by Neureiter et al. (2021). And the adequacy check is blind to it: it flags the trend scenario no more often than pure BM, because a trend shifts all contemporaneous tips equally and leaves the contrasts untouched. The misspecification that damages the homeland most is the one the data cannot reveal (Section 11.8). 11.13.4 Ancient languages restore identifiability Now suppose some of the languages are ancient, attested at earlier times. We mimic this by shortening ten randomly chosen terminal branches, so that those tips are “sampled” between a few centuries and a few millennia before the present, and simulate locations with the same eastward trend. With tips at different heights \(h_i\) (distance from the root), the expected location of tip \(i\) is \(x_{	ext{root}} + \mu h_i\), so we can estimate both the homeland and the trend by GLS regression of location on tip height, using the phylogenetic covariance matrix. We compare this with the undirected BM estimate, which ignores the trend. This is a parameter-recovery experiment for the drift model, and a robustness experiment for the undirected one. gls_drift <- function(tr, x) { C <- vcv(tr)[names(x), names(x)] h <- diag(C) # root-to-tip heights X <- cbind(root = 1, trend = h) Ci <- solve(C) beta <- solve(t(X) %*% Ci %*% X, t(X) %*% Ci %*% x) drop(beta) } ancient_rep <- function(n = 30, n_anc = 10, mu = 0.4) { tr <- pbtree(n = n, scale = 6) term <- which(tr$edge[, 2] <= n) pick <- sample(term, n_anc) tr$edge.length[pick] <- tr$edge.length[pick] * runif(n_anc, 0.05, 0.5) x <- fastBM(tr, a = 0, sig2 = 0.36, mu = mu) c(bm_root = unname(fastAnc(tr, x)[1]), gls_drift(tr, x)) } set.seed(2) anc_res <- t(replicate(150, ancient_rep())) round(rbind(mean = colMeans(anc_res), sd = apply(anc_res, 2, sd)), 2) #> bm_root root trend #> mean 2.13 -0.23 0.45 #> sd 0.83 1.76 0.28 The undirected BM estimate is again biased eastward, while the drift model recovers both the homeland (true value 0) and the trend (true value 0.4) on average, albeit with substantial uncertainty from replicate to replicate. The lesson for linguistics is concrete: ancient languages placed at their attested dates and locations are not just useful for calibrating the clock (Chapter 10); they are the main source of information about the direction of an expansion. The simulation assumes that the ancient tips were located where their lineages were; an administrative language attested far from its speakers’ core area (Section 11.11) would mislead the drift model too. 11.13.5 Discrete phylogeography: regions, rates and Markov jumps For discrete phylogeography we divide the map into four regions arranged in a ring (R1 to R4, with R1 adjacent to R2 and R4, and so on) and simulate the region of each lineage on the same tree, starting in R1, under a symmetric CTMC in which lineages move only between adjacent regions, quickly between R1 and R2 and slowly elsewhere. We then fit three models with fitMk(): equal rates, symmetric rates, and a ring model in which only adjacent regions exchange lineages (rates between R1 and R3, and between R2 and R4, fixed at zero). The ring model, which here happens to be the true model family, is the simplest example of a geographically constrained rate matrix, a hand-built version of what BSSVS learns from the data. regions <- c("R1", "R2", "R3", "R4") Qtrue <- matrix(0.05, 4, 4, dimnames = list(regions, regions)) Qtrue["R1", "R3"] <- Qtrue["R3", "R1"] <- 0 # non-adjacent regions Qtrue["R2", "R4"] <- Qtrue["R4", "R2"] <- 0 Qtrue["R1", "R2"] <- Qtrue["R2", "R1"] <- 0.4 # a fast corridor diag(Qtrue) <- 0; diag(Qtrue) <- -rowSums(Qtrue) set.seed(8) area <- sim.Mk(tree, Qtrue, anc = "R1") table(area) #> area #> R1 R2 R3 R4 #> 14 12 3 1 ring <- matrix(c(0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 0, 4, 0), 4, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(regions, regions)) fits <- list(ER = fitMk(tree, area, model = "ER"), SYM = fitMk(tree, area, model = "SYM"), ring = fitMk(tree, area, model = ring)) knitr::kable(data.frame( model = names(fits), k = sapply(fits, function(f) attr(logLik(f), "df")), logL = round(sapply(fits, logLik), 2), AIC = round(sapply(fits, AIC), 2)), row.names = FALSE, caption = "Discrete phylogeographic models fitted to simulated region data: number of free rate parameters (k), log-likelihood and AIC.") Table 11.4: Discrete phylogeographic models fitted to simulated region data: number of free rate parameters (k), log-likelihood and AIC. model k logL AIC ER 1 -35.39 72.78 SYM 6 -27.66 67.32 ring 4 -27.66 63.32 The marginal posterior probabilities of each region at the root and at the other internal nodes are obtained with ancr() (Chapter 12 explains marginal reconstruction in detail). Figure 11.2 shows them as pie charts. best <- fits[[which.min(sapply(fits, AIC))]] anc_area <- ancr(best) round(anc_area$ace[1, ], 3) # root (homeland) probabilities #> R1 R2 R3 R4 #> 0.546 0.448 0.005 0.001 cols <- setNames(c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3", "#e7298a"), regions) plotTree(tree, fsize = 0.7, ftype = "i", offset = 0.5) nodelabels(pie = anc_area$ace, piecol = cols, cex = 0.4) tiplabels(pie = to.matrix(area[tree$tip.label], regions), piecol = cols, cex = 0.3) legend("bottomleft", legend = regions, pch = 21, pt.bg = cols, pt.cex = 1.5, bty = "n") Figure 11.2: Marginal ancestral region probabilities under the best-fitting discrete model, shown as pie charts at internal nodes. Tip colors give the observed regions of the 30 simulated languages. The ring model is preferred by AIC (Table 11.4), as it should be. Even in this idealized setting, with the true tree and a correctly specified model, the root probability is split between the true homeland R1 and its neighbor R2: because lineages move quickly along the R1-R2 corridor, the data cannot tell which end of the corridor the family started from. A single discrete character carries limited information about deep nodes, and this is the typical situation in linguistic discrete phylogeography. Finally, stochastic character mapping (make.simmap(); Section 12.6) samples complete histories of movement and lets us count the expected number of moves between each pair of regions, the Markov jump counts of Section 11.4.3. set.seed(7) Qhat <- as.Qmatrix(best) maps <- make.simmap(tree, area, Q = unclass(Qhat)[regions, regions], nsim = 50, pi = "fitzjohn", message = FALSE) jumps <- describe.simmap(maps)$count round(colMeans(jumps), 2) # expected moves by type #> N R1,R2 R1,R3 R1,R4 R2,R1 R2,R3 R2,R4 R3,R1 R3,R2 R3,R4 R4,R1 R4,R2 #> 29.68 13.78 0.00 0.00 12.22 2.14 0.00 0.00 0.14 1.20 0.00 0.00 #> R4,R3 #> 0.20 Most of the roughly thirty expected moves are back-and-forth exchanges along the fast R1-R2 corridor, with a handful of moves into R3 and R4. Counts of this kind are what one would report for questions such as how often lineages entered or left a given habitat. 11.13.6 Homelands and rates over a sample of trees So far the tree was known. We now carry the analysis over a mock posterior sample of 100 trees, built by perturbing the true tree: three random nearest-neighbor interchanges, lognormal noise on every branch length, and a root age drawn around six millennia with a standard deviation of about 20% on the log scale, roughly the dating uncertainty of a well-calibrated family. (A real analysis would use trees sampled by BEAST or MrBayes from the lexical data; Section 17.11 shows how to read them.) On each tree we estimate the homeland’s east coordinate with its standard error, the east-west diffusion rate (by REML, as the mean squared standardized contrast), and the probability that the root lay in region R1 under the equal-rates discrete model. We then do the same on the MCC tree of the sample, computed with maxCladeCred() from phangorn, which returns the sampled tree with the highest clade credibility, branch lengths included. library(phangorn) set.seed(5) post <- lapply(1:100, function(i) { t <- rNNI(tree, moves = 3) # topological noise t$edge.length <- t$edge.length * rlnorm(nrow(t$edge), 0, 0.3) t <- force.ultrametric(t, method = "extend", message = FALSE) age <- 6 * rlnorm(1, 0, 0.2) # root-age uncertainty t$edge.length <- t$edge.length * age / max(node.depth.edgelength(t)) t }) class(post) <- "multiPhylo" mcc <- maxCladeCred(post) per_tree <- function(t) { x <- tips[t$tip.label, "east"] f <- fastAnc(t, x, CI = TRUE) c(root_age = max(node.depth.edgelength(t)), east = unname(f$ace[1]), se_east = unname(diff(f$CI95[1, ])) / (2 * 1.96), sig2 = mean(pic(x, t)^2), # REML diffusion rate p_R1 = ace(area[t$tip.label], t, type = "discrete", model = "ER")$lik.anc[1, "R1"]) } res <- t(sapply(post, per_tree)) on_mcc <- per_tree(mcc) op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1)) hist(res[, "east"], breaks = 15, col = "gray80", border = "white", main = "", xlab = "homeland, east (100 km)") abline(v = 0, lty = 2); abline(v = on_mcc["east"], col = "red", lwd = 2) plot(res[, "root_age"], res[, "sig2"], pch = 16, col = "gray50", xlab = "root age (kyr)", ylab = "diffusion rate (east)") points(on_mcc["root_age"], on_mcc["sig2"], pch = 18, col = "red", cex = 2) hist(res[, "p_R1"], breaks = 15, col = "gray80", border = "white", main = "", xlab = "P(root in R1)") abline(v = on_mcc["p_R1"], col = "red", lwd = 2) Figure 11.3: A two-step phylogeographic analysis over a mock posterior sample of 100 trees. Left: estimates of the homeland’s east coordinate on each tree. Center: diffusion rate against root age, one point per tree. Right: probability that the root lay in region R1 under the equal-rates discrete model. Red marks the analysis of the MCC tree alone; the dashed line in the left panel is the true homeland. par(op) Pooling across trees, with the total variance of the homeland estimate computed as the average within-tree variance plus the between-tree variance (the rule explained in Section 13.12.1), gives the following summaries, compared with the MCC tree alone: m <- nrow(res) pooled_se <- sqrt(mean(res[, "se_east"]^2) + (1 + 1 / m) * var(res[, "east"])) q <- function(v, p) unname(quantile(v, p)) round(rbind( MCC_tree = on_mcc[c("east", "se_east", "sig2", "p_R1")], over_trees = c(mean(res[, "east"]), pooled_se, mean(res[, "sig2"]), mean(res[, "p_R1"])), lower_95 = c(q(res[, "east"], 0.025), NA, q(res[, "sig2"], 0.025), q(res[, "p_R1"], 0.025)), upper_95 = c(q(res[, "east"], 0.975), NA, q(res[, "sig2"], 0.975), q(res[, "p_R1"], 0.975))), 3) #> east se_east sig2 p_R1 #> MCC_tree 0.104 0.606 0.361 0.516 #> over_trees 0.105 0.581 0.300 0.566 #> lower_95 -0.017 NA 0.167 0.381 #> upper_95 0.205 NA 0.451 0.771 cor(res[, "root_age"], res[, "sig2"]) #> [1] -0.782 p_true <- ace(area, tree, type = "discrete", model = "ER")$lik.anc[1, "R1"] Figure 11.3 shows the uneven effects described in Section 11.10. The homeland barely moves from tree to tree: the between-tree spread is small compared with the within-tree standard error, so the MCC tree and the pooled analysis agree. The diffusion rate is a different matter. It varies by more than a factor of two across the sample, mostly because the root age varies (the two are strongly negatively correlated), and the single MCC value sits wherever the dates of that one sampled tree happen to put it. A rate or velocity reported from the MCC tree would carry none of this uncertainty. The discrete root probability, finally, ranges widely across trees, and its value on the MCC tree is one draw from that range. On the true tree the same model gives 0.31, a reminder that the posterior, here as in real analyses, need not be centered on the true tree. The dependence of rates on the time scale can be made exact. Rescaling every branch of the true tree by the same factor, as a different root age would, leaves the reconstructed homeland unchanged and divides the rate by that factor: rate_by_age <- t(sapply(c(4, 6, 9), function(T) { tr <- tree tr$edge.length <- tr$edge.length * T / 6 c(root_age = T, root_east = unname(fastAnc(tr, tips[, "east"])[1]), sig2_east = mean(pic(tips[, "east"], tr)^2)) })) round(rate_by_age, 3) #> root_age root_east sig2_east #> [1,] 4 0.093 0.708 #> [2,] 6 0.093 0.472 #> [3,] 9 0.093 0.315 The diffusion rate is identifiable only relative to the dates of the tree (Table 11.2). 11.13.7 Bayes factors for BSSVS routes BSSVS itself requires MCMC in BEAST, but turning its output into route Bayes factors is simple arithmetic, and one consequence is worth knowing before reading any published route map. With four regions, three of the six possible routes are needed for connectivity, so the prior inclusion probability of each route is high (about 0.62), and even a posterior inclusion probability of 0.81 yields only a modest Bayes factor of about 2.7. With twenty regions and 190 possible routes the prior inclusion probability is about 0.1, and the same posterior inclusion probability yields a Bayes factor of about 37. Bayes factors from BSSVS are therefore not comparable across analyses with different numbers of regions, and a route can look “strongly supported” partly because the map was cut into many regions. The function bssvs_bf(), which computes route Bayes factors from posterior inclusion probabilities read from a BEAST log, and the worked numbers above, are in Section D.1.2. 11.13.8 Planar versus spherical distance Finally, a small calculation shows why diffusion on unprojected longitude and latitude is a problem at continental scales (Section 11.5.3). We compute the great-circle (haversine) distance between pairs of points separated by ten degrees of longitude at different latitudes, and compare it with the “planar” distance implied by treating degrees as equal units everywhere. haversine <- function(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2, R = 6371) { rad <- pi / 180 dlat <- (lat2 - lat1) * rad; dlon <- (lon2 - lon1) * rad a <- sin(dlat / 2)^2 + cos(lat1 * rad) * cos(lat2 * rad) * sin(dlon / 2)^2 2 * R * asin(sqrt(a)) } lat <- c(0, 20, 40, 50, 60, 70) sph <- haversine(0, lat, 10, lat) knitr::kable(data.frame(latitude = lat, planar_km = round(10 * 111.2), great_circle_km = round(sph), ratio = round(10 * 111.2 / sph, 2)), caption = "Distance between two points ten degrees of longitude apart at various latitudes: planar approximation on raw degrees versus great-circle distance.") Table 11.5: Distance between two points ten degrees of longitude apart at various latitudes: planar approximation on raw degrees versus great-circle distance. latitude planar_km great_circle_km ratio 0 1112 1112 1.00 20 1112 1045 1.06 40 1112 851 1.31 50 1112 714 1.56 60 1112 555 2.00 70 1112 380 2.93 As Table 11.5 shows, at the latitude of the Pontic-Caspian steppe (around 50 degrees north) the planar approximation overstates east-west distances by more than half; at the latitude of northern Scandinavia or Siberia it roughly doubles or triples them. A planar random walk on raw coordinates therefore treats east-west movement at high latitudes as far more costly than it is, which can bias homeland and route reconstructions for Eurasian families. Projecting coordinates or, better, using spherical diffusion avoids the problem. Classical homeland methods (linguistic paleontology, the diversity principle, migration theory) are informal; phylogeography makes the assumptions about movement explicit and quantifies uncertainty under them. In discrete phylogeography, location is a character evolving under a CTMC on regions. BSSVS selects the dispersal routes needed to explain the data and yields route-specific Bayes factors that depend on the number of regions; Markov jumps count movements; GLMs relate dispersal rates to predictors such as distance and habitat. In continuous phylogeography, coordinates diffuse along branches under Brownian motion or a relaxed random walk. Under BM, the ML homeland is a phylogenetically weighted average of present-day locations. Undirected diffusion models cannot detect directional expansions from contemporaneous languages. They place the homeland near the center of the range with overconfident uncertainty, and adequacy checks on present-day locations cannot reveal the problem. Ancient languages at their attested times and places are the main remedy. A posterior over an ancestral location is a statement about language lineages under a model. It is not evidence that the model describes how speech communities moved; that requires adequacy checks, alternative process models and independent evidence. Diffusion rates and velocities are identifiable only relative to the dates of the tree and inherit their uncertainty. Analyses over a sample of trees show this; analyses on a single MCC tree hide it. Linguistic sampling bias, the displacement of speech communities and the replacement of early branches are serious and often undetectable sources of error. DEC/BioGeoBEARS, GeoSSE, the structured coalescent and phylodynamic GLMs offer largely unexploited tools for modeling ranges, area-dependent diversification and the drivers of linguistic dispersal. 11.14 Exercises Conceptual A study reports a Bayes factor of 50 in favor of an Anatolian rather than a steppe homeland for a language family. List the information you would need before accepting this as evidence about the homeland (consider the sizes of the two regions, the prior on the root location, the dates of the tree, and whether the model could have favored a peripheral homeland at all). Explain in your own words why adding the same eastward drift to every lineage cannot be detected from contemporaneous languages, and why ancient languages help. What must be assumed about where the ancient languages are attested? A dataset contains 40 languages from one region and 5 from another, because the first region has been far better documented. Explain how this affects a discrete and a continuous phylogeographic reconstruction, and propose two robustness analyses. A paper reports that a family expanded at “1.2 km per year”. Which modeling choices and which external inputs does this number depend on, and what would you need to know before reading it as the speed at which people moved? Distinguish demic diffusion from language shift. For each, describe what the movement of a lineage along a branch of the language tree corresponds to historically, and say whether a diffusion model can tell the two apart. Computational Using one_rep(), vary the trend mu over 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 and plot the coverage of the Brownian root interval against \(\mu T\). At what displacement does coverage fall below 80%? Does the adequacy check (flagged) ever respond? Modify ancient_rep() so that the ten ancient languages all belong to one clade (choose terminal branches below a single node with getDescendants()). How do the bias and standard deviation of the drift estimates change? Repeat with n_anc equal to 2, 5 and 20. With the mock posterior post, compute for each tree the dispersal distance implied by the REML rate over the root age, \(\sqrt{2\hat\sigma^2 T}\), and compare its 95% range across trees with the single value from the MCC tree. Then double the standard deviation of the root-age noise used to build post and repeat. Fit the ring model of Section 11.13.5 with fitMk() to the first 20 trees in post, and record how often it is preferred to the ER model by AIC. Then pool Markov jump counts across trees by running make.simmap() with nsim = 10 on each tree and combining the describe.simmap() counts. Add noise to the tip locations in one_rep() (for example x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5), mimicking displaced speech communities) and record coverage and the adequacy check. Which kinds of misspecification does the contrast-kurtosis check detect, and why? Research You are planning a phylogeographic study of a South American family with 70 languages, a third of which were relocated during the twentieth century and a handful of which are known only from colonial-era sources. Design the analysis: how you would code locations (points, polygons, historical locations), which diffusion models you would compare, which adequacy checks you would run, how you would use the colonial-era sources, and what you would and would not claim about the movements of speech communities. Design a phylogeographic GLM to test whether the Bantu expansion followed habitats suitable for cereal cultivation. Specify the regions, the predictors and how they would be measured for the relevant period, the analysis over trees, and what result would count as evidence that habitat shaped dispersal rather than merely correlating with it. For Austronesian, argue for or against a continuous relaxed random walk, a discrete model on island groups, and a DEC+J biogeographic model. For each, state which historical quantities it could estimate and which it would misrepresent. 11.15 Further reading Lemey et al. (2009): The paper that introduced Bayesian discrete phylogeography with BSSVS. Written for virologists, but the model description is clear and general. Lemey et al. (2010): The relaxed random walk for continuous phylogeography. Required reading before running a continuous analysis in BEAST. Bouckaert et al. (2012): The landmark linguistic application to Indo-European. Read it together with the critique of Pereltsvaig and Lewis (2015) and the later work of Chang et al. (2015) and Heggarty et al. (2023). Neureiter et al. (2021): A simulation study of how well relaxed random walks recover linguistic homelands and migrations. It shows where they fail. Bouckaert (2016): Spherical diffusion and its implementation in BEAST 2. It explains why planar models break down at large scales. Grollemund et al. (2015) and Koile et al. (2022): Two contrasting phylogeographic analyses of the Bantu expansion. Together they are an excellent case study in how modeling choices shape conclusions. Wichmann, Müller, et al. (2010): The quantitative diversity-based approach. It is a useful baseline for any phylogeographic study. Ree and Smith (2008) and Matzke (2014): DEC and BioGeoBEARS, the core of model-based historical biogeography and a promising and largely untried framework for languages. Lemey et al. (2014): Phylogeographic GLMs that relate dispersal rates to predictors. This is a template for testing hypotheses about the causes of language spread. Nichols (1992): The classic linguistic treatment of spread zones and residual zones. It gives the geographical intuitions any phylogeographic model should respect. References

Chapter 12 Ancestral State Reconstruction Historical linguistics is, at its core, a science of reconstruction. The comparative method recovers the sounds, words and grammatical structures of languages that were never written down, and Proto-Indo-European, Proto-Austronesian and Proto-Bantu are known to us only through such reconstruction. Evolutionary biology has its own, largely independent, tradition of ancestral state reconstruction (ASR): given a tree and the states of a character at its tips, infer the states at the internal nodes. The two traditions use the same word for different operations. This chapter develops the biological toolkit (parsimony, likelihood and Bayesian reconstruction, and stochastic character mapping), shows how its answers depend on the model, the root and the tree, and asks what it can add to the linguist’s own methods of reconstruction, and what it cannot replace. After reading this chapter you should be able to: distinguish the reconstruction of coded character states, the reconstruction of historical linguistic forms (proto-forms and sound changes) and the reconstructions of the comparative method, and say what kind of evidence each uses; compute and interpret parsimony, marginal and joint reconstructions, and explain why marginal and joint answers can disagree; assess how root priors, rate models and hidden rate heterogeneity affect a reconstruction, and check which quantity a software function reports; use stochastic character mapping to count changes and explain why the counts exceed parsimony counts; reconstruct a named ancestor over a sample of trees, and explain why a reconstruction on a single MCC tree can mislead; evaluate published reconstructions of the proto-lexicon, of grammar and of sound systems, including the limits of their agreement with expert reconstructions as evidence. 12.1 What is an ancestral state? Consider the word for ‘five’ across the Austronesian family. In Malay and Indonesian it is lima, in Tagalog lima, in Fijian lima, in Hawaiian lima (where it also means ‘hand’ or ‘arm’), in Malagasy dimy. Comparative Austronesianists reconstruct Proto-Austronesian *lima ‘five; hand’, and the reconstruction is about as secure as any in the field. Now consider a less clear case: a meaning for which some branches use one cognate set, some another, and a few a third. Which word did the proto-language use? Or consider a structural feature: Proto-Oceanic is usually reconstructed with basic subject-verb-object order, but many Oceanic languages of New Guinea have verb-final order, apparently under the influence of neighboring Papuan languages. Which order did the common ancestor of a particular subgroup have, and how many times did the change happen? Questions of this kind have the same logical structure. There is a tree, which for the moment we take as known; there is a character (a meaning slot with cognate classes as its states, a binary feature such as presence of grammatical gender, a multistate feature such as basic word order); and there are observed states at the tips. ASR infers the states at internal nodes, or more generally the history of the character along the branches. Two clarifications prevent common misunderstandings. First, an internal node of a phylogeny is not a language in the everyday sense. It represents the last common ancestor of a set of lineages, an idealized moment in a speech community that was certainly internally variable. A reconstructed state at a node is a statement about the variety from which the descendants inherited their state, not a claim that a uniform proto-language existed. The comparative method makes the same idealization, which is why reconstructed proto-languages are often described as “uniform” or “idealized” systems. Second, the inference is conditional on a model. Even parsimony, which looks model-free, embodies a model: one in which change is rare and every change costs the same. All probabilistic reconstructions depend on the tree, its branch lengths, the rate matrix and the root prior. A probability of 0.9 for SOV order at the root of a family is the probability under the assumed model, and a different but equally defensible model can produce a different answer. Much of this chapter is about how to make these dependencies explicit and how to propagate uncertainty about them. For the same reason some authors prefer to speak of ancestral state estimation rather than reconstruction, since the latter suggests a certainty that the inference does not have (Goldstein 2020). 12.2 Three kinds of reconstruction The word “reconstruction” covers at least three different operations in the literature that this chapter reviews, and much confusion, in both directions, comes from treating them as one. Reconstruction by the comparative method. A comparative reconstruction such as Proto-Austronesian *lima is a hypothesis about a form, embedded in a system: a set of cognates, a set of regular sound correspondences, a proto-phoneme for each correspondence set, and sound laws that derive each daughter form from the proto-form. Its evidence is the regularity of the correspondences across many words, and its strength comes from that system-wide consistency, not from the distribution of the form over a tree. It is not tied to a dated node, it rarely comes with a probability, and its status is debated: some linguists read reconstructed forms as approximations of real speech, others as formulas summarizing the correspondences (Fox 1995; Campbell 2013). It also produces the data that the other two kinds of reconstruction take as given. Cognate sets, in particular, are judgments of the comparative method (Chapter 3), and reconstructed proto-languages are themselves hypotheses rather than observations (Section 3.2.3). Model-based reconstruction of linguistic forms. A second family of methods reconstructs the forms themselves, or the sound changes that relate them, with explicit probabilistic models: stochastic transducers on the branches of a tree, or concerted changes in sound correspondences (Sections 12.11 and 12.12). These methods take cognate sets and usually a tree as input and output strings or sound laws. They are closer to the comparative method in what they produce, and closer to phylogenetics in how they reason. Phylogenetic reconstruction of character states. Most of this chapter concerns a third operation. A character is coded from the data, and the reconstruction is a probability distribution over its states at a node of a tree. If the character is the meaning slot ‘hand’ with cognate classes as states, the output is “cognate class 3 was the word for ‘hand’ at this node with probability 0.8”. This presupposes the cognate classes and says nothing about the form of the word. If the character is a typological feature such as basic word order, the states are categories defined for modern languages in databases such as WALS or Grambank, and the reconstruction presupposes that the proto-language can be described in the same terms, which is not guaranteed (a proto-language might have had a word-order system that fits none of the modern categories well). Table 12.1 summarizes the contrast. The three operations are complementary. Character-state reconstruction is quick, quantitative and comparable across families, but it reconstructs codes, not languages. Comparative reconstruction reconstructs languages, but without probabilities. Model-based reconstruction of forms aims at both, and is the least developed. Section 12.13 returns to the relationship, including the question of what agreement between them does and does not show. Table 12.1: Three kinds of reconstruction in historical linguistics. Comparative method Model-based reconstruction of forms Phylogenetic character-state reconstruction What is reconstructed Proto-forms, proto-phonemes, sound laws, constructions Proto-forms as strings; sound changes on branches Probabilities of coded states at tree nodes Main evidence Regularity of correspondences across many words Aligned cognate forms and a tree Distribution of states over the tips of a tree Role of the tree Mainly primary subgrouping Full tree, often fixed Full topology and branch lengths Output Starred forms, sometimes with alternatives Forms with model-based uncertainty Posterior probabilities under a model Presupposes Cognacy and regularity (established within the method) Cognate sets, alignments Cognate sets or typological codes from earlier analysis 12.3 Parsimony reconstruction 12.3.1 Fitch and Sankoff The oldest algorithmic approach is maximum parsimony: choose the assignment of states to internal nodes that minimizes the number (or total cost) of changes on the tree. For unordered characters with equal costs, Fitch (1971) gave a two-pass algorithm. In the downpass (from tips to root), each node receives a set of candidate states: the intersection of its children’s sets if they overlap, and otherwise their union, at the cost of one change. The number of unions is the parsimony score of the character on the tree. An uppass then refines the sets into the most parsimonious reconstructions (MPRs) at each node: the set of states that appear in at least one most-parsimonious assignment. Sankoff (1975) generalized this to arbitrary cost matrices, in which a change from state \(i\) to state \(j\) costs \(c_{ij}\). Sankoff parsimony accommodates ordered characters (changes only between adjacent states of a scale, as for a series of vowel heights), irreversible characters (Dollo-like costs, in which gaining a state is expensive and losing it cheap, a natural model for cognate presence; Chapter 7) and directional sound changes (a cost matrix in which \(p > f\) is cheap and \(f > p\) expensive). Its recursion has exactly the structure of the likelihood pruning algorithm of Chapter 5: replace “minimum” by “sum”, “plus” by “times” and costs by transition probabilities, and Sankoff’s algorithm becomes Felsenstein’s. The Fitch and Sankoff recursions, Equations (D.4) and (D.5), and a hand-coded Fitch downpass checked against phangorn are in Section D.2.1. When several reconstructions are equally parsimonious, conventions are needed to choose among them. ACCTRAN (accelerated transformation) places changes as close to the root as possible, favoring reversals over parallel changes; DELTRAN (delayed transformation) places them as close to the tips as possible, favoring parallel changes (Swofford and Maddison 1987). For linguistic characters the choice is substantive. ACCTRAN treats a feature shared by two non-sister subgroups as inherited and later lost in between; DELTRAN treats it as independently innovated twice. These correspond to two of the classical options historical linguists weigh when a feature has a patchy distribution: retention with losses, or parallel innovation (or contact). The convention also changes how certain a reconstruction looks. phangorn’s ancestral.pars() offers type = "MPR", which returns at every node all the states that appear in at least one most-parsimonious reconstruction, and type = "ACCTRAN", which commits to one of them. Plotted as pie charts, ACCTRAN reconstructions therefore look more decisive than the data warrant, and MPR is the honest summary of what parsimony alone can say. A second trap is circularity. A character that was used to infer the tree is not independent evidence about its own history on that tree, because its distribution has already shaped the topology. Reconstructing a morphological innovation on a tree inferred from a character set that includes it will tend to make the reconstruction look cleaner than it should. Characters that are the object of a reconstruction are best left out of the tree inference, or the sensitivity of the result to their exclusion checked. 12.3.2 What parsimony ignores Parsimony is fast, intuitive and close to the reasoning of the comparative method, but it has well-known limitations (Cunningham et al. 1998). It ignores branch lengths, so a change on a branch representing five thousand years of separation counts the same as one on a branch of fifty years. It gives no measure of uncertainty beyond the existence of multiple equally parsimonious solutions. And it is biased when rates of change are high: the minimum number of changes is then systematically less than the actual number, and reconstructions at deep nodes become unreliable in ways that parsimony itself cannot detect. These are the same considerations that favor likelihood over parsimony for tree inference (Chapter 4), and they are, if anything, more serious for ASR, because a single character carries far less information than a whole data matrix. 12.4 Likelihood reconstruction: marginal and joint 12.4.1 The Mk model Probabilistic ASR starts from a continuous-time Markov model of character change, the same machinery used for cognate data (Chapter 7) and for discrete phylogeography (Chapter 11). For a character with \(k\) states, an instantaneous rate matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) specifies the rate \(q_{ij}\) of change from state \(i\) to state \(j\), and \(\mathbf{P}(t) = e^{\mathbf{Q}t}\) gives transition probabilities over a branch of length \(t\). For morphological characters in biology this is known as the Mk model (Lewis 2001); the general likelihood framework for discrete characters on trees, including tests of correlated evolution, goes back to Pagel (1994). As in Chapter 11, the rate matrix can be equal-rates (ER: one rate), symmetric (SYM: \(k(k-1)/2\) rates) or all-rates-different (ARD: \(k(k-1)\) rates), or can be constrained by hand (for example, an ordered model with changes only between adjacent states). For basic word order with three states (SOV, SVO, VSO), an ARD model has six rates. It is natural to suspect that changes are asymmetric: many typologists have argued that SOV to SVO is common and the reverse rare, and that VSO tends to arise from SVO. A fitted ARD model on a large enough sample of trees could test this, which is what Maurits and Griffiths (2014) set out to do (Section 12.10). The likelihood of the tip data given the tree \(\tau\) and parameters \(\theta\) (the rates and the root distribution \(\pi\)) is computed by Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm. The algorithm computes, for every node \(v\) and state \(i\), the conditional likelihood \(L_v(i)\): the probability of the tip states below \(v\) given that \(v\) is in state \(i\). The likelihood of the whole tree is then \(L(\theta) = \sum_i \pi_i\, L_{\text{root}}(i)\). Parameters are estimated by maximizing \(L(\theta)\), and reconstruction proceeds in one of two ways. The pruning recursion for \(L_v(i)\), Equation (D.6), and an implementation in R that reproduces the log-likelihood reported by fitMk(), are in Section D.2.2. 12.4.2 Marginal reconstruction The marginal reconstruction at node \(v\) is the probability distribution of the state at \(v\), summing over all possible states at every other node: \[\begin{equation} P(X_v = i \mid D, \hat\theta) = \frac{\sum_{\text{assignments with } X_v = i} P(D, \text{assignment} \mid \hat\theta)}{L(\hat\theta)}. \tag{12.1} \end{equation}\] At the root this is simply \(\pi_i L_{\text{root}}(i) / \sum_j \pi_j L_{\text{root}}(j)\), which follows directly from the pruning pass. For other nodes, one must combine the information from below \(v\) (its conditional likelihoods \(L_v(i)\)) with the information from the rest of the tree (the “outside” likelihood \(U_v(i)\), computed in a second, root-to-tips pass), so that \(P(X_v = i \mid D) \propto L_v(i)\, U_v(i)\). An equivalent and conceptually simple approach is to re-root the tree at each node in turn and use the root formula; this re-rooting algorithm is implemented in several R functions, and the resulting node probabilities are the empirical Bayes reconstructions introduced for molecular sequences by Yang et al. (1995). Two points about marginal reconstruction are often confused. First, the conditional likelihood \(L_v(i)\) normalized over \(i\) is not the marginal posterior at \(v\), except at the root: it ignores everything outside the subtree. Second, the marginal probabilities computed at the maximum-likelihood estimate \(\hat\theta\) are empirical Bayes posterior probabilities (Yang et al. 1995; Koshi and Goldstein 1996): they treat the estimated rates as if they were known exactly. With small trees and single characters, the uncertainty in \(\hat\theta\) can be large, and empirical Bayes reconstructions are overconfident. The R section shows the first point concretely. In R, ape::ace(..., type = "discrete") returns marginal posterior probabilities in its lik.anc component under its default setting marginal = FALSE. Setting marginal = TRUE returns, despite the name, the scaled conditional likelihoods of each node given only its descendants, which are not marginal reconstructions except at the root. The phytools function ancr() returns marginal reconstructions by default and joint reconstructions with type = "joint". Always check which quantity a function reports before interpreting it, and say which one you report. 12.4.3 Joint reconstruction The joint reconstruction is the single assignment of states to all internal nodes that maximizes the joint probability of the data and the assignment: \[\begin{equation} (\hat x_{n+1}, \ldots, \hat x_{2n-1}) = \arg\max_{x_{n+1}, \ldots, x_{2n-1}} \pi_{x_{\text{root}}} \prod_{\text{branches } (a \to c)} P_{x_a x_c}(t_c), \tag{12.2} \end{equation}\] where tip states are fixed at their observed values. A naive search over all \(k^{n-1}\) assignments is infeasible for large trees, but Pupko et al. (2000) gave a dynamic-programming algorithm, the max-product analogue of pruning, which finds the best assignment in time linear in the number of nodes. The Pupko algorithm, Equation (D.7), and a hand-coded version that agrees exactly with ancr(..., type = "joint") are in Section D.2.3. Marginal and joint reconstructions answer different questions. Marginal probabilities say what we believe about one node at a time, and they are the right quantity when interest centers on a particular proto-language (“what was the basic word order of Proto-Oceanic?”). The joint reconstruction is a single coherent history and is the right quantity when the reconstruction will be used as a whole, for example to count the minimum number of changes it implies. The two can disagree: the state with the highest marginal probability at a node need not be the state it takes in the most probable joint assignment, and the R section shows an example. Neither reports the uncertainty of an entire history; that is what stochastic mapping is for. 12.4.4 The root prior The root distribution \(\pi\) has a large and often unappreciated effect on reconstructions near the root, which is usually where linguistic interest lies. Common choices are: Equal (flat): \(\pi_i = 1/k\). The default in many programs. Stationary: \(\pi\) equal to the equilibrium distribution of \(\mathbf{Q}\). This assumes the process had been running long before the root, which is natural for a family that is itself part of a deeper history. Estimated: \(\pi\) treated as free parameters, which is rarely well identified. FitzJohn: \(\pi_i \propto L_{\text{root}}(i)\), weighting root states by their own conditional likelihoods, proposed by FitzJohn et al. (2009) in the context of diversification models and now widely used. Fixed: the root state set to a particular value, for example to test a hypothesis by comparing likelihoods with the root fixed to each state. With an asymmetric \(\mathbf{Q}\), the stationary distribution can favor states that are rare at the tips, and a stationary root prior can then dominate the reconstruction at the root. Reporting the sensitivity of the root reconstruction to the root prior is good practice. Programs differ in their defaults, and the default is not always visible in a script: fitMk() in phytools uses the flat prior unless told otherwise, whereas RevBayes uses the stationary distribution of \(\mathbf{Q}\) when no root frequencies are given. Harmon (2019) adds a third source of root probabilities, outside information such as attested ancient languages or an outgroup, and notes that the flat and stationary choices coincide only under equal rates. An estimated root distribution needs a particular warning. For a single character with a uniform prior on \(\pi\), the marginal likelihood and the root reconstruction are exactly those of the flat prior, and the posterior of \(\pi\) hardly moves from its prior, because one character supplies a single draw from the root distribution. Root frequencies become estimable only when many characters share them. 12.4.5 Constraints and priors that decide the answer A rate matrix with zeros in it does more than express a hypothesis: it can settle the reconstruction before the data are consulted. Cathcart (2018) made the point with the study of “dative sickness” in Germanic by Dunn et al. (2017), which modelled how the case of the subjects of particular verbs changed among accusative (A), dative (D) and nominative (N). The model the authors preferred allowed only the changes A \(\to\) D, A \(\to\) N and D \(\to\) N, the directions of the hypothesized drift, and its reconstructions agreed with the philological ones, which they read as support for it. Under that model, however, a nominative subject can be reconstructed at a node only if every descendant language has one, and wherever an accusative subject is attested at a tip, the root must have had an accusative subject. The agreement was therefore largely built into the constraints, and the constrained model was not the one favored by the likelihood. A weaker form of the hypothesis, in which the disfavored changes are rare rather than impossible, can be tested by comparing the estimated rates; Cathcart’s reanalysis of the published data found the rates in the favored directions to be higher on average, but not significantly so. Agreement between a reconstruction and expert judgement is a useful sanity check. It is not evidence for the model that produced the reconstruction, and it should play no part in choosing among models (compare Section 12.13). Constraints are easier to defend when they rest on evidence from outside the character being modelled. Goldstein (2022a) fixed the Indo-European root at “no articles” and excluded the loss of articles, because the earliest attested Indo-European languages lack articles and each class of articles descended from a common ancestral article is confined to a single major branch (Section 13.7). His rate estimates are conditional on that judgement; a model that allows rare losses could test it. Softer modelling choices act in the same way, only less visibly. Whether a character is given one rate or separate rates of gain and loss can change reconstructions substantially (Mooers and Schluter 1999). Irreversibility is hard to detect from the states of living languages alone. Harmon (2019) shows a case in which a model with different rates of gain and loss fitted no better than a one-rate model, although the biological expectation of asymmetry was strong, and notes that outside knowledge would have to enter as an informative prior. Historical linguistics has much knowledge of this kind about the direction of change, and using it is one of the natural meeting points of the two traditions (Section 12.13). The price is that the prior then contributes to the answer, and its contribution has to be reported. The Indo-European augment, a past-tense verbal prefix found in Greek, Armenian and Indo-Iranian, shows how these choices interact with subgrouping. Whether it was present in Proto-Indo-European remains uncertain, and Goldstein (2020) uses it to show that the dependence runs both ways. To treat a shared feature as a subgrouping innovation one must know its ancestral state, and to reconstruct an ancestral state one must know the subgrouping. Phylogenetic ASR makes the second half of this circle explicit, but it does not break it. For a feature attested in only a few branches, the reconstruction depends on the tree, on the asymmetry of gain and loss, and on the root treatment, and the data alone may not decide between “inherited and lost” and “gained more than once”. Section D.2.6 computes the root reconstruction of a rare, augment-like feature exactly under flat, stationary, estimated and fixed roots, and shows why an estimated root frequency for one character reproduces the flat prior. The RevBayes version, with marginal likelihoods for seven root treatments and rate priors, is in Section H.5.21. 12.5 Bayesian ASR: integrating over trees and parameters Empirical Bayes reconstruction conditions on one tree and one set of rates. A fully Bayesian reconstruction integrates over both: \[\begin{equation} P(X_v = i \mid D) = \int\!\!\int P(X_v = i \mid D, \tau, \theta)\; p(\tau, \theta \mid D)\; d\tau\, d\theta. \tag{12.3} \end{equation}\] In practice the integral is approximated by averaging over a posterior sample of trees (usually from an earlier analysis of the lexical data) and over a posterior sample of rates for the character of interest, obtained by MCMC on each tree or jointly across trees. Huelsenbeck and Bollback (2001) compared empirical and hierarchical Bayesian approaches and showed that ignoring uncertainty in the tree and the parameters can give overconfident reconstructions. Pagel et al. (2004) developed the approach implemented in BayesTraits, in which a reversible-jump MCMC samples both the rates and the model structure (which rates are equal, which are zero) across a sample of trees. A complication specific to integrating over trees is that a node of interest may not exist in every tree. If the question is “what was the word order of Proto-Germanic?”, the relevant node is the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the Germanic languages, which exists in every tree that contains those languages but may differ in its descendants, its age and its position from tree to tree. Pagel et al. (2004) proposed reconstructing the state at the MRCA of a specified set of tips in each tree, and also showed how to fix (or “fossilize”) the state of a node and compare the marginal likelihoods of models with the node fixed to different states, which gives a Bayes factor for competing reconstructions. This is particularly useful when a linguistic hypothesis concerns a specific proto-language (“Proto-Indo-European had three genders”) rather than a node in a particular tree. The MRCA approach also exposes a subtlety. If the named languages do not form a clade in some trees, their MRCA in those trees is a deeper node, the ancestor of the named group and of other languages, and the reconstruction there answers a different historical question. A reconstruction averaged over trees then mixes answers to two questions, and it should be reported together with the posterior probability that the group is a clade. Tree uncertainty can matter as much as parameter uncertainty, and the general reasons why a single summary tree misleads in downstream analyses are set out in Section 11.10. For ASR two of them are especially important. A reconstruction on the maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree treats every clade in it as certain, so the answer for “Proto-X” is reported even when X is a clade in only half of the posterior trees. And reconstructions are nonlinear functions of the tree, so the reconstruction on a summary tree is not the average reconstruction. The R section shows both on a small example (Section 12.15.7). 12.6 Stochastic character mapping Node reconstructions say nothing directly about what happened along the branches: how many times a character changed, when, and in which direction. Stochastic character mapping (Nielsen 2002; Huelsenbeck et al. 2003) answers these questions by sampling complete histories of the character from their posterior distribution given the tip data, the tree and the model. Each sampled history (“map”) specifies the state at every point on every branch. Averaging over many maps gives posterior distributions of the number of changes of each type, the time spent in each state, and the states at nodes. A map is sampled in three steps: a root state is drawn from its marginal posterior; the states of the other nodes are drawn one by one from the root toward the tips, each conditional on its parent’s state and on the data below it; and, finally, a history along each branch is simulated conditional on the states at its two ends. The first two steps draw a joint assignment of node states from its exact posterior; the third fills in the changes along the branches. The conditional distribution used in the second step, Equation (D.8), and the rejection and uniformization methods for the third, are in Section D.2.4. The method was popularized by the SIMMAP software (Bollback 2006) and is implemented in R as make.simmap() in phytools. In the original formulation, the rates are either fixed at their maximum-likelihood values (empirical Bayes) or sampled from their posterior; phytools supports both. Stochastic maps answer many questions that node reconstructions cannot. How many times did SOV order change to SVO in the history of a family, and is that number larger than the number of changes in the opposite direction? Did a feature change mostly on long branches or in bursts? How much of a family’s history was spent with a particular state, and did changes in one character tend to follow changes in another (as a test of correlated evolution; see Chapter 13)? The expected number of changes is also computable analytically (Minin and Suchard 2008), but maps are more flexible because any function of the history can be summarized. The posterior expected number of changes from a stochastic map is usually larger than the parsimony count, often considerably. Parsimony counts the minimum number of changes needed; stochastic mapping counts the expected number under a model that allows multiple changes along a branch, including changes that are later reversed. When historical linguists say that a feature “changed only once” in a family, they are usually making a parsimony argument. A model-based count can be an instructive check. 12.7 Heterogeneous and hidden-rate models The standard Mk model assumes that the rates of change are the same on every branch of the tree. Linguistic characters often violate this. Basic word order has been stable for millennia in some lineages (the Japonic and Koreanic languages have been verb-final throughout their recorded history), while it has changed repeatedly in others (in the history of English, from mixed OV/VO with verb-second in Old English to rigid SVO). A model that assumes a single rate everywhere will underestimate change in the labile lineages and overestimate it in the stable ones, and reconstructions at deep nodes can be badly affected. Hidden-rate models (Beaulieu et al. 2013) address this by augmenting each observed state with a hidden rate category. With two categories, “slow” and “fast”, a binary character with observed states 0 and 1 has four hidden states (0-slow, 1-slow, 0-fast, 1-fast). Each category has its own rates of change between the observed states, and lineages switch between categories at further rates. Only the observed state is known at the tips; the likelihood sums over hidden categories. The model is a phylogenetic version of the covarion model (Chapter 7), and Boyko and Beaulieu (2021) generalized it into a broad family of hidden Markov models for comparative data, implemented in the R package corHMM. phytools provides a similar model through fitHRM(). The block structure of the hidden-rate rate matrix, Equation (D.9), is in Section D.2.5. Hidden-rate models are attractive for linguistics because they formalize the intuition that some lineages are “conservative” and others “innovative” for a given feature, without having to specify in advance which ones. Their parameters are, however, hard to estimate from a single character on a tree of modest size, and model comparison (by AIC or marginal likelihood) should be used to check that the extra complexity is warranted. A different kind of heterogeneity arises when several characters are related. Basic word order is often coded as a single character with six states (SOV, SVO, VSO, VOS, OVS, OSV), but it can also be decomposed into binary characters (OV versus VO, subject-initial or not) whose evolution may be correlated. Models of correlated discrete characters (Pagel 1994) are the subject of Chapter 13. Here it is enough to note that the choice of coding changes the reconstruction, because it changes the model. 12.8 How reliable are ancestral reconstructions? Ancestral reconstructions are estimates, and their accuracy depends on several factors that can be stated in general terms. Depth and rate. Information about a node decays with the time separating it from the tips, relative to the rate of change. A character that changes on average once every few thousand years retains information about nodes a few thousand years deep but very little about nodes ten thousand years deep. At the limit, the posterior at the root converges to the root prior. Studies in biology have repeatedly found that reconstructions of fast-evolving characters at deep nodes are unreliable (Schluter et al. 1997; Cunningham et al. 1998). A simple check is to compare the fitted Mk model with a model that ignores the tree and draws each language’s state independently from the observed frequencies. When the rate is so high that the likelihood surface has a long flat ridge, the two likelihoods coincide, and the character carries no information about its history; Harmon (2019) calls this the “total garbage” test (Section D.2.7). Tree shape and sampling. A node supported by many descendant lineages that are independently informative (a star-like radiation) is reconstructed more precisely than a node with a single long stem. Unsampled lineages, including extinct ones, do not contribute information. Dense sampling of one subgroup can, as in phylogeography, pull reconstructions toward that subgroup’s states when the model is misspecified. Tree uncertainty. A reconstruction at a node is only as secure as the node itself. If the clade below the node of interest is poorly supported, or if the dates of the tree are uncertain, the reconstruction varies from tree to tree (Section 12.5). Model adequacy. Reconstructions are only as good as the model. Rate heterogeneity among lineages, asymmetric rates, correlations with other characters and contact-induced change all violate the simple Mk model, and violations tend to produce overconfident reconstructions rather than visibly uncertain ones. Diversification. If the state of a character affects the rate at which lineages split or die out, reconstructions that ignore this are biased toward the state associated with higher diversification (Maddison 2006). For languages, a feature associated with expanding, rapidly splitting populations (perhaps a feature of the languages of agricultural expansions) could be overrepresented at the tips and wrongly reconstructed as ancestral. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, simulations in which characters evolve under an Mk model and are reconstructed under the same model test only parameter recovery; reconstructions are far more often wrong because the model is misspecified than because the algorithm fails. There is a small but instructive literature that tests ASR against known histories. In biology, Hillis et al. (1992) generated a known phylogeny by serial propagation of bacteriophage in the laboratory, and Oakley and Cunningham (2000) used the same system to show that reconstruction of continuous ancestral states was much less accurate than estimation of evolutionary correlations from the same data. In linguistics, the natural test cases are families with a documented ancestor: reconstructing Latin from the Romance languages, Sanskrit or Middle Indo-Aryan from modern Indo-Aryan languages, or Classical Chinese from modern Sinitic varieties. Such tests are a recurring theme in work on automated reconstruction (Section 12.12) and in evaluations of lexical ASR (Section 12.9). Attested ancient languages are valuable for ASR in a second way. Biologists have shown that including fossil observations at internal positions in a tree improves the accuracy of ancestral reconstructions of continuous traits (Slater et al. 2012). The linguistic analogue is to include ancient languages as tips (or as sampled ancestors; Chapter 10) whenever they are available, rather than reconstructing the deep history from modern languages alone. 12.9 Reconstructing the proto-lexicon The most direct linguistic application of ASR is to the vocabulary of proto-languages. There are two ways to pose the question, corresponding to the two ways of coding lexical data described in Chapter 3. Semasiological reconstruction: was this word present? Under binary cognate coding, each character is a cognate set, and its state in a language is 1 if the language has a reflex of the set (in the relevant meaning) and 0 otherwise. ASR then gives, for each cognate set, the probability that it was present in a proto-language. Under the stochastic Dollo model (Chapter 7), each cognate set is born exactly once on the tree, so a set present in two primary branches must have been present at the root; the reconstruction of the proto-lexicon under such a model follows almost directly from the inferred tree and the pattern of presence. Under reversible binary models, in contrast, a cognate set present in two primary branches might instead have been gained twice, and the root reconstruction depends on the relative rates of gain and loss. Onomasiological reconstruction: which word expressed this meaning? Under multistate coding, each character is a meaning slot (say ‘hand’) and its states are the cognate classes used for that meaning. ASR then gives the probability that each cognate class was the word for ‘hand’ in the proto-language. This is the question the comparative method typically answers when it lists a reconstructed proto-form with its gloss. The two framings can give inconsistent answers. If presence/absence characters for the competing cognate classes of a single meaning are reconstructed separately, nothing forces their probabilities to sum to one: the reconstruction may imply that the proto-language had no word for ‘hand’ or several. The multistate framing builds in the constraint that one word fills the slot, though it has its own unrealistic assumption that a language has exactly one word per meaning (synonymy and polysemy are common).
