The R section demonstrates the inconsistency on a toy example. Jäger and List (2018) made the first systematic evaluation of ASR methods for onomasiological reconstruction. They compared parsimony (including Sankoff parsimony with different coding schemes) and likelihood-based methods with binary and multistate coding, applying them to multilingual wordlists from families for which expert reconstructions of the proto-language vocabulary exist, and they scored each method by how often it recovered the expert’s choice of word for each meaning. The study showed that ASR can recover a substantial proportion of expert onomasiological reconstructions automatically, and that both the method and the coding choice affect the result. It also clarified the conceptual difference between asking whether a cognate set existed and asking which cognate set filled a meaning slot, which earlier work had often blurred. The design is a test of agreement with the comparative method rather than of truth: the cognate sets fed to the algorithms and the expert reconstructions used to score them come from the same scholarly tradition, so agreement shows that ASR reproduces expert reasoning from the distribution of cognates, not that both are right. Lexical ASR has been used, implicitly or explicitly, in many studies that use language trees to reconstruct culture. If a word for ‘pig’, ‘taro’ or ‘canoe outrigger’ can be reconstructed with high probability for a node, the referent was presumably known to its speakers. This is linguistic paleontology (Chapter 11) given a probabilistic footing, and it inherits the same problem of semantic change: the probability that a cognate set existed at a node is not the probability that it had the same meaning there. The Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database (Greenhill et al. 2008) and comparative dictionaries such as Blust and Trussel’s Austronesian Comparative Dictionary are the obvious resources for such work, because their cognate sets can be compared with the reconstructions of specialists. 12.10 Reconstructing grammar Structural features, such as basic word order, the presence of grammatical gender, the alignment of case marking or the position of adpositions, are natural targets for ASR. Their states are discrete and well defined in typological databases such as WALS and Grambank (Chapter 3), and the questions are of wide interest: was Proto-Indo-European verb-final? Did the ancestor of all languages have SOV order? 12.10.1 Basic word order Gell-Mann and Ruhlen (2011) assembled a tree of the world’s languages from published classifications and argued, from the distribution of basic word orders across it, that the ancestral order of all (or nearly all) attested languages was SOV, with subsequent drift toward SVO and from there to VSO and VOS. Their reconstruction relied on informal, essentially parsimony-like reasoning over a deep and largely conjectural tree, and it was criticized for that reason. It nevertheless posed the question in a form that probabilistic ASR can address. Maurits and Griffiths (2014) addressed it with Bayesian phylogenetic methods. They modeled basic word order (the six orders of subject, object and verb) as a character evolving under a continuous-time Markov chain, with a single set of transition rates shared across many language families, and they integrated over trees for each family generated from published classifications combined with priors on branch lengths. Pooling families allowed the rates to be estimated from far more transitions than any one family provides. They then computed posterior distributions over ancestral word orders at the roots of the families. Their results favored SOV as the ancestral order in many of the families examined, broadly in line with the qualitative claim of Gell-Mann and Ruhlen (2011), but with considerable uncertainty that depended on the family and on the assumptions about the trees. The study is a model of careful ASR: it is explicit about the trees, it pools information across families by estimating a single set of transition rates shared by all of them (a choice its authors supported by model comparison), and it reports uncertainty rather than a single answer. The approach of Maurits and Griffiths (2014) assumes that word order evolves under the same process in every family. The opposite assumption, that each family has its own process, underlies the analysis of Dunn et al. (2011), who fitted separate models of correlated evolution between word-order features in four families and found that the dependencies between features differ across families (Chapter 13). Between these two extremes lie hierarchical models in which family-specific rates are drawn from a shared distribution, an approach that, to our knowledge, has rarely been applied to ancestral word order but that is standard in other areas of Bayesian statistics. 12.10.2 Structural phylogenetics In Island Melanesia, the Papuan (non-Austronesian) languages of the Solomon Islands and the Bismarck Archipelago share almost no demonstrable cognate vocabulary, and the comparative method cannot establish whether they form one or several families. Dunn et al. (2005) proposed structural phylogenetics: coding over one hundred abstract structural features (properties of phonology, morphology and syntax) for these Papuan languages and for neighboring Oceanic (Austronesian) languages, and analyzing them with maximum parsimony and the NeighborNet network method. For the Oceanic languages, whose subgrouping is known from the comparative method, the structural tree recovered much of the accepted structure, which served as a check on the method. For the Papuan languages, the structural tree suggested a deep genealogical signal of the kind that lexical methods could not detect, though the authors were careful to note that structural similarity can also reflect contact. A longer methodological treatment (Dunn et al. 2008) explored the sensitivity of the results to coding and methods. Structural phylogenetics is relevant to ASR in two ways. The structural trees provide a scaffold for reconstructing the grammars of ancestral nodes. And the approach raises the question of how fast and how independently structural features change, which ASR on trees with known structure can help answer. A related analysis by Reesink et al. (2009) used population-genetic clustering (STRUCTURE) on structural features of the languages of Sahul and is discussed in Chapter 16. 12.10.3 Indo-European morphosyntax Indo-European offers the richest test bed for grammatical ASR, because its early history is documented in Hittite, Vedic Sanskrit, Ancient Greek, Latin and other ancient languages, and because its proto-grammar has been reconstructed by the comparative method in great detail. Several studies have combined dated Indo-European trees with grammatical features to reconstruct the history of particular constructions. Widmer et al. (2017) studied the recursion of noun phrases (whether modifiers such as possessors can themselves contain further modifiers in the same construction type) and argued, from Bayesian phylogenetic analyses of 55 Indo-European languages, that although particular NP construction types can gain or lose the ability to embed recursively within a few centuries, it is extremely unlikely that recursive NP embedding was ever lost altogether at any stage of the family: when one construction type becomes unavailable for recursion, an unconstrained alternative is very likely to develop. Recursion in this sense behaves as a strong diachronic bias, which the authors suggest may be universal. Carling and Cathcart (2021) reconstructed the evolution of a large set of Indo-European grammatical features with phylogenetic methods and compared their reconstructions of Proto-Indo-European grammar with those of the comparative tradition, finding substantial agreement for many features and informative disagreements for others. Here too, agreement is partly built in: the feature codes for ancient languages and the comparative reconstructions draw on the same philological analyses, so the disagreements are at least as informative as the agreements. Cathcart et al. (2018) showed that areal (contact) pressure in addition to inheritance shapes the evolution of grammatical features in Indo-European, a reminder that ASR under a purely vertical model can mistake contact-induced convergence for inheritance. Calude and Verkerk (2016) studied the typology and diachrony of higher numerals across Indo-European with phylogenetic comparative methods. Goldstein (2022a) estimated that indefinite articles arose faster in Indo-European languages that already had a definite article (Section 13.7). Shirtz et al. (2021) compared models for the evolution of negative existential constructions in 106 Indo-European languages and found that the unidirectional Negative Existential Cycle alone fits worse than models that allow other and multiple transitions between strategies, while noting that the skewed distribution of types in the sample limits what such models can resolve. A recurring finding of this literature is that grammatical features are not uniformly more stable than vocabulary. Using a large set of structural and lexical characters across Austronesian, Greenhill et al. (2017) found that rates of change of grammatical features vary widely, with some changing faster than basic vocabulary, and that grammatical features are more susceptible to the influence of neighboring languages. The implication for ASR is that structural reconstructions at deep nodes should not be assumed reliable merely because “grammar is conservative”. Recent studies have tried to model grammatical change more realistically. Ebert et al. (2025) replaced a single word-order feature per language with object-verb order in 46 parallel sentences from a corpus of 36 Indo-European languages. A mixture model grouped the sentence contexts into three classes with distinct dynamics: contexts with nominal objects changed slowly, pronominal objects changed fast, and complement clauses had a strong bias toward VO. Stochastic character mapping reconstructed VO order for nominal objects in Proto-Indo-European, while the fast rates for pronominal objects did not allow a reliable reconstruction at all, a clear illustration of the depth-and-rate limit of Section 12.8. For argument marking, Phillips and Bowern (2022) used a Brownian-motion model to trace splits in ergative marking across Pama-Nyungan and found evidence for an ergative-accusative split traceable to Proto-Pama-Nyungan, and Hong et al. (2026) modelled ergative, non-ergative and split alignment of case marking in over 200 languages from eleven families. Their best model required two evolutionary regimes that cut across families, one favoring non-ergative and one favoring split-ergative alignment, an example of the heterogeneous-rate models of Section 12.7 applied to grammar. 12.11 Reconstructing sound systems and sound change Sound systems are the domain where the comparative method is most powerful and where phylogenetic ASR has been least used. The comparative method reconstructs proto-phonemes from regular correspondences, using the directionality of sound change (lenition is more common than fortition, palatalization before front vowels is common and the reverse rare) to decide between alternative reconstructions. Several kinds of phylogenetic work bear on this. Phonological characters on trees. Phoneme inventories can be coded as presence/absence of each segment, and their evolution modeled on trees. The database BDPROTO compiles reconstructed proto-language inventories and has been used to study diachronic trends in inventory structure (Moran et al. 2021). Macklin-Cordes et al. (2021) showed that phonotactic properties (which sequences of sounds are permitted) carry phylogenetic signal in Pama-Nyungan, so that they can in principle be treated as characters for both tree inference and ASR. Note that the presence of a phoneme in an inventory is a character state, not a reconstruction of the sound system: an ASR saying that a node “had /f/” with probability 0.7 does not say which words contained it or by which correspondences it is known. Sound changes as characters. In the computational cladistics of Ringe et al. (2002) (Chapter 4), sound changes such as Grimm’s Law were coded as characters, on the assumption that a complex sound change is very unlikely to happen twice independently. In ASR terms, these are characters with strongly asymmetric (nearly irreversible) rates. They also illustrate the dependence on the comparative method: whether a language underwent Grimm’s Law is itself established by comparative reconstruction. Regular sound change as concerted evolution. Hruschka et al. (2015) proposed a Bayesian phylogenetic model in which sound correspondences across a large set of Turkic cognates are treated as characters that can change together, so that a regular sound change appears as a concerted shift in many characters at once on a single branch. The model detects branches on which such concerted changes occurred, an automated version of the comparative method’s identification of sound laws, and it adapts the biological concept of concerted evolution (the homogenization of gene copies within a lineage) to the regularity of sound change. Directional models. The asymmetries that historical phonologists rely on (for example, that /p/ > /f/ is far more common than /f/ > /p/) are naturally expressed as asymmetric rate matrices. Cross-linguistic databases of attested sound changes could in principle supply informative priors for such matrices, a possibility that, to our knowledge, remains largely unexploited. Garrett and Johnson (2013) develop a typology of asymmetric sound changes grounded in biases of motor planning, aerodynamics, gestural mechanics and perceptual parsing; a typology of this kind is what an informative prior on a directional rate matrix would have to encode, and it would also say which zero rates are defensible (Section 12.4.5). Irregular reflexes and dialect layers. Where sound change looks irregular, probabilistic models can help to separate its sources before any tree-based reconstruction is attempted. Cathcart (2022) applied a Bayesian model based on a hierarchical Dirichlet process to the irregular reflexes of West Iranian (Persian, Kurdish, Balochi and others). He argued that the usual explanation, borrowing from some stage of Persian, is too simple: Persian may not be the only donor, irregularity is not always introduced by lexical borrowing, and some apparent irregularities may reflect different outcomes in different conditioning environments. How a rare sound spreads: bilabial trills in Malekula. Bilabial trills are among the rarest speech sounds in the world’s languages, yet several Oceanic languages of Malekula Island in Vanuatu have them. King et al. (2025) built a lexical phylogeny of the Malekula languages from the Vanuatu Voices database and then reconstructed, on that phylogeny, the presence of a trill in fourteen separate meanings whose words contain one in at least some languages. Treating each word as its own character, rather than coding “has a trill” once per language, let them follow the sound through the lexicon. They found a surprising degree of dynamism: trills spread gradually through the vocabulary, were frequently lost and regained, and their distribution was consistent with frequent borrowing between neighboring languages. The authors suggest that the low functional load of the trills, and speakers’ attachment to them as a marker of identity, explain the rapid change and the borrowing. The study shows how ASR on a lexical tree can address the diffusion of a sound change, a question the comparative method usually treats qualitatively. It also inherits the caveats of this chapter: fourteen characters on one tree of a small island give limited power, and reconstructed gains and losses are conditional on the tree, which may itself have been affected by contact. 12.12 Automated reconstruction of word forms The most ambitious form of linguistic ASR reconstructs not states of a coded character but the actual phonological shapes of proto-words, the second kind of reconstruction in Section 12.2. Bouchard-Côté et al. (2013) developed a probabilistic model in which each branch of a language tree carries a stochastic string transducer, a model of sound change that rewrites a parent word form into a child word form by context-dependent substitutions, insertions and deletions. The parameters of the transducers are shared across words on a branch (so that sound change is regular in the model) but can differ between branches, and the unobserved proto-forms at internal nodes are inferred jointly with the parameters by approximate inference. Applied to a large set of Austronesian languages drawn from the Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database, the system reconstructed proto-forms for hundreds of cognate sets. The automated reconstructions were compared with the manual reconstructions in Blust’s comparative work on Austronesian, and a large majority came within a single character edit of the expert’s reconstruction. The authors also used the model to test the functional load hypothesis, the long-standing idea that sound contrasts that distinguish many words are less likely to be lost through merger, and found support for it. Earlier work by the same group (Bouchard-Côté et al. 2007) had developed the approach on Romance, where the reconstructions can be checked against attested Latin. Later work has explored neural network models trained to map descendant forms to ancestral forms. Meloni et al. (2021) trained sequence-to-sequence models to reconstruct Latin forms from their Romance reflexes, and Ciobanu and Dinu (2018) addressed a similar task with other machine-learning methods. List, Forkel, and Hill (2022) proposed a framework that reconstructs proto-forms from aligned cognate sets using sound correspondence patterns and trimmed alignments, designed to be fast, transparent and evaluable on datasets in the CLDF format (Chapter 3). The same sound-correspondence logic can be run forwards. Bodt and List (2022) predicted the most likely forms of words missing from their Western Kho-Bwa (Sino-Tibetan) data from the correspondences in related cognate sets, preregistered the predictions, and then compared them with forms elicited in later fieldwork, an unusually direct out-of-sample test of a reconstruction-based model. Lu et al. (2024) reduced the need for training data with a semisupervised architecture that learns from a few cognate sets with known proto-forms and many without, and that builds in a principle of the comparative method: a reconstructed form must be transformable back into its reflexes. These methods differ from the character-state ASR of the rest of this chapter in an important way. Neural approaches typically require training data consisting of known ancestral forms, so they learn to imitate expert reconstructions (or attested ancestors) and are best seen as tools for extending or checking reconstructions, not as independent discovery procedures. The model of Bouchard-Côté et al. (2013), in contrast, is a generative model of sound change on a tree that needs no proto-forms for training, only the cognate sets and the tree. Its close agreement with expert reconstructions is therefore stronger evidence than agreement from a supervised model. It is still not fully independent: the cognate sets it starts from were established by the same comparative scholarship whose reconstructions it is scored against, and the hardest part of the comparative method, deciding which words are cognate, has been done in advance. The Romance case, where Latin is attested, is the cleaner test. To our knowledge, joint inference of trees, cognate sets, alignments and proto-forms in a single model, the linguistic equivalent of statistical alignment in biology (Redelings and Suchard 2005), remains an open goal. A partial step is the TKF91-based model of Goldstein et al. (2026), which infers trees directly from aligned cognate word forms and can be used to study segmental stability and the evolution of phonological inventories. 12.13 ASR and the comparative method How does phylogenetic ASR relate to the reconstructions of traditional historical linguistics? The comparative method (Fox 1995; Campbell 2013; Ringe and Eska 2013) reconstructs proto-forms by (1) establishing cognate sets, (2) identifying recurrent sound correspondences, (3) reconstructing for each correspondence set the proto-sound that best explains its reflexes, using knowledge of the directionality and naturalness of sound changes, and (4) assembling the reconstructed sounds into proto-words. Grammar is reconstructed by analogous reasoning on paradigms and constructions, with internal reconstruction (the use of irregularities within one language) as a complementary tool. Skirgård (2024) made the comparison explicit for grammar. Using Grambank data, she compared reconstructions of the grammar of ancestral Oceanic languages from the historical-linguistic literature with reconstructions by maximum parsimony and maximum likelihood, and found a high degree of agreement, with a tendency for classical reconstruction to ignore branch lengths. She argued that taking branch lengths into account is more conceptually sound, and that the most promising path combines computational methods with qualitative knowledge. Several points of contact and contrast stand out; Table 12.2 summarizes them. Both are tree-based, but differently. The comparative method uses the tree mainly through the principle that a feature attested in two primary branches is likely to be inherited, which is a parsimony argument. Phylogenetic ASR uses the full topology and the branch lengths. The comparative method uses directionality heavily, ASR rarely does. The comparative method’s knowledge of what is a likely sound change is, in modeling terms, a strongly informative prior on an asymmetric rate matrix. Most phylogenetic ASR uses symmetric or uninformative models. Bringing typological knowledge of change into ASR through informative priors is a natural meeting point. ASR quantifies uncertainty; the comparative method rarely does. Reconstructions marked with a question mark, or alternative reconstructions discussed in the text, are the comparative method’s expression of uncertainty. ASR provides probabilities, but probabilities that are conditional on a model whose adequacy has to be argued. They work at different levels. The comparative method reconstructs forms, sounds and constructions; most phylogenetic ASR reconstructs coded states of characters (Section 12.2). Automated reconstruction of word forms (Section 12.12) begins to close the gap. The input to ASR is the output of the comparative method. Cognate judgments, the basis of lexical phylogenetics, are themselves made by the comparative method (or by automated approximations to it; Chapter 3). Phylogenetic ASR does not replace the comparative method, it builds on it. The last point has a consequence for how agreement is read. When a phylogenetic reconstruction agrees with the comparative method’s reconstruction of the same proto-language, as in the evaluations of Jäger and List (2018), Carling and Cathcart (2021) and Bouchard-Côté et al. (2013), the agreement shows that the two procedures extract the same answer from overlapping evidence. It is not independent confirmation, because the cognate sets, the subgrouping that shapes the tree and often the coding of ancient languages come from the comparative tradition itself, and because cognate sharing is not the same as shared innovation. The most informative cases are the disagreements, which point either to a weakness of the model (contact, rate heterogeneity, the coding) or to a place where the comparative reconstruction rests on an assumption that the distributional evidence does not support. Frequency heuristics, explicit trees and tree samples. When the tree is uncertain, Indo-Europeanists have often decided whether a form goes back to the proto-language by counting. A long-standing lower-bound heuristic, already in Meillet’s Introduction, accepts a word as Proto-Indo-European if it is attested in at least three (preferably non-contiguous) branches and borrowing is not suspected; a majority-rule heuristic reconstructs the state found in most daughters; an Anatolian criterion asks for attestation in Anatolian and at least one other branch. Goldstein (2022b) argues that all three amount to reconstruction on a consensus tree with an unresolved node, and that this cannot work. On each fully resolved tree compatible with the consensus, the reconstruction is fixed by the topology and the optimality criterion, not by the count of daughters. The lower-bound rule can only place a form at the root and ignores the possibility that it arose at a shallower node; it treats forms attested in one branch as innovations, although any of them could be an archaism; and the threshold of three has no stated justification. Hale (2007) makes a related argument against majority rule: if a flat tree stands for a set of equally possible subgroupings, the number of daughters with a feature is no evidence about the proto-language, and counting daughters lets the sociopolitical status of varieties, which decides what gets documented as a separate “language”, influence the reconstruction. Olander (2018) proposes a cladistic approach instead. A feature shared by several subgroups is first reconstructed only to their lowest common node in an explicit, binary tree, and pushing it further back requires a separate argument that it was lost in the other lineages. On his working tree, the augment of Greek, Armenian and Indo-Iranian becomes an innovation of the node that unites these branches with Balto-Slavic, followed by loss in Balto-Slavic. A feature attested only in a deeply embedded subgroup, such as Baltic, becomes an unlikely archaism, because many independent innovations would be needed elsewhere. The approach makes reconstructions explicit, but it makes them conditional on one tree. Goldstein’s alternative is Bayesian ASR over a sample of trees (Section 12.5). Reconstructing presence and absence over 100 trees from an analysis in the framework of Chang et al. (2015), he obtained a posterior probability above 0.95 for the conjunction *kʷe ‘and’ at the root, in line with the traditional reconstruction, but only 0.56 for the absence of the augment, which leaves its Proto-Indo-European status open (compare Section 12.4.5). Both results are conditional on a binary presence/absence coding and a simple Markov model, and the augment result shows what the heuristics conceal: uncertainty in the tree becomes uncertainty in the reconstruction. Table 12.2: Ancestral state reconstruction in biology and the comparative method in linguistics. Aspect Phylogenetic ASR Comparative method Unit of reconstruction Coded character states, sometimes sequences Sounds, word forms, morphemes, constructions Use of the tree Full topology and branch lengths Mainly primary branching and subgrouping Model of change Explicit CTMC, usually symmetric Implicit, strongly directional knowledge of likely changes Uncertainty Posterior probabilities (model-conditional) Qualitative (question marks, alternatives) Contact Usually ignored Identified by irregular correspondences, cultural knowledge Validation Simulation, known histories Attested ancestors, internal consistency 12.14 From the biologist’s toolbox Ancestral sequence resurrection. Molecular biologists reconstruct ancestral protein sequences and then synthesize and test them in the laboratory, to study the functional properties of ancient molecules (Thornton 2004). The linguistic analogue of resurrection would be the experimental testing of reconstructed proto-forms (for example, psycholinguistic tests of how reconstructed proto-words are perceived), which is unusual but not unthinkable. More practically, the statistical methods used in molecular ASR, including joint reconstruction with insertions and deletions and reconstruction that accounts for alignment uncertainty, are directly relevant to automated reconstruction of word forms. The threshold model. Many linguistic features are discrete manifestations of an underlying continuum: a language is coded as “having” a phonemic tone contrast or not, as “having” grammatical gender or not, but the underlying systems vary continuously in their extent. The threshold model of quantitative genetics treats a discrete character as determined by an unobserved continuous liability that evolves under Brownian motion; the character changes state when the liability crosses a threshold (Felsenstein 2012). ASR under the threshold model reconstructs the liability at internal nodes (Revell 2014), and the model naturally produces the kind of “lineage-specific propensity” seen in linguistic features (lineages near the threshold flip often, lineages far from it rarely). To our knowledge, the threshold model has rarely if ever been applied to linguistic features; Sections 13.9.3 and 16.5.2 discuss it further. Structured Markov models. For characters whose states are logically hierarchical (a feature can only take a value if another feature is present: a language can only have gender agreement on verbs if it has gender), naive coding as independent characters is incoherent. Tarasov (2019) developed structured Markov models that combine dependent characters into a single rate matrix respecting these logical dependencies. Grambank-style data, with many logically dependent features, would benefit directly. Model averaging by reversible jump. Rather than choose one rate model for a character, BayesTraits samples over all ways of setting rates equal or to zero by reversible-jump MCMC (Pagel and Meade 2006), so that ASR averages over model uncertainty. This is available to linguists and used occasionally, but much ASR in the linguistic literature still reports reconstructions from a single chosen model. Fossils and sampled ancestors. Integrating fossil observations improves ancestral reconstruction of continuous traits (Slater et al. 2012). Attested ancient languages placed as tips or sampled ancestors play the same role for linguistic characters, and should be included whenever available. Polymorphic characters. Languages often have more than one value for a feature: several basic word orders with no dominant one, or two competing words for the same meaning. Biologists model polymorphism explicitly as an intermediate state (for example, the polymorphic Mk models of phytools, fitpolyMk(), described in Revell and Harmon (2022)). Coding “no dominant order” or synonymy as polymorphism rather than as missing data, or as an arbitrary choice of one state, would be more faithful to the data. 12.15 Ancestral state reconstruction in R We work with a toy dataset: a hand-built, ultrametric tree of fourteen hypothetical languages in four subgroups (A to D), with branch lengths in millennia and a root age of 5,000 years, and the basic word order of each language (SOV, SVO or VSO). The data are invented, but the pattern is realistic: subgroup A is mostly verb-final, subgroups B and D mostly SVO, and subgroup C mostly VSO (Figure 12.1, which also shows the node numbers used below). library(phytools) library(phangorn) tree <- read.tree(text = paste0( "((((A1:1,A2:1):1.5,(A3:1.2,A4:1.2):1.3):1,", "((B1:0.8,B2:0.8):1.2,B3:2):1.5):1.5,", "(((C1:1,C2:1):1,C3:2):1.5,((D1:0.5,D2:0.5):2,(D3:1.5,D4:1.5):1):1):1.5);")) wo <- c(A1 = "SOV", A2 = "SOV", A3 = "SOV", A4 = "SVO", B1 = "SVO", B2 = "SVO", B3 = "SOV", C1 = "VSO", C2 = "VSO", C3 = "SVO", D1 = "SVO", D2 = "SVO", D3 = "SOV", D4 = "SVO") wo <- factor(wo[tree$tip.label]) cols <- setNames(c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3"), levels(wo)) plotTree(tree, offset = 0.6, fsize = 0.9) tiplabels(pie = to.matrix(wo, levels(wo)), piecol = cols, cex = 0.4) nodelabels(frame = "none", cex = 0.7, adj = c(1.2, -0.4)) # node numbers legend("topleft", legend = levels(wo), pch = 21, pt.bg = cols, pt.cex = 1.5, bty = "n") Figure 12.1: A toy tree of fourteen hypothetical languages in four subgroups with their basic word orders. Branch lengths are in millennia. 12.15.1 Parsimony phangorn computes the parsimony score and the most-parsimonious reconstruction (MPR) sets at every node. pd <- phyDat(matrix(as.character(wo), dimnames = list(names(wo), "wo")), type = "USER", levels = levels(wo)) pscore <- parsimony(tree, pd) pscore #> [1] 5 mpr <- ancestral.pars(tree, pd, type = "MPR") root <- Ntip(tree) + 1 round(t(sapply(root:(root + 3), function(v) mpr[[v]][1, ])), 2) #> [,1] [,2] [,3] #> [1,] 0.5 0.5 0 #> [2,] 0.5 0.5 0 #> [3,] 0.5 0.5 0 #> [4,] 1.0 0.0 0 The minimum number of changes is five. At the root, parsimony cannot choose between SOV and SVO (each receives weight 0.5 in the MPR sets), and it says nothing about how likely either is. 12.15.2 Fitting Mk models We fit equal-rates, symmetric and all-rates-different Mk models with fitMk() and compare them by AIC (Table 12.3). fits <- list(ER = fitMk(tree, wo, model = "ER"), SYM = fitMk(tree, wo, model = "SYM"), ARD = fitMk(tree, wo, model = "ARD")) knitr::kable(data.frame( model = names(fits), k = sapply(fits, function(f) attr(logLik(f), "df")), logL = round(sapply(fits, logLik), 3), AIC = round(sapply(fits, AIC), 2)), row.names = FALSE, caption = "Mk models of word-order change fitted to the toy data.") Table 12.3: Mk models of word-order change fitted to the toy data. model k logL AIC ER 1 -13.76 29.53 SYM 3 -12.36 30.72 ARD 6 -11.97 35.94 fitER <- fits$ER Q <- unclass(as.Qmatrix(fitER))[levels(wo), levels(wo)] round(Q, 3) #> SOV SVO VSO #> SOV -0.343 0.171 0.171 #> SVO 0.171 -0.343 0.171 #> VSO 0.171 0.171 -0.343 With fourteen languages, the simplest model wins: the data cannot support six separate rates. This is typical of single-character analyses on small trees and is a reason to pool information across families, as Maurits and Griffiths (2014) did. 12.15.3 Marginal reconstruction with ape and phytools We now compare the marginal reconstructions at every node from ancr() and from ace() with its default settings, and the output of ace() with marginal = TRUE, at node 16, the ancestor of subgroups A and B. marg <- ancr(fitER)$ace ace_default <- ace(wo, tree, type = "discrete", model = "ER")$lik.anc ace_marginal <- ace(wo, tree, type = "discrete", model = "ER", marginal = TRUE)$lik.anc node <- 16 # ancestor of subgroups A and B rbind(ancr_marginal = marg[as.character(node), ], ace_default = ace_default[node - Ntip(tree), ], ace_marginal_TRUE = ace_marginal[node - Ntip(tree), ]) |> round(3) #> SOV SVO VSO #> ancr_marginal 0.494 0.367 0.139 #> ace_default 0.494 0.367 0.139 #> ace_marginal_TRUE 0.533 0.324 0.143 round(marg[1, ], 3) # the root #> SOV SVO VSO #> 0.352 0.418 0.230 The ancr() and default ace() results agree: these are the marginal posteriors. The marginal = TRUE result is different. It equals the scaled conditional likelihoods of node 16 given only the languages below it (Section D.2.2 verifies this by hand), which ignore the information from subgroups C and D on the other side of the root and therefore overstate the support for SOV at node 16. This is the caution of Section 12.4.2 made concrete. 12.15.4 Joint reconstruction ancr(..., type = "joint") returns the most probable joint assignment of states to all nodes. We compare it, node by node, with the state that has the highest marginal probability. jt <- ancr(fitER, type = "joint") nodes <- as.character(root:(root + tree$Nnode - 1)) data.frame(node = nodes, joint = as.character(jt$ace[nodes]), marginal_best = colnames(marg)[apply(marg, 1, which.max)], marginal_prob = round(apply(marg, 1, max), 2), row.names = NULL) #> node joint marginal_best marginal_prob #> 1 15 SVO SVO 0.42 #> 2 16 SVO SOV 0.49 #> 3 17 SVO SOV 0.64 #> 4 18 SOV SOV 0.94 #> 5 19 SVO SOV 0.58 #> 6 20 SVO SVO 0.49 #> 7 21 SVO SVO 0.94 #> 8 22 SVO SVO 0.52 #> 9 23 SVO VSO 0.46 #> 10 24 VSO VSO 0.90 #> 11 25 SVO SVO 0.64 #> 12 26 SVO SVO 0.99 #> 13 27 SVO SVO 0.59 c(joint_logP = as.numeric(jt$logLik), logL = as.numeric(logLik(fitER))) #> joint_logP logL #> -17.45 -13.76 Compare the joint and marginal columns. At the ancestor of subgroup A (node 17), the state with the highest marginal probability is SOV, at about 0.64, but the single most probable joint history assigns SVO there. That history makes the tree as a whole more probable, even though SOV is the better bet for node 17 considered alone. The same happens at nodes 16 and 19, and at node 23 (the ancestor of subgroup C) for VSO. Note also that the joint log-probability (about \(-17.4\)) is much lower than the log-likelihood (about \(-13.8\)): the latter sums over all histories, the former is the probability of one history. 12.15.5 Root priors How much does the root prior matter here? We refit the ER model with a flat root prior and with the FitzJohn prior. root_with <- function(pi) ancr(fitMk(tree, wo, model = "ER", pi = pi))$ace[1, ] rbind(flat = root_with("equal"), fitzjohn = root_with("fitzjohn")) |> round(3) #> SOV SVO VSO #> flat 0.352 0.418 0.230 #> fitzjohn 0.347 0.530 0.123 Under the ER model the stationary distribution is flat, so the stationary prior would coincide with the flat prior. The FitzJohn prior sharpens the reconstruction toward the state that is already favored, SVO. With an asymmetric rate matrix the differences can be much larger. 12.15.6 Stochastic character mapping We sample 200 stochastic maps under the fitted ER model and summarize them (Figure 12.2). set.seed(12) pi_flat <- rep(1 / 3, 3) maps <- make.simmap(tree, wo, Q = Q, pi = pi_flat, nsim = 200, message = FALSE) summ <- describe.simmap(maps) round(colMeans(summ$count), 2) # expected number of changes by type #> N SOV,SVO SOV,VSO SVO,SOV SVO,VSO VSO,SOV VSO,SVO #> 10.97 2.63 1.03 2.71 1.44 1.31 1.85 round(summ$ace[1:4, ], 2) # node frequencies, first four nodes #> SOV SVO VSO #> 15 0.32 0.43 0.26 #> 16 0.50 0.39 0.12 #> 17 0.66 0.26 0.09 #> 18 0.96 0.03 0.02 par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(maps[[1]], colors = cols, fsize = 0.8, ftype = "i") # plotSimmap leaves zero margins; restore room for the axes par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1)) hist(summ$count[, "N"], breaks = seq(-0.5, max(summ$count[, "N"]) + 0.5, 1), main = "", xlab = "Total number of changes", col = "gray80", border = "white") abline(v = pscore, lty = 2) Figure 12.2: One stochastic character map of word order sampled under the fitted equal-rates model (left), and the posterior distribution of the total number of changes across 200 maps (right). The dashed line marks the parsimony minimum of five changes. The frequencies of states at nodes across maps approximate the marginal posteriors computed above, as they should, since the maps are sampled from the same posterior. The expected total number of changes, about eleven, is more than twice the parsimony minimum of five, because the model allows changes that are later reversed and multiple changes on long branches. Asking how often SOV became SVO, and how often the reverse happened, is now a matter of reading off the columns of summ$count. 12.15.7 Reconstructing a named ancestor over a sample of trees In a real analysis the tree is uncertain. Suppose the lexical data leave the position of language B3 unresolved: in 60% of the posterior trees it is the sister of B1 and B2, as in the toy tree, and in 40% it branches off the stem of subgroup A instead. We build a mock posterior sample of 100 trees with this mixture, add lognormal noise to every branch length, and ask the question a linguist would ask: what was the word order of Proto-B, the ancestor of B1, B2 and B3? Following Pagel et al. (2004) we reconstruct, on each tree, the state at the MRCA of those three languages, and we record whether they form a clade. We then compare the answer with the one obtained on the MCC tree of the sample (Figure 12.3). set.seed(3) A <- paste0("A", 1:4); B <- c("B1", "B2", "B3") alt <- drop.tip(tree, "B3") # B3 moved next to A alt <- bind.tip(alt, "B3", where = getMRCA(alt, A), position = 0.5) trees <- lapply(1:100, function(i) { t2 <- if (runif(1) < 0.6) tree else alt t2$edge.length <- t2$edge.length * rlnorm(nrow(t2$edge), 0, 0.2) t2 }) class(trees) <- "multiPhylo" mcc <- maxCladeCred(trees) recon <- function(t2) { a <- ace(wo[t2$tip.label], t2, type = "discrete", model = "ER")$lik.anc c(B_clade = is.monophyletic(t2, B), protoB_SOV = unname(a[getMRCA(t2, B) - Ntip(t2), "SOV"]), a[1, ]) } res <- t(sapply(trees, recon)) on_mcc <- recon(mcc) round(rbind(MCC_tree = on_mcc, mean_over_trees = colMeans(res)), 3) #> B_clade protoB_SOV SOV SVO VSO #> MCC_tree 1.00 0.348 0.345 0.419 0.235 #> mean_over_trees 0.65 0.444 0.355 0.431 0.215 round(tapply(res[, "protoB_SOV"], res[, "B_clade"], mean), 3) #> 0 1 #> 0.511 0.408 par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1)) stripchart(res[, "protoB_SOV"] ~ factor(res[, "B_clade"], c(1, 0), c("B a clade", "B not a clade")), method = "jitter", pch = 16, col = "gray40", vertical = TRUE, ylab = "P(SOV) at MRCA of B1, B2, B3", ylim = c(0, 1)) abline(h = on_mcc["protoB_SOV"], col = "red", lwd = 2) boxplot(res[, levels(wo)], col = cols, ylab = "P(root state)", ylim = c(0, 1)) Figure 12.3: Reconstructions over a mock posterior sample of 100 trees in which language B3 is placed with subgroup B in 60% of trees and with subgroup A in 40%. Left: probability of SOV at the MRCA of B1, B2 and B3 on each tree, by whether the three form a clade; the red line is the value on the MCC tree. Right: marginal probability of each word order at the root across the 100 trees. The MCC tree contains the majority topology, in which subgroup B is a clade, and it reports a single probability of SOV for Proto-B. Over the sample, three things are hidden by that single number. First, Proto-B exists as a clade in only about two-thirds of the trees; in the others, the MRCA of the three B languages is the ancestor of subgroups A and B together, which is a different proto-language, and the reconstruction there answers a different question. Second, the probability of SOV is systematically higher in those trees, because B3 is then a close relative of the SOV-speaking subgroup A, so the average over trees differs from the MCC answer. Third, even among trees with the same topology, branch-length uncertainty spreads the reconstruction over a wide range. The root reconstruction varies less, but still noticeably. A reconstruction reported from a single summary tree would hide all of this; reporting the reconstruction over trees together with the probability that the named group is a clade does not. 12.15.8 Hidden rates A hidden-rate model with two rate categories can be fitted with fitHRM(). We compare it with the ordinary ER model. invisible(capture.output( hrm <- fitHRM(tree, wo, model = "ER", ncat = 2, niter = 2))) c(ER_logL = as.numeric(logLik(fitER)), HRM_logL = as.numeric(logLik(hrm)), ER_AIC = AIC(fitER), HRM_AIC = AIC(hrm)) #> ER_logL HRM_logL ER_AIC HRM_AIC #> -13.76 -13.76 29.53 33.53 The hidden-rate model does not improve the likelihood, so its extra parameters are not justified (its AIC is worse by about four units): with fourteen languages there is no detectable rate heterogeneity. The same analysis on a large tree with stable and labile lineages could tell a different story. For hidden Markov models with more structure, the corHMM package is the standard tool. The call below fits a comparable model with two rate categories and sums the marginal reconstructions over the hidden categories. In this fit all the probability falls in one rate category, so the summed reconstructions coincide with those of the ordinary equal-rates model: the second category is not used, which is another way of seeing that the data contain no signal of rate heterogeneity. library(corHMM) dat <- data.frame(lang = names(wo), wo = as.character(wo)) fit_hmm <- corHMM(phy = tree, data = dat, rate.cat = 2, model = "ER", node.states = "marginal") #> State distribution in data: #> States: 1 2 3 #> Counts: 5 7 2 #> Beginning thorough optimization search -- performing 0 random restarts #> Finished. Inferring ancestral states using marginal reconstruction. fit_hmm$loglik #> [1] -13.76 # fit_hmm$states has one column per (observed state, rate category) pair, # (1,R1), (2,R1), (3,R1), (1,R2), ...; states are numbered in sorted order. # Sum over the two rate categories: n_obs <- ncol(fit_hmm$states) / 2 anc <- fit_hmm$states[, 1:n_obs] + fit_hmm$states[, n_obs + 1:n_obs] colnames(anc) <- sort(unique(dat$wo)) round(head(anc, 3), 3) # the first row is the root #> SOV SVO VSO #> [1,] 0.352 0.418 0.230 #> [2,] 0.494 0.367 0.139 #> [3,] 0.642 0.264 0.094 12.15.9 Lexical reconstruction: one slot or many characters? Finally, a lexical example. Suppose the fourteen languages use three cognate classes, labeled k, m and t, for the meaning ‘hand’. We reconstruct the proto-word for ‘hand’ in two ways: as one multistate character (the onomasiological framing), and as three separate presence/absence characters, one per cognate class. hand <- c(A1 = "k", A2 = "k", A3 = "k", A4 = "k", B1 = "m", B2 = "m", B3 = "k", C1 = "t", C2 = "t", C3 = "m", D1 = "m", D2 = "t", D3 = "k", D4 = "m") hand <- factor(hand[tree$tip.label]) multi <- ancr(fitMk(tree, hand, model = "ER"))$ace[1, ] binary <- sapply(levels(hand), function(cl) { b <- setNames(as.integer(hand == cl), names(hand)) ancr(fitMk(tree, b, model = "ARD"))$ace[1, "1"] }) round(rbind(multistate = multi, binary_presence = binary), 3) #> k m t #> multistate 0.414 0.328 0.259 #> binary_presence 0.457 0.500 0.506 c(sum_multistate = sum(multi), sum_binary = sum(binary)) #> sum_multistate sum_binary #> 1.000 1.462 The multistate reconstruction distributes a probability of one across the three candidate words, favoring k. The three binary reconstructions, each fitted separately, each give a probability of around one half that the cognate class was present in the proto-language, and their sum is well above one: taken at face value, they imply that the proto-language most likely had more than one word for ‘hand’. Neither answer is “right” in general, since synonymy exists, but the comparison shows that the framing of the question is part of the model, as Jäger and List (2018) emphasized. Neither answer, either, says what the word for ‘hand’ sounded like: that is the business of the comparative method and of the form-based models of Section 12.12. “Reconstruction” covers three operations: the comparative method’s reconstruction of forms and systems, model-based reconstruction of word forms and sound changes, and phylogenetic reconstruction of coded character states. The third presupposes the outputs of the first and reconstructs codes, not languages. Ancestral state reconstruction infers the states of characters at internal nodes, or their complete histories, from tip data and a tree. Every reconstruction is conditional on a model. Parsimony (Fitch, Sankoff) minimizes changes and is close to the reasoning of the comparative method, but ignores branch lengths and gives no probabilities. Under Mk models, marginal reconstruction gives the posterior of each node separately, joint reconstruction gives the single most probable history, and the two can disagree. Check whether software reports marginal posteriors or subtree-only conditional likelihoods. Rates fixed at zero, informative priors on the direction of change and the root treatment can settle a reconstruction before the data are consulted. Report them, and do not count agreement with expert reconstructions as support for a constrained model. Root priors, tree uncertainty and parameter uncertainty can change deep reconstructions substantially. Reconstruct named ancestors over a sample of trees, and report how often the named group is a clade; a single MCC tree hides both the spread and the cases in which the node does not exist. Stochastic character mapping samples complete histories. It gives expected numbers and directions of changes, which typically exceed parsimony counts. Hidden-rate, threshold and structured Markov models represent lineage-specific propensities and logical dependencies among features. They are largely untried in linguistics. Agreement between phylogenetic and comparative reconstructions is not independent confirmation, because the inputs to phylogenetic ASR come from the comparative method. Disagreements are often more informative. 12.16 Exercises Conceptual For the Austronesian word for ‘five’, state what each of the three kinds of reconstruction in Section 12.2 would produce, what evidence it would use, and what it would presuppose. (1995) and Pupko et al. (2000): The foundational papers for empirical Bayes marginal reconstruction and for the joint reconstruction algorithm, written for molecular sequences but fully general. Pagel (1999b): A clear introduction to likelihood-based reconstruction of discrete characters and its uncertainty. Pagel et al. (2004): Bayesian ASR integrating over trees and parameters, with the “fossilization” approach to testing hypotheses about particular ancestors. Huelsenbeck et al. (2003): The key paper on stochastic character mapping of morphological characters. It includes tests of character correlation from mapped histories. Beaulieu et al. (2013): Hidden-rate models for discrete characters, with a biological case study that has many linguistic analogues. Jäger and List (2018): The best introduction to lexical ASR in linguistics. It covers the semasiological and onomasiological framings and evaluates methods against expert reconstructions. Maurits and Griffiths (2014): A careful Bayesian reconstruction of ancestral word order across families. Read it alongside Gell-Mann and Ruhlen (2011). Skirgård (2024): A systematic comparison of classical and computational reconstructions of Oceanic grammar, with a clear discussion of what branch lengths add. Nunn (2011), chapters 3 and 4: An accessible account of parsimony, likelihood and Bayesian reconstruction of ancestral states, with examples from anthropology. Olander (2018) and Goldstein (2022b): Two Indo-Europeanist arguments that reconstruction cannot be separated from the tree, the first reconstructing on one explicit binary tree, the second over a posterior sample of trees. King et al. (2025): ASR applied to the spread of a rare sound through the lexicon, with borrowing between neighbors as the likely mechanism. Dunn et al. (2005): Structural phylogenetics of Papuan and Oceanic languages. It shows the promise and the pitfalls of reconstructing deep history from grammar. Bouchard-Côté et al. (2013): Automated reconstruction of Austronesian proto-forms with a generative model of sound change. It is the most complete bridge so far between phylogenetic ASR and the comparative method. Revell and Harmon (2022): A practical, R-based textbook covering Mk models, ASR, stochastic mapping, hidden rates and threshold models with phytools. Harmon (2019), chapters 7 and 8: A concise, openly available introduction to the Mk model and its extensions, the treatment of the root, and fitting by maximum likelihood and MCMC. Cathcart (2018): A short exposition for linguists of the mathematics behind continuous-time Markov models, pruning, MCMC and stochastic mapping, with a sharp discussion of how constrained models can predetermine ancestral reconstructions. Chapter 13 Phylogenetic Comparative Methods in Linguistics Linguistic typology has always been a comparative science. Its central questions are about patterns across languages. Do languages with object-verb order tend to have postpositions? Are tone languages more common in humid climates? Do languages spoken by large populations have simpler morphology? Every such question runs into the same obstacle. Languages are not independent data points, because they descend from common ancestors and borrow from their neighbors. Anthropologists have called this Galton’s problem since the 1880s. This chapter is about the statistical tools that biologists built to solve the same problem for species, phylogenetic comparative methods (PCMs), and about how to use them well in quantitative typology: how to design a language sample, which tree and which branch lengths to use, how to carry tree uncertainty into the results, and what a phylogenetically controlled association can and cannot say about causes. After reading this chapter you should be able to: explain Galton’s problem, demonstrate by simulation why ordinary regression and contingency tests on related languages give inflated false positive rates, and say what genealogical sampling does and does not fix; design a language sample for a comparative question, and compute the effective number of independent observations that a sample provides under a phylogenetic model; describe the Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and Pagel models of trait evolution, measure phylogenetic signal, and interpret the results as patterns rather than processes; fit and interpret phylogenetic regressions (PGLS, phylogenetic logistic regression, phylogenetic mixed models) and Pagel’s test for correlated evolution with standard R packages; assess the sensitivity of a result to branch lengths (including Glottolog topologies with arbitrary branch lengths) and to tree uncertainty, by repeating the analysis over a sample of trees and pooling the results; separate phylogenetic and spatial dependence, and state which confounders a phylogenetic control removes and which it leaves untouched; critically read the debates over word-order universals and over environmental and social effects on language structure. suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(ape) # trees, vcv(), pic(), corBrownian(), corPagel(), ace() library(phytools) # pbtree(), fastBM(), phylosig(), fitPagel(), sim.Mk() library(geiger) # fitContinuous(), rescale() library(nlme) # gls() library(caper) # comparative.data(), pgls(), phylo.d() library(phylolm) # phylolm(), phyloglm(), rbinTrait() }) 13.1 Why comparison needs phylogeny 13.1.1 The logic of cross-linguistic correlation Typologists look for regularities in the distribution of structural features across the languages of the world. The most famous example is the set of word-order generalizations of Greenberg (1963). One of them is Universal 4: “With overwhelmingly greater than chance frequency, languages with normal SOV order are postpositional.” Later typologists, above all Dryer (1992), tested and refined these generalizations on much larger samples. The result was a list of word-order correlations: pairs of features whose values co-occur more often than chance. Languages with object-verb (OV) order, like Japanese, Turkish or Hindi, tend to have postpositions (Tokyo ni ‘Tokyo to’). They also tend to put genitives before nouns and relative clauses before the noun they modify. Languages with verb-object (VO) order, like English, Indonesian or Swahili, tend to have prepositions and postnominal relative clauses. How should we test whether such a correlation is real? The simplest approach is to sample languages, tabulate the two features in a \(2 \times 2\) contingency table, and apply a \(\chi^2\) test or a logistic regression. For a continuous variable, such as the size of a phoneme inventory or the number of speakers, we would use an ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression. Every one of these tests assumes that the observations are independent and identically distributed. That is, knowing the value for one language tells us nothing extra about the value for another, beyond what the predictors already say. For languages this assumption is false, and badly so. The Romance languages are verb-object and prepositional because Latin was (or more precisely, because late spoken Latin was). They did not each arrive at this combination independently. If we count French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Romanian, Catalan and fifty Romance dialects as separate data points, we inflate our apparent sample size enormously. We are counting one historical event many times over. The same is true at deeper levels. Hundreds of Bantu languages share SVO order and prepositions from Proto-Bantu. Hundreds of Austronesian languages share a set of structural features from Proto-Austronesian or Proto-Malayo-Polynesian. Languages also influence each other through contact. The languages of the Balkans, of Mainland Southeast Asia, or of the Ethiopian highlands share structural features that cut across family boundaries. This two-fold dependence, through descent and through diffusion, is the central methodological problem of comparative typology. 13.1.2 Galton’s problem The problem was first stated in anthropology, not linguistics. In 1888 Edward Tylor presented to the Royal Anthropological Institute a statistical study of the “adhesions” between customs across several hundred societies. He looked, for instance, at whether the custom of avoidance between a man and his mother-in-law co-occurred with particular rules of residence after marriage (Tylor 1889). Francis Galton, who chaired the meeting, raised an objection in the discussion. Many of the societies might have shared their customs by borrowing or by common descent, so they were not independent instances. Tylor’s “adhesions” might reflect history rather than any functional connection between customs. The objection became known as Galton’s problem. Naroll (1961) reviewed early solutions in anthropology, and the problem has shaped cross-cultural research ever since. Galton’s problem has two faces. The first is statistical. Non-independent observations carry less information than independent ones, so standard errors computed under independence are too small and \(p\)-values are too optimistic. The second is inferential. Even a correctly estimated association may reflect a historical accident rather than a causal or functional link. If an ancestral language happened to have two features, and its many descendants retained both out of inertia, then the features will be associated across the descendants. Yet nothing about one feature need favor the other. Biologists know this second face well. A trait inherited from a common ancestor is called a homology, and a shared trait that arose independently is called a homoplasy or convergence. Only independent origins (convergent evolution) provide evidence that two traits are functionally linked. Mace and Pagel (1994) brought the biological solution to anthropology in an influential paper in Current Anthropology. Their argument was simple. Comparative biologists had faced Galton’s problem for species and had developed methods to solve it by modeling evolution along a phylogeny. Anthropologists, and by extension linguists, could do the same, using language trees as estimates of the historical relationships among societies. This chapter is about those methods and how linguists have used them. Chapter 14 follows the same program into cultural evolution. 13.1.3 Sampling-based solutions in typology Typologists recognized the problem long before they adopted phylogenetic methods. Their response was to design samples that reduce non-independence (Rijkhoff et al. 1993). Three strategies stand out. The first is genealogical stratification. The idea is to sample at most one language per family, or per subgroup of a given age, so that no historical lineage is counted twice. Dryer (1989) made this operational with the notion of the genus: a group of languages whose relatedness is fairly obvious without systematic comparative analysis, with a time depth comparable to the subfamilies of Indo-European (Germanic, Romance, Slavic), perhaps 2,500 to 4,000 years. Dryer counted genera rather than languages. A genus was scored as having a feature if most of its languages had it. The genera were then grouped into large macroareas (Africa, Eurasia, Southeast Asia and Oceania, Australia and New Guinea, North America, South America). A correlation was accepted as a universal tendency only if it held in a majority of genera in every macroarea, or nearly every one (Dryer 1989, 1992). The macroarea criterion deals with the second face of Galton’s problem, contact, at a very coarse scale. It asks whether a pattern recurs in regions that have had little historical contact. The second strategy is diversity sampling. Here the goal is to maximize the range of structural types represented, for instance by sampling in proportion to the internal diversity of families (Rijkhoff et al. 1993; Miestamo et al. 2016). This is useful for discovering what is possible, but less useful for testing correlations. The third strategy, more recent, is to replace counting with modeling of the processes that produce the distribution. Maslova (2000) pointed out that the present-day distribution of types is a snapshot of a dynamic system. If languages change from type to type at certain rates, then the cross-linguistic frequency of a type reflects the stationary distribution of that process rather than a timeless preference. A universal is then a claim about transition rates, which is exactly what phylogenetic models of discrete characters estimate. Cysouw (2011) makes the link explicit. For a binary feature with change probabilities \(p_{AB}\) and \(p_{BA}\), the stable frequency of type A is \(p_{BA}/(p_{AB}+p_{BA})\), whatever the time unit. The converse does not hold: very different pairs of rates give the same stable frequency, so present-day frequencies alone cannot identify the rates. And reading the observed frequencies as stable frequencies assumes that the system has reached its stationary distribution; in a young family the observed frequencies may still reflect the ancestral state (a founder effect) rather than the stable state. Bickel (2011) and Bickel (2013) developed the Family Bias method. It asks whether families tend to be biased in the same direction, toward the same value of a feature, more often than chance. For large families the bias can be estimated directly from the daughter languages. For small families and isolates it is extrapolated from the large families. A distributional universal, on this view, is a consistent bias across families that diversify independently. The method is explicitly diachronic in spirit. It treats each family as an independent experiment in language change, while making no attempt to model the internal tree of each family. A related approach uses mixed-effects models. Family and area are treated as random effects, which lets observations within the same family or area be correlated (Jaeger et al. 2011). This was an important step toward modeling dependence directly. But a random effect for “family” treats all languages in a family as equally related to each other. It cannot represent the fact that Spanish and Portuguese are much closer to each other than either is to Hindi. A phylogenetic model can. Macklin-Cordes and Round (2022) make the link between the two traditions explicit. They argue that phylogenetic comparative methods address the same problem as balanced sampling, statistical non-independence due to genealogy, but whereas sampling can never achieve independence and discards most of the data, phylogenetic methods model the dependence and use all of it. Their paper introduces phylogenetic signal, typological averages that are sensitive to genealogy and the treatment of tree uncertainty for typologists, with a case study of the laminal contrast in Pama-Nyungan. 13.1.4 What a phylogeny adds All sampling solutions throw away information. If we keep one language per genus, we discard every other language, and with it every within-genus change. Yet those changes are exactly the independent evolutionary events that tell us whether two traits evolve together. Suppose the change from OV to VO has happened twenty times within Indo-European alone. We would like to know whether the adposition order changed along with it. A one-language-per-genus sample cannot tell us. Stratified samples also depend on an arbitrary time threshold, and they treat relatedness as all-or-nothing: Germanic and Romance count as independent genera although they are related, only less closely than Spanish and Portuguese. Phylogenetic comparative methods take the opposite approach. They keep all the languages and model the dependence explicitly. Relatedness is represented by a phylogeny with branch lengths, and trait evolution by a stochastic process running along the branches. The expected similarity between two languages then follows from how much history they share. Two languages that split 500 years ago are expected to be very similar. Two languages that split 6,000 years ago are expected to be much less so, and two languages from different families not at all (unless contact has intervened). The phylogeny thus works as a covariance structure. A regression or correlation test that uses it gives each language the weight its independent information deserves. A simulation makes the point concrete. We generate a tree for 60 languages, scaled so that the root lies 6,000 years in the past, and let two continuous traits (say, the proportion of suffixing morphology and the mean word length in a corpus) evolve along it completely independently of each other. We then test for a correlation that, by construction, does not exist, 500 times over, and count how often each method declares a significant correlation at the 5% level. A valid test should do so about 5% of the time. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, this checks the robustness under misspecification of OLS, whose assumption of independent languages the data violate; PGLS is applied to data simulated under its own assumptions. set.seed(13) tree <- pbtree(n = 60, scale = 6) # pure-birth tree, depth 6 (kyr) tree$tip.label <- sprintf("L%02d", 1:60) H <- nodeHeights(tree) # assign every tip to the lineage that crosses a given time slice cut_tree <- function(tree, height) { H <- nodeHeights(tree) crossing <- which(H[, 1] < height & H[, 2] >= height) grp <- integer(Ntip(tree)) for (k in seq_along(crossing)) { d <- getDescendants(tree, tree$edge[crossing[k], 2]) grp[d[d <= Ntip(tree)]] <- k } setNames(grp, tree$tip.label) } genus <- cut_tree(tree, height = 6 - 3.5) # 3.5 kyr before the present n_genera <- length(unique(genus)) cols <- hcl.colors(n_genera, "Dark 3") plot(tree, cex = 0.6, label.offset = 0.05, tip.color = cols[genus], edge.width = 1.2) abline(v = 6 - 3.5, lty = 2, col = "grey40") axisPhylo(cex.axis = 0.8) mtext("thousands of years before present", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8) Figure 13.1: A simulated family of 60 languages with a root age of 6,000 years. Colors mark the ‘genera’ obtained by cutting the tree 3,500 years before the present, a Dryer-style grouping used below for genealogically stratified sampling. The tree in Figure 13.1 has 10 lineages crossing the 3,500-year line. These are our “genera”. We compare three procedures: an OLS regression on all 60 languages, an OLS regression on a stratified sample with one language per genus, and a phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) regression that uses the tree’s covariance structure (Section 13.6). For speed, the PGLS fit is computed by “whitening” the data with the Cholesky factor of the inverse covariance matrix, which is exactly what PGLS does internally. C <- vcv(tree) # BM covariance matrix W <- chol(solve(C)) # whitening matrix: W'W = C^-1 one_per_genus <- tapply(seq_along(genus), genus, function(i) i[1]) nrep <- 500 pvals <- matrix(NA, nrep, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("OLS", "Genus", "PGLS"))) for (r in seq_len(nrep)) { x <- fastBM(tree) # trait 1, Brownian motion y <- fastBM(tree) # trait 2, independent of trait 1 g <- one_per_genus pvals[r, "OLS"] <- summary(lm(y ~ x))$coefficients[2, 4] pvals[r, "Genus"] <- summary(lm(y[g] ~ x[g]))$coefficients[2, 4] Xw <- W %*% cbind(1, x); yw <- W %*% y # transformed (whitened) data pvals[r, "PGLS"] <- summary(lm(yw ~ Xw - 1))$coefficients[2, 4] } fpr <- colMeans(pvals < 0.05) round(fpr, 3) #> OLS Genus PGLS #> 0.406 0.082 0.044 ci <- sapply(fpr, function(p) p + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nrep)) bp <- barplot(fpr, ylim = c(0, max(ci) * 1.15), col = c("grey70", "grey50", "grey30"), names.arg = c("OLS, all languages", "OLS, one per genus", "PGLS"), ylab = "false positive rate", border = NA) arrows(bp, ci[1, ], bp, ci[2, ], angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.05) abline(h = 0.05, lty = 2) Figure 13.2: Galton’s problem in a simulation. Two traits evolved independently by Brownian motion on the simulated 60-language tree. Bars show the proportion of 500 replicates in which each test reported a significant correlation at the 5% level, with 95% binomial intervals. The dashed line marks the nominal 5% rate. The result (Figure 13.2) is stark. Ordinary regression on all languages finds a “significant” correlation between two unrelated traits in about 41% of replicates, roughly 8 times the nominal rate. Stratified sampling helps but does not fully solve the problem, with a false positive rate of about 8%: the genera are still related through the deeper part of the tree, and the sample is much smaller. PGLS keeps all the languages and achieves the nominal rate (4%). Nothing in the simulation is unusual. Pure-birth trees and Brownian motion are, if anything, a mild scenario compared with real language families, in which a single deep split, such as that between OV and VO branches, can create a strong association that rests on just one historical event. Galton’s problem is just as acute for discrete features. Below, two binary features evolve independently on the same tree, each with a low rate of change, as typological features often do. For a symmetric two-state process with rate \(q\), a branch of length \(t\) ends in a different state from the one it started in with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1 - e^{-2qt})\), so we visit the branches from the root toward the tips and flip the state with this probability. We then apply Fisher’s exact test to the \(2 \times 2\) table of the two features. sim_binary <- function(tree, q) { tree <- reorder(tree, "cladewise") # parents before children state <- integer(Ntip(tree) + tree$Nnode) state[Ntip(tree) + 1] <- rbinom(1, 1, 0.5) # root drawn from stationarity p_flip <- 0.5 * (1 - exp(-2 * q * tree$edge.length)) flips <- rbinom(nrow(tree$edge), 1, p_flip) for (e in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) state[tree$edge[e, 2]] <- abs(state[tree$edge[e, 1]] - flips[e]) setNames(state[seq_len(Ntip(tree))], tree$tip.label) } p_fisher <- replicate(500, { a <- sim_binary(tree, 0.15); b <- sim_binary(tree, 0.15) if (length(unique(a)) < 2 || length(unique(b)) < 2) NA else fisher.test(table(a, b))$p.value }) fpr_discrete <- mean(p_fisher < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) fpr_discrete #> [1] 0.184 Here too the naive test rejects the true null hypothesis of independence far more often than it should: in about 18% of replicates rather than 5%. The phylogenetic alternative, Pagel’s test for correlated evolution, is developed in Section 13.7. Dryer’s genera and macroareas. Dryer (1992) tested several dozen putative word-order correlations on a database of some 625 languages grouped into genera and six macroareas. A pair of features counted as correlated only if the preferred combination was found in more genera than the dispreferred combination in each macroarea (or in all but one). The analysis confirmed some of Greenberg’s correlations, such as those involving adpositions, genitives and relative clauses, and rejected others. The most famous rejected case is adjective-noun order, which Greenberg had expected to correlate with verb-object order and which turned out not to. Dryer’s procedure was a pragmatic, transparent and remarkably successful answer to Galton’s problem. Its limitations are those discussed above. It counts each genus once, whatever its internal history. It treats the genus threshold as a sharp boundary. And it says nothing about the dynamics of change that produced the distribution. It nonetheless remains the benchmark against which phylogenetic results on word order are judged, and it played a central role in the debate that followed Dunn et al. (2011) (Section 13.8). 13.2 Designing a language sample Phylogenetic methods do not make sampling irrelevant. They change what sampling is for. A sampling design for a comparative study should answer five questions before any data are coded. What is the target of inference? A claim about “the languages of the world” today, a claim about the possible languages, and a claim about the processes of change (a universal as a bias in transition rates; Section 13.1.3) call for different samples. For the first, the sampling frame is a list such as Glottolog (Hammarström et al. 2024); for the third, the unit of replication is the family or the independent change, not the language. How much independent information will the sample contain? Under a phylogenetic model the information in a sample is not its number of languages. A useful summary is the effective sample size for estimating a mean, \(n_{\text{eff}} = \mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{1}\), where \(\mathbf{R}\) is the phylogenetic correlation matrix (the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) of Section 13.3.1 scaled to unit diagonal). It equals the number of languages when they are independent and approaches the number of deep, independent lineages when languages cluster in shallow clades. For tests of association, what matters is the number of independent changes in the predictor, which can be smaller still. Does the predictor vary within families? An association estimated from a sample in which a predictor varies only between families rests on as many data points as there are families, whatever the number of languages. Variation within families is what lets a phylogenetic model see coupled change. How are languages, dialects and families delimited? Splitting one language into five dialects adds five tips to a shallow clade. PCMs down-weight them, but only to the extent that the tree represents their closeness correctly. Lumping varieties into one tip, or splitting them, changes \(\mathbf{C}\), and decisions should be made before seeing the results (Section 15.8). Which languages are missing, and why? Typological databases over-represent well-described languages, which are often larger, written, or spoken in regions with a long tradition of description. If documentation is related to the variables under study (population size and morphological complexity are a clear example), restricting the analysis to documented languages can create or mask associations (Section 13.11.4). The code below makes point 2 concrete. It computes \(n_{\text{eff}}\) for random subsamples of the 60-language tree, under Brownian motion (\(\lambda = 1\)) and under a weaker phylogenetic dependence (\(\lambda = 0.5\); Section 13.3.4), and for the one-language-per-genus sample. neff <- function(tr, lambda = 1) { R <- cov2cor(vcv(tr)) # phylogenetic correlations R <- lambda * R + (1 - lambda) * diag(nrow(R)) sum(solve(R)) # 1' R^-1 1 } set.seed(14) neff_tab <- t(sapply(c(5, 10, 20, 40, 60), function(k) { v <- replicate(50, { tr <- keep.tip(tree, sample(tree$tip.label, k)) c(neff(tr), neff(tr, 0.5)) }) c(languages = k, n_eff_BM = mean(v[1, ]), n_eff_lambda_0.5 = mean(v[2, ])) })) round(neff_tab, 1) #> languages n_eff_BM n_eff_lambda_0.5 #> [1,] 5 3.5 4.1 #> [2,] 10 4.8 6.3 #> [3,] 20 6.2 9.1 #> [4,] 40 6.8 11.2 #> [5,] 60 7.0 12.2 genus_tree <- keep.tip(tree, tree$tip.label[one_per_genus]) c(genera = n_genera, n_eff_genera = round(neff(genus_tree), 1)) #> genera n_eff_genera #> 10.0 5.8 Under Brownian motion, sixty languages from this family are worth about seven independent observations of the family mean, and most of that value is already reached with twenty languages. The one-per-genus sample is worth less than its number of genera, because the genera are themselves related. With weaker dependence the value of extra languages is greater. Real families are more unbalanced than this pure-birth tree, and a global sample is a forest of families of very different sizes, so it is worth computing \(n_{\text{eff}}\) for the actual sample and tree before an analysis. Two practical consequences follow. Adding languages from an already well-sampled clade buys little; adding families or isolates buys a lot, even though each contributes little information about rates of change within lineages. For estimating rates, the balance tips the other way: following Maslova (2000), Cysouw (2011) suggests that a 100-language sample built as pairs of closely related languages from 50 groups, or as about ten densely sampled groups, says more about change than 100 languages from different genealogical units. And reporting results family by family alongside pooled results shows whether a global association is carried by a few large families. Modeling dependence also relaxes the classical demand for a balanced, probability-based sample. Guzmán Naranjo and Becker (2022) combined a phylogenetic regression term with a two-dimensional Gaussian process for areal effects and argued that, with both controls in the model, strict probability sampling is not required, provided the sample is a variety sample large enough to cover different families and areas. Their test case is instructive: an apparent effect of VO order on the choice between prefixing and suffixing disappeared once genealogical and areal effects were both controlled, and the areal effects were as important as the genealogical ones. The design questions above do not go away, but they shift from “which languages may I include?” to “how much independent information about my question does this sample contain, and where does it come from?” 13.3 Models of trait evolution Every phylogenetic comparative method rests on a model of how traits change along the branches of a tree. For discrete characters the standard models are the continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) introduced in Chapter 5 and developed for cognate data in Chapter 7. For continuous characters the workhorse is Brownian motion and its relatives. Continuous characters are less common in linguistics than in biology, but far from rare. Examples include phoneme inventory size, the ratio of consonants to vowels, mean word length, measures of morphological synthesis or fusion, entropy-based measures of word-order freedom, lexical rates of change, and even latitude and longitude (Chapter 11). Many discrete features can also be modeled as continuous liabilities that cross a threshold (Section 13.9.3). 13.3.1 Brownian motion Brownian motion (BM) is a random walk in continuous time. Let \(X(t)\) be the value of a trait at time \(t\). Under BM, the change over any short interval \(dt\) is normally distributed with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\,dt\): \[\begin{equation} X(t + dt) - X(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2\, dt), \tag{13.1} \end{equation}\] and changes over non-overlapping intervals are independent. The parameter \(\sigma^2\) is the evolutionary rate. Over a branch of length \(t\), the change is \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 t)\). The process has no tendency to return to any particular value. It simply diffuses, so the variance among independent lineages grows linearly with time. BM is often described as a model of “neutral drift”, and for genetic drift in quantitative traits it can be derived from population genetics. But its usefulness does not depend on that interpretation. BM also arises when a trait is pushed around by many small, independent influences whose direction varies randomly over time: shifting social preferences, contact with changing neighbors, analogical leveling here and sound change there.
