It is the natural null model for “change happens, but in no particular direction.” Now place BM on a tree. Each lineage inherits its ancestor’s value at the moment of splitting and then wanders independently. Two languages \(i\) and \(j\) share the path from the root to their most recent common ancestor. Along that shared path, they have experienced the same changes. After the split, their changes are independent. Hence the covariance between their trait values equals \(\sigma^2\) times the length of the shared path, \(s_{ij}\). The variance of a single language equals \(\sigma^2\) times its distance from the root, \(T_i\). Collecting these into a matrix, the vector of tip values \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top\) is multivariate normal: \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}_n\!\left(\mu \mathbf{1},\; \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}\right), \qquad C_{ij} = s_{ij}, \quad C_{ii} = T_i, \tag{13.2} \end{equation}\] where \(\mu\) is the value at the root and \(\mathbf{1}\) is a vector of ones. The matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) is the phylogenetic variance-covariance matrix. It is the single most important object in this chapter. Everything a Gaussian PCM knows about the tree is contained in it. In R, ape::vcv() computes it. For a four-language tree in which A and B split 1,000 years ago, C and D 2,000 years ago, and the two pairs 3,000 years ago: toy <- read.tree(text = "((A:1,B:1):2,(C:2,D:2):1);") vcv(toy) #> A B C D #> A 3 2 0 0 #> B 2 3 0 0 #> C 0 0 3 1 #> D 0 0 1 3 Read the matrix row by row. A and B share 2 units of history (the branch from the root to their ancestor), so their covariance is 2. A and C share nothing, so their covariance is 0. Each tip has variance 3, the full depth of the tree. The maximum-likelihood estimate of the root value \(\mu\) is then a weighted mean of the tip values, and it is also the ML estimate of the ancestral state at the root (Chapter 12). It down-weights clusters of closely related languages, since they carry largely redundant information: a family with 400 Bantu languages and a single isolate does not get a root estimate that is 400/401 Bantu. The Brownian likelihood, Equation (D.10), and the maximum-likelihood estimates of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\), Equation (D.11), are in Section D.3.1. 13.3.2 The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process Brownian motion lets a trait wander without bound. Many linguistic quantities, however, plausibly stay within a range. Phoneme inventories rarely shrink below about a dozen segments or grow beyond about a hundred. The proportion of a lexicon that is borrowed is bounded by 0 and 1. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process adds a deterministic pull toward an optimum, or attractor, \(\theta\): \[\begin{equation} dX(t) = \alpha\,[\theta - X(t)]\,dt + \sigma\, dW(t), \tag{13.3} \end{equation}\] where \(dW(t)\) is the increment of a standard Brownian motion and \(\alpha \ge 0\) is the strength of the pull. When \(\alpha = 0\), OU reduces to BM. When \(\alpha > 0\), the trait fluctuates around \(\theta\) with stationary variance \(\sigma^2/(2\alpha)\). The phylogenetic half-life, \(t_{1/2} = \ln 2/\alpha\), is the expected time for a lineage to move halfway from its ancestral value toward the optimum. Comparing \(t_{1/2}\) with the depth of the tree tells us whether the pull is weak (half-life longer than the tree) or strong (half-life much shorter, in which case the phylogeny barely matters). Under OU, the covariance between two languages decays exponentially with the time separating them, rather than linearly as under BM. OU was introduced to comparative biology by Hansen (1997) as a model of stabilizing selection toward an adaptive optimum. Butler and King (2004) extended it to multiple optima on different parts of the tree, for example one optimum for languages in one ecological or social setting and another for languages in a different setting. Such multi-optimum models are a natural way to formalize hypotheses that a feature is “adapted” to some environment. A linguistic version might specify one optimum for languages of large, open societies and another for languages of small, close-knit ones. The OU covariance between two tips, Equation (D.12), and the early-burst covariance, Equation (D.13), are in Section D.3.2. OU models are easy to fit and easy to over-interpret. With small trees, likelihood-ratio tests favor OU over BM much more often than they should. Measurement error, or a few unusual languages, can also mimic an OU process. And the “stabilizing selection” reading of \(\alpha\) is only one of several processes that produce the same pattern (Cooper et al. 2016; Ho and Ané 2014b). For trees of a few dozen languages, \(\alpha\) and \(\sigma^2\) are often weakly identifiable. Report the half-life with its uncertainty, check the result by simulation, and avoid talking about “selection” unless there is independent reason to. 13.3.3 Early burst and related models The early burst (EB) model, also called ACDC (accelerating-decelerating), lets the rate of BM change exponentially through time: \(\sigma^2(t) = \sigma_0^2\, e^{r t}\). With \(r < 0\), change is fast early in the history of the clade and slows down later. This is the signature expected under adaptive radiation, when a lineage enters new ecological space and its descendants quickly diversify into vacant niches (Blomberg et al. 2003; Harmon et al. 2010). Linguistic analogues are easy to imagine. A language family expanding into a new and diverse landscape, such as Austronesian into the Pacific or Bantu across sub-Saharan Africa, might diversify structurally faster in its early phases than later. Punctuational bursts of lexical change at language splits (Atkinson et al. 2008), discussed in Chapter 9, are a different phenomenon, linked to splitting events rather than to clade age, but they raise the same general question: is the rate of change constant through time? In biology, Harmon et al. (2010) found that early bursts are actually rare in comparative data on body size and shape. That result is a useful warning against assuming them. 13.3.4 Pagel’s tree transformations: lambda, kappa and delta Pagel (1997) and Pagel (1999a) introduced three transformations of the tree, or equivalently of \(\mathbf{C}\). They are a flexible way to test how well BM on the given tree describes the data. Each transformation is controlled by a single parameter, and each has a natural interpretation. Lambda (\(\lambda\)) multiplies all off-diagonal elements of \(\mathbf{C}\) by \(\lambda\) and leaves the diagonal unchanged: \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{C}(\lambda) = \lambda\,\mathbf{C} + (1 - \lambda)\,\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{C}). \tag{13.4} \end{equation}\] When \(\lambda = 1\) we have pure BM on the original tree. When \(\lambda = 0\) the tree becomes a “star” in which all languages are independent. Intermediate values shrink the internal branches relative to the terminal ones. Lambda is the most widely used measure of phylogenetic signal (Section 13.4). Note that \(\lambda\) can exceed 1 slightly, up to the value at which \(\mathbf{C}(\lambda)\) ceases to be a valid covariance matrix. Most software restricts it to \([0, 1]\). Kappa (\(\kappa\)) raises every branch length to the power \(\kappa\). When \(\kappa = 1\) the tree is unchanged. When \(\kappa = 0\) all branches have equal length, so change is proportional to the number of splits rather than to time. This is a model of punctuational or speciational change, in which evolution is concentrated at splitting events. Kappa is therefore directly relevant to the linguistic hypothesis of punctuational bursts discussed in Chapter 9. Delta (\(\delta\)) raises the node heights (the distances from the root) to the power \(\delta\). With \(\delta < 1\), the deep parts of the tree are stretched relative to the shallow parts: change is concentrated early, as in an early burst. With \(\delta > 1\), change is concentrated toward the tips, as expected under accelerating evolution or for traits that evolve fast and lose their deep phylogenetic signal. These transformations matter twice over for linguists. As models, they describe how a trait evolved. As tools, they let the data adjust branch lengths that were chosen arbitrarily, which is how they are often used with Glottolog-based trees (Section 13.12.2). Figure 13.3 shows the effect of each transformation on the tree from Figure 13.1, using geiger::rescale(). # cex = 1 keeps full-size titles despite five panels op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 5), mar = c(1, 0.5, 2.5, 0.5), cex = 1) plot(tree, show.tip.label = FALSE, main = "original", cex.main = 0.9) plot(rescale(tree, "lambda", 0.3), show.tip.label = FALSE, main = expression(lambda == 0.3), cex.main = 0.9) plot(rescale(tree, "kappa", 0), show.tip.label = FALSE, main = expression(kappa == 0), cex.main = 0.9) plot(rescale(tree, "delta", 3), show.tip.label = FALSE, main = expression(delta == 3), cex.main = 0.9) plot(rescale(tree, "OU", alpha = 0.5), show.tip.label = FALSE, main = expression(OU ~ alpha == 0.5), cex.main = 0.9) Figure 13.3: Pagel’s branch-length transformations applied to the simulated language tree. From left to right: the original tree; lambda = 0.3 (internal branches shortened); kappa = 0 (all branches equal, a speciational model); delta = 3 (change concentrated near the tips); and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck transformation with alpha = 0.5. par(op) A traitgram, or phenogram, plots the tree with the trait value on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. It is a good way to see the difference between BM and OU. Under BM, lineages fan out, and their spread grows with time. Under OU with a strong pull, they stay within a band around the optimum, and the spread barely depends on how long ago two languages split (Figure 13.4). set.seed(21) x_bm <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1, internal = TRUE) x_ou <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1, alpha = 1.5, theta = 0, internal = TRUE) op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) phenogram(tree, x_bm, ftype = "off", spread.labels = FALSE, xlab = "time from root (kyr)", ylab = "trait", main = "Brownian motion") phenogram(tree, x_ou, ftype = "off", spread.labels = FALSE, xlab = "time from root (kyr)", ylab = "trait", main = "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck") Figure 13.4: Traitgrams of a continuous trait simulated on the same tree under Brownian motion (left) and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a strong pull toward an optimum of zero (right; alpha = 1.5, half-life about 0.46 thousand years). Internal node values are the simulated ancestral values. par(op) 13.3.5 Fitting and comparing models All of these models can be fitted by maximum likelihood and compared with information criteria such as AIC or its small-sample correction AICc (Chapter 5). The function geiger::fitContinuous() (Pennell et al. 2014) fits BM, OU, EB, lambda, kappa, delta and a “white noise” model in which languages are independent draws from a single normal distribution. Below we fit five models to the BM and OU traits just simulated. fit_models <- function(x) { models <- c("BM", "OU", "EB", "lambda", "white") sapply(models, function(m) fitContinuous(tree, x, model = m, control = list(niter = 10))$opt$aicc) } tips <- tree$tip.label aicc <- rbind(BM_trait = fit_models(x_bm[tips]), OU_trait = fit_models(x_ou[tips])) delta_aicc <- t(apply(aicc, 1, function(a) a - min(a))) knitr::kable(round(delta_aicc, 1), caption = "Differences in AICc from the best model (0 = best) for traits simulated under Brownian motion and under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.") Table 13.1: Differences in AICc from the best model (0 = best) for traits simulated under Brownian motion and under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. BM OU EB lambda white BM_trait 0.0 2.1 2.2 2.2 64.3 OU_trait 18.2 0.0 20.4 6.3 4.2 With 60 tips, the model comparison usually recovers the generating process. You will find, though, that it is quite easy to construct cases where it does not. Re-running the simulation with different seeds is instructive. Model selection among continuous models is a good exploratory tool. It is a weak basis for strong claims about evolutionary mechanism. 13.3.6 Discrete characters Most typological features are discrete. Word order is OV or VO. A language has or lacks tone, grammatical gender, a dual number or a definite article. As in previous chapters, such characters are modeled by a CTMC with rate matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\). The simplest version is the Mk model of Lewis (2001). Its variants include the equal-rates (ER), symmetric (SYM) and all-rates-different (ARD) models, as well as ordered models in which changes can only happen between adjacent states. Chapter 12 uses these models for ancestral state reconstruction. Here they will serve as the building blocks of Pagel’s test for correlated evolution (Section 13.7). One feature of the Mk model matters for comparative analysis. Its equilibrium frequencies, the stationary distribution \(\pi\) of \(\mathbf{Q}\), are what the “preferences” of typology look like in a dynamic view (Maslova 2000). A strongly preferred type is a type that languages change into readily and out of reluctantly. 13.4 Phylogenetic signal Phylogenetic signal is the tendency of related languages to resemble each other more than languages drawn at random from the same tree (Blomberg et al. 2003; Münkemüller et al. 2012). It is the first thing to measure in any comparative analysis. It tells us how strongly Galton’s problem affects a feature, and so whether phylogenetic correction matters. It is also of interest in its own right. Features with strong signal are stable, inherited properties of lineages. Features with weak signal are labile, easily borrowed or easily innovated. The stability of linguistic features, which typologists have long discussed (Wichmann and Holman 2009b; Dediu and Cysouw 2013), is closely related to phylogenetic signal. The two are not the same thing, though, as we will see. 13.4.1 Pagel’s lambda The most common measure of signal for continuous traits is Pagel’s \(\lambda\) (Equation (13.4)), estimated by maximum likelihood. A value near 1 means that the trait covaries among languages as expected under BM on the tree. A value near 0 means that the tree tells us nothing about trait similarity. A likelihood-ratio test of \(\lambda = 0\) against the ML value tests for the presence of signal. A test of \(\lambda = 1\) tests for departure from BM. 13.4.2 Blomberg’s K, Moran’s I and the D statistic Blomberg et al. (2003) proposed the statistic \(K\), which compares how much of a trait’s variance lies between clades rather than within them with the amount expected under BM on the tree. \(K = 1\) is the BM expectation. \(K < 1\) means that relatives resemble each other less than expected under BM; \(K > 1\) means that they resemble each other more. Significance is assessed by permuting trait values across the tips. In biology, Blomberg et al. (2003) famously found that behavioral traits have lower \(K\) than morphological ones, being “more labile”. The analogous claim in linguistics, that some kinds of structure are more stable than others, is explored below. Moran’s I (Moran 1950), borrowed from spatial statistics, measures autocorrelation with respect to a matrix of weights. Gittleman and Kot (1990) proposed using phylogenetic proximity as the weights. Moran’s I has the advantage that the same statistic can be computed with geographic weights, which makes it convenient for comparing phylogenetic and spatial autocorrelation of a feature. It is not tied to an explicit model of evolution, though, and it depends on the choice of weights. For binary features, Fritz and Purvis (2010) proposed the statistic \(D\), which compares the observed differences between sister clades with their distribution under random reshuffling of the trait and under a threshold model in which the binary trait arises from a Brownian liability. \(D \approx 1\) indicates a random (phylogenetically unstructured) distribution, \(D \approx 0\) a distribution as clumped as expected under the Brownian threshold model, and \(D < 0\) an even more clumped one. It is implemented as caper::phylo.d(). The formulas for \(K\), Moran’s I and \(D\), Equations (D.14), (D.15) and (D.16), and code computing Moran’s I and \(D\) for simulated traits, are in Section D.3.3. 13.4.3 Signal in R The code below estimates \(\lambda\) and \(K\) for the BM trait simulated above, and for a “trait” that is pure noise. noise <- setNames(rnorm(Ntip(tree)), tips) lam <- function(v) phylosig(tree, v, method = "lambda", test = TRUE)$lambda sig <- rbind( BM = c(lambda = lam(x_bm[tips]), K = phylosig(tree, x_bm[tips], method = "K")), noise = c(lambda = lam(noise), K = phylosig(tree, noise, method = "K"))) round(sig, 3) #> lambda K #> BM 1.012 0.953 #> noise 0.095 0.114 phylosig(tree, x_bm[tips], method = "K", test = TRUE, nsim = 999)$P #> [1] 0.001001 phylosig(tree, noise, method = "K", test = TRUE, nsim = 999)$P #> [1] 0.6557 The BM trait has \(\lambda\) close to 1 and \(K\) close to or above 1, and the noise trait has values near 0. Phylogenetic signal is a pattern, not a process. Revell et al. (2008) showed by simulation that high signal can arise under processes with high or low rates, and that low signal can arise from a strong pull toward an optimum (OU), from fast evolution, or from measurement error. “This feature has high \(\lambda\), so it evolves slowly” does not follow. Under BM, \(\lambda\) is 1 whatever the rate. Stability, in the sense of a low rate of change per unit time, is better estimated directly as a rate parameter in a CTMC or BM model on a dated tree (Dediu 2011; Greenhill et al. 2017). And signal estimated on a tree with arbitrary branch lengths (Section 13.12.2) depends on those branch lengths. 13.4.4 Phylogenetic signal in linguistic features How strong is phylogenetic signal in grammatical features? This question goes back to old debates about “stability” in typology, and phylogenetic methods have given new answers. Wichmann and Holman (2009b) proposed a stability metric computed from WALS (Dryer and Haspelmath 2013), and Dediu and Cysouw (2013) compared it with six other stability estimates, most of them non-phylogenetic but including the Bayesian phylogenetic rates of Dediu (2011). The methods agree only partially, although some features come out as consistently stable and others as consistently unstable across methods. Dediu (2011): stability of linguistic features on language trees. Dediu (2011) used Bayesian phylogenetic methods to estimate rates of change for WALS features on samples of trees for a number of language families. He treated the estimated rate of change as a measure of instability and, by integrating over tree uncertainty, obtained a ranking of features by stability. He then used the estimates to revisit an earlier hypothesis linking the distribution of tone to population frequencies of particular alleles of two brain-related genes (Dediu and Ladd 2007). The analysis is a good example of a common design: a large set of typological features analyzed one at a time on samples of trees for several families. It also shows a characteristic limitation. Many families contribute little variation for many features, and the trees themselves are uncertain, so the per-feature estimates are noisy. The largest analysis to date is that of Grambank, a database of 195 binary and multistate grammatical features coded for more than 2,400 languages (Skirgård et al. 2023). Skirgård and colleagues fitted Bayesian spatiophylogenetic models (Section 13.10). These decompose the variance of each feature into a phylogenetic component, based on a global language tree, and a spatial component, based on geographic distances. Across features, the phylogenetic component was on average larger than the spatial one. In other words, inheritance from ancestors explained more of the present-day distribution of grammatical features than proximity to neighbors did, although the strength of the phylogenetic effect varied considerably between features and the spatial effect was, on average, small. The paper is discussed further in Section 13.8.4. Greenhill et al. (2017) took a different approach. They estimated rates of change for structural (grammatical) features and for basic vocabulary on the same Austronesian trees. Contrary to a widespread expectation, grammatical features were not more stable than vocabulary: on average, most grammatical features changed faster than items of basic vocabulary, although both kinds of data showed a wide range of rates and each contained a core of highly stable features. Both rates and signal, then, are properties of individual features, not of “grammar” or “lexicon” as a whole. Other studies point the same way. Dediu and Levinson (2012) estimated stability profiles of structural features within several families and found both tendencies shared across families and family-specific ones. Hübler (2022), defining stability as high phylogenetic signal combined with a low rate of change, measured both for 171 structural features in Japonic, Koreanic, Mongolic, Tungusic and Turkic languages; signal and rate were correlated, and features of argument marking, derivation and valency came out among the most stable. Wichmann (2015) reviews the older and newer approaches to stability in typology. Chapter 9 discusses rates of change in more detail. 13.5 Phylogenetically independent contrasts The first general solution to Galton’s problem for continuous traits was Felsenstein’s method of phylogenetically independent contrasts [PIC; Felsenstein (1985b)]. It is still the most intuitive. The insight is that although the trait values of languages are not independent, the differences between sister lineages are. Under BM, the change from the ancestor of Spanish and Portuguese to Spanish is independent of the change from that ancestor to Portuguese. It is also independent of every change elsewhere in the tree. So the difference between Spanish and Portuguese is an independent evolutionary “experiment”. So is the difference between French and Italian, and so is the difference between the ancestor of the Ibero-Romance languages and the ancestor of French and Italian, once suitably estimated. The algorithm works from the tips toward the root, computing a difference between each pair of sister lineages, standardized by the square root of the branch lengths that separate them, and replacing each pair by an estimated ancestral value. A tree with \(n\) tips yields \(n - 1\) contrasts, which are independent and identically distributed with mean zero under BM. To test for correlated evolution of two traits, we compute contrasts for each and regress the contrasts of \(y\) on those of \(x\) through the origin. There is no intercept because the sign of each contrast is arbitrary. PIC was revolutionary because it turned a problem with unknown dependencies into a standard regression on independent data. It was quickly adopted in biology (Harvey and Pagel 1991; Garland et al. 1992). It has two limitations. It assumes BM (although branch lengths can be transformed first). And it is awkward to extend to multiple predictors, categorical predictors or non-normal data. Both limitations are removed by PGLS, of which PIC is a special case. The contrast algorithm step by step, Equation (D.17), and a numerical check that the contrast slope equals the PGLS slope under BM, are in Section D.3.4. set.seed(31) x <- fastBM(tree) y <- 2 + 0.6 * x + fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.5) # true slope 0.6 u_x <- pic(x, tree); u_y <- pic(y, tree) fit_pic <- lm(u_y ~ u_x - 1) # regression through origin coef(summary(fit_pic)) #> Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) #> u_x 0.6405 0.1079 5.937 1.729e-07 13.6 Phylogenetic generalized least squares 13.6.1 The model Phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) is ordinary linear regression with a non-diagonal residual covariance matrix (Grafen 1989; Martins and Hansen 1997). The model is \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{V}), \tag{13.5} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{y}\) is the response for \(n\) languages, \(\mathbf{X}\) is the \(n \times p\) design matrix (a column of ones and the predictors), and \(\mathbf{V}\) is a phylogenetic correlation structure. Under BM, \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{C}\). Under Pagel’s lambda model, \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{C}(\lambda)\). Under OU, \(\mathbf{V}\) has the OU covariance. The coefficients are estimated by generalized least squares, which is equivalent to transforming (“whitening”) the data so that the transformed residuals are independent with equal variance, and then running ordinary least squares on the transformed data. This is exactly what we did in the Galton simulation. Independent contrasts are one particular whitening transformation, which is why the PIC slope through the origin is identical to the PGLS slope under BM (Rohlf 2001; Blomberg et al. 2012). The GLS estimator and its variance, Equations (D.18) and (D.19), the whitening transformation, Equation (D.20), and the profile likelihood of \(\lambda\), Equation (D.21), are in Section D.3.5; the general theory of GLS is in Section A.11. A few points about Equation (13.5) are worth stressing, because they are often misunderstood. The phylogenetic structure is in the residuals, not in the variables (Revell 2010). A strongly inherited predictor does not by itself call for PGLS. If the predictor explains all the phylogenetic structure in the response, the residuals may show no signal, and estimating \(\lambda\) jointly with the regression will reveal this (Section 13.6.2). Conversely, testing the response for signal and skipping PGLS if none is found is bad practice. The predictors are treated as fixed and measured without error, as in any regression. Error in the predictor (for example, poorly estimated speaker numbers) biases the slope toward zero. The intercept is the estimated value at the root of the tree for a language with all predictors equal to zero. It is not the mean of the sample. PGLS handles any number of continuous or categorical predictors and their interactions, exactly as in ordinary regression. The only change is \(\mathbf{V}\). 13.6.2 Estimating lambda jointly In practice we rarely know how strong the phylogenetic dependence of the residuals is. The standard solution is to estimate Pagel’s \(\lambda\) jointly with \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) by maximum likelihood, with \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{C}(\lambda)\) (Freckleton et al. 2002). For each value of \(\lambda\) the regression coefficients have a closed form, so the likelihood can be maximized over \(\lambda\) alone, which is fast. The estimated \(\lambda\) then tells us where the analysis sits between OLS (\(\lambda = 0\)) and PGLS under BM (\(\lambda = 1\)). Its confidence interval tells us how well the data pin this down. With a few dozen languages, the interval is often wide. 13.6.3 PGLS in R There are three common routes to PGLS in R, and it is useful to know all of them. The nlme::gls() function (Pinheiro and Bates 2000) accepts correlation structures from ape such as corBrownian(), corPagel() and corMartins() (an OU structure). The caper package (Orme et al. 2013) provides pgls(), which estimates \(\lambda\), \(\kappa\) and \(\delta\) and offers profile plots and diagnostics. The phylolm package (Ho and Ané 2014a) fits the same models with a linear-time algorithm, which matters for trees with thousands of tips such as global language phylogenies. We simulate a scenario of the kind discussed in Section 13.11. A predictor, logpop, stands in for the logarithm of speaker population. A response, complexity, stands in for an index of morphological complexity. Their relationship has a true slope of \(-0.3\), and the residual variation has phylogenetic signal \(\lambda = 0.7\). Both variables are inherited. Population size, too, has a history: languages of a large, expanding branch tend to be large. set.seed(43) logpop <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.4) + 9 resid <- fastBM(rescale(tree, "lambda", 0.7), sig2 = 0.15) complexity <- 5 - 0.3 * logpop + resid langs <- data.frame(lang = tips, logpop = logpop[tips], complexity = complexity[tips], row.names = tips) head(langs, 4) #> lang logpop complexity #> L01 L01 7.750 1.556 #> L02 L02 7.913 2.066 #> L03 L03 7.399 1.435 #> L04 L04 6.747 2.269 First, the three models fitted with nlme::gls(): OLS (via gls() without a correlation structure), PGLS under BM, and PGLS with \(\lambda\) estimated. m_ols <- gls(complexity ~ logpop, data = langs, method = "ML") m_bm <- gls(complexity ~ logpop, data = langs, method = "ML", correlation = corBrownian(1, phy = tree, form = ~lang)) m_lam <- gls(complexity ~ logpop, data = langs, method = "ML", correlation = corPagel(0.5, phy = tree, form = ~lang)) tab <- t(sapply(list(OLS = m_ols, BM = m_bm, lambda = m_lam), function(m) c(summary(m)$tTable["logpop", c("Value", "Std.Error", "p-value")], AIC = AIC(m)))) lambda_hat <- coef(m_lam$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE) knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3, caption = "Slope of complexity on log population under OLS, PGLS with Brownian motion, and PGLS with Pagel's lambda estimated by maximum likelihood (simulated data; true slope -0.3, true lambda 0.7).") Table 13.2: Slope of complexity on log population under OLS, PGLS with Brownian motion, and PGLS with Pagel’s lambda estimated by maximum likelihood (simulated data; true slope -0.3, true lambda 0.7). Value Std.Error p-value AIC OLS -0.125 0.084 0.140 170.9 BM -0.342 0.141 0.018 160.2 lambda -0.262 0.127 0.044 151.5 The estimated \(\lambda\) is 0.81, close to the true value of 0.7, and the lambda model is clearly preferred by AIC. Notice what happens to the slope. In this replicate OLS gives an estimate of -0.13 with \(p =\) 0.14. The real effect is masked by the phylogenetically structured noise, because a few large clades happen to have residuals that run against the trend. The lambda model, which down-weights redundant information from those clades, recovers a slope of -0.26 with \(p =\) 0.044. This is a useful corrective to a common belief. Phylogenetic correction is often thought of as a conservative procedure that can only remove “significant” results. In fact, it makes estimates more efficient as well as more honest, and it can reveal an effect that OLS misses as easily as it can remove a spurious one. Which estimate is closest to the truth in a single replicate is partly a matter of luck. What is not luck is that OLS standard errors and \(p\)-values are systematically wrong when residuals have phylogenetic structure (Figure 13.2). The same lambda model fitted with caper gives identical estimates, and caper also reports likelihood-ratio tests of \(\lambda = 0\) and \(\lambda = 1\) and a confidence interval for \(\lambda\): cd <- comparative.data(phy = tree, data = langs, names.col = lang, vcv = TRUE) m_caper <- pgls(complexity ~ logpop, data = cd, lambda = "ML") summary(m_caper)$coefficients #> Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) #> (Intercept) 4.3347 1.2991 3.337 0.001484 #> logpop -0.2624 0.1273 -2.061 0.043754 m_caper$param.CI$lambda[c("opt", "ci.val", "bounds.p")] #> $opt #> lambda #> 0.8116 #> #> $ci.val #> [1] 0.4838 0.9657 #> #> $bounds.p #> [1] 3.661e-06 1.046e-03 par(mar = c(7, 4, 1, 1)) # room for the two-line subtitle below the axis plot(pgls.profile(m_caper, "lambda")) Figure 13.5: Profile log-likelihood of Pagel’s lambda for the PGLS of complexity on log population, computed with caper. The vertical lines mark the ML estimate and its 95% confidence interval. Finally, phylolm fits the lambda model and also an OU model for the residuals, which we can compare by AIC: p_lam <- phylolm(complexity ~ logpop, data = langs, phy = tree, model = "lambda") p_ou <- phylolm(complexity ~ logpop, data = langs, phy = tree, model = "OUrandomRoot") rbind(lambda = c(coef(p_lam), AIC = AIC(p_lam)), OU = c(coef(p_ou), AIC = AIC(p_ou))) #> (Intercept) logpop AIC #> lambda 4.335 -0.2624 151.5 #> OU 3.700 -0.2110 149.1 13.6.4 Diagnostics PGLS has the same diagnostics as ordinary regression, applied to the normalized (whitened) residuals. These are what should be approximately independent and normal. In nlme, residuals(m, type = "normalized") returns them. caper offers plot() methods for its model objects. Outlying languages deserve particular attention. In a phylogenetic regression a single language on a long branch, such as an isolate or the only representative of a deep branch, can be highly influential, because nothing else in the sample shares its history. Re-fitting without such languages, and without each large clade in turn, is cheap and often revealing. Correlated predictors need a diagnostic of their own. Many candidate predictors in linguistic typology travel together: speaker population, the proportion of adult second-language learners and the area a language is spoken over; humidity, temperature and latitude. Inherited predictors are correlated for a second reason, because closely related languages share values of all of them. When two predictors carry nearly the same information, a regression that includes both can estimate their joint effect but not how to divide it between them. Each coefficient is then a partial effect, the association with one predictor holding the other fixed, and its standard error grows with the correlation. The simulation below makes the point with two inherited predictors that are almost interchangeable and contribute equally to the response. set.seed(7) x1 <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.4) x2 <- x1 + fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.05) # x2 tracks x1 closely y <- 1 + 0.3 * x1 + 0.3 * x2 + fastBM(rescale(tree, "lambda", 0.7), sig2 = 0.15) d2 <- data.frame(lang = tips, x1 = x1[tips], x2 = x2[tips], y = y[tips]) round(cor(d2$x1, d2$x2), 3) #> [1] 0.991 fit_lam <- function(f) gls(f, data = d2, method = "ML", correlation = corPagel(0.5, phy = tree, form = ~lang)) fits <- list(x1 = fit_lam(y ~ x1), x2 = fit_lam(y ~ x2), both = fit_lam(y ~ x1 + x2)) coef_se <- function(m, v) if (v %in% rownames(summary(m)$tTable)) summary(m)$tTable[v, c("Value", "Std.Error")] else c(NA, NA) tab_col <- t(sapply(fits, function(m) c(coef_se(m, "x1"), coef_se(m, "x2"), AIC = AIC(m)))) colnames(tab_col) <- c("slope x1", "SE x1", "slope x2", "SE x2", "AIC") knitr::kable(tab_col, digits = 2, caption = paste( "PGLS (Pagel's lambda) with two nearly collinear inherited predictors,", "each with a true slope of 0.3 (simulated data).")) Table 13.3: PGLS (Pagel’s lambda) with two nearly collinear inherited predictors, each with a true slope of 0.3 (simulated data). slope x1 SE x1 slope x2 SE x2 AIC x1 0.51 0.11 NA NA 163.8 x2 NA NA 0.44 0.10 165.6 both 0.55 0.41 -0.04 0.37 165.8 Fitted alone, either predictor has a clear positive slope, because it stands in for both. Fitted together, the standard errors are about four times larger, one slope is close to zero, and neither is distinguishable from the other; by AIC the two-predictor model is no better than either single-predictor model, although it is the true model. None of this is a failure of PGLS. It is what the data can say: languages in which \(x_1\) is high and \(x_2\) low, which alone could separate the two effects, hardly exist in the sample. The practical consequences are to report the correlations among predictors (and their phylogenetic signal), to interpret coefficients as partial effects, to compare models with and without each predictor rather than reading single \(p\)-values, and to recognize that choosing between correlated predictors is a substantive question about mechanism (Section 13.11.4) that the regression cannot settle on its own. Population size and rates of language change. Several studies have used phylogenetic regressions to ask whether languages spoken by larger populations change faster or slower. Bromham et al. (2015) compared pairs of closely related Polynesian languages that differ in population size, an explicitly phylogenetic “sister-pair” design that echoes independent contrasts. They found that languages with larger populations gained new words faster, while smaller populations lost words faster. Greenhill et al. (2018) extended the sister-pair design to 153 pairs of closely related languages in Indo-European, Austronesian and Bantu, comparing numbers of word gains and losses between sisters and using branch lengths from published dated trees to correct for divergence time. They found that the Polynesian pattern did not generalize consistently: smaller Indo-European languages showed significantly higher rates of word loss, but there was no significant pattern in Austronesian or Bantu. These studies illustrate a recurring theme. The response variable (a rate) is itself an output of a phylogenetic analysis, so it inherits that analysis’s uncertainty and assumptions. And the effect sizes are modest relative to the noise. Chapter 9 discusses them as findings about rates. Here they matter as examples of design: sister pairs are a sampling design that guarantees variation within lineages (Section 13.2). 13.7 Correlated evolution of discrete characters 13.7.1 Pagel’s model Most of the classic questions of typology concern discrete features. For these, the standard phylogenetic tool is the method of Pagel (1994). The idea is to model two binary characters jointly as a single four-state character, and to compare a model in which the two evolve independently with one in which the rate of change in each depends on the current state of the other. Let \(X\) be the order of object and verb (0 = OV, 1 = VO) and \(Y\) the order of adposition and noun (0 = postpositions, 1 = prepositions). The joint character has four states: \((0,0)\) = OV with postpositions, \((0,1)\) = OV with prepositions, \((1,0)\) = VO with postpositions and \((1,1)\) = VO with prepositions. The first and last are the “harmonic” combinations of Greenberg’s Universal 4 and its mirror image. Change happens in continuous time, and only one character changes at a time. Under the dependent model, every one of the eight permitted transitions has its own rate: \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{Q}_{\text{dep}} = \begin{pmatrix} \cdot & q_{12} & q_{13} & 0 \\ q_{21} & \cdot & 0 & q_{24} \\ q_{31} & 0 & \cdot & q_{34} \\ 0 & q_{42} & q_{43} & \cdot \end{pmatrix}, \tag{13.6} \end{equation}\] with rows and columns in the order \((0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\) and diagonal elements chosen so that rows sum to zero. Under the independent model, each character has its own gain and loss rates whatever the state of the other character, so the eight rates collapse to four (for example, \(q_{13} = q_{24}\): the rate at which OV becomes VO does not depend on adposition order). Both models are fitted by maximum likelihood with the pruning algorithm on the four-state character (Chapter 5), and compared with a likelihood-ratio statistic \[\begin{equation} \text{LR} = 2\,[\ell(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\text{dep}}) - \ell(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\text{ind}})], \tag{13.7} \end{equation}\] which is referred to a \(\chi^2\) distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. In a Bayesian implementation, such as BayesTraits (Pagel and Meade 2006), the comparison is made with a Bayes factor. The log marginal likelihoods of the two models are estimated, for example by stepping-stone sampling (Chapter 6), and their difference is interpreted on the scale of Kass and Raftery (1995). Values of \(2\log\text{BF}\) above about 2 are often treated as “positive” evidence, above 6 as “strong” and above 10 as “very strong”. The independent rate matrix, Equation (D.22), and the constraints that turn the dependent model into it are in Section D.3.6. The dependent model says more than “the two features are correlated.” It describes the dynamics of the correlation, and its rate parameters can be read directly. If \(q_{24}\) (OV-with-prepositions to VO-with-prepositions) is much larger than \(q_{13}\) (OV-with-postpositions to VO-with-postpositions), then a language with prepositions is more likely to switch to VO than a language with postpositions. In other words, adposition order conditions change in verb-object order. A pair of large rates leading out of the disharmonic states and small rates leading out of the harmonic ones means that disharmonic combinations are transient. They are visited, but quickly abandoned. This is just the kind of claim about pathways of change that diachronic typologists have made (Maslova 2000; Croft et al. 2011). More specific hypotheses can be tested by constraining particular rates. For example: Contingent change: does \(X\) change faster when \(Y = 1\) than when \(Y = 0\)? Test \(q_{13} = q_{24}\) (and/or \(q_{31} = q_{42}\)) against the unconstrained dependent model. Direction of dependence: is the dependence of \(X\) on \(Y\), or of \(Y\) on \(X\), or both? The function fitPagel() in phytools offers the arguments dep.var = "x", "y" or "xy" for this. Temporal order: which change usually comes first? The ratio of rates out of the two disharmonic states suggests whether languages typically pass through OV-with-prepositions or through VO-with-postpositions on the way between the harmonic types. In BayesTraits, reversible-jump MCMC can sample over all patterns of equality constraints among the rates, so that the posterior concentrates on the best-supported simplified model (Pagel and Meade 2006). Correlated grammaticalization of articles in Indo-European. Goldstein (2022a) coded the presence of definite and indefinite articles in 94 Indo-European languages as a single four-state character and fitted a dependent model in RevBayes over a sample of 100 trees from the ancestry-constrained posterior of Chang et al. (2015). Because the earliest attested languages lack articles, the root was fixed at “no articles” and losses were excluded, so the model is irreversible. The estimated rate of gaining an indefinite article was more than an order of magnitude higher in lineages that already had a definite article (posterior medians 0.00064 and 0.000036, with non-overlapping 95% HPD intervals), while the rate of gaining a definite article did not clearly depend on the presence of an indefinite one (overlapping intervals). A model with separate rates of indefinite-article gain was preferred over one with a single rate by a log Bayes factor of 5.31. The results are consistent with a trajectory from no articles, to a definite article, to both, and they show how an implicational universal can be restated as a claim about conditional rates of change (compare Cysouw 2011). Three caveats apply, and they illustrate Section 13.7.3. The result rests on many events, not one: the author counts at least 17 independent origins of definite and 15 of indefinite articles. The hyperpriors on the numbers of transitions, which the author describes as strong, were informed by counts of article origins in the same languages. And contact, which plausibly helped spread articles in parts of Europe, violates the assumption that change on different branches is independent. Cathcart et al. (2020) used a related design for Indo-Iranian, asking whether the development of sortal numeral classifiers is linked to the loosening of obligatory plural marking, as a diachronic reading of the Greenberg–Sanches–Slobin generalization predicts, rather than being due only to contact with neighbouring non-Indo-European languages. Estimating transition rates on 65 languages, with reconstructions constrained by historically attested states, they found broad support for the diachronic reading but no evidence for a strong bias against the synchronic co-occurrence of classifiers and obligatory plural marking, and a stronger effect in Iranian than in Indo-Aryan. 13.7.2 Pagel’s test in R We simulate a family of 100 languages and let VO order and prepositions evolve under a dependent model. In this model the harmonic states (OV with postpositions, VO with prepositions) are stable, with low rates of change out of them. The disharmonic states are unstable, with rates of leaving them ten times as high. states <- c("OV|Po", "OV|Pr", "VO|Po", "VO|Pr") Qdep <- matrix(0, 4, 4, dimnames = list(states, states)) Qdep["OV|Po", c("OV|Pr", "VO|Po")] <- 0.2 # leaving a harmonic state: slow Qdep["VO|Pr", c("VO|Po", "OV|Pr")] <- 0.2 Qdep["OV|Pr", c("OV|Po", "VO|Pr")] <- 2 # leaving a disharmonic state: fast Qdep["VO|Po", c("VO|Pr", "OV|Po")] <- 2 diag(Qdep) <- -rowSums(Qdep) set.seed(7) tree100 <- pbtree(n = 100, scale = 3) joint <- sim.Mk(tree100, Qdep) VO <- setNames(ifelse(grepl("^VO", joint), "VO", "OV"), names(joint)) Pr <- setNames(ifelse(grepl("Pr$", joint), "Pr", "Po"), names(joint)) table(VO, Pr) #> Pr #> VO Po Pr #> OV 55 6 #> VO 7 32 traits <- data.frame(VO = factor(VO), Pr = factor(Pr), row.names = names(VO)) plotTree.datamatrix(tree100, traits, fsize = 0.45, yexp = 1.1, sep = 1.5, colors = list(c(OV = "#E69F00", VO = "#56B4E9"), c(Po = "#009E73", Pr = "#CC79A7"))) legend("topleft", legend = c("OV", "VO", "Postp.", "Prep."), pch = 15, bty = "n", col = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#CC79A7"), cex = 0.8, ncol = 2) Figure 13.6: Simulated verb-object order (left column: OV or VO) and adposition order (right column: postpositions or prepositions) for 100 languages evolving under a dependent model in which the harmonic combinations are stable. fitPagel() fits the independent and dependent models and computes the likelihood-ratio test. We use method = "ace", which calls ape::ace() internally and is much faster than the default for this size of problem. fit_xy <- fitPagel(tree100, VO, Pr, method = "ace") fit_xy #> #> Pagel's binary character correlation test: #> #> Assumes "ARD" substitution model for both characters #> #> Independent model rate matrix: #> OV|Po OV|Pr VO|Po VO|Pr #> OV|Po -0.4320 0.2021 0.2299 0.0000 #> OV|Pr 0.3043 -0.5342 0.0000 0.2299 #> VO|Po 0.3596 0.0000 -0.5617 0.2021 #> VO|Pr 0.0000 0.3596 0.3043 -0.6639 #> #> Dependent (x & y) model rate matrix: #> OV|Po OV|Pr VO|Po VO|Pr #> OV|Po -0.3169 0.1659 0.1509 0.0000 #> OV|Pr 0.6849 -4.4520 0.0000 3.7671 #> VO|Po 1.7550 0.0000 -2.3991 0.6440 #> VO|Pr 0.0000 0.5455 0.2866 -0.8321 #> #> Model fit: #> log-likelihood AIC #> independent -86.78 181.6 #> dependent -72.45 160.9 #> #> Hypothesis test result: #> likelihood-ratio: 28.6606 #> p-value: 9.16161e-06 #> #> Model fitting method used was ace The dependent model is strongly preferred, and the estimated rate matrix recovers the structure of the generating process. The rates leading out of the disharmonic states (OV|Pr and VO|Po) are large, and those leading out of the harmonic states are small. We can also ask whether the dependence runs in one direction only: # dep.var = "x": VO depends on Pr; "y": Pr depends on VO fit_x <- fitPagel(tree100, VO, Pr, method = "ace", dep.var = "x") fit_y <- fitPagel(tree100, VO, Pr, method = "ace", dep.var = "y") aic <- c(independent = fit_xy$independent.AIC, VO_depends = fit_x$dependent.AIC, Pr_depends = fit_y$dependent.AIC, both = fit_xy$dependent.AIC) round(aic - min(aic), 1) #> independent VO_depends Pr_depends both #> 24.5 0.0 3.7 3.8 The independent model is decisively rejected. The differences among the dependent models are much smaller. In this replicate, a model in which only VO order depends on adposition order fits as well as the full model, or better, even though the generating process had dependence in both directions. This is typical. Detecting that two features are coupled requires far less data than establishing how they are coupled, and claims about the direction of dependence deserve correspondingly more caution. For contrast, here is the same test on two features that evolve independently on the same tree. It correctly finds no evidence for dependence: set.seed(8) Q1 <- matrix(c(-0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5), 2, 2, dimnames = list(c("a", "b"), c("a", "b"))) f1 <- sim.Mk(tree100, Q1); f2 <- sim.Mk(tree100, Q1) fit_null <- fitPagel(tree100, f1, f2, method = "ace") c(LR = fit_null$lik.ratio, p = fit_null$P) #> LR p #> 1.3428 0.8541 13.7.3 What Pagel’s test can and cannot show Maddison and FitzJohn (2015) identified a deep problem with all tests of this kind, which they called the “unsolved challenge” for phylogenetic correlation tests of categorical characters. A strongly significant result can arise from a single evolutionary event. Imagine that one branch deep in the tree saw both a change from OV to VO and a change from postpositions to prepositions, and that both states were then inherited by a large clade. The two characters will be perfectly associated across the tips, and the dependent model will fit far better than the independent one. The reason is that under the independent model it is improbable for both characters to change on the same branch and nowhere else. Yet a single co-occurrence is weak evidence for a functional link. It is one data point, not a hundred. The code below shows how easily this happens. # pick a clade of about 40 languages; both characters change once, on its stem n <- Ntip(tree100) nodes <- (n + 2):(n + tree100$Nnode) clade_size <- sapply(nodes, function(nd) sum(getDescendants(tree100, nd) <= n)) stem <- nodes[which.min(abs(clade_size - 40))] members <- getDescendants(tree100, stem) in_clade <- seq_len(n) %in% members c1 <- setNames(ifelse(in_clade, "VO", "OV"), tree100$tip.label) c2 <- setNames(ifelse(in_clade, "Pr", "Po"), tree100$tip.label) table(c1, c2) #> c2 #> c1 Po Pr #> OV 54 0 #> VO 0 46 fit_single <- fitPagel(tree100, c1, c2, method = "ace") c(LR = fit_single$lik.ratio, p = fit_single$P) #> LR p #> 16.30159 0.00264 The test is “significant” at conventional levels, although the data contain exactly one co-occurring pair of changes. The problem is not a bug in the software. It reflects the question the test answers, which is whether the dependent model describes the data better than the independent one. The test does not ask how many independent instances of correlated change the data contain. Maddison and FitzJohn (2015) proposed that analyses report the number of independent origins of the associated states and treat results driven by one or two events with great skepticism. Uyeda et al. (2018) made a broader version of the same point. Phylogenetic comparative models describe macroevolutionary patterns, and singular historical events, such as one shift on one branch, can dominate both continuous and discrete analyses. They recommended explicitly modeling such events, for instance with models that allow shifts in rate or state on particular branches. Several other caveats apply with special force to language: Hidden heterogeneity. If rates of change vary across lineages for reasons unrelated to the other character (for instance, because some branches experienced intense contact), Pagel’s test can mistake that heterogeneity for dependence. Hidden-rate models (Chapter 12), which add unobserved rate categories, help diagnose this (Beaulieu et al. 2013; Boyko and Beaulieu 2021). Contact. The models assume that change happens independently on each branch. Borrowing of word-order patterns from neighbors violates this. A pair of features may be associated because both spread through the same contact zone. Coding. Typological features are often coded from WALS-style categories with a “no dominant order” value that must be dropped or merged. These coding decisions can affect the result. Tree and branch lengths. The rates are in units of the tree’s branch lengths. Results on trees with arbitrary branch lengths (Section 13.12.2) need cautious interpretation. 13.7.4 Pathways of acquisition Some linguistic hypotheses are not about correlation in general but about the order in which two features arise. Implicational hierarchies such as the sequence of basic color terms of Berlin and Kay (1969), and grammaticalization clines in which one function of a construction develops before another, predict that a language acquires feature \(Y\) only after it has acquired feature \(X\). Pagel’s four-state coding expresses such a claim directly. If change is restricted to gains and the root is fixed at \((0,0)\), four rates remain: \(q_{12}\) and \(q_{13}\) for gaining \(Y\) or \(X\) first, and \(q_{24}\) and \(q_{34}\) for completing the pair. The strict hierarchy “\(X\) before \(Y\)” sets \(q_{12} = q_{24} = 0\); a weaker version, in which \(Y\) can arise alone but does not lead on to \(X\), sets only \(q_{24} = 0\). These hypotheses can be compared by marginal likelihood, or the model structure can itself be sampled. Reversible-jump MCMC can let each rate be exactly zero with some prior probability, so that the posterior probability of a zero rate measures the evidence that a route is closed, and a categorical model indicator can switch among a small set of pathway models within one analysis. Both can be run over a posterior sample of trees, so that the answer does not depend on one tree. Haynie and Bowern (2016) used reversible-jump MCMC over a posterior sample of Pama-Nyungan trees in this way to study the gain and loss of color terms (Section 14.10). Two cautions apply. The gain-only coding with a fixed root makes the state of the root an assumption rather than a result, so the analysis cannot also be used to reconstruct the root (Section 12.4.5). And the Maddison-FitzJohn problem of the previous section applies with full force: a route can look closed simply because the data contain few lineages in which it could have been taken. Simulated data are a useful check on whether the data are informative at all. In the RevBayes implementation of Section H.5.22, which analyses 30 simulated feature pairs over a sample of 100 trees, the posterior probability that the absent route was closed was above 0.99, the three open routes were never closed, and the model indicator put a probability above 0.99 on the generating pathway. These are parameter-recovery results in the sense of Section 6.10, obtained with 30 replicate pairs evolving under the same process; with a single pair of features, as in most linguistic applications, the same analysis is likely to be much less decisive. The study of articles described in Section 13.7 also illustrates three practical points about pathway models. First, each rate is best read as a change in a background state: \(q_{24}\) and \(q_{13}\) in Equation (13.6) describe the same change in the first character, made with and without the second, so the hypothesis “the second feature promotes the first” becomes the inequality \(q_{24} > q_{13}\), which a posterior sample of the two rates addresses directly. Semi-dependent models, in which only one character’s rates depend on the state of the other, sit between the independent and the fully dependent model and are the natural way to ask which way the conditioning runs. Second, the gain-only restriction and the root state \((0,0)\) can rest on the comparative method rather than on convenience, as they do for the articles (Section 12.4.5); the rate estimates are then conditional on that philological judgement. Third, priors on the rates of a gain-only model are easiest to set in terms of the expected number of changes on the whole tree: an exponential prior whose mean is \(c\) divided by the tree length says that roughly \(c\) changes of that kind would be expected over the history of the sample if every lineage remained able to make them, a quantity on which a specialist can usually express an opinion. Because such counts are easily informed by the same languages that are being analysed, as the caveats to the article study note, the sensitivity of the conclusions to \(c\) should be reported. 13.8 Word-order universals on language trees 13.8.1 Dunn, Greenhill, Levinson and Gray (2011) “Evolved structure of language shows lineage-specific trends in word-order universals.” Dunn et al. (2011) applied Pagel’s method, in its Bayesian form in BayesTraits, to eight word-order features in four large language families: Austronesian, Bantu, Indo-European and Uto-Aztecan. The features were the orders of adjective and noun, adposition and noun, demonstrative and noun, genitive and noun, numeral and noun, relative clause and noun, object and verb, and subject and verb. For every pair of features in every family, they compared the dependent and independent models by Bayes factors, integrating over samples of trees estimated from lexical cognate data. The striking result was that the networks of strongly supported dependencies differed from family to family. Several dependencies were supported in one family but not in others, and the familiar Greenbergian correlations were not recovered as a uniform set across all four. The authors concluded that word-order dependencies are largely lineage-specific. On this view the structure of a language reflects the cultural evolutionary history of its lineage, with each family following its own pathways, rather than universal cognitive or processing constraints. The paper was published in Nature and received wide attention well beyond linguistics. The study was a landmark in two ways. It was the first large-scale attempt to test typological universals with explicit models of diachronic change on dated trees. And it moved the question from “which combinations are frequent?” to “which changes are coupled?” It also provoked one of the most substantial methodological debates in modern typology, much of it collected in a 2011 issue of Linguistic Typology. 13.8.2 The responses Dryer (2011) argued that the study did not test the correlations as typologists had formulated them. The correlations are claims about the languages of the world as a whole, established across genera and macroareas. Four families are a small and unrepresentative sample of that whole. Within a single family, many features show little variation: most Bantu languages are VO and prepositional, for example. A test within that family therefore has little power, and failure to find a dependency there is weak evidence against it. Dryer also argued that the strength of the evidence for a correlation should be judged by how often the preferred combinations arise across independent lineages worldwide, which is what his genus-based method measures. His own data, he noted, show the correlations clearly. Croft et al. (2011) situated the debate within diachronic typology. Greenbergian universals have long been interpreted as constraints on pathways of change, so a model of change on trees is the right kind of tool. But a test of universal constraints needs to pool information across families, and needs to model the transitions that the constraints are about. They also raised statistical concerns about drawing conclusions from family-specific results based on few independent changes. Levy and Daumé III (2011) put a similar point sharply in their title: “computational methods are invaluable for typology, but the models must match the questions”. A universal is a hypothesis that the same dependency holds in all families. That hypothesis should be tested with a model in which the families share parameters, or at least a hierarchical model in which family-specific parameters are drawn from a common distribution. Separate analyses of four families cannot distinguish “the dependency is absent in this family” from “this family provides too little information”. A model with shared parameters across families would have far more power to detect a universal tendency, and would test it directly. Bickel (2011), also in the Linguistic Typology discussion, argued for distributional methods that treat families as independent replicates of diachronic processes, of which his Family Bias method is an example. Cysouw (2011) examined what the transition probabilities estimated by such models mean and how they relate to observed frequencies. Because the independent model is nested in the dependent one, he noted, the test can show that dependence is not supported but cannot give strong support for independence, so most of the weak results are absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Combining the family-level Bayes factors with Fisher’s method (under a frequentist calibration of Bayes factors that is itself debatable), he found support across the families for four classical pairings, among them adposition order with object–verb order. For that pair the stable distributions implied by the published rates are similar in Austronesian and Indo-European; in Austronesian, postpositions with OV order occur in only about 6 percent of the sampled languages but have a stable frequency of about 24 percent, a difference he attributes to the founder effect of a young family. Longobardi and Roberts (2011) responded from the perspective of generative syntax, questioning which kind of universals, if any, the study could bear on. Levinson et al. (2011) replied to the critics. They maintained that if universal dependencies exist, they should be detectable in the history of individual families, and that the family-specific approach makes explicit what claims of universality predict. With hindsight, the debate settled some issues and sharpened others. Few would now dispute that cross-linguistic correlations should be studied as properties of change, or that phylogenetic models provide the natural framework for doing so. Few would dispute either that analyses confined to a handful of families, each with limited variation, lack the power to establish the absence of a universal tendency. In the terms of Section 13.2, the debate was largely about sampling: about what the target of inference was and how many independent changes each family supplied. The real open question is whether the tendencies are weak and universal, strong but lineage-specific, or some mixture of the two. Hierarchical models that let rates vary across families around a shared mean can answer it, because they estimate both the shared tendency and the between-family variance. 13.8.3 Later work Several later studies took up this agenda. Maurits and Griffiths (2014) used Bayesian phylogenetic models of basic word order (the six orders of subject, object and verb) on trees for many families to estimate ancestral word orders and transition rates. They found evidence that SOV is the most likely ancestral state for many families and that changes among word orders follow characteristic pathways (see Chapter 12). Jäger and Wahle (2021) developed what they called phylogenetic typology. They used posterior samples of trees inferred for each family from ASJP lexical data, in the manner of Jäger (2018), with the Glottolog classification as a constraint (Hammarström et al. 2024), and fitted CTMC models of the kind discussed above to pairs of WALS word-order features, pooling information across 175 lineages. In contrast to the impression left by the 2011 debate, they reported support for a number of the classical word-order correlations once data from many lineages were combined in a single phylogenetic model. Not every proposed correlation was supported, though. Their work shows that the answer depends heavily on the scope of the sample and on whether information is pooled across families, which is exactly what Levy and Daumé III (2011) had argued. 13.8.4 Grambank Grambank and the relative weight of genealogy and geography. Skirgård et al. (2023) introduced Grambank, a database of 195 grammatical features coded for more than 2,400 languages by a large team, with explicit coding protocols and sources. One of their analyses addressed the old question of whether languages are more similar because of shared descent or because of shared geography. For each feature they fitted a Bayesian model with three latent components: a phylogenetic effect, with covariance derived from a global language phylogeny; a spatial effect, with covariance decaying with geographic distance; and residual variation. Models of this type are called spatiophylogenetic models, and they were fitted with the integrated nested Laplace approximation [INLA; Rue et al. (2009)]. Averaged across features, phylogeny accounted for more variance than space, and the relative contributions varied widely between features. The study also illustrated the cost of language endangerment for typology. Simulated loss of the currently endangered languages would reduce the structural diversity documented in Grambank only moderately at the global scale, but much more severely in some regions, so that the loss would be strikingly uneven. Methodologically, the paper marks the point at which spatiophylogenetic models, long used in ecology, became a standard tool in typology. Section 13.10 shows a small example. Grambank has since become the reference dataset for testing typological universals and claims about social and environmental effects on grammar with phylogenetic and spatial controls, as in the analysis of Shcherbakova et al. (2023) discussed in Section 13.11. Testing 191 universals at once. Verkerk, Shcherbakova, et al. (2025) used Grambank to test 191 proposed grammatical universals with Bayesian analyses that account for both genealogical descent and geographic proximity. About a third of the proposed universals received statistical support, most of them word-order universals and hierarchical universals, the two types that have been most prominent in earlier work. Evolutionary analyses suggested that languages tend to change in ways that converge on the preferred patterns, which the authors interpret as evidence that shared cognitive and communicative pressures repeatedly push languages toward similar solutions. Two features of the design matter for interpretation. Testing many universals at once guards against the selective reporting that has plagued single-universal studies, but the result for each universal depends on how its features are coded in Grambank and on the global tree used as a scaffold. And support for a universal under a spatiophylogenetic model is evidence of a statistical tendency in change, not of a particular cognitive mechanism. Other Grambank-based studies have moved from correlation toward explicit causal models. Shcherbakova et al. (2024) analyzed case marking, verbal indexing and word order in 1,705 languages with phylogenetic causal graph methods and concluded that verb-final order tends to give rise to case marking and, more surprisingly, that case marking tends to lead to flexible word order. Because Grambank’s features were designed for coverage rather than statistical independence, Graff, Chousou-Polydouri, et al. (2025) derived curated versions of Grambank and of other structural databases in which logically dependent and strongly correlated features are reduced, for analyses that treat features as independent. 13.9 Phylogenetic regression for non-Gaussian responses Pagel’s test handles pairs of discrete features. Many questions, though, call for a regression: a binary or count response, with several predictors, some continuous. Does the probability that a language has tone depend on humidity, controlling for latitude? Does the presence of grammatical gender depend on population size and on the number of neighboring languages? PGLS is not appropriate for binary responses. Three families of methods fill the gap: phylogenetic logistic regression, phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models, and the threshold model. 13.9.1 Phylogenetic logistic regression Ives and Garland (2010) developed a phylogenetic logistic regression in which the binary response evolves along the tree as a two-state Markov process. The rates of this process are chosen so that the expected value of the response for language \(i\) follows the usual logistic form, \[\begin{equation} \Pr(y_i = 1) = \mu_i = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}}, \tag{13.8} \end{equation}\] while a parameter \(\alpha\) controls how fast the process “forgets” its past. When \(\alpha\) is large, the state of a language is almost independent of its ancestors, and the model approaches ordinary logistic regression. When \(\alpha\) is small, related languages are strongly correlated, and the effective sample size shrinks. Estimation is by maximum penalized likelihood. The penalty, due to Firth (1993), reduces the small-sample bias of logistic regression and keeps estimates finite when the data are nearly separated, a common situation when a feature is almost fixed within large clades. The method is implemented as phylolm::phyloglm() (Ho and Ané 2014a). Below we simulate a binary response (call it tone, present or absent) whose probability depends on a continuous predictor (call it humid, a standardized humidity index). Both variables are phylogenetically structured. We then compare ordinary and phylogenetic logistic regression. set.seed(11) humid <- rTrait(n = 1, phy = tree100, model = "BM", parameters = list(sigma2 = 0.4)) tone <- rbinTrait(n = 1, phy = tree100, beta = c(-0.5, 1), alpha = 0.5, X = cbind(1, humid)) dtone <- data.frame(lang = tree100$tip.label, humid = humid, tone = tone, row.names = tree100$tip.label) table(dtone$tone) #> #> 0 1 #> 64 36 fit_glm <- glm(tone ~ humid, data = dtone, family = binomial) fit_plr <- phyloglm(tone ~ humid, data = dtone, phy = tree100, method = "logistic_MPLE") rbind(glm = coef(summary(fit_glm))["humid", c(1, 2, 4)], phyloglm = coef(summary(fit_plr))["humid", c(1, 2, 4)]) #> Estimate Std. Error Pr(>|z|) #> glm 0.6739 0.2603 0.009628 #> phyloglm 0.7440 0.3124 0.017230 fit_plr$alpha #> #> 0.7874 The comparison mirrors the Gaussian case. The ordinary logistic regression treats the 100 languages as independent observations, and its standard error is correspondingly optimistic. The phylogenetic model estimates \(\alpha\) and adjusts the standard errors to the amount of independent information in the data. In real analyses the two often disagree not only in precision but in the sign or magnitude of the effect. That happens when a few large clades with particular values of both variables drive the ordinary regression. 13.9.2 Phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models The most general and flexible framework is the phylogenetic generalized linear mixed model (PGLMM). It comes from quantitative genetics, where a pedigree plays the role of the phylogeny (Lynch 1991; Housworth et al. 2004; Hadfield and Nakagawa 2010). The model has a linear predictor with a random effect for each language whose covariance is proportional to the phylogenetic correlation matrix: \[\begin{equation} g\big(\mathbb{E}[y_i]\big) = \eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + a_i + e_i, \qquad \mathbf{a} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2_a \mathbf{A}), \quad e_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_e), \tag{13.9} \end{equation}\] where \(g\) is a link function (identity for Gaussian, logit or probit for binary data, log for counts), \(\mathbf{A}\) is the phylogenetic correlation matrix (\(\mathbf{C}\) scaled to unit diagonal for an ultrametric tree), and \(e_i\) is a language-level residual. For a Gaussian response, the phylogenetic heritability \[\begin{equation} H^2 = \frac{\sigma^2_a}{\sigma^2_a + \sigma^2_e} \tag{13.10} \end{equation}\] is equivalent to Pagel’s \(\lambda\) (Housworth et al. 2004). For non-Gaussian responses it is defined on the latent scale. The PGLMM framework has several advantages that matter for linguistic data: Multiple observations per language. The model separates between-language variation (phylogenetic and non-phylogenetic) from within-language variation. This is useful for corpus data, for speaker-level data in sociolinguistics, or for multiple sources coding the same language. Several random effects at once. A spatial random effect, a random effect for macroarea, and a random effect for the coding source can sit alongside the phylogenetic one (Section 13.10). Multi-response models. Two or more features can be modeled jointly, with phylogenetic and residual correlations between them estimated separately (Hadfield and Nakagawa 2010). A phylogenetic correlation means that the features have coevolved over the long term. A residual correlation means that they covary among languages in ways not attributable to shared history, as expected under contact or a recent functional coupling. This decomposition is directly relevant to the debate over lineage-specific versus universal dependencies, and to our knowledge it has rarely if ever been used in typology. Bayesian inference. The two standard implementations are MCMCglmm (Hadfield 2010) and brms (Bürkner 2017), the latter an interface to Stan. Bayesian inference makes it natural to integrate over a sample of trees (Section 13.12.1). Ecologists have developed closely related models for communities of species (Ives and Helmus 2011), and the frequentist phyr package fits PGLMMs quickly. In linguistics, mixed models with random effects for family and area (Jaeger et al. 2011; Bentz and Winter 2013) can be seen as coarse PGLMMs with a block-diagonal \(\mathbf{A}\). Every language within a family is assumed to be equally related to every other. The following code fits a Gaussian PGLMM to the complexity data from Section 13.6.3 with MCMCglmm, using a short chain. The phylogeny enters as the inverse of the relatedness matrix, computed by inverseA(). library(MCMCglmm) set.seed(5) Ainv <- inverseA(tree, nodes = "TIPS", scale = TRUE)$Ainv prior <- list(G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)), R = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)) m_mc <- MCMCglmm(complexity ~ logpop, random = ~lang, ginverse = list(lang = Ainv), data = langs, prior = prior, nitt = 23000, burnin = 3000, thin = 20, verbose = FALSE) summary(m_mc)$solutions #> post.mean l-95% CI u-95% CI eff.samp pMCMC #> (Intercept) 4.4432 1.8352 7.28648 1000 0.002 #> logpop -0.2747 -0.5443 -0.03021 1000 0.046 H2 <- m_mc$VCV[, "lang"] / rowSums(m_mc$VCV) hpd <- HPDinterval(H2) c(posterior_mean_H2 = mean(H2), lower95 = hpd[1, 1], upper95 = hpd[1, 2]) #> posterior_mean_H2 lower95 upper95 #> 0.8325 0.6122 0.9999 The posterior mean of the slope is close to the ML estimate from PGLS. The phylogenetic heritability plays the role of \(\lambda\), and its posterior shows how uncertain that quantity is with 60 languages. For real analyses, chains should be much longer. Convergence should be checked as described in Chapter 6, and the sensitivity of variance components to their priors should be examined. Weakly informative or parameter-expanded priors are generally preferable to the inverse-gamma prior used here. The same model in brms, with notes on the sampler settings it needs, is in Section D.3.7. 13.9.3 The threshold model Many discrete linguistic features plausibly reflect an underlying continuous tendency. The degree of reliance on suffixation, the strength of a preference for head-final structures, or the degree of grammaticalization of a construction may vary continuously while being coded as present or absent. The threshold model of quantitative genetics, introduced to comparative biology by Felsenstein (2005, 2012), formalizes this idea. Each language has an unobserved liability \(l_i\) that evolves by Brownian motion on the tree. The observed state is 1 when the liability exceeds a threshold (conventionally 0) and 0 otherwise: \[\begin{equation} y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } l_i > 0, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \qquad \mathbf{l} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta, \mathbf{C}). \tag{13.11} \end{equation}\] Multistate ordered characters use several thresholds. The model has properties that Markov models lack. A lineage whose liability lies close to the threshold may flip back and forth quickly, while one far from it is very stable. The probability of change therefore depends on the lineage’s history, and not only on its current state. Correlations between two discrete characters, or between a discrete and a continuous one, are simply correlations between liabilities (Felsenstein 2012). Ancestral states can be reconstructed on the liability scale (Revell 2014), which is implemented in phytools::ancThresh() and threshBayes(). A threshold PGLMM is a probit PGLMM with the residual variance fixed; in MCMCglmm it is available as family = "threshold". To our knowledge, threshold models have been used only rarely on linguistic data, although many typological features seem natural candidates for them. They deserve a place alongside Mk models in typological work (see also Section 16.5.2). A threshold model for the simulated tone data fitted with MCMCglmm, and the conversion between its probit-scale coefficients and the logistic coefficients above, are in Section D.3.8. From the biologist’s toolbox: multivariate and shift models. Comparative biology has moved well beyond single-trait BM. Several families of methods could be applied directly to typological and lexical data. (1) Multivariate BM and OU models, implemented in mvMORPH (Clavel et al. 2015), estimate evolutionary covariance matrices among several continuous traits. With them one can ask, for example, whether measures of fusion and exponence coevolve, and whether that coupling differs between families. (2) Phylogenetic factor analysis (Tolkoff et al. 2018) reduces many traits to a few latent factors that evolve along the tree. It could be used to find coevolving “modules” of grammatical features in Grambank-scale data. (3) Rate-shift models detect branches or clades where the rate of evolution changes. Examples are the reversible-jump approach of Eastman et al. (2011) and the variable-rates model of Venditti et al. (2011). Applied to typology, they would identify lineages with bursts of structural change, for instance after intense contact or language shift. (4) Multi-optimum OU models, with regimes specified in advance (Butler and King 2004; Beaulieu et al. 2012) or detected from the data (Uyeda and Harmon 2014; Khabbazian et al. 2016), could test whether languages in different social or ecological settings are drawn toward different optima. (5) Hidden-rate and structured Markov models for discrete characters (Beaulieu et al. 2013; Boyko and Beaulieu 2021) allow the dependence between features to switch on and off across the tree. They are a principled way to represent “lineage-specific” dependencies, which is the very issue raised by Dunn et al. (2011). (6) Measurement-error and within-species variation models (Ives et al. 2007) could represent dialect variation and coding uncertainty. Most of these methods are available in R and run on the same tree and data objects used in this chapter. To our knowledge, few if any have been applied to linguistic data so far. 13.10 Space and phylogeny together Galton’s problem has two faces: descent and diffusion. The methods so far address only descent. Languages that are geographically close share features through contact. They also tend to be closely related, which makes the two sources of similarity hard to separate. A phylogenetic regression that ignores space will attribute some areal similarity to the tree, or leave it in the residuals. A spatial regression that ignores phylogeny will make the opposite mistake. The natural generalization is a model with separate covariance components for phylogeny and space: \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}, \quad \mathbf{a} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2_p \mathbf{C}), \; \mathbf{s} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2_s \mathbf{S}), \; \mathbf{e} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2_e \mathbf{I}), \tag{13.12} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{S}\) is a spatial correlation matrix, for instance \(S_{ij} = \exp(-d_{ij}/\rho)\) with \(d_{ij}\) the geographic distance and \(\rho\) a range parameter. Freckleton and Jetz (2009) developed a version of this model for comparative biology. In ecology it is usually fitted in a Bayesian framework with INLA or MCMC.
