The proportions \(\sigma^2_p/(\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_s + \sigma^2_e)\) and \(\sigma^2_s/(\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_s + \sigma^2_e)\) measure the relative importance of descent and diffusion. These are the quantities reported by Skirgård et al. (2023). Mixed models with crossed random effects for family and macroarea (Jaeger et al. 2011) are a coarse version of the same idea. Below we simulate languages whose locations are themselves inherited along the tree, as they would be if languages spread by migration from a homeland (Chapter 11). A trait then receives a phylogenetic component, a spatial component and noise, each contributing a known share of the variance. Because the true shares are known, this is a parameter-recovery experiment. set.seed(99) lon <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1) + rnorm(Ntip(tree), 0, 0.3) lat <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1) + rnorm(Ntip(tree), 0, 0.3) D <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(lon, lat))) S <- exp(-D / 1) # spatial correlation, range 1 L_s <- t(chol(S + diag(1e-8, nrow(S)))) a_phy <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1 / max(diag(C))) # phylogenetic part, variance 1 s_sp <- drop(L_s %*% rnorm(Ntip(tree))) # spatial part, variance 1 trait <- 0.8 * a_phy + 0.8 * s_sp + rnorm(Ntip(tree), 0, 0.5) true_share <- c(0.64, 0.64, 0.25) / sum(c(0.64, 0.64, 0.25)) round(true_share, 2) # phylo, space, noise #> [1] 0.42 0.42 0.16 The model of Equation (13.12) can be fitted in MCMCglmm with two random effects for the same languages, one with the inverse phylogenetic correlation matrix and one with the inverse spatial correlation matrix. The range \(\rho\) is held fixed at its true value for simplicity; real analyses estimate it or compare several values. dsp <- data.frame(lang = tips, lang_sp = tips, y = trait[tips]) Sinv <- as(solve(S + diag(1e-6, nrow(S))), "CsparseMatrix") dimnames(Sinv) <- list(tips, tips) px <- list(V = 1, nu = 1, alpha.mu = 0, alpha.V = 1000) # parameter-expanded prior_sp <- list(G = list(G1 = px, G2 = px), R = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)) set.seed(1) m_sp <- MCMCglmm(y ~ 1, random = ~lang + lang_sp, data = dsp, prior = prior_sp, ginverse = list(lang = Ainv, lang_sp = Sinv), nitt = 33000, burnin = 3000, thin = 30, verbose = FALSE) share <- m_sp$VCV / rowSums(m_sp$VCV) colnames(share) <- c("phylo", "space", "noise") round(rbind(posterior_mean = colMeans(share), t(HPDinterval(share))), 2) #> phylo space noise #> posterior_mean 0.38 0.57 0.06 #> lower 0.00 0.07 0.00 #> upper 0.90 1.00 0.31 The posterior means are in the right region, and the model correctly attributes most of the variance to the two structured components rather than to noise. But the 95% intervals for the phylogenetic and spatial shares are very wide: with 60 languages whose locations are themselves inherited, the two components are partly confounded, and the data cannot apportion the variance between them precisely. Real analyses use larger samples, estimate the range parameter, and report full posterior distributions of the variance shares, as here. The example shows the key logic: two non-independence structures can be modeled simultaneously and their contributions compared. A maximum-likelihood fit of the same model written from scratch, and its comparison with phylogeny-only and space-only models by AIC, are in Section D.3.9. Separating phylogeny from space is fundamentally difficult when related languages are also neighbors, which is the normal situation. In such cases, the data contain little information about which of the two structures is responsible for similarity, and the variance shares can depend heavily on priors, on the range parameter and on the tree’s branch lengths. Large families that have spread over wide areas (Austronesian, Bantu, Indo-European), and contact zones that cut across families, are where the two can be told apart. 13.11 Environment, society and language: causal claims Since about 2010, a growing literature has claimed that properties of languages are shaped by the physical or social environment of their speakers. Examples include humidity and tone, altitude and ejectives, population size and morphology, and the proportion of adult learners and case marking. These claims are interesting because they cut against a long-standing assumption in linguistics: that language structure is independent of the environment, apart from the lexicon. They are also exactly the kind of claim that Galton’s problem threatens most. Environmental and social variables are strongly spatially and phylogenetically structured. A few large families (Niger-Congo, Austronesian, Sino-Tibetan) dominate global samples, so a handful of historical accidents can produce a worldwide correlation. Ladd et al. (2015) review such correlational studies, both of linguistic features with one another and of features with properties of speakers and environments, and trace much of the scepticism of linguists to differences in assumptions and methods between large-scale quantitative work and traditional historical and theoretical research. This section reviews the most prominent cases, and then asks what phylogenetic control contributes to a causal argument. 13.11.1 Tone and humidity Climate, vocal folds and tonal languages. Everett et al. (2015) observed that languages with complex tone systems (three or more tones) are concentrated in humid regions, such as sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia and parts of New Guinea and the Americas. They are rare in very dry or cold regions. The authors argued for a physiological mechanism. Dry air desiccates the vocal folds and makes precise control of pitch harder, so that over many generations the transmission of complex tone would be slightly less successful in arid climates. They tested the pattern on a large sample of languages, using resampling procedures designed to control for relatedness and area, and found that it held across several families and regions. The paper generated a lively exchange. In the inaugural issue of the Journal of Language Evolution, Everett et al. (2016) restated and extended the case for climatic adaptation in a target article that drew a series of commentaries. Hammarström (2016) argued that once genealogical and areal dependencies are properly controlled, the evidence for a desiccation effect largely disappears. Collins (2016) argued, with simulations, that the global pattern can be explained by the spread of tone through contact in a few large areas, which happen to be humid. Everett and colleagues replied to the commentaries in the same issue. Roberts (2018) used the debate as a case study for a broader methodological argument: claims of linguistic adaptation should be tested in multiple, independent ways, combining large-scale correlational studies with experimental and causal-inference approaches, rather than relying on a single regression. The tone-humidity debate illustrates a general structure. A global correlation exists. Its interpretation depends on whether the effective number of independent observations is large (many families and areas showing the pattern) or small (a few large tonal areas). Phylogenetic and spatial models are the formal way to settle that question. Their answer depends on how well the trees and spatial structure are represented, and on the statistical power left once dependencies are accounted for. 13.11.2 Population size and morphological complexity The linguistic niche hypothesis. Lupyan and Dale (2010) analyzed more than 2,000 languages in WALS and found that languages spoken by larger populations, over larger areas and with more neighboring languages tend to use less inflectional morphology. They rely more on lexical and syntactic strategies. Lupyan and Dale proposed the linguistic niche hypothesis. Languages adapt to the social environments in which they are learned and used, and “esoteric” niches (small, close-knit communities with few adult learners) favor complex morphology, while “exoteric” niches (large populations with many adult learners) favor simplification. Related work by Bentz and Winter (2013), using mixed-effects models with random effects for family and area, found that languages with a larger proportion of second-language speakers are less likely to have nominal case. Bentz et al. (2015) reported a related effect on lexical diversity (fewer distinct word forms in languages with more non-native speakers). Koplenig (2019) reanalyzed similar data and found that the number of speakers was associated with some structural measures, but that the proportion of non-native speakers was not, once relatedness and area were controlled. The most comprehensive test to date is that of Shcherbakova et al. (2023). They used Grambank data and Bayesian spatiophylogenetic models of grammatical complexity measures, with population size and the proportion of L2 speakers as predictors. They found no support for the claim that “societies of strangers” speak less complex languages, which is also the title of their paper. This line of research shows how conclusions can change as methods for handling non-independence improve: from global correlations, to mixed models with family and area effects, to explicit spatiophylogenetic models on new data. It also illustrates that “complexity” is not one variable. Different operationalizations (number of inflectional categories, fusion, informativity, number of case markers) can behave differently, and choosing among them after seeing the data inflates false positives just as surely as ignoring phylogeny does. 13.11.3 Other environmental and demographic claims Several other claims follow the same pattern. Phoneme inventories and distance from Africa. Atkinson (2011) reported that phoneme inventory size declines with distance from a putative origin in southwestern Africa. He interpreted this as a serial founder effect during the human expansion out of Africa, analogous to the decline of genetic diversity. Critics argued that the analysis did not adequately control for relatedness and area, that phoneme counts are not comparable across sources, and that the result is sensitive to modeling choices (Jaeger et al. 2011; Cysouw et al. 2012). Altitude and ejectives. Everett (2013) argued that ejective consonants are more common in languages spoken at high altitude, proposing an aerodynamic mechanism. Later analyses questioned the robustness of the pattern once areal and genealogical structure was taken into account (Urban and Moran 2021). Bite configuration and labiodentals. Blasi et al. (2019) argued that labiodental sounds (such as f and [v]) became more common after the Neolithic, because softer diets preserved the overbite and overjet of adolescence into adulthood. The argument combined biomechanical modeling, cross-linguistic distributional analysis with controls for relatedness, and historical reconstruction within Indo-European. Future tense and saving. Chen (2013) reported that speakers of languages that grammatically mark future time save less, smoke more and exercise less. Roberts et al. (2015) re-tested the claim with explicit control for linguistic relatedness and geography, using phylogenetic and mixed-model approaches. They found that the relationship was considerably weaker, and not robust across all methods, once historical non-independence was taken into account. Spurious correlations. Roberts and Winters (2013) made the general point vividly. They showed that cultural and linguistic traits correlate with all kinds of unrelated variables in cross-national data, and that such correlations are expected from shared history and geography alone. A related argument in the cross-cultural literature, Bromham, Hua, et al. (2018), showed that correlations between pathogen load and cultural traits are highly sensitive to controls for relatedness, proximity and covariation among predictors. Ecology and diversity. Hua et al. (2019) examined the ecological correlates of language diversity worldwide, analyzing the density of languages rather than their structure. They too had to deal with spatial autocorrelation and with the confounding of climate, topography and history. 13.11.4 What phylogenetic control does and does not do It helps to state the causal logic explicitly, in the language of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) (Pearl 2009). Galton’s problem is a problem of confounding. Shared history (\(H\)) affects both a predictor \(X\) and a response \(Y\), because a proto-language passed on its values of both, so \(X\) and \(Y\) are associated across its descendants even if neither affects the other: \(X \leftarrow H \rightarrow Y\). A phylogenetic regression controls for \(H\) to the extent that the tree and the evolutionary model capture it. In effect, it compares changes in \(X\) with changes in \(Y\) along independent branches, a within-lineage comparison analogous to a fixed-effects design in econometrics. The estimand is therefore an evolutionary association: whether lineages that changed in \(X\) also tended to change in \(Y\). Several other routes from \(X\) to \(Y\) remain open, and Table 13.4 lists the most important. Contact creates associations among neighbors whatever their ancestry. Environmental variables such as climate are not inherited at all (speakers move, climates change), and they are structured in space, so they can confound a regression on any other spatially structured variable. A single deep event can produce an association that looks strong but rests on one observation (Section 13.7.3). The process that determines which languages are documented, and so enter the sample, can itself create associations: if large, written languages are more likely to be described in detail, and description affects how complexity is coded, conditioning on documentation conditions on a common effect of population size and coded complexity. And with observational data the direction of causation is not given: population size might affect morphology, or the history that produced a large population might also have produced a particular kind of morphology. Table 13.4: Sources of cross-linguistic association other than a causal effect of \(X\) on \(Y\), and what addresses each. Source of association Example What addresses it Shared inheritance Bantu languages share SVO and prepositions from Proto-Bantu Phylogenetic covariance (PGLS, PGLMM), if the tree and model are adequate Contact and areal diffusion Tone spreading through Mainland Southeast Asia Spatial covariance, area effects, explicit contact models Shared environment that is not inherited Humidity and latitude both structured in space Measuring and including the environmental covariates; spatial models A single historical event One branch changes both features, then radiates Counting independent origins; dropping large clades; shift models Selective documentation Well-described languages are larger and coded in more detail Modeling missingness; restricting to uniformly coded data; sensitivity analyses Reverse causation Language structure affecting group size or spread Temporal order on dated trees; directional models of coevolution Measurement and coding choices Several operationalizations of “complexity” Pre-specification; reporting all codings; multiple-testing control Three practical conclusions follow. First, phylogenetic control is necessary but not sufficient: it removes one confounder, the one represented by the tree. Second, the strength of an argument depends on the number of independent changes in \(X\) that the sample contains (Section 13.2), not on the number of languages. Third, the most persuasive studies combine several lines of evidence, as advocated by Roberts (2018): large-sample comparative analyses with phylogenetic and spatial controls, within-family tests where the predictor varies, experiments on learning and production, and mechanistic models. Databases such as CHIELD, which records causal hypotheses in evolutionary linguistics as explicit causal graphs (Roberts et al. 2020), help make such hypotheses explicit and comparable. Dated trees add one thing that a cross-sectional sample cannot: the order of changes. Directional versions of Pagel’s test (Section 13.7) ask whether changes in \(X\) tend to precede changes in \(Y\); temporal precedence is weaker than causation, but it rules out some causal stories. 13.11.5 Phylogenetic path analysis When the hypotheses involve several variables, a useful framework is phylogenetic confirmatory path analysis (Hardenberg and Gonzalez-Voyer 2013). It combines PGLS with the d-separation test of Shipley (2000). A causal hypothesis is written as a DAG. Every DAG implies a set of conditional independencies: pairs of variables that should be independent given certain others. For example, the DAG “population size \(\rightarrow\) proportion of L2 speakers \(\rightarrow\) morphological complexity” implies that population size and complexity are independent once the L2 proportion is controlled for. Each implied independence is tested with a PGLS regression, which yields a \(p\)-value \(p_k\), and the results are combined with Fisher’s statistic \[\begin{equation} C = -2\sum_{k=1}^{K} \ln p_k \sim \chi^2_{2K}. \tag{13.13} \end{equation}\] A small \(C\) (large \(p\)) means that the DAG is consistent with the data. Competing DAGs can be ranked with an information criterion based on \(C\). The R package phylopath (Bijl 2018) automates the procedure. The steps are simple enough to carry out directly, which also makes the logic visible. We simulate data under a mediation DAG and compare it with a “common cause” DAG in which population size affects both L2 proportion and complexity directly. set.seed(77) pop <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.3) # log population l2 <- 0.7 * pop + fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.1) # L2 proportion (latent scale) morph <- -0.6 * l2 + fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.1) # morphological complexity pdat <- data.frame(lang = tips, pop = pop[tips], l2 = l2[tips], morph = morph[tips]) pgls_p <- function(formula, term) { # p-value of one term in a BM PGLS m <- gls(formula, data = pdat, correlation = corBrownian(1, tree, form = ~lang)) summary(m)$tTable[term, "p-value"] } # DAG A (mediation): pop -> l2 -> morph. # Implied independence: morph _||_ pop | l2 p_A <- pgls_p(morph ~ l2 + pop, "pop") # DAG B (common cause): l2 <- pop -> morph. # Implied independence: morph _||_ l2 | pop p_B <- pgls_p(morph ~ pop + l2, "l2") C_stat <- -2 * log(c(A_mediation = p_A, B_common_cause = p_B)) cbind(C = C_stat, p = pchisq(C_stat, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)) #> C p #> A_mediation 0.9843 6.113e-01 #> B_common_cause 26.3115 1.934e-06 The mediation DAG, which generated the data, is consistent with them: its implied independence holds. The common-cause DAG is rejected, because complexity is not independent of L2 proportion once population size is controlled for. The logic extends to larger graphs, in which each DAG implies several independencies, and to PGLS with \(\lambda\) estimated or to phylogenetic logistic regression for binary variables. Its limits are those of any DAG-based method. The candidate DAGs must be specified in advance, unmeasured confounders (including every row of Table 13.4 except the first) can create spurious dependencies, and several DAGs may imply the same independencies (they are then Markov equivalent and cannot be distinguished by the data). 13.12 Practicalities 13.12.1 Integrating over tree uncertainty All the analyses so far have treated the tree as known. In practice, language trees are estimated, often with considerable uncertainty in topology and branch lengths (Chapter 6). There are three common ways to handle this. Use a single summary tree, such as a maximum clade credibility tree. This is simple, but it ignores uncertainty and can give overconfident results; Section 11.10 explains why a summary tree can mislead even when its topology looks plausible, and Section 12.15.7 shows an example for a named ancestor. Repeat the analysis on a sample of trees from the posterior and summarize the distribution of estimates. For frequentist analyses, the estimates can be combined with the rules developed for multiple imputation (Rubin 1987), whose use for phylogenetic uncertainty in comparative analyses was set out by Nakagawa and Villemereuil (2019). If \(\hat\beta_m\) and \(s_m\) are the estimate and its standard error on tree \(m\) of \(M\), the pooled estimate and its total variance are \[\begin{equation} \bar\beta = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} \hat\beta_m, \qquad T = \underbrace{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} s_m^2}_{\text{within trees}} + \left(1 + \frac{1}{M}\right) \underbrace{\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M} (\hat\beta_m - \bar\beta)^2}_{\text{between trees}}. \tag{13.14} \end{equation}\] The between-tree term is what a single-tree analysis leaves out. Integrate over trees within a Bayesian analysis. BayesTraits does this by sampling trees from the posterior sample as part of the MCMC (Pagel et al. 2004). In MCMCglmm or brms one can fit the model to each tree in turn and pool the posterior samples. Below we create a mock “posterior sample” of 100 trees by applying random nearest-neighbor interchanges and branch-length noise to the true tree. We then fit the BM PGLS of complexity on log population to each tree, combine the results with Equation (13.14), and compare them with an analysis of the MCC tree of the sample alone. set.seed(2025) tree_sample <- phangorn::rNNI(tree, moves = 4, n = 100) tree_sample <- lapply(tree_sample, function(t) { t$edge.length <- t$edge.length * rlnorm(length(t$edge.length), 0, 0.25); t }) class(tree_sample) <- "multiPhylo" gls_bm <- function(tr, y, x) { # fast BM GLS via whitening Wt <- chol(solve(vcv(tr)[names(y), names(y)])) f <- lm(Wt %*% y ~ Wt %*% cbind(1, x) - 1) coef(summary(f))[2, 1:2] } y_c <- setNames(langs$complexity, tips); x_c <- setNames(langs$logpop, tips) est <- t(sapply(tree_sample, gls_bm, y = y_c, x = x_c)) M <- nrow(est) pooled <- mean(est[, 1]) total_se <- sqrt(mean(est[, 2]^2) + (1 + 1 / M) * var(est[, 1])) mcc_s <- phangorn::maxCladeCred(tree_sample) tab_unc <- rbind(true_tree = gls_bm(tree, y_c, x_c), MCC_tree = gls_bm(mcc_s, y_c, x_c), over_trees = c(pooled, total_se)) cbind(tab_unc, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(tab_unc[, 1] / tab_unc[, 2]))) #> Estimate Std. Error p #> true_tree -0.3416 0.1406 0.01510 #> MCC_tree -0.2660 0.1401 0.05752 #> over_trees -0.3369 0.1470 0.02192 hist(est[, 1], breaks = 20, col = "grey80", border = "white", main = "", xlab = "PGLS slope (Brownian motion)") abline(v = tab_unc["true_tree", 1], lty = 2) abline(v = tab_unc["MCC_tree", 1], col = "red", lwd = 2) abline(v = pooled, lwd = 2) Figure 13.7: Distribution of PGLS slope estimates for complexity on log population across 100 trees representing phylogenetic uncertainty. The dashed line marks the estimate on the true tree, the red line the estimate on the MCC tree, and the solid black line the pooled estimate. In this example the topological and branch-length uncertainty is moderate, so the slope estimates vary somewhat across trees, and the pooled standard error is somewhat larger than that of a single-tree analysis. The MCC tree gives just one of the slopes in the histogram (here -0.27, against a pooled estimate of -0.34), with a standard error that reflects none of their spread. In this replicate the MCC tree happens to lie in the tail of the distribution, and its \(p\)-value falls on the other side of the conventional threshold from the pooled one. The direction of the error is a matter of chance: on another sample the MCC tree could just as well make a weak result look strong. With real posterior samples the variation can be much larger, particularly when the deep structure of a family is uncertain. Pooling is also a diagnostic. If the estimates on different trees disagree in sign, the data do not support a conclusion about the association whatever the pooled \(p\)-value says, and the trees on which the result depends deserve inspection. 13.12.2 Global analyses on Glottolog topologies with arbitrary branch lengths Typological questions are often global, and no dated phylogeny covers all the world’s languages. The usual workaround is to take the classification in Glottolog (Hammarström et al. 2024), convert it to a tree, and assign arbitrary branch lengths. Common choices are to make all branches equal in length, or to use Grafen’s method (Grafen 1989), in which a node’s height is proportional to the number of tips below it, minus one, raised to a power. Families are then joined at a root, either as a “star” or under a deep node of arbitrary age. This produces a usable covariance structure, but its consequences need to be understood: Glottolog classifications are topologies, often with many polytomies, and they reflect the uneven state of comparative research. Well-studied families have deep, detailed subgrouping, while poorly studied ones are flat. The covariance structure therefore partly encodes the history of scholarship, and the same is true of the cognate-based trees used elsewhere, whose cognate judgments come from the comparative method. With arbitrary branch lengths, rates and transition probabilities are in arbitrary units, and the strength of phylogenetic signal depends on the branch-length scheme. Joining families at a common root implies covariance among them, unless the families are treated as independent (block-diagonal \(\mathbf{C}\)). A star of families is usually the more defensible choice, because relationships among families are by definition not demonstrated. Equal branch lengths treat every split as equally deep. Grafen’s method makes large clades deep and small ones shallow, which is closer to what dated trees usually show but has no historical basis for any particular family. Three strategies reduce the arbitrariness. The first is to let the data adjust the branch lengths through a transformation estimated jointly with the model (\(\lambda\), \(\kappa\) or \(\delta\); Section 13.3.4). The second is to replace the topology of individual families by dated trees where they exist (Chapter 10), stitched into the global structure. The third is to use global phylogenies estimated from lexical data, such as those of Jäger (2018), which used ASJP word lists with Glottolog constraints and give data-driven branch lengths, at the cost of strong modeling assumptions. Whichever option is chosen, sensitivity analyses across branch-length schemes are essential. The code below estimates \(\lambda\) for the BM trait simulated earlier, first on the true tree, then on several “Glottolog-like” versions of it, with short internal branches collapsed into polytomies and branch lengths replaced by arbitrary schemes. glotto <- di2multi(tree, tol = 0.25) # collapse short branches glotto$edge.length <- NULL # keep topology only schemes <- list( true = tree, equal_branches = compute.brlen(glotto, 1), grafen_1 = compute.brlen(glotto, method = "Grafen", power = 1), grafen_0.5 = compute.brlen(glotto, method = "Grafen", power = 0.5)) brlen_tab <- t(sapply(schemes, function(tr) { ps <- phylosig(tr, x_bm[tips], method = "lambda") c(internal_nodes = tr$Nnode, lambda = ps$lambda, logL = ps$logL) })) knitr::kable(brlen_tab, digits = 2, caption = "Pagel's lambda for the same simulated trait estimated on the true tree and on topology-only trees with arbitrary branch lengths.") Table 13.5: Pagel’s lambda for the same simulated trait estimated on the true tree and on topology-only trees with arbitrary branch lengths. internal_nodes lambda logL true 59 1.01 -99.72 equal_branches 48 1.00 -110.61 grafen_1 48 0.84 -112.91 grafen_0.5 48 1.03 -110.70 The estimates of \(\lambda\) and the log-likelihoods differ among branch-length schemes, even though the trait and the topology (apart from the collapsed branches) are the same. Polytomies themselves are not a problem for GLS, since a polytomy is just a block of equal covariances. But arbitrary branch lengths change the relative weight of shallow and deep structure, and so they change both the estimated signal and the effective sample size. The consequences for a regression are shown next: the PGLS of complexity on log population, with \(\lambda\) estimated, on each scheme. brlen_pgls <- t(sapply(schemes, function(tr) { f <- phylolm(complexity ~ logpop, data = langs, phy = tr, model = "lambda") cf <- summary(f)$coefficients c(slope = cf["logpop", "Estimate"], se = cf["logpop", "StdErr"], p = cf["logpop", "p.value"], lambda = f$optpar) })) round(brlen_pgls, 3) #> slope se p lambda #> true -0.262 0.127 0.044 0.812 #> equal_branches -0.241 0.133 0.076 0.933 #> grafen_1 -0.244 0.142 0.093 0.826 #> grafen_0.5 -0.250 0.139 0.076 0.854 The slope is similar on every scheme, but its standard error and \(p\)-value move enough that a conventional significance threshold is crossed on some schemes and not on others. A result that holds on one branch-length scheme only should be reported as fragile. 13.12.3 Data issues Several practical issues recur in comparative analyses of linguistic data: Matching. Language names, ISO 639-3 codes and Glottocodes must be matched between the trait database and the tree. Dialects and closely related varieties may map onto one tip or several. Missing data. WALS is famously sparse: most features are coded for a minority of languages. Dropping languages with missing values is simple, but it is unbiased only if the data are missing at random with respect to the variables of interest. Data are often missing for poorly documented languages, which tend to be small and spoken in particular regions. Phylogenetic imputation, which predicts missing values from relatives, is possible within Bayesian PGLMMs. It should be reported as such. Coding. Multistate features are often collapsed to binary ones. Categories such as “no dominant order” or “both orders” must be handled consistently. Results can depend on these choices, which should be decided before the analysis and checked for sensitivity afterward. Sample composition. Large families dominate, and isolates and small families contribute little information about rates of change, however well the model handles dependence. A global analysis can be driven by a few families. Reporting family-level results alongside the global ones helps reveal this (Section 13.2). 13.13 Pitfalls We end with a list of common errors, many of them illustrated earlier in this chapter. Ignoring phylogeny. Ordinary regressions and contingency tests on samples of related languages give inflated false positive rates (Figure 13.2). Genus-based sampling helps but does not eliminate the problem. Confusing languages with information. Sixty languages may be worth a handful of independent observations (Section 13.2). Compute the effective sample size and count the independent changes in the predictor. Testing the variables instead of the residuals. The need for phylogenetic correction depends on the residuals of the model, not on the phylogenetic signal in the response or predictor alone (Revell 2010). Estimate \(\lambda\) jointly with the regression. Counting events as if they were languages. A significant Pagel test or PGLS can rest on one or two historical events, such as a single deep split (Maddison and FitzJohn 2015; Uyeda et al. 2018). Report the number of independent origins, inspect the data on the tree, and do a sensitivity analysis that drops large clades. Treating the tree as known. Integrate over a sample of trees and pool the results, or at least check robustness across a few plausible trees; do not rely on the MCC tree alone. Arbitrary branch lengths. Results on Glottolog-style trees depend on the branch-length scheme. Analyze several schemes and report all of them. Ignoring contact. A tree models descent only. Areal diffusion is a second source of non-independence that phylogenetic models do not address. Add spatial components, area random effects, or at least check whether residuals are spatially autocorrelated. Over-interpreting model parameters. A preference for OU does not demonstrate stabilizing selection (Cooper et al. 2016). A high \(\lambda\) does not demonstrate slow change (Revell et al. 2008). A dependent model in Pagel’s test does not demonstrate a functional link. Confusing correlation with causation. Phylogenetic control removes one confounder (Table 13.4). Causal claims about environment and language need multiple lines of evidence (Roberts 2018). Lack of power. Within single families, features often vary little, and failure to reject independence says little about the absence of a dependency. Simulate data under the alternative to estimate power before interpreting a null result. Forking paths. With many features, codings, trees and model variants, some combination will be “significant.” Pre-register analyses where possible, correct for multiple comparisons, and report all analyses performed. Galton’s problem, the non-independence of related and neighboring languages, inflates false positive rates of naive cross-linguistic tests, often dramatically. Sampling one language per genus reduces but does not remove the problem. Phylogenetic methods change the purpose of sampling rather than removing it. The information in a sample is measured by its effective sample size and by the number of independent changes in the predictor, which can be far smaller than the number of languages. Gaussian phylogenetic comparative methods rest on a covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) derived from the tree under Brownian motion. OU, early-burst and Pagel’s \(\lambda\), \(\kappa\) and \(\delta\) models modify \(\mathbf{C}\) in interpretable ways. Phylogenetic signal (\(\lambda\), \(K\), Moran’s I, \(D\)) measures how strongly related languages resemble each other. It is a pattern, not a rate, and it should be estimated on residuals when the goal is regression. Independent contrasts and PGLS are equivalent under Brownian motion. PGLS generalizes to multiple predictors, estimated \(\lambda\) and other covariance structures. Pagel’s 1994 test compares independent and dependent four-state Markov models for pairs of binary features. It describes the dynamics of coupled change, but it can be driven by single events. Dunn et al. (2011) found lineage-specific word-order dependencies in four families. The responses stressed limited power within families and the need for models that pool information across them. Later global analyses found support for a number of classical correlations. Phylogenetic logistic regression, PGLMMs (MCMCglmm, brms) and threshold models extend phylogenetic regression to binary and other non-Gaussian responses. Spatiophylogenetic models add a spatial component, as in the Grambank analyses. Phylogenetic control removes the confounding represented by the tree, and nothing else. Contact, non-inherited environment, single events, selective documentation and reverse causation need their own designs; causal claims require multiple lines of evidence. Tree uncertainty and arbitrary branch lengths can move a result across a significance threshold. Repeat analyses over a sample of trees and several branch-length schemes, and pool with Rubin’s rules. 13.14 Exercises Conceptual Explain the two faces of Galton’s problem with a linguistic example of each, and say which face genealogical stratification addresses and which it does not. Explain why a significant Pagel test can arise from a single historical event, and describe two analyses that would reveal whether this has happened. Why does joining all families under a common root in a Glottolog-based tree imply something about their history? When would a block-diagonal covariance be preferable? Choose one environmental claim reviewed in Section 13.11 and design a multi-pronged test in the spirit of Roberts (2018), combining a comparative analysis with at least one other kind of evidence. 13.15 Further reading Harvey and Pagel (1991), The Comparative Method in Evolutionary Biology. The classic statement of the problem and its early solutions. It is still the best conceptual introduction to why comparative data need phylogenies. Harmon (2019), Phylogenetic Comparative Methods: Learning from Trees. A free, rigorous textbook covering BM, OU, discrete characters and diversification models, with clear derivations. Revell and Harmon (2022), Phylogenetic Comparative Methods in R. A hands-on guide by the author of phytools, covering nearly every method in this chapter with code.
