In cophylogenetic terms, the population tree is the host and the language tree is the parasite. Cospeciation corresponds to a population and its language splitting together; host switching corresponds to language shift, in which a population adopts the language of another; duplication corresponds to a language split without a corresponding genetic split; and loss corresponds to the disappearance of a lineage’s language without trace. Studies comparing genetic and linguistic relationships, such as that of Hunley et al. (2008) for Northern Island Melanesia and the global analysis of Barbieri et al. (2022), have documented both concordance and frequent mismatches. We simulate a language tree for 12 populations, derive a genetic tree that mostly follows it but differs by two random local rearrangements, and then introduce two language shifts: populations PopB and PopK each adopt the other’s language. ParaFit tests the global congruence of the two trees, and its per-link statistics can flag the associations that contribute least to it. Because the shifts are built into the simulation, this is a parameter-recovery exercise for the test, not evidence that it works on real populations. set.seed(1605) lang_tree <- pbtree(n = 12, scale = 1, tip.label = paste0("Lang", LETTERS[1:12])) gene_tree <- lang_tree gene_tree$tip.label <- sub("Lang", "Pop", gene_tree$tip.label) gene_tree <- rNNI(gene_tree, moves = 2) # genetic noise and admixture links <- cbind(gene_tree$tip.label, sub("Pop", "Lang", gene_tree$tip.label)) links[links[, 1] == "PopB", 2] <- "LangK" # language shifts links[links[, 1] == "PopK", 2] <- "LangB" A <- unclass(table(factor(links[, 1], levels = gene_tree$tip.label), factor(links[, 2], levels = lang_tree$tip.label))) pf <- parafit(cophenetic(gene_tree), cophenetic(lang_tree), A, nperm = 199, test.links = TRUE, correction = "cailliez", silent = TRUE) invisible(capture.output( cp <- cophylo(gene_tree, lang_tree, assoc = links, rotate = TRUE))) plot(cp, link.lty = "solid", link.col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.7), fsize = 0.8) Figure 16.3: Cophylogeny of a simulated population (genetic) tree, left, and a language tree, right. Lines link each population to the language it speaks. Two populations, PopB and PopK, have shifted language, producing crossing links. link_tab <- data.frame(population = rownames(A)[pf$link.table[, "Host"]], language = colnames(A)[pf$link.table[, "Parasite"]], F1 = round(pf$link.table[, "F1.stat"], 2), p = pf$link.table[, "p.F1"]) list(global_p = pf$p.global, weakest_links = head(link_tab[order(link_tab$F1), ], 4)) #> $global_p #> [1] 0.005 #> #> $weakest_links #> population language F1 p #> 2 PopB LangK 0.62 0.785 #> 11 PopK LangB 1.94 0.465 #> 8 PopH LangH 2.95 0.385 #> 12 PopL LangL 4.93 0.295 The global test indicates that the trees are more congruent than expected by chance (with 199 permutations the smallest attainable \(p\)-value is 0.005). The per-link statistics then single out the links that contribute least to the congruence, and in this simulation the two weakest links are the two simulated language shifts, PopB-LangK and PopK-LangB. With only 12 tips the individual link tests have little power, none of them is significant on its own, and in real data a link may contribute weakly because of admixture or sampling rather than language shift. Assessment: cophylogeny. Tier B; barely applied. Preserved: two genealogies linked at their tips, with events that explain mismatches. Violated: human populations exchange genes continuously, so a population “tree” is a poor summary of genetic history; language shift is often partial, so the links between populations and languages are not one-to-one; and the two trees are estimated with very different uncertainties, which event-based methods ignore unless they integrate over samples of both. What would show it works: recovery of language shifts documented historically, with event costs calibrated by simulation, and robustness of the inferred shifts across posterior samples of both trees. Research programme. Apply event-based reconciliation (with costs chosen to reflect the relative plausibility of co-divergence, language shift and loss) to paired genetic and linguistic trees for regions with good data on both, such as Island Southeast Asia and the Pacific, Africa south of the equator, or the Caucasus. Calibrate the event costs with simulation, and validate them against historically documented language shifts. Run the reconciliation over posterior samples of both trees rather than on two summary trees. The output would be explicit hypotheses of language shift, each tied to a pair of branches and a time window. Visual tanglegrams and Mantel tests between genetic and linguistic distances are common (Chapter 14), but formal event-based reconciliation of language and population trees is, to our knowledge, rare. 16.5 Question 4: Shared or lineage-specific mechanisms of feature evolution? Do grammatical features evolve under the same rules in every family, or does each lineage have its own dynamics? The question is behind the debate over word-order universals (Section 13.8): Dunn et al. (2011) found family-specific dependencies, while Jäger and Wahle (2021), with a larger sample, found that a model with the same dynamics in every lineage fitted better. Biology offers two ways of making the question sharper. One reduces many correlated features to a few latent dimensions and asks whether those dimensions, and their rates, are shared. The other treats discrete features as thresholds on continuous latent variables, so that “the same mechanism” becomes “the same correlation between liabilities”. Both turn a question about many transition rates into a question about a few interpretable parameters, which can then be allowed to vary among families in a hierarchical model and compared with a model in which they are shared. 16.5.1 Phylogenetic factor analysis and multivariate models How it works. Many traits are measured together, and their covariation partly reflects shared ancestry. Ordinary principal component analysis treats species as independent and can produce components that mainly reflect phylogenetic structure (Revell 2009). Phylogenetic factor analysis (PFA) models a matrix of traits \(\mathbf{Y}\) (species by traits) as \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{E}, \tag{16.4} \end{equation}\] where the latent factors \(\mathbf{F}\) evolve along the tree by Brownian motion, \(\mathbf{L}\) is a loading matrix linking factors to observed traits, and \(\mathbf{E}\) is residual variation (Tolkoff et al. 2018). Extensions handle discrete traits through latent liabilities and large numbers of traits efficiently (Hassler et al. 2022). The linguistic mapping. Typological databases such as Grambank and WALS record hundreds of structural features per language. Many are correlated: head-marking and dependent-marking features, word-order features, and features related to morphological complexity cluster together. Grambank analyses have combined phylogenetic and spatial controls when studying individual features and summary scores (Skirgård et al. 2023), and the question of whether typological features form a few latent dimensions has a long history. PFA would recover such dimensions while accounting for phylogeny, and it would also estimate how fast each latent dimension evolves. Fitting it separately to several families and comparing the loadings is a direct test of whether the dimensions, and hence the mechanisms that link features, are shared. Assessment: phylogenetic factor analysis. Tier B; not applied. Preserved: correlated traits evolving along a tree, with the correlation carried by a few latent factors. Violated: binary features are linked to the factors through liabilities whose Brownian motion is an assumption, not an observation; contact makes neighbouring languages similar in ways the tree does not explain, so a spatial term is needed; and Grambank features are coded with logical dependencies (a feature that only applies if another is present), which create correlations that are artefacts of coding. What would show it works: recovery of known factor structure in simulated binary data with realistic missingness and contact; stability of the loadings across families and feature subsets; and factors that predict held-out features better than a model without them. Research programme. Apply PFA, through its liability extension for binary features, to Grambank features for a family with a well-supported dated tree (Austronesian or Bantu), and ask whether the latent factors correspond to classical typological dimensions (for example, head direction or synthesis). Repeat the analysis on a second family, compare the loadings, and compare the rate of evolution of each factor with lexical rates estimated on the same tree. Fit the model over a posterior sample of trees, not a single summary tree. 16.5.2 Threshold models How it works. The threshold model of quantitative genetics, brought into phylogenetics by Felsenstein (2005) and Felsenstein (2012), treats a discrete character as the visible expression of a continuous, unobserved liability that evolves by Brownian motion along the tree. When the liability crosses a threshold, the discrete state changes. Correlated evolution between two discrete characters is modelled as correlation between their liabilities; discrete and continuous characters can be analyzed together; and ordered multistate characters correspond to several thresholds. Ancestral states can be reconstructed under the model (Revell 2014), and Bayesian implementations are available in phytools (Revell 2012). The linguistic mapping. Many typological features are coarse categorical summaries of underlying gradient properties. Basic word order is coded as a single category, but corpora show that languages differ in how rigid or flexible their orders are; a “case system” feature may summarize a gradient degree of morphological marking. The threshold model fits this situation better than a Markov model in which categories switch abruptly. It also offers an alternative to the discrete correlated-evolution test of Pagel (1994) used by Dunn et al. (2011): two word-order features would be correlated if their liabilities are correlated, with a single correlation coefficient that is easier to interpret, and easier to compare across families, than a matrix of transition rates. Chapter 13 (Section 13.9.3) shows a fit in R. Assessment: threshold models. Tier B; not applied to linguistic questions beyond illustration. Preserved: discrete states as coarse readings of a continuous variable. Violated: the liability is unobserved, so its Brownian motion is an assumption that cannot be checked directly; for features without an obvious gradient basis (presence of a grammatical category) the liability has no linguistic interpretation; and threshold models predict that change between distant categories passes through the intermediate ones, which may not hold. What would show it works: where corpus measures of the gradient property exist (for instance word-order entropy), the inferred liabilities should correlate with them, and the model should predict held-out categorical codings at least as well as Markov models. Research programme. Re-analyze the word-order features of Dunn et al. (2011) under bivariate threshold models and compare lineage-specific correlations with the results of the original discrete analysis and its critiques (Chapter 13). A hierarchical version, with family-specific correlations drawn from a shared distribution, would turn the debate over universals into an estimate of how much the correlations vary among families. A second project would use corpus-based measures of word-order entropy where available as continuous data alongside categorical codings, linking the two through the liability. 16.6 Question 5: How do languages diversify? Why do some families have thousands of languages and others a handful, and did families split faster during expansions than afterwards? These are questions about the process that generated the tree itself, which in Bayesian dating is represented only by the tree prior. Biology has a large toolkit for them, together with hard-won knowledge of how easily it misleads. A second question is how diversification proceeded: by clean splits, or by the gradual break-up of a dialect network. Answering either requires the tree to be well sampled, which motivates the last method of the section, the placement of poorly documented languages. 16.6.1 Diversification models How it works. A dated phylogeny of living species carries information about the history of speciation and extinction that produced it. The simplest model is the birth-death process: each lineage splits at rate \(\lambda\) and goes extinct at rate \(\mu\), independently of all other lineages. The net diversification rate is \(r = \lambda - \mu\) and the turnover (or relative extinction) is \(\epsilon = \mu / \lambda\). Starting from \(n_0\) lineages, the expected number of lineages after time \(t\) grows exponentially, \[\begin{equation} E[N(t)] = n_0\, e^{(\lambda - \mu) t}. \tag{16.5} \end{equation}\] The phylogeny we observe is the reconstructed tree, which contains only lineages with living descendants. Its branching times follow a known distribution that depends on both \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), not only on their difference (Nee et al. 1994; Nee 2006). This is what makes it possible, in principle, to estimate extinction from a tree of living species: lineages that arose recently have had less time to go extinct, so with \(\mu > 0\) the reconstructed tree shows an excess of recent branching, the “pull of the present”. A lineages-through-time (LTT) plot, the number of lineages in the reconstructed tree against time on a logarithmic scale, makes this visible. Under a pure-birth (Yule) process the expected LTT plot is a straight line; extinction bends it upward near the present; a slowdown of diversification, as might occur when a radiation fills available space, bends it downward. The \(\gamma\) statistic of Pybus and Harvey (2000) summarizes the shape: negative values indicate that internal nodes are concentrated toward the root (early bursts or slowdowns), positive values that they are concentrated toward the tips. Many extensions exist (Morlon 2014). Time-varying models let \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) change through time, for example in piecewise-constant intervals, as in the birth-death skyline (Stadler et al. 2013). Lineage-varying models let rates differ among clades: BAMM (Rabosky 2014) identifies discrete rate shifts on the tree, while ClaDS (Maliet et al. 2019) lets every lineage inherit a slightly perturbed rate from its parent. State-dependent speciation and extinction (SSE) models tie rates to a character: in BiSSE (Maddison et al. 2007), species in state 0 or 1 have their own \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), and transitions between states occur at rates \(q_{01}\) and \(q_{10}\). MuSSE generalizes to several states, GeoSSE to geographic ranges (Goldberg et al. 2011), and HiSSE (Beaulieu and O’Meara 2016) adds hidden states to distinguish genuine trait-dependent diversification from rate variation that merely happens to correlate with the trait. Most of these models are implemented in R packages such as diversitree (FitzJohn 2012). Three cautions from the biological literature are essential. First, SSE models have high false-positive rates when applied naively: with a single large clade that happens to have both a particular trait and a high diversification rate, BiSSE will often find trait-dependent diversification even if the trait is irrelevant (Rabosky and Goldberg 2015). HiSSE and character-independent null models were developed in response. Second, BAMM’s treatment of rate shifts and its priors have been criticized (Moore et al. 2016), and its results should be interpreted cautiously. Third, and most fundamentally, Louca and Pennell (2020) showed that for any tree of extant species, there are infinitely many time-varying birth-death histories that yield exactly the same likelihood. Only certain combinations of parameters (such as the “pulled” diversification rate) are identifiable from extant trees alone. Inferences of extinction rates and of the timing of rate changes from extant trees must therefore rest on strong assumptions, unless extinct lineages are sampled. Incomplete sampling is another major issue. If only some extant species are in the tree, the estimates must account for the sampling fraction (Stadler 2009). Random sampling of tips tends to remove recent nodes disproportionately, which mimics a slowdown in diversification. The linguistic mapping. The mapping is direct: a language family tree is a reconstructed tree, language splits are speciation events, and language death is extinction. Language extinction is, moreover, extremely common, both historically (most languages of the past left no descendants) and today. Diversification models could address questions such as these: Did families diversify faster during agricultural expansions than afterwards? Do island colonizations drive bursts of splitting? Are there clades with exceptionally high or low rates of language formation? Does a trait, such as a subsistence mode, a writing tradition, or a mountainous environment, affect the rates at which languages split or die? The Bayesian tree priors used in linguistic dating are themselves birth-death models (Chapter 6), so every BEAST analysis with a birth-death prior implicitly estimates \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\). These estimates are rarely reported or interpreted, and for good reason: they are sensitive to the prior, to calibrations, and to the sampling fraction. Atkinson et al. (2008) related the number of nodes on root-to-tip paths to the amount of lexical change, which is a diversification-related question but concerns rates of change rather than rates of splitting. Work on the “pulses and pauses” of Austronesian settlement (Gray et al. 2009) is also, in effect, a claim about time-varying diversification in a geographic setting. We simulate a family of 80 languages under a birth-death process with \(\lambda = 0.6\) and \(\mu = 0.3\) splits and deaths per lineage per millennium, keeping only languages that survive to the present. We then fit a birth-death model by maximum likelihood with ape::birthdeath and a pure-birth model with ape::yule. This is parameter recovery under the model’s own assumptions, with a single replicate. set.seed(1603) family <- pbtree(b = 0.6, d = 0.3, n = 80, extant.only = TRUE) root_age <- max(nodeHeights(family)) bd_fit <- birthdeath(family) yule_fit <- yule(family) eps_hat <- unname(bd_fit$para["d/b"]) r_hat <- unname(bd_fit$para["b-d"]) lambda_hat <- r_hat / (1 - eps_hat) data.frame( quantity = c("root age (millennia)", "net diversification r", "turnover mu/lambda", "lambda", "mu", "Yule lambda", "AIC birth-death", "AIC Yule"), estimate = c(root_age, r_hat, eps_hat, lambda_hat, lambda_hat * eps_hat, yule_fit$lambda, bd_fit$dev + 2 * 2, -2 * yule_fit$loglik + 2), truth = c(NA, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.3, NA, NA, NA) ) #> quantity estimate truth #> 1 root age (millennia) 9.9396 NA #> 2 net diversification r 0.2678 0.3 #> 3 turnover mu/lambda 0.6730 0.5 #> 4 lambda 0.8192 0.6 #> 5 mu 0.5513 0.3 #> 6 Yule lambda 0.4983 NA #> 7 AIC birth-death -277.0538 NA #> 8 AIC Yule -271.9175 NA The estimates are of the right order, but the individual rates are imprecise even with 80 languages and a correctly specified model; in this replicate both rates, and hence the turnover, are overestimated, and printing bd_fit shows wide profile-likelihood confidence intervals. This is typical. Net diversification is estimated much more precisely than extinction: in the vocabulary of Section 6.10, the extinction rate is identifiable under the model but barely estimable in practice from a tree of this size. sub_family <- keep.tip(family, sample(family$tip.label, 25)) op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1)) lt_full <- ltt(family, plot = FALSE) lt_sub <- ltt(sub_family, plot = FALSE) plot(lt_full$times - max(lt_full$times), lt_full$ltt, type = "s", log = "y", xlab = "Time before present (millennia)", ylab = "Lineages (log scale)", las = 1) lines(lt_sub$times - max(lt_sub$times), lt_sub$ltt, type = "s", lty = 2) # log-linear growth from 2 lineages at the root to 80 at the present lines(c(-root_age, 0), c(2, Ntip(family)), lty = 3) legend("topleft", c("80 languages", "25 sampled"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n") g_full <- replicate(100, gammaStat(pbtree(n = 80))) g_sub <- replicate(100, { tr <- pbtree(n = 80) gammaStat(keep.tip(tr, sample(tr$tip.label, 25))) }) br <- seq(floor(min(g_full, g_sub)), ceiling(max(g_full, g_sub)), by = 0.5) hist(g_full, breaks = br, col = adjustcolor("grey50", 0.5), border = "white", main = "", xlab = expression(gamma ~ "statistic"), ylim = c(0, 35), las = 1) hist(g_sub, breaks = br, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5), border = "white", add = TRUE) abline(v = -1.645, lty = 2) Figure 16.4: Left: lineages-through-time plot for the simulated 80-language family (solid) and for a random subsample of 25 languages (dashed), on a log scale. The dotted line joins 2 lineages at the root to 80 at the present: the straight line expected on this scale if lineages accumulated at a constant rate with no extinction. Right: distribution of Pybus and Harvey’s gamma statistic over 100 pure-birth trees of 80 languages, analyzed with all languages (grey) or with a random 25 languages (blue). Incomplete sampling alone pushes gamma toward negative values, mimicking a slowdown in diversification. par(op) c(gamma_full_tree = gammaStat(family), gamma_subsample = gammaStat(sub_family), prop_sig_full = mean(g_full < -1.645), prop_sig_sub = mean(g_sub < -1.645)) #> gamma_full_tree gamma_subsample prop_sig_full prop_sig_sub #> 2.5823 0.1454 0.0400 0.4300 Figure 16.4 illustrates both the pull of the present (the full tree’s LTT curve bends upward near the present, as expected with extinction) and the sampling artifact: subsampling languages flattens the recent part of the curve and makes \(\gamma\) negative, suggesting a slowdown where there was none. The right panel is a robustness test in the sense of Section 6.10: the data violate the assumption of complete sampling, and the statistic fails. Since almost every language phylogeny is a sample (many languages in a family are undocumented or omitted), this artifact is a serious concern for any linguistic diversification analysis. And because a single tree hides the uncertainty in node ages, any such statistic should be computed over a posterior sample of trees, not on one summary tree. Language samples are rarely random. Well-documented subgroups are oversampled, and analysts often choose one representative per dialect cluster, which removes shallow nodes systematically and produces an apparent slowdown in diversification toward the present. Before interpreting an LTT plot, a \(\gamma\) statistic or a fitted extinction rate for a language family, state the sampling fraction for each clade (Glottolog counts are a reasonable starting point) and use methods that account for it. Assessment: diversification models. Tier B; barely applied. Preserved: lineages that split and die. Violated: language “speciation” is gradual and often a matter of classification (Section 16.2.5), so the timing and even the number of splits depend on the lumping and splitting of varieties; extinction and sampling are not independent of traits (languages of small, unwritten communities are both more likely to die and less likely to be documented); and the extant-tree non-identifiability of Louca and Pennell (2020) applies in full. What would show it works: recovery of simulated rate shifts under realistic, non-random sampling of tips and with dialect lumping; agreement between rate changes inferred from the tree and independently dated archaeological phases that were not used as calibrations; and, for SSE models, rejection of character-independent nulls by more than the false-positive rate found in simulation. Research programme. Fit a birth-death skyline model to a well-sampled, densely dated family, such as Austronesian or Bantu, with time intervals chosen a priori to correspond to archaeologically defined phases, and test whether splitting rates were higher during the expansion phases. Use GeoSSE with island versus mainland as a geographic state to test whether island colonization elevates splitting rates in Austronesian, using HiSSE-style hidden states and character-independent null models to guard against false positives. Throughout, specify sampling fractions per clade from Glottolog counts, report only identifiable combinations of parameters, in line with Louca and Pennell (2020), and repeat the analysis over the posterior sample of trees. A complementary project would use dated ancient languages as sampled extinct lineages (Section 16.3.2), which improves the identifiability of extinction. 16.6.2 Phylodynamics How it works. Phylodynamics is the study of how epidemiological, ecological and evolutionary processes jointly shape pathogen phylogenies (Grenfell et al. 2004; Volz et al. 2013). Its core insight is that the shape of a dated phylogeny reflects the population dynamics of the organisms it describes. Coalescent-based methods estimate the history of effective population size: the Bayesian skyline (Drummond et al. 2005), skyride (Minin et al. 2008) and skygrid (Gill et al. 2013) reconstruct \(N_e(t)\) as a piecewise or smooth function by relating the rate of coalescence at each time to the population size at that time (fewer lineages coalesce per unit time in a larger population). Birth-death-based methods estimate time-varying transmission (birth), recovery (death) and sampling rates, and from these the effective reproduction number, using the birth-death skyline (Stadler et al. 2013). Structured versions estimate migration between subpopulations (Kühnert et al. 2016). The methods are implemented in BEAST 2 and BEAST X. The linguistic mapping. Two mappings are possible, at two scales. At the level of a language family, the spread of a family across a landscape resembles an epidemic spreading through a host population: lineages (languages) “infect” new territory and split, and some “recover” (die). The birth-death skyline then estimates time-varying rates of language formation and loss, as discussed above, and structured birth-death models with geographic demes could estimate rates of movement between regions in a way that is coupled to diversification, unlike the CTMC phylogeography of Chapter 11. At the level of a single language or dialect continuum, coalescent methods could, in principle, estimate the history of the “effective size” of a speech community from the genealogy of its lexical variants, if multiple idiolects or local varieties were sampled. Section 16.2.2 shows why that effective size would measure the speed of sorting rather than the number of speakers. Assessment: phylodynamics. Tier B for structured birth-death models of family expansion; tier C for coalescent skylines of speech communities. Not applied in the formal sense. Preserved: lineages that branch, move and die at rates that change through time. Violated: languages are sampled by documentation, not at random through time; the coalescent effective size of a speech community is not a population size (Table 16.1); and token genealogies cannot be read off word lists. What would show it works: for family-level models, agreement of inferred rate changes with archaeological proxies that were not used as calibrations; for community-level skylines, recovery of known demographic histories (for instance documented immigration into a city) from densely sampled sociolinguistic data. Research programme. Treat a densely sampled expansion (Bantu is the obvious candidate, given its large datasets and archaeological record) with a structured birth-death model in which geographic regions (for instance, rainforest versus savanna) are demes, and ask whether rates of splitting and of movement between regions differed. The results could be compared directly with archaeological proxies for population growth, such as summed radiocarbon date distributions, providing an independent test. The pulses-and-pauses analysis of Austronesian (Gray et al. 2009) and phylogeographic work on Bantu share the spirit of this proposal without its formal model. 16.6.3 Simulation-based inference: ABC and deep learning How it works. Some models are easy to simulate from but have likelihoods that are impossible to compute, for instance agent-based models of speakers in space, models of borrowing on a dynamic contact network, or the token model of Section 16.2.2 with social biases. Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) avoids the likelihood: draw parameters \(\theta\) from the prior, simulate a dataset \(D^{\text{sim}}\), compute summary statistics \(S(\cdot)\), and accept \(\theta\) if \[\begin{equation} \rho\big(S(D^{\text{sim}}), S(D)\big) < \varepsilon \tag{16.6} \end{equation}\] for a distance \(\rho\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\). The accepted values approximate the posterior (Beaumont et al. 2002; Csilléry et al. 2010). The quality of the approximation depends critically on the choice of summary statistics. Deep learning offers a way to learn summaries, or to bypass them. Neural networks trained on simulated alignments can infer quartet topologies (Suvorov et al. 2020; Zou et al. 2020), and networks trained on simulated trees can estimate epidemiological and diversification parameters from tree shape (Voznica et al. 2022; Lambert et al. 2023). The trained network then acts as a fast amortized estimator: once trained, it can be applied to many datasets at negligible cost. The linguistic mapping. Simulation-based inference fits language data well in situations where the generative process is understood but the likelihood is intractable. Examples include the wave model, in which innovations spread over overlapping areas of a dialect continuum; models in which borrowing probability depends on geographic distance and population size; and models combining language splits with demographic processes. Deep learning has been used in computational historical linguistics mainly for cognate detection rather than tree inference (for example, Rama 2016). Assessment: simulation-based inference. Tier B for ABC with explicit process models; tier C for deep-learning estimators trained on simulated language data. Barely applied. Preserved: whatever the simulator assumes; the method imposes no likelihood. At risk: everything rests on the simulator, so the inference is only as good as the model of tree-like or wave-like change it encodes; summaries chosen for convenience may discard the information that separates the hypotheses; and a network trained on simulations will confidently classify real data that resemble none of them. What would show it works: calibration of posterior intervals on held-out simulations, classification accuracy on simulations from models not used in training (a robustness test), and correct classification of families whose mode of diversification is known historically. Research programme. Use ABC or a neural classifier to decide between tree-like and wave-like diversification for a given dataset. Simulate cognate data under a tree model with varying borrowing rates and under a spatially explicit wave model of overlapping innovations, compute summaries (delta scores, Q-residuals, the shape of the split network, the \(D\) statistics of Section 16.4.1), and train a classifier or ABC procedure to identify which process generated the data and with what parameters. Validate it on simulated data and on families where historical evidence about the mode of diversification exists, such as Oceanic linkages (François 2015) or Romance. A second project would fit the token model itself by ABC to datasets that record synonyms, estimating innovation rates and the strength of conformity from the distribution of synonyms per meaning. 16.6.4 Phylogenetic placement How it works. When a reference tree for a group of organisms is well established and a new sequence (often a short environmental read) needs to be classified, re-inferring the whole tree is wasteful. Phylogenetic placement holds the reference tree fixed and evaluates the likelihood of attaching the new sequence to each branch. pplacer (Matsen et al. 2010) and the evolutionary placement algorithm EPA and its successor EPA-ng (Berger et al. 2011; Barbera et al. 2019) do this efficiently for millions of sequences. For each branch \(e\), the method optimizes the attachment position and the length of the pendant branch, and converts the resulting likelihoods \(L_e\) into likelihood weight ratios, \[\begin{equation} w_e = \frac{L_e}{\sum_{e'} L_{e'}}, \tag{16.7} \end{equation}\] which express how confidently the new sequence can be placed. A spread of weight across several neighbouring branches signals that the data cannot pin down the placement. The linguistic mapping. Many languages are known only from short word lists: in archival materials, in the notes of early explorers, or in recent but brief documentation. Others are extinct and known from a handful of glosses. Glottolog lists a number of languages as unclassified, and many more have classifications based on limited evidence. Placement offers a principled way to classify such languages onto a reference tree inferred from well-documented relatives, with an explicit measure of uncertainty. For diversification analyses it is also a way to raise the sampling fraction. And it scales: global lexical datasets such as ASJP (Jäger 2018) could be extended by placing new lists on a fixed tree without re-running a global analysis. We simulate binary cognate data for 13 languages, delete 85% of the data for one of them (the “query” language, as if it were known only from a short list), infer a reference tree from the other 12 languages by maximum likelihood, and then place the query on each branch in turn. The data follow the placement model exactly, so this is parameter recovery; it shows what the method can do, not that it works on archival word lists. set.seed(1604) full13 <- pbtree(n = 13, scale = 1, tip.label = c(sprintf("L%02d", 1:12), "Query")) m13 <- as.character(simSeq(full13, l = 500, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), rate = 1.2)) m13 <- m13[, colSums(m13 == "1") > 0] m13["Query", runif(ncol(m13)) < 0.85] <- "?" # 85% missing d13 <- phyDat(m13, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?") ref_names <- setdiff(full13$tip.label, "Query") ref_fit <- optim.pml(pml(NJ(dist.hamming(subset(d13, ref_names))), subset(d13, ref_names)), optNni = TRUE, control = pml.control(trace = 0)) ref_tree <- midpoint(ref_fit$tree) # root for display only place_on_edge <- function(i, pendant = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8)) { child <- ref_tree$edge[i, 2] cand <- bind.tip(ref_tree, "Query", where = child, position = ref_tree$edge.length[i] / 2, edge.length = 0.1) q_edge <- which(cand$edge[, 2] == which(cand$tip.label == "Query")) max(sapply(pendant, function(pl) { cand$edge.length[q_edge] <- pl pml(cand, d13)$logLik })) } edge_ll <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(ref_tree$edge)), place_on_edge) lwr <- exp(edge_ll - max(edge_ll)); lwr <- lwr / sum(lwr) true_sis <- full13$tip.label[Siblings(full13, which(full13$tip.label == "Query"))] labs <- ifelse(ref_tree$tip.label %in% true_sis, paste0(ref_tree$tip.label, " *"), ref_tree$tip.label) pal <- colorRampPalette(c("grey80", "darkorange", "firebrick"))(101) shown <- ref_tree shown$tip.label <- labs plot(shown, edge.color = pal[round(100 * lwr / max(lwr)) + 1], edge.width = 1 + 6 * lwr / max(lwr), cex = 0.9, label.offset = 0.02 * max(node.depth.edgelength(shown))) add.scale.bar(cex = 0.8) Figure 16.5: Likelihood-based phylogenetic placement of a poorly documented language. The reference tree of 12 languages is fixed; edges are colored and thickened in proportion to the likelihood weight ratio of placing the query language on them. The asterisk marks the query’s true sister in the simulation. top <- order(lwr, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3] data.frame(edge_to = sapply(top, function(i) paste( ref_tree$tip.label[unlist(Descendants(ref_tree, ref_tree$edge[i, 2], "tips"))], collapse = ",")), LWR = round(lwr[top], 3)) #> edge_to LWR #> 1 L11 0.833 #> 2 L12 0.164 #> 3 L11,L12 0.002 c(observed_characters = sum(m13["Query", ] != "?"), true_sister = true_sis) #> observed_characters true_sister #> "66" "L12" With only about 15% of its characters observed, the query is still placed in the right part of the tree (Figure 16.5): almost all of the weight falls on the two branches leading to L11 and L12, which are adjacent to the true attachment point (the query’s true sister is L12). The LWRs show that the data identify the small clade but cannot fully resolve the exact attachment point, which is the honest answer given so little data. A real analysis would also optimize the attachment point along the branch and integrate over uncertainty in the reference tree; pplacer’s Bayesian mode does the latter. Assessment: phylogenetic placement. Tier B; not applied in the likelihood or Bayesian sense, although distance-based automated classification of languages from short word lists has a long history in the ASJP tradition. Preserved: the assumptions of ordinary tree inference, applied to one new tip. Violated or at risk: archival lists are not random samples of a modern word list (they over-represent salient and borrowed vocabulary), transcriptions are inconsistent, so cognate judgements are less certain; a query with many loans from one neighbour will be placed next to the donor (Section 15.4); and the reference tree is treated as known. What would show it works: a calibration study in which well-classified languages are reduced to lists of archival size and quality, placed, and scored for how often the highest-weight placement is correct, with LWRs that are calibrated (placements with weight 0.9 correct about 90% of the time). Research programme. Build reference trees for several large families from Lexibank data, and place every language that Glottolog lists as unclassified within (or possibly within) those families, as well as archival word lists of extinct languages. Report LWRs and, crucially, run the calibration study just described before interpreting any placement. 16.7 Summary table Table 16.2 gathers the assessments. “Question” refers to the five sections of this chapter, “tier” to the classification of Section 16.1, and the last two columns give the assumption most likely to fail for language data and the kind of evidence that would show the adaptation works. And every row of the last-but-one column asks for more than parameter recovery: the validating evidence is either robustness to a specified linguistic complication or agreement with a historically documented case that the method did not use. A biological method is a stochastic model of how data arise; it transfers to language only if the mapping, the process assumptions, the available data and the identifiability of its parameters all survive. We classify methods as established in linguistics (A), plausible extensions (B) or speculative analogies (C). In an explicit model of lexical transmission, a concept-level genealogy is the copying history of word tokens, and cognate classes are the partition induced by innovations on it. Under neutral, exchangeable copying without borrowing, the genealogy of one token per language approximates the multispecies coalescent; conformity, prestige, selection, dialect structure and borrowing break the approximation in different ways. The symmetry of discordant patterns, the basis of the lexical \(D\) statistic, survives most social biases but not borrowing or ancestral dialect structure. The amount of discordance does not survive them, so coalescent “population sizes” of speech communities measure the speed of sorting, not numbers of speakers. Rates of change are best informed by dated ancient languages, sound-level models and adequacy checks; under neutral copying the replacement rate equals the innovation rate, independent of community size. Network coalescent models, reconciliation, clustering and cophylogeny follow the genealogies of concepts, word families, feature profiles and populations through borrowing and language shift. Diversification models are directly applicable in form but suffer from non-identifiability of extinction, false positives and strong sensitivity to the non-random sampling of languages. Every proposal needs validation beyond parameter recovery: robustness under realistic misspecification, empirical adequacy and agreement with documented histories. 16.8 Exercises Conceptual Latin ignis and Sanskrit agní- continue the same Proto-Indo-European word for ‘fire’. In the placement simulation, vary the proportion of missing characters for the query from 50% to 95%, and record the likelihood weight ratio of the edge leading to the true sister. Over 50 replicates per level, are placements with a weight above 0.8 correct about 80% of the time or more? Research You suspect that some conflict in a Bantu lexical dataset reflects sorting of ancestral synonymy rather than contact. Design a study: what data you would need (for example, synonyms recorded per meaning, or several varieties per language), which simulations you would run under the token model (which biases, which borrowing scenarios), which statistics you would compute, and what result would persuade a sceptic. A colleague proposes to use GeoSSE to test whether mountainous terrain slows language splitting in the Caucasus. Identify the threats to validity (lumping of varieties, non-random sampling, extinction, contact, tree uncertainty) and justify each modelling choice you would make, including the null models and the treatment of the posterior sample of trees. Propose an adaptation of DTL reconciliation for Romance word families, in which Latin learned borrowings coexist with inherited reflexes (French frêle and fragile). Define the events of the model, say which assumptions of the biological method fail, and describe the validation data you would use. 16.9 Further reading Degnan and Rosenberg (2009): A clear review of gene-tree discordance and the multispecies coalescent; read it with the “fire” example of this chapter in mind. Reali and Griffiths (2010) and Newberry et al. (2017). Two complementary ways of treating linguistic variants as alleles, one theoretical and one empirical. Baxter et al. (2006) and Blythe and Croft (2012). Explicit models of variant competition in a speech community, and the case that documented changes require selection as well as drift; the starting point for any coalescent theory of words. Morlon (2014): An accessible review of diversification methods; pair it with Louca and Pennell (2020) on the limits of what extant trees can tell us. Rabosky and Goldberg (2015): Essential reading before running any state-dependent diversification analysis. Szöllősi, Tannier, et al. (2013): The probabilistic reconciliation framework for transfers, including transfers from unsampled lineages, which has close analogues in borrowing from extinct languages. Bouchard-Côté et al. (2013): The most ambitious sequence-level model of sound change applied to a whole language family. Heath et al. (2014) and Gavryushkina et al. (2014). The fossilized birth-death process and sampled ancestors, the framework behind current treatments of ancient languages. Brown and Thomson (2018): A review of model adequacy testing that translates directly to cognate data. Matsen et al. (2010): The standard reference for likelihood and Bayesian phylogenetic placement. Reesink et al. (2009): A model for how to transfer a population-genetic method to language data with an explicit justification. References

Chapter 17 A Complete Workflow in R The previous chapters introduced the methods of linguistic phylogenetics one at a time. A real study has to chain them together. Every stage, from the word list to the published tree and the comparative analysis built on it, takes the output of the stage before and inherits its assumptions. This chapter asks how the pieces fit into one reproducible pipeline, and how one can tell whether that pipeline works. We first run it on a simulated family of 24 languages, where the true tree is known and every estimate can be scored against it. We then run it on real Polynesian data, where the answer is not known and the data are far less tidy. Along the way we prepare input files for MrBayes, BEAST 2, BEASTling and RevBayes, read the stored output of runs of those programs, and carry tree uncertainty into a downstream analysis. Every chunk of R code that is not marked as illustrative runs as printed, in well under a minute. After reading this chapter you should be able to: turn a long-format cognate table into a binary presence/absence matrix, scoring unrecorded meanings as missing, and explain the character dependencies and the ascertainment bias that this coding creates; infer distance, parsimony and maximum-likelihood trees with phangorn, compare binary models by AIC, and score each tree against a known tree with the normalized Robinson-Foulds distance; export a matrix as NEXUS, PHYLIP and a BEAST 2 data block, and identify the parts of MrBayes, BEAST 2, BEASTling and RevBayes input files; read posterior tree samples and parameter logs into R, check convergence with ESS and PSRF, and summarize the trees as MCC trees, consensus trees and DensiTree plots; repeat a comparative analysis over a posterior sample of trees, and explain why a single summary tree can distort the result; build a character matrix from a real CLDF dataset, with explicit decisions about reconstructions, loans and language identifiers; state which kind of validation (Section 6.10) each analysis in the chapter provides, and explain why agreement with expert subgroups is not independent validation. 17.1 The shape of a phylogenetic project A phylogenetic analysis of a language family is a pipeline. Each stage takes the output of the previous one, and each makes assumptions that the next stage inherits. Table 17.1 lists the stages we will work through, the questions each answers, the tools we use for the toy data, and the tools one would typically use in a real study. Table 17.1: The stages of a linguistic phylogenetic analysis, with the tools used for the toy data in this chapter and typical tools for a real study. Stage Question In this chapter In a real study 1. Data assembly Which languages, which meanings, which forms? simulation Lexibank, IE-CoR, ABVD, fieldwork; Glottolog for language identity 2. Cognate coding Which forms are related by descent? known by construction expert judgment, EDICTOR, LingPy/LexStat 3. Character matrix How are cognate sets turned into characters? presence/absence coding in R R, Python (pycldf, lingpy), BEASTling 4. Exploration Is the signal tree-like? Are some languages odd? distances, delta scores, NeighborNet the same, plus SplitsTree 5. Tree inference What is the best-supported tree? UPGMA, NJ, parsimony, ML (phangorn) IQ-TREE, RAxML-NG, MrBayes, BEAST 2, RevBayes 6. Support How sure are we about each clade? nonparametric bootstrap bootstrap, UFBoot, posterior clade probabilities 7. Dating When did the splits happen? input files for MrBayes, BEAST 2, BEASTling and RevBayes; stored output of short runs relaxed clocks and calibrations in BEAST 2 or RevBayes 8. Summaries What does the sample of trees say? MCC tree, consensus, DensiTree TreeAnnotator, phangorn, ggtree, DensiTree 9. Downstream use What do the trees imply about other traits? PGLS over a tree sample BayesTraits, MCMCglmm, brms, RevBayes 10. Reporting Can someone else reproduce it? seeds, versions, files archived data and code (CLDF, Zenodo) Two features of this pipeline deserve emphasis before we begin. The first is that the most consequential decisions are made early, during data assembly and cognate coding (Chapter 3), and they are rarely revisited once the expensive inference has started. A Bayesian analysis of a large family can run for weeks. An error in a cognate judgment, or a dialect included twice under two names, will be faithfully propagated into every tree in the posterior. The second is that real projects are iterative. Exploratory analyses usually reveal problems in the data, such as a language with far too many singletons that turns out to reflect a coding error or a heavily borrowed lexicon. These problems are fixed before the main inference, and the cycle is repeated. A tidy project layout pays for itself many times over. A common arrangement keeps raw data (for example a cloned CLDF dataset) in data-raw/, derived matrices in data/, scripts numbered in the order they are run (01-build-matrix.R, 02-ml-tree.R, and so on), BEAST or RevBayes input files in analyses/, and figures in figures/. Raw data are never edited by hand: every transformation is done by a script, so the whole analysis can be rerun from scratch. The renv package can record the exact versions of the R packages used, and the git commit hash or version number of each CLDF dataset should be recorded alongside the results. 17.2 Packages and reproducibility We use ape for basic tree handling (Paradis and Schliep 2019), phangorn for distance, parsimony and likelihood inference and for summarizing tree sets (Schliep 2011), phytools for simulation and comparative methods (Revell 2012, 2024), ggtree for plotting (Yu et al. 2017), and nlme for phylogenetic generalized least squares (Pinheiro and Bates 2000). All are available from CRAN, except ggtree and its companion treeio (Wang et al. 2020), which are distributed through Bioconductor. suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(ape) library(phangorn) library(phytools) library(ggtree) library(ggplot2) library(nlme) }) set.seed(17) # every random step below depends on this seed pkgs <- c("ape", "phangorn", "phytools", "ggtree", "ggplot2", "nlme") data.frame(package = pkgs, version = vapply(pkgs, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)), ""), row.names = NULL) #> package version #> 1 ape 5.8.1 #> 2 phangorn 2.12.1 #> 3 phytools 2.5.2 #> 4 ggtree 4.2.0 #> 5 ggplot2 4.0.3 #> 6 nlme 3.1.170 Setting the random seed once, at the top of the script, makes the whole chapter reproducible: rerunning it produces exactly the same tree, data and results. In a real analysis one should also report the seeds used by external programs (BEAST 2 and MrBayes both print theirs at startup) and the versions of every program, since default priors and operators change between releases. 17.3 Step 1: Simulating a language family Why simulate at all? There are two reasons, one practical and one methodological. The practical reason is that simulated data are small, free of licensing restrictions, and available offline. The methodological reason is more important. For a real language family we never know the true tree, so we cannot tell whether a method has succeeded or failed. For simulated data we know the truth by construction, and can measure how close each method comes. Simulation studies of this kind have a long history in phylogenetics and have been used to good effect in linguistics. Barbançon et al. (2013) simulated the evolution of lexical and morphological characters on known trees, with and without borrowing, and compared the accuracy of distance, parsimony, compatibility and Bayesian methods. Greenhill et al. (2009) used simulation to ask how much borrowing it takes to mislead a Bayesian tree analysis. The workflow in this chapter is a miniature version of the same logic, with one important difference. Our simulator stays close to the assumptions of the inference models: there is a tree, there is no borrowing, and meanings evolve independently. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, Steps 4 to 9 are therefore tests of parameter recovery. They show whether the pipeline can recover a history when its assumptions hold. They are not evidence of empirical adequacy for real language data, and they say nothing about robustness under misspecification unless the simulation deliberately breaks the models’ assumptions, as Section 17.15 and the exercises suggest. 17.3.1 The tree We assume that the family diversified under a Yule (pure-birth) process (Yule 1925): each lineage splits into two at a constant rate \(\lambda\), and no lineage ever dies out. The Yule process is the simplest of the tree priors discussed in Chapter 6, and it is a common default in BEAST 2 analyses of language families. When there are \(k\) lineages, the waiting time until the next split is exponentially distributed with rate \(k\lambda\). We simulate a tree with 24 tips with phytools::pbtree() and rescale it so that the root lies 6 time units before the present. It is convenient to think of the unit as a millennium, so the family has a time depth of 6,000 years, comparable to Austronesian or Bantu (Chapter 10). n_lang <- 24 true_tree <- pbtree(b = 1, n = n_lang, scale = 6) true_tree$tip.label <- sprintf("L%02d", seq_len(n_lang)) true_tree <- reorder(true_tree, "cladewise") c(tips = Ntip(true_tree), root_age = max(node.depth.edgelength(true_tree)), ultrametric = is.ultrametric(true_tree)) #> tips root_age ultrametric #> 24 6 1 To see later whether the inferred trees recover the major subgroups of the family, we define “subgroups” as the clades descended from the lineages that were alive at a given moment in the past. Cutting the true tree 3,000 years after the root (that is, 3,000 years before the present) and collecting the descendants of each lineage alive at that time gives a set of subgroups, much as a historical linguist speaks of the primary or secondary branches of a family. subgroups_at <- function(tree, cut_time) { H <- node.depth.edgelength(tree) # distance of each node from the root e <- tree$edge crossing <- which(H[e[, 1]] < cut_time & H[e[, 2]] >= cut_time) grp <- character(Ntip(tree)) for (k in seq_along(crossing)) { desc <- getDescendants(tree, e[crossing[k], 2]) grp[desc[desc <= Ntip(tree)]] <- LETTERS[k] } setNames(grp, tree$tip.label) } subgroup <- subgroups_at(true_tree, cut_time = 3) table(subgroup) #> subgroup #> A B C D #> 12 7 1 4 Figure 17.1 shows the true tree, with time running from the root on the left to the present on the right, and with tips colored by subgroup. okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#0072B2", "#999999", "#000000", "#F0E442") sg_levels <- sort(unique(subgroup)) sg_cols <- setNames(okabe_ito[seq_along(sg_levels)], sg_levels) tip_info <- data.frame(label = names(subgroup), subgroup = subgroup) p_true <- ggtree(true_tree) %<+% tip_info + geom_tippoint(aes(color = subgroup), size = 1.6) + geom_tiplab(aes(color = subgroup), size = 3, offset = 0.08, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_color_manual(values = sg_cols, name = "Subgroup") + theme_tree2() + labs(x = "Time since the root (thousands of years)") + xlim(0, 6.6) p_true Figure 17.1: The simulated true tree of 24 languages, with a time depth of 6,000 years. Tip labels are colored by subgroup, that is, by the lineage alive 3,000 years before the present from which each language descends. 17.3.2 Lexical replacement Next we let vocabulary evolve along the tree. Our model is the simplest one that still captures the essentials of lexical change in a basic vocabulary list. Each of \(M\) meanings (concepts such as ‘hand’, ‘water’ or ‘two’) is expressed in the root language by a single word, which founds cognate class 1 for that meaning. Along each branch, the word for meaning \(m\) is replaced by a new, unrelated word at rate \(r_m\) per millennium. Replacements occur as a Poisson process, so the probability that the word survives a branch of length \(t\) unchanged is \[\begin{equation} P(\text{no replacement on a branch of length } t) = e^{-r_m t}. \tag{17.1} \end{equation}\] This is precisely the assumption of glottochronology (Swadesh 1955; Lees 1953), applied separately to each meaning and each branch. Every replacement creates a cognate class that has never existed before, so a class can be born only once and, once lost, never comes back. In the terms of Chapter 7, cognate classes evolve under a perfectly Dollo-like process with no homoplasy. Real meanings differ greatly in their rates of replacement. Words for ‘two’, ‘who’ or ‘I’ are replaced far more slowly than words for ‘dirty’ or ‘to throw’, and frequency of use is a good predictor of the difference (Pagel et al. 2007). We capture this by drawing the rate of each meaning from a gamma distribution with mean \(\bar r\) and shape \(\alpha\), \[\begin{equation} r_m \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\ \alpha / \bar r), \qquad \mathbb{E}[r_m] = \bar r, \quad \mathrm{Var}[r_m] = \bar r^2 / \alpha. \tag{17.2} \end{equation}\] With \(\alpha = 1\) the rates are exponentially distributed, so a few meanings change very fast and many change slowly. We set the mean rate to \(\bar r = 0.1\) replacements per meaning per millennium. Over a 6,000-year tree this produces a realistic mix of very stable and very unstable meanings. Finally, each language-meaning cell is deleted with a small probability, to mimic the missing data that are ubiquitous in real word lists. simulate_cognates <- function(tree, n_meanings = 110, mean_rate = 0.1, gamma_shape = 1, p_missing = 0.03) { tree <- reorder(tree, "cladewise") # parents are visited before children n_tip <- Ntip(tree) rates <- rgamma(n_meanings, shape = gamma_shape, rate = gamma_shape / mean_rate) states <- matrix(NA_integer_, n_tip + tree$Nnode, n_meanings) states[n_tip + 1, ] <- 1L # the root has class 1 for every meaning last_id <- rep(1L, n_meanings) # highest class number used so far for (i in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) { parent <- tree$edge[i, 1] child <- tree$edge[i, 2] s <- states[parent, ] k <- rpois(n_meanings, rates * tree$edge.length[i]) # replacements hit <- k > 0 last_id[hit] <- last_id[hit] + k[hit] # only the last replacement survives s[hit] <- last_id[hit] states[child, ] <- s } tips <- states[seq_len(n_tip), , drop = FALSE] concepts <- sprintf("C%03d", seq_len(n_meanings)) cog <- data.frame( Language_ID = rep(tree$tip.label, times = n_meanings), Parameter_ID = rep(concepts, each = n_tip), Cognateset_ID = paste0(rep(concepts, each = n_tip), "-", as.vector(tips)) ) keep <- runif(nrow(cog)) > p_missing # random missing data list(cognates = cog[keep, ], rates = setNames(rates, concepts)) } sim <- simulate_cognates(true_tree) cog <- sim$cognates head(cog, 8) #> Language_ID Parameter_ID Cognateset_ID #> 1 L01 C001 C001-2 #> 2 L02 C001 C001-1 #> 3 L03 C001 C001-1 #> 4 L04 C001 C001-1 #> 5 L05 C001 C001-1 #> 6 L06 C001 C001-1 #> 7 L07 C001 C001-1 #> 8 L08 C001 C001-1 The output is a long table with one row per word: a language, a meaning (Parameter_ID) and the cognate class to which the word belongs (Cognateset_ID). We have deliberately used the column names of the CLDF standard (Forkel et al. 2018), in which a Lexibank dataset stores its words in a FormTable and its cognate judgments in a CognateTable (Section 17.13). Code written for this toy table therefore works, almost unchanged, on real data. n_classes <- tapply(cog$Cognateset_ID, cog$Parameter_ID, function(x) length(unique(x))) summary(as.vector(n_classes)) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 1.00 2.00 3.00 4.04 5.00 15.00 Each meaning is now represented by between 1 and 15 cognate classes across the family. Meanings with a single class are those whose word was never replaced anywhere on the tree; meanings with many classes are the fast-evolving ones. Our simulator leaves out most of what makes real lexical data difficult. There is no borrowing, so every shared cognate reflects common descent. There are no synonyms, so each language has exactly one word per meaning. There is no semantic shift that brings an old cognate class into a new meaning, no parallel innovation, no partial cognacy, and no coding error. Real data violate all of these assumptions (Chapters 3, 8 and 15). The results below are therefore a best case. It is good practice to rerun a pipeline on simulated data that do include these complications, and to see which conclusions survive. 17.4 Step 2: From cognate table to character matrix Phylogenetic programs need a matrix of languages by characters. As discussed in Chapter 3, the dominant coding in lexical phylogenetics is binary presence/absence coding. Each cognate class becomes a character, scored 1 in the languages that have a word belonging to the class for the relevant meaning, and 0 in the languages whose word for that meaning belongs to some other class. If a language has no recorded word for the meaning at all, every character belonging to that meaning is scored as missing (?), not as absent. Getting this last point right matters: scoring an unrecorded meaning as 0 would assert that the language lacks the cognate, and would make poorly documented languages look artificially divergent. cognates_to_binary <- function(cog) { langs <- sort(unique(cog$Language_ID)) sets <- sort(unique(cog$Cognateset_ID)) set_concept <- cog$Parameter_ID[match(sets, cog$Cognateset_ID)] m <- matrix("0", length(langs), length(sets), dimnames = list(langs, sets)) m[cbind(match(cog$Language_ID, langs), match(cog$Cognateset_ID, sets))] <- "1" attested <- table(factor(cog$Language_ID, levels = langs), factor(cog$Parameter_ID, levels = unique(set_concept))) for (cc in colnames(attested)) { # unattested meaning -> all '?' absent <- attested[, cc] == 0 if (any(absent)) m[absent, set_concept == cc] <- "?" } attr(m, "concept") <- set_concept m } bin <- cognates_to_binary(cog) dim(bin) #> [1] 24 444 table(bin) #> bin #> ? 0 1 #> 306 7793 2557 The matrix has 24 languages and 444 binary characters, and about 3% of its cells are missing. Because the function uses only the three columns Language_ID, Parameter_ID and Cognateset_ID, it handles synonyms (two cognate sets for the same language and meaning) without modification: both characters are simply scored 1. It does assume that cognate set identifiers are unique across meanings; in real data it is safest to paste the meaning identifier onto the cognate set identifier, as our simulator does. It is worth looking at how the characters are distributed across the family, because the distribution determines what a phylogenetic method can learn from them. n_present <- colSums(bin == "1") table(cut(n_present, breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10, n_lang - 1, n_lang), labels = c("1 (singleton)", "2", "3-5", "6-10", paste0("11-", n_lang - 1), paste0(n_lang, " (all)")))) #> #> 1 (singleton) 2 3-5 6-10 11-23 #> 173 48 95 40 79 #> 24 (all) #> 9 About 39% of the characters are singletons, present in a single language. Singletons tell us nothing about the branching order, since they do not group any languages together, but they are informative about branch lengths: a language with many singletons has replaced much of its vocabulary since it split from its relatives. A handful of characters are present in every language; these belong to meanings whose word was never replaced. Notice what is never observed: a character that is absent from every language. A cognate class that has disappeared from every sampled language leaves no trace and cannot be coded. This is the ascertainment bias discussed in Chapter 7. It is the reason MrBayes and RevBayes offer a noabsencesites coding option and BEAST 2 analyses of cognate data include an ascertainment correction (Lewis 2001; Nicholls and Gray 2008). We return to it in Step 6. Figure 17.2 displays the whole matrix, with languages ordered as on the true tree and characters grouped by meaning. Closely related languages share long runs of identical columns. tip_order <- true_tree$tip.label[ true_tree$edge[true_tree$edge[, 2] <= n_lang, 2]] num <- matrix(match(bin[tip_order, ], c("0", "1", "?")), nrow = n_lang, dimnames = list(tip_order, colnames(bin))) op <- par(mar = c(2, 4, 1, 1)) image(t(num[n_lang:1, ]), col = c("grey92", "grey20", "#D55E00"), axes = FALSE, useRaster = TRUE) axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_lang), labels = rev(tip_order), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.6, tick = FALSE) mtext("cognate classes (grouped by meaning)", side = 1, line = 0.5, cex = 0.8) Figure 17.2: The binary cognate matrix. Rows are languages, ordered as in the true tree; columns are cognate classes, grouped by meaning. Dark cells are presences, light cells absences and orange cells missing data. par(op) Finally, we convert the character matrix into a phyDat object, the data format used by phangorn. We declare a user-defined alphabet with the two states 0 and 1, and tell phangorn that ? means “either state”. cog_data <- phyDat(bin, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?") cog_data #> 24 sequences with 444 character and 299 different site patterns. #> The states are 0 1 phangorn compresses identical columns into site patterns, which is why it reports fewer patterns than characters. All the likelihood calculations below are done once per pattern and weighted by the number of times each pattern occurs. 17.5 Step 3: Exploring the data Before inferring a tree it is wise to look at the data in ways that do not presuppose one. The most natural summary for lexical data is the lexicostatistical distance between two languages: the proportion of meanings, among those recorded for both, for which they do not share a cognate. If \(S_{ij}\) is the number of meanings for which languages \(i\) and \(j\) share a cognate and \(N_{ij}\) the number of meanings recorded for both, \[\begin{equation} d_{ij} = 1 - \frac{S_{ij}}{N_{ij}}. \tag{17.3} \end{equation}\] This is the quantity that classical lexicostatistics computed by hand (Chapter 1). It is computed directly from the long cognate table. lexical_distance <- function(cog) { langs <- sort(unique(cog$Language_ID)) n <- length(langs) D <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(langs, langs)) by_lang <- split(cog, cog$Language_ID) for (i in seq_len(n - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):n) { a <- by_lang[[langs[i]]] b <- by_lang[[langs[j]]] common <- intersect(a$Parameter_ID, b$Parameter_ID) shared <- intersect(a$Cognateset_ID[a$Parameter_ID %in% common], b$Cognateset_ID[b$Parameter_ID %in% common]) n_shared_meanings <- length(unique(sub("-[0-9]+$", "", shared))) D[i, j] <- D[j, i] <- 1 - n_shared_meanings / length(common) } as.dist(D) } D_lex <- lexical_distance(cog) summary(as.vector(D_lex)) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 0.00971 0.31719 0.47573 0.42855 0.56636 0.64583 The closest pair of languages differ in about 1% of their recorded meanings, the most distant pair in about 65%. Under the glottochronological model of Equation (17.1) with a single rate \(r\), the expected distance between two languages separated by a total path length \(T\) would be \(1 - e^{-rT}\), a curve that flattens as \(T\) grows. With rates varying among meanings it flattens even more, because the fast meanings are quickly saturated while the slow ones are still informative. This is one reason why converting lexicostatistical distances directly into dates is unreliable (Chapter 9). How tree-like are these distances? Chapter 8 introduced two diagnostics. The delta score of Holland et al. (2002) measures how far each quartet of languages departs from a perfect tree and averages over quartets. Values near 0 indicate tree-like data, and Gray et al. (2010) found considerably higher values in some language datasets than in others. A NeighborNet (Bryant and Moulton 2004) displays conflicting signal as boxes in a split network. Both are available in phangorn. round(c(mean = delta.score(cog_data, arg = "mean"), sd = delta.score(cog_data, arg = "sd")), 3) #> mean sd #> 0.128 0.199 nnet <- neighborNet(D_lex) op <- par(mar = rep(1.5, 4), xpd = NA) pn <- plot(nnet, type = "2D", show.tip.label = FALSE, edge.width = 1) net_labels(pn, nnet$tip.label, # label placement: see the appendix col = sg_cols[subgroup[nnet$tip.label]]) Figure 17.3: NeighborNet of the lexicostatistical distances, with tips colored by subgroup. Because there is no borrowing in the simulation, conflicting signal is weak and the network is close to a tree. par(op) The mean delta score is low and the network in Figure 17.3 has only small boxes, as expected for data simulated without borrowing. The residual conflict comes from short internal branches on which few or no replacements occurred, and from the random noise of a finite word list. In real data, a language that sits at the center of large boxes in a NeighborNet, or that takes part in an unusually large share of the non-tree-like quartets (the arg = "all" option returns the score of every quartet, which can be averaged per language), is a candidate for extensive borrowing or coding problems and deserves a closer look before tree inference. The figures of this chapter use two small plotting helpers: net_labels(), which places tip labels around a split network without overlaps, and support_layers(), which places support values next to the nodes of a ggtree plot. They are defined in hidden chunks, and their code is printed in Section E.3.1. 17.6 Step 4: Distance trees The quickest route from a distance matrix to a tree is a clustering algorithm (Chapter 4). UPGMA repeatedly joins the two closest clusters and assumes that distances are ultrametric, that is, that every language has changed at the same rate since the root. Neighbor-joining (Saitou and Nei 1987) relaxes this assumption and produces an unrooted tree with branch lengths that may differ among lineages. We compute both from the lexicostatistical distances, and also a neighbor-joining tree from the Hamming distances between rows of the binary matrix, the proportion of cognate characters (rather than meanings) in which two languages differ. tree_upgma <- upgma(D_lex) tree_nj <- NJ(D_lex) tree_nj_ham <- NJ(dist.hamming(cog_data)) To judge these trees we need a measure of distance from the truth. The Robinson-Foulds (RF) distance (Robinson and Foulds 1981) counts the bipartitions (splits) found in one tree but not the other (Chapter 2). For two fully resolved unrooted trees with \(n\) tips, each has \(n-3\) nontrivial splits, so the RF distance ranges from 0 to \(2(n-3)\), and dividing by this maximum gives a normalized distance between 0 (identical topologies) and 1 (no split in common): \[\begin{equation} \mathrm{RF}_{\text{norm}}(\tau_1, \tau_2) = \frac{|\Sigma(\tau_1) \,\triangle\, \Sigma(\tau_2)|}{2(n-3)}, \tag{17.4} \end{equation}\] where \(\Sigma(\tau)\) is the set of nontrivial splits of tree \(\tau\) and \(\triangle\) denotes the symmetric difference. We also count how many of the true subgroups with more than one member are recovered as clades. Since several of the methods produce unrooted trees, we ask whether each subgroup forms a clade under some rooting, which is what ape::is.monophyletic() checks for an unrooted tree. truth_unrooted <- unroot(true_tree) multi_groups <- names(which(table(subgroup) > 1)) score_tree <- function(tree) { rf <- RF.dist(unroot(tree), truth_unrooted, normalize = TRUE) groups_ok <- vapply(multi_groups, function(g) is.monophyletic(tree, names(subgroup)[subgroup == g]), logical(1)) c(RF_normalized = round(rf, 3), subgroups_recovered = sum(groups_ok), subgroups_total = length(groups_ok)) } rbind(UPGMA = score_tree(tree_upgma), `NJ (lexical)` = score_tree(tree_nj), `NJ (Hamming)` = score_tree(tree_nj_ham)) #> RF_normalized subgroups_recovered subgroups_total #> UPGMA 0.143 3 3 #> NJ (lexical) 0.238 3 3 #> NJ (Hamming) 0.238 3 3 On these data the distance methods already recover most of the true tree, including its subgroups. This is not surprising: the data were generated under a clock-like process with no borrowing, which is exactly the setting in which UPGMA’s assumptions hold. With real data, where some lineages change faster than others, UPGMA can be badly misled, and NJ is generally preferred among distance methods (Chapter 4). The remaining differences from the truth lie on the short internal branches, where few replacements happened and the data carry little information either way. 17.7 Step 5: Maximum parsimony Parsimony seeks the tree that requires the fewest changes to explain the data (Chapter 4). phangorn searches tree space with the parsimony ratchet (Nixon 1999), which alternates between searches on the original data and on randomly reweighted data in order to escape local optima. We then assign branch lengths by the ACCTRAN criterion, which places changes as close to the root as possible, and report the tree length together with the consistency index (CI) and retention index (RI), two classical measures of how much homoplasy the data contain on the tree. tree_mp <- pratchet(cog_data, trace = 0, minit = 50, all = FALSE) tree_mp <- acctran(tree_mp, cog_data) c(length = parsimony(tree_mp, cog_data), CI = round(CI(tree_mp, cog_data), 3), RI = round(RI(tree_mp, cog_data), 3)) #> length CI RI #> 560.000 0.768 0.862 score_tree(tree_mp) #> RF_normalized subgroups_recovered subgroups_total #> 0.19 3.00 3.00 The data were simulated without homoplasy, so why is the CI below 1? The answer lies in the coding. Under binary presence/absence coding, a single replacement event on one branch produces two changes: the old cognate class goes from 1 to 0, and the new class goes from 0 to 1. Moreover, a cognate class that is lost independently in two lineages (because the meaning was replaced separately in each) produces two 1-to-0 changes for the same character, which parsimony counts as homoplasy even though no cognate class was ever born twice. This dependence among the binary characters that encode a single meaning is one of the well-known costs of presence/absence coding (Chapters 7 and 15), and the stochastic Dollo models of Chapter 7 were designed with precisely this situation in mind. 17.8 Step 6: Maximum likelihood 17.8.1 Fitting and comparing models A likelihood analysis requires an explicit model of character change. For binary cognate characters, the standard choice is a two-state continuous-time Markov chain with rate matrix \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{Q} = \begin{pmatrix} -\pi_1 & \pi_1 \\ \pi_0 & -\pi_0 \end{pmatrix}, \tag{17.5} \end{equation}\] scaled so that the expected number of changes per unit branch length is 1, where \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_1\) are the stationary frequencies of absence and presence. If \(\pi_0 = \pi_1 = 1/2\) the model is the binary analogue of the Jukes-Cantor model, sometimes called the Mk model with \(k=2\) (Lewis 2001). We compare three models: equal frequencies; estimated frequencies; and estimated frequencies with gamma-distributed rate variation among characters, using four discrete rate categories. Each model is fitted with an NNI tree search starting from the NJ tree, and the models are compared by AIC (Chapter 5). ctrl <- pml.control(trace = 0) fit_start <- pml(tree_nj, cog_data) fit_mk <- optim.pml(fit_start, optNni = TRUE, control = ctrl) fit_mkf <- optim.pml(fit_mk, optNni = TRUE, optBf = TRUE, control = ctrl) fit_mkfg <- optim.pml(update(fit_mkf, k = 4), optNni = TRUE, optBf = TRUE, optGamma = TRUE, control = ctrl) model_table <- data.frame( model = c("equal frequencies", "estimated frequencies", "estimated frequencies + gamma"), logLik = sapply(list(fit_mk, fit_mkf, fit_mkfg), logLik), df = sapply(list(fit_mk, fit_mkf, fit_mkfg), function(f) attr(logLik(f), "df"))) model_table$AIC <- -2 * model_table$logLik + 2 * model_table$df model_table$dAIC <- model_table$AIC - min(model_table$AIC) model_table$logLik <- round(model_table$logLik, 1) model_table$AIC <- round(model_table$AIC, 1) model_table$dAIC <- round(model_table$dAIC, 1) knitr::kable(model_table, caption = paste( "Comparison of binary substitution models by AIC.", "The degrees of freedom include the branch lengths.")) Table 17.2: Comparison of binary substitution models by AIC. The degrees of freedom include the branch lengths. model logLik df AIC dAIC equal frequencies -2552 45 5195 198.6 estimated frequencies -2452 46 4996 0.0 estimated frequencies + gamma -2453 47 5000 3.3 best_fit <- fit_mkf round(c(pi_absent = fit_mkfg$bf[1], pi_present = fit_mkfg$bf[2], gamma_shape = fit_mkfg$shape), 3) #> pi_absent pi_present gamma_shape #> 0.753 0.247 99.999 score_tree(best_fit$tree) #> RF_normalized subgroups_recovered subgroups_total #> 0.238 3.000 3.000 Estimating the stationary frequencies improves the fit enormously, as Table 17.2 shows. This makes sense: in a presence/absence matrix most cells are 0, because each language has only one of the several cognate classes for each meaning, and a model that assumes equal frequencies of 0 and 1 is badly misspecified. The estimated frequency of presence, about 0.25, is close to the overall proportion of 1s among the non-missing cells. Adding gamma rate variation, by contrast, does not improve the fit enough to justify the extra parameter, and the gamma shape parameter is estimated to be very large (100, close to the upper bound of the optimizer). A large shape parameter means that the binary characters show little rate variation, even though we simulated strong rate variation among meanings. The reason is again the coding. A fast meaning does not produce a few fast-changing characters; it produces many cognate classes, each of which is born once and then lost, so each individual character changes only once or twice on the tree. Rate variation among meanings is thus partly converted into variation in the number of characters per meaning rather than into variation in rates among characters. Models that work at the level of meanings, such as multistate models or binary models with meaning-level partitions, address this mismatch (Chapter 7). In what follows we use the model preferred by AIC, the binary model with estimated frequencies and no rate variation, as our best-fitting model. With real cognate data, which are messier than ours, among-character rate variation is usually strongly supported. 17.8.2 Ascertainment correction The likelihoods above treat the observed characters as if they were a random sample of all possible characters, but, as noted in Step 2, a cognate class absent from every language can never be observed. phangorn implements the Lewis correction for unobservable constant characters through the argument ASC = TRUE (Lewis 2001). This corrects for the absence of both all-0 and all-1 columns, so to use it consistently we must first remove the few characters that are present in every language. Because optim.pml() in phangorn 2.12.1 did not reliably optimize branch lengths under ASC = TRUE in our tests, we use it only for the topology search and then re-optimize the branch lengths with refine_asc_edges() (Section 7.5). The frequency of presence is held at its estimate from the full matrix; in our trials optBf = TRUE did not reliably update it under the correction either, and a direct joint maximization drove it to about 0.01, close to the stochastic Dollo limit of the reversible model (Section 7.7.4), as one might expect for data in which every cognate class arises only once. constant <- apply(bin, 2, function(x) all(x[x != "?"] == "1")) bin_var <- bin[, !constant] cog_var <- phyDat(bin_var, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?") fit_asc <- optim.pml(pml(best_fit$tree, cog_var, ASC = TRUE, bf = best_fit$bf), optNni = TRUE, control = ctrl) fit_asc <- refine_asc_edges(fit_asc) # branch lengths on corrected likelihood c(constant_removed = sum(constant), logLik = round(logLik(fit_asc), 1)) #> constant_removed logLik #> 14 -2210 score_tree(fit_asc$tree) #> RF_normalized subgroups_recovered subgroups_total #> 0.238 3.000 3.000 This log-likelihood is not comparable with those of Table 17.2, because it is computed on a different dataset.
