Removing constant characters and correcting for them is the closest phangorn comes to the noabsencesites correction of MrBayes and RevBayes, which conditions only on the absence of all-0 columns. For binary cognate data the latter is the more appropriate correction, since a cognate class present in all languages is perfectly observable. Here the correction leaves the topology unchanged but shortens the tree considerably, from a total length of 1.65 to 0.97 expected changes per character: without it, the model reads the shortage of all-absent characters as evidence of change and inflates the branch lengths. In Bayesian dating analyses this matters directly, because branch lengths become inferred dates. As Chapter 7 explains, the correction can also be applied per meaning, since each meaning necessarily has at least one cognate class present in some language. 17.8.3 Rooting The binary model of Equation (17.5) is time-reversible, so the likelihood does not depend on where the root is placed, and maximum-likelihood trees are unrooted. To interpret a tree historically we must root it. With real data, the usual options are an outgroup (a language or subgroup believed to have split off first, such as Anatolian for Indo-European or the Formosan languages for Austronesian, both of which are themselves debated choices), midpoint rooting, which places the root halfway along the longest path between two tips and assumes a roughly clock-like process, or a clock model that estimates the root jointly with the tree (Chapter 9). Here we use midpoint rooting, which works well because the data were simulated under a strict clock. 17.9 Step 7: Bootstrap support and comparison with the truth The nonparametric bootstrap (Felsenstein 1985a) resamples characters with replacement to create pseudo-replicate datasets of the same size, re-estimates the tree from each, and reports for each clade of the best tree the proportion of replicate trees that contain it. We use 50 replicates, enough for illustration; published analyses typically use 100 to 1,000. Each replicate repeats the NNI search under the best-fitting model. bs_trees <- bootstrap.pml(best_fit, bs = 50, optNni = TRUE, control = ctrl) ml_tree <- plotBS(midpoint(best_fit$tree), bs_trees, type = "none", p = 0) bs_support <- as.numeric(ml_tree$node.label) if (max(bs_support, na.rm = TRUE) <= 1) bs_support <- 100 * bs_support bs_support[1] <- NA # the root has no meaningful support ml_tree$node.label <- ifelse(is.na(bs_support), "", round(bs_support)) summary(bs_support) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. NAs #> 20 53 92 79 100 100 1 Half of the internal nodes have support of at least 92%, and 10 of the 22 nodes with a support value reach 95% or more. Bootstrapping characters in a cognate matrix raises a subtle issue. The binary characters belonging to one meaning are not independent, so resampling them individually breaks up meanings and can overstate support. A more faithful scheme resamples whole meanings, with all their characters, which is straightforward to implement by resampling the Parameter_ID values of the long table and rebuilding the matrix. We leave this as an exercise; the code in Step 2 does all the work. Figure 17.4 shows the midpoint-rooted ML tree with bootstrap support at the internal nodes and tips colored by their true subgroup. p_ml <- ggtree(ml_tree) %<+% tip_info + geom_tippoint(aes(color = subgroup), size = 1.6) + geom_tiplab(aes(color = subgroup), size = 3, offset = 0.004, show.legend = FALSE) + support_layers(2.6) + # support labels: see the appendix scale_color_manual(values = sg_cols, name = "Subgroup") + theme_tree2() + labs(x = "Expected changes per character") p_ml + xlim(0, max(node.depth.edgelength(ml_tree)) * 1.15) Figure 17.4: Maximum-likelihood tree (binary model with estimated frequencies), midpoint-rooted, with bootstrap support values (percent of 50 replicates). Tip colors show the true subgroups. Branch lengths are in expected changes per character. We can now compare all the estimates with the true tree (Table 17.3). comparison <- rbind( UPGMA = score_tree(tree_upgma), `NJ (lexical distance)` = score_tree(tree_nj), `NJ (Hamming distance)` = score_tree(tree_nj_ham), `Maximum parsimony` = score_tree(tree_mp), `ML, equal frequencies` = score_tree(fit_mk$tree), `ML, estimated frequencies` = score_tree(fit_mkf$tree), `ML, frequencies + gamma` = score_tree(fit_mkfg$tree), `ML, ascertainment-corrected` = score_tree(fit_asc$tree)) knitr::kable(comparison, caption = paste( "Normalized Robinson-Foulds distances between each estimated tree and", "the true tree (0 = identical), and the number of true multi-language", "subgroups recovered as clades.")) Table 17.3: Normalized Robinson-Foulds distances between each estimated tree and the true tree (0 = identical), and the number of true multi-language subgroups recovered as clades. RF_normalized subgroups_recovered subgroups_total UPGMA 0.143 3 3 NJ (lexical distance) 0.238 3 3 NJ (Hamming distance) 0.238 3 3 Maximum parsimony 0.190 3 3 ML, equal frequencies 0.238 3 3 ML, estimated frequencies 0.238 3 3 ML, frequencies + gamma 0.238 3 3 ML, ascertainment-corrected 0.238 3 3 Two lessons from Table 17.3 generalize well beyond this toy example. First, when the data are clean and the process is close to clock-like, all methods do reasonably well and differ mainly in how they resolve the shortest internal branches. Second, the differences that remain are concentrated precisely on those branches, which are also the ones with low bootstrap support. The bootstrap is doing its job: low support flags the parts of the tree where the data are not decisive, and where different methods are free to disagree. Do not be surprised if a more sophisticated model does not win on any particular simulated dataset. The truth is a single random draw, and with only a few hundred characters the sampling error of any method is substantial. Meaningful comparisons of methods require many replicate simulations, as in the studies of Barbançon et al. (2013) and Rama et al. (2018). And all of these comparisons are parameter recovery on data that fit the methods’ assumptions closely. A method that wins here has passed the easiest test, not shown that it fits real cognate data. A tanglegram (Figure 17.5) is the most direct visual comparison of two trees: the true tree is drawn on the left, the ML tree on the right, and lines connect the same language in both. phytools rotates nodes to minimize line crossings. co <- cophylo(true_tree, ml_tree, rotate = TRUE, print = FALSE) #> Rotating nodes to optimize matching... #> Done. plot(co, fsize = 0.65, link.type = "curved", link.lwd = 1.2, link.col = adjustcolor("#0072B2", 0.6)) Figure 17.5: Tanglegram of the true tree (left) and the midpoint-rooted ML tree (right). Crossing lines indicate topological differences. Barbançon et al. (2013) carried out what remains one of the most careful simulation comparisons of phylogenetic methods for linguistic data. They simulated lexical and morphological characters on model trees, with up to three contact edges, under a range of conditions, including different degrees of deviation from a lexical clock, rate variation among characters, homoplasy and borrowing. They then compared the accuracy of six methods: UPGMA, neighbor-joining, maximum parsimony, weighted maximum parsimony, weighted maximum compatibility and the Bayesian method of Gray and Atkinson, run in MrBayes. Among their findings was that UPGMA, the method closest to classical lexicostatistics, was the least accurate, and that its error grew the most as the clock assumption was relaxed. The ranking of the unweighted methods (maximum parsimony first, then Gray and Atkinson’s method, then neighbor-joining) was remarkably consistent across conditions, whereas the performance of the weighted methods depended on the weighting scheme and the amount of homoplasy. The study is a model for how to evaluate a pipeline: simulate under conditions that match what is known about real language change, vary those conditions systematically, and measure accuracy against the known truth. 17.10 Step 8: Exporting data for Bayesian software Bayesian dating analyses with relaxed clocks, calibrations and stochastic Dollo or covarion models are rarely run in R. They are run in dedicated programs: MrBayes (Ronquist, Teslenko, et al. 2012), BEAST 2 (Bouckaert et al. 2014, 2019), RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) or TraitLab (Nicholls and Gray 2008), often with BEASTling (Maurits et al. 2017) to write the BEAST 2 input file. R is nevertheless the natural place to prepare their inputs, because the matrix, the language metadata and the calibrations already live there. In this section we write the files these programs need into a temporary directory. The external programs are not part of the book’s build. We ran each of them on exactly these files, with shorter chains than a real analysis would use, and kept the input files, a thinned copy of the output, the scripts and the run logs in the folder software-runs/ of the book’s repository. Its file run_all.sh repeats every run, and its README.md lists the program versions, run times and diagnostics. Appendix F lists where to obtain the programs. out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "workflow-export") dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE) 17.10.1 NEXUS NEXUS (Chapter 2) is the lingua franca of phylogenetic software. A NEXUS data block declares the number of taxa and characters, the data type and the symbols for missing data, followed by the matrix. Two data types are relevant for cognate data. MrBayes uses DATATYPE=RESTRICTION for binary characters, which enables its ascertainment options; most other programs read DATATYPE=STANDARD with symbols 01. It is also useful to record which characters belong to which meaning, as character sets (CHARSET), so that analyses can be partitioned by meaning or apply ascertainment correction per meaning. The following function writes both. write_nexus_binary <- function(m, file, datatype = c("restriction", "standard"), extra = NULL) { datatype <- match.arg(datatype) fmt <- if (datatype == "restriction") { "FORMAT DATATYPE=RESTRICTION MISSING=? GAP=-;" } else { "FORMAT DATATYPE=STANDARD SYMBOLS=\"01\" MISSING=? GAP=-;" } w <- max(nchar(rownames(m))) rows <- sprintf(" %-*s %s", w, rownames(m), apply(m, 1, paste, collapse = "")) concept <- attr(m, "concept") r <- rle(concept) ends <- cumsum(r$lengths) starts <- ends - r$lengths + 1 # spaces around '-': RevBayes's NEXUS reader rejects "1-4" charsets <- sprintf(" CHARSET %s = %d - %d;", r$values, starts, ends) lines <- c("#NEXUS", "", "BEGIN DATA;", sprintf(" DIMENSIONS NTAX=%d NCHAR=%d;", nrow(m), ncol(m)), paste0(" ", fmt), " MATRIX", rows, " ;", "END;", "", "BEGIN ASSUMPTIONS;", charsets, "END;") if (!is.null(extra)) lines <- c(lines, "", extra) writeLines(lines, file) invisible(file) } nexus_std <- file.path(out_dir, "toy_cognates_standard.nex") write_nexus_binary(bin, nexus_std, datatype = "standard") show_file <- function(file, n = 12, width = 72) { x <- readLines(file, n = n) x <- ifelse(nchar(x) > width, paste0(substr(x, 1, width), " ..."), x) cat(x, sep = "\n") } show_file(nexus_std) #> #NEXUS #> #> BEGIN DATA; #> DIMENSIONS NTAX=24 NCHAR=444; #> FORMAT DATATYPE=STANDARD SYMBOLS="01" MISSING=? GAP=-; #> MATRIX #> L01 01001010001000001000001001010100000000010100010001000????100010 ... #> L02 1000??100010000001000010010100010000000101000100100000100100010 ... #> L03 100010100010000000100010010100001000001001000101000000100100010 ... #> L04 100010100010000010000010010101000000001001000101000000100100010 ... #> L05 100010100010000010000010010101000000001001000??1000000100100010 ... #> L06 10001010001???????????10010101000000001001000101000000100010010 ... It is always worth reading an exported file back in to check that nothing was lost or garbled on the way. check <- read.nexus.data(nexus_std) c(languages = length(check), characters = length(check[[1]]), identical = all(sapply(names(check), function(l) all(check[[l]] == bin[l, ])))) #> languages characters identical #> 24 444 1 17.10.2 MrBayes MrBayes reads commands from a mrbayes block appended to the NEXUS file. The block below specifies a binary (restriction-site) model with stationary frequencies estimated under a flat Dirichlet prior, gamma rate variation, and the noabsencesites ascertainment correction for the unobservable all-absent characters. It sets up a relaxed clock with independent gamma rates (IGR), a uniform prior on node ages, and one calibration. Since this is a toy, we invent the calibration by pretending that subgroup D is known, from written records, to have begun to diverge within half a millennium of its true age. We generate the block in R, so the language names and the calibration are filled in automatically. calib_tips <- names(subgroup)[subgroup == "D"] calib_age <- unname(branching.times(true_tree)[ as.character(getMRCA(true_tree, calib_tips))]) mb_block <- c( "BEGIN MRBAYES;", " set autoclose=yes nowarn=yes seed=17 swapseed=17;", " [ binary model with ascertainment correction and gamma rates ]", " lset coding=noabsencesites rates=gamma ngammacat=4;", " prset statefreqpr=dirichlet(1,1);", " [ relaxed clock; time unit = 1,000 years ]", " prset brlenspr=clock:uniform clockvarpr=igr;", " prset clockratepr=lognormal(-2.3,1.0);", " prset treeagepr=uniform(3,12);", sprintf(" constraint subgroupD = %s;", paste(calib_tips, collapse = " ")), sprintf(" calibrate subgroupD = uniform(%.1f,%.1f);", max(calib_age - 0.5, 0.1), calib_age + 0.5), " prset topologypr=constraints(subgroupD) nodeagepr=calibrated;", " mcmc ngen=5000000 samplefreq=1000 printfreq=10000 nchains=4 nruns=2;", " sump relburnin=yes burninfrac=0.25;", " sumt relburnin=yes burninfrac=0.25 contype=allcompat;", "END;") nexus_mb <- file.path(out_dir, "toy_cognates_mrbayes.nex") write_nexus_binary(bin, nexus_mb, datatype = "restriction", extra = mb_block) cat(mb_block, sep = "\n") #> BEGIN MRBAYES; #> set autoclose=yes nowarn=yes seed=17 swapseed=17; #> [ binary model with ascertainment correction and gamma rates ] #> lset coding=noabsencesites rates=gamma ngammacat=4; #> prset statefreqpr=dirichlet(1,1); #> [ relaxed clock; time unit = 1,000 years ] #> prset brlenspr=clock:uniform clockvarpr=igr; #> prset clockratepr=lognormal(-2.3,1.0); #> prset treeagepr=uniform(3,12); #> constraint subgroupD = L21 L22 L23 L24; #> calibrate subgroupD = uniform(0.1,1.1); #> prset topologypr=constraints(subgroupD) nodeagepr=calibrated; #> mcmc ngen=5000000 samplefreq=1000 printfreq=10000 nchains=4 nruns=2; #> sump relburnin=yes burninfrac=0.25; #> sumt relburnin=yes burninfrac=0.25 contype=allcompat; #> END; Running mb toy_cognates_mrbayes.nex would perform two independent runs of four Metropolis-coupled chains each (Chapter 6), report the average standard deviation of split frequencies between the runs as a convergence diagnostic, and write the sampled trees to .t files and the parameters to .p files. MrBayes 3.2.9 reads the file as written; it skips the ASSUMPTIONS block, and in batch mode it exits when the block is done. For the book we shortened the run to 1 million generations with two chains per run (mcmc ngen=1000000 samplefreq=500 nchains=2 nruns=2), which took 6 to 11 minutes on one core, depending on the load of the machine. The average standard deviation of split frequencies fell to 0.006, and every PSRF was below 1.12. But the effective sample sizes of the tree height, the clock rate and the state frequencies were only 20 to 40. These parameters are strongly correlated with each other and mix slowly, which is why a real analysis needs the longer run of the block above. The priors here are placeholders. In a real analysis each would need to be justified, and the analysis rerun under alternatives to check that the conclusions do not depend on them (Chapter 15). Note in particular that constraining subgroup D to be monophyletic is a strong assumption that is only justified if the subgroup is securely established by the comparative method. 17.10.3 BEAST 2 BEAST 2 reads a single XML file that describes the data, the model, the priors, the MCMC operators and the output. The file is normally generated with the graphical program BEAUti or, for linguistic data, with BEASTling, rather than written by hand. Writing it from scratch is error-prone, because a typical file for a relaxed-clock covarion analysis runs to many hundreds of lines. It is nevertheless useful to know its structure, and to be able to generate the data part from R. Each language becomes a sequence element whose value attribute is that language’s row of the matrix. For the ascertainment correction, we put a dummy all-absent column in front of the matrix and mark it with the alignment’s ascertained, excludefrom and excludeto attributes. BEAST 2 then leaves column 0 out of the likelihood and conditions on characters not being absent from every language, the equivalent of noabsencesites in MrBayes. seq_lines <- sprintf( ' <sequence id="seq_%s" taxon="%s" totalcount="2" value="0%s"/>', rownames(bin), rownames(bin), apply(bin, 1, paste, collapse = "")) beast_data <- c(paste('<data id="cognates" spec="Alignment" dataType="binary"', 'ascertained="true" excludefrom="0" excludeto="1">'), seq_lines, "</data>") writeLines(beast_data, file.path(out_dir, "toy_cognates_beast_data.xml")) cat(substr(beast_data[1:4], 1, 72), " ...", sep = "\n") #> <data id="cognates" spec="Alignment" dataType="binary" ascertained="true #> <sequence id="seq_L01" taxon="L01" totalcount="2" value="00100101000 #> <sequence id="seq_L02" taxon="L02" totalcount="2" value="01000??1000 #> <sequence id="seq_L03" taxon="L03" totalcount="2" value="01000101000 #> ... The rest of a BEAST 2.7 file for these data specifies the restriction-site model with estimated frequencies and gamma rate variation, a strict clock, a Yule tree prior, the subgroup-D calibration and the root-age prior of the MrBayes block. The skeleton below shows how the file is organized. It has four parts: the state (everything the MCMC samples: the tree, the birth rate, the clock rate, the gamma shape and the frequencies); the posterior, the product of the priors and the likelihood; the operators, which propose new values for each part of the state; and the loggers, which write the parameter trace and the sampled trees. The full file, about 140 lines long, is software-runs/beast2/toy_beast.xml in the book’s repository, and it runs as it stands. Class names changed in BEAST 2.7, when the core packages were moved to the beast.base namespace, so XML written for BEAST 2.6 or earlier does not run in 2.7 without editing. <beast version="2.7" namespace="beast.base.core:beast.base.inference:..."> <data id="cognates" spec="Alignment" dataType="binary" ascertained="true" excludefrom="0" excludeto="1"> ... </data> <run id="mcmc" spec="MCMC" chainLength="3000000"> <state id="state"> ... </state> <!-- 1. what is sampled --> <distribution id="posterior" spec="CompoundDistribution"> <distribution id="prior" ...> ... </distribution> <!-- 2a --> <distribution id="likelihood" ...> ... </distribution> <!-- 2b --> </distribution> <operator ... /> ... <!-- 3. proposals --> <logger ... > ... </logger> <!-- 4. output files --> </run> </beast> A longer annotated excerpt of the BEAST 2.7 file, with the priors, the calibration, the substitution model and the operators written out, is in Section E.3.2. The strict clock is a StrictClockModel element inside the likelihood. For a relaxed clock it is replaced by an uncorrelated lognormal clock (UCRelaxedClockModel) or by the optimized relaxed clock of the ORC package. For a covarion model, the substitution model becomes BinaryCovarion. 17.10.4 BEASTling BEASTling (Maurits et al. 2017) was written to spare linguists the work of writing BEAST 2 XML. The user writes a short configuration file in a simple key = value format, and BEASTling generates a complete and internally consistent XML file, including ascertainment correction, rate variation among features, calibrations and monophyly constraints. Language identities can be matched to Glottolog (Hammarström et al. 2024), which allows constraints such as “keep every Glottolog subgroup monophyletic” to be stated in a single line. BEASTling reads long-format data with one row per language and feature, which is exactly what our cognate table is, so we export it with a Value column holding the cognate class. beastling_data <- data.frame(Language_ID = cog$Language_ID, Parameter_ID = cog$Parameter_ID, Value = sub("^C[0-9]+-", "", cog$Cognateset_ID)) write.csv(beastling_data, file.path(out_dir, "toy_cognates_long.csv"), row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE) head(beastling_data, 4) #> Language_ID Parameter_ID Value #> 1 L01 C001 2 #> 2 L02 C001 1 #> 3 L03 C001 1 #> 4 L04 C001 1 A configuration for a covarion analysis with a relaxed clock and one calibration might look as follows. We generate it in R so that the calibrated clade and its age range match the MrBayes block above; BEASTling expects calibration ages in years. Note the uniform() around the age range. A bare range such as 129-1129 would be read as the 95% interval of a normal distribution, not as the bounds of a uniform one. The option names below are those of BEASTling 1.5.1, the most recent release. beastling_conf <- c( "[admin]", "basename = toy_family", "", "[MCMC]", "chainlength = 10000000", "", "[model lexicon]", "model = covarion", "data = toy_cognates_long.csv", "rate_variation = True", "", "[clock default]", "type = relaxed", "", "[calibration]", sprintf("%s = uniform(%d, %d)", paste(calib_tips, collapse = ","), round(1000 * max(calib_age - 0.5, 0.1)), round(1000 * (calib_age + 0.5)))) writeLines(beastling_conf, file.path(out_dir, "toy_family.conf")) cat(beastling_conf, sep = "\n") #> [admin] #> basename = toy_family #> #> [MCMC] #> chainlength = 10000000 #> #> [model lexicon] #> model = covarion #> data = toy_cognates_long.csv #> rate_variation = True #> #> [clock default] #> type = relaxed #> #> [calibration] #> L21,L22,L23,L24 = uniform(129, 1129) Running beastling toy_family.conf writes toy_family.xml, a 775-line BEAST 2 file with one likelihood per meaning, each with its own ascertainment correction. BEASTling leaves out the meanings that have only one cognate class, since they carry no information. There is a catch. BEASTling has not been updated since version 1.5.1 (2021). It writes XML for BEAST 2.6 and does not run under Python 3.14. BEAST 2.7 cannot read the old class names (it stops with “Class could not be found”), so the file must either be run with BEAST 2.6 or have its class names translated to the 2.7 namespace. We did the latter with a short script, software-runs/beastling/beast26_to_27.py, ran BEASTling 1.5.1 under Python 3.12, and ran the converted file with beast toy_family_beast27.xml in BEAST 2.7.7, which needs the BEASTLabs package for BEASTling’s starting tree. The covarion model with a relaxed clock is much slower than the strict-clock analysis of the previous section, about 14 minutes per million states on one core, and a 500,000-state test run was far from converged (an ESS of 5 for the posterior). A real analysis of this kind needs tens of millions of states. 17.10.5 RevBayes RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) takes a different approach from BEAST 2. The model is written as a script in the Rev language, which specifies a probabilistic graphical model one variable at a time. This makes RevBayes the most flexible of the four programs: any parameter can be given any prior, and new models can be assembled from existing pieces without writing Java or C++. The script below specifies an unrooted analysis of the binary matrix under the Mk model with gamma rate variation, conditioned on variable characters (the Mkv correction of Lewis (2001)), with two independent runs. It follows the structure of the RevBayes tutorials on discrete morphological characters. The excerpt below shows the data and the model; the moves, the monitors and the summary of the tree sample are left out. # excerpt of toy_cognates.Rev (run with: rb toy_cognates.Rev) data <- concatenate(readDiscreteCharacterData("toy_cognates_standard.nex")) ... # tree prior: uniform topology, exponential branch lengths topology ~ dnUniformTopology(taxa) br_lens[i] ~ dnExponential(10.0) # in a loop over the branches phylogeny := treeAssembly(topology, br_lens) # substitution model: symmetric two-state Mk model with gamma rates Q <- fnJC(2) alpha ~ dnExponential(1.0) site_rates := fnDiscretizeGamma(alpha, alpha, 4) # likelihood, conditioned on variable characters (Mkv) seq ~ dnPhyloCTMC(tree = phylogeny, Q = Q, siteRates = site_rates, type = "Standard", coding = "variable") seq.clamp(data) ... mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 2, combine = "mixed") mymcmc.run(generations = 10000) The complete script, as it was run, is printed in Section E.3.3. Two details of the script needed care in RevBayes 1.4.1. Because the NEXUS file defines a CHARSET for each meaning, readDiscreteCharacterData() returns 110 separate matrices, one per meaning, and concatenate() joins them again. The 14 characters present in every language that records the meaning are incompatible with coding = "variable", and RevBayes drops them with a warning. The two runs of 10,000 iterations, each with about 76 moves per iteration, took 8 minutes on one core. After a 25% burn-in, every parameter had an ESS above 200 in each run, and the maximum a posteriori tree differed from the true tree in 4 of its 21 internal splits. Replacing the symmetric Mk model with an asymmetric binary model, the coding option with an ascertainment scheme suited to presence/absence data, or the unrooted tree prior with a birth-death prior and a relaxed clock, are each changes of a few lines. The RevBayes tutorials on dating, clock models and model comparison show how. An exported file is only as good as the matrix that went into it, and a Bayesian analysis is only as good as its priors. Three checks are worth making every time. First, re-import the exported file and compare it with the original matrix (as we did for the NEXUS file above). Second, run the analysis once with the data removed (BEAST 2 has a “sample from prior” option; in MrBayes use mcmc data=no; in RevBayes, simply omit the clamp) and inspect the resulting distributions of dates and rates. This prior-only run is part of implementation validation: it shows the prior that the program actually uses, which is not always the one the analyst wrote down. The marginal prior on the root age, after calibrations and tree prior have interacted, can be very different from what was intended (Chapter 10). Third, run at least two independent chains from different starting points and confirm that they agree. 17.11 Step 9: Working with posterior samples of trees A Bayesian analysis produces not one tree but a sample of thousands of trees from the posterior distribution, together with a trace of every parameter. Summarizing this sample is a task in its own right. We use the output of the complete BEAST 2 analysis of Section 17.10.3: the binary model with ascertainment correction and gamma rate variation, a strict clock, a Yule prior, the subgroup-D calibration and a uniform prior between 3,000 and 12,000 years on the root age. We ran BEAST 2.7.7 twice, with seeds 1 and 2, for 3 million states each, sampling every 2,000 states. Each run took about seven minutes on one processor core. A real analysis would run longer, but here every parameter reached an effective sample size above 500 (see below). The book’s repository keeps the two parameter logs in full and every tenth sampled tree (151 trees per run), so the code below runs offline. 17.11.1 Reading tree files and diagnosing convergence The first steps are to read the tree files, discard the burn-in (the initial part of the chain, before it reached the region of high posterior probability), and check convergence. BEAST 2 and MrBayes write trees in NEXUS format, which ape::read.nexus() reads, and parameter traces as tab-delimited text. RevBayes writes its trees as a table with one Newick tree per row, which read.tree(text = ...) can parse. beast_dir <- "software-runs/beast2" runs <- c("run1", "run2") read_trees <- function(run) { trees <- read.nexus(file.path(beast_dir, run, "toy_thinned.trees")) trees[-seq_len(floor(0.1 * length(trees)))] # discard the first 10% } posterior <- do.call(c, lapply(runs, read_trees)) read_log <- function(run) { trace <- read.table(file.path(beast_dir, run, "toy.log"), header = TRUE, comment.char = "#") trace[-seq_len(floor(0.1 * nrow(trace))), ] } traces <- lapply(runs, read_log) pars <- c("posterior", "TreeHeight", "clockRate", "freqParameter.2", "gammaShape", "mrca.age.subgroupD.") ess <- sapply(traces, function(tr) coda::effectiveSize(tr[, pars])) colnames(ess) <- runs psrf <- coda::gelman.diag(coda::mcmc.list(lapply(traces, function(tr) coda::mcmc(tr[, pars]))), autoburnin = FALSE)$psrf[, 1] round(cbind(ess, PSRF = psrf), 2) #> run1 run2 PSRF #> posterior 1351.0 1351.0 1 #> TreeHeight 1351.0 1475.2 1 #> clockRate 743.2 602.1 1 #> freqParameter.2 516.5 492.0 1 #> gammaShape 1351.0 759.8 1 #> mrca.age.subgroupD. 1332.7 1351.0 1 c(trees = length(posterior), root_age_median = median(unlist(lapply(traces, `[[`, "TreeHeight")))) #> trees root_age_median #> 272.00 3.65 Every parameter has an ESS of several hundred in each run. The potential scale reduction factor (PSRF) of Gelman and Rubin (1992) compares the variance within and between the two runs; values close to 1 indicate that they have converged to the same distribution. The posterior median of the root age, about 3,600 years, is well below the true 6,000 years. With a strict clock, the absolute dates rest on the calibrations and priors, and our one young calibration, together with the prior on the clock rate, pulls the whole tree toward the lower end of the root-age prior. This is a reminder that dates are only as good as the calibrations (Chapter 10). In the terms of Section 6.10, the absolute root age is identifiable under the model only through the calibration and the priors. With a single young calibration it is not practically estimable from these data, even though the true value lies inside the 95% interval. TreeAnnotator, distributed with BEAST 2, summarizes the tree sample as a maximum clade credibility tree (Section 17.11.2) and annotates each node with the median and 95% highest posterior density (HPD) interval of its age. We ran it on the two runs combined, after a 10% burn-in, with median node heights: treeannotator -burnin 0 -height median combined.trees toy_mcc.tree treeio reads the annotated tree, and Figure 17.6 draws the HPD intervals as bars. We draw the bars with geom_segment() from the stored interval limits. ggtree’s geom_range() gives bars of the right width, but it centers them on the node, which misplaces skewed intervals such as the root’s. mcc_beast <- treeio::read.beast(file.path(beast_dir, "toy_mcc.tree")) p_hpd <- revts(ggtree(mcc_beast)) # x axis: time before the present nodes <- subset(p_hpd$data, !isTip) hpd <- do.call(rbind, nodes$height_0.95_HPD) nodes$lower <- -hpd[, 2] nodes$upper <- -hpd[, 1] p_hpd + geom_segment(data = nodes, aes(x = lower, xend = upper, y = y, yend = y), color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 2) + geom_tiplab(size = 3, offset = 0.06) + theme_tree2() + labs(x = "Thousands of years before present") Figure 17.6: The maximum clade credibility tree from TreeAnnotator, with median node ages and 95 percent HPD intervals of node ages (bars), from the BEAST 2 analysis. The effective sample size (ESS) of a parameter estimates how many independent draws the autocorrelated MCMC sample is worth (Chapter 6). Tracer (Rambaut et al. 2018) reports it for BEAST and MrBayes logs, and the R package coda (Plummer et al. 2006) computes it from any trace. A common rule of thumb asks for an ESS of at least 200 for every parameter of interest. We can see what ESS measures with a simulated trace that starts far from its stationary distribution and is strongly autocorrelated, as an unconverged log-likelihood trace typically is (Figure 17.7). n_iter <- 2000 ar_part <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.95), n = n_iter, sd = 2)) loglik_trace <- -2400 + ar_part - 300 * exp(-(seq_len(n_iter)) / 60) burn <- seq_len(0.1 * n_iter) op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) plot(loglik_trace, type = "l", col = "grey30", xlab = "sample", ylab = "log-likelihood") rect(0, min(loglik_trace) - 10, max(burn), max(loglik_trace) + 10, col = adjustcolor("#D55E00", 0.15), border = NA) Figure 17.7: A simulated MCMC trace of the log-likelihood. The first 10 percent of the samples (shaded) are a burn-in phase that has not yet reached the stationary distribution. par(op) round(c(ESS_all = unname(coda::effectiveSize(loglik_trace)), ESS_after_burnin = unname(coda::effectiveSize(loglik_trace[-burn])))) #> ESS_all ESS_after_burnin #> 18 42 Two thousand samples are worth only a few dozen independent ones, because each sample is highly correlated with the previous one. Including the burn-in makes things look even more misleading: the trend at the start inflates the variance and distorts the estimate. The remedy for a low ESS is to run the chain longer, to thin less aggressively, or to improve the mixing with better proposals, not to report the estimates anyway. For tree topologies, which have no single numerical value, convergence is assessed by comparing split frequencies between independent runs (the ASDSF reported by MrBayes, Chapter 6) or with tools such as RWTY (Warren et al. 2017). The R package convenience (Fabreti and Höhna 2022) combines checks for continuous parameters and for splits and reports whether a run passes them, and Barido-Sottani et al. (2023) give a practical guide to diagnosing runs that do not. 17.11.2 Summary trees There is no single best way to summarize a posterior sample of trees (Chapter 2). The maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree is the tree in the sample that maximizes the product of the posterior probabilities of its clades; it is the default in BEAST’s TreeAnnotator and in phangorn’s maxCladeCred() (Heled and Bouckaert 2013). The majority-rule consensus tree contains exactly those clades found in more than half the trees, and is the default in MrBayes. Each internal node of either tree is labeled with its clade credibility, the proportion of posterior trees that contain the clade. mcc <- maxCladeCred(posterior) clade_cred <- prop.clades(mcc, posterior, rooted = TRUE) / length(posterior) mcc$node.label <- sprintf("%.2f", clade_cred) mcc$node.label[1] <- "" # the root is always present mrc <- consensus(posterior, p = 0.5, rooted = TRUE) c(MCC_internal_nodes = mcc$Nnode, consensus_internal_nodes = mrc$Nnode, MCC_RF_to_truth = RF.dist(unroot(mcc), truth_unrooted, normalize = TRUE)) #> MCC_internal_nodes consensus_internal_nodes #> 23.0000 21.0000 #> MCC_RF_to_truth #> 0.1429 The MCC tree is fully resolved, because it is one of the sampled trees, whereas the majority-rule consensus collapses every clade with support below 50% and is therefore less resolved. Which to report depends on the purpose. The MCC tree is convenient for plotting dates, but it can contain clades with very low support, and its node heights must be summarized separately (TreeAnnotator offers mean, median or common-ancestor heights; Chapter 6). Figure 17.8 shows the MCC tree with clade credibilities. p_mcc <- ggtree(mcc) %<+% tip_info + geom_tippoint(aes(color = subgroup), size = 1.6) + geom_tiplab(aes(color = subgroup), size = 3, offset = 0.08, show.legend = FALSE) + support_layers(2.5) + scale_color_manual(values = sg_cols, name = "Subgroup") + theme_tree2() revts(p_mcc) + scale_x_continuous(labels = abs, limits = c(-6.2, 0.8)) + labs(x = "Thousands of years before present") Figure 17.8: Maximum clade credibility tree of the BEAST 2 posterior sample, computed with phangorn, with clade credibilities at internal nodes and tips colored by true subgroup. The time axis is in thousands of years before the present. 17.11.3 Visualizing uncertainty A summary tree hides the uncertainty that the posterior sample expresses. A DensiTree (Bouckaert 2010) draws every tree in the sample on top of the others with transparent lines, so that well-supported parts of the tree appear as sharp, dark branches and uncertain parts as a blurred cloud (Figure 17.9). The original DensiTree program is distributed with BEAST 2; phangorn provides an R implementation. densiTree(posterior, consensus = mcc, alpha = 0.03, col = "#0072B2", cex = 0.7, type = "phylogram") Figure 17.9: DensiTree plot of the BEAST 2 posterior sample of trees. Sharp regions indicate well-supported clades and node heights; blurred regions indicate uncertainty. The sample can also be compared with the truth tree by tree. The distribution of RF distances between the posterior trees and the true tree shows how much topological uncertainty remains. rf_post <- sapply(posterior, function(tr) RF.dist(unroot(tr), truth_unrooted, normalize = TRUE)) summary(rf_post) #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 0.0476 0.1429 0.1429 0.1647 0.1905 0.2857 The stored output of the other programs can be scored in the same way. Table 17.4 compares the summary tree of each program with the true tree, using the function score_tree() of Step 4. For the two dated analyses it also gives the median root age. sr <- "software-runs" mb_con <- treeio::read.mrbayes( file.path(sr, "mrbayes", "toy_mrbayes_run.nex.con.tre")) summary_trees <- list( `MrBayes, consensus` = mb_con@phylo, `BEAST 2, MCC (TreeAnnotator)` = mcc_beast@phylo, `RevBayes, MAP tree` = read.nexus(file.path(sr, "revbayes", "output", "toy_map.tre")), `IQ-TREE, ML tree` = read.tree(file.path(sr, "iqtree", "ch17_gtr2.treefile")), `RAxML-NG, ML tree` = read.tree(file.path(sr, "raxml-ng", "ch17.raxml.bestTree"))) root_age <- function(td, col) { # median age of the root node d <- treeio::get.data(td) as.numeric(d[[col]][d$node == Ntip(td@phylo) + 1]) } programs <- data.frame(t(sapply(summary_trees, score_tree)), root_age = c(root_age(mb_con, "age_median"), root_age(mcc_beast, "height_median"), NA, NA, NA)) knitr::kable(programs, digits = 2, caption = paste( "Summary trees from the external programs compared with the true tree:", "normalized Robinson-Foulds distance, true subgroups recovered, and", "median root age in thousands of years (true value 6).")) Table 17.4: Summary trees from the external programs compared with the true tree: normalized Robinson-Foulds distance, true subgroups recovered, and median root age in thousands of years (true value 6). RF_normalized subgroups_recovered subgroups_total root_age MrBayes, consensus 0.14 3 3 4.08 BEAST 2, MCC (TreeAnnotator) 0.14 3 3 3.65 RevBayes, MAP tree 0.19 2 3 NA IQ-TREE, ML tree 0.19 3 3 NA RAxML-NG, ML tree 0.19 3 3 NA All five programs recover the same tree up to a few splits. The differences from the truth are again on the short internal branches. Agreement among programs is a weak form of implementation validation. The programs were written independently, so a gross error in one of them would show up as a disagreement. But they share models, conventions and file formats, and they did not run identical models here, so agreement cannot show that any of them is exactly right. MrBayes and BEAST 2 date the root at about 4,000 and 3,600 years, with 95% intervals that reach 7,600 and 7,000 years. Both are pulled toward the lower bound of the root-age prior, for the reason given above. 17.12 Step 10: A comparative analysis over a sample of trees Language trees are increasingly used not as ends in themselves but as scaffolds for testing hypotheses about other traits, as Chapters 13 and 14 describe. The basic problem is Galton’s problem: related languages are not independent observations, so a correlation across languages can arise from shared inheritance alone. Phylogenetic comparative methods solve this by modeling the expected covariance among languages given the tree. And since the tree is itself uncertain, a careful analysis repeats the comparative analysis over a sample of trees and reports the spread of results. We illustrate with a continuous predictor \(x\) and a continuous response \(y\). Think of \(x\) as the logarithm of the speaker population and \(y\) as some numerical typological index, although nothing hinges on the interpretation. We simulate both by Brownian motion on the true tree (Chapter 13), with a true regression slope of 0.6: \[\begin{equation} y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}), \tag{17.6} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{C}\) is the matrix of shared branch lengths between pairs of languages implied by the tree. Phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) fits this model by generalized least squares (Grafen 1989); ordinary least squares (OLS) wrongly assumes \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{I}\). set.seed(2) # a separate seed, so this section does not depend on earlier ones x <- fastBM(true_tree, sig2 = 1) y <- 0.6 * x + fastBM(true_tree, sig2 = 0.5) traits <- data.frame(lang = names(x), x = x, y = y[names(x)]) fit_ols <- lm(y ~ x, data = traits) fit_pgls_true <- gls(y ~ x, data = traits, correlation = corBrownian(1, true_tree, form = ~lang)) rbind(OLS = coef(summary(fit_ols))["x", c(1, 2, 4)], `PGLS, true tree` = coef(summary(fit_pgls_true))["x", c(1, 2, 4)]) #> Estimate Std. Error Pr(>|t|) #> OLS 0.7062 0.1791 0.000692 #> PGLS, true tree 0.5418 0.1840 0.007497 Now we repeat the PGLS on every tree in the posterior sample, as one would with a real posterior. We also estimate Pagel’s \(\lambda\) (Pagel 1999a) for the response on every tree, as a measure of phylogenetic signal (Chapter 13). pgls_one <- function(tr) { m <- try(gls(y ~ x, data = traits, correlation = corBrownian(1, tr, form = ~lang)), silent = TRUE) if (inherits(m, "try-error")) return(c(slope = NA, se = NA, p = NA)) cf <- coef(summary(m))["x", ] c(slope = cf[["Value"]], se = cf[["Std.Error"]], p = cf[["p-value"]]) } pgls_post <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(posterior, pgls_one))) lambda_post <- sapply(posterior, function(tr) phylosig(tr, setNames(traits$y, traits$lang), method = "lambda")$lambda) round(rbind( slope = quantile(pgls_post$slope, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE), lambda = quantile(lambda_post, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))), 3) #> 2.5% 50% 97.5% #> slope 0.371 0.491 0.595 #> lambda 0.999 1.007 1.018 c(share_p_below_0.05 = mean(pgls_post$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)) #> share_p_below_0.05 #> 0.9412 ggplot(pgls_post, aes(x = slope)) + geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "grey70", color = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") + geom_vline(xintercept = coef(fit_ols)[["x"]], linetype = "dotted") + geom_vline(xintercept = coef(fit_pgls_true)[["x"]]) + labs(x = "PGLS slope estimate", y = "Number of trees") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) Figure 17.10: Distribution of PGLS slope estimates across the trees of the BEAST 2 posterior sample. The dashed line is the true slope (0.6), the dotted line the OLS estimate, and the solid line the PGLS estimate on the true tree. Three things are worth noticing in these results. First, phylogenetic signal in the response is strong (\(\lambda\) close to 1 on every tree), as expected for a trait that evolves by Brownian motion, so ignoring the tree is not an option. Second, the OLS and PGLS point estimates (0.71 and 0.54 against a true value of 0.6) need not differ much in any one dataset. The main problem with OLS is that it treats the 24 languages as independent data points, whereas much of their variation is shared within subgroups. Its standard errors are therefore too small, and with phylogenetically structured data it rejects true null hypotheses far more often than its nominal error rate (Chapter 13). Third, the spread of PGLS estimates across the tree sample is a direct measure of how much phylogenetic uncertainty matters for the conclusion. Here 94% of the trees yield a significant positive slope, so the conclusion is robust to tree uncertainty. In a real study the spread is often wider, and it should be reported. This is also why a downstream analysis should not be run on the MCC tree alone. The MCC tree is one tree from the sample, with summary node heights; using it as if it were known treats every clade, including those with low credibility, as certain, and it can shift or narrow the estimate even when its topology looks plausible. A fully Bayesian alternative integrates over trees within a single analysis. BayesTraits, for example, samples a new tree from the posterior at each step of its chain (Pagel et al. 2004). Alternatively, one can fit a Bayesian phylogenetic mixed model separately on each tree and pool the posterior samples, as in the following code with MCMCglmm (Hadfield 2010). Twenty trees and short chains keep it fast; a real analysis would use more of both. # a Bayesian phylogenetic mixed model over 20 trees of the posterior sample library(MCMCglmm) set.seed(4) prior <- list(G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)), R = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)) some_trees <- posterior[round(seq(1, length(posterior), length.out = 20))] draws <- lapply(some_trees, function(tr) { Ainv <- inverseA(tr, nodes = "TIPS")$Ainv m <- MCMCglmm(y ~ x, random = ~lang, ginverse = list(lang = Ainv), data = traits, prior = prior, nitt = 13000, burnin = 3000, thin = 10, verbose = FALSE) m$Sol[, "x"] }) quantile(unlist(draws), c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)) # slope, integrating over trees #> 2.5% 50% 97.5% #> 0.09289 0.50572 0.91922 17.13 Step 11: From toy data to real data Everything above runs on a simulated table with three columns. Replacing it with real data is mostly a matter of reading the right files and joining them correctly. Real linguistic datasets are increasingly published in the Cross-Linguistic Data Formats (CLDF) (Forkel et al. 2018), a standard built on plain CSV files plus a JSON metadata file that describes their contents. Lexibank (List, Forkel, Greenhill, et al. 2022) distributes more than a hundred wordlists in CLDF, with concepts linked to Concepticon (List et al. 2016) and languages linked to Glottolog (Hammarström et al. 2024); Grambank (Skirgård et al. 2023) distributes structural data in the same format. Appendix G describes these and other resources. 17.13.1 The CLDF data model A CLDF dataset is a directory of tables, each of a standard type, plus a metadata file (for example cldf-metadata.json or Wordlist-metadata.json) that declares which file holds which table and which columns hold which standard properties. Table 17.5 lists the tables most relevant to phylogenetics. Table 17.5: The CLDF tables most often used in phylogenetic work. CLDF component Usual file Key columns Content LanguageTable languages.csv ID, Name, Glottocode, Latitude, Longitude one row per language variety ParameterTable parameters.csv ID, Name, Concepticon_ID one row per concept (wordlists) or feature (structural data) FormTable forms.csv ID, Language_ID, Parameter_ID, Value, Form, Segments one row per word form CognateTable cognates.csv ID, Form_ID, Cognateset_ID one row per cognate judgment ValueTable values.csv ID, Language_ID, Parameter_ID, Value, Code_ID one row per language-feature value (structural data) CodeTable codes.csv ID, Parameter_ID, Name the possible values of each categorical feature Because every table refers to the others by identifiers (Language_ID, Parameter_ID, Form_ID), building the input for cognates_to_binary() amounts to two joins. The code below is not run when the book is built, because it requires a downloaded dataset. We tested it on walworthpolynesian (version 1.1), a Lexibank wordlist of 31 Polynesian languages with expert cognate judgments. There it produces a matrix of 31 languages and 1,456 cognate characters in a few seconds. # not run: requires a Lexibank dataset with cognate judgments, e.g. # git clone https://github.com/lexibank/<dataset>.git # (tested with <dataset> = walworthpolynesian, release v1.1) library(readr) library(dplyr) cldf_dir <- "<dataset>/cldf" forms <- read_csv(file.path(cldf_dir, "forms.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) cognates <- read_csv(file.path(cldf_dir, "cognates.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) languages <- read_csv(file.path(cldf_dir, "languages.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) cog_real <- cognates |> inner_join(forms, by = c("Form_ID" = "ID")) |> transmute(Language_ID, Parameter_ID, # make cognate set identifiers unique within meanings Cognateset_ID = paste(Parameter_ID, Cognateset_ID, sep = "-")) |> distinct() bin_real <- cognates_to_binary(cog_real) # label languages by Glottocode, to join with other datasets later; # check the identifiers before anything is built from the matrix glotto <- setNames(languages$Glottocode, languages$ID) ids <- unname(glotto[rownames(bin_real)]) if (anyNA(ids)) stop("no Glottocode for: ", paste(rownames(bin_real)[is.na(ids)], collapse = ", ")) if (anyDuplicated(ids)) stop("varieties sharing a Glottocode: ", paste(unique(ids[duplicated(ids)]), collapse = ", ")) rownames(bin_real) <- ids data_real <- phyDat(bin_real, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?") Several practical issues arise with real data that the toy example hides. Some datasets list more than one variety per Glottocode, so labeling by Glottocode can create duplicate row names; decide in advance whether to keep one variety per language or to use the dataset’s own identifiers. Some cognate judgments are flagged as doubtful (a Doubt column in the CognateTable), or as loans (a Loan column in the FormTable of some datasets), and a principled decision is needed about whether to exclude them, code them as missing, or run the analysis both ways (Chapter 8). Datasets also differ in their concept lists, so combining two datasets means matching concepts through their Concepticon identifiers rather than their names. The R package rcldf reads a CLDF dataset directly from its metadata file and returns its tables as data frames, which saves hard-coding file names. # not run: rcldf is available from GitHub (SimonGreenhill/rcldf); # tested with rcldf 1.6.3 ds <- rcldf::cldf("<dataset>/cldf/cldf-metadata.json") names(ds$tables) # "FormTable", "LanguageTable", "CognateTable", ... head(ds$tables$FormTable) 17.13.2 When there are no cognate judgments Many Lexibank datasets contain word forms segmented into sounds but no expert cognate judgments. For these, automated cognate detection (Chapter 3) can supply provisional cognate sets. The standard tool is the LexStat algorithm in the Python library LingPy (List et al. 2017), which learns language-pair-specific sound correspondences and clusters words within each meaning. The following Python code (not run) reads a Lexibank dataset, runs LexStat, and writes a table with a cognate set identifier for each word, which can then be read into R and passed to cognates_to_binary(). # not run: Python with lingpy installed (pip install lingpy); # tested with lingpy 2.6.14 from lingpy import Wordlist, LexStat wl = Wordlist.from_cldf("<dataset>/cldf/cldf-metadata.json") wl.output("tsv", filename="wordlist") # writes wordlist.tsv lex = LexStat("wordlist.tsv") lex.get_scorer(runs=10000) # permutation test for correspondences lex.cluster(method="lexstat", threshold=0.55, ref="cogid") lex.output("tsv", filename="wordlist-cognates") We ran this code on the Polynesian dataset used in Section 17.14. The permutation test is the slow step, and the whole run took about 20 minutes on one processor core. LexStat grouped the 7,518 words into 1,897 cognate sets, where the experts recognize 1,456. Compared with the expert judgments, the automatic sets had a B-cubed precision of 0.95 and a recall of 0.79. The algorithm rarely groups words that the experts keep apart, but it splits some expert cognate sets, typically where sound change has made related words look dissimilar. How much does it matter whether cognates are judged by experts or by an algorithm? Rama et al. (2018) addressed this question directly. They inferred cognate sets automatically for several language families with expert cognate judgments available, built binary matrices from both the automatic and the expert cognates, inferred Bayesian trees from each, and compared the trees with expert classifications from Glottolog. Trees from automatically detected cognates came reasonably close to those from expert cognates, although expert judgments generally remained better. The study suggests a practical division of labor: automated detection makes it possible to analyze families for which no expert cognate coding exists and to check expert codings for inconsistencies, but it is not yet a substitute for expert judgment where that is available. Jäger (2018) pushed the automated approach to a global scale, inferring cognate classes and trees from the ASJP word lists for thousands of languages. 17.13.3 Structural data and Glottolog trees Grambank (Skirgård et al. 2023) codes nearly two hundred grammatical features for more than two thousand languages, mostly as binary presence/absence features. Its CLDF ValueTable can be reshaped into a matrix and analyzed with exactly the tools of Steps 4 to 7 (with the caveats about structural data discussed in Chapter 3), or, more commonly, used as trait data in a comparative analysis over a lexical tree. Since both Grambank and Lexibank identify languages by Glottocode, joining them is straightforward. # not run: requires a clone of https://github.com/grambank/grambank # (tested with release v1.0.3) library(tidyr) gb_values <- read_csv("grambank/cldf/values.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) gb <- gb_values |> select(Language_ID, Parameter_ID, Value) |> pivot_wider(names_from = Parameter_ID, values_from = Value) gb_mat <- as.matrix(gb[, -1]) rownames(gb_mat) <- gb$Language_ID # Grambank uses Glottocodes gb_mat[is.na(gb_mat)] <- "?" # unrecorded -> missing # keep the languages in both the lexical tree and Grambank shared <- intersect(rownames(gb_mat), mcc_real$tip.label) # mcc_real: a summary tree from a real analysis, tips labeled by Glottocode tree_gb <- keep.tip(mcc_real, shared) trait <- gb_mat[shared, 1] # any one feature as a trait # multistate features can be split into binary indicators before analysis We tested this code on Grambank 1.0.3, with a neighbor-joining tree of the 31 Polynesian languages of walworthpolynesian, labeled by Glottocode, standing in for mcc_real. It builds a matrix of 2,467 languages by 195 features, and 26 of the 31 Polynesian languages are in Grambank. For comparisons across many families, no dated lexical tree exists, and analysts often fall back on the Glottolog classification as a topology, with branch lengths assigned by a rule such as Grafen’s method (ape::compute.brlen()), or on a global tree inferred from ASJP data. Chapter 13 discusses the consequences of such arbitrary branch lengths. Reading Glottolog’s Newick trees requires some care, because the node labels contain characters with special meaning in Newick; community R packages such as glottoTrees help with parsing, pruning and combining them. 17.13.4 Scaling up the inference For a few dozen languages, phangorn is fast enough for maximum-likelihood analysis. For hundreds of languages, dedicated programs are much faster. IQ-TREE (Minh, Schmidt, et al. 2020) and RAxML-NG (Kozlov et al. 2019) both support binary characters, ascertainment correction and fast bootstrap approximations. Both read the PHYLIP format, which phangorn writes directly. phylip_file <- file.path(out_dir, "toy_cognates.phy") write.phyDat(cog_var, file = phylip_file, format = "phylip") show_file(phylip_file, n = 3) #> 24 430 #> L01 0100101000000001000001001010100000000010100010001000????100010000000 ... #> L02 1000??10000000001000010010100010000000101000100100000100100010000000 ... # run in a shell, not in R: maximum likelihood with a binary model, # estimated state frequencies, gamma rates, ascertainment correction # (variable characters only) and 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates # (IQ-TREE 3 is called iqtree3; IQ-TREE 2 is called iqtree2) iqtree3 -s toy_cognates.phy -m GTR2+FO+G4+ASC -B 1000 # the corresponding RAxML-NG analysis with 100 standard bootstrap replicates raxml-ng --all --msa toy_cognates.phy --model BIN+G+ASC_LEWIS --bs-trees 100 The resulting tree files are Newick, read with ape::read.tree(), and bootstrap tree sets can be summarized with the same functions we used above. BEASTling (Maurits et al. 2017) was designed to make the workflow of this chapter easier for linguists. Its authors observed that writing BEAST 2 XML by hand was a serious barrier, and that the files were rarely published, which made analyses hard to reproduce. BEASTling instead takes a short human-readable configuration file and a data file, and generates the XML. Because the configuration file is short, it can be printed in full in a paper’s supplementary material, and anyone with the same data and BEASTling version can regenerate the identical XML. BEASTling also integrates Glottolog, so that languages can be selected by family or macro-area and Glottolog subgroups can be imposed as monophyly constraints, and it supports models for lexical and typological data in the same analysis. The approach illustrates a general principle: the more of a pipeline that is specified in short, declarative, version-controlled files, the easier it is to reproduce and to vary. Lexibank (List, Forkel, Greenhill, et al. 2022) is an attempt to do for lexical data what GenBank did for DNA sequences. It aggregates more than a hundred published wordlists, converts each to CLDF with a reproducible conversion script (written with the cldfbench and pylexibank Python packages), links every concept to Concepticon and every language to Glottolog, and standardizes phonetic transcriptions so that words can be segmented into sounds automatically. The result is a single collection of wordlists covering thousands of language varieties, in which every dataset is versioned, archived on Zenodo and citable. For the workflow of this chapter the consequence is that Step 1 (data assembly) and much of Step 2 (matrix building) can be done with a few lines of code for any dataset in the collection, and that an analysis can cite the exact version of the data it used. 17.14 A case study with real data: Polynesian We now run the same pipeline on a real language family. The data are the Polynesian wordlist of Walworth (2018) in its Lexibank version (Walworth 2024), released under a CC BY 4.0 licence. It records Blust’s list of 210 basic meanings for 30 Polynesian languages and a Proto-Polynesian reconstruction, with expert cognate judgments. Polynesian is a good first family: it is small, its history is short (the Polynesian homeland in Tonga and Samoa was settled roughly three thousand years ago) (Gray et al. 2009), and its main subgroups are well established. The four CLDF tables the analysis needs, about 1.5 MB, are stored in the book’s repository in data/case-study/, together with the Glottolog classification of each language (Hammarström et al. 2024), so the section runs offline. 17.14.1 From CLDF to a character matrix The code is that of Section 17.13.1, with two decisions specific to this dataset. The Proto-Polynesian “language” is a reconstruction made with the comparative method from the daughter languages. It is not independent evidence, so we leave it out. And 213 forms are flagged as loans in the Loan column of the FormTable. We drop them, so that a meaning whose only recorded word in a language is a loan is scored as missing for that language (Chapter 8). library(readr) library(dplyr) cs_dir <- "data/case-study" read_cs <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(cs_dir, f), show_col_types = FALSE) forms_p <- read_cs("forms.csv") cognates_p <- read_cs("cognates.csv") languages_p <- read_cs("languages.csv") cog_poly <- cognates_p |> inner_join(forms_p, by = c("Form_ID" = "ID")) |> filter(Language_ID != "Polynesian", # Proto-Polynesian, a reconstruction !Loan) |> # forms flagged as loans transmute(Language_ID, Parameter_ID, Cognateset_ID = paste(Parameter_ID, Cognateset_ID, sep = "-")) |> distinct() bin_poly <- cognates_to_binary(cog_poly) # identifiers: the dataset's language IDs, which are readable names; # check them and their Glottocodes before building anything from the matrix glotto_poly <- setNames(languages_p$Glottocode, languages_p$ID)[rownames(bin_poly)] stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(rownames(bin_poly)), !anyNA(glotto_poly), !anyDuplicated(glotto_poly)) data_poly <- phyDat(bin_poly, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?") c(languages = nrow(bin_poly), meanings = length(unique(cog_poly$Parameter_ID)), characters = ncol(bin_poly), missing = round(mean(bin_poly == "?"), 3), singletons = sum(colSums(bin_poly == "1") == 1)) #> languages meanings characters missing singletons #> 30.000 210.000 1396.000 0.071 769.000 The Glottolog classification gives the subgroups we will look for. We take every Glottolog subgroup below Polynesian that contains at least two of the 30 languages. gl <- read_cs("glottolog_classification.csv") lineage <- strsplit(setNames(gl$Classification, gl$Glottocode)[glotto_poly], " > ") names(lineage) <- rownames(bin_poly) groups <- unique(unlist(lapply(lineage, `[`, -1))) members <- lapply(setNames(groups, groups), function(g) names(lineage)[vapply(lineage, function(l) g %in% l, logical(1))]) members <- members[lengths(members) >= 2 & lengths(members) < nrow(bin_poly)] lengths(members) #> Nuclear Polynesian #> 28 #> Vanuatu-Loyalty Outliers #> 3 #> Mele-Futuna #> 2 #> Northern Outlier Polynesian-East Polynesian #> 16 #> Solomons Northern Outlier Polynesian-East Polynesian #> 15 #> Central Northern Outlier Polynesian-East Polynesian #> 14 #> East Polynesian #> 12 #> East Polynesian Proximal #> 9 #> Central Northern Outlier Polynesian #> 2 #> East Polynesian Distal #> 3 #> Far East Polynesian #> 2 #> Southern East Polynesian Proximal #> 8 #> Tongic #> 2 #> Ellicean #> 3 #> Pukapukic #> 2 #> Tahitian-Austral #> 3 #> Austral #> 2 These are nested. Tongic (Tongan and Niuean) and Nuclear Polynesian (all the rest) form the primary split. Within Nuclear Polynesian, the East Polynesian languages, from Hawaiian to Rapanui and Māori, form the most famous subgroup. They descend from the language of the settlers who reached East Polynesia less than a thousand years ago (Wilmshurst et al. 2011). Several intermediate groupings link East Polynesian with Polynesian Outliers spoken in the Solomon Islands and Micronesia. 17.14.2 Exploration and maximum likelihood The delta score and the NeighborNet of Step 3 show how tree-like the data are (Figure 17.11). d_poly <- dist.hamming(data_poly) delta_poly <- c(mean = delta.score(data_poly, arg = "mean"), sd = delta.score(data_poly, arg = "sd")) round(delta_poly, 3) #> mean sd #> 0.337 0.271 nnet_poly <- neighborNet(d_poly) tip_col <- ifelse(nnet_poly$tip.label %in% members[["Tongic"]], "#D55E00", ifelse(nnet_poly$tip.label %in% members[["East Polynesian"]], "#0072B2", "grey20")) op <- par(mar = c(1.5, 1.5, 3, 1.5), xpd = NA) pn_poly <- plot(nnet_poly, type = "2D", show.tip.label = FALSE) net_labels(pn_poly, nnet_poly$tip.label, col = tip_col) # helper (appendix) Figure 17.11: NeighborNet of the Hamming distances between the 30 Polynesian languages. Tongic languages (Tongan, Niuean) and East Polynesian languages are marked in color. par(op) We then fit the binary model by maximum likelihood, with and without gamma rate variation, starting from a neighbor-joining tree, and assess the NJ tree with 100 bootstrap replicates. tree_nj_poly <- NJ(d_poly) bs_nj_poly <- bootstrap.phyDat(data_poly, function(x) NJ(dist.hamming(x)), bs = 100) fit_poly <- optim.pml(pml(tree_nj_poly, data_poly), optNni = TRUE, optBf = TRUE, control = ctrl) fit_poly_g <- optim.pml(update(fit_poly, k = 4), optNni = TRUE, optBf = TRUE, optGamma = TRUE, control = ctrl) round(c(AIC_no_gamma = AIC(fit_poly), AIC_gamma = AIC(fit_poly_g), gamma_shape = fit_poly_g$shape, pi_present = fit_poly_g$bf[2]), 3) #> AIC_no_gamma AIC_gamma gamma_shape pi_present #> 23270.788 22922.139 2.584 0.180 A nonparametric bootstrap of the ML search in phangorn takes a few seconds per replicate on these data, which is too slow for the book’s build. We therefore ran the same model in IQ-TREE on the variable characters, with the ultrafast bootstrap. The PHYLIP file is written as in Step 11, and the output is stored in software-runs/case-study/. poly_var <- bin_poly[, !apply(bin_poly, 2, function(x) all(x[x != "?"] == "1"))] write.phyDat(phyDat(poly_var, type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?"), file = file.path(out_dir, "poly.phy"), format = "phylip") seq_poly <- sprintf( ' <sequence id="seq_%s" taxon="%s" totalcount="2" value="0%s"/>', rownames(bin_poly), rownames(bin_poly), apply(bin_poly, 1, paste, collapse = "")) writeLines(c(paste('<data id="cognates" spec="Alignment" dataType="binary"', 'ascertained="true" excludefrom="0" excludeto="1">'), seq_poly, "</data>"), file.path(out_dir, "poly_beast_data.xml")) iqtree3 -s poly.phy -m GTR2+FO+G4+ASC -B 1000 -T 1 -seed 17 --prefix poly iq_poly <- read.tree(file.path("software-runs", "case-study", "iqtree", "poly.treefile")) iq_poly <- root(iq_poly, outgroup = "Tongan", resolve.root = TRUE, edgelabel = TRUE) # Tongic is not monophyletic here tip_info_poly <- data.frame( label = rownames(bin_poly), group = ifelse(rownames(bin_poly) %in% members[["Tongic"]], "Tongic", ifelse(rownames(bin_poly) %in% members[["East Polynesian"]], "East Polynesian", "other Nuclear Polynesian"))) ggtree(iq_poly) %<+% tip_info_poly + geom_tippoint(aes(color = group), size = 1.4) + geom_tiplab(aes(color = group), size = 3, offset = 0.002, show.legend = FALSE) + support_layers(2.4, drop = c("", "Root")) + # plotting helper (appendix) scale_color_manual(values = c(Tongic = "#D55E00", `East Polynesian` = "#0072B2", `other Nuclear Polynesian` = "grey20"), name = NULL) + theme_tree2() + xlim(0, max(node.depth.edgelength(iq_poly)) * 1.3) + labs(x = "Expected changes per character") Figure 17.12: Maximum-likelihood tree of the 30 Polynesian languages from IQ-TREE (binary model with estimated frequencies, gamma rates and ascertainment correction), rooted on Tongan, with ultrafast bootstrap support (percent) at internal nodes. Colors as in the NeighborNet. 17.14.3 A Bayesian analysis For the Bayesian analysis we adapted the BEAST 2 file of Section 17.10.3 (software-runs/case-study/poly_beast.xml): the same binary model with ascertainment correction and gamma rates, and a Yule prior. We used no calibrations. The strict clock has its rate fixed at 1, so node heights are in expected changes per character, a relative time scale. Two runs of 1.5 million states each, sampled every 1,000 states, took about 13 minutes each on one processor core. Every parameter reached an ESS above 600 in each run. As before, the book keeps every tenth sampled tree. poly_dir <- file.path("software-runs", "case-study", "beast2") read_poly <- function(run, file) file.path(poly_dir, run, file) post_poly <- do.call(c, lapply(runs, function(run) { tr <- read.nexus(read_poly(run, "poly_thinned.trees")) tr[-seq_len(floor(0.1 * length(tr)))] })) traces_poly <- lapply(runs, function(run) { tr <- read.table(read_poly(run, "poly.log"), header = TRUE, comment.char = "#") tr[-seq_len(floor(0.1 * nrow(tr))), ] }) pars_poly <- c("posterior", "TreeHeight", "gammaShape", "freqParameter.2") round(sapply(traces_poly, function(tr) coda::effectiveSize(tr[, pars_poly]))) #> [,1] [,2] #> posterior 821 815 #> TreeHeight 919 977 #> gammaShape 931 907 #> freqParameter.2 1088 1198 mcc_poly <- maxCladeCred(post_poly) cred <- prop.clades(mcc_poly, post_poly, rooted = TRUE) / length(post_poly) mcc_poly$node.label <- ifelse(seq_along(cred) == 1, "", sprintf("%.2f", cred)) ggtree(mcc_poly) %<+% tip_info_poly + geom_tippoint(aes(color = group), size = 1.4) + geom_tiplab(aes(color = group), size = 3, offset = 0.002, show.legend = FALSE) + support_layers(2.4) + # plotting helper (appendix) scale_color_manual(values = c(Tongic = "#D55E00", `East Polynesian` = "#0072B2", `other Nuclear Polynesian` = "grey20"), name = NULL) + theme_tree2() + xlim(0, max(node.depth.edgelength(mcc_poly)) * 1.3) + labs(x = "Expected changes per character since the root") Figure 17.13: Maximum clade credibility tree of the BEAST 2 posterior sample for Polynesian, with clade credibilities at internal nodes. The horizontal axis is in expected changes per character, measured from the root; there are no calibrations. Colors as in the NeighborNet. 17.14.4 Which subgroups are recovered? Table 17.6 checks each Glottolog subgroup against the NJ and ML trees, with the NJ bootstrap support, and gives its posterior probability in the BEAST 2 sample. iq_unrooted <- unroot(iq_poly) recovered <- function(tree, g) is.monophyletic(unroot(tree), g) support <- function(trees, g, rooted = FALSE) mean(vapply(trees, function(tr) if (rooted) is.monophyletic(tr, g) else recovered(tr, g), logical(1))) poly_table <- data.frame( languages = lengths(members), NJ = vapply(members, function(g) recovered(tree_nj_poly, g), logical(1)), NJ_bootstrap = vapply(members, function(g) support(bs_nj_poly, g), 0), ML = vapply(members, function(g) recovered(iq_unrooted, g), logical(1)), BEAST_posterior = vapply(members, function(g) support(post_poly, g, rooted = TRUE), 0)) knitr::kable(poly_table, digits = 2, caption = paste( "Glottolog subgroups with at least two of the 30 languages: whether the", "NJ and IQ-TREE ML trees contain them, their NJ bootstrap support, and", "their posterior probability in the BEAST 2 sample (rooted clades).")) The mean delta score is 0.34, against 0.13 for the simulated family. The NeighborNet shows large boxes in the center, where the Outliers, Samoan, Tuvaluan and the Tongic languages meet. Rate variation among characters, which the simulated data hardly showed, is strongly supported: adding gamma rates lowers the AIC by 349 units. Support is also lower. Many internal nodes of the ML tree have ultrafast bootstrap values well below 95%, and the methods disagree with each other on about half of their splits. Only 3 of the 17 Glottolog subgroups appear in the ML tree. One of them is East Polynesian, the best-established subgroup in the family, which has a posterior probability of 1 in the BEAST 2 sample. The deeper structure is not recovered. Tongan and Niuean do not form a Tongic clade. East Uvean and East Futunan are placed next to Niuean or Tongan rather than among the other Nuclear Polynesian languages, and in the BEAST 2 tree Tongan groups with Samoan. This is the expected signature of contact. East Uvean, in particular, borrowed heavily from Tongan, and borrowings that the coders did not recognize as loans look like shared inheritance (Chapter 8). Pukapuka joins East Polynesian, whereas Glottolog places it with Samoan and Tuvaluan, which is again consistent with later contact. In the strict-clock BEAST 2 analysis, the root falls between East Polynesian (with Pukapuka) and all other languages, with a posterior probability of 0.99, instead of between Tongic and Nuclear Polynesian. The East Polynesian languages have long branches. A strict clock interprets that extra change as extra time and places the root on their side. A relaxed clock, an outgroup or a prior on the root position would be needed to root this tree credibly (Chapter 9). The intermediate groupings that link East Polynesian with particular Outliers rest on few shared innovations, and a basic-vocabulary list of 210 meanings is unlikely to resolve them. These comparisons need a caveat. Agreement with the expert subgroups is not independent validation of the methods. The cognate judgments are themselves products of the comparative method, and the Glottolog subgrouping comes from the same method, applied by overlapping communities of scholars to overlapping data. Moreover, a shared cognate is not the same thing as a shared innovation: two languages can share a cognate because both retained it. A tree that reproduces the classification may partly reproduce the judgments that went into the coding, and a disagreement may reflect either the method or the coding. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10, the Polynesian analysis is a first step toward empirical adequacy (the delta score and the NeighborNet show where the tree model fits poorly) and toward historical interpretation, not a validation of the methods. The simulation is the only setting in which we know the right answer. The real data show where a pipeline that works well on clean data runs into the problems discussed in Chapters 8 and 15: contact, rate variation among lineages, and short internal branches. 17.15 Validating the pipeline The analyses of this chapter provide different kinds of evidence, and it helps to name them with the vocabulary of Section 6.10. Implementation validation asks whether the software computes what the model says. Three checks in this chapter are of this kind: reading the exported NEXUS file back in (Step 8), running similar models in five independent programs (Table 17.4), and running each Bayesian analysis without data to see the prior it actually uses. The second is the weakest, for the reasons given in Step 9. Parameter recovery asks whether the pipeline recovers a history simulated under its own assumptions. Steps 4 to 9 on the toy family are tests of this kind. Strictly, the simulator and the models differ slightly: the simulator is Dollo-like and varies rates among meanings, whereas the inference models are reversible and binary. The data are still much closer to the models than any real dataset. Robustness under misspecification asks how the results change when the data violate the model in realistic ways, through borrowing, rate shifts in one lineage, coding error or missing languages. The simulations of this chapter do not test it; the second computational exercise shows how to begin, and Chapter (ref?)(issues) gives examples. Empirical model adequacy asks whether the fitted model could have produced the real data. AIC and Bayes factors measure only relative fit. For the Polynesian data, the delta score and the NeighborNet already show aspects of the data that a tree model does not capture, and the posterior predictive checks described below would make the question formal. Historical interpretation asks whether the clades, dates and rates correspond to historical events. For Polynesian, the uncalibrated BEAST 2 tree has no time scale at all, and its root position reflects the clock model as much as the history. Simulation is also the most powerful way to validate a real analysis, beyond parameter recovery on a toy. Take the tree and parameters estimated from the real data and simulate many new datasets from them, with the same numbers of languages, meanings and missing cells. Then run the whole pipeline on each and check whether it recovers what was simulated. If a method systematically misplaces a particular subgroup, or overestimates the root age, on data simulated from a known history, it will do the same on real data. Simulation can also introduce violations of the model deliberately, such as borrowing between particular languages, faster change in one lineage, or coding errors, to see which conclusions are robust to them (Greenhill et al. 2009). That turns a parameter-recovery study into a test of robustness under misspecification. The function simulate_cognates() above, extended with borrowing events, is all that is needed to begin (see the second computational exercise). Evolutionary biologists have developed two formal versions of this idea that have only recently been applied systematically to linguistic phylogenetic pipelines (King 2026b, 2026a). Simulation-based calibration (Talts et al. 2018) checks that a Bayesian program is computing the posterior correctly: draw parameters (including a tree) from the prior, simulate data from them, run the inference, and record where the true value falls among the posterior samples. If the software and the model implementation are correct, these ranks are uniformly distributed, and departures from uniformity reveal bugs or poor mixing. It has become a standard test for new phylogenetic models in packages for BEAST 2 and RevBayes. Posterior predictive simulation checks whether the model is adequate for the data: simulate datasets from parameters drawn from the posterior, compute summary statistics such as the number of singletons per language, the distribution of cognate-class sizes or the delta score, and compare them with the observed values (Chapter 15). A model that cannot reproduce the observed number of singletons, for example, is probably mis-describing the process of lexical replacement. Both checks are straightforward to implement with the tools of this chapter, and both would make published linguistic phylogenies considerably more convincing. Applied to the standard BEAST 2 set-up for cognate data, the first revealed that the default weighting of meaning-partition rates miscalibrates the posterior, and the second that the covarion model fails to reproduce several features of Indo-European cognate data (King 2026b). A third practice worth borrowing is the continuously updated, fully scripted pipeline exemplified by Nextstrain in pathogen phylodynamics (Hadfield et al. 2018), in which a single command rebuilds every analysis from the raw data whenever the data change. 17.16 A reporting checklist A phylogenetic analysis is reproducible only if a reader can reconstruct every step from the data to the figures. Table 17.7 collects the information that should be reported, drawing on the stages of this chapter. Chapter 15 gives a complementary checklist focused on the substantive pitfalls. Table 17.7: Information to report for a reproducible linguistic phylogenetic analysis.
