D Technical Notes: Space, Ancestral States and Comparative Methods D.1 Chapter 11: Phylogeography and Homelands D.2 Chapter 12: Ancestral State Reconstruction D.3 Chapter 13: Phylogenetic Comparative Methods D.4 Chapter 14: Language Trees as Scaffolds for Cultural Evolution

D Technical Notes: Space, Ancestral States and Comparative Methods This appendix collects the derivations, algorithms and longer pieces of code that support Chapters 11 to 14. Each section corresponds to one chapter and can be read alongside it. Every code chunk here is self-contained: the trees and data it needs are recreated with the same random seeds as in the chapter, so the objects are identical to those the chapter uses unless stated otherwise. The general background on likelihood, multivariate normal distributions, generalized least squares and continuous-time Markov chains is in Appendix A, especially Sections A.7, A.10 and A.11. suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(ape) library(phytools) library(phangorn) }) D.1 Chapter 11: Phylogeography and Homelands D.1.1 Pruning for discrete locations In discrete phylogeography (Section 11.4.1) the location of a lineage is one of \(K\) regions, evolving under a rate matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) with transition probabilities \(\mathbf{P}(t) = e^{\mathbf{Q}t}\). The likelihood of the observed tip regions is computed by Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm. For each node \(v\) and each region \(i\), the partial likelihood \(L_v(i)\) is the probability of the tip regions below \(v\) given that \(v\) was in region \(i\). It is computed from the tips toward the root: \[\begin{equation} L_v(i) = \prod_{c \in \text{children}(v)} \sum_{j=1}^{K} P_{ij}(t_c)\, L_c(j), \tag{D.1} \end{equation}\] with \(L_v(i) = 1\) if tip \(v\) is in region \(i\) and \(0\) otherwise, and \(t_c\) the length of the branch leading to child \(c\). The likelihood of the whole tree is \(\sum_i \pi_i L_{\text{root}}(i)\), where \(\pi_i\) is a prior on the root region, and the posterior probability that the root was in region \(i\) is \(\pi_i L_{\text{root}}(i) / \sum_j \pi_j L_{\text{root}}(j)\). Marginal probabilities at other internal nodes need a second, root-to-tips pass, or equivalently re-rooting at each node in turn (Section 12.4.2). An implementation of the recursion for any discrete character is given in Section D.2.2. D.1.2 Route Bayes factors in BSSVS Under the BSSVS prior of Equation (11.3), the number of active symmetric routes is \(K - 1\) plus a Poisson variable with mean \(\ln 2\), so the expected number of active routes is \(\ln 2 + K - 1\) out of \(K(K-1)/2\) possible ones. The prior inclusion probability of any one route is therefore \(q = (\ln 2 + K - 1) / [K(K-1)/2]\). If \(p_{ij}\) is the posterior inclusion probability of route \(i \leftrightarrow j\) (the posterior mean of \(\delta_{ij}\), read from the MCMC log), the Bayes factor for including the route is the ratio of posterior to prior odds: \[\begin{equation} \text{BF}_{ij} = \frac{p_{ij}/(1 - p_{ij})}{q/(1 - q)}, \qquad q = \frac{\ln 2 + K - 1}{K(K-1)/2}. \tag{D.2} \end{equation}\] The function below computes it. The posterior inclusion probabilities are invented, as if read from a BEAST log file for an analysis with four regions. bssvs_bf <- function(post_incl, K, poisson_mean = log(2)) { q <- (poisson_mean + K - 1) / (K * (K - 1) / 2) # prior inclusion probability post_incl <- pmin(post_incl, 1 - 1e-6) # guard against p = 1 (post_incl / (1 - post_incl)) / (q / (1 - q)) } post <- c("R1-R2" = 0.99, "R1-R3" = 0.12, "R1-R4" = 0.55, "R2-R3" = 0.81, "R2-R4" = 0.08, "R3-R4" = 0.93) round(bssvs_bf(post, K = 4), 1) #> R1-R2 R1-R3 R1-R4 R2-R3 R2-R4 R3-R4 #> 61.8 0.1 0.8 2.7 0.1 8.3 # the same posterior inclusion probability with 4 and with 20 regions round(c(K4 = bssvs_bf(0.81, K = 4), K20 = bssvs_bf(0.81, K = 20)), 1) #> K4 K20 #> 2.7 36.9 With four regions the prior inclusion probability is about 0.62, so a posterior inclusion probability of 0.81 gives a Bayes factor below 3; with twenty regions the prior inclusion probability is about 0.1 and the same posterior gives a Bayes factor above 30. A posterior inclusion probability that hits 1 in every sample gives an infinite Bayes factor; the guard in the function caps it, and in practice such routes are reported as “BF > 1000” or similar. Because the Poisson prior can be changed by the analyst, and because \(q\) depends on \(K\), route Bayes factors should always be reported together with \(K\) and the prior. D.1.3 The multivariate normal model for coordinates Under bivariate Brownian motion (Equation (11.5)), the location of each tip is the root location plus the sum of independent normal displacements along the branches from the root to the tip. Two tips \(i\) and \(j\) share the displacements on the path from the root to their most recent common ancestor, so the covariance between any coordinate of \(i\) and any coordinate of \(j\) is the corresponding entry of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) multiplied by the length of the shared path, \(C_{ij}\). Writing \(\mathbf{C}\) for the \(n \times n\) phylogenetic covariance matrix (with \(C_{ii}\) the root-to-tip time of tip \(i\)) and stacking the coordinates of the \(n\) tips into a vector \(\mathbf{X}\) of length \(2n\) (tip by tip), \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}_{2n}\!\left(\mathbf{1}_n \otimes \mathbf{x}_{\text{root}},\; \mathbf{C} \otimes \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right), \tag{D.3} \end{equation}\] where \(\otimes\) is the Kronecker product. The likelihood can be evaluated directly from this formula for small trees, or in time linear in the number of tips by a pruning algorithm analogous to Equation (D.1), in which the partial likelihoods are normal densities summarized by their means and variances (Felsenstein 1985b). For a single coordinate \(\mathbf{x}\) the model is \(\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}_n(x_{\text{root}} \mathbf{1}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{C})\), a linear model with a single intercept and correlated errors. Maximizing the log-likelihood \[\ell(x_{\text{root}}, \sigma^2) = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \tfrac12 \log\det\mathbf{C} - \frac{(\mathbf{x} - x_{\text{root}}\mathbf{1})^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - x_{\text{root}}\mathbf{1})}{2\sigma^2}\] with respect to \(x_{\text{root}}\) gives the generalized least squares estimator of Equation (11.6) (Section A.11). Its variance follows from the general GLS result \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) with the design matrix \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{1}\). Note that neither the weights \(\mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1} / \mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{1}\) nor the variance depends on the observed locations. The chunk below recreates the tree and locations of Section 11.13.1 and checks that the GLS mean equals the maximum-likelihood root location returned by fastAnc(). set.seed(11) tree <- pbtree(n = 30, scale = 6) tree$tip.label <- paste0("L", 1:30) Sigma <- matrix(c(0.36, 0.10, 0.10, 0.36), 2) XY <- sim.corrs(tree, vcv = Sigma, anc = c(0, 0), internal = TRUE) tips <- XY[tree$tip.label, ] colnames(tips) <- c("east", "north") C <- vcv(tree)[rownames(tips), rownames(tips)] one <- rep(1, nrow(C)) Ci <- solve(C) w <- drop(one %*% Ci) / drop(one %*% Ci %*% one) # GLS weights, sum to 1 c(gls = sum(w * tips[, "east"]), fastAnc = unname(fastAnc(tree, tips[, "east"])[1])) #> gls fastAnc #> 0.09339 0.09339 range(w) # all weights positive here #> [1] 0.00589 0.12728 The weights are all positive, so the homeland estimate is a convex combination of the present-day locations and lies inside their convex hull. D.1.4 Why standardized contrasts serve as an adequacy statistic The adequacy check of Section 11.13.3 uses the standardized independent contrasts of a coordinate (Section D.3.4). Under Brownian motion on the correct tree, the \(n - 1\) standardized contrasts are independent and identically distributed \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), whatever the shape of the tree. Their kurtosis, \(\overline{u^4} / (\overline{u^2})^2\), is invariant to \(\sigma^2\), so its null distribution can be simulated from standard normal draws without reference to the tree. A relaxed random walk inflates the variance of the contrasts on some branches and not others, which produces a mixture of normals with heavier tails than any single normal, and so a larger kurtosis. A directional trend leaves the contrasts unchanged when all tips are contemporaneous. Under BM with drift \(\mu\), a tip at height \(h\) has expected value \(x_{\text{root}} + \mu h\), so on an ultrametric tree of depth \(T\) every tip has the same expectation, \(x_{\text{root}} + \mu T\). The drift adds this constant to every tip and changes nothing else: the covariances are those of BM without drift. Every value used by the contrast algorithm is either a tip value or a weighted average of tip values with weights summing to one, so each has the same expectation, and every contrast, being a difference of two such values, has expectation zero and the same variance as without drift. The contrasts therefore have exactly the distribution they would have without drift. No statistic computed from the contrasts, and more generally no statistic that is invariant to a common shift of all tips, can detect a trend from contemporaneous tips. This is the formal reason why the adequacy check in Table 11.3 flags the trend scenario no more often than pure Brownian motion. With non-contemporaneous tips the cancellation fails and the drift becomes visible, which is what the drift regression of Section 11.13.4 exploits. D.2 Chapter 12: Ancestral State Reconstruction The code in this section uses the toy tree and word-order data of Section 12.15, recreated in the first chunk. tree <- read.tree(text = paste0( "((((A1:1,A2:1):1.5,(A3:1.2,A4:1.2):1.3):1,", "((B1:0.8,B2:0.8):1.2,B3:2):1.5):1.5,", "(((C1:1,C2:1):1,C3:2):1.5,((D1:0.5,D2:0.5):2,(D3:1.5,D4:1.5):1):1):1.5);")) wo <- c(A1 = "SOV", A2 = "SOV", A3 = "SOV", A4 = "SVO", B1 = "SVO", B2 = "SVO", B3 = "SOV", C1 = "VSO", C2 = "VSO", C3 = "SVO", D1 = "SVO", D2 = "SVO", D3 = "SOV", D4 = "SVO") wo <- factor(wo[tree$tip.label]) root <- Ntip(tree) + 1 fitER <- fitMk(tree, wo, model = "ER") Q <- unclass(as.Qmatrix(fitER))[levels(wo), levels(wo)] pi_flat <- rep(1 / 3, 3) D.2.1 Fitch and Sankoff algorithms In Fitch’s downpass (from tips to root), each node \(v\) with children \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) is assigned a set of candidate states: \[\begin{equation} S_v = \begin{cases} S_{c_1} \cap S_{c_2} & \text{if } S_{c_1} \cap S_{c_2} \neq \emptyset, \\ S_{c_1} \cup S_{c_2} & \text{otherwise (cost} + 1\text{)}. \end{cases} \tag{D.4} \end{equation}\] The total number of unions is the parsimony score. An uppass from the root then refines the sets into the most parsimonious reconstructions at each node. Sankoff’s generalization allows an arbitrary cost \(c_{ij}\) for a change from state \(i\) to state \(j\). The downpass computes, for each node \(v\) and state \(i\), the minimum cost \(S_v(i)\) of the subtree below \(v\) given that \(v\) is in state \(i\): \[\begin{equation} S_v(i) = \sum_{c \in \text{children}(v)} \min_{j} \left[ c_{ij} + S_c(j) \right], \tag{D.5} \end{equation}\] with \(S_v(i) = 0\) if tip \(v\) is in state \(i\) and \(\infty\) otherwise. The minimum over \(i\) of \(S_{\text{root}}(i)\) is the parsimony score. The recursion has the structure of Equation (D.6) with minimum and addition in place of sum and product, which is why Sankoff parsimony and likelihood pruning are often presented together. The function below implements the Fitch downpass and checks its score against phangorn. fitch_down <- function(tree, x) { n <- Ntip(tree) sets <- vector("list", n + tree$Nnode) for (i in 1:n) sets[[i]] <- as.character(x[tree$tip.label[i]]) cost <- 0 parents <- rev(unique(rev(reorder(tree, "postorder")$edge[, 1]))) for (v in parents) { # each node after all its children ch <- tree$edge[tree$edge[, 1] == v, 2] I <- Reduce(intersect, sets[ch]) if (length(I) > 0) sets[[v]] <- I else { sets[[v]] <- Reduce(union, sets[ch]); cost <- cost + 1 } } list(sets = sets, cost = cost) } fd <- fitch_down(tree, wo) pd <- phyDat(matrix(as.character(wo), dimnames = list(names(wo), "wo")), type = "USER", levels = levels(wo)) c(hand = fd$cost, phangorn = parsimony(tree, pd)) #> hand phangorn #> 5 5 fd$sets[[root]] # downpass set at the root #> [1] "SOV" "SVO" The downpass set at the root contains both SOV and SVO, matching the tie in the most-parsimonious reconstruction sets reported in Section 12.15.1. D.2.2 Pruning and conditional likelihoods by hand Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm computes the conditional likelihood \(L_v(i)\), the probability of the tip states below node \(v\) given that \(v\) is in state \(i\), from the tips toward the root: \[\begin{equation} L_v(i) = \prod_{c \in \text{children}(v)} \sum_{j} P_{ij}(t_c)\, L_c(j), \qquad L(\theta) = \sum_i \pi_i\, L_{\text{root}}(i), \tag{D.6} \end{equation}\] with \(L_v(i) = 1\) for the observed state of a tip and 0 otherwise. The function below implements the recursion, with transition probabilities computed from an eigendecomposition of \(\mathbf{Q}\) (Section A.6). Pt <- function(Q, t) { e <- eigen(Q) Re(e$vectors %*% diag(exp(e$values * t)) %*% solve(e$vectors)) } prune <- function(tree, x, Q) { tree <- reorder(tree, "postorder") n <- Ntip(tree); K <- ncol(Q) L <- matrix(1, n + tree$Nnode, K, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Q))) L[1:n, ] <- 0 L[cbind(1:n, match(as.character(x[tree$tip.label]), colnames(Q)))] <- 1 for (e in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) { par <- tree$edge[e, 1]; ch <- tree$edge[e, 2] L[par, ] <- L[par, ] * (Pt(Q, tree$edge.length[e]) %*% L[ch, ]) } L } L <- prune(tree, wo, Q) c(hand = log(sum(pi_flat * L[root, ])), fitMk = as.numeric(logLik(fitER))) #> hand fitMk #> -13.76 -13.76 round(pi_flat * L[root, ] / sum(pi_flat * L[root, ]), 3) # root posterior #> SOV SVO VSO #> 0.352 0.418 0.230 The hand-computed log-likelihood matches fitMk(), and the normalized root vector is the marginal posterior at the root. At other nodes the normalized conditional likelihoods are not marginal posteriors, because they ignore the rest of the tree. The chunk below shows that they are what ace(..., marginal = TRUE) returns, as stated in Section 12.15.3. node <- 16 # ancestor of subgroups A and B rbind( ancr_marginal = ancr(fitER)$ace[as.character(node), ], ace_marginal_TRUE = ace(wo, tree, type = "discrete", model = "ER", marginal = TRUE)$lik.anc[node - Ntip(tree), ], hand_subtree_only = L[node, ] / sum(L[node, ])) |> round(3) #> SOV SVO VSO #> ancr_marginal 0.494 0.367 0.139 #> ace_marginal_TRUE 0.533 0.324 0.143 #> hand_subtree_only 0.533 0.324 0.143 D.2.3 Joint reconstruction: the Pupko algorithm Pupko et al. (2000) find the joint reconstruction of Equation (12.2) by dynamic programming, the max-product analogue of pruning. For each non-root node \(c\) with parent \(a\), and each possible parent state \(i\), define \[\begin{equation} \Lambda_c(i) = \max_j \left[ P_{ij}(t_c) \prod_{d \in \text{children}(c)} \Lambda_d(j) \right], \qquad C_c(i) = \arg\max_j \left[ \cdots \right], \tag{D.7} \end{equation}\] where for a tip \(c\) in observed state \(s\), \(\Lambda_c(i) = P_{is}(t_c)\). At the root, choose \(\hat x_{\text{root}} = \arg\max_i \pi_i \prod_{d} \Lambda_d(i)\), and then trace back down the tree: each child takes the state \(C_c(\hat x_a)\) recorded for its parent’s chosen state. The implementation below works on the log scale and is checked against ancr(..., type = "joint"). joint_pupko <- function(tree, x, Q, pi) { tree <- reorder(tree, "postorder") n <- Ntip(tree); K <- ncol(Q); states <- colnames(Q); N <- n + tree$Nnode S <- matrix(0, N, K) # sum of log Lambda over children best <- matrix(NA_integer_, N, K) # C_c(i): best child state, parent i for (e in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) { par <- tree$edge[e, 1]; ch <- tree$edge[e, 2] lP <- log(Pt(Q, tree$edge.length[e])) if (ch <= n) { j <- match(as.character(x[tree$tip.label[ch]]), states) lv <- lP[, j]; b <- rep(j, K) } else { M <- lP + matrix(S[ch, ], K, K, byrow = TRUE) lv <- apply(M, 1, max); b <- apply(M, 1, which.max) } best[ch, ] <- b; S[par, ] <- S[par, ] + lv } r <- n + 1; st <- integer(N); st[r] <- which.max(log(pi) + S[r, ]) pre <- reorder(tree, "cladewise") for (e in seq_len(nrow(pre$edge))) st[pre$edge[e, 2]] <- best[pre$edge[e, 2], st[pre$edge[e, 1]]] list(nodes = setNames(states[st[r:N]], r:N), logL = max(log(pi) + S[r, ])) } jp <- joint_pupko(tree, wo, Q, pi_flat) jt <- ancr(fitER, type = "joint") all(jp$nodes == as.character(jt$ace[names(jp$nodes)])) #> [1] TRUE c(hand = jp$logL, ancr = as.numeric(jt$logLik)) #> hand ancr #> -17.45 -17.45 D.2.4 Sampling a stochastic map A stochastic character map is drawn in three steps, using the conditional likelihoods \(L_v(i)\) from a pruning pass. Root state. Draw the root state \(i\) with probability \(\pi_i L_{\text{root}}(i) / \sum_j \pi_j L_{\text{root}}(j)\). Node states, from root to tips. For each child \(c\) of a node \(a\) whose state \(i\) has been drawn, draw the state \(j\) of \(c\) with probability \[\begin{equation} P(X_c = j \mid X_a = i, D) = \frac{P_{ij}(t_c)\, L_c(j)}{\sum_{l} P_{il}(t_c)\, L_c(l)}. \tag{D.8} \end{equation}\] Together, steps 1 and 2 draw a joint assignment of node states from its exact posterior. Branch histories. For each branch, simulate the history of the character between the now-fixed start and end states, conditional on those endpoints. The simplest method is rejection sampling: simulate forward from the start state using exponential waiting times with rate \(-q_{ii}\) in state \(i\) and jump probabilities \(q_{ij}/(-q_{ii})\), and accept the history only if it ends in the required state. Rejection is inefficient on long branches and for improbable endpoints. Uniformization instead draws the number of potential changes on a branch from a Poisson distribution with a rate \(\mu \ge \max_i(-q_{ii})\), and then the states at those events from the discrete-time chain with transition matrix \(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{Q}/\mu\), conditional on the endpoints; it never rejects. Irvahn and Minin (2014) built on uniformization a stochastic mapping algorithm that avoids matrix exponentiation altogether, which pays off when the state space is large. Averages over many maps estimate posterior expectations of any function of the history, such as the number of changes of each type or the time spent in each state. The analytical alternative for expected counts and dwelling times is the method of Minin and Suchard (2008). D.2.5 Hidden-rate models With two hidden rate categories, slow (S) and fast (F), a character with observed states \(1, \ldots, k\) has \(2k\) hidden states, and the rate matrix has block structure: \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{Q} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{Q}_S - \mathbf{D}_{SF} & \mathbf{D}_{SF} \\ \mathbf{D}_{FS} & \mathbf{Q}_F - \mathbf{D}_{FS} \end{pmatrix}, \tag{D.9} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{Q}_S\) and \(\mathbf{Q}_F\) are the rate matrices for observed-state changes within each category (with their own diagonals) and \(\mathbf{D}_{SF}\), \(\mathbf{D}_{FS}\) are diagonal matrices of switching rates between categories. At a tip with observed state \(s\), the partial likelihood is 1 for both hidden states \(s_S\) and \(s_F\) and 0 otherwise, so the pruning algorithm sums over the hidden category automatically. Marginal reconstructions of the observed state are obtained by summing the reconstructed probabilities of \(s_S\) and \(s_F\), as in the corHMM example of Section 12.15.8. Two identifiability issues are worth knowing. The labels of the categories can be swapped without changing the likelihood unless the model constrains, for example, the rates in \(\mathbf{Q}_S\) to be smaller than those in \(\mathbf{Q}_F\); and with one character on a small tree the switching rates are typically poorly estimated, so that the model can fit no better than the ordinary Mk model even when rates do vary. D.2.6 Root treatments for a rare feature, computed exactly Section 12.4.5 argued that, for a feature attested in only a few branches, the root reconstruction depends on the root treatment as much as on the data. For a binary character the Bayesian answer can be computed exactly, by integrating the pruning likelihood over the two rates on a grid, because the transition probabilities have the closed form \(P_{01}(t) = \pi_1 (1 - e^{-(q_{01} + q_{10})t})\) and \(P_{10}(t) = \pi_0 (1 - e^{-(q_{01} + q_{10})t})\), with \(\pi_1 = q_{01} / (q_{01} + q_{10})\) the stationary frequency of state 1 (Section A.7). The feature below is present in two languages of subgroup A and two of subgroup C, on opposite sides of the root of the toy tree; both rates have Exponential(1) priors. rare <- setNames(rep(0, Ntip(tree)), tree$tip.label) rare[c("A1", "A2", "C1", "C2")] <- 1 # root conditional likelihoods L0, L1 for vectors of rates (closed form) root_L <- function(q01, q10) { tr <- reorder(tree, "postorder"); n <- Ntip(tr) L <- array(1, c(n + tr$Nnode, 2, length(q01))) for (i in 1:n) { L[i, , ] <- 0; L[i, rare[tr$tip.label[i]] + 1, ] <- 1 } a <- q01 + q10; p1 <- q01 / a for (e in seq_len(nrow(tr$edge))) { pa <- tr$edge[e, 1]; d <- tr$edge[e, 2] ex <- exp(-a * tr$edge.length[e]) P01 <- p1 * (1 - ex); P10 <- (1 - p1) * (1 - ex) L[pa, 1, ] <- L[pa, 1, ] * ((1 - P01) * L[d, 1, ] + P01 * L[d, 2, ]) L[pa, 2, ] <- L[pa, 2, ] * (P10 * L[d, 1, ] + (1 - P10) * L[d, 2, ]) } list(L0 = L[n + 1, 1, ], L1 = L[n + 1, 2, ]) } # integrate over q01, q10 ~ Exponential(1) on a grid in log q u <- seq(log(1e-5), log(60), length.out = 300); du <- u[2] - u[1] g <- expand.grid(a = exp(u), b = exp(u)) wt <- du^2 * g$a * g$b * dexp(g$a) * dexp(g$b) rl <- root_L(g$a, g$b) pi1 <- g$a / (g$a + g$b) # stationary P(present) m0 <- sum(wt * rl$L0); m1 <- sum(wt * rl$L1) m_stat <- sum(wt * ((1 - pi1) * rl$L0 + pi1 * rl$L1)) data.frame( root = c("flat", "stationary", "fixed absent", "fixed present"), lnML = round(log(c((m0 + m1) / 2, m_stat, m0, m1)), 3), P_present = round(c(m1 / (m0 + m1), sum(wt * pi1 * rl$L1) / m_stat, 0, 1), 3)) #> root lnML P_present #> 1 flat -8.784 0.462 #> 2 stationary -8.836 0.272 #> 3 fixed absent -8.710 0.000 #> 4 fixed present -8.864 1.000 Three things are worth noticing. First, the marginal likelihoods differ by less than 0.2 log units, so the data cannot choose among the root treatments, and the Bayes factor for “present at the root” against “absent at the root” (fixing the root, as in the approach of Pagel et al. (2004)) is close to 1. Second, the posterior probability that the feature was present at the root is nevertheless 0.46 under the flat prior and 0.27 under the stationary prior: the stationary prior gives the root the frequencies of a process in which the rarely attested state is rare. Third, the flat-prior answer is exactly the Bayes factor turned into a probability, \(m_1 / (m_0 + m_1)\), because a flat root is an equal mixture of the two fixed roots. An estimated root frequency adds nothing for a single character. With a uniform (Dirichlet(1, 1)) prior on \(\pi_1\), the likelihood averaged over the prior is \(\int_0^1 [\pi_1 L_1 + (1 - \pi_1) L_0]\, d\pi_1 = (L_0 + L_1)/2\), the flat-prior likelihood, at any rates; and the posterior mean of \(\pi_1\) is \((2 L_1 + L_0) / 3(L_0 + L_1)\), which can range only between 1/3 and 2/3. The chunk checks both at one pair of rates. r1 <- root_L(0.2, 0.4) p <- seq(0.0005, 0.9995, by = 0.001) # grid over pi_1 lik_pi <- p * r1$L1 + (1 - p) * r1$L0 c(estimated = mean(lik_pi), flat = (r1$L0 + r1$L1) / 2) #> estimated flat #> 0.0007825 0.0007825 c(posterior_mean_pi1 = sum(p * lik_pi) / sum(lik_pi), formula = (2 * r1$L1 + r1$L0) / (3 * (r1$L0 + r1$L1))) #> posterior_mean_pi1 formula #> 0.4876 0.4876 Maximum likelihood shows the same contrast. In phytools, pi = "estimated" sets the root prior to the stationary distribution of the fitted rate matrix. x <- setNames(factor(rare), names(rare)) fit_flat <- fitMk(tree, x, model = "ARD", pi = "equal") invisible(capture.output( # silence the message on pi fit_stat <- fitMk(tree, x, model = "ARD", pi = "estimated"))) rbind(flat = ancr(fit_flat)$ace[1, ], stationary = ancr(fit_stat)$ace[1, ]) |> round(3) #> 0 1 #> flat 0.519 0.481 #> stationary 0.830 0.170 The RevBayes script of Section H.5.21 fits the same kinds of model to a simulated rare feature, adds informative rate priors and a loss-only model, and reproduces the exact values computed in this way. D.2.7 A test for historical signal in one character Harmon (2019) proposes a blunt check of whether a character carries any information about its history. The comparison model ignores the tree and draws the state of each language independently, with probability \(p_k\) for state \(k\); its maximized log-likelihood is \(\sum_k n_k \log(n_k/n)\), where \(n_k\) languages are in state \(k\). As the rates of an Mk model grow, the tip states become independent draws from the stationary distribution, so the Mk likelihood approaches this value along a flat ridge. If the best Mk likelihood is no higher than the tree-free likelihood, the rates cannot be estimated and nothing can be said about ancestral states. The chunk compares two binary characters on the toy tree, one that follows the primary split and one scattered across the subgroups, and then the word-order data. garbage <- function(x) { n <- table(x); sum(n * log(n / sum(n))) } tips <- tree$tip.label split_cd <- setNames(as.integer(substr(tips, 1, 1) %in% c("C", "D")), tips) scattered <- setNames(as.integer(tips %in% c("A1", "A3", "B2", "C1", "C3", "D2", "D4")), tips) sapply(list(follows_split = split_cd, scattered = scattered), function(y) c(Mk_ARD = as.numeric(logLik(fitMk(tree, y, model = "ARD"))), tree_free = garbage(y))) |> round(3) #> follows_split scattered #> Mk_ARD -4.001 -9.704 #> tree_free -9.704 -9.704 c(word_order_ER = as.numeric(logLik(fitER)), tree_free = garbage(wo)) #> word_order_ER tree_free #> -13.76 -13.89 For the scattered character the two likelihoods are identical: the Mk fit has run onto the ridge, and any reconstruction would only restate the root prior. The word-order data of Chapter 12 are better than that, but not by much: the equal-rates model improves on the tree-free model by about 0.13 log-likelihood units with one parameter fewer, a reminder that fourteen languages and one feature carry little historical information. D.3 Chapter 13: Phylogenetic Comparative Methods The code in this section recreates the simulated 60-language tree of Section 13.1 and the traits simulated from it, with the same seeds as in the chapter. suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(nlme); library(caper); library(phylolm); library(MCMCglmm) }) set.seed(13) tree <- pbtree(n = 60, scale = 6) tree$tip.label <- sprintf("L%02d", 1:60) tips <- tree$tip.label C <- vcv(tree) set.seed(21) x_bm <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1, internal = TRUE) # as in pcms-traitgram D.3.1 The Brownian likelihood Under Brownian motion the tip values are multivariate normal, \(\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}_n(\mu\mathbf{1}, \sigma^2\mathbf{C})\) (Equation (13.2)), so the likelihood is the multivariate normal density (Section A.10): \[\begin{equation} L(\mu, \sigma^2 \mid \mathbf{x}, \tau) = \frac{\exp\!\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mu\mathbf{1})^\top (\sigma^2\mathbf{C})^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mu\mathbf{1})\right]}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\, \det(\sigma^2\mathbf{C})^{1/2}}. \tag{D.10} \end{equation}\] Setting the derivatives of its logarithm with respect to \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) to zero gives the maximum-likelihood estimates \[\begin{equation} \hat\mu = (\mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{1})^{-1}\, \mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{x}, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{(\mathbf{x} - \hat\mu\mathbf{1})^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \hat\mu\mathbf{1})}{n}. \tag{D.11} \end{equation}\] The estimate \(\hat\mu\) is the GLS mean, a weighted average of the tip values with weights \(\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{C}^{-1}\) (the same estimator as the Brownian homeland of Equation (11.6)). The REML estimate of \(\sigma^2\) uses the divisor \(n - 1\) instead of \(n\), and it equals the mean squared standardized independent contrast (Section D.3.4). x <- x_bm[tips] Ci <- solve(C); one <- rep(1, length(x)) mu_hat <- drop(one %*% Ci %*% x) / drop(one %*% Ci %*% one) s2_ml <- drop(t(x - mu_hat) %*% Ci %*% (x - mu_hat)) / length(x) c(mu_hat = mu_hat, fastAnc_root = unname(fastAnc(tree, x)[1]), s2_REML = s2_ml * length(x) / (length(x) - 1), mean_pic2 = mean(pic(x, tree)^2)) #> mu_hat fastAnc_root s2_REML mean_pic2 #> 0.2138 0.2138 1.0072 1.0072 D.3.2 Covariances under the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and early-burst models For the OU process of Equation (13.3) on an ultrametric tree of depth \(T\), with the root value drawn from the stationary distribution, the covariance between two tips separated by a patristic distance \(d_{ij} = 2(T - s_{ij})\) is \[\begin{equation} \operatorname{Cov}(x_i, x_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\alpha}\, e^{-\alpha d_{ij}}. \tag{D.12} \end{equation}\] Covariance thus decays exponentially with the distance between languages, rather than linearly as under BM. As \(\alpha \to 0\) the stationary variance \(\sigma^2 / (2\alpha)\) diverges, which is why software either fixes the root value or conditions on it when \(\alpha\) is small; the two parameterizations are labelled OUfixedRoot and OUrandomRoot in phylolm. For the early-burst model, in which the Brownian rate changes as \(\sigma^2(t) = \sigma_0^2 e^{rt}\), the covariance between two tips is the integral of the rate over their shared history: \[\begin{equation} C_{ij} = \int_0^{s_{ij}} \sigma_0^2 e^{rt}\, dt = \sigma_0^2\, \frac{e^{r s_{ij}} - 1}{r}. \tag{D.13} \end{equation}\] With \(r < 0\) most of the variance is generated early, so deep splits dominate the covariance structure. On an ultrametric tree, the delta transformation of Section 13.3.4 maps \(C_{ij}\) to \(C_{ij}^{\delta}\); delta and EB are therefore alternative ways of concentrating change early or late. D.3.3 Signal statistics Blomberg’s K. Let \(\text{MSE}_0 = (\mathbf{x} - \hat\mu\mathbf{1})^\top(\mathbf{x} - \hat\mu\mathbf{1})/(n-1)\) measure dispersion around the phylogenetic mean while ignoring the tree, and \(\text{MSE} = (\mathbf{x} - \hat\mu\mathbf{1})^\top\mathbf{C}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \hat\mu\mathbf{1})/(n-1)\) measure dispersion using the tree. Then \[\begin{equation} K = \frac{\text{MSE}_0 / \text{MSE}}{\dfrac{1}{n-1}\left[\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{C}) - \dfrac{n}{\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{1}}\right]}, \tag{D.14} \end{equation}\] where the denominator is the expected value of the ratio under BM, so that \(K = 1\) is the BM expectation (Blomberg et al. 2003). Moran’s I. With weights \(w_{ij}\) (for example \(w_{ij} = 1/d_{ij}\) for patristic distance \(d_{ij}\)), \[\begin{equation} I = \frac{n}{\sum_{i \ne j} w_{ij}} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i \ne j} w_{ij}(x_i - \bar x)(x_j - \bar x)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}. \tag{D.15} \end{equation}\] Its expected value under no autocorrelation is \(-1/(n-1)\). The D statistic. For a binary trait, \(\Sigma d\) is the sum of differences between sister clades computed by a contrast-like algorithm. The observed value is compared with its mean under random reshuffling of the trait across tips (\(\overline{\Sigma d_r}\)) and under a Brownian threshold model (\(\overline{\Sigma d_b}\)): \[\begin{equation} D = \frac{\Sigma d_{\text{obs}} - \overline{\Sigma d_b}}{\overline{\Sigma d_r} - \overline{\Sigma d_b}}. \tag{D.16} \end{equation}\] The chunks below compute Moran’s I for the BM trait of the chapter and for a noise trait (drawn here with its own seed, so it differs from the noise trait in Section 13.4), and \(D\) for a binary trait derived by thresholding the BM trait at its median. set.seed(22) noise <- setNames(rnorm(Ntip(tree)), tips) w <- 1 / cophenetic(tree); diag(w) <- 0 Moran.I(x_bm[tips], w)$observed # phylogenetic Moran's I, BM trait #> [1] 0.2375 Moran.I(noise, w)$observed # ... and for noise (expected ~ -1/(n-1)) #> [1] -0.007312 bin_dat <- data.frame(lang = tips, feature = as.integer(x_bm[tips] > median(x_bm[tips]))) cd_bin <- comparative.data(tree, bin_dat, names.col = "lang") d_res <- phylo.d(cd_bin, binvar = feature, permut = 200) round(c(D = unname(d_res$DEstimate), P_random = d_res$Pval1, P_brownian = d_res$Pval0), 3) #> D P_random P_brownian #> -0.247 0.000 0.805 The BM trait has a clearly positive Moran’s I and the noise trait a value near its null expectation. The binary feature derived from the BM trait has \(D\) near or below zero: it is significantly more clumped than random, and not distinguishable from the Brownian threshold expectation. D.3.4 Independent contrasts Take two sister tips \(i\) and \(j\) with trait values \(x_i, x_j\) and branch lengths \(v_i, v_j\) to their common ancestor \(k\). Compute the standardized contrast \[\begin{equation} u_{ij} = \frac{x_i - x_j}{\sqrt{v_i + v_j}}. \tag{D.17} \end{equation}\] Under BM the raw difference has variance \(\sigma^2(v_i + v_j)\), so the standardized contrast has variance \(\sigma^2\) whatever the branch lengths. Estimate the value at node \(k\) as the weighted average \(x_k = (x_i/v_i + x_j/v_j)/(1/v_i + 1/v_j)\). The weights favor the descendant on the shorter branch. Lengthen the branch below \(k\) by \(v_i v_j/(v_i + v_j)\) to account for the error in the estimate of \(x_k\). Prune \(i\) and \(j\), treat \(k\) as a tip, and repeat. A tree with \(n\) tips yields \(n - 1\) contrasts, independent and identically distributed \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) under BM. The regression of the contrasts of \(y\) on those of \(x\) through the origin gives exactly the PGLS slope under BM (Rohlf 2001; Blomberg et al. 2012), as the chunk below confirms for the data of Section 13.5. set.seed(31) x <- fastBM(tree) y <- 2 + 0.6 * x + fastBM(tree, sig2 = 0.5) fit_pic <- lm(pic(y, tree) ~ pic(x, tree) - 1) dat_pic <- data.frame(lang = tips, x = x[tips], y = y[tips]) m_pic_gls <- gls(y ~ x, data = dat_pic, correlation = corBrownian(1, tree, form = ~lang)) c(PIC = unname(coef(fit_pic)), PGLS_BM = unname(coef(m_pic_gls)["x"])) #> PIC PGLS_BM #> 0.6405 0.6405 D.3.5 Generalized least squares and the lambda profile For the model of Equation (13.5), the generalized least squares estimator and its covariance are \[\begin{equation} \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{V}^{-1} \mathbf{X})^{-1}\, \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{V}^{-1} \mathbf{y}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{V}^{-1} \mathbf{X})^{-1}, \tag{D.18} \end{equation}\] with \[\begin{equation} \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top \mathbf{V}^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n - p}. \tag{D.19} \end{equation}\] When \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}\), these reduce to the familiar OLS formulas. GLS is OLS on transformed data. Factor \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top\), for example by a Cholesky decomposition, and premultiply the model by \(\mathbf{L}^{-1}\): \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{L}^{-1}\boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{L}^{-1}\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}. \tag{D.20} \end{equation}\] The transformed residuals are independent with equal variance, so OLS on the transformed data is optimal (the Gauss-Markov theorem; Section A.11). The Galton simulation in Section 13.1 uses the upper-triangular factor \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{V}^{-1}\), which is an equivalent whitening. When \(\lambda\) is estimated jointly, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) and \(\hat\sigma^2\) follow from Equations (D.18) and (D.19) for each value of \(\lambda\), with \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{C}(\lambda)\). Substituting them into the log-likelihood gives the profile log-likelihood of \(\lambda\) (Freckleton et al. 2002): \[\begin{equation} \ell(\lambda) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\hat\sigma^2_\lambda) - \frac{1}{2}\log\det \mathbf{C}(\lambda) - \frac{n}{2}, \tag{D.21} \end{equation}\] with \(\hat\sigma^2_\lambda\) computed with divisor \(n\) for ML (or \(n - p\), with an adjustment, for REML). Maximizing this one-dimensional function is fast, and the profile curve gives a likelihood interval for \(\lambda\), as plotted in Figure 13.5. D.3.6 Pagel’s independent model With the joint states of two binary characters ordered \((0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\), the independent model gives each character its own gain and loss rates, \(\alpha_X, \beta_X\) and \(\alpha_Y, \beta_Y\), regardless of the state of the other character: \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{Q}_{\text{ind}} = \begin{pmatrix} \cdot & \alpha_Y & \alpha_X & 0 \\ \beta_Y & \cdot & 0 & \alpha_X \\ \beta_X & 0 & \cdot & \alpha_Y \\ 0 & \beta_X & \beta_Y & \cdot \end{pmatrix}. \tag{D.22} \end{equation}\] It is the special case of the dependent model of Equation (13.6) with \(q_{12} = q_{34} = \alpha_Y\), \(q_{21} = q_{43} = \beta_Y\), \(q_{13} = q_{24} = \alpha_X\) and \(q_{31} = q_{42} = \beta_X\): four constraints, hence the four degrees of freedom of the likelihood-ratio test. The zeros on the anti-diagonal encode the assumption that the two characters never change at exactly the same instant. Two caveats about the \(\chi^2_4\) reference distribution are worth knowing. It is an asymptotic approximation that can be poor for small trees and for rates near zero (on the boundary of the parameter space), and the test is a test of the model, not of the number of independent co-occurring changes (Section 13.7.3). A parametric bootstrap, simulating data under the fitted independent model and refitting both models, gives a better calibrated \(p\)-value. D.3.7 Phylogenetic GLMM in brms The Gaussian PGLMM of Section 13.9.2 can also be fitted in brms, which passes the model to Stan. The code below is not run here, because it requires compiling a Stan model. We ran it with brms 2.23 and rstan 2.32, which took a few minutes, most of them spent compiling. With the default adapt_delta = 0.8, the first model produced about 300 divergent transitions and an effective sample size below 100 for the residual standard deviation. Phylogenetic and residual variance are hard to separate with 60 languages, and the posterior has the funnel shape that Stan’s sampler finds difficult. With adapt_delta = 0.99, as below, there were no divergent transitions and every effective sample size was above 350. The estimated slope (posterior mean \(-0.27\), 95% interval \(-0.54\) to \(0.00\)) agrees with the PGLS and MCMCglmm estimates. The second model needs a spatial correlation matrix S for the languages of tree100, with row and column names matching lang. library(brms) A <- vcv(tree, corr = TRUE) m_brms <- brm(complexity ~ logpop + (1 | gr(lang, cov = A)), data = langs, data2 = list(A = A), family = gaussian(), chains = 4, iter = 4000, cores = 4, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99)) # binary response, with a spatial random effect alongside the phylogenetic one # (S: a spatial correlation matrix, e.g. exp(-distance / range)) m_tone <- brm(tone ~ humid + (1 | gr(lang, cov = A)) + (1 | gr(lang2, cov = S)), data = transform(dtone, lang2 = lang), data2 = list(A = vcv(tree100, corr = TRUE), S = S), family = bernoulli()) D.3.8 The threshold model in MCMCglmm The chunk below recreates the 100-language tree and the simulated tone data of Section 13.9.1 and fits a threshold model, a probit PGLMM with the residual variance fixed at 1, in MCMCglmm. set.seed(7) tree100 <- pbtree(n = 100, scale = 3) set.seed(11) humid <- rTrait(n = 1, phy = tree100, model = "BM", parameters = list(sigma2 = 0.4)) tone <- rbinTrait(n = 1, phy = tree100, beta = c(-0.5, 1), alpha = 0.5, X = cbind(1, humid)) dtone <- data.frame(lang = tree100$tip.label, humid = humid, tone = tone, row.names = tree100$tip.label) set.seed(6) Ainv100 <- inverseA(tree100, nodes = "TIPS", scale = TRUE)$Ainv prior_t <- list(G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 1000, alpha.mu = 0, alpha.V = 1)), R = list(V = 1, fix = 1)) m_thr <- MCMCglmm(tone ~ humid, random = ~lang, ginverse = list(lang = Ainv100), family = "threshold", data = dtone, prior = prior_t, nitt = 23000, burnin = 3000, thin = 20, verbose = FALSE) summary(m_thr)$solutions #> post.mean l-95% CI u-95% CI eff.samp pMCMC #> (Intercept) -1.292 -3.1214 0.1431 861.5 0.104 #> humid 1.353 0.5693 2.4679 433.3 0.001 The coefficient of humid is on the liability (probit) scale. It is therefore not directly comparable with the logistic coefficients of Section 13.9.1, which are larger by a factor of roughly 1.6 to 1.8 for the same effect (the ratio of the standard deviations of the logistic and standard normal distributions is \(\pi/\sqrt{3} \approx 1.81\), and approximations based on matching slopes at the center give about 1.6 to 1.7). The prior used here is a parameter-expanded prior on the phylogenetic variance; with the residual variance fixed, the latent scale is identified only up to that convention, so variance components from threshold and logistic models are not comparable either. D.3.9 A spatiophylogenetic model by maximum likelihood The chunk below recreates the simulated locations and trait of Section 13.10 and fits Equation (13.12) by maximum likelihood, holding the range \(\rho\) fixed, for three nested covariance structures: phylogeny with noise, space with noise, and all three components. The intercept is profiled out by GLS for each value of the variance components, which are optimized on the log scale. set.seed(99) lon <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1) + rnorm(Ntip(tree), 0, 0.3) lat <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1) + rnorm(Ntip(tree), 0, 0.3) D <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(lon, lat))) S <- exp(-D / 1) # spatial correlation, range 1 Cs <- C / max(diag(C)) # phylogenetic correlation L_s <- t(chol(S + diag(1e-8, nrow(S)))) a_phy <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1 / max(diag(C))) # phylogenetic part, variance 1 s_sp <- drop(L_s %*% rnorm(Ntip(tree))) # spatial part, variance 1 trait <- 0.8 * a_phy + 0.8 * s_sp + rnorm(Ntip(tree), 0, 0.5) negloglik <- function(logv, comps, y) { V <- Reduce(`+`, Map(`*`, exp(logv), comps)) R <- chol(V); Xm <- matrix(1, length(y), 1) Ri <- backsolve(R, diag(length(y))) # V^-1 = Ri Ri' Vinv <- Ri %*% t(Ri) b <- solve(t(Xm) %*% Vinv %*% Xm, t(Xm) %*% Vinv %*% y) r <- y - Xm %*% b 0.5 * (2 * sum(log(diag(R))) + t(r) %*% Vinv %*% r + length(y) * log(2 * pi)) } I_n <- diag(Ntip(tree)) fits <- list(phylogeny_only = list(phylo = Cs, noise = I_n), space_only = list(space = S, noise = I_n), both = list(phylo = Cs, space = S, noise = I_n)) res <- t(sapply(fits, function(comps) { o <- optim(rep(log(0.3), length(comps)), negloglik, comps = comps, y = trait[tips]) share <- setNames(rep(NA, 3), c("phylo", "space", "noise")) share[names(comps)] <- exp(o$par) / sum(exp(o$par)) c(AIC = 2 * o$value + 2 * (length(comps) + 1), share) })) knitr::kable(res, digits = 2, caption = "Maximum-likelihood fits of phylogeny-only, space-only and spatiophylogenetic models to a simulated trait, with the estimated share of variance attributed to each component.") Table D.1: Maximum-likelihood fits of phylogeny-only, space-only and spatiophylogenetic models to a simulated trait, with the estimated share of variance attributed to each component. AIC phylo space noise phylogeny_only 181.6 0.43 NA 0.57 space_only 181.0 NA 0.68 0.32 both 173.2 0.37 0.63 0.00 In this replicate the full model, with both phylogenetic and spatial components, is preferred by AIC (Table D.1). It apportions the variance between phylogeny and space, while the noise component shrinks toward zero; the true shares were about 0.42, 0.42 and 0.16. Maximum-likelihood estimates of variance components are biased downward in small samples and can sit on the boundary at zero, as the noise component nearly does here; the Bayesian fit in the chapter reports the full posterior instead, which makes the uncertainty in the shares visible. D.4 Chapter 14: Language Trees as Scaffolds for Cultural Evolution D.4.1 Borrowing as a transformation of the covariance matrix In the horizontal transmission simulation of Section 14.14, each society \(i\) replaces a fraction \(h\) of its trait value with the value of a contact partner \(p(i)\): \(x_i' = (1 - h)\,x_i + h\,x_{p(i)}\). In matrix form, \(\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}\) with \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{B} = (1 - h)\,\mathbf{I} + h\,\mathbf{P}, \tag{D.23} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{P}\) has a single 1 in each row, in the column of that society’s partner. If \(\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu\mathbf{1}, \sigma^2\mathbf{C})\) under Brownian motion on the tree, then \(\mathbf{x}' \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu\mathbf{1}, \sigma^2\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B}^\top)\), because each row of \(\mathbf{B}\) sums to one. A PGLS that uses \(\mathbf{C}\) is therefore misspecified, and how badly depends on how different \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B}^\top\) is from \(\mathbf{C}\). When partners are close relatives, \(C_{i,p(i)} \approx C_{ii}\) and the transformation changes little; when partners are distant, it adds covariance where \(\mathbf{C}\) has almost none, and the regression treats similar societies as independent observations. If the contact network and the borrowing fraction were known, a GLS with \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B}^\top\) would be correctly specified. The chunk below recreates the tree and the geographic partners of the chapter, and compares the false positive rates of PGLS with \(\mathbf{C}\) and of GLS with \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B}^\top\) at \(h = 0.3\). set.seed(12) htree <- pbtree(n = 60, scale = 5) htree$tip.label <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:60) Ch <- vcv(htree) geo <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(runif(120), 60, 2))); diag(geo) <- Inf partner <- apply(geo, 1, which.min) # nearest neighbor in space h <- 0.3 P <- matrix(0, 60, 60); P[cbind(1:60, partner)] <- 1 B <- (1 - h) * diag(60) + h * P gls_p <- function(y, x, V) { Wv <- chol(solve(V)) coef(summary(lm(Wv %*% y ~ Wv %*% cbind(1, x) - 1)))[2, 4] } V_borrow <- B %*% Ch %*% t(B) set.seed(13) p <- replicate(300, { x <- drop(B %*% fastBM(htree)); y <- drop(B %*% fastBM(htree)) c(PGLS_tree = gls_p(y, x, Ch), GLS_borrowing = gls_p(y, x, V_borrow)) }) rowMeans(p < 0.05) # false positive rates #> PGLS_tree GLS_borrowing #> 0.6067 0.0600 The GLS that knows the contact structure has close to the nominal 5% false positive rate. In practice the network and \(h\) are unknown, so they have to be modeled: neighbor-graph models (Towner et al. 2012) and spatial covariance components (Section 13.10) are approximations to \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B}^\top\) in which the contact structure is represented by geographic proximity and its strength is estimated from the data. E Technical Notes: Methods from Evolutionary Biology This appendix collects the technical material behind Chapters 15 to 17: simulation code, derivations and complete input files that would interrupt the argument of those chapters. Each section corresponds to one chapter and can be read, and run, on its own; every code chunk recreates the data it needs. Chapter 18 has no technical notes. E.1 Chapter 15: Critiques, Pitfalls and Controversies E.1.1 A robustness study for the forty-language scenario The worked scenario of Section 15.13 asks whether borrowing between two subgroups could move a disputed language from one to the other, and whether it changes the amount of change on the tree, on which dates depend. This section gives a small simulation study of that question. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10 it is a test of robustness under misspecification: the data are generated with borrowing and uneven missingness, and analyzed with methods that assume neither. In a real application the tree, the rates and the pattern of missing cells would be taken from the fitted model and the real data, and the inference would be the full Bayesian analysis; here, to keep the code fast, we simulate the tree and use neighbor-joining and maximum likelihood branch lengths on a fixed topology. The simulator works on meanings, as in Chapter 17: each meaning has its own replacement rate, drawn from a gamma distribution, and every replacement creates a new cognate class. Missing cells are concentrated in twelve poorly documented languages. Borrowing copies the word of a random member of a donor subgroup into members of a recipient subgroup, with a higher rate for one disputed language of the recipient subgroup. library(phangorn) set.seed(1510) n_lang <- 40 tree40 <- phytools::pbtree(n = n_lang, scale = 1, tip.label = sprintf("L%02d", seq_len(n_lang))) # two non-sister clades of 5 to 10 languages with a stem branch long # enough to be recoverable: recipient A and donor B clades <- lapply(Ntip(tree40) + seq_len(tree40$Nnode), function(nd) tree40$tip.label[unlist(Descendants(tree40, nd, "tips"))]) sizes <- lengths(clades) nodes <- Ntip(tree40) + seq_len(tree40$Nnode) stem <- tree40$edge.length[match(nodes, tree40$edge[, 2])] cand <- clades[sizes >= 5 & sizes <= 10 & !is.na(stem) & stem > 0.05] pick <- NULL for (i in seq_along(cand)) for (j in seq_along(cand)) { if (is.null(pick) && i < j && !length(intersect(cand[[i]], cand[[j]])) && !is.monophyletic(tree40, c(cand[[i]], cand[[j]]))) pick <- c(i, j) } group_A <- cand[[pick[1]]]; group_B <- cand[[pick[2]]] disputed <- group_A[1] poor <- sample(setdiff(tree40$tip.label, c(group_A, group_B)), 12) sim_meanings <- function(tree, n_mean = 200, mean_rate = 2, shape = 1) { tree <- reorder(tree, "cladewise") rates <- rgamma(n_mean, shape, shape / mean_rate) st <- matrix(0L, Ntip(tree) + tree$Nnode, n_mean) next_id <- 1L for (i in seq_len(nrow(tree$edge))) { p <- tree$edge[i, 1]; ch <- tree$edge[i, 2] hit <- rpois(n_mean, rates * tree$edge.length[i]) > 0 st[ch, ] <- st[p, ] st[ch, hit] <- next_id + seq_len(sum(hit)) - 1L next_id <- next_id + sum(hit) } m <- st[seq_len(Ntip(tree)), ] rownames(m) <- tree$tip.label m } borrow <- function(m, b) { # A copies from B; disputed copies more for (j in seq_len(ncol(m))) { for (l in group_A) { p <- if (l == disputed) 2 * b else b / 2 if (runif(1) < p) m[l, j] <- m[sample(group_B, 1), j] } } m } add_missing <- function(m) { # uneven documentation for (l in rownames(m)) { p <- if (l %in% poor) 0.5 else 0.1 m[l, runif(ncol(m)) < p] <- NA } m } to_binary <- function(m) { # one 0/1 column per cognate class cols <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(m)), function(j) { cl <- sort(unique(na.omit(m[, j]))) x <- sapply(cl, function(k) ifelse(m[, j] == k, "1", "0")) x <- matrix(x, nrow(m)) x[is.na(m[, j]), ] <- "?" x }) b <- do.call(cbind, cols) rownames(b) <- rownames(m) b[, colSums(b == "1") < nrow(b), drop = FALSE] } For each level of borrowing, we simulate ten datasets, infer a neighbor-joining tree from Hamming distances, and record four quantities: the normalized RF distance to the true tree, whether the recipient subgroup is recovered as a clade, whether the disputed language is placed with the donor subgroup, and the total length of the tree under a binary model with branch lengths optimized on the inferred topology (a stand-in for the amount of change from which dates are derived). one_run <- function(b) { m <- add_missing(borrow(sim_meanings(tree40), b)) d <- phyDat(to_binary(m), type = "USER", levels = c("0", "1"), ambiguity = "?") nj <- NJ(dist.hamming(d)) fit <- optim.pml(pml(nj, d), optEdge = TRUE, optNni = FALSE, control = pml.control(trace = 0)) c(b = b, RF = RF.dist(nj, tree40, normalize = TRUE, rooted = FALSE), A_is_clade = is.monophyletic(unroot(nj), group_A), disputed_with_B = is.monophyletic(unroot(nj), c(group_B, disputed)), tree_length = sum(fit$tree$edge.length)) } res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3), function(b) t(replicate(10, one_run(b))))) round(aggregate(cbind(RF, A_is_clade, disputed_with_B, tree_length) ~ b, data = as.data.frame(res), FUN = mean), 3) #> b RF A_is_clade disputed_with_B tree_length #> 1 0.0 0.392 1.0 0.0 1.702 #> 2 0.1 0.411 1.0 0.0 1.703 #> 3 0.2 0.419 0.9 0.0 1.743 #> 4 0.3 0.454 0.0 0.9 1.788 The output shows the pattern of Section 15.4 in a larger tree. The overall RF distance changes little. The recipient subgroup is recovered in every replicate without borrowing, but once borrowing is strong enough the disputed language is placed with the donors instead, and the recipient subgroup is no longer a clade. The total length of the tree also changes, here growing, because borrowed words that conflict with the inferred tree must be explained as extra changes; in a dated analysis the effect on node ages depends on where the conflict falls, which is why the check must be run with the real model. In a real study, a borrowing rate of the size suggested by the flagged loans would be simulated, and if it moves the disputed language as often as the real analysis places it in the other subgroup, the lexical data cannot decide the question. The same design, with the Bayesian analysis in place of neighbor-joining, gives the corresponding check for dates. E.2 Chapter 16: The Biologist’s Toolbox This section collects the simulators and derivations behind the discussion of sorting and borrowing in Chapter 16. Everything below runs in a fresh R session. E.2.1 A coalescent simulator for concept trees sim_msc_tree() simulates one concept-level genealogy inside a language tree whose branch lengths are in coalescent units. Each lineage is stored as a Newick string together with its height above the present. Working from the youngest internal node of the language tree to the oldest, the lineages entering each branch coalesce at rate \(k(k-1)/2\) (Equation (16.1)) until the top of the branch is reached; the survivors are passed to the parent branch, and the root branch is open-ended, so that all lineages eventually coalesce. library(phangorn) library(phytools) set.seed(1601) # Coalesce a pool of lineages from height h_start until h_end (or until one # lineage is left). Each lineage is a Newick string plus its height. coalesce_branch <- function(pool, h_start, h_end) { t <- h_start while (length(pool) > 1) { k <- length(pool) t <- t + rexp(1, rate = k * (k - 1) / 2) if (t > h_end) break pick <- sample(k, 2) a <- pool[[pick[1]]]; b <- pool[[pick[2]]] merged <- list(nwk = sprintf("(%s:%.6f,%s:%.6f)", a$nwk, t - a$h, b$nwk, t - b$h), h = t) pool <- c(pool[-pick], list(merged)) } pool } # Simulate one concept (gene) tree inside an ultrametric language tree `sp` sim_msc_tree <- function(sp) { ntip <- Ntip(sp) height <- max(node.depth.edgelength(sp)) - node.depth.edgelength(sp) pools <- vector("list", ntip + sp$Nnode) for (i in seq_len(ntip)) pools[[i]] <- list(list(nwk = sp$tip.label[i], h = 0)) internal <- (ntip + 1):(ntip + sp$Nnode) for (node in internal[order(height[internal])]) { kids <- sp$edge[sp$edge[, 1] == node, 2] pools[[node]] <- do.call(c, lapply(kids, function(k) coalesce_branch(pools[[k]], height[k], height[node]))) } root_pool <- coalesce_branch(pools[[ntip + 1]], height[ntip + 1], Inf) read.tree(text = paste0(root_pool[[1]]$nwk, ";")) } We check the simulator against Equation (16.2) for three languages. In the vocabulary of Section 6.10 this is implementation validation: it shows that the code computes what the coalescent says, and nothing about whether words follow the coalescent. T_grid <- c(0.02, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3) p_sim <- sapply(T_grid, function(T) { sp3 <- read.tree(text = sprintf("((A:1,B:1):%f,C:%f);", T, 1 + T)) mean(replicate(400, is.monophyletic(sim_msc_tree(sp3), c("A", "B")))) }) curve(1 - 2/3 * exp(-x), from = 0, to = 3.2, ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1, xlab = "Internal branch length T (coalescent units)", ylab = "P(concept tree matches language tree)") points(T_grid, p_sim, pch = 19) abline(h = 1/3, lty = 2) Figure E.1: Probability that a concept tree matches the language tree ((A,B),C) as a function of the internal branch length T in coalescent units. Points: proportion of 400 simulated concept trees with A and B as sisters. Curve: the analytical result of Equation (16.2). The dashed line marks 1/3, the value expected if the concept trees carried no information about the language tree. The simulated proportions lie on the analytical curve (Figure E.1). When the internal branch is short in coalescent units, concept trees are only weakly informative about the language tree. E.2.2 The token model and its coalescent limit The model. A speech community has \(N\) speakers, and each speaker uses one word, of some cognate class, for a given concept. In each generation every learner chooses a model in the previous generation and copies its word; with probability \(u\) the learner instead innovates a word of a new class (the infinitely-many-alleles assumption: every innovation is new). Let \(
u_i\) be the number of learners who copy speaker \(i\), so that \(\sum_i 
u_i = N\). Under neutral copying each learner chooses a model uniformly at random, \((
u_1, \ldots, 
u_N)\) is multinomial with equal probabilities, and the model is the Wright-Fisher model (Wright 1931). More generally, if the joint distribution of the \(
u_i\) is exchangeable (no speaker is favoured a priori) and the same in every generation, the model is a Cannings model, which includes the Moran model (Moran 1950) and models with highly variable numbers of imitators. Pair coalescence. Follow two tokens back one generation. They have the same parent token with probability \[ egin{equation} c_N =  rac{\mathbb{E}[
u_1(

The time back to their common ancestor is geometric with mean \(1/c_N\) generations, and \(N_e = 1/c_N\) is the coalescent effective size of the community. The Kingman limit. If \(c_N 	o 0\) as \(N\) grows and simultaneous mergers of three lineages are rare compared with mergers of two, in the sense that \[ egin{equation}  rac{\mathbb{E}[

u_1-2)]}{N^2 c_N} 	o 0, 	ag{E.2} \end{equation}\] then the genealogy of a sample of \(n\) tokens, with time measured in units of \(1/c_N\) generations, converges to Kingman’s coalescent, in which each pair of lineages merges at rate 1 and the total rate with \(k\) lineages is \(k(k-1)/2\) (Kingman 1982; Möhle and Sagitov 2001). Neutral Wright-Fisher and Moran copying satisfy the condition. If the condition fails because single speakers are occasionally copied by a non-negligible fraction of the community, the limit is a \(\Lambda\)-coalescent, in which several lineages can merge at once (Möhle and Sagitov 2001; Eldon and Wakeley 2006). Innovation on the genealogy. Innovations occur on each lineage with probability \(u\) per generation, that is, at rate \(u N_e = 	heta/2\) per coalescent time unit, with \(	heta = 2 N_e u\). Because every innovation creates a new class, the cognate classes of a sample are the partition obtained by cutting the genealogy at the innovations, and their distribution is given by Ewens’ sampling formula. Two consequences are used in the chapter. Two tokens belong to the same class with probability \(1/(1 + 	heta)\), and the expected number of classes among \(n\) tokens is \[ egin{equation} \mathbb{E}[K_n] = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}  rac{	heta}{	heta + i}. 	ag{E.3} \end{equation}\] The replacement rate. A new class starts in one speaker. Under neutral copying its probability of eventually being used by everyone is \(1/N\), and about \(Nu\) new classes arise per generation, so the class that is fixed in a community is replaced at rate \(Nu 	imes 1/N = u\) per generation, independently of \(N\). If a new class has a fixed advantage \(s\) in copying, its fixation probability in the haploid Wright-Fisher model is approximately \((1 - e^{-2s})/(1 - e^{-2Ns})\), and the replacement rate \(Nu(1 - e^{-2s})/(1 - e^{-2Ns})\) grows with \(N\) when \(s > 0\) and shrinks with \(N\) when \(s < 0\). Whether rates of lexical change depend on community size (Section 9.10) is therefore a question about whether replacement is neutral. Several communities. A language split divides a community into two that copy only from themselves. Two tokens from different daughter communities cannot share a parent until their ancestry reaches the ancestral community, so, backward in time, lineages coalesce within each branch of the language tree according to the coalescent of that branch and merge into a common pool at the split. This is the multispecies coalescent (Rannala and Yang 2003), with the length of a branch in coalescent units equal to its length in generations divided by its \(N_e\) (or \(\int dt / N_e(t)\) if the size changes). The triplet result of Equation (16.2) follows as in the chapter. If a learner in community \(i\) copies a model in community \(j\) with probability \(m_{ij}\), then, backward in time, a lineage in \(i\) moves to \(j\) at rate \(m_{ij}\) per generation, and the genealogy is a structured coalescent with migration rather than the MSC. A founder event, in which a daughter community starts from a few speakers, is a short branch of very small \(N_e\), and therefore a burst of coalescence at the split. Conformity. Under the conformist rule of the chapter, a learner meets a first model and two further models; if the two further models agree, the learner adopts their word with probability \(c\), and otherwise copies the first model. For a class at frequency \(x\), the probability that a learner adopts it is \[ egin{equation} g(x) = c\,x^2 +  ig(1 - c\,[x^2 + (1-x)^2] ig)\,x = x + c\,x(1-x)(2x-1), 	ag{E.4} \end{equation}\] when there are two classes. The term \(c\,x(1-x)(2x-1)\) is frequency-dependent selection: it pushes a class below frequency \(1/2\) down and a class above \(1/2\) up. A new innovation starts at frequency \(1/N\) and is selected against until it happens to drift towards \(1/2\), so its fixation probability is far below \(1/N\), polymorphism is lower than Ewens’ formula predicts, and the replacement rate is lower than \(u\). The genealogy of tokens is affected less, because the rule chooses among speakers of the same class, as the chapter’s simulation shows. In general, when copying depends on the classes of the models, the genealogy and the classes are no longer independent, and the genealogy is not Kingman’s coalescent; for selection it can be represented by the ancestral selection graph (Neuhauser and Krone 1997). Prestige. Under the prestige rule, in each generation with probability \(\varepsilon\) a fraction \(\psi\) of the learners copy one speaker. Two tokens then share a parent with probability \[ egin{equation} c_N \approx  rac{1}{N} + \varepsilon \psi^2, 	ag{E.5} \end{equation}\] and three share a parent with probability about \(\varepsilon \psi^3\), which is not negligible compared with \(c_N\) when \(\varepsilon\psi^2\) is comparable to \(1/N\). Condition (E.2) fails, and the genealogy is the \(\Lambda\)-coalescent of Eldon and Wakeley (2006). Because one speaker is imitated for every concept at once, mergers in different concepts happen in the same generations, so concepts are not independent loci. Checking the simulator. The functions below are those of the chapter. We run the neutral model for several innovation probabilities and compare the number of classes per concept among all \(N\) speakers with Equation (E.3), and we compare the prestige curve with the geometric prediction \(1 - (1 - c_N)^t\) from Equation (E.5). Both are implementation checks. # Speech community: speakers in rows, concepts in columns; `cls` holds the # cognate class each speaker uses, `tag` the ancestor of the token at a # reference time, so that genealogies can be followed forward in time. choose_models <- function(cls, bias, conform = 0.5, eps = 0.1, psi = 0.5) { N <- nrow(cls); K <- ncol(cls) col <- rep(seq_len(K), each = N) draw <- function() sample.int(N, N * K, replace = TRUE) par <- draw() # neutral: a random model if (bias == "conformist") { # two further models that agree win p2 <- draw(); p3 <- draw() agree <- cls[cbind(p2, col)] == cls[cbind(p3, col)] use <- agree & runif(N * K) < conform par[use] <- p2[use] } if (bias == "prestige" && runif(1) < eps) { # one speaker copied by many fans <- rep(runif(N) < psi, K) par[fans] <- sample.int(N, 1) } cbind(par, col) # (model, concept) for every learner } learn <- function(state, u, bias, ...) { idx <- choose_models(state$cls, bias, ...) d <- dim(state$cls) cls <- matrix(state$cls[idx], d[1], d[2]) inn <- runif(length(cls)) < u # innovation: a new class cls[inn] <- state$next_id + seq_len(sum(inn)) list(cls = cls, tag = matrix(state$tag[idx], d[1], d[2]), next_id = state$next_id + sum(inn)) } pair_identity <- function(m) { # P(two distinct speakers share a label) N <- nrow(m) mean(apply(m, 2, function(x) { n <- tabulate(match(x, unique(x))) sum(n * (n - 1)) / (N * (N - 1)) })) } run_bias <- function(bias, N = 30, K = 400, u = 0.01, t_max = 2 * N, every = 3, ...) { st <- list(cls = matrix(1L, N, K), tag = matrix(1L, N, K), next_id = 1L) for (i in seq_len(4 * N)) st <- learn(st, u, bias, ...) # burn-in st$tag[] <- seq_len(N) # the reference time out <- NULL for (t in seq_len(t_max)) { st <- learn(st, u, bias, ...) if (t %% every == 0) out <- rbind(out, c(T = t / N, coal = pair_identity(st$tag))) } list(curve = out, classes = mean(apply(st$cls, 2, function(x) length(unique(x))))) } set.seed(1608) N <- 30 ewens <- function(theta, n) sum(theta / (theta + 0:(n - 1))) check_u <- sapply(c(0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02), function(u) { s <- run_bias("neutral", N = N, K = 300, u = u, t_max = 3) c(u = u, simulated = s$classes, ewens = ewens(2 * N * u, N)) }) round(t(check_u), 3) #> u simulated ewens #> [1,] 0.002 1.430 1.454 #> [2,] 0.005 2.027 2.069 #> [3,] 0.010 3.047 2.967 #> [4,] 0.020 4.640 4.456 prest <- run_bias("prestige", N = N, K = 300) c_N <- 1 / N + 0.1 * 0.5^2 round(cbind(prest$curve, geometric = 1 - (1 - c_N)^(prest$curve[, "T"] * N), kingman_N = 1 - exp(-prest$curve[, "T"]))[c(5, 10, 15, 20), ], 3) #> T coal geometric kingman_N #> [1,] 0.5 0.536 0.594 0.393 #> [2,] 1.0 0.713 0.835 0.632 #> [3,] 1.5 0.930 0.933 0.777 #> [4,] 2.0 0.962 0.973 0.865 The neutral simulations reproduce Ewens’ expectation, and the prestige curve follows the geometric prediction with \(c_N \approx 0.058\), an effective size of about 17 for a community of 30 speakers, not the Kingman curve for \(N = 30\). The occasional large jumps in the prestige curve are the multiple mergers. E.2.3 The lexical \(D\) statistic Null expectation. Take four languages with tree \((((P_1, P_2), P_3), O)\), one token sampled from each, and an infinitely-many-classes model of innovation. Write \(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_O\) for the classes. A meaning is an ABBA pattern if \(X_2 = X_3 
eq X_1 = X_O\) and a BABA pattern if \(X_1 = X_3 
eq X_2 = X_O\). Suppose that \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are founded by the same split from the same ancestral community, follow the same copying rule after the split, are sampled in the same way, and exchange no words with \(P_3\) or \(O\). Then the joint distribution of \((X_1, X_2, X_3, X_O)\) is unchanged when \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are swapped, and the swap turns every ABBA pattern into a BABA pattern. Hence \(\mathbb{E}[n_{	ext{ABBA}}] = \mathbb{E}[n_{	ext{BABA}}]\), and \(D\) of Equation (16.3) has expectation zero. The argument needs exchangeability of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), not neutral copying or a Kingman genealogy, which is why the test survives conformity and prestige when both sister languages are subject to them. It does not need equal replacement rates either: both patterns require that neither sampled token acquired a new class after the split of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), so a difference in innovation rates multiplies both expected counts by the same factor. It fails if the sister languages differ in their copying rules (a conformist \(P_1\) retains the commonest ancestral class more often), in the way they were documented (more synonyms recorded for \(P_2\) give it more chances to share), if the ancestors of \(P_2\) and \(P_3\) were neighbouring dialects of a structured ancestral community, and, by design, if \(P_2\) or \(P_1\) borrowed from \(P_3\). Standard error. Under the null, each informative meaning is ABBA or BABA with probability \(1/2\), so with \(n = n_{	ext{ABBA}} + n_{	ext{BABA}}\) independent informative meanings, \(n_{	ext{ABBA}}\) is binomial and \(D\) has standard error \(1/\sqrt{n}\). Meanings linked by polysemy, by shared semantic fields or by prestige effects are not independent; a delete-one-block jackknife over \(B\) blocks of meanings then gives \[ egin{equation} \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(D)^2 =  rac{B-1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B}  ig(D_{(-b)} -  ar D ig)^2, 	ag{E.6} \end{equation}\] where \(D_{(-b)}\) is the statistic computed without block \(b\) and \( ar D\) is their mean. A simulation. We simulate concept trees for four languages with sim_msc_tree(), place innovations on each concept tree as a Poisson process with rate \(	heta/2 = 0.5\) per coalescent unit, and read off the classes. In a proportion \(b\) of meanings, \(P_2\) borrows its word from \(P_3\) (using the regrafting of the chapter). The function lexical_D() computes the patterns from a long table with the CLDF columns used in Chapter 17, so it can be applied unchanged to real data. This is a parameter-recovery exercise for the test. set.seed(1609) lang4 <- read.tree(text = "(((P1:1,P2:1):0.5,P3:1.5):1,O:2.5);") # classes at the tips: cut the concept tree at Poisson innovations classes_on_tree <- function(g, rate = 0.5) { hit <- rpois(nrow(g$edge), rate * g$edge.length) > 0 lab <- integer(Ntip(g) + g$Nnode) # class 0 at the root for (i in seq_len(nrow(g$edge))) { # edges in preorder lab[g$edge[i, 2]] <- if (hit[i]) g$edge[i, 2] else lab[g$edge[i, 1]] } setNames(lab[seq_len(Ntip(g))], g$tip.label) } borrow_into <- function(g, recipient, donor, t_contact = 0.3) { g2 <- drop.tip(g, recipient) bind.tip(g2, recipient, where = which(g2$tip.label == donor), position = t_contact, edge.length = t_contact) } simulate_cognate_table <- function(n_meanings, b) { do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_meanings), function(i) { g <- reorder(sim_msc_tree(lang4), "cladewise") if (runif(1) < b) g <- reorder(borrow_into(g, "P2", "P3"), "cladewise") x <- classes_on_tree(g) data.frame(Language_ID = names(x), Parameter_ID = sprintf("C%03d", i), Cognateset_ID = paste0(i, "-", x)) })) } lexical_D <- function(cog, p1, p2, p3, o, n_blocks = 20) { w <- tapply(cog$Cognateset_ID, list(cog$Parameter_ID, cog$Language_ID), function(z) z[1]) # one form per language and meaning w <- w[stats::complete.cases(w[, c(p1, p2, p3, o)]), , drop = FALSE] abba <- w[, p2] == w[, p3] & w[, p1] == w[, o] & w[, p1] != w[, p2] baba <- w[, p1] == w[, p3] & w[, p2] == w[, o] & w[, p1] != w[, p2] d_of <- function(k) (sum(abba[k]) - sum(baba[k])) / (sum(abba[k]) + sum(baba[k])) blocks <- cut(seq_len(nrow(w)), n_blocks, labels = FALSE) d_jack <- sapply(seq_len(n_blocks), function(b) d_of(blocks != b)) se <- sqrt((n_blocks - 1) / n_blocks * sum((d_jack - mean(d_jack))^2)) D <- d_of(rep(TRUE, nrow(w))) c(ABBA = sum(abba), BABA = sum(baba), D = D, SE = se, z = D / se) } round(rbind( `no borrowing` = lexical_D(simulate_cognate_table(1000, 0), "P1", "P2", "P3", "O"), `b = 0.1` = lexical_D(simulate_cognate_table(1000, 0.1), "P1", "P2", "P3", "O")), 3) #> ABBA BABA D SE z #> no borrowing 0 1 -1 NaN NaN #> b = 0.1 3 0 1 0 Inf Without borrowing the two patterns are about equally frequent and \(|z|\) is small; with a tenth of the meanings borrowed from \(P_3\) into \(P_2\), ABBA patterns are in clear excess. Real applications need the robustness studies described in the chapter, because the simulation shares every assumption of the null model except the borrowing. The input files and the output of every run are kept in the folder software-runs/ of the book’s repository, whose README.md lists the program versions, run times and diagnostics. E.3.1 Plotting helpers The chapter draws its trees with ggtree and its split networks with phangorn. Two helpers keep the labels of these figures readable. Both are pure functions, defined in hidden chunks of the chapter, and are printed here. net_labels() labels the tips of a network drawn with plot(..., show.tip.label = FALSE). It needs the object that plot() returns for a network, whose .plot$vertices element holds the coordinates of the vertices. Each label is first placed just outside its tip, on the line from the centre of the network through the tip. Overlapping labels are then pushed apart vertically, pair by pair, until no two overlap, and labels that had to move far from their tip are joined to it by a thin grey line. # Tip labels for a network drawn with show.tip.label = FALSE: each label starts # just outside its tip (away from the network's centre); overlapping labels are # then pushed apart vertically and joined to their tips by thin grey lines. net_labels <- function(pn, labels, col = "black", cex = 0.7) { v <- pn$.plot$vertices[seq_along(labels), , drop = FALSE] d <- sweep(v, 2, colMeans(pn$.plot$vertices)) u <- d / sqrt(rowSums(d^2)) w <- strwidth(labels, cex = cex, font = 3) * 1.1 h <- strheight("Lg", cex = cex, font = 3) * 1.5 lab <- v + u * (0.5 * w + 0.5 * h)[row(u)] for (iter in 1:500) { moved <- FALSE for (i in seq_len(nrow(lab) - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):nrow(lab)) { ox <- (w[i] + w[j]) / 2 - abs(lab[i, 1] - lab[j, 1]) oy <- h - abs(lab[i, 2] - lab[j, 2]) if (ox > 0 && oy > 0) { s <- if (lab[i, 2] >= lab[j, 2]) 1 else -1 lab[i, 2] <- lab[i, 2] + s * (oy / 2 + 1e-9) lab[j, 2] <- lab[j, 2] - s * (oy / 2 + 1e-9) moved <- TRUE } } if (!moved) break } far <- sqrt(rowSums((lab - v)^2)) > 0.9 * (0.5 * w + 0.5 * h) segments(v[far, 1], v[far, 2], lab[far, 1] - u[far, 1] * w[far] / 2, lab[far, 2] - u[far, 2] * h / 3, col = "grey60", lwd = 0.6) text(lab[, 1], lab[, 2], labels, cex = cex, font = 3, col = col) } support_layers() returns two ggtree text layers for the node labels of a tree, such as bootstrap values or clade credibilities. Each value is placed at the right end of its stem branch: above the branch for the upper of two daughters and below it for the lower one, so that no value crosses the vertical line of its parent. Labels listed in drop (for example an empty root label) are skipped. It is used as ggtree(tree) + support_layers(2.6). # Support values: each one sits at the right end of its stem branch, above the # branch for an upper daughter and below it for a lower daughter, so it never # crosses the parent's vertical line (which spans only between the daughters). support_layers <- function(size, drop = "") { pick <- function(up) function(d) { py <- d$y[match(d$parent, d$node)] d[!d$isTip & d$node != d$parent & !is.na(d$label) & !d$label %in% drop & (d$y >= py) == up, ] } list(geom_text(data = pick(TRUE), aes(label = label), size = size, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.4, color = "grey30"), geom_text(data = pick(FALSE), aes(label = label), size = size, hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.4, color = "grey30")) } E.3.2 The BEAST 2 input file The excerpt below shows the components of the BEAST 2.7 analysis of the toy family in Section 17.10.3: the restriction-site model with estimated frequencies and gamma rate variation, a strict clock, a Yule tree prior, the subgroup-D calibration and the root-age prior of the MrBayes block. Some operators, priors and log entries have been left out (...). The full file, about 140 lines long, is software-runs/beast2/toy_beast.xml, and it runs as it stands in BEAST 2.7.7. The data block is the one written by chunk workflow-beast-data of the chapter: one sequence element per language, preceded by a dummy all-absent column that the ascertained, excludefrom and excludeto attributes remove from the likelihood. <beast version="2.7" namespace="beast.base.core:beast.base.inference:..."> <data id="cognates" spec="Alignment" dataType="binary" ascertained="true" excludefrom="0" excludeto="1"> ... </data> <taxonset id="subgroupD" spec="TaxonSet"> <taxon id="L21" spec="Taxon"/> ... </taxonset> <run id="mcmc" spec="MCMC" chainLength="3000000"> <!-- 1. State: everything the MCMC samples --> <state id="state"> <tree id="Tree" name="stateNode"> <taxonset id="TaxonSet.cognates" spec="TaxonSet" alignment="@cognates"/> </tree> <parameter id="birthRate" name="stateNode" lower="0.0">1.0</parameter> <parameter id="clockRate" name="stateNode" lower="0.0">0.1</parameter> <parameter id="gammaShape" name="stateNode" lower="0.0">1.0</parameter> <parameter id="freqParameter" name="stateNode" dimension="2" lower="0.0" upper="1.0">0.5</parameter> </state> <init spec="RandomTree" initial="@Tree" taxa="@cognates" rootHeight="6.0"> ... </init> <!-- 2. Posterior = prior x likelihood --> <distribution id="posterior" spec="CompoundDistribution"> <distribution id="prior" spec="CompoundDistribution"> <distribution id="YuleModel" spec="YuleModel" tree="@Tree" birthDiffRate="@birthRate"/> <distribution id="clockRatePrior" spec="Prior" x="@clockRate"> <distr spec="beast.base.inference.distribution.LogNormalDistributionModel" M="-2.3" S="1.0"/> </distribution> <!-- calibration: an MRCA prior on a set of taxa --> <distribution id="subgroupD.prior" spec="MRCAPrior" tree="@Tree" taxonset="@subgroupD" monophyletic="true"> <distr spec="beast.base.inference.distribution.Uniform" lower="0.1" upper="1.1"/> </distribution> ... </distribution> <distribution id="likelihood" spec="CompoundDistribution"> <distribution id="treeLikelihood" spec="TreeLikelihood" data="@cognates" tree="@Tree"> <siteModel spec="SiteModel" gammaCategoryCount="4" shape="@gammaShape"> <parameter name="mutationRate" estimate="false">1.0</parameter> <!-- two-state model with estimated frequencies --> <substModel spec="GeneralSubstitutionModel"> <parameter name="rates" dimension="2" estimate="false">1.0</parameter> <frequencies spec="Frequencies" frequencies="@freqParameter"/> </substModel> </siteModel> <branchRateModel spec="StrictClockModel" clock.rate="@clockRate"/> </distribution> </distribution> </distribution> <!-- 3. Operators: proposals for each state node --> <operator id="subtreeSlide" spec="SubtreeSlide" tree="@Tree" weight="15.0"/> <operator id="clockRateScaler" spec="ScaleOperator" parameter="@clockRate" scaleFactor="0.75" weight="5.0"/> ... <!-- 4.
