The mutationRate of the site model is fixed at 1, so that the clock rate alone sets the number of expected changes per unit of time. Replacing the strict clock or the substitution model changes only the branchRateModel or the substModel element, together with the parameters, priors and operators they need. E.3.3 The RevBayes script This is the complete script of Section 17.10.5, as it was run with RevBayes 1.4.1 on the file toy_cognates_standard.nex written by the chapter. It specifies an unrooted analysis under the symmetric two-state Mk model with gamma rate variation, conditioned on variable characters, with two independent runs. # toy_cognates.Rev -- run with: rb toy_cognates.Rev # the CHARSETs split the file into one matrix per meaning; rejoin them data <- concatenate(readDiscreteCharacterData("toy_cognates_standard.nex")) taxa <- data.taxa() n_taxa <- data.ntaxa() n_branches <- 2 * n_taxa - 3 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() # tree prior: uniform topology, exponential branch lengths topology ~ dnUniformTopology(taxa) moves.append( mvNNI(topology, weight = n_taxa) ) moves.append( mvSPR(topology, weight = n_taxa / 5.0) ) for (i in 1:n_branches) { br_lens[i] ~ dnExponential(10.0) moves.append( mvScale(br_lens[i], weight = 1.0) ) } TL := sum(br_lens) phylogeny := treeAssembly(topology, br_lens) # substitution model: symmetric two-state Mk model with gamma rates Q <- fnJC(2) alpha ~ dnExponential(1.0) moves.append( mvScale(alpha, weight = 2.0) ) site_rates := fnDiscretizeGamma(alpha, alpha, 4) # likelihood, conditioned on variable characters (Mkv) seq ~ dnPhyloCTMC(tree = phylogeny, Q = Q, siteRates = site_rates, type = "Standard", coding = "variable") seq.clamp(data) mymodel = model(phylogeny) monitors.append( mnModel(filename = "output/toy.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnFile(filename = "output/toy.trees", printgen = 10, phylogeny) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 1000, TL) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 2, combine = "mixed") mymcmc.run(generations = 10000) trace = readTreeTrace("output/toy.trees", treetype = "non-clock") map_tree = mapTree(trace, "output/toy_map.tre") q() The moves define the proposals of the MCMC: NNI and SPR moves on the topology, and scaling moves on every branch length and on the gamma shape. The monitors write the parameters to output/toy.log every 10 iterations, the trees to output/toy.trees, and a progress line to the screen. readTreeTrace() reads the sampled trees and mapTree() summarizes them as the maximum a posteriori tree. Run times and convergence diagnostics are reported in Section 17.10.5. References

F Software This appendix is an annotated guide to the software used in linguistic phylogenetics. It covers Bayesian platforms and their extension packages, maximum-likelihood, parsimony and distance programs, network software, tools for summarizing and visualizing trees, tools for preparing linguistic data, and the R and Python libraries most often used alongside them. For each program we say what it does, what it is typically used for with language data, and where to obtain it. Software changes quickly: version numbers, package names and web addresses given here were correct at the time of writing, but readers should always check the current documentation and cite the version they actually used. The workflow chapter (Chapter 17) shows how several of these programs fit together in practice. F.1 Choosing software No single program does everything. Table F.1 maps the common tasks of a linguistic phylogenetic project to the programs most often used for them. It is the most widely used program for dated language phylogenies. Its core supports a wide range of substitution models (including binary, covarion and general discrete-state models suitable for cognate data), strict and relaxed clocks, tree priors from the Yule and birth-death families and the coalescent, node calibrations, and flexible priors on all parameters. Models are specified in an XML file, usually created with the graphical program BEAUti; the companion programs LogCombiner, TreeAnnotator and DensiTree combine runs, build summary trees and visualize tree sets. Much of BEAST 2’s power comes from its package system: extensions are installed from within BEAUti through the package manager. The textbook by Drummond and Bouckaert (2015) is the standard introduction. Website: https://www.beast2.org. F.2.2 BEAST 2 packages relevant to linguistics BEASTling is not a BEAST 2 package but a standalone Python program that writes BEAST 2 XML files for linguistic analyses from short configuration files (Maurits et al. 2017). It reads data in CSV or CLDF format, links languages to Glottolog, can impose Glottolog subgroups as monophyly constraints, and supports models for lexical (cognate) and typological data, rate variation across features, relaxed clocks and calibrations. Its configuration files make analyses easy to publish and reproduce. However, BEASTling has not been updated since version 1.5.1 (2021). It writes XML for BEAST 2.6, which BEAST 2.7 cannot read without renaming classes to the new beast.base namespace. It also fails to start under Python 3.14, and it needs older versions of clldutils (2.x) and pycldf (below 1.15). Chapter 17 shows a working route. Source: https://github.com/lmaurits/BEASTling. Babel is a BEAST 2 package developed by Remco Bouckaert specifically for linguistic data. It provides models and tools used in published language phylogenies, including stochastic Dollo-type and pseudo-Dollo covarion models for cognate data, ascertainment-correction schemes suitable for cognate presence/absence data, and utilities for preparing and summarizing linguistic analyses. Source: https://github.com/rbouckaert/Babel. BEAST_CLASSIC ports to BEAST 2 several models originally developed in BEAST 1, most importantly discrete-trait phylogeography with Bayesian stochastic search variable selection (BSSVS) (Lemey et al. 2009) and continuous-trait diffusion models used in continuous phylogeography. Source: https://github.com/BEAST2-Dev/beast-classic. GEO_SPHERE implements phylogeographic diffusion on the surface of a sphere and related landscape-aware diffusion models (Bouckaert 2016). Spherical diffusion avoids the distortions of planar diffusion models over large areas, which matters for language families spread across continents. Landscape-aware variants allow diffusion to depend on features such as land and water, an idea first explored for language data in the Indo-European analysis of Bouckaert et al. (2012). SA (sampled ancestors) implements the fossilized birth-death process with sampled ancestors (Gavryushkina et al. 2014), which allows sampled taxa to lie directly on the lineages leading to other taxa rather than only at the tips. For linguistics, this allows ancient languages such as Latin or Vedic Sanskrit to be modeled as possible direct ancestors of modern languages, the approach taken by Heggarty et al. (2023). Source: https://github.com/CompEvol/sampled-ancestors. ORC (optimized relaxed clock) provides a reparameterized uncorrelated relaxed clock with improved operators that make relaxed-clock analyses mix much faster (Douglas et al. 2021). Source: https://github.com/jordandouglas/ORC. bModelTest performs Bayesian site-model averaging, sampling over substitution models and rate-heterogeneity options within the MCMC rather than selecting a single model in advance (Bouckaert and Drummond 2017). It was designed for nucleotide data, but the approach of averaging over models rather than choosing one is relevant to any data type. Source: https://github.com/BEAST2-Dev/bModelTest. MASCOT implements the marginal approximation of the structured coalescent, a phylogeographic model in which migration between discrete locations is modeled within a population-genetic framework rather than as a trait evolving on a fixed tree (Müller et al. 2018). It has, to our knowledge, rarely if ever been applied to language data (Chapter 11). Source: https://github.com/CompEvol/Mascot. Model selection packages. The NS package implements nested sampling for estimating marginal likelihoods and their uncertainty (Maturana Russel et al. 2019); the MODEL_SELECTION package implements path sampling and stepping-stone sampling. Both are used to compute Bayes factors between models (Chapter 6). CoupledMCMC implements Metropolis-coupled MCMC (parallel tempering) with adaptive temperatures for BEAST 2, which can help with multimodal posteriors (Müller and Bouckaert 2020). BDSKY implements the birth-death skyline model, in which birth and death rates change through time in a piecewise-constant way (Stadler et al. 2013). Developed for epidemiology, it could be used to study changes in the rate of language diversification through time (Chapter 16). F.2.3 BEAST X and BEAST 1 BEAST 1, whose most widely cited release is BEAST 1.10 (Suchard et al. 2018), is the original BEAST, developed in parallel with BEAST 2 by a partly different team with a strong focus on viral phylodynamics and phylogeography. Its successor, BEAST X, extends the platform with new models and faster inference methods, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for many parameters (Baele et al. 2025). BEAST 1 and BEAST X provided the original implementations of discrete phylogeography with BSSVS (Lemey et al. 2009), relaxed random walk continuous phylogeography (Lemey et al. 2010) and phylogeographic generalized linear models with predictors. BEAST 1 and BEAST X files are not compatible with BEAST 2. Website: https://beast.community. F.2.4 RevBayes RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) is a Bayesian phylogenetics platform built around probabilistic graphical models. Models are written in Rev, an interpreted language resembling R, in which every random variable, deterministic function and constant is declared explicitly. This makes RevBayes the most flexible general-purpose platform: unusual combinations of models, priors and data types can be specified without programming new code. It supports discrete morphological (Mk) models and restriction-site models suitable for cognate data, relaxed clocks, a wide range of tree priors including the fossilized birth-death process, ancestral state reconstruction, stochastic character mapping, and marginal likelihood estimation by path sampling and stepping-stone sampling. The extensive tutorials (https://revbayes.github.io/tutorials/) are among the best learning resources in phylogenetics. The R package RevGadgets visualizes RevBayes output (Tribble et al. 2022). Website: https://revbayes.github.io. F.2.5 MrBayes MrBayes (Huelsenbeck and Ronquist 2001; Ronquist, Teslenko, et al. 2012) is a long-established Bayesian phylogenetics program controlled by commands in a NEXUS block. It supports restriction-site (binary) data with ascertainment options such as noabsencesites and variable, standard discrete (morphological) data, covarion models, gamma rate variation, strict and relaxed clocks, node calibrations and tip dating, and Metropolis-coupled MCMC with multiple independent runs and a built-in convergence diagnostic (the average standard deviation of split frequencies). It also estimates marginal likelihoods by stepping-stone sampling. MrBayes is fast and well documented, and is a good choice for undated or simply dated analyses of cognate data. Website: https://nbisweden.github.io/MrBayes/. F.2.6 TraitLab TraitLab is a MATLAB package that implements the stochastic Dollo model for binary trait data, in which each cognate class is born once and then may be lost independently on different lineages (Nicholls and Gray 2008). It also handles missing data and catastrophic rate changes on branches (Ryder and Nicholls 2011), and lateral transfer between lineages (Kelly and Nicholls 2017). TraitLab was developed specifically for language data and remains the reference implementation of these models (Chapter 7). It is distributed by its authors; current versions are available through code repositories linked from the publications. F.2.7 BayesTraits BayesTraits analyzes the evolution of traits on samples of phylogenetic trees (Pagel et al. 2004; Pagel and Meade 2006). It implements discrete-trait models (including the test of correlated evolution between binary traits of Pagel (1994), with reversible-jump MCMC over model structures), continuous-trait models with Pagel’s \(\lambda\), \(\kappa\) and \(\delta\) transformations, regression, variable-rates models, and ancestral state reconstruction. Because it integrates over a posterior sample of trees, it is a standard tool for comparative studies in linguistics and cultural evolution, including the word-order study of Dunn et al. (2011) (Chapter 13). It is distributed by the Evolution Group at the University of Reading. F.2.8 Other Bayesian programs PhyloBayes (Lartillot et al. 2009) implements the CAT family of site-heterogeneous profile mixture models. These models, developed for protein data, let different sites have different equilibrium frequencies. To our knowledge they have rarely if ever been applied to linguistic data, but they are relevant to the question of rate and pattern heterogeneity among meanings (Chapter 7). BAli-Phy (Redelings 2021) jointly estimates sequence alignments and phylogenies; it is a natural model for future work on the joint alignment of word forms (Chapter 16). Website: https://www.bali-phy.org. F.3 Maximum likelihood IQ-TREE (Nguyen et al. 2015; Minh, Schmidt, et al. 2020) is a fast and widely used program for maximum-likelihood tree inference. It supports binary (JC2, GTR2) and general discrete morphological (MK) models with ascertainment-bias correction (+ASC), gamma and free-rate heterogeneity, partitioned analyses, automatic model selection with ModelFinder (Kalyaanamoorthy et al. 2017), the ultrafast bootstrap (Hoang et al. 2018), and tests of tree topology. Website: https://iqtree.github.io. RAxML-NG (Kozlov et al. 2019) is the successor of RAxML, designed for speed and scalability. It supports binary data (BIN) and general multistate data, ascertainment-bias corrections (for example +ASC_LEWIS), and standard and transfer bootstrap support. Source: https://github.com/amkozlov/raxml-ng. PhyML (Guindon et al. 2010) is a widely used maximum-likelihood program with fast SPR-based tree search and approximate likelihood-ratio tests of branch support. phangorn (R; Schliep (2011)) provides maximum-likelihood inference for user-defined discrete data including binary cognate data, with ascertainment correction, model comparison and bootstrapping. It is slower than IQ-TREE or RAxML-NG but integrates seamlessly with the rest of the R ecosystem; it is used throughout this book. F.4 Parsimony and distance methods PAUP* (Swofford 2003) (Phylogenetic Analysis Using Parsimony, and other methods) is a classic program for parsimony, distance and likelihood analysis, with powerful heuristic tree searches and support for character weighting, constraints and consensus methods. Website: https://paup.phylosolutions.com. TNT (Tree analysis using New Technology) (Goloboff et al. 2008; Goloboff and Catalano 2016) is the fastest program for parsimony analysis of large datasets, with sophisticated search strategies (ratchet, sectorial searches, tree drifting and fusing) and implied weighting. Website: https://www.lillo.org.ar/phylogeny/tnt/. PHYLIP (Felsenstein 1989) (Phylogeny Inference Package) is a long-standing collection of programs for distance, parsimony (including Dollo and Camin-Sokal parsimony) and likelihood methods. Its file format, the PHYLIP format, is still widely used for data exchange. FastME (Lefort et al. 2015) implements balanced minimum-evolution tree construction from distance matrices, with tree rearrangements that improve on neighbor-joining. phangorn and ape (R) provide UPGMA, neighbor-joining, BIONJ, FastME-style minimum evolution and parsimony (Fitch and Sankoff, with the parsimony ratchet), as illustrated in Chapters 4 and 17. F.5 Networks SplitsTree (Huson and Bryant 2006) computes and displays split networks, including NeighborNet (Bryant and Moulton 2004), split decomposition and median networks, together with statistics such as delta scores. It has been the standard tool for exploratory network analysis of language data. Recent versions (SplitsTree 6) have been rewritten with an interactive interface. Source: https://github.com/husonlab/splitstree6. PhyloNet (Than et al. 2008; Wen et al. 2018) infers explicit phylogenetic networks, in which reticulation nodes represent hybridization or other horizontal events, from gene trees or sequence data, under parsimony, likelihood and Bayesian criteria. PhyloNetworks (Solís-Lemus et al. 2017) is a Julia package for estimating and analyzing explicit phylogenetic networks, including SNaQ, a pseudolikelihood method that accounts for incomplete lineage sorting (Solı́s-Lemus and Ané 2016). Source: https://github.com/JuliaPhylo/PhyloNetworks.jl. Gabmap (Nerbonne et al. 2011) is a web application for dialectometry: it computes aggregate distances between dialect sites from transcriptions or categorical data, and visualizes them with maps, clustering and multidimensional scaling. It is useful for dialect continua where tree models are inappropriate. phangorn (R) implements NeighborNet, consensus networks and delta scores, and plots split networks (Chapter 8). F.6 Convergence diagnostics, summaries and visualization Tracer (Rambaut et al. 2018) reads the parameter logs of BEAST, MrBayes and other programs, and displays traces, marginal posterior distributions, effective sample sizes and summary statistics. It is the standard first check on any Bayesian run. Source: https://github.com/beast-dev/tracer. TreeAnnotator and LogCombiner are distributed with BEAST 2 and BEAST X. LogCombiner combines and resamples log and tree files from several runs, removing burn-in; TreeAnnotator builds a summary tree (maximum clade credibility or other) with node heights and highest posterior density intervals (Heled and Bouckaert 2013). DensiTree (Bouckaert 2010), distributed with BEAST 2, draws all trees of a posterior sample on top of each other to visualize uncertainty in topology and node heights. FigTree is a graphical viewer for trees, widely used for displaying annotated BEAST trees. Source: https://github.com/rambaut/figtree. IcyTree (Vaughan 2017) is a browser-based tree viewer that handles annotated trees and networks without installation. Website: https://icytree.org. iTOL (Interactive Tree Of Life) (Letunic and Bork 2021) is an online tool for displaying and annotating large trees with associated data. Website: https://itol.embl.de. SpreaD3 (Bielejec et al. 2016) visualizes phylogeographic reconstructions from BEAST as animated maps. RWTY (Warren et al. 2017) (R) provides convergence diagnostics specifically for tree topologies, including split-frequency comparisons between runs and visualizations of tree space. F.7 Tools for linguistic data LingPy (List et al. 2017; List, Walworth, et al. 2018) is a Python library for quantitative historical linguistics. It provides phonetic alignment (including the SCA method), automated cognate detection (LexStat, SCA-based and edit-distance-based clustering, with Infomap or UPGMA-style partitioning), distance computation, and export to phylogenetic formats. Website: https://lingpy.org; source: https://github.com/lingpy/lingpy. LingRex extends LingPy with methods for partial cognate detection, correspondence pattern inference and related tasks. Source: https://github.com/lingpy/lingrex. EDICTOR (List 2017) is a web-based interactive tool for creating, inspecting and editing etymological datasets: aligning word forms, assigning cognate sets (including partial cognates) and inspecting correspondence patterns. It runs in the browser and works with the same TSV formats as LingPy. Website: https://edictor.org. cldfbench and pylexibank (Forkel and List 2020) are Python packages for creating CLDF datasets reproducibly from raw sources. Each Lexibank dataset is a cldfbench project with a conversion script that downloads or reads the original data, maps concepts to Concepticon and languages to Glottolog, segments transcriptions, and writes validated CLDF. Sources: https://github.com/cldf/cldfbench and https://github.com/lexibank/pylexibank. pycldf reads, writes and validates CLDF datasets in Python, and provides command-line tools for inspecting them. Source: https://github.com/cldf/pycldf. The CLDF specification itself is documented at https://cldf.clld.org (Forkel et al. 2018). Other CLDF ecosystem tools. pyglottolog gives programmatic access to the Glottolog data repository (https://github.com/glottolog/pyglottolog); pyconcepticon does the same for Concepticon (https://github.com/concepticon/pyconcepticon); pyclts provides the Cross-Linguistic Transcription Systems reference catalog (https://github.com/cldf-clts/pyclts); and segments tokenizes transcriptions using orthography profiles (https://github.com/cldf/segments). F.8 R packages R is the most common environment for preparing data, analyzing trees and running comparative methods. Table F.2 lists the packages most relevant to linguistic phylogenetics. F.10 Citing software Software is part of the method. A methods section should name every program and package used, with version numbers, and should cite the publications that describe them, as their authors request. For BEAST 2, the packages used (and their versions) should also be cited, since many of the models in a typical linguistic analysis come from packages rather than from the core. In R, citation("<package>") prints the preferred citation for any installed package, and sessionInfo() records the versions used. Archiving the input files (XML, Rev scripts, NEXUS files with command blocks, BEASTling configuration files) alongside the data allows others to reproduce the analysis exactly (Chapter 17). G Data Resources This appendix describes the main databases used in linguistic phylogenetics and in the comparative study of language and culture. For each resource we describe what it contains, how it is organized, how it has been used in phylogenetic work, and where to find it. Many of these resources are now published in the Cross-Linguistic Data Formats (CLDF) (Forkel et al. 2018) and archived in versioned releases on Zenodo, which makes them easy to load with the tools described in Chapter 17 and Appendix F. Most of the databases that follow the CLDF model have a web interface built with the clld toolkit, usually at an address of the form https://<name>.clld.org, and a GitHub repository with the CLDF data. Two general points apply throughout. First, always cite the specific version of a database that was used, since databases are corrected and extended between releases. Second, read the documentation on how the data were collected and coded; every database embodies decisions (which concepts, which sources, which coding conventions) that affect what it can and cannot be used for (Chapters 3 and 15). Table G.1 gives an overview. Table G.1: Overview of major data resources. Coverage figures are approximate and change between releases. Each languoid (a language, dialect or family) has a stable identifier, the Glottocode (for example stan1293 for Standard English), together with its position in a genealogical classification, geographic coordinates, macro-area, endangerment status and an extensive bibliography of descriptive sources. Glottolog’s classification is deliberately conservative: it recognizes only families whose unity has been demonstrated by the comparative method, and lists a large number of isolates and unclassified languages. This makes it a reliable scaffold, but means that its trees are mostly unresolved at higher levels and have no branch lengths. Glottocodes have become the standard identifier for linking linguistic datasets: Lexibank, Grambank, WALS (via mappings), PHOIBLE, D-PLACE and many others use them, so data from different sources can be joined by Glottocode (Chapter 17). Glottolog’s classification trees are distributed in Newick format and through its CLDF dataset (https://github.com/glottolog/glottolog-cldf), and are often used as topologies in global comparative analyses, with branch lengths assigned by rule (Chapter 13). Glottolog is published in numbered versions; analyses should cite the version used. G.1.2 Other catalogues Ethnologue is a commercial catalogue of the world’s languages with information on speaker numbers, vitality and location, identified by ISO 639-3 codes. Its classification is less conservative than Glottolog’s, and access to much of its data requires a subscription. ISO 639-3 codes, which Ethnologue maintains on behalf of the International Organization for Standardization, remain widely used and are mapped to Glottocodes by Glottolog. G.2 Lexical databases G.2.1 ASJP The Automated Similarity Judgment Program (ASJP) database (Wichmann et al. 2022) contains short word lists for a 40-item subset of the Swadesh list, transcribed in a simplified phonetic alphabet (ASJPcode) for several thousand languages and dialects. The 40 items were chosen for their stability and their usefulness for classification (Holman et al. 2008). Because every list uses the same concepts and transcription, ASJP is the largest uniform lexical dataset available. It has been used for automated classification based on normalized Levenshtein distances (Brown et al. 2008), for dating language families with a calibrated distance-based method (Holman et al. 2011), and for global phylogenies based on automatically inferred cognates (Jäger 2018). ASJP lists do not contain cognate judgments; cognacy must be inferred (Chapter 3). G.2.2 Lexibank Lexibank (List, Forkel, Greenhill, et al. 2022) is a public repository of standardized word lists. It aggregates more than a hundred published datasets, each converted to CLDF by a reproducible script, with concepts linked to Concepticon, languages linked to Glottolog, and transcriptions standardized and segmented according to the CLTS reference catalogue. Many datasets include expert cognate judgments; others contain only word forms, for which Lexibank provides automatically computed features. Lexibank datasets are hosted on GitHub (https://github.com/lexibank) and archived on Zenodo, and include CLDF versions of several of the datasets described below (for example the ABVD and datasets used in published Sino-Tibetan and other phylogenies). Lexibank is the natural starting point for any new lexical phylogenetic analysis (Chapter 17). G.2.3 Indo-European: IELex, IE-CoR and related databases IELex (the Indo-European Lexical Cognacy Database) was assembled by Michael Dunn and collaborators, building on the Swadesh-list data of Dyen et al. (1992), and was used, with modifications, in several influential Bayesian analyses of Indo-European, including Bouckaert et al. (2012) and Chang et al. (2015). Its cognate judgments and meaning definitions were criticized and revised over time. IE-CoR (Indo-European Cognate Relationships) (Heggarty et al. 2023) is a newer database designed to address these problems. It covers about 160 Indo-European languages, including ancient languages, for a list of 170 meanings, with explicit protocols for selecting the word for each meaning, for coding cognacy (including loanwords and parallel semantic shifts), and for documenting sources. It was developed from the earlier CoBL (Cognates in Basic Lexicon) project and underlies the analysis of Heggarty et al. (2023). Website: https://iecor.clld.org. The data of Ringe et al. (2002), which code lexical, phonological and morphological characters for 24 Indo-European languages, remain an important resource for character-based analyses of Indo-European, and were used in comparisons of phylogenetic methods (Nakhleh, Warnow, et al. 2005). G.2.4 Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database (ABVD) The ABVD (Greenhill et al. 2008) contains word lists for 210 basic meanings for well over a thousand Austronesian language varieties, with cognate judgments for a large subset. It underlies many of the best-known phylogenetic studies of Austronesian, including Gray et al. (2009), and has been used extensively as a scaffold for studies of cultural evolution in the Pacific (Chapter 14). The ABVD is available online (https://abvd.clld.org) and in CLDF through Lexibank. Sister databases built with the same software have been set up for some other families. G.2.5 Bantu Several lexical datasets underlie phylogenetic work on Bantu. The lexicostatistical study of Bastin et al. (1999) compiled basic vocabulary for several hundred Bantu languages, and has been reused in later work. Grollemund et al. (2015) assembled 100-meaning word lists with cognate judgments for over 400 Bantu and related languages, which were also used by Koile et al. (2022). The Bantu Lexical Reconstructions (BLR) database at the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Tervuren collects reconstructed Proto-Bantu roots, and is a resource for cognate identification. Several Bantu datasets are available in CLDF through Lexibank. G.2.6 Sino-Tibetan The Sino-Tibetan Etymological Dictionary and Thesaurus (STEDT) project at Berkeley (Matisoff 2015) compiled a large database of lexical forms from several hundred Sino-Tibetan varieties, organized by etymological sets, and published a reconstruction of Proto-Tibeto-Burman. Website: https://stedt.berkeley.edu. The datasets of Sagart et al. (2019) and Zhang et al. (2019), which include cognate judgments for basic vocabulary, are available in CLDF. G.2.7 Uralic: UraLex UraLex is a basic-vocabulary dataset for the Uralic languages, with cognate judgments and documentation of sources, compiled to support phylogenetic analyses of the family (Syrjänen et al. 2013). It has been used to examine how the choice of meaning list affects inferred Uralic trees, and as the basis of dated analyses (Honkola et al. 2013). G.2.8 Australia: Chirila Chirila (Contemporary and Historical Resources for the Indigenous Languages of Australia) (Bowern 2016) is a large database of lexical data for Australian Aboriginal languages, compiled from published and archival sources. It underlies phylogenetic studies of Pama-Nyungan (Bowern and Atkinson 2012; Bouckaert et al. 2018) and studies of lexical change in Australian languages. Website: https://doi.org/10.60600/YU/XHPJXB. G.2.9 NorthEuraLex NorthEuraLex (Dellert et al. 2020) contains word lists for over 1,000 concepts for more than a hundred languages of northern Eurasia, from Uralic, Indo-European, Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusic and other families, all in a uniform phonetic transcription. Its long concept list makes it useful for automated cognate detection, studies of sound correspondences, and comparisons across many families. Website: http://northeuralex.org. G.2.10 Intercontinental Dictionary Series and World Loanword Database The Intercontinental Dictionary Series (IDS) (Key and Comrie 2015) provides word lists for a standard list of roughly 1,300 concepts for several hundred languages, compiled from dictionaries. The World Loanword Database (WOLD) (Haspelmath and Tadmor 2009b) gives, for 41 languages from around the world, the vocabulary for a list of about 1,460 meanings together with expert judgments of whether each word is a loan, from which source, and how certain the judgment is. A companion handbook summarizes the findings (Haspelmath and Tadmor 2009a). WOLD’s “borrowability” scores for meanings are relevant to choosing meaning lists for phylogenetic analysis, and its loanword data can be used to validate borrowing detection methods (Chapter 8). Websites: https://ids.clld.org and https://wold.clld.org. G.2.11 Other lexical resources The Sound Comparisons project (https://soundcomparisons.com) provides recorded audio and transcriptions of comparable word lists for dialects and languages of several families, useful for studies of phonetic variation and dialect continua. The DiACL database (Carling et al. 2018) (Diachronic Atlas of Comparative Linguistics) combines lexical cognate data and typological data for several language families, including Indo-European, with good coverage of ancient languages; it has been used in phylogenetic studies of grammatical change. The CLDF datasets accompanying many recent phylogenetic papers, such as those for Dravidian (Kolipakam et al. 2018) and Tupi-Guarani, are often available through Lexibank or from the authors’ repositories. G.3 Concepts, polysemy and sounds G.3.1 Concepticon Concepticon (List et al. 2016) links the concept lists used in linguistics (Swadesh lists, Leipzig-Jakarta list, ASJP list, questionnaires and the concept lists of individual datasets) to a common set of concept sets with stable identifiers and definitions. Linking a dataset’s concepts to Concepticon makes it possible to combine datasets with different concept lists, to see which concepts are shared, and to compare the stability or borrowability of concepts across studies. Website: https://concepticon.clld.org. G.3.2 CLICS The Database of Cross-Linguistic Colexifications (CLICS) (List, Greenhill, et al. 2018; Rzymski et al. 2020) records cases in which a single word expresses two concepts (for example ‘tree’ and ‘wood’, or ‘arm’ and ‘hand’) across thousands of language varieties, aggregated from Lexibank datasets. Colexification networks reveal semantic associations and are relevant to modeling semantic change and to understanding why some cognate sets shift meaning. Website: https://clics.clld.org. G.3.3 CLTS The Cross-Linguistic Transcription Systems (CLTS) reference catalogue (Anderson et al. 2018) defines a standardized set of speech sounds with phonetic feature descriptions, and maps the transcription conventions of many datasets and databases (including PHOIBLE) to it. It underlies the standardization of transcriptions in Lexibank, which makes automated alignment and sound-correspondence analysis possible across datasets. Website: https://clts.clld.org. G.3.4 PHOIBLE PHOIBLE (Moran and McCloy 2019) is a database of phoneme inventories for more than two thousand languages, compiled from multiple sources (some languages have several inventories from different descriptions), with features for each segment. It is used in typological studies of sound systems and in phylogenetic comparative studies of phonological evolution (Chapters 12 and 13). Website: https://phoible.org. G.4 Structural (typological) databases G.4.1 WALS The World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS) (Dryer and Haspelmath 2013) contains data on about 190 phonological, grammatical and lexical features for about 2,600 languages, each feature compiled by a specialist and documented in a chapter. WALS was the first large typological database freely available online, and has been used in a great many comparative studies, including early phylogenetic tests of word-order correlations and studies of the stability of features (Dediu 2011; Wichmann and Holman 2009b). Its main limitation for phylogenetic work is its sparsity: most languages are coded for only a minority of features, and different features are coded for different language samples. Website: https://wals.info. G.4.2 Grambank Grambank (Skirgård et al. 2023) codes about 195 grammatical features for more than 2,400 languages, with a design that addresses the main limitations of WALS: features are mostly binary, defined with detailed coding instructions, and coded for every language in the sample from the same reference grammars, so that coverage is much more complete. It was compiled by a large team using a common questionnaire and is published in CLDF. Grambank is now the standard resource for phylogenetic comparative studies of grammar and for global analyses of structural diversity (Chapter 13). Website: https://grambank.clld.org; data: https://github.com/grambank/grambank. G.4.3 AUTOTYP AUTOTYP (Bickel et al. 2022) is a typological database built on the principle of autotypologizing: categories are defined bottom-up from the data rather than imposed in advance, and complex phenomena are coded as many fine-grained variables. It covers several thousand languages for some variables, with particular depth in morphology, alignment and clause linkage, and includes a genealogical and areal classification. Data: https://github.com/autotyp/autotyp-data. G.4.4 Other structural resources The Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures (APiCS) (Michaelis et al. 2013) provides comparable structural data for 76 pidgin and creole languages, relevant to questions about contact languages and their place in (or outside) family trees (Chapter 8). Website: https://apics-online.info. Areal and family-specific structural databases, such as the South American Indigenous Language Structures database, and family-specific questionnaires used in studies such as Dunn et al. (2005), complement the global databases. G.5 Cultural, environmental and historical data G.5.1 D-PLACE D-PLACE (Database of Places, Language, Culture and Environment) (Kirby et al. 2016) links cultural data on about 1,400 societies, drawn principally from the Ethnographic Atlas (Murdock 1967) and other ethnographic datasets, to their languages (via Glottocodes), locations and environmental variables such as climate and ecology. Crucially for phylogenetic work, D-PLACE also collects published language phylogenies, so that cultural traits can be analyzed on a tree with the matching societies. It is the main data source for phylogenetic studies of cultural evolution (Chapter 14). Website: https://d-place.org; data: https://github.com/D-PLACE/dplace-cldf. G.5.2 Pulotu Pulotu (Watts, Sheehan, et al. 2015) is a database of supernatural beliefs and practices, together with social and environmental variables, for over one hundred Austronesian cultures, coded from ethnographic sources with careful attention to the historical period described. It was designed for phylogenetic analysis on Austronesian language trees and underlies studies of the coevolution of religion and political complexity (Watts, Greenhill, et al. 2015; Watts et al. 2016). It is now distributed in CLDF. G.5.3 Seshat Seshat: Global History Databank (Turchin et al. 2015) codes social complexity, warfare, religion, agriculture and many other variables for hundreds of historical polities, sampled through time from the Neolithic onward. It is used to study the dynamics of social complexity through time rather than across a tree, but can be combined with language trees for regions where polities are linked to languages. Website: https://seshatdatabank.info. G.5.4 Kinbank Kinbank (Passmore et al. 2023) is a global database of kinship terminology, recording the terms used for a standard set of kin relationships in more than a thousand languages, linked to Glottolog. It enables phylogenetic studies of the evolution of kinship systems, one of the classic topics of cultural phylogenetics (Chapter 14). G.5.5 Genes and languages The GeLaTo database (Genes and Languages Together) (Barbieri et al. 2022) pairs human population-genetic data with linguistic information for the same populations, and has been used to quantify how often genetic and linguistic histories match. Such resources are essential for formal joint models of genetic and linguistic history (Chapters 14 and 18). G.6 Published trees Phylogenetic comparative studies need trees, preferably full posterior samples rather than single summary trees. Several sources collect published language phylogenies: D-PLACE includes a collection of published language phylogenies (with posterior samples where available), matched to the societies in its cultural datasets. Phlorest, a collection of language phylogenies standardized in CLDF format by the CLDF team (https://github.com/phlorest), aims to make published trees uniformly accessible. Glottolog provides classification trees for every family, without branch lengths, which can be combined into a global tree. Global lexical trees have been inferred from ASJP data (Jäger 2018) and are available from the authors’ repositories. Supplementary data of individual papers, often deposited in Dryad, Zenodo, OSF or GitHub, remain the main source for many trees. Authors who deposit their full posterior tree samples, input files and data make their work far more useful to others (Chapter 17). G.7 Data formats The Cross-Linguistic Data Formats (CLDF) (Forkel et al. 2018) are the standard format for most of the resources in this appendix. A CLDF dataset consists of CSV tables (languages, parameters, forms, cognates, values, codes, and others) and a JSON metadata file that describes them, following the W3C recommendation for CSV on the web. Specifications and validation tools are documented at https://cldf.clld.org. Chapter 17 shows how to read CLDF data into R, and Appendix F lists the Python tools (pycldf, cldfbench, pylexibank) used to create and validate CLDF datasets. NEXUS, PHYLIP and Newick (Chapter 2) remain the formats for exchanging matrices and trees with phylogenetic software. References

H RevBayes Implementations The Bayesian models described in this book are implemented in RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) in the folder revbayes/ that accompanies the book. We call this collection RevLingPhy. RevBayes is well suited to the purpose because it expresses a model as an explicit probabilistic graphical model. Every rate matrix, prior, clock and tree process is written out in a few lines of the Rev language rather than hidden behind a menu. Each script can therefore be read as a precise statement of the model that the corresponding chapter describes in words and equations. Every script was run with RevBayes 1.4.1 on a small simulated dataset, with between six and sixteen languages, for which the true parameter values are known. A companion R script compares the posterior with the truth. This appendix documents each model, shows its Rev code, and reports the result of that check. H.1 Layout and use The package has the following structure. Table H.1: Folders of the RevLingPhy package. Folder Contents data/ R scripts (sim_<group>.R) that simulate each test dataset, and the simulated data with its true parameter values analyses/<group>/ One standalone Rev script per model, numbered within each group output/<group>/ MCMC logs, sampled trees, ancestral states and marginal likelihoods tests/ R scripts (check_<group>.R) that compare posteriors with the true values, and their results docs/ The documentation reproduced in this appendix The scripts are grouped by topic. The lexical group covers substitution models for cognate data, tree priors, model comparison and model adequacy (Chapters 5, 6 and 7). The time group covers clock models, calibration, tip-dating and diversification (Chapters 9, 10 and 16). The traits group covers phylogeography, ancestral states and comparative methods (Chapters 11, 12, 13 and 14). To run a single analysis, change into the revbayes/ folder and call RevBayes on the script. Chain lengths can be increased for real data by passing an argument after --args. cd revbayes rb analyses/lexical/01_binary_ctmc_asc.Rev rb analyses/lexical/01_binary_ctmc_asc.Rev --args 50000 # longer chain Rscript tests/check_lexical.R # compare with the truth The scripts are written for clarity and for small test datasets. For real datasets, chains must be much longer, convergence must be checked with two or more independent runs (Section 6.5), and priors should be chosen for the problem at hand rather than copied from the test settings. 22_pathway_rj_tree_sample reversible jump over rates 13 3/4 501 pass, miss H.3 Models of lexical evolution This section documents the RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) scripts for the models of lexical evolution of Chapter 7, together with the Bayesian devices of Chapter 6 that matter most for cognate data (tree-length priors, marginal likelihoods, posterior predictive checks). Every script was run on a small data set simulated by revbayes/data/sim_lexical.R with known parameter values (revbayes/data/lexical/true_values.csv), and revbayes/tests/check_lexical.R compares the posterior with the truth and, where possible, with an independent computation in R (the book’s own likelihood code or phangorn). Conventions. All data sets have ten languages (L01 to L10). The true tree (revbayes/data/lexical/true_time_tree.tre) is a Yule tree re-scaled to a root age of 4 millennia; unrooted analyses use the same tree with branch lengths multiplied by a rate, so that branch lengths are expected changes per character. Binary cognate matrices never contain all-absent columns (every cognate class is attested somewhere), so the binary models use the no-absence ascertainment correction of Section 7.4 unless stated otherwise. Scripts are run from revbayes/: cd revbayes Rscript data/sim_lexical.R # simulate all data sets rb analyses/lexical/01_ctmc_ascertainment.Rev # one analysis, default settings rb analyses/lexical/09_model_comparison.Rev --args 2 500 # one model, 500 generations per stone bash tests/run_lexical.sh # all analyses, recording run times Rscript tests/check_lexical.R # writes tests/results_lexical.csv In each verification table, Truth is the simulated value, HPD the 95% highest posterior density interval, and ESS the effective sample size after discarding 10% burn-in. Status is pass if the truth lies inside the HPD and ESS is at least 100, pass (low ESS) if the truth is covered with ESS below 100, fail otherwise, and info for descriptive rows (prior sensitivity, independent maximum-likelihood estimates, topology summaries). Rows marked pass (bias shown) belong to a deliberately misspecified model, for which missing the truth is the expected and desired outcome. Run times (runtime_s in the CSV) were measured on a shared 12-core machine with several other RevBayes jobs running and are therefore pessimistic. The simulated Yule tree has three very short internal branches (0.06 to 0.14 millennia) and four long ones. With ten languages and a few hundred to a thousand characters the four long splits are recovered with posterior probability close to 1 in every analysis, while the three short ones are genuinely uncertain (posterior probabilities mostly between 0.05 and 0.6). The topology rows in the tables therefore report the Robinson-Foulds distance of the most probable sampled topology to the truth, the posterior probability of the true topology and the support of each true split, with status info; they are a property of the simulated tree, not a failure of the models. H.3.1 Implementation devices Three devices recur, because RevBayes 1.4.1 has no built-in stochastic Dollo likelihood and offers ascertainment correction only for 2-state data. Hidden-state binary models (covarion, stochastic Dollo, pseudo-Dollo) are written as CTMCs on 3 or 4 hidden states, and the observed binary matrix is expanded with expandCharacters(2), which turns an observed 0 into the ambiguity (0 2) and a 1 into (1 3). No-absence correction for hidden-state models. The required likelihood is \(\prod_i P(D_i)/(1-P_0)^N\), where \(P_0\) is the probability that all languages lack the class (Equation (7.4)). We clamp a second copy Z of the CTMC to a single all-absent column, so that \(\log P_0\) is available as Z.lnProbability(), cancel Z’s own contribution with a clamped Exponential(rate \(1/P_0\)) node at 0, and add \(-N\log(1-P_0)\) with \(N\) clamped Exponential(rate \(1/(1-P_0)\)) nodes at 0 (an exponential density at 0 equals its rate). check_lexical.R recomputes the corrected likelihood in R for posterior samples; the two agree to better than \(10^{-3}\) log-units. Two RevBayes 1.4.1 quirks had to be worked around and are worth knowing: a deterministic node defined only as Z.lnProbability() is not re-evaluated when the tree or the rate matrix changes (its children keep stale probabilities, which silently removes the correction), so the scripts add 0 * (a function of every parameter) to it; and model() crashes when entered from the tree in such a graph, so it is entered from the sink node (model(asc)). A user-defined Rev function computing \(P_0\) by pruning works but is about a hundred times slower. H.3.2 Binary CTMC and ascertainment correction Script 01 fits the binary CTMC of Section 7.3 (restriction-site or Mk2 model with an estimated frequency of presence \(\pi_1\), Equation (7.1), Felsenstein (1992)) on an unrooted tree with i.i.d. exponential branch lengths, three times: to data without all-absent columns with no correction (coding="all"), to the same data with the no-absence correction (coding="noabsencesites"), and to the variable-only version of the data with the Lewis correction (coding="variable", Lewis (2001)). The uncorrected fit shows the bias described in Section 7.4: \(\pi_1\) is inflated to 0.398 (truth 0.3) and the tree length to 2.82 (truth 1.85). Both corrected fits recover the truth, and agree with an independent maximum-likelihood fit with the book’s corrected likelihood function. ################################################################################ # 01_ctmc_ascertainment.Rev # Model : binary CTMC (restriction-site / Mk2 with free stationary frequency # pi1) on cognate presence/absence, unrooted tree, i.i.d. exponential # branch-length prior. # Book : Chapter 7, Sections lexical-models-ctmc and lexical-models-ascertainment # (Equations lexical-models-Q and lexical-models-asc). # Estimates: pi1, topology, branch lengths, tree length (expected changes per # cognate character), under three ascertainment schemes: # (A) "uncorrected": data without all-absent columns, coding="all" (biased) # (B) "noabsence" : same data, coding="noabsencesites" (correct) # (C) "variable" : data without all-absent AND all-present columns, # coding="variable" (Lewis Mkv) (correct) # Data : data/lexical/d01_noabsence.nex, d01_variable.nex (truth: pi1 = 0.3, # TL = 1.854; see data/lexical/true_values.csv) # Runtime : about 1.5 minutes for the three chains (default n_gen = 12000) # Usage : rb analyses/lexical/01_ctmc_ascertainment.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(101) n_gen = 12000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/lexical/01_ctmc_ascertainment/" schemes = ["uncorrected", "noabsence", "variable"] files = ["data/lexical/d01_noabsence.nex", "data/lexical/d01_noabsence.nex", "data/lexical/d01_variable.nex"] codings = ["all", "noabsencesites", "variable"] for (s in 1:3) { data <- readDiscreteCharacterData(files[s]) taxa <- data.taxa() n_branches <- 2 * taxa.size() - 3 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() # --- tree: uniform topology, i.i.d. exponential branch lengths (mean 0.2) psi ~ dnUniformTopologyBranchLength(taxa, branchLengthDistribution = dnExponential(5.0)) moves.append( mvNNI(psi, weight = 10) ) moves.append( mvSPR(psi, weight = 5) ) moves.append( mvBranchLengthScale(psi, weight = n_branches) ) TL := psi.treeLength() # --- binary CTMC: Q = beta * [[-pi1, pi1], [pi0, -pi0]], normalised so that # one unit of branch length = one expected change per character pi ~ dnDirichlet(v(1, 1)) moves.append( mvBetaSimplex(pi, alpha = 20, weight = 3) ) pi1 := pi[2] Q := fnF81(pi) seq ~ dnPhyloCTMC(tree = psi, Q = Q, type = "Binary", coding = codings[s]) seq.clamp(data) mymodel = model(psi) monitors.append( mnModel(filename = out_dir + schemes[s] + ".log", printgen = 12) ) monitors.append( mnFile(psi, filename = out_dir + schemes[s] + ".trees", printgen = 60) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 5000, pi1, TL) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 1) mymcmc.burnin(generations = 500, tuningInterval = 100) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen) trace = readTreeTrace(out_dir + schemes[s] + ".trees", treetype = "non-clock", burnin = 0.1) map_tree = mapTree(trace, out_dir + schemes[s] + "_map.tre") } q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status binary CTMC, coding=all on no-absence data (uncorrected) pi1 0.300 0.398 0.382 0.413 901.0 pass (bias shown) binary CTMC, coding=all on no-absence data (uncorrected) TL 1.853 2.817 2.611 3.003 785.8 pass (bias shown) binary CTMC, coding=noabsencesites pi1 0.300 0.310 0.289 0.329 803.5 pass binary CTMC, coding=noabsencesites TL 1.853 1.990 1.823 2.161 514.3 pass binary CTMC, coding=noabsencesites topology_RF_MAP 0.000 6.000 NA NA NA info (MAP topology differs) binary CTMC, coding=variable (Mkv) on variable-only data pi1 0.300 0.308 0.286 0.331 772.1 pass binary CTMC, coding=variable (Mkv) on variable-only data TL 1.853 1.997 1.822 2.186 436.6 pass ML (R, true topology, branch-length scale free), noabsence correction pi1 0.300 0.307 NA NA NA info H.3.3 Gamma rate variation among characters Script 02 adds discrete-gamma rate variation (four categories, Equation (7.5), Yang (1994)), the model of Gray and Atkinson (2003). The data were simulated with rates drawn from the same 4-category discrete gamma (\(\alpha = 0.5\)), so that \(\alpha\) is directly verifiable; with continuous-gamma data the discrete model estimates a smaller \(\alpha\), as the book’s phangorn example also shows. The gamma shape and the tree length lie on a ridge (fast categories saturate), so the branch-length prior matters; script 02 uses the compound Dirichlet prior of Rannala et al. (2012) and Zhang et al. (2012) with tree length \(\sim\) Gamma(1, 0.2), and script 14 shows the sensitivity. ################################################################################ # 02_ctmc_gamma.Rev # Model : binary CTMC + discrete-gamma among-character rate variation # (4 equiprobable categories, mean rate 1), no-absence ascertainment # correction, unrooted tree with a gamma-Dirichlet branch-length prior. # Book : Chapter 7, Section lexical-models-rates (Equation lexical-models-gamma); # this is the "restriction site + Gamma" model of Gray & Atkinson (2003). # Estimates: gamma shape alpha, pi1, topology, tree length. # Data : data/lexical/d02_gamma.nex (truth: alpha = 0.5, pi1 = 0.25, TL = 6.95; # rates drawn from the 4-category discrete gamma, i.e. the fitted model) # Runtime : about 2.5 minutes (default n_gen = 10000) # Usage : rb analyses/lexical/02_ctmc_gamma.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(202) n_gen = 10000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/lexical/02_ctmc_gamma/" data <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/lexical/d02_gamma.nex") taxa <- data.taxa() n_branches <- 2 * taxa.size() - 3 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() # gamma-Dirichlet (compound Dirichlet) branch-length prior, Rannala et al. A 4-state chain \(U \to P \to D\) (“unborn”, “present”, “dead”, plus an unused copy of “present” for the ambiguity coding) with a vanishing birth rate \(\varepsilon = 10^{-5}\), death rate \(\mu\) and root frequency \(\varepsilon/\mu\) for “present” gives \(P(x) = \varepsilon\, a_x + O(\varepsilon^2)\) for every observable pattern \(x\), with \(a_x = \Lambda_x/\lambda\) (the expected number of classes with pattern \(x\) per unit birth rate), and \(1-P_0 = \varepsilon A\) with \(A = \Lambda/\lambda\). Conditioning on observability (device 2) therefore yields the Dollo multinomial likelihood \(\prod_x (a_x/A)^{n_x}\), with relative error of order \(\varepsilon \times\) tree length, and a clamped Poisson node \(N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda A)\) completes the full likelihood. This is the limit argument of Section 7.7.4 turned into an implementation. The time tree has its root age fixed at 4 millennia, because only \(\mu t\) is identifiable. The check script evaluates the book’s own R implementation of the Dollo likelihood (dollo_rates()) on posterior samples: the RevBayes likelihood differs from it only by the constant \(-\log N!\) (maximum deviation 0.0092 log-units), and the maximum-likelihood estimate on the true tree agrees with the posterior. Catastrophes and the missing-data extension of Ryder and Nicholls (2011) are not implemented. ################################################################################ # 04_stochastic_dollo.Rev # Model : stochastic Dollo model of Nicholls & Gray (2008) on a time tree: # cognate classes are born once (Poisson process, rate lambda per # lineage per millennium; Poisson(lambda/mu) classes at the root) and # die independently at rate mu; all-absent classes are unobservable. # Book : Chapter 7, Section lexical-models-dollo (the Nicholls-Gray likelihood: # Poisson pattern counts with means Lambda_x; full likelihood # exp(-Lambda) prod_x Lambda_x^n_x / n_x!). # Estimates: mu, lambda, tree topology and node ages (root age fixed at 4.0 # millennia; only mu*t is identifiable without a calibration). # # IMPLEMENTATION (RevBayes 1.4.1 has no dnPhyloCTMCDollo): # The Dollo likelihood is obtained as an exact limit of a CTMC. Consider the # 4-state chain U (unborn) --eps--> P (present) --mu--> D (dead), plus an # unused copy P' of "present" (state 4) that only serves the ambiguity coding. # Root frequencies: P = eps/mu, U = 1 - eps/mu. Observed 0 = {U, D}, 1 = {P, P'}. # To first order in eps, P(pattern x) = eps * a_x with a_x = Lambda_x / lambda of # the book's Dollo section (birth on the branch above v with rate eps, # survival e^{-mu(t-s)}, root term eps/mu * S_root), and 1 - P(0...0) = eps * A. # Hence prod_x [P(x) / (1 - P0)]^{n_x} -> prod_x (a_x / A)^{n_x}, the Dollo # multinomial likelihood conditional on N. The relative error is O(eps * tree # length) ~ 2e-4 for eps = 1e-5. The no-absence conditioning is done explicitly # (dummy all-absent column Z and the two RevBayes 1.4.1 work-arounds, # see 03_covarion.Rev), and the Poisson factor for the # number of observed classes, N ~ Poisson(lambda * A) with A = (1 - P0)/eps, # completes the full Nicholls-Gray likelihood (up to the # constant sum(log n_x!) - log N!). The check script verifies this against the # book's own R implementation of the Dollo likelihood (dollo_rates()). # Data : data/lexical/d04_dollo.nex (truth: lambda = 20, mu = 0.3, root age 4) # Runtime : about 2 minutes (default n_gen = 8000) # Usage : rb analyses/lexical/04_stochastic_dollo.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(404) n_gen = 8000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/lexical/04_stochastic_dollo/" eps <- 1e-5 # Truth: r = (0.237, 0.789, 1.974), TL = 3.475 # Runtime : about 1.5 minutes (default n_gen = 15000) # Usage : rb analyses/lexical/06_meaning_mk.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(606) n_gen = 15000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/lexical/06_meaning_mk/" K <- 5 n_part <- 3 part_start <- [1, 61, 121] part_end <- [60, 120, 180] for (k in 1:n_part) { part[k] <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/lexical/d06_meanings.nex") part[k].excludeAll() part[k].includeCharacter(part_start[k]:part_end[k]) } taxa <- part[1].taxa() n_branches <- 2 * taxa.size() - 3 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() psi ~ dnUniformTopologyBranchLength(taxa, branchLengthDistribution = dnExponential(5.0)) moves.append( mvNNI(psi, weight = 10) ) moves.append( mvSPR(psi, weight = 5) ) moves.append( mvBranchLengthScale(psi, weight = n_branches) ) TL := psi.treeLength() # The tree is fixed at the true time tree: with one likelihood object per meaning, every tree move recomputes 150 likelihoods, which is too slow for the time budget. The residual term \(\varepsilon_m\) of the book’s regression is omitted. ################################################################################ # 07_frequency_regression.Rev # Model : meaning-specific replacement rates predicted by word frequency, # embedded in the phylogenetic likelihood: # log rho_m = a + b * log(freq_m) (one partition per meaning) # Each meaning is a multistate (K = 5) Mk character on the dated tree # (root age 4 millennia), so that a (log rate per millennium of a word of # average log-frequency) is identifiable, not only b. # Design : the time tree is FIXED at the true tree. With one CTMC object per # meaning (150 partitions) every tree move recomputes 150 likelihoods, # which is far too slow for the 3-minute budget (about 1.4 generations # per second in a test); conditioning on the tree isolates the # regression, which is what this script verifies. # Book : Chapter 7, Section "Word frequency as a rate predictor" # (the regression log rho_m = beta0 + beta1 log(frequency_m) + eps_m; # here eps_m = 0, i.e. the pure regression; Pagel et al. 2007). # Estimates: intercept a, slope b (tree fixed). # Data : data/lexical/d07_frequency.nex (150 meanings) and # d07_logfreq.txt (centred, standardised log frequencies). # Truth: a = log(0.15) = -1.897, b = -0.6. # Runtime : about 3 minutes (default n_gen = 3000) # Usage : rb analyses/lexical/07_frequency_regression.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(707) n_gen = 3000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/lexical/07_frequency_regression/" K <- 5 data <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/lexical/d07_frequency.nex") lf_tab <- readDataDelimitedFile("data/lexical/d07_logfreq.txt", header = FALSE) M <- data.nchar() for (m in 1:M) logf[m] <- lf_tab[m][1] taxa <- data.taxa() moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() psi <- readTrees("data/lexical/true_time_tree.tre")[1] a ~ dnNormal(0.0, 2.0) # log rate (per millennium) at mean log frequency b ~ dnNormal(0.0, 1.0) # frequency effect moves.append( mvSlide(a, delta = 0.2, weight = 1) ) moves.append( mvSlide(b, delta = 0.2, weight = 1) ) Q <- fnJC(K) for (m in 1:M) { rho[m] := exp(a + b * logf[m]) part[m] <- data part[m].excludeAll() part[m].includeCharacter(m) seq[m] ~ dnPhyloCTMC(tree = psi, Q = Q, branchRates = rho[m], type = "Standard", coding = "all") seq[m].clamp(part[m]) } mymodel = model(a) monitors.append( mnModel(filename = out_dir + "frequency.log", printgen = 3, exclude = ["rho"]) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 500, a, b) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 1) mymcmc.burnin(generations = 300, tuningInterval = 30) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen) q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status per-meaning Mk rates, log rho = a + b log f (time tree) a -1.897 -1.844 -1.952 -1.712 458.0 pass per-meaning Mk rates, log rho = a + b log f (time tree) b -0.600 -0.519 -0.647 -0.399 555.9 pass per-meaning Mk rates, log rho = a + b log f (time tree) topology_RF_MAP 0.000 4.000 NA NA NA info (MAP topology differs) H.3.9 Dated analyses with Yule and birth-death tree priors Script 08 dates a binary cognate matrix with a strict clock, the no-absence correction and a root calibration (root age \(\sim\) Lognormal(\(\log 4\), 0.05)), once under a Yule prior and once under a constant-rate birth-death prior (Section 6.2). The equal-rates model is rejected: it predicts far too few universally shared cognates (slow characters) and too little spread in cognate-set sizes. The gamma model reproduces all four statistics. In RevBayes 1.4.1, the built-in simulator for a binary CTMC with coding="noabsencesites" and gamma rate categories rejects all-absent columns but keeps the rate category of the rejected column, so slow categories are over-represented and the replicates contain about twice the correct share of all-present cognates (the exact conditional expectation was computed analytically at posterior samples); an unconditioned (coding="all") simulation with site rates was also wrong. The check script therefore draws the replicates in R from the RevBayes posterior samples (tree, \(\pi\), \(\alpha\)), with exact rejection of all-absent columns; for the equal-rates model the built-in replicates agree with them, and the biased built-in gamma replicates are shown in a separate row. ################################################################################ # 10_posterior_predictive.Rev # Model : posterior predictive model adequacy (Bollback 2002; Hoehna et al. # 2018 "P3") for cognate data: the equal-rates binary CTMC and the # CTMC + Gamma model are fitted to data simulated WITH strong rate # heterogeneity (d02, alpha = 0.5); posteriorPredictiveSimulation() # simulates replicate datasets from posterior draws. Data: 50 meanings with rate 0.05 and 50 with rate 0.5 per millennium on the fixed true tree. The posterior puts most weight on two strata with equal weights; the slow rate is recovered, the fast rate (about 12 expected changes per character over the tree, so nearly saturated) is slightly underestimated, its HPD ending just below the truth. holds a set of cognate classes, with entry of new words and competition-dependent loss, “can be written down as a CTMC on subsets and specified in general-purpose software such as RevBayes”. Script 15 does so for \(K = 3\) classes: seven states (the non-empty subsets of \(\{A, B, C\}\)), entry at rate \(\gamma\) for each absent class, loss of each word at rate \(\delta\) times the number of its competitors (so a slot is never empty), and root frequencies equal to the stationary distribution, proportional to \((\gamma/\delta)^{|S|-1}/(|S|-1)!\). Each language’s observed set of classes for a meaning is one 7-state character. The closed set of three classes (a lost class may re-enter) is a simplification of the open process. The ratio \(\gamma/\delta\), and with it the stationary frequency of synonymy, is sharply identified; the absolute rates trade off against the node ages, and the loss rate is underestimated, its HPD ending just below the truth (maximum likelihood on the true tree, computed in the check script, gives estimates closer to the truth). ################################################################################ # 15_synonymy_slot_model.Rev # Model : explicit model of replacement with synonymy for meaning slots: each # language's slot holds a SET of cognate classes (polymorphism allowed), # written as a CTMC on the non-empty subsets of K = 3 classes {A, B, C}: # states 1 {A} 2 {B} 3 {C} 4 {A,B} 5 {A,C} 6 {B,C} 7 {A,B,C} # * a new class enters the slot at rate g_in (for each absent class); # * each present word is lost at rate d_out x (number of competitors), # so a slot is never empty and loss accelerates with synonymy. # The chain is reversible with stationary frequencies proportional to # (g_in/d_out)^(|S|-1) / (|S|-1)!, used as root frequencies. # Book : Chapter 7, Section lexical-models-replacement (row 10 of Table # lexical-models-comparison: "small state spaces can be specified in # RevBayes"). Script 16 relaxes this in the way that morphological phylogenetics does for binary characters (Wright et al. 2016): each character belongs to one of four categories whose \(\pi_1\) values are the mean-discretized quantile classes of a Beta distribution (fnDiscretizeBeta), each category has an F81 rate matrix rescaled to one expected change per unit branch length, and the likelihood sums over the unknown category of each character (siteMatrices). In morphology the Beta is usually symmetric, \(\text{Beta}(s, s)\), because the labels 0 and 1 are arbitrary; for cognate presence and absence they are not, so the script parameterizes the Beta by its mean \(m\) and concentration \(\phi\), \(\text{Beta}(m\phi, (1 - m)\phi)\). The data (925 observed cognate classes on the fixed true time tree, strict clock 0.3) were simulated under this asymmetric mixture with \(\text{Beta}(1, 3)\), and five models are compared by stepping-stone and path sampling (Section 6.7), all with the no-absence correction: the binary Jukes-Cantor (Mk) model with \(\pi_1 = 1/2\), F81 with one estimated \(\pi_1\), F81 with gamma rates, and the asymmetric and symmetric Beta mixtures. This is a parameter-recovery and model-recovery experiment in the sense of Section 6.10; it does not show that real cognate data contain this kind of heterogeneity. The generating model wins clearly, by about 40 log-units over F81 with gamma rates. Gamma rate variation thus absorbs part of the heterogeneity in \(\pi_1\), but only part, because characters with a low \(\pi_1\) differ from the others in their pattern of presence and not only in their rate. The binary Jukes-Cantor model, which forces \(\pi_1 = 1/2\), is worst by far, and the symmetric mixture, which keeps the mean of \(\pi_1\) at one half, recovers only a fraction of the difference: for presence-absence data the mean frequency must be free. Parameter recovery under the generating model is mixed. The concentration, \(b\) and the clock rate are covered by their 95% HPD intervals, but the mean frequency of presence is overestimated (posterior mean 0.292, truth 0.25) and the interval for \(a\) ends just above the truth. The check script recomputes the mixture likelihood independently in R (agreement to \(10^{-3}\) log-units at posterior samples) and finds the same estimate by maximum likelihood on the same data, while maximum-likelihood fits to four further simulated data sets of 3,000 classes give \(m\) between 0.245 and 0.254. The offset is therefore a property of this one simulated data set, a reminder that a single replicate can miss the truth by chance, and not a bias of the model or of RevBayes. ################################################################################ # 16_f81_beta_mixture.Rev # Model : F81 mixture across cognate characters ("Beta mixture" of stationary # frequencies): every character belongs to one of four categories, # each with its own frequency of presence pi1[k] taken from the four # mean-discretized quantile classes of a Beta distribution, and each # with an F81 rate matrix rescaled to one expected change per unit # branch length. The four equiprobable categories of the discrete gamma (script 02) are a numerical convention, not a hypothesis about language. Script 17 asks what the choice costs. The data (809 observed cognate classes on the fixed true time tree, strict clock 0.3, \(\pi_1 = 0.25\)) were simulated with rates drawn from the continuous Gamma(0.4, 0.4) distribution, so that none of the five fitted models is the generating one: the discrete gamma with two, four and eight categories; four gamma categories with free weights (a Dirichlet prior on siteRatesProbs, which lets the mean rate depart from one, a departure absorbed by the clock rate); and a three-category FreeRate model with free rates and free weights whose weighted mean is fixed at one (Yang 1995; Soubrier et al. 2012). All use the F81 binary CTMC with the no-absence correction and are compared by stepping-stone and path sampling (16 stones of 300 generations). Two categories are clearly too few (about 17 log-units worse than four), while eight categories differ from four by about one log-unit, which is within the Monte Carlo error of estimates from runs of this length. Neither the free weights nor the FreeRate model improves on four gamma categories: with a few hundred characters, the extra parameters cost more in marginal likelihood than they gain in fit when the true rates are gamma-shaped. A short MCMC under the four-category model recovers the simulated values of \(\alpha\), \(\pi_1\) and the clock rate within their 95% HPD intervals, and the check script recomputes the four-category likelihood independently in R at posterior samples. This is a model-recovery experiment on data that follow the gamma shape; FreeRate models are worth considering precisely when real cognate data contain rate classes that the gamma cannot represent, such as a block of almost invariant meanings next to fast ones (Section 7.5). ################################################################################ # 17_rate_categories.Rev # Model : How many rate categories, and of which kind? H.4 Clocks, calibrations, tree priors and diversification This section documents the RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) scripts for the models of Chapters 9 and 10, and for the time-tree models of the biologist’s toolbox in Chapter 16: strict, relaxed and local clocks, punctuational change, node and tip calibration, sampled ancestors, tree priors, the multispecies coalescent and diversification models. Every script was run on a small data set simulated by revbayes/data/sim_time.R with known parameter values (revbayes/data/time/true_values.csv), and revbayes/tests/check_time.R compares the posterior with the truth. Conventions. Time is measured in millennia (ky) before the present. Branch lengths are expected numbers of changes per binary cognate character, so clock rates are changes per character per millennium (true value 0.15 in most data sets). Unless stated otherwise the characters are binary cognate-presence characters evolving under a two-state F81 model with an estimated stationary frequency of presence (true value 0.35), simulated without ascertainment (constant columns are kept, and every model uses coding="all"). Ascertainment correction and other lexical substitution models are covered by the scripts for Chapter 7. Scripts are run from revbayes/, for example cd revbayes rb analyses/time/01_strict_clock_calibrations.Rev # default settings rb analyses/time/06_punctuational_bursts.Rev --args 15000 punct0 bash analyses/time/run_time.sh # all analyses, 2 at a time Rscript tests/check_time.R # writes tests/results_time.csv In each verification table, Truth is the simulated value, HPD the 95% highest posterior density interval, and ESS the effective sample size after discarding 25% burn-in (summed over runs where two runs were made). Status is pass if the truth lies inside the HPD (or a model-specific criterion stated in the notes of results_time.csv is met) and ESS is at least 100, warn if the criterion is met with ESS below 100, fail otherwise, and info for descriptive rows. Rows prefixed info- belong to deliberately misspecified models, for which missing the truth is the expected outcome. Five devices recur in the scripts. Calibration densities as observations. RevBayes has no “calibration prior” object. A density \(f\) on a node age $t = $ tmrca(tree, clade) is imposed by clamping an observation whose density, as a function of \(t\), equals \(f(t)\). For the offset lognormal of Equation (C.12), obs ~ dnLognormal(mu, sigma, offset=-t) clamped at \(-a\) gives \((t-a) \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). For the soft-bounded uniform, the density dnSoftBoundUniformNormal(min=a-t, max=b-t, sd, p=0.95) evaluated at 0 equals the soft uniform density of \(t\) on \([a,b]\), because the density is translation invariant. As in BEAST, the joint prior is the product of the tree prior and the calibration densities (Section 10.3.2), and script 14 shows the resulting effective prior. Fixed topology. The relaxed-clock, punctuational, tree-prior and gamma scripts date the true topology (node ages free, starting from the true topology with all ages multiplied by 1.5). This is a standard “dating a given tree” analysis, and it lets branch-specific rates be matched to their true values. Scripts 01, 07, 08 and 11 estimate the topology, starting from a UPGMA tree or a random draw from the prior. Branch indices. The relaxed-clock scripts write branch_index.txt, which maps each RevBayes branch index to its set of descendant languages. check_time.R uses it to match branch_rates[k] to the simulated rates. Node order. RevBayes numbers internal nodes so that a parent always has a larger index than its children, with the root at \(2n-1\). Looping over branches from index \(2n-2\) down to 1 therefore defines a parent’s rate before its children’s rates. The autocorrelated and random local clocks rely on this. Runtimes. The runtimes in the tables are wall-clock seconds recorded by run_time.sh on a shared 12-core machine with two RevBayes processes at once. On an idle core they are about half as long. H.4.2 Uncorrelated lognormal relaxed clock Script 02_ucln_relaxed_clock.Rev implements Equation (C.9) (Drummond et al. 2006): each of the 22 branch rates is an independent lognormal draw with mean \(\bar r\) and log-scale standard deviation \(\sigma\), so the multipliers have mean one. The data were simulated with \(\bar r = 0.15\) and \(\sigma = 0.5\) (CV 0.53). Rates are sampled as continuous values rather than discretized categories. Mixing is helped by mvRateAgeBetaShift, which moves a node age and rescales the rates of the adjacent branches so that their lengths in changes stay the same. This is the joint rate-age proposal at the heart of the optimized relaxed clock (Section 9.5.4). An up-down scale move stretches the tree and shrinks all rates together. Besides \(\bar r\), \(\sigma\) and the root age, the check reports what fraction of the true branch rates fall inside their branch-wise 95% HPD, and the correlation between posterior-mean and true log rates. ################################################################################ # 02_ucln_relaxed_clock.Rev # # Model : uncorrelated lognormal (UCLN) relaxed clock (Drummond et al. 2006): # r_j = rbar * eps_j, ln eps_j ~ N(-sigma^2/2, sigma^2) # (Equation clocks-ucln), binary cognate CTMC (2-state F81), # Yule tree prior, node calibrations C1 (soft uniform) and # C2 (offset lognormal) as in script 01. RevBayes 1.4.1 has no built-in distribution for autocorrelated rates, so the model is written out node by node. Each node’s log rate is normal around its parent’s log rate minus \(\nu t/2\), with variance \(\nu t\), where \(t\) is the branch duration, a deterministic function of the moving node ages (timetree.branchLength(k)). Each branch rate is the exponential of the mean of the log rates at its two ends, exactly as in the R simulation of Section 9.5.6. Besides single-node slides, an mvUpDownSlide move shifts all log rates together.
