H.4.5 Random local clock Script 05_random_local_clock.Rev implements the random local clock of Section 9.5.3 (Drummond and Suchard 2010). RevBayes 1.4.1 has no dedicated distribution for it, so the script uses the reversible-jump indicator formulation that the book describes. Each branch has a multiplier that is exactly 1 (no shift) with prior probability \(1-q\), or a LogNormal(0, 1) draw (a shift) with probability \(q\), via dnReversibleJumpMixture with mvRJSwitch. A branch’s rate is its parent branch’s rate times its own multiplier, so a shift is inherited by the whole clade below it until the next shift. Setting \(q = 1-0.5^{1/22}\) makes the prior probability of no shift anywhere one half, matching the Poisson(\(\ln 2\)) prior of Drummond and Suchard. The data contain a single threefold shift on the stem of a four-language clade. The checks require a posterior shift probability above 0.5 on that branch and below 0.5 on every other branch. ################################################################################ # 05_random_local_clock.Rev # # Model : random local clock (Drummond & Suchard 2010). Each branch j has a # rate multiplier m_j that is exactly 1 (no shift) with probability # 1-q or drawn from LogNormal(0, 1) (a shift) with probability q, # via a reversible-jump mixture. A branch inherits the rate of its # parent branch times its own multiplier, so a shift applies to the # whole subtree until the next shift: # r_j = r_parent(j) * m_j, r for the root's children = base rate * m_j # q = 1 - 0.5^(1/22) gives P(no shift anywhere) = 0.5, as in the # Poisson(ln 2) prior on the number of shifts of Drummond & Suchard. # Binary cognate CTMC, Yule prior, calibrations C1/C2, fixed topology. # RevBayes 1.4.1 has no dedicated RLC distribution; this is the # standard RJ-indicator formulation built from dnReversibleJumpMixture. # Book : Ch. 9 "Local clocks and random local clocks" (clocks-local) # Estimates: base rate, number and placement of shifts (posterior probability # per branch), shift multiplier, node ages, root age # Data : data/time/clock_rlc.nex (one x3 shift on the stem of a 4-language clade) # Runtime : ~2 min # Usage : cd revbayes && rb analyses/time/05_random_local_clock.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(505) n_gen = 15000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/time/05_random_local_clock/" data <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/time/clock_rlc.nex") taxa <- data.taxa() n_taxa <- taxa.size() n_branches <- 2 * n_taxa - H.4.6 Punctuational bursts at splits Script 06_punctuational_bursts.Rev implements the punctuational model of Section 9.8 (Atkinson et al. 2008) as a generative model rather than a regression. Every branch starts at a split and receives a burst of \(\beta\) expected changes per character on top of gradual change, so that \(b_j = r t_j + \beta\) and the expected root-to-tip path is \(rT + \beta n_i\) (Equation (9.5)). On a time tree this is written as the branch rate \(r + \beta / t_j\). The parameter \(\beta\) has a reversible-jump prior that puts probability 0.5 on \(\beta = 0\) (purely gradual change) and otherwise draws \(\beta\) from an exponential distribution with mean 0.05, so the posterior probability that \(\beta > 0\) is directly a Bayes factor for punctuational change. The script runs on two data sets on the same 16-language tree: one with \(\beta = 0.05\) and a negative control with \(\beta = 0\). The tree is the most unbalanced of 200 Yule trees, with 1 to 11 splits between the root and a tip. It was chosen this way because \(\beta\) is identified only through differences in node counts among tips: bursts that were the same on every root-to-tip path could be absorbed by moving the node ages. A floor of one year on branch durations keeps \(\beta/t_j\) finite when a node slides onto its child. As an independent check, check_time.R regresses the ML (phangorn) branch lengths on the true topology against the true durations, \(b = r t + \beta k\), using the short branches whose ML lengths are not saturated. ################################################################################ # 06_punctuational_bursts.Rev # # Model : punctuational (speciational) change, after Atkinson et al. (2008): # every branch starts at a split and receives a burst of beta # expected changes per character in addition to gradual change, # b_j = r * t_j + beta, # so the expected root-to-tip path is r*T + beta*n_i (Equation # clocks-punct). Implemented with branch rates r + beta/t_j on a # time tree. beta has a reversible-jump prior: beta = 0 (purely # gradual) with probability 0.5, else beta ~ Exponential(mean 0.05); # the posterior probability of beta > 0 is then a Bayes factor # (prior odds 1). Strict clock otherwise; calibrations C1/C2; # fixed (true) topology of 16 languages; the tree is unbalanced # (1 to 11 splits between the root and a tip) to give the test power. # Book : Ch. 9 "Punctuational bursts at language splits" (clocks-punctuational) # Estimates: beta, P(beta > 0 | data), clock rate r, node ages, root age # Data : data/time/punct.nex (beta = 0.05) by default; # data/time/punct0.nex (beta = 0, negative control) with --args n_gen punct0 # Runtime : ~1-2 min # Usage : cd revbayes && rb analyses/time/06_punctuational_bursts.Rev [--args n_gen dataset] ################################################################################ seed(606) n_gen = 15000 dataset = "punct" if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) if (args.size() > 2) dataset = args[3] out_dir = "output/time/06_punctuational_bursts/" + dataset + "_" data <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/time/" + dataset + ".nex") taxa <- data.taxa() n_taxa <- taxa.size() n_branches <- 2 * n_taxa - 2 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() #### tree prior; fixed topology ################################################ root_age ~ dnUniform(0.5, 30.0) birth_rate ~ dnExponential(1.0) timetree ~ dnBDP(lambda=birth_rate, mu=0.0, rho=1.0, rootAge=root_age, taxa=taxa) start_tree <- readTrees("data/time/tree16_start.tre")[1] root_age.setValue(start_tree.rootAge()) timetree.setValue(start_tree) moves.append( mvScale(birth_rate, lambda=1.0, tune=true, weight=1.0) ) moves.append( mvSlide(root_age, delta=0.5, tune=true, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvTreeScale(tree=timetree, rootAge=root_age, delta=0.5, tune=true, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvNodeTimeSlideUniform(timetree, weight=15.0) ) moves.append( mvSubtreeScale(timetree, weight=5.0) ) #### calibrations ############################################################## source("data/time/calibrations_tree16.Rev") age_C1 := tmrca(timetree, clade_C1) age_C2 := tmrca(timetree, clade_C2) obs_C1 ~ dnSoftBoundUniformNormal(min=C1_min - age_C1, max=C1_max - age_C1, sd=C1_sd, p=0.95) obs_C1.clamp(0.0) obs_C2 ~ dnLognormal(mean=C2_mu, sd=C2_sd, offset=-age_C2) obs_C2.clamp(-C2_offset) #### gradual clock + punctuational bursts ##################################### clock_rate ~ dnExponential(2.0) moves.append( mvScale(clock_rate, lambda=0.5, tune=true, weight=5.0) ) beta ~ dnReversibleJumpMixture(constantValue=0.0, baseDistribution=dnExponential(20.0), p=0.5) moves.append( mvRJSwitch(beta, weight=5.0) ) moves.append( mvScale(beta, lambda=0.5, tune=true, weight=5.0) ) burst_present := ifelse(beta > 0.0, 1, 0) # The burst is spread over the branch as a rate beta/t_j. H.4.7 Tip-dating with ancient languages Script 07_tip_dating_serial_bd.Rev implements tip-dating (Section 10.5) with nine modern and three ancient languages attested 3.0, 2.2 and 1.4 ky ago. The ages come from tipdate_taxa.tsv through readTaxonData. The tree prior is the serially sampled birth-death process dnBDSTP with removal probability \(r = 1\), so an ancient language cannot be an ancestor of another sample. No node is calibrated: the clock rate is informed only by the fact that the ancient languages have had less time to change (Drummond et al. 2003). The script can also be run on the sampled-ancestor data set of script 08 (--args 15000 fbd). This shows what happens, as discussed in Section 10.6, when a true ancestor (Latin) is forced onto a side branch of its own. ################################################################################ # 07_tip_dating_serial_bd.Rev # # Model : tip-dating with ancient (non-contemporaneous) languages. H.4.9 Clock-model comparison by marginal likelihood Script 09_clock_model_comparison_ss.Rev estimates the log marginal likelihood of a strict or a UCLN clock by stepping-stone sampling (Xie et al. 2011) and path sampling (Lartillot and Philippe 2006) from a single powerPosterior run with 20 power steps (Section 6.7). It is run four times: both models on the UCLN data of script 02 and both on the strict data of script 01. The log Bayes factor favours the UCLN when it is positive. The check passes if the generating model is chosen. In RevBayes, clamped calibration “observations” count as part of the likelihood that is raised to each power. The estimate is still the marginal likelihood of the full model, because the remaining prior (uniform root age, proper priors on everything else) is proper. ################################################################################ # 09_clock_model_comparison_ss.Rev # # Model : Bayesian clock-model comparison by marginal likelihood. Fits a # strict clock or a UCLN relaxed clock (same tree prior, same node # calibrations, same binary cognate CTMC, fixed true topology) and # estimates log marginal likelihoods by stepping-stone sampling # (Xie et al. 2011) and path sampling (Lartillot & Philippe 2006) # from one powerPosterior run. # Book : Ch. 9 "Choosing a clock model" (clocks-choice) and "The strict # clock" (Bayes-factor comparison); Ch. 6 marginal likelihoods # Estimates: log marginal likelihood of the chosen model on the chosen dataset # Data : data/time/clock_ucln.nex (generated under UCLN, sigma = 0.5) or # data/time/clock_strict.nex (generated under a strict clock) # Runtime : ~1-2.5 min per model/dataset combination # Usage : cd revbayes && rb analyses/time/09_clock_model_comparison_ss.Rev --args MODEL DATASET [CATS] # MODEL in {strict, ucln}; DATASET in {clock_ucln, clock_strict} # The four combinations are run by analyses/time/run_time.sh. ################################################################################ seed(909) model_name = "ucln" dataset = "clock_ucln" n_cats = 20 if (args.size() > 1) model_name = args[2] if (args.size() > 2) dataset = args[3] if (args.size() > 3) n_cats = int(args[4]) out_dir = "output/time/09_clock_model_comparison_ss/" stem = out_dir + dataset + "_" + model_name data <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/time/" + dataset + ".nex") taxa <- data.taxa() n_taxa <- taxa.size() n_branches <- 2 * n_taxa - 2 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() #### tree prior; fixed topology ################################################ root_age ~ dnUniform(0.5, 30.0) birth_rate ~ dnExponential(1.0) timetree ~ dnBDP(lambda=birth_rate, mu=0.0, rho=1.0, rootAge=root_age, taxa=taxa) start_tree <- readTrees("data/time/tree12_start.tre")[1] root_age.setValue(start_tree.rootAge()) timetree.setValue(start_tree) moves.append( mvScale(birth_rate, lambda=1.0, tune=true, weight=1.0) ) moves.append( mvSlide(root_age, delta=0.5, tune=true, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvTreeScale(tree=timetree, rootAge=root_age, delta=0.5, tune=true, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvNodeTimeSlideUniform(timetree, weight=10.0) ) moves.append( mvSubtreeScale(timetree, weight=3.0) ) #### calibrations ############################################################## source("data/time/calibrations_tree12.Rev") age_C1 := tmrca(timetree, clade_C1) age_C2 := tmrca(timetree, clade_C2) obs_C1 ~ dnSoftBoundUniformNormal(min=C1_min - age_C1, max=C1_max - age_C1, sd=C1_sd, p=0.95) obs_C1.clamp(0.0) obs_C2 ~ dnLognormal(mean=C2_mu, sd=C2_sd, offset=-age_C2) obs_C2.clamp(-C2_offset) #### clock model ############################################################### mean_rate ~ dnExponential(2.0) moves.append( mvScale(mean_rate, lambda=0.5, tune=true, weight=5.0) ) if (model_name == "strict") { branch_rates := mean_rate } else { sigma ~ dnExponential(1.0) moves.append( mvScale(sigma, lambda=0.5, tune=true, weight=5.0) ) for (j in 1:n_branches) { branch_rates[j] ~ dnLognormal(ln(mean_rate) - H.4.11 Multispecies coalescent in a dialect continuum Script 11_multispecies_coalescent.Rev implements the multispecies coalescent of Section 16.2.1 (Rannala and Yang 2003; Heled and Drummond 2010). The five “species” are languages, each sampled at two local varieties (“individuals”). Eight “loci” are concept blocks, each with 200 binary cognate characters that share one concept tree (gene tree). The concept trees grow inside the language tree under dnMultiSpeciesCoalescent, with incomplete sorting of ancestral lexical variation across the short internal branches. The language-tree topology and ages and the effective population size \(N_e\) are the targets. The clock rate is fixed at its true value, because the absolute time scale and \(N_e\) cannot both be identified without a calibration. Treating a block of characters as one locus with a single history is an idealization: in real lexical data each meaning would be a separate, very short locus. In RevBayes 1.4.1 a pair of lineages coalesces at rate \(2/N_e\) per unit of tree time, so the expected time to coalescence of two lineages is \(N_e/2\) rather than the \(N_e\) implied by the units of Equation (16.1). We verified this by simulating from dnMultiSpeciesCoalescent and by recomputing its log density by hand, and the R simulator uses the same parameterization. The script has two modes, and the table shows both. genetrees clamps the eight true concept trees. This tests the MSC density and the inference of the language tree and \(N_e\) on their own. joint (the default) estimates the concept trees from the cognate characters together with everything else. Getting the joint mode to run at all took three changes, and all three are documented in the script. Runaway towards \(N_e \to 0\). With an exponential prior on \(N_e\), the sampler repeatedly ran away towards \(N_e \to 0\), with log densities above \(10^{60}\). This happened when root-age or subtree-scale proposals produced language trees with negative branch lengths, or concept trees incompatible with the language tree. A clamped “guard” observation now gives zero density to negative species-tree branches, mvSpeciesSubtreeScaleBeta is not used, and \(N_e\) has a Uniform(0.05, 5) prior. Starting tree. The language tree starts from a data-derived UPGMA tree, because from a random start the joint sampler stayed on a wrong topology. Mixing. Even with these changes the joint mode mixes poorly in a few minutes. The topology is recovered, but the ages stay near their starting values and their HPDs are far too narrow, so those rows fail. The genetrees mode recovers every parameter. Running the joint model reliably would need much longer chains or better joint species-gene moves. ################################################################################ # 11_multispecies_coalescent.Rev # # Model : multispecies coalescent (Rannala & Yang 2003; Heled & Drummond # 2010) for a dialect continuum: 5 languages ("species"), each # sampled at 2 local varieties ("individuals"); 8 independent # concept blocks ("loci"), each with its own concept tree (gene # tree) evolving inside the language tree with incomplete lineage # sorting of ancestral lexical variation. Each block is a set of # binary cognate characters sharing one history (an idealisation: # in real lexical data each meaning would be one short "locus"). # Gene trees ~ dnMultiSpeciesCoalescent(language tree, Ne); # characters ~ binary CTMC on the gene trees with a known clock rate. # Note: in RevBayes 1.4.1 a pair of lineages coalesces at rate 2/Ne # (time units of the tree), i.e. E[pair coalescence time] = Ne/2; # data/sim_time.R simulates with the same parameterisation. # Book : Ch. 16 "The multispecies coalescent and incomplete lineage # sorting" (biology-toolkit-msc) # Estimates: language (species) tree topology and ages, Ne, 8 concept trees # Data : data/time/msc_locus1..8.nex, msc_species_map.tsv, msc_setup.Rev # Runtime : ~2-3 min (one run; A proposal on the root # age can put the root below one of its children; with no character data on # the species tree nothing else rejects such a state, and the MSC density of # RevBayes 1.4.1 then becomes arbitrarily large (we observed the chain running # away to Ne -> 0 with log densities > 1e60). "genetrees") { # verification of the MSC density alone: the true concept trees are observed true_gene_trees <- readTrees("data/time/msc_gene_trees_true.tre") for (l in 1:n_loci) { gene_tree[l] ~ dnMultiSpeciesCoalescent(speciesTree=sptree, Ne=Ne, taxa=taxa) gene_tree[l].clamp(true_gene_trees[l]) } } else { # full model: concept trees estimated from binary cognate characters pi ~ dnDirichlet(v(1, 1)) Q := fnF81(pi) moves.append( mvBetaSimplex(pi, alpha=20, tune=true, weight=2.0) ) for (l in 1:n_loci) { gene_tree[l] ~ dnMultiSpeciesCoalescent(speciesTree=sptree, Ne=Ne, Language splitting has its own rate in each of three intervals (0 to 1.5, 1.5 to 3 and more than 3 ky ago); language death has one constant rate. The tree is larger than the others in this appendix because rates are estimated from branching times alone. Extinction is held constant to respect the non-identifiability of fully time-varying birth and death rates from trees of living languages (Louca and Pennell 2020). H.4.13 State-dependent diversification (BiSSE) Script 13_bisse_state_dependent_diversification.Rev implements BiSSE (Maddison et al. 2007) with the character-dependent birth-death process dnCDBDP, on a fixed tree of 150 languages simulated by diversitree (FitzJohn 2012) with a binary trait under which state-1 languages split twice as fast. The tree is clamped with clamp and the tip states with clampCharData. check_time.R compares the posterior with the diversitree maximum-likelihood estimates. HiSSE (Beaulieu and O’Meara 2016) uses the same distribution with four states (two observed by two hidden) and ambiguous tip coding, and the character-independent null models it needs are built the same way. We have not run these, because a convincing test of HiSSE needs much larger trees than are practical here. The caution of Rabosky and Goldberg (2015) applies: a single clade with both the trait and a high rate can produce spurious support for state dependence. All six rates are covered by their 95% HPDs. However, the posterior probability that \(\lambda_1 > \lambda_0\) is only about 0.91, below the 0.95 threshold, so that row is reported as a fail. The diversitree ML estimates show the same weak contrast in this simulated tree (\(\hat\lambda_0 = 0.64\), \(\hat\lambda_1 = 0.78\), against true values 0.4 and 0.8). The shortfall is a property of this simulated data set rather than of the implementation: 150 languages are too few to detect a twofold difference in splitting rate reliably. H.4.14 Effective priors of calibrated nodes Script 14_effective_prior_calibrations.Rev puts into practice the advice of Section 10.3.2 to always sample from the prior. It runs the model of script 01 without the cognate data and records the effective (marginal) prior of the two calibrated nodes and the root. For the calibrated nodes, Truth is the mean of the density the analyst specified, so the difference between it and the posterior-mean column measures how much the tree prior and the ordering constraints have shifted the effective prior (Heled and Drummond 2012; Warnock et al. 2012). In RevBayes 1.4.1, run(underPrior=true) reported “no effect” for this model, so the script leaves out the dnPhyloCTMC node. That keeps the calibration densities and drops only the data. The results illustrate two pitfalls. First, the soft-bounded uniform on C1 (95% of its mass in [0.96, 1.96] ky) becomes an effective prior centred near 1.9 ky, half a millennium older than the analyst specified, because of the Yule prior and the older calibration C2 above it. Second, the effective prior on the uncalibrated root is narrow and young, about 4.3 ky. With the topology free under the prior, the clade C2 (all languages except one) almost always contains the root, so the C2 calibration ends up dating the root itself. Once the data fix the topology, the root is no longer calibrated, and the posterior of script 01 is far wider (4.0 to 10.3 ky). A calibration on a large clade whose monophyly is not enforced can therefore act on a different node from the one intended. The notes column of results_time.csv reports how often this happens. ################################################################################ # 14_effective_prior_calibrations.Rev # # Model : the model of script 01 (Yule prior x calibration densities C1, C2, # strict clock, binary CTMC) sampled WITHOUT the data # (mcmc(..., underPrior=TRUE)) to obtain the effective (marginal) # prior on calibrated and uncalibrated node ages. The book's advice # "always sample from the prior": the effective prior on a # calibrated node is the product of the calibration density, the # tree prior and the ordering constraints, and can differ from the # specified density. tests/check_time.R compares it with the # specified densities and with the posterior from script 01. # Book : Ch. 10 "How calibrations interact" (divergence-interaction) # Estimates: effective prior of age_C1, age_C2 and the root age # Data : taxon names of data/time/clock_strict.nex only # Runtime : ~30 s # Usage : cd revbayes && rb analyses/time/14_effective_prior_calibrations.Rev [--args n_gen] ################################################################################ seed(1414) n_gen = 50000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/time/14_effective_prior_calibrations/" data <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/time/clock_strict.nex") taxa <- data.taxa() moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() root_age ~ dnUniform(0.5, 30.0) birth_rate ~ dnExponential(1.0) timetree ~ dnBDP(lambda=birth_rate, mu=0.0, rho=1.0, rootAge=root_age, samplingStrategy="uniform", condition="time", taxa=taxa) start_tree <- readTrees("data/time/clock_strict_upgma_start.tre")[1] root_age.setValue(start_tree.rootAge()) timetree.setValue(start_tree) moves.append( mvScale(birth_rate, lambda=1.0, tune=true, weight=1.0) ) moves.append( mvSlide(root_age, delta=1.0, tune=true, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvTreeScale(tree=timetree, rootAge=root_age, delta=0.5, tune=true, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvNodeTimeSlideUniform(timetree, weight=10.0) ) moves.append( mvSubtreeScale(timetree, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvNarrow(timetree, weight=3.0) ) moves.append( mvFNPR(timetree, weight=2.0) ) source("data/time/calibrations_tree12.Rev") age_C1 := tmrca(timetree, clade_C1) age_C2 := tmrca(timetree, clade_C2) obs_C1 ~ dnSoftBoundUniformNormal(min=C1_min - H.4.16 Models not implemented Three models from Chapters 9, 10 and 16 have no script here. Penalized likelihood and rate smoothing (Section 9.5.5) are not Bayesian. They are covered by ape::chronos() in the book itself. The optimized relaxed clock (Section 9.5.4) is a set of MCMC proposals for the UCLN model rather than a different model. Script 02 uses the corresponding RevBayes moves (mvRateAgeBetaShift, mvUpDownScale). Stratigraphic-range FBD models (dnFBDRP), skyline FBD models with a sampling rate that changes when writing appears (the timeline and psiTimeline arguments of dnFBDP), HiSSE and calibration cross-validation can all be expressed with the RevBayes 1.4.1 functions listed above. They are left as extensions, because verifying them would need either more ancient languages or much larger trees than these small test data sets have. H.5 Phylogeography, ancestral states and comparative models This section documents the RevBayes (Höhna et al. 2016) scripts for the trait models of Chapters 11, 12, 13 and 14: discrete and continuous phylogeography, range evolution, Mk models and ancestral states, stochastic character mapping, hidden rates, correlated evolution, Brownian motion and its relatives, phylogenetic regression and signal, threshold and spatial models. Each model has one standalone script in revbayes/analyses/traits/, run on a small data set simulated with known parameter values by revbayes/data/sim_traits.R (true values in revbayes/data/traits/true_values.csv); revbayes/tests/check_traits.R reads the output, computes posterior means, 95% highest-posterior-density (HPD) intervals and effective sample sizes (ESS, coda), checks whether the truth is covered and runs the model-specific checks described below, writing revbayes/tests/results_traits.csv. Conventions. Most scripts condition on one fixed, known time tree of 16 languages (data/traits/tree16.tre, a Yule tree with root age 4; time is in millennia, so rates are per thousand years). Three scripts integrate over tree uncertainty instead (13, 14 and 22). Coordinates are planar, in units of 100 km. Scripts are run from revbayes/: cd revbayes Rscript data/sim_traits.R # simulate all data sets rb analyses/traits/05_mk_asr.Rev # one analysis, default settings rb analyses/traits/02_continuous_phylogeo_bm.Rev --args 20000 # longer chain bash tests/run_traits.sh # all analyses, 2 at a time Rscript tests/check_traits.R # writes tests/results_traits.csv The first command-line argument after --args is the number of MCMC generations. Several scripts fit more than one model; each then also estimates the marginal likelihood of every model by stepping-stone and path sampling (powerPosterior, Chapter 6) and writes them to marginal_likelihoods.csv in its output folder. Two RevBayes pitfalls shaped these scripts. First, model(x) collects every node connected to x, including through shared constant nodes (a tree object, a prior constant such as rate <- 2.0) and through the elements of one Rev vector (x[1] and x[2]). Two models built in the same script that share such a node are silently merged, and a power posterior then adds their likelihoods. Each model in a multi-model script therefore has its own tree copy and its own variable names. Second, inside a loop an index such as i <- n - j is a constant node that is re-evaluated when it is reassigned, so every distribution created with tree.branchLength(i) ends up using the last value; loops therefore run over the loop variable itself (for (i in (n - 1):1)). The verification standard is the one used throughout this appendix: the script runs; the 95% HPD interval of each key parameter contains the simulated value (or the failure is explained); ESS is reported (100 or more counts as adequate); model comparisons are reported whether or not they pick the generating model; and, where possible, the Bayesian result is compared with an independent calculation (maximum likelihood from ape, phytools, geiger or nlme, or an exact numerical result). With 16 languages and one character, many parameters are only weakly identified: wide intervals that contain the truth are the expected outcome, and so are model comparisons that cannot separate similar models. The table summarizes the checks; “miss” marks a check that did not come out as the generating model would predict, “expected_miss” a failure that the book itself predicts (script 16), and “warn_ess” an ESS below 100. Four regions A-D lie on a line, and the data were simulated with only the three adjacent routes (AB, BC, CD) active, at rate 0.3 per millennium, from a homeland in A. Each of the six symmetric route rates is a reversible-jump mixture of a point mass at zero (route absent) and an exponential rate, so the indicators \(\delta_{ij}\) are the moves of a reversible-jump sampler (dnReversibleJumpMixture + mvRJSwitch). The book’s prior puts Poisson(\(\ln 2\)) plus \(K - 1\) on the number of active routes; RevBayes has no built-in prior on the sum of indicators, so the script uses independent indicators with the same expected number of active routes, i.e. prior inclusion probability \(q = (\ln 2 + K - 1)/(K(K-1)/2) = 0.62\), which makes the book’s Bayes factor formula exact. H.5.2 Continuous phylogeography: bivariate Brownian diffusion 02_continuous_phylogeo_bm.Rev implements Equation (11.5) (Section 11.5.1): the coordinates of every node are parameters, each child is bivariate normal around its parent with covariance \(t_c \boldsymbol\Sigma\), and the tip locations are clamped. The diffusion matrix is built from two rates and a correlation with fnVarCovar, and the root location (the homeland) has a vague bivariate normal prior. Since the internal locations are sampled, the same script gives ancestral locations for every proto-language. ################################################################################ # 02_continuous_phylogeo_bm.Rev # # Model: Continuous phylogeography by bivariate Brownian diffusion of # projected coordinates (x = km east, y = km north, units of 100 km). # Every node location is a parameter (data augmentation): # x_c | x_a ~ N_2(x_a, t_c * Sigma), # Sigma = [[s_x^2, rho s_x s_y], [rho s_x s_y, s_y^2]]. # Tip locations are clamped to the observed coordinates. # Book: Chapter 11, "Brownian diffusion" (#phylogeography-bm), # Eq. phylogeography-bm and phylogeography-mvn. # Estimates: root location (homeland), diffusion rates s_x, s_y and rho; # ancestral locations of all internal nodes. # Data: data/traits/coords_bm.tsv on data/traits/tree16.tre # Run: cd revbayes && rb analyses/traits/02_continuous_phylogeo_bm.Rev [--args n_gen] # Runtime: about 2 minutes (2 runs x 7,000 generations) ################################################################################ seed(1102) n_gen = 7000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/traits/02_continuous_phylogeo_bm/" t_start = time("seconds") tree <- readTrees("data/traits/tree16.tre")[1] coords = readDataDelimitedFile("data/traits/coords_bm.tsv", header = TRUE, delimiter = "\t") n_tips <- tree.ntips() n_nodes <- tree.nnodes() root_idx <- tree.getRootIndex() # observed tip coordinates, indexed by RevBayes node index for (r in 1:coords.size()) { obs[tree.tipIndex(coords[r][1])] <- [ coords[r][2], coords[r][3] ] } moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() # diffusion matrix sigma_x ~ dnLognormal(0.0, 1.0) sigma_y ~ dnLognormal(0.0, 1.0) rho ~ dnUniform(-1.0, 1.0) Sigma := fnVarCovar([sigma_x, sigma_y], [rho]) moves.append( mvScale(sigma_x, lambda = 0.3, weight = 3.0) ) moves.append( mvScale(sigma_y, lambda = 0.3, weight = 3.0) ) moves.append( mvSlide(rho, delta = 0.2, weight = 3.0) ) # root location: vague bivariate normal prior (sd = 10, i.e. 1000 km) # (mvVectorSlide element indices are 0-based) loc[root_idx] ~ dnMultivariateNormal([0.0, 0.0], covariance = fnVarCovar([10.0, 10.0], [0.0])) loc[root_idx].setValue([0.0, 0.0]) moves.append( mvVectorSlide(loc[root_idx], delta = 0.5, weight = 3.0) ) moves.append( mvVectorSlide(loc[root_idx], elements = [0], delta = 0.5, weight = 2.0) ) moves.append( mvVectorSlide(loc[root_idx], elements = [1], delta = 0.5, weight = 2.0) ) # all other nodes, from the root down (parents have larger indices than children) # NB: the loop index must be the loop variable itself (a constant node such as # `i <- n_nodes - j` would be re-evaluated when it is reassigned). for (i in (n_nodes - 1):1) { loc[i] ~ dnMultivariateNormal(loc[tree.parent(i)], covariance = Sigma, scale = tree.branchLength(i)) if (i <= n_tips) { loc[i].clamp(obs[i]) } else { loc[i].setValue([0.0, 0.0]) moves.append( mvVectorSlide(loc[i], elements = [0], delta = 0.3, weight = 1.0) ) moves.append( mvVectorSlide(loc[i], elements = [1], delta = 0.3, weight = 1.0) ) } } root_x := loc[root_idx][1] root_y := loc[root_idx][2] mymodel = model(Sigma) monitors.append( mnFile(sigma_x, sigma_y, rho, root_x, root_y, filename = out_dir + "model.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 5000, root_x, root_y, sigma_x) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 2, combine = "none") mymcmc.burnin(generations = 1000, tuningInterval = 100) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen, tuningInterval = 0) write("runtime_s", time("seconds") - t_start, filename = out_dir + "runtime.txt", separator = "\t") q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status bivariate BM diffusion root_x 2.0 2.223 -0.176 4.337 694 pass bivariate BM diffusion root_y -1.0 -2.342 -3.982 -0.576 588 pass bivariate BM diffusion sigma_x 1.0 1.166 0.761 1.624 739 pass bivariate BM diffusion sigma_y 0.7 0.815 0.555 1.124 863 pass bivariate BM diffusion rho 0.4 0.480 0.130 0.829 1200 pass bivariate BM diffusion root_vs_GLS NA 0.108 NA NA NA pass All five parameters are covered. The posterior mean homeland agrees with the generalized least-squares root of Equation (11.6), computed independently in R, to within about 10 km (root_vs_GLS). H.5.3 Relaxed random walk 03_relaxed_random_walk.Rev implements the lognormal relaxed random walk of Section 11.5.2 (Equation (11.7)). Each branch has a variance multiplier \(\phi_b\) with mean one, and the internal locations are integrated out by dnPhyloMultivariateBrownianREML (the per-branch argument of that distribution is a standard-deviation multiplier, so it receives \(\sqrt{\phi_b}\)). The multipliers use a non-centered parameterization, \(\phi_b = \exp(-s^2/2 + s z_b)\) with \(z_b \sim N(0, 1)\). The model is unchanged, but a first, centered version got stuck in the “funnel” near \(s = 0\) (ESS below 20). The script also reports a weighted diffusion rate. ################################################################################ # 03_relaxed_random_walk.Rev # # Model: Relaxed random walk (RRW) for continuous coordinates. Bivariate # Brownian diffusion with diffusion matrix Sigma, where every branch b # has its own variance multiplier phi_b ~ Lognormal(-s^2/2, s) (mean 1): # x_c | x_a, phi_b ~ N_2(x_a, phi_b * t_c * Sigma). # The root and internal locations are integrated out analytically # (restricted likelihood, dnPhyloMultivariateBrownianREML). # Book: Chapter 11, "The relaxed random walk" (#phylogeography-rrw), # Eq. phylogeography-rrw (lognormal version). # Estimates: sigma_x, sigma_y, rho, the spread s of the log multipliers, # branch multipliers phi_b, and the weighted diffusion rate. # Data: data/traits/coords_rrw.nex on data/traits/tree16.tre # Run: cd revbayes && rb analyses/traits/03_relaxed_random_walk.Rev [--args n_gen] # Runtime: about 1 minute ################################################################################ seed(1103) n_gen = 30000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/traits/03_relaxed_random_walk/" t_start = time("seconds") tree <- readTrees("data/traits/tree16.tre")[1] coords <- readContinuousCharacterData("data/traits/coords_rrw.nex") n_branches <- tree.nnodes() - 1 moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() sigma_x ~ dnLognormal(0.0, 1.0) sigma_y ~ dnLognormal(0.0, 1.0) rho ~ dnUniform(-1.0, 1.0) Sigma := fnVarCovar([sigma_x, sigma_y], [rho]) moves.append( mvScale(sigma_x, lambda = 0.3, weight = 2.0) ) moves.append( mvScale(sigma_y, lambda = 0.3, weight = 2.0) ) moves.append( mvSlide(rho, delta = 0.2, weight = 2.0) ) # lognormal branch multipliers with mean one; s has an exponential prior. # Non-centred parameterization, phi_b = exp(-s^2/2 + s z_b) with z_b ~ N(0, 1), # which is the same model as phi_b ~ Lognormal(-s^2/2, s) but avoids the # "funnel" between s and the phi_b that traps a centred sampler near s = 0. s_phi ~ dnExponential(1.0) moves.append( mvScale(s_phi, lambda = 0.3, weight = 3.0) ) m_phi := -0.5 * s_phi * s_phi for (b in 1:n_branches) { z_phi[b] ~ dnNormal(0.0, 1.0) moves.append( mvSlide(z_phi[b], delta = 1.0, weight = 1.0) ) phi[b] := exp(m_phi + s_phi * z_phi[b]) # the REML likelihood takes per-branch standard-deviation multipliers br_sd[b] := sqrt(phi[b]) } X ~ dnPhyloMultivariateBrownianREML(tree, branchRates = br_sd, rateMatrix = Sigma) X.clamp(coords) # weighted diffusion rate: expected squared displacement per unit time in the # plane is (sigma_x^2 + sigma_y^2) times the time-weighted mean multiplier for (b in 1:n_branches) bl[b] <- tree.branchLength(b) total_time <- sum(bl) for (b in 1:n_branches) w_phi[b] := phi[b] * bl[b] / total_time mean_phi := sum(w_phi) weighted_diffusion := (sigma_x * sigma_x + sigma_y * sigma_y) * mean_phi / 4.0 mymodel = model(Sigma) monitors.append( mnModel(filename = out_dir + "model.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 5000, sigma_x, sigma_y, s_phi) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 1) mymcmc.burnin(generations = 2000, tuningInterval = 100) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen, tuningInterval = 0) write(tree, filename = out_dir + "tree_index.txt") write("runtime_s", time("seconds") - t_start, filename = out_dir + "runtime.txt", separator = "\t") q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status relaxed random walk (lognormal) sigma_x 0.8 0.756 0.444 1.145 2129 pass relaxed random walk (lognormal) sigma_y 0.8 0.665 0.387 0.999 2119 pass relaxed random walk (lognormal) rho 0.3 0.390 -0.112 0.800 2851 pass relaxed random walk (lognormal) s_phi 0.8 0.503 0.001 1.315 1078 pass relaxed random walk (lognormal) cor(true phi, posterior phi) NA 0.172 NA NA NA pass The diffusion parameters and the spread \(s\) are covered. H.5.4 DEC range evolution 04_dec.Rev implements the dispersal-extinction-cladogenesis model described in the biologist’s toolbox of Chapter 11 (Section 11.12; Ree et al. (2005); Ree and Smith (2008)), for three areas. The anagenetic rate matrix comes from fnDECRateMatrix (dispersal rate \(d\) per area pair, local extinction rate \(e\); the null range is excluded, so a single-area range cannot be lost) and cladogenesis from fnDECCladoProbs with subset sympatry and allopatry (probType = "class": a class is chosen with probability clado_probs, then a pattern uniformly within it, which is exactly how sim_traits.R simulates). Ranges are coded as presence/absence per area and converted with formatDiscreteCharacterData(..., "DEC"). ################################################################################ # 04_dec.Rev # # Model: DEC (dispersal-extinction-cladogenesis) range evolution, three areas # A, B, C. Anagenetic CTMC on ranges (dispersal rate d per area pair, # local extinction rate e per area; the null range is excluded, so a # single-area range cannot be lost), plus cladogenetic range # inheritance at nodes: narrow sympatry for one-area ranges, and # subset sympatry ("s") or allopatry ("a") for wider ranges. # Book: Chapter 11, "From the biologist's toolbox" (#phylogeography-toolbox), # the DEC paragraph (Ree & Smith 2008), Bayesian version of Landis et al. 2013. # Estimates: d, e, the cladogenetic class probability of subset sympatry, and # the ancestral range at the root. # Data: data/traits/ranges.nex (presence/absence in A, B, C) on tree16.tre # Run: cd revbayes && rb analyses/traits/04_dec.Rev [--args n_gen] # Runtime: about 1 minute ################################################################################ seed(1104) n_gen = 10000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/traits/04_dec/" t_start = time("seconds") tree <- readTrees("data/traits/tree16.tre")[1] rng01 <- readDiscreteCharacterData("data/traits/ranges.nex") n_areas <- rng01.nchar() n_states <- 2^n_areas rng = formatDiscreteCharacterData(rng01, "DEC", n_states) moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() dispersal ~ dnExponential(2.0) extirpation ~ dnExponential(2.0) moves.append( mvScale(dispersal, lambda = 0.5, weight = 3.0) ) moves.append( mvScale(extirpation, lambda = 0.5, weight = 3.0) ) for (i in 1:n_areas) { for (j in 1:n_areas) { dr[i][j] := dispersal er[i][j] <- 0.0 } } for (i in 1:n_areas) er[i][i] := extirpation Q_DEC := fnDECRateMatrix(dispersalRates = dr, extirpationRates = er, nullRange = "Exclude") # cladogenesis: probability of subset sympatry vs allopatry (class weights) clado_probs ~ dnDirichlet([1, 1]) moves.append( mvSimplexElementScale(clado_probs, alpha = 10.0, weight = 2.0) ) p_sympatry := clado_probs[1] P_DEC := fnDECCladoProbs(eventProbs = clado_probs, eventTypes = ["s", "a"], numCharacters = n_areas, probType = "class") # flat prior over the non-empty ranges at the root rf <- rep(1, n_states) rf[1] <- 0 root_freq <- simplex(rf) m_bg ~ dnPhyloCTMCClado(tree = tree, Q = Q_DEC, cladoProbs = P_DEC, rootFrequencies = root_freq, type = "NaturalNumbers", nSites = 1) m_bg.clamp(rng) mymodel = model(m_bg) monitors.append( mnModel(filename = out_dir + "model.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnJointConditionalAncestralState(tree = tree, ctmc = m_bg, type = "NaturalNumbers", withTips = TRUE, withStartStates = TRUE, filename = out_dir + "states.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 5000, dispersal, extirpation) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 1) mymcmc.burnin(generations = 1000, tuningInterval = 100) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen, tuningInterval = 0) write(tree, filename = out_dir + "tree_index.txt") write("runtime_s", time("seconds") - t_start, filename = out_dir + "runtime.txt", separator = "\t") q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status DEC dispersal 0.40 0.577 0.193 1.132 951 pass DEC extirpation 0.15 0.300 0.001 0.853 951 pass DEC p_sympatry 0.50 0.395 0.004 0.754 951 pass DEC root_state 0.00 0.176 NA NA NA pass \(d\), \(e\) and the cladogenetic probability are covered. H.5.7 Hidden-rates model 07_hidden_rates.Rev implements the hidden-rates model of Section 12.7 (Equation (D.9)) with a slow and a fast category. H.5.8 Pagel’s test of correlated evolution 08_pagel_correlated.Rev implements Section 13.7: two binary features coded as one four-state character, with the independent model of Equation (D.22) and the dependent model of Equation (13.6), compared by stepping-stone sampling. A third, reversible-jump analysis samples over the dependence itself, in the spirit of BayesTraits. Each of the four pairs of rates that the independent model sets equal is written as a base rate and a multiplier that is exactly 1 with prior probability 1/2. The independent model is the state in which all four multipliers equal 1 (prior probability 1/16). The data follow the book’s simulation (harmonic states stable, disharmonic states left ten times faster), with 20 independent feature pairs on the 16-tip tree so that the test has some power. H.5.10 Early burst 10_early_burst.Rev implements the EB model of Section 13.3.3. RevBayes 1.4.1 has fnEarlyBurst, but its rate parameter is restricted to be positive, so the model is written out exactly instead. The variance that accumulates on a branch running from time \(s_0\) to \(s_1\) after the root is \(\sigma_0^2(e^{r s_1} - e^{r s_0})/r\), which reproduces the covariance of Equation (D.13). It enters dnPhyloBrownianREML as a per-branch multiplier computed from the node ages. Four independent traits were simulated with \(r = -0.8\). ################################################################################ # 10_early_burst.Rev # # Model: Early-burst (EB, ACDC) model: Brownian motion whose rate changes # exponentially with time since the root, sigma2(s) = sigma2_0 exp(r s) # (r < 0: fast early, slow late). RevBayes has no dedicated EB # distribution with r < 0 allowed, so the model is expressed exactly # through per-branch rate multipliers: the variance accumulated on a # branch from s0 to s1 (time since root) is # sigma2_0 * (exp(r s1) - exp(r s0)) / r, # which reproduces the EB covariance C_ij = sigma2_0 (exp(r s_ij) - 1) / r # (Eq. pcms-eb). The restricted (REML) likelihood integrates the root. # EB is compared with constant-rate BM by stepping-stone sampling # (both REML, so their marginal likelihoods are comparable). # Book: Chapter 13, "Early burst and related models" (#pcms-eb). # Estimates: r, sigma2_0; ln marginal likelihoods of EB and BM. # Data: data/traits/trait_eb.nex (4 independent traits, r = -0.8, # sigma2_0 = 2) on H.5.11 Evolutionary correlation and phylogenetic regression 11_mvbm_correlation.Rev fits bivariate BM with an evolutionary correlation (dnPhyloMultivariateBrownianREML). The slope \(\rho\sigma_2/\sigma_1\) is the phylogenetic regression slope that PGLS estimates (Section 13.6, Equation (D.18)). ################################################################################ # 11_mvbm_correlation.Rev # # Model: Bivariate Brownian motion with an evolutionary correlation: # (x1, x2) evolve with rate matrix # Sigma = [[s1^2, rho s1 s2], [rho s1 s2, s2^2]], # i.e. X ~ N(1 (x) root, C (x) Sigma), with the root integrated out # (restricted likelihood, dnPhyloMultivariateBrownianREML). The # phylogenetic regression slope of x2 on x1 is beta = rho s2 / s1, # the quantity that PGLS estimates (the GLS slope equals the slope of # Sigma, Eq. pcms-pgls). # Book: Chapter 13, "Phylogenetic generalized least squares" (#pcms-pgls), # "Phylogenetically independent contrasts" (#pcms-pic), the multivariate # BM models of the chapter's toolbox box and Chapter 16 # (#biology-toolkit-pfa). # Estimates: s1, s2, rho, slope; compared in tests/check_traits.R with PGLS # (nlme::gls + ape::corBrownian) and with the non-phylogenetic OLS # slope and Pearson correlation. # Data: data/traits/corr_traits.nex on tree16.tre # Run: cd revbayes && rb analyses/traits/11_mvbm_correlation.Rev [--args n_gen] # Runtime: about 10 s ################################################################################ seed(1111) n_gen = 20000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/traits/11_mvbm_correlation/" t_start = time("seconds") tree <- readTrees("data/traits/tree16.tre")[1] dat <- readContinuousCharacterData("data/traits/corr_traits.nex") moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() sigma_1 ~ dnLognormal(0.0, 1.0) sigma_2 ~ dnLognormal(0.0, 1.0) rho ~ dnUniform(-1.0, 1.0) moves.append( mvScale(sigma_1, lambda = 0.3, weight = 2.0) ) moves.append( mvScale(sigma_2, lambda = 0.3, weight = 2.0) ) moves.append( mvSlide(rho, delta = 0.2, weight = 3.0) ) Sigma := fnVarCovar([sigma_1, sigma_2], [rho]) slope := rho * sigma_2 / sigma_1 X ~ dnPhyloMultivariateBrownianREML(tree, rateMatrix = Sigma) X.clamp(dat) mymodel = model(Sigma) monitors.append( mnFile(sigma_1, sigma_2, rho, slope, filename = out_dir + "model.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 5000, rho, slope) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 1) mymcmc.burnin(generations = 1000, tuningInterval = 100) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen, tuningInterval = 0) write("runtime_s", time("seconds") - t_start, filename = out_dir + "runtime.txt", separator = "\t") q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status bivariate BM sigma_1 1.000 1.215 0.828 1.663 1901 pass bivariate BM sigma_2 0.800 0.957 0.660 1.293 1901 pass bivariate BM rho 0.750 0.693 0.408 0.898 1901 pass bivariate BM slope 0.600 0.555 0.252 0.836 2046 pass bivariate BM slope_vs_PGLS 0.608 0.555 NA NA NA pass The correlation (true 0.75) and slope (true 0.6) are recovered. H.5.12 Pagel’s lambda 12_pagel_lambda.Rev estimates Pagel’s \(\lambda\) (Equation (13.4)). For an ultrametric tree of height \(T\), \(\mathbf{C}(\lambda)\) is BM on a tree whose internal branches are multiplied by \(\lambda\) and whose terminal branches become \(\lambda t_b + (1-\lambda)T\), so \(\lambda\) enters as deterministic per-branch rate multipliers with a uniform prior. The threshold model, the other half of this item, is script 17. ################################################################################ # 12_pagel_lambda.Rev # # Model: Brownian motion on a lambda-transformed tree (Pagel's lambda), # C(lambda) = lambda C + (1 - lambda) diag(C) (Eq. pcms-lambda). # For an ultrametric tree of height T this is BM on a tree whose # internal branches are multiplied by lambda and whose terminal # branches t_b become lambda t_b + (1 - lambda) T. We express it # through per-branch variance multipliers (lambda on internal branches, # lambda + (1 - lambda) T / t_b on terminal branches), so lambda is an # ordinary parameter with a Uniform(0, 1) prior. The root is # integrated out (REML). # A threshold model for a binary trait is in 17_threshold_model.Rev. # Book: Chapter 13, "Pagel's tree transformations" (#pcms-transforms), # "Phylogenetic signal" (#pcms-signal), "Estimating lambda jointly" # (#pcms-pgls-lambda). # Estimates: lambda, sigma2; compared with the ML estimate of phytools::phylosig. # Data: data/traits/trait_lambda.nex (lambda = 0.4, sigma2 = 1) on tree16.tre # Run: cd revbayes && rb analyses/traits/12_pagel_lambda.Rev [--args n_gen] # Runtime: about 10 s ################################################################################ seed(1112) n_gen = 20000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/traits/12_pagel_lambda/" t_start = time("seconds") tree <- readTrees("data/traits/tree16.tre")[1] dat <- readContinuousCharacterData("data/traits/trait_lambda.nex") n_tips <- tree.ntips() n_branches <- tree.nnodes() - 1 T <- tree.rootAge() for (b in 1:n_branches) { bl[b] <- tree.branchLength(b) is_tip[b] <- ifelse(b <= n_tips, 1.0, 0.0) } moves = VectorMoves() monitors = VectorMonitors() lambda ~ dnUniform(0.0, 1.0) lambda.setValue(0.5) sigma2 ~ dnLoguniform(1e-3, 100.0) moves.append( mvSlide(lambda, delta = 0.2, weight = 3.0) ) moves.append( mvScale(sigma2, lambda = 0.5, weight = 2.0) ) for (b in 1:n_branches) { # internal: lambda; terminal: lambda + (1 - lambda) T / t_b lam_mult[b] := abs(lambda + is_tip[b] * (1.0 - lambda) * T / bl[b]) br[b] := sqrt(sigma2 * lam_mult[b]) } X ~ dnPhyloBrownianREML(tree, branchRates = br, nSites = 1) X.clamp(dat) mymodel = model(sigma2) monitors.append( mnFile(lambda, sigma2, filename = out_dir + "model.log", printgen = 10) ) monitors.append( mnScreen(printgen = 5000, lambda, sigma2) ) mymcmc = mcmc(mymodel, monitors, moves, nruns = 1) mymcmc.burnin(generations = 1000, tuningInterval = 100) mymcmc.run(generations = n_gen, tuningInterval = 0) write("runtime_s", time("seconds") - t_start, filename = out_dir + "runtime.txt", separator = "\t") q() Model Parameter Truth Post. mean HPD low HPD high ESS Status BM with Pagel’s lambda lambda 0.4 0.380 0.0 0.820 1654 pass BM with Pagel’s lambda sigma2 1.0 0.929 0.3 1.797 1742 pass The posterior of \(\lambda\) is wide but centered near the truth (mean 0.38, true 0.4). H.5.16 Trend, ancient languages and identifiability 16_bm_trend_ancient_tips.Rev reproduces the argument of Section 11.5.5 (Equation (11.8)) in a Bayesian setting. The data are a simulated eastward expansion from a homeland at (0, 0) with drift 0.8 per millennium; four languages are ancient, sampled 0.9-1.8 millennia ago. With the internal nodes integrated out, each coordinate is multivariate normal with mean \(x_{\text{root}} + \mu h_i\) and covariance \(\sigma^2\mathbf{C}\). That is the GLS regression on tip height described in the book. There are three analyses: (a) undirected BM on the 12 modern languages; (b) BM with trend on the modern languages; (c) BM with trend on all 16. Analysis (b) is sampled in the equivalent parameterization \(x_{\text{end}} = x_{\text{root}} + \mu T\), which has the same prior but lets the chain move along the ridge that contemporaneous tips cannot resolve. ################################################################################ # 16_bm_trend_ancient_tips.Rev # # Model: Brownian diffusion with a directional trend (drift) and the role of # ancient (non-contemporaneous) languages in identifying it: # x_c | x_a ~ N_2(x_a + mu t_c, t_c sigma^2 I) (Eq. phylogeography-trend). # Integrating out the internal nodes, each coordinate of the tips is # multivariate normal with mean x_root + mu h_i (h_i = time from the # root to tip i) and covariance sigma^2 C (C = shared path lengths), # which is what the script uses: the GLS-regression form of the book. # Three analyses of the same simulated eastward expansion (true root # (0, 0), drift mu = (0.8, 0) per kyr): # (a) undirected BM, 12 contemporary languages only; # (b) BM + trend, 12 contemporary languages only (root and drift # not separately identifiable: only root + mu T is, so the # posterior follows the prior along a ridge); # (c) BM + trend, the 12 contemporary plus 4 ancient languages # (sampled 0.9-1.8 kyr ago), which restores identifiability. # Book: Chapter 11, "Trend, ancient languages and identifiability" # (#phylogeography-trend) and its R section (#phylogeography-r-ancient). # Estimates: root location (homeland), drift mu, sigma, in each analysis. # Note: the covariance is passed as sigma^2 * C (a deterministic matrix); the # `scale` argument of dnMultivariateNormal is not used because a # stochastic scale did not enter the likelihood in RevBayes 1.4.1 tests. # Data: data/traits/trend_{modern,ancient}.tsv (x, y, depth) and # data/traits/trend_C_{modern,ancient}.tsv (covariance matrices) # Run: cd revbayes && rb analyses/traits/16_bm_trend_ancient_tips.Rev [--args n_gen] # Runtime: about 2 minutes ################################################################################ seed(1116) n_gen = 6000 if (args.size() > 1) n_gen = int(args[2]) out_dir = "output/traits/16_bm_trend_ancient_tips/" t_start = time("seconds") # NB: model() collects every node connected to its argument, including through # shared constant nodes and through the elements of one Rev vector. The three # analyses therefore use separate data objects and separate variable names. ############################ data dm = readDataDelimitedFile("data/traits/trend_modern.tsv", header = TRUE, delimiter = "\t") Cm = readDataDelimitedFile("data/traits/trend_C_modern.tsv", header = TRUE, delimiter = "\t") da = readDataDelimitedFile("data/traits/trend_ancient.tsv", header = TRUE, delimiter = "\t") Ca = readDataDelimitedFile("data/traits/trend_C_ancient.tsv", header = TRUE, delimiter = "\t") nm <- dm.size() na <- da.size() for (i in 1:nm) { xm[i] <- dm[i][2] ym[i] <- dm[i][3] hm[i] <- dm[i][4] sdm[i] <- sqrt(Cm[i][i + 1]) } for (i in 1:na) { xa[i] <- da[i][2] ya[i] <- da[i][3] ha[i] <- da[i][4] sda[i] <- sqrt(Ca[i][i + 1]) } k = 0 for (i in 1:(nm - H.5.23 Models not implemented as stated Every model on the list was implemented. Four were expressed through general building blocks rather than a dedicated RevBayes function, and are labelled as such in their scripts: the BSSVS prior on the number of active routes (independent indicators with the same expected number, script 01); the early-burst model (exact per-branch multipliers, script 10); Pagel’s \(\lambda\) (exact per-branch multipliers, script 12); the hidden-rates matrix (fnFreeK rather than fnHiddenStateRateMatrix, script 07). Spherical diffusion (Section 11.5.3), landscape-aware models and phylogenetic logistic regression were not attempted. RevBayes 1.4.1 has no spherical diffusion distribution. Phylogenetic logistic regression in the sense of Ives and Garland (2010) is a penalized-likelihood method; its Bayesian counterpart is the threshold model (script 17) with covariates in the liability. I Glossary This glossary defines the technical terms used in the book, from both historical linguistics and evolutionary biology. Definitions are brief; the chapter indicated in parentheses, where given, treats the term in detail. Terms in italics within a definition have their own entries. A Acceptance probability In the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, the probability with which a proposed new state of the Markov chain is accepted. It depends on the ratio of posterior densities and on the proposal distribution (Chapter 6). ACCTRAN “Accelerated transformation”, a rule for placing character changes on a parsimony tree as close to the root as possible, favoring reversals over parallel changes. Its counterpart is DELTRAN (Chapter 4). Ancestral state reconstruction (ASR) Inference of the character states (for example, a cognate class, a word order, or a phoneme) of ancestral nodes of a tree, by parsimony, maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods (Chapter 12). Areal feature A linguistic feature shared by languages in a geographic area because of contact rather than common descent, as in a Sprachbund. Ascertainment bias A bias arising because some kinds of characters cannot be observed. In cognate data, a cognate class absent from every sampled language is never coded, so models must condition on observable patterns; this is done by an ascertainment correction (Chapter 7). ASJP The Automated Similarity Judgment Program, a database of 40-item word lists in a simplified transcription for thousands of languages, and the distance-based methods developed with it (Appendix G). Autapomorphy A derived character state unique to a single terminal taxon; in cognate data, a singleton cognate class. Autapomorphies carry no information about branching order. B Basic vocabulary Meanings thought to be universal, culturally neutral and resistant to borrowing, such as body parts, low numerals, pronouns and basic actions, used to build word lists for comparison. The Swadesh list is the classic example (Chapter 3). Bayes factor The ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two models, used to compare them in Bayesian inference. Values above about 20 (or a log Bayes factor above about 3) are conventionally taken as strong evidence (Chapter 6). Bayesian inference Statistical inference that combines a prior distribution with the likelihood of the data to obtain a posterior distribution of parameters, including trees (Chapter 6). BEAST A family of programs (BEAST 2, BEAST 1 and BEAST X) for Bayesian inference of time-calibrated phylogenies (Appendix F). Bipartition See split. Birth-death process A model of diversification in which lineages split at rate \(\lambda\) (birth) and go extinct at rate \(\mu\) (death); used as a tree prior (Chapter 6). Bootstrap A resampling procedure that estimates the support for clades by re-inferring the tree from many pseudo-replicate datasets formed by sampling characters with replacement (Chapter 4). Borrowing The adoption of a word or structural feature from another language through contact. Borrowing is the linguistic analogue of horizontal gene transfer (Chapter 8). Branch length The length of an edge of a tree, measured either in time or in expected amount of change. Brownian motion A model of continuous trait evolution in which changes are normally distributed with variance proportional to time, so that trait covariances between species are proportional to shared branch length (Chapter 13). Burn-in The initial portion of an MCMC run, before the chain has reached its stationary distribution, which is discarded before summarizing the posterior. C Calibration Information about the age of a node (or a tip) used to convert relative branch lengths into absolute time, often expressed as a prior distribution on the node’s age (Chapter 10). Character A feature of the languages under study that can take different states, such as the presence or absence of a cognate class, a word-order type, or a sound correspondence. Chronogram A tree whose branch lengths represent time, so that all contemporary tips are equidistant from the root. Compare phylogram. Clade A group consisting of an ancestor and all of its descendants; a monophyletic group. Clade credibility The posterior probability of a clade, estimated as the proportion of trees in a posterior sample that contain it. CLDF Cross-Linguistic Data Formats, a standard for publishing linguistic data as CSV tables with JSON metadata (Appendix G). Clock model A model of how rates of change vary across branches of a tree. A strict clock assumes a single rate; relaxed clocks allow rates to vary (Chapter 9). Coalescent A population-genetic model that describes the ancestry of a sample of gene copies backward in time within a population; also used as a tree prior. Cognate A word that descends from the same ancestral word as a word in another related language, for example English two, German zwei and Latin duo. Cognate class (cognate set) The set of words, across languages, that are cognate with each other for a given meaning. Comparative method The method of historical linguistics that establishes genetic relationship and reconstructs proto-languages by identifying systematic sound correspondences among cognates. Compatibility A criterion for tree inference that seeks the tree on which the largest number (or weight) of characters can evolve without homoplasy (Chapter 4). Consensus tree A tree that summarizes a set of trees, such as a strict consensus (clades present in all trees) or majority-rule consensus (clades present in more than half) (Chapter 2). Consistency index (CI) A measure of homoplasy on a parsimony tree: the minimum possible number of changes divided by the observed number. A value of 1 indicates no homoplasy. Continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) A stochastic process in which a character moves among discrete states at rates given by a rate matrix; the basis of most substitution models (Chapter 5). Convergence In MCMC, the state in which a chain is sampling from the target posterior distribution; assessed with diagnostics such as ESS, trace plots and comparisons between independent runs. Covarion model A substitution model in which each character switches between “on” (evolving) and “off” (invariant) states along the tree, so that rates vary through time as well as among characters (Chapter 7). Credible interval An interval containing a specified proportion (often 95%) of the posterior probability of a parameter. See HPD interval. D Delta score A measure of how far a distance matrix departs from tree-likeness, computed over quartets of taxa. Low values indicate tree-like data (Chapter 8). DELTRAN “Delayed transformation”, a rule for placing character changes on a parsimony tree as far from the root as possible, favoring parallel changes over reversals. DensiTree A visualization that draws all trees of a posterior sample superimposed, so that uncertainty in topology and node heights is visible. Dialect continuum A chain of geographically adjacent varieties in which neighbors are mutually intelligible but the ends are not, typically poorly described by a tree. Discrete phylogeography Phylogeographic inference that treats location as a discrete character evolving on the tree under a CTMC (Chapter 11). Distance method A tree-building method that works from a matrix of pairwise distances between taxa, such as UPGMA or neighbor-joining (Chapter 4). Diversification rate The net rate at which lineages multiply, the speciation (splitting) rate minus the extinction rate. Dollo’s law The principle that a complex character, once lost, cannot be regained. In linguistics, a cognate class is born only once. See stochastic Dollo model. E Edge A branch of a tree. Effective sample size (ESS) The number of independent samples that an autocorrelated MCMC sample is equivalent to; values above about 200 are commonly required. Equilibrium frequencies See stationary distribution. F Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm The dynamic-programming algorithm that computes the likelihood of a tree efficiently by working from the tips toward the root (Chapter 5). Fossilized birth-death (FBD) process A tree prior that includes the sampling of extinct lineages (fossils) through time, allowing them to be placed in the tree as tips or sampled ancestors (Chapter 10). G Galton’s problem The problem that cross-cultural or cross-linguistic observations are not independent because of shared ancestry and contact, named after Francis Galton’s objection to an early comparative study (Chapter 13). Gamma rate heterogeneity Modeling variation in rates among characters by drawing each character’s rate from a gamma distribution, usually approximated with a few discrete categories (Chapter 5). Glottochronology The method, developed by Swadesh and Lees, of estimating the time since two languages separated from the proportion of shared basic vocabulary, assuming a constant rate of replacement (Chapter 1). Glottocode The stable identifier assigned to every languoid in Glottolog, used to link linguistic datasets. Glottolog A comprehensive catalogue and classification of the world’s languages, dialects and families (Appendix G). H Highest posterior density (HPD) interval The shortest interval containing a specified proportion of the posterior probability; commonly reported for node ages. Homeland The geographic area in which the ancestral language (proto-language) of a family was spoken (Chapter 11). Homology Similarity due to common ancestry. Cognacy is the linguistic counterpart of homology. Homoplasy Similarity not due to common ancestry, arising from parallel change, convergence or reversal; in language data, also from undetected borrowing or chance resemblance. Horizontal transmission Transfer of traits between lineages other than by descent; in biology, horizontal gene transfer or hybridization; in linguistics, borrowing. I Incomplete lineage sorting Persistence of ancestral variation through several speciation events, so that gene trees differ from the species tree. A linguistic analogue is the persistence of synonyms or variants across language splits. Independent contrasts Felsenstein’s method of transforming trait values on a tree into independent differences for regression and correlation analysis (Chapter 13). Ingroup The set of taxa under study, as opposed to an outgroup. Innovation A change shared by a group of languages that defines a subgroup, in contrast to a retention. Shared innovations are the basis of subgrouping in the comparative method. J Joint reconstruction Ancestral state reconstruction that finds the most probable combination of states at all nodes simultaneously, in contrast to marginal reconstruction. K Kendall-Colijn metric A tree distance that compares rooted trees by the depths of the most recent common ancestors of pairs of tips, optionally weighting topology and branch lengths (Chapter 2). L Languoid In Glottolog, any language, dialect or family, treated as a unit of classification. Lateral transfer See horizontal transmission. Levenshtein distance The minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another; normalized versions are used to compare word forms (Chapter 4). Lexicostatistics The quantitative comparison of languages by the proportions of cognates they share in basic vocabulary lists (Chapter 1). Likelihood The probability of the observed data given a model and its parameter values, viewed as a function of the parameters (Chapter 5). Lineage-specific Describing a pattern or dependency that holds within one family or lineage but not universally. Loanword A word adopted from another language. See borrowing. Long-branch attraction The tendency of some methods, notably parsimony, to group long branches together erroneously because of convergent changes (Chapter 4). M Majority-rule consensus A consensus tree containing all clades found in more than 50% of a set of trees. Marginal likelihood The probability of the data under a model, averaged over all parameter values weighted by their prior; the quantity compared in Bayes factors. It is estimated by methods such as path sampling, stepping-stone sampling or nested sampling (Chapter 6). Marginal reconstruction Ancestral state reconstruction that gives the probability of each state at each node separately, integrating over states at other nodes. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) A family of algorithms that sample from a probability distribution by constructing a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is that distribution (Chapter 6). Maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree The tree in a posterior sample that maximizes the product of the posterior probabilities of its clades; a common summary tree. Maximum likelihood (ML) The method of choosing parameter values (including the tree) that maximize the likelihood (Chapter 5). Meaning slot A meaning (concept) in a word list, considered as a multistate character whose states are the cognate classes used to express it (Chapter 7). Metropolis-coupled MCMC (MC3) An MCMC variant that runs several “heated” chains in parallel and swaps states among them, to help the cold chain move between peaks of the posterior. Midpoint rooting Rooting an unrooted tree at the midpoint of the longest path between two tips. Missing data Cells of a data matrix for which the state is unknown, coded as “?”. In cognate data, a meaning with no recorded word in a language. Mk model A model for discrete characters with \(k\) states in which all changes occur at equal rates; with correction for unobserved invariant characters it is called Mkv (Chapter 7). Model adequacy Whether a model can reproduce key features of the observed data, assessed for example by posterior predictive simulation (Chapter 15). Monophyletic Describing a group that contains an ancestor and all of its descendants. See clade. Multistate character A character with more than two possible states. N Neighbor-joining (NJ) A distance method that builds an unrooted tree by successively joining pairs of taxa that minimize the total tree length (Chapter 4). NeighborNet A method that builds a planar split network from a distance matrix, displaying conflicting signal as boxes (Chapter 8). Nested sampling A method for estimating marginal likelihoods, together with an estimate of their uncertainty, by sampling from progressively constrained regions of the prior. Newick format A text format for trees using nested parentheses, for example ((A,B),C); (Chapter 2). NEXUS format A block-structured file format for phylogenetic data, trees and commands, used by many programs (Chapter 2). Node A point in a tree: an internal node represents an ancestor, a terminal node (tip, leaf) an observed taxon. Node density effect The correlation between the number of nodes on a root-to-tip path and the amount of change along it, used as evidence of punctuational change (Chapter 9). O Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model A model of continuous trait evolution in which the trait is pulled toward an optimum while also drifting randomly (Chapter 13). Outgroup A taxon known to lie outside the group of interest, used to root the tree. P Paraphyletic Describing a group that contains an ancestor and some, but not all, of its descendants. Parsimony The criterion that prefers the tree requiring the fewest character changes (Chapter 4). Partial cognate A word that is cognate with a word in another language in only some of its morphemes, as in compounds (Chapter 3). Partitioning Dividing the characters into subsets that evolve under separate models or parameters. Path sampling A method for estimating marginal likelihoods by sampling along a path between the prior and the posterior. Compare stepping-stone sampling. PGLS Phylogenetic generalized least squares, regression that models residual covariance among taxa according to the tree (Chapter 13). Phylogenetic comparative methods (PCMs) Statistical methods that account for shared ancestry when analyzing traits across taxa (Chapter 13). Phylogenetic network A graph that represents evolutionary history with reticulation. Explicit networks represent specific events such as hybridization or borrowing, while implicit (split) networks display conflicting signal (Chapter 8). Phylogenetic signal The tendency of related taxa to resemble each other more than random taxa, measured for example by Pagel’s \(\lambda\) or Blomberg’s \(K\) (Chapter 13). Phylogeography The study of the geographic history of lineages using phylogenies (Chapter 11). Phylogram A tree whose branch lengths represent amounts of change. Compare chronogram. Polytomy A node with more than two descendant branches. It may be “hard” (simultaneous splitting) or “soft” (unresolved). Posterior distribution The probability distribution of parameters given the data, obtained by Bayes’ theorem. Posterior predictive simulation Simulating new datasets from parameters drawn from the posterior and comparing them with the observed data, to assess model adequacy. Prior distribution The probability distribution assigned to parameters before observing the data. Proto-language The reconstructed common ancestor of a language family, such as Proto-Indo-European. Pseudo-Dollo model A model for cognate data that approximates the stochastic Dollo assumption (each cognate class born once) within a CTMC framework, often combined with a covarion process (Chapter 7). Punctuational change Change concentrated at speciation events or language splits rather than spread evenly over time (Chapter 9). Q Q-matrix (rate matrix) The matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) of instantaneous rates of change between states in a CTMC. Transition probabilities over time \(t\) are given by \(\mathbf{P}(t) = e^{\mathbf{Q}t}\). Quartet A set of four taxa; the smallest unit for which unrooted tree topologies differ, used in quartet-based distances and delta scores. R Rate heterogeneity Variation in rates of change among characters, among lineages, or through time. Relaxed clock A clock model that allows rates of change to vary among branches, either independently (uncorrelated) or with rates inherited from parent branches (autocorrelated) (Chapter 9). Restriction-site model A binary substitution model originally developed for restriction-site data and used for cognate presence/absence data in MrBayes and RevBayes. Retention A feature inherited unchanged from the proto-language; shared retentions do not define subgroups. Retention index (RI) A measure of the fit of characters to a parsimony tree that, unlike the consistency index, is not affected by autapomorphies. Reticulation Network-like evolution in which lineages exchange material, such as hybridization, horizontal gene transfer or borrowing. Robinson-Foulds (RF) distance A tree distance that counts the splits present in one tree but not in the other (Chapter 2). Root The node representing the most recent common ancestor of all taxa in a rooted tree. Root-meaning coding A coding of lexical data in which characters represent etyma (roots) regardless of the meaning they now express (Chapter 3). S Sampled ancestor A sampled taxon (such as an ancient language) that lies directly on the lineage leading to other taxa, rather than at the tip of a separate branch (Chapter 10). Singleton A character (such as a cognate class) present in only one taxon. See autapomorphy. Sister group The closest relative of a clade; two clades that share an immediate common ancestor. Sound correspondence A regular, recurring match between sounds in cognate words of related languages, such as Latin p corresponding to Germanic f (pater, father). Split A bipartition of the taxa into two groups, defined by an edge of an unrooted tree. Trees can be described by their sets of splits. Split network A network that displays a set of splits, some of which may be incompatible with any single tree. See NeighborNet. Sprachbund A linguistic area in which languages from different families share features through prolonged contact. Stationary distribution The long-run frequencies of states in a CTMC, denoted \(\pi\). Stepping-stone sampling A method for estimating marginal likelihoods using a series of distributions between prior and posterior. Stochastic character mapping Simulation of complete histories of character change on a tree, conditional on the observed tip states, to estimate the number and timing of changes (Chapter 12). Stochastic Dollo model A model for binary trait data in which each trait (cognate class) is born once on the tree and may be lost independently on any lineage (Chapter 7). Strict clock A clock model in which the rate of change is the same on all branches. Subgroup A set of languages within a family that share a more recent common ancestor with each other than with other members, established by shared innovations. Substitution model A model of how character states change over time, typically a CTMC defined by a rate matrix. Swadesh list A list of basic meanings (in versions of 100 or 200 items) compiled by Morris Swadesh for lexicostatistics and still widely used. Synapomorphy A shared derived character state, the evidence for a clade; the biological counterpart of a shared innovation. T Taxon A unit of analysis at the tips of a tree; in linguistics, a language or dialect. Tip dating Dating a tree using the known ages of sampled tips (for example ancient languages) rather than, or in addition to, node calibrations. Topology The branching pattern of a tree, ignoring branch lengths. Tree prior The prior probability distribution on tree topologies and branch lengths or node ages, such as the Yule or birth-death prior. Tree space The set of all possible trees for a given set of taxa, with a notion of distance or neighborhood among them (Chapter 2). Treelikeness The degree to which data are consistent with a single tree rather than a network. U Ultrametric tree A rooted tree in which all tips are equidistant from the root, as expected when branch lengths represent time and all tips are contemporary. Unrooted tree A tree that specifies relationships without a root, and therefore without a direction of time. UPGMA Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic mean, a clustering method that produces an ultrametric tree and assumes a constant rate of change (Chapter 4). W Wave model The model of language diversification, associated with Johannes Schmidt (Wellentheorie), in which innovations spread across overlapping areas of a dialect network rather than splitting lineages cleanly (Chapter 1). Word list A list of words for a fixed set of meanings in a set of languages, the basic data of lexical phylogenetics. Y Yule process A pure-birth model of diversification in which lineages split at a constant rate and never go extinct; used as a tree prior.
